translation_en: It's useless to talk about GTA 5, everything that had to be said about it, criticized and admired, has already been said. But in a brief summary, the game opens the doors to a satirical Los Angeles, full of stereotypes and realities. Part of what makes it most fun is that it's a freedom simulator; steal cars, murder people on the street, buy guns, explosives, use them to blow up a gas station and then rob everything in sight. More than a great story—a bit short, but good—GTA 5's strong suit is its great reflection of American reality, ready and served up for us players to entertain ourselves and taste it. GTA 5 includes GTA Online, which is possibly the game I've dedicated the most time to in my life. In this one, freedom expands to friends, businesses, cars, properties, hookers, bars, night clubs, casinos, nearby islands, and above all: Money. Tons of content, so much density on the web pages, the radio, the map, weapons, and more. A phenomenal experience. For this and much more, the second best-selling game in the world: GTA 5. It deserves to be enjoyed forever.

translation_en: A friendly piece of advice for China: The internet is full of games that scam elementary school kids out of their money, and you do nothing about it. Every website you click on is filled with games using broken Mandarin, and you do nothing about it. Games with official websites selling cheats, and you do nothing about it. Yet you crack down on AAA masterpieces? Violence? Pornography? Look at the ads plastered all over domestic websites—every single one of them is more revealing than anything on STEAM, but you don't give a damn, and instead you target STEAM. You have the luxury and free time, why don't you do something about the Chinese film industry? It's more deformed than Lu Benwei. Look at your CCTV, then look at the BBC. What a gap. You stomp out the cultural confidence you built up yourself, and why? Because you refuse to reform your management style, and yet you drag a massive platform down with you. Even though a lot of Chinese gamers just use STEAM as a launcher, at least it gave people a sense of copyright awareness. Just as we're finally making some progress, we're getting knocked right back to square one. What, are you encouraging everyone to pirate games now? Forget about so-called democracy, why can't we have a ratings system? A ratings system could solve most of these problems. Do you think this is fun? You "experts" are seriously retarded. Every day you pull this useless crap, why don't you just ban the internet altogether and stop letting normal people use it? Organising people every day to shout slogans and farm fields??? Or why not just go straight back to primitive society? What I actually care about is if the games I bought become unplayable, who am I supposed to ask for compensation? Perfect World, or the state? But I guess in the end, it'll just mean we players who insist on supporting official releases take a total loss, only to be smugly mocked by real-life pirating snobs. Retarded. Awesome job, my country,呵呵. Emperor Qin, this prosperous era is just as you wished. Some people and their friends grew up playing Legend and CS when they were kids, and none of them went around hacking, slashing, or committing crimes. Today's brats watch Pleasant Goat and roast other kids—is that really the fault of games and anime, or is it the fault of irresponsible parenting and schooling? Everyone knows the truth. You're just gonna abandon the 100-year goal of socialism like this? What is the Chinese Dream? Study hard, get your physical body out of the Great Firewall. Gaming belongs to the ninth art. Any major masterpiece inherently embodies the author's thoughts and philosophy. But given our country's currently closed-off value system, foreign reflections on the future and bizarre fantasies simply cannot be accepted by the SARFT. As for domestic games right now, due to factors like STEAM and consoles, you can still make a boatload of cash just by churning out garbage. They know that as long as the game's quality is barely passable, and they design some "micro-operations" to show off in-game, alongside all sorts of horny character art, and all sorts of second-rate character modeling and lines, they can scam people out of money. The plot of the game itself has to be trash—it can't have any depth, it has to be simple and easy to understand. Productions like this actually make way more money than games where you genuinely put effort into the plot and development. STEAM might seem like a lot of people know about it in China now, but before *PUBG* came out, if you walked down the street, hardly anyone knew what STEAM even was. In fact, China's real-name verification system is already more advanced than foreign countries. UnionPay and WeChat Pay both require a national ID card, so why haven't they rolled out a ratings policy yet? Because right now, whether something passes review is entirely up to the ultimate discretionary power of the Ministry of Culture and the SARFT; there are no relevant laws or regulations to determine whether a game passes review or not. There was once a domestic single-player game developer that made a wuxia game and submitted it for review. Since they were a domestic developer, they knew the censorship mechanism very well, so before submitting, they removed blood and dismemberment effects, and turned all the corpses black. But even then, it still failed review! The censorship body said that the player character in this game could just go to prison for ten days after killing someone, which would easily cause a negative social impact. Later on, through endless revisions, it basically turned into a wuxia game where you could only ride horses. Meanwhile, Tencent's *Moonlight Blade* has to face zero consequences after slaughtering human enemies—you just keep on massacring. Doesn't that cause an even bigger social impact? Yet *Moonlight Blade* passed review. Why does this happen? Tencent makes a fortune every single day; they can afford to pay. That small developer had pretty much no money left after finishing their game. So the development of Chinese single-player games isn't about how good your production quality is, nor is it about whether your marketing is on point—it’s about whether you can afford to pay up first. And what do the relevant Chinese authorities claim their basis is during censorship? It's the so-called social mainstream, the Core Socialist Values. What does this kind of thing resemble? Ancient monarchs would always find a statement that aligned with legal principles to justify their power: the Mandate of Heaven, "I am the True Dragon and Son of Heaven," claiming all their power was bestowed upon them by the heavens. The Core Socialist Values are just acting as a tool for this exact purpose, giving their illegitimate, unlawful power and acquired benefits a seemingly reasonable pretext. Hong Kong and Macao are Special Administrative Regions (let's modify this: Taiwan does not belong to a region), and their social, economic, political, and cultural systems are completely different from the mainland's. Has anyone ever thought about why this is the case? Actually, it's very simple: the squeaky wheel gets the grease. Take Hong Kong for example—if it had been the mainland system when it was returned in '97, they would have gone on massive strikes and student boycotts, making it impossible for society to function normally. Plus, at the time, many eyes both domestic and international were watching Hong Kong, so they became a Special Administrative Region. And what about us mainlanders? When they blocked the foreign internet, we endured it. When they censored *World of Warcraft*, we endured that too. We have never spoken up for our own rights. And now things are getting worse and worse, and a Chinese version of STEAM is about to come out. The best-case scenario is that a Chinese store launches, and all existing mainland region payment methods and low-price regional discounts get migrated over to it. If we silently endure this time, what about next time? I'm afraid we're going to turn into North Korea's Kwangmyong. A lot of people treat these things as if they're only natural, whether it's blocking the foreign internet, censoring games, *Baozou Dajishi*, or now the Chinese version of STEAM. But what are the facts? In Europe, there are terrorist activities on Instagram and Twitter—did they just simply build a firewall to block these social media apps? No, they wage cyber warfare against those terrorists and drive them off those social platforms. If that's the case, why can't the CCP do it? Is it just because building a wall is cheaper? Are our rights and our spaces for entertainment and relaxation worth less than the cost of waging a cyber war? Do Chinese people just have to compromise and swallow their anger while foreigners get to protect their rights? Please spread these words far and wide. Speak up for your own rights and for STEAM! I don't know which version of "being represented" is better: the one they claim—that banning and censoring *World of Warcraft*, *Baozou Dajishi*, and other free media, social apps, and single-player/online games represents the will of the people and players—or what I'm posting today, which represents the interests of STEAM players. But I know that everything I'm saying comes from the bottom of my heart, spoken with a bittersweet mix of emotions after experiencing all of this. I am speaking with a clear conscience, whereas they aren't necessarily doing the same. I hope everyone spreads these words. I know that nine times out of ten it won't do any good, but how can we stay silent just because our voices are small? As an ordinary resident living in China who loves STEAM and loves the joy STEAM brings, this is all I can do. Thank you everyone, this represents personal opinions only. Please award this comment, give me a like.

translation_en: I no longer recommend anyone to buy this game just to play GTA Online. Its lifecycle is basically over, and what's left is just gasping for air with updates that keep getting more and more trash. Players gave Rockstar a full year, and the stuff they've been putting out is absolute "heavyweight" garbage. Here is why I don't recommend anyone to buy it. · Extremely terrible online environment If you go to a public lobby—meaning a session with a bunch of strangers—you are almost guaranteed to run into hackers. Even if you try to keep to yourself, you'll easily fall victim to things like all players being teleported into cages and killed. You'll also be killed repeatedly to the point where you can't even open the pause menu, and sometimes hackers will straight up crash your game. If you're planning to play with friends, you can avoid this, but that's assuming you haven't been targeted by any cheaters. Otherwise, hackers will be able to endlessly join your lobby or missions, teleport you into cages to kill you again, or crash your game. Even if you've never messed with a single motherfucking hacker, you still have to deal with the god-awful "ballstorture" random invites (a year-long indiscriminate invite spam that even forcibly drags players into new lobbies). And what is Rockstar's solution to this? They disabled the feature that lets players invite public lobby players to missions from a private session, and players can no longer search for active missions across different lobbies (which used to be a thing). So with players making all these sacrifices, you'd think the hacker problem has gotten a lot better, right? Well, just on Chinese forums alone, you can find at least 4 different hacks being used to indiscriminately invite, harass, and attack players across entire servers, and one of them is literally ballstorture! That's their attitude towards hackers! They don't give a shit about hacks that affect global lobbies, so those petty, motherfucking script kiddies are way beyond what they're willing to manage. · Extremely trash updates If you can avoid the absolute trash environment by completely isolating yourself, there's one big problem you can never escape: the increasingly trash updates. If last summer's ULP mission update at least had some extra features worth praising (hidden contacts, categorization options at the auto shop—yes, features that should have been made ages ago that they dragged their feet on for almost 10 years), this year there is practically nothing worth bragging about! The winter update's god-awful Acid Trip missions felt as lazy as taking some minor side missions, splitting them up individually, and telling you this is a major update! A major update! Players who haven't played might not know what a usual major mission update is like. Setting aside PvP updates, past major mission updates were typically massive heists like the Heists (Apartments), Doomsday Heist (the coolest and most sci-fi one), Diamond Casino Heist, and Cayo Perico. The Apartment Heists, being the pioneer of 4-player co-op, go without saying—a must-play for groups of four. The Doomsday Heist featured all sorts of badass weapons and vehicles, with action scenes rivaling a blockbuster movie. Casino and Cayo Perico added multiple playstyles, allowing for stealth or loud approaches with plenty of tactical variety. Meanwhile, the Acid Trip update was even split into two parts, with the second part dragging on for almost half a year just to be squeezed out, and they even dragged out adding a Hard Mode (which just means one less life) for several months! This level of efficiency is unprecedented and infuriating. Maybe you think trash missions are fine and you can just play other stuff, but what comes next is absolute heavyweight material. · Extremely trash business model Grand Theft Auto—crimes related to stealing cars, right? The focus is on stealing and cars, AUTO! In their latest update, they deleted nearly 200 good cars! And that number is apparently still growing! What reason did Rockstar give? "To optimize the browsing experience." So, Rockstar must really care about the players' browsing experience, right? Oh, aside from deleting nearly 200 great cars, they barely added a few categories. And what else? Is there a search-by-name function? Are there more filter options? When you check out a car's description and hit back, does it stay where you were scrolling or does it reset to the top? None of it! A flying motorcycle that used to cost 2 million, after several price hikes, they raised it to 8 million! This is equivalent to grinding Cayo Perico at least 5 times in a row, and every single time it has to be a 1.8 million payout (meaning solo primary target split + glitching + being lucky enough to spawn the highest-value loot to fill your bag), just so you can afford this one vehicle. If you aren't that lucky, you have to grind even more times! At the same time, I don't know if Rockstar has some kind of fetish for limited-time collection garbage. They constantly push all sorts of god-awful tasks that not only have terrible rewards, but also suck to play. For example, last Halloween's limited-time event to collect 200 jack-o'-lanterns within a week, randomly slapped with effects like explosions or electrocution, or collecting 100 prop bags, only to get an outfit at the end that doesn't even look good and feels super low-effort. On top of that, they constantly pull stunts like time-gated logins just to get XX outfit. This way of manufacturing "FOMO" is deeply sickening. Just to add a shred of collector's value to their profoundly lazy outfits, they pull this extremely repulsive limited-time collection bullshit. Whoever does it just feels disgusted by it, artificially inflating the difficulty of getting the item to fake some kind of value. Yet, even after getting it, I still wouldn't wear it in-game, which is just pathetic. Then there's the Rockstar Creator. They keep adding more and more restrictions to it. The latest update even introduced a blacklist on props, making most fun, player-created maps unplayable—though they eventually walked it back after getting flak from players, nobody can guarantee when they'll just delete those features again. On top of that, they restrict player earning speeds. Cayo Perico, the most profitable heist, got hit with a god-awful 3-hour cooldown for solo runners and a 48-minute cooldown for playing with others. Other major jobs also got slapped with a 48-minute cooldown (all forcing multiplayer), meaning even solo players aren't spared from Rockstar's retarded management. Before players get to experience the game fully, some might think that limiting how fast you make money helps players appreciate the progression. But when faced with shitty guns that cost hundreds of thousands (more expensive than many properties), most people won't complain that the cooldowns are too short—they'll just bitch about Los Santos's insane hyperinflation. After all, Rockstar knows that if players made money and bought things too easily, they wouldn't buy GTA+ subscriptions or Shark Cards. · Endless bugs and crashes The game's harmless fun bugs that help players make more money in jobs get promptly fixed, while game-breaking bugs—like bullets getting swallowed, making players lose hundreds of thousands in ammo costs every time, or crashes that eat your payouts—are left entirely for the community to deal with (even the optimization for loading times was made by players before being officially adopted). Bullets still randomly disappear to this day, and recently a new bug popped up where vehicles don't get insurance payouts when destroyed. Sometimes players can't even get into the game, save files get lost or reset. Fun bugs get patched immediately, while infuriating, game-breaking bugs pile up forever and are never actually fixed. An online environment this trash is truly one-of-a-kind among all open-world games. It just keeps getting worse! If you don't want to update it, then stop updating! If a year from now a massive chunk of content is locked behind GTA+ subscriptions—especially those 200 deleted cars—I wouldn't be surprised at all, because that is 100% something Rockstar would pull!

translation_en: There was a guy who had a crush on a high school classmate for a long time. He made his move and chased her from the second year of high school all the way to his junior year of college, but she never agreed to be with him. The guy remembers confessing his feelings three times, and not once did it work out. Along the way, the girl went through four bad breakups, and every single time, the guy was right there by her side during her lowest points. He helped her get through her emotional slumps, thinking that as long as she was happy, he would be happy too. Every time she got a new boyfriend, even though it hurt, the guy would still wish them well. He walked her to and from class, went to cram school with her, prepped for the college entrance exams together, hung out on weekends, and joined the same club, even though they ended up going to different universities. But whenever they came home for the holidays, they would still go out to eat, chat, and catch up. Yet, they remained just good friends. The guy didn't want to give up; he refused to accept it. He believed that his hard work would eventually touch her heart. Just like that, he chased her for five years. This was his first love. Until recently, the girl broke up with her boyfriend again, and the guy, who had always been right by her side, tried his best to comfort her. "Since you're single now, you must be free this Christmas, right?" the guy mustered up the courage to ask. "Um..." she replied. "Then... let's two single folks have dinner together this time?" he said. "Sure, thanks!" the girl replied. The guy made up his mind. He was going to confess one more time. This time it was do-or-die. He had to put in the absolute maximum effort to move her! So the clumsy guy started knitting a woolen scarf—something extremely difficult for him. He bought a bunch of materials, and despite failing art class, he made a Christmas card. The guy kept thinking, it might look pathetic, but it's the thought that counts, right?! ... Finally, today was Christmas. Even though they agreed on seven in the evening, the excited guy showed up at six. He stood in front of the East Gate, silently practicing the confession lines he'd rehearsed so many times, wearing an outfit he put together from a magazine, and secretly checking his reflection in shop windows over and over to fix his hair. 10 minutes... 20 minutes... 30 minutes... The guy's phone rang. It was the girl. "Sorry, have you arrived yet? My boyfriend just said he wanted to give me a surprise, and we might get back together... So... I probably can't make it tonight. You probably haven't left yet anyway, there's still half an hour..." "It's fine, I'm still in my dorm and haven't left yet, hahahahaha... Congrats..." "I'm so sorry, we made plans and everything..." "It's totally fine, go have fun. Merry Christmas. Hahahaha..." "Um, Merry Christmas." "Hey..." Should he confess? "Hmm?" "Nothing, never mind... Bye then." "Yeah, bye." After hanging up, I shoved the scarf I knitted and the card straight into the trash can at the East Gate. I knew I had a scowl on my face, but I felt oddly numb. So I stood blankly in front of the East Gate for another 30 minutes, pretending to wait for someone while watching couples walk by. Then, come dinnertime, I went to a restaurant, ordered two steaks, and wolfed them both down. I paid for two people as well. Afterward, I went to see *Life of Pi*, and on the way back, I muttered my well-rehearsed confession lines out loud, pretending as if I'd actually confessed. Just like that, I ended up walking to the train station. I originally meant to go back to the dorm, but instead, I bought a ticket to Zhunan, Miaoli. I decided to just go home. I was so tired. I must have been exhausted. When I got home, my mom saw that my expression was off, but she didn't say anything and let me go into my room alone. I felt surprisingly calm. Really, unexpectedly calm. So I opened my computer, logged into Bahamut, and started typing out this story—belonging only to me—as a memorial. But typing this out, my tears are blurring the verification code on the screen so badly that I can't even see it. That's when I realize just how heartbroken I am. Merry Christmas, and I hope you find happiness and joy, so I don't have to worry about you anymore.

Also, here's some need-to-know info for beginners starting online mode ([u] highly recommend playing story mode first to get used to the controls [/u]) [h1] Main Game Controls [/h1] [b] P [/b] Pause menu [b] HOME [/b](above arrow keys) Rockstar menu, used for adding friends [b] M [/b] Interaction menu (has all kinds of functions, highly recommend trying them out one by one) [b] V [/b] Switch perspective (first-person is faster than third-person when running up and down stairs) [b] C [/b] Look behind [b] TAB [/b] Weapon wheel (while the wheel is open you can press C to eat snacks for health or press V to put on armor, provided you actually have them, which you can check in the menu before starting a mission) [b] Q [/b] Take cover (while in cover you can press left click to blind fire, or right click first to aim out of cover) [b] CTRL [/b] Stealth [b] R [/b] Reload, also does a melee attack if your mag is full [b] G [/b] Detonate sticky bombs [b] Press G while aiming [/b] Throw throwable (throws whatever throwable is currently selected on your weapon wheel) [b] Press movement key + Space while aiming [/b] Roll in the direction you're moving [b] T [/b] Global chat (on win 10 press ALT+SHIFT to switch input methods, Microsoft Pinyin is recommended) [b] Y [/b] Crew chat [b] Z [/b] HUD info (shows car name, how much money you have, level, session player list) [b] Double-click Z [/b] Enlarge mini-map [b] B [/b] Point finger where your crosshair is pointing (pretty much useless, but I'm writing it down just in case you run into some foreigner and have a language barrier emergency) [b] X [/b] Oppressor rocket boost [hr][/hr] Other stuff: If you want to grind cargo and do work in peace, I recommend going into story mode first, then go to Settings - Online - Play GTA Online - choose Closed Friend Session or Invite-Only Session. Because you're the only one in there, you won't get stuck in the cloud loading screens. I recommend changing your startup setting in the options to default to story mode. Going straight to online will put you in a public session and leave you stuck in the clouds for ages. How to get a solo public session: In settings, turn off "Pause Game on Focus Loss", press ALT+ENTER to go into windowed mode, press the Windows key to pull your mouse out, right-click the game's top window border, wait 6 seconds, then left-click back into the game window. Done. You can use this if you're being chased or want to get away from annoying ad spammers. Switching to first-person view has a ton of perks. You run faster, going up and down stairs is way more responsive, and moving left and right while aiming is much more agile.

translation_en: Some tips for beginners: 1. After buying the game, it's best to master the offline mode first—learn how to fly planes and helicopters, and get familiar with all the weapons before jumping into Online. Think of it as building a foundation for Online. 2. Public lobbies in Online can be pretty laggy and are full of cheaters. I feel like public lobbies are only necessary when you're doing apartment heists that require four people for setups and finales. Stuff like Cayo Perico preps, CEO and nightclub cargo can all be done solo in invite-only sessions. (Joining Online directly without a VPN usually takes forever. I recommend newbies load into Story Mode first, press Esc, find "Online" in the tabs across the top, click the bottom option, and then enter an invite-only session.) 3. The public lobby environment is trash. You can ignore any chat messages advertising menus/cheats, and it's best not to join random QQ groups either. (I joined one once, and it was basically all cheaters and menu sellers). If you want to join a GTAO QQ group, I suggest looking for fan groups of GTAO content creators on Bilibili. 4. You honestly don't need cheats anywhere in Online. If you have a long drive ahead of you, just be patient and you'll usually get there. In heavy-combat areas like Cayo Perico or Act III of Doomsday, as long as you've got skill you can beat them without god mode—even the Criminal Mastermind challenge. So I don't recommend beginners buying cheats right off the bat; it doesn't improve your skill and ruins the game experience. Getting carried by a cheater in a modded vehicle is pointless too. If you play patiently, the money will come. 5. Some of my personal tips for reference: ① For pistols and SMGs, I recommend the Armor Piercing Pistol, followed by the Micro SMG. They're great for drive-bys. ② For assault rifles, beginners should go with the Special Carbine. Once you're a higher level, switch to the Carbine Rifle and upgrade it to Mk II. ③ For sniper rifles, beginners should use the cheap semi-auto sniper (not the one below the Heavy Sniper). Later on, buy the Heavy Sniper at a weapon workshop and upgrade it to Mk II. (If you make money fast and have plenty of cash, you can buy a weapon workshop in places like the Kosatka or the MOC. This lets you bypass level restrictions to buy certain weapons. For example, the Heavy Sniper normally unlocks at level 80-90 or 100, but you can buy it and upgrade it to Mk II right away at a workshop.) ④ As for shotguns, you *have* to get the Assault Shotgun. It's fully automatic and packs a serious punch. With an extended clip, it's arguably the second best shotgun in the game (the absolute best being the Mk II with explosive rounds). ⑤ Heavy weapons have limited options early on. The Homing Launcher runs out of ammo fast, and its tracking is pretty much useless—you have to use it like a regular RPG and lead your shots. If you've got extra cash, buy the Widowmaker. ⑥ For throwables, buy sticky bombs. They're super strong. The most important thing for beginners is to fully experience the offline mode before coming to Online. Don't buy or sell cheats, and be careful joining random QQ groups advertised in the in-game chat.

[h1] Things I Liked [/h1] 〽️The game never repeats itself in main missions. There are 69 different main missions, and in all 69 of these missions, we do things that are different from one another. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2930486755 〽️The 3-character system is successfully integrated into the open world and missions. 〽️The graphics are good and more than enough for our time. 〽️It has a huge map with tons of things to do, offering a very diverse and fun gameplay. 〽️It's open to modding and has a ton of mods. From SMGs to a ray gun, from shotguns to RPGs, various rifles, and even broken bottles to brass knuckles, there is a huge number of weapons available. Almost all of these weapons can be modified down to the finest detail. 〽️There are 30 different open-world side activities, 60 random events, and 58 Strangers and Freaks missions. Since these missions are all different from each other, they are absolute bliss. In short, the game rarely gets repetitive, which boosts its replayability. 〽️Vehicle variety and customization are no different from the weapon variety. There are commercial planes, stunt planes, seaplanes, warplanes, helicopters, boats, jet skis, ATVs, off-road vehicles, and many more usable vehicles. Also, the car mechanics are legendary. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2971832866 〽️We can't skip mentioning the gunplay and hit feedback. It has a gunplay feel that doesn't even exist in games coming out today. Enemies react based on where you hit them, making firefights much more realistic. In short, GTA V is a magnificent production in every single detail. It's a masterpiece to me. Even almost 10 years after its release, it continues to be one of the best examples of the open-world genre. It would have been even better if they had spent a bit more time on the online part. translation_en: My first time encountering this game was during the summer vacation of the third grade of elementary school. Some stuff had happened at home, nobody was looking after me, and as a result, I lost interest in everything. At the time, I saw this game on Youku, clicked on it, and saw the words "Ludendorff, North Yankton, 9 Years Ago" pop up in Traditional Chinese. PC specs weren't very high back then, and looking back now, the graphics definitely weren't as good as today's, but it honestly blew my mind for the longest time. I still remember staying up all night watching all of that creator's videos, and even after finishing them, I couldn't fall asleep. Back then I didn't even know what Steam was, so I could only search the web, found a bunch of cracked pirate versions, the kind that were loaded with viruses, and eventually I just had to give up. Later, when I went to play at my cousin's house, I saw *Vice City* on his computer. I asked him what game this was, and he told me it was GTA. I knew this wasn't the GTA I had in mind, so I searched for related info online and found out there were several GTA games. Later on, I downloaded *Vice City* and *San Andreas* from uploaders on Bilibili, beat both games in over half a year, and that's what dragged me down this rabbit hole. Around late 2019 or early 2020, my dad bought me a PC with a 2060 graphics card, so I quickly registered on Steam. I remember it was the New Year sale, 50% off. I bought the game that I had been dreaming about for so many years for 59 RMB. By that time, I had already watched countless content creators' playthroughs of it. A week later, watching the original trio push Devin down into the ocean, I leaned back in my chair. Finally, Trevor's pacing and the sunset in the dusk—right then, I knew how much I loved this game. The dream I had in the third grade of elementary school came true the year I was in the seventh grade. Now it's the summer vacation of the ninth grade, and the online community of this game is completely unplayable due to all the hackers. I tried to forget about this game along the way, but I realized that no matter how much I circled back, no other game could replace it. This game gave me a ray of light during the darkest time of my life, and I love it. —— July 8, 2022, 5:38 PM

translation_en: Suggestions for the development of China's gaming industry: Those who try to turn games into mere commodities, those who try to turn games into social platforms, and those who try to turn games into political tools—all of you can fuck right off! The internet is full of games that fleece kids of their pocket money and then bail, and you do nothing about it. You do nothing about web games where every single ad features broken, unnatural Mandarin. You do nothing about websites openly selling hacks and cheats. But you crack down on AAA blockbusters? Violence? Sexual content? Take a look at the ads plastered all over domestic websites—every single one of them is more revealing than anything on Steam. You don't do a damn thing about that, yet you come after Steam? Stop trying to drag a massive platform down into the dirt, alright? Even though many Chinese players just use Steam as a game launcher, it at least fostered the concept of supporting legitimate, licensed software. Just as we're finally making a bit of progress, you're about to drag us back to square one. Are you trying to encourage everyone to pirate games instead? Setting aside the whole "democracy" debate, why can't we have a ratings system? A ratings board could resolve most of these issues. Is pulling shit like this supposed to be funny? You "experts" are seriously fucking retarded. Every day you churn out this useless garbage, crying about "electronic opium" and the need to "cure internet addiction." And what was the result? A few years ago, a high school student, in order to "cure his internet addiction," secretly chopped off his own hand behind his family's back. Is that shit reasonable? And what about people like Professor Yang, who used "internet addiction" as an excuse to rake in crazy amounts of money, causing endless human tragedies and shattering families left and right? Is that reasonable? Of course, having your life ruined by crap like this is a low-probability event anyway. What I care about much more is this: If the game I bought stops working, who the fuck is going to compensate me? Perfect World, or Tencent? At the end of the day, it'll probably just mean us players who insist on buying legitimate copies take a total loss for nothing—just like back in 2018 with the WeGame version of *Monster Hunter: World*. The game got pulled, a bunch of players who wanted to support domestic industry refused to let them issue refunds, and in the end, Tencent just swallowed the money, while probably getting to smugly laugh in the faces of real-life players who actually buy legit games. Games belong to the ninth art. Any major blockbuster inherently embodies the author's thoughts and philosophy. Amidst the collision and blending of various ideological cultures, foreign thoughts about the future and their wild, countless fantasies simply cannot be accepted by the SARFT or the Ministry of Culture. But if the authorities won't accept them, the real question is: can the players accept them? As things stand right now in the domestic market—due to Steam, consoles, and various other factors—you can still make a boatload of cash by just churning out absolute garbage. They know that as long as the game's quality is barely passable, and they design a few flashy "micro-operations" to flex on people, slap on some horny character art, and use edgy-ass character models and dialogue, they can scam people out of their money. The story has to be complete nonsense—no depth, super simple and easy to understand. It's even better if you can stir up a bunch of drama, good or bad, to trigger some public outrage. A prime example is *Tower of Fantasy*—you guys must have been eating that popcorn drama up. At the same time, you pump out some ads for a marketing push, and a piece of shit put together like that will make you way more money than a game whose story you actually sat down and carefully crafted. Even though Steam seems like it's well-known in China, the truth is, before *PUBG* blew up, if you walked down the street, hardly anyone even knew what Steam was. Actually, China's real-name verification system is already way ahead of foreign countries. UnionPay and WeChat Pay both strictly require an ID card. So why the hell is there still a delay in rolling out a game ratings policy? In foreign countries, rating systems are agreements between major gaming companies. If that were implemented domestically... well, what's the very first company that pops into your head? Tencent? NetEase? You know how greedy they are, you get what I mean. Furthermore, the Ministry of Culture and the SARFT currently hold absolute veto power over what gets approved. There are no clear, relevant laws or regulations determining whether a game passes censorship or not. Back in the day, a domestic single-player game developer made a wuxia game and submitted it for review. Because they were a domestic studio, they knew the censorship mechanism inside and out, so before submitting it, they stripped out all the blood and dismemberment effects, and turned all the corpses black. But even then, it still failed censorship! The censors said that the player character in the game only has to serve ten days in prison after killing someone, which could easily cause a negative social impact. After going back and revision after revision, it eventually turned into a wuxia game where you can literally do nothing except ride horses. Meanwhile, Tencent's *Moonlight Blade* lets you slaughter human enemies and face zero consequences—you just keep right on butchering people. Doesn't that cause an even bigger social impact? Yet *Moonlight Blade* passed censorship just fine. Why does that happen? Tencent makes a fortune every single day; they can afford to pay up, they can afford endless trial and error. But that small developer had no money left after finishing the game, so they just dropped dead on the spot. Therefore, the development of Chinese single-player games isn't about your production standards, nor is it about whether your marketing hits the mark—it's first and foremost about whether you can afford to pay the bribe. The original intention behind the Great Firewall was good—it was meant to block the export of Western ideology, consolidate the ideological high ground, and reduce the invasion of undesirable culture. But poorly reasoned policies have made it damn near impossible for the domestic gaming industry to grow. Precisely because of this reason, a lot of people have come to take this shit for granted. Whether it's blocking foreign internet access, censoring games, *Baozou Dashijian*, or the upcoming Steam China edition, or being force-fed a bowl of lukewarm shit by WeGame and various localized console versions. So many things have been castrated, pulled from shelves, and banned: Easter eggs in *StarGraft 2*, the blood color in *Chicken Dinner*, certain content in *That Game 5*, Bilibili's philosophy content, as well as *World of Warcraft*, *Baozou Dashijian*, and so on. So much, so much. There's no going back. They left a brilliant, dazzling mark in our memories, because these are the things we love and cherish. They say they're maintaining the internet environment, but do they know how we feel? Do they understand our pain?! Now, when you really think about it, has the purpose of the Firewall drifted away from what it was originally set up to do? The wall was supposed to keep out rotting culture, but now, it's also isolating excellent games, allowing certain domestic, rotting forms of capital to suck the blood of all players without any pressure whatsoever. The wall has been weaponized by certain people to rake in huge profits, and the country's gaming market has been turned by certain groups into a breeding ground for corruption. Policies desperately need to be reformed, otherwise, there will definitely be grave consequences down the road. I know saying all this is probably nine times out of ten useless. Just treat it as me venting; some things have been bottled up for too long, and if I don't say it, my chest feels too heavy. As an ordinary gamer who loves Steam and loves the joy Steam brings—even though a blanket ban is quick and easy, it treats the symptoms rather than the disease. It's about time China's gaming industry policies were reformed. Many of us are hard-working and silently swallow our grievances. When they blocked the foreign internet and censored games, we complied. And what was the result? Facebook, Twitter, and Google were replaced at home by Tencent, Baidu, and the like. Now those tech giants have already occupied massive swathes of the domestic gaming industry. Following WeGame, Perfect World, and the fake Steam platform, the official Steam China version is now about to launch. We can all easily imagine what kind of greedy, ugly face this "China version" is going to have.

translation_en: Advice for the development of China's gaming industry: To those who try to turn games into mere commodities, to those who try to turn games into social platforms, to those who try to turn games into political tools—get the fuck out of here! The internet is full of games designed to milk kids of their money, and you do nothing about it. You go to web pages and every single ad is in broken-ass Mandarin, and you do nothing about it. There are official websites openly selling hacks and cheats, and you do nothing about it. But you crack down on AAA blockbusters? Violence? Pornography? Look at the images plastered all over web ads everywhere in this country—every single one of them is more revealing than anything on STEAM, and you don't give a shit, but you come after STEAM? Can't you leave a great platform out of this, please? Even though STEAM is just treated as a game launcher by a lot of Chinese players, at least it gave people an awareness of buying genuine copies. Just as we're finally making a bit of progress, you're about to drag us right back to square one. What, you wanna encourage everyone to play cracked games? Not even talking about so-called democracy, why can't we just have an age-rating system? A rating system could solve most of these issues. Do you think pulling this shit is fun? You "experts" are fucking brilliant. Every day you churn out this useless garbage, talking about "electronic opium" and how we need to cure internet addiction. And what was the result? A few years ago, a high school student actually chopped off his own hand behind his family's back just to cure his so-called "internet addiction." Is that reasonable? And what about people like Professor Yang, using internet addiction as an excuse to rake in crazy amounts of money, causing endless human tragedies and shattered families? Is that reasonable? Of course, ruining your life over shit like this is a low-probability event anyway. What I care about more is: if the game I bought stops working, who the fuck is going to compensate me? Perfect World, or Tencent? Though I guess it'll just end up with us players who insist on buying genuine games taking a total loss. Take the 2018 WeGame version of *Monster Hunter: World*, for example. The game got pulled from shelves, a bunch of players who wanted to support domestic industries insisted on not getting a refund, and in the end, Tencent just swallowed the money—probably while getting mocked by a bunch of smug, real-life pirates riding their high horses. Gaming belongs to the ninth art. Any blockbuster game inherently embodies the author's philosophy and worldview. Amidst the collision and blending of various ideological cultures, foreign thoughts about the future and all sorts of bizarre fantasies are simply unacceptable to the SARFT and the Ministry of Culture. But hey, if the bureaus won't accept them, the real question is whether the *players* can accept them. As things stand right now in the domestic market, thanks to all the restrictions around Steam and consoles, you can still make a pile of absolute garbage and rake in cash. Game developers know that as long as the game's quality is barely passable, all they need to do is design some micro-management features for players to flex their "skills" in-game, throw in all sorts of horny original art, and slap on some edgy-ass character models and dialogue, and they can scam people out of their money. The plot of the game itself has to be complete nonsense—no depth whatsoever, just keep it shallow and easy to understand. It's even better if you can stir up a bunch of drama, good or bad, to manipulate public opinion. Take *Tower of Fantasy* as a prime example; I'm sure you guys have eaten plenty of drama over that one. At the same time, pump out some ads and run a PR campaign, and that kind of production will make you way more money than a game where you actually sat down and carefully crafted a storyline. Even though a lot of people in China seem to know about Steam now, before *PUBG* came out, if you walked down the street, hardly anyone even knew Steam existed. Actually, real-name verification in China is already way ahead of foreign countries. UnionPay and WeChat Pay both require a National ID card, so why the hell are they still dragging their feet on introducing an age-rating policy? Foreign rating systems are just agreements between major game publishers. If you applied that domestically, well, what's the very first company that pops into your head? Tencent? NetEase? You know what they look like when they're eating—you get my drift. Moreover, the Ministry of Culture and SARFT currently hold absolute veto power over what gets approved. There are no actual laws or regulations governing whether a game passes censorship. Back in the day, a domestic single-player game developer made a wuxia game and submitted it for review. Because they were a domestic studio, they knew the censorship system inside out, so before submitting it, they stripped out all the blood and dismemberment effects, and turned all the corpses black. But even then, it still failed review. The censors said that in this game, the player character only has to spend ten days in jail after killing someone, which could easily cause a negative social impact. After going through round after round of revisions, it eventually turned into a wuxia game where you can literally only ride horses. Meanwhile, in Tencent's *Moonlight Blade*, after you slaughter humanoid enemies you don't have to bear any responsibility at all—you can just keep right on butchering. Doesn't that create a much worse social impact? Yet *Moonlight Blade* got approved. Why does this happen? Because Tencent makes a killing every single day. They can afford the fines and fees, they can afford endless trial and error. But that small studio had basically no money left after finishing their game, so they just dropped dead on the spot. Therefore, the development of Chinese single-player games isn't about your production quality, nor is it about whether your marketing is on point—it’s about whether you can afford to pay off the gatekeepers first. The original intention behind the Great Firewall was good—to block the export of Western ideologies, consolidate the ideological high ground, and reduce the invasion of harmful cultures. But poorly implemented policies have made it damn near impossible for the domestic gaming industry to develop. And precisely because of this reason, a lot of people now just take this shit as a matter of course. Whether it's blocking foreign websites, censoring games, shows like *Baozou Dashijian*, or the upcoming Steam China, or getting force-fed a bowl of cold mush by WeGame and various localized console editions. So many things have been castrated, taken down, and banned: Easter eggs in *Starcraft 2*, the blood color in *PUBG*, certain content in *That Game 5* (GTA V), Bilibili's philosophy content, *World of Warcraft*, *Baozou Dashijian*, and so on. So much, so damn much. There's no turning back. In our memories, they left a brilliant and dazzling mark, because these are the things we loved and cherished. They say they're maintaining the internet environment, but do they know how we feel? Do they understand our pain?! Now, thinking about it carefully, has the purpose of the Firewall drifted away from its original design? The Wall was meant to block decadent culture, but now, it’s also shutting out brilliant games, allowing certain corrupt domestic capitalists to suck the blood of all players without any pressure. The Wall has been weaponized by some people as a tool for extortion, and this country's gaming market has been turned by certain factions into a breeding ground for corruption. Policies desperately need to be reformed, otherwise there will definitely be severe consequences down the road. I know saying all this is probably 90% useless. Just treat me as blowing off some steam—some things have been bottled up for too long, and if I don't say it, my chest feels tight. As an ordinary gamer who loves Steam and loves the joy Steam brings, a one-size-fits-all ban is quick, but it treats the symptoms and not the disease. It's about time the policies surrounding China's gaming industry were overhauled. A lot of us are uncomplaining and hardworking, just constantly swallowing our pride. When they blocked foreign websites and censored games, we complied. And what was the result? Facebook, Twitter, and Google got replaced in the domestic market by Tencent, Baidu, and their ilk. Now those tech giants have already occupied vast territories of the domestic gaming industry. Following WeGame, Perfect World, and the fake Steam platform, Steam China is about to drop. I'm sure you can all imagine what kind of ugly mugs those guys are going to make while devouring this market.

translation_en: At 1:13 AM on June 1, 2022, with almost 1,900 hours on record, my GTA Online account got hit with a 30-day ban and a full character wipe. So why am I writing this review at 1:13 AM on June 14? Because I didn't want to wait 30 days, so I bought GTA again on another Steam account and started over, only to get hit with *another* 30-day ban and wipe on the night of June 13. I have never used any cheats. I have never modified any game files. When I found out I was banned, I was in absolute shock, and having my progress completely wiped just left my mind totally blank. On top of that, Rockstar support won't accept your appeals; they just keep copy-pasting: "All suspension and ban decisions and character resets are final and cannot be appealed," and "We do not provide further details regarding security detections or security measures taken against player accounts." It took me three or four days just to process this. Later, I still wanted to play but didn't want to wait 30 days, so on the night of June 4, I bought another copy of GTA on a different Steam account, playing completely legit and walking on eggshells to start over. But on the night of June 13, I got banned again. I honestly have no fucking clue why. I've racked my brain and can't come up with a single reason. I've always been a cautious, hoarder-type player. For the longest time, I've known to avoid public lobbies as much as possible because they're an absolute shitshow of modders doing god knows what, which might somehow drag you down with them. But it's impossible to completely avoid public lobbies because certain features require you to go into one first before you can trick it into a solo public session. To be honest, Rockstar's detection system is trash. You have no fucking clue how it even works; the moment it thinks you're dodgy, it bans you without a second thought and wipes your data along with it. All I can say is I'm deeply disappointed. After my first ban, I actually chose to trust Rockstar, bought the game again, and got fucked over a second time. I've also seen countless people mocking those who get banned: "If you got banned, you're obviously doing something wrong," "Rockstar doesn't hand out false bans," "You know damn well what you did," "Stop crying about getting banned for cheating, it's pathetic," and all that bullshit. I used to think like that to some extent too, but until you get wrongfully banned yourself, you have no idea how infuriating these people are. All of the above only applies to GTA Online. GTA V single-player is actually really well made. But I genuinely do not recommend giving Rockstar another dime. The online mode is an absolute mess, and you never know when a ban is gonna randomly drop on your head. Even if you only want to play single-player, I wouldn't recommend buying it—just pirate the damn thing. A developer like this doesn't deserve your money anymore.

translation_en: Grand Theft Auto V is a fantastic game that I can recommend to pretty much anyone, as long as you have the mindset of "I'm not playing GTA Online." Driving around in your favorite car, going for a scenic flight in your favorite aircraft, shooting people with guns, and gambling at the casino are all a blast. But you can only fully and safely enjoy those things offline. The price might feel a little steep, but there's easily enough content just in the offline story mode to make it worth it. Hell, offline is even treated better than GTA Online, with fewer bugs and special abilities. So if you're gonna play it, just stick to offline. If you casually step into the world of GTA Online with a mindset like, "Well, GTA Online is included, might as well check it out," what's waiting for you is pure hell. There's no such thing as "peacefully" having fun goofing off with random strangers online in GTA Online, which has been a lawless wasteland since way back. PKs (Player Kills) by no-lifes run rampant without a care in the world, and cheaters roam wild all over the place. There's trash talk, racist remarks, political and ideological rants, arguments sparked by those things, and you constantly see spam advertising cheats. Disconnecting during missions happens all the time, and the matchmaking time when hosting a mission (depending on the type) currently takes anywhere up to several tens of minutes. The only reason people still play GTA Online despite all that is probably because of the vehicles unique to Online, high-difficulty missions, and attractions you can only find there, but it is definitely not something I'd recommend to beginners. If you're interested in the vehicles exclusive to GTA Online, I recommend a playstyle where you do jobs bit by bit in invite-only sessions and casually grind for cash. To sum up this long-ass review, unless you're specifically looking for a lawless wasteland kind of game, you're better off just enjoying the offline mode. "A ruthless city where you can't trust anyone, let alone each other"—that kind of shit is plenty enough inside fiction.

translation_en: Originally I just wanted to knock out a community task, write a review for a game, and get a little bit of XP. But seeing GTA V brought all these memories flooding back. Dear Taco_tuesday_, What's up, old friend! This is my main account that got banned for modding money. When I first stepped into Los Santos, I couldn't resist the bait of the ads and went full-on multi-millionaire mode overnight. As everyone knows how things go in Los Santos, my level 2000+ female character was constantly getting blown to pieces and dragged into modder firefights. Being a total noob back then, I bought a bunch of properties and cars that I thought looked badass but had zero cost-efficiency. I also bought every single business. At the time, I thought, is this really the whole online mode of this game? And then? Where was the story? Cluelessly hitting enter on phone invites, I somehow ended up tagging along with all sorts of people from everywhere to complete easy or hard missions. About a week after moving into Los Santos, I realized my level 2000 female character was a total dumbass. Fine, I'll switch to my other account, a male character just a little over level 100—neither too high nor too low. And that was the day an invitation popped up on my phone. I hit enter, entered your lobby, and that was our very first meeting. It was a Doomsday Heist prep mission—Server Farm. Looking back now, you were probably already pretty much maxed out by then. You saw I was ready and started right away. It was pitch black, and I stuck to you like glue, watching you take out cameras and silently one-shot the guards with a suppressed weapon. I was so terrified of getting lost and holding you back, following you right up to the rooftop. You were so badass, seamlessly finding the entrance. Once inside, I saw so many red dots on the map and had no idea what to aim at. Before I could even do anything, you rushed past me and wiped them out in two, three moves, like a god of war. You probably realized I was a total noob and went ahead to do the four-node hacking task all by yourself. Meanwhile, I tried my best not to die—I sure as hell didn't want to fail the mission. When it came to the last node, I caught up with you, ready to bail. Right as we made a run for it, a massive wave of NOOSE reinforcements showed up. In the chaos of escaping, I accidentally burned through a life. Crawling up to the roof, I found the whole place surrounded, and once we dropped down, the gunfire was insane. How was I supposed to not hold us back? We hid behind some planters, and I was freaking out so bad. Seeing you stay still, I just hunkered down next to you, until I suddenly saw a tank spawn right downstairs. Without even thinking, I bolted for it. In the end, your tank saved both of you and me. Mission passed. Hilariously, back then I actually thought you were the one who called in that vehicle. After the mission ended, it started pouring rain in Los Santos, thunder and lightning crashing everywhere. You called in your Pegassi Zentorno, pitch-black body with purple underglow. That minimalist color scheme you always liked. Once you got in, I jumped into the passenger seat too, wondering if you'd think I sucked and shoot me. But you didn't. You started the car and typed to ask if I was Chinese. I said yes. Radio playing inside the car, wind and rain lashing outside, you driving all over the place because you were busy typing. We just went tearing wildly through the wilderness in northern Los Santos with no destination in mind. I typed that I was getting carsick—though I wasn't really—and it just felt so damn good. That was our first real conversation, and we added each other on WeChat after that. But over the next few months, I never once heard your voice. That Pegassi Zentorno became the car you drove the most over the following months, and I was always sitting right there in the passenger seat. The turning point came when my account got banned for modding money—for thirty days. I couldn't wait that long, so I immediately registered a new Steam account and bought GTAV again. I’d been honest with you about the money modding before we even hung out, so you kind of saw it coming. When I asked you what kind of mods were good to use, you told me I didn't need to buy any menus, you could just carry me and we could play together. You were always so ridiculously polite. Every single day when you logged off, you'd tell me goodnight / night night, so I'd say goodnight / night night right back. Just like that, we spent over 3 months of days and nights together. My little alt account went from having absolutely nothing to being fully maxed out. You were the one who carried me through the whole thing step by step. Of course, our teamwork just got smoother and smoother over time; we never once used voice chat for any of our missions. I always knew what you were thinking, and you'd always turn around to check on me. Eventually, I finally became a capable little mute in Los Santos too. Actually, I copied you ages ago and bought a Pegassi Zentorno myself, but I was too shy to drive it out where you could see. I'd buy outfits almost identical to whatever you were wearing and put them on my little mute. But the second you logged on, I'd quickly change out of them. I loved that unspoken chemistry we had. Whenever I lagged into a solo public session, you'd always join straight away. Seeing your name online when I hit the 'Z' key made me immediately go check if you had gone back to your apartment. I loved it when you drove me back to my hillside house, and I loved waiting for you downstairs at your place. You'd always ask me, "Got enough cash? Doing Cayo?" Lol, seriously, all my assets were stolen from El Rubio because you dragged me along. I remember getting griefed by tryhards in our lobby, and when I kept getting farmed by some dude while riding my Oppressor Mark II, you stood on the ground with a sniper rifle, dropping them one by one with absolute precision. We've been hunted by modders, and we've hunted modders. We've watched the scenery together, gone scuba diving, gone up to the mountain to look at the ghost, sharing who knows how many days and nights in Los Santos. I also remember that massive brawl triggered by a cargo sale—I was the unlucky bastard running the goods, and it was like an all-out war with the whole LSPD mobilized. Once again, you saved me from the depths of hell. Huge shoutout to your tank. You asked me why there were so many people, and I typed that I was just glad you came, you were way too cool. I remember you seeing a TikTok about using the Scramjet's boost to fly up onto a rooftop, and we actually pulled it off. I remember how every time we did a race, you'd wait for me at the finish line, helping me practice until I could finally make it into the top five against full lobbies. I remember the Pacific Standard heist, where my motorcycle skills were absolute garbage and I had to ride on the back of your bike just so I wouldn't drag the team down. But then we hit a stupid glitch during the parachute section and the mission failed because of some scumbag modder. But your mental was always so rock solid—during the Doomsday Heist, you carried a whole team solo for over an hour just to get us through it. Every single time I pulled off a good play in the nick of time, you'd send me a WeChat message hyping me up, saying "so good, so good." Thank you for protecting my little mute for so long. Even though nothing dramatic ever happened between us, and we had zero connection in real life, all we had was that pure, unspoken chemistry right there in Los Santos. When you deleted me back then, it hurt pretty bad. Maybe the fact that there was no reason at all is what makes it hurt the most. After you left and I realized you'd wiped me completely from your friends list, I didn't even want to log into the game to check anything. But one day on a whim, I went back to Los Santos, pulled that Pegassi Zentorno out of the garage, and customized it from memory to look exactly like yours. I even changed my car horn to your favorite—"Soviet Connection" from GTA IV. I drove that car down the familiar streets, but even though it was the same car, the driver was gone, and I didn't have a passenger seat to sit in anymore. That building was still that building, but you didn't live there anymore, and I’d never wait for that little mute again. I’ll never see your pure white WeChat profile picture light up again either. Ah, it's been almost a year in the blink of an eye. Honestly, back then, having you around truly meant the world to me. I was just coming off a devastating breakup in real life that left me completely wrecked, but because of you, I slowly pulled myself out of it. I really, truly appreciate you keeping me company. The game is genuinely amazing, the scenery I saw is unforgettable, and Online doesn't need a script—we wrote our own story. P.S. I bought Red Dead Redemption 2, which was on your Steam wishlist. Wonder if you ever bought it? I bought Forza Horizon 4 too, since I saw you playing it before. translation_en: The other day I walked past the Pacific Standard bank and accidentally realized that you can actually get inside without launching a heist. Using the ATM inside, I thought of my level 40-50 self, stumbling around trying to leech off heists, thought of those clumsy friends of mine, and all those countless days and nights in Los Santos. Such a deserted bank, such a lonely feeling. Before I knew it, I had made it to the second floor, jumped down, and walked out of the bank. The blinding sunlight hit my head, my whole body flashed white for a second before returning to normal. In this sunny Los Santos, I couldn't feel any warmth. When I first started playing Online, it was a Gerald mission double cash event, and me and a few good buddies grinded those missions endlessly. Relying on the 100k from the starter pack, I scraped together enough for an arcade, and me and the boys clumsily grinded the Casino. Not long after, Cayo Perico dropped, and one of my homies straight up used a Shark Card to buy the Kosatka. I still remember our first time on the island, going in through the drainage tunnel, everything so unfamiliar and fresh. Later, that Shark Card bro led us swimming into the compound through the drainage pipe. He cut the grate, went forward and to the right, and we just kept swimming, swimming all the way until today, surfacing and pushing open that room's door. We stuffed our bags as much as we could, yet we could never fill our desires. We ran it over and over, until one day, we got sick of it. We started cleaning up Agent 13's mess; we met back up at the Diamond Casino, pressing PageUp over and over again, trying out new approaches and routes; and we replayed the old heists. For the final finale, I was no longer the hacker. Spraying bullets in the lobby, looking at the screaming NPCs on the floor, I thought of the first time doing the Pacific Standard with my boys, when the guy on crowd control said he got killed by a hostage. We half-believed him, crying and laughing. But honestly, we haven't improved much since then. Getting on the motorcycle still means a restart. That final payout of just over a million felt so heavy, way heavier than the casino diamonds or Cayo Perico gold. Hit the gas, pop a wheelie, bail off the bike, pull the chute. Shouting over party chat, the canyon scenery spread out below, driving the boat under the bridge, reaching an endless end. That bridge is the one I once sped across in my Omnis. Back then, that worried kid finally shook off the sadness that clung so tightly to him, dreaming back into the city of Los Santos—how many times has the real world hurt me? Later on, I got the MK2, got sports cars, properties, and all the assets. The most recent asset I bought was Eclipse Towers, which a lot of people bought way early on. I stand in front of the floor-to-ceiling windows, Vespucci Beach and the amusement park to the west, the mountains to the east, the pier to the south. In this not-so-big Los Santos, I just want to shrink into this apartment of my own. That good buddy who loves driving is always bantering with the Shark Card bro, telling me, "Man, I wish the money in Los Santos could turn into real cash. I'd trade a billion in-game for a single buck in real life." It's true. Standing on piles of cash all over my office, the thought suddenly hit me: "An inch of time is an inch of gold, but an inch of gold can't buy an inch of time." This is the gold I traded my time for. This is the feeling when the pride and a sense of accomplishment in a virtual world collide with the frustration of real life—that surge of helplessness, loneliness, desolation, confusion, and numbness. I wish I wasn't that all-powerful overlord of Los Santos who slaughters everything in sight. I wish I was just an ordinary person. Being an ordinary person is no easy task. If you think what I'm saying is absurd and meaningless, then go out onto the streets of Los Santos and ask the pedestrians, my friend. Ask them about their life expectancy, ask them if their personal cars are still in one piece. Of course, my friend, you could also turn off your PC, go out on the street and ask the strangers passing you by, chat with an Uber driver, and ask them what they're hustling for, why they feel like life is worse than death, and what life means to them.

translation_en: 960 hours in. I was actually planning to drag it out to a thousand hours, hit 100 million, take a nice screenshot, and leave Los Santos with no regrets. But suddenly, this wave of loneliness grabbed me. From playing solo, to playing with three people, down to two, and back to solo again. Every day repeating the same heists with routines I know by heart, self-absorbed in those just-right, picture-perfect moments. I really can't take it anymore. Carrying noobs, beefing, sourcing cargo, stealing cars, grinding heists—everything has just become completely meaningless. I know it's time to go, but I can't bear to let go. I want to linger here and look at my assets scattered across the map. Sure, the interaction is pitifully little, but just looking at it makes me content. That's my love letter to GTA. The actual useful info is below. I know most people have the habit of reading negative reviews to buy a game, while positive ones are mostly about nostalgia that leaves newbies totally clueless. So, let me add just a few tips. Roughly 1/3 of public sessions in GTA 5 are God-mode cheaters, so don't be too hostile to others. But some lawless human beings will attack indiscriminately, and you can't start missions, source goods, or sell cargo without being in a public session. That's why the magical solo-public lobby trick exists. Just like it sounds, to glitch into a solo public session: press Alt+Enter to window the screen, then Ctrl+Alt+Delete to bring up Task Manager. Right-click the top window bar, hold it for about 10 seconds, then left-click back onto the screen, and you'll be all alone in the session. Without money, you get zero gaming experience. Ignore any NPCs who call you. The Premium Edition gives you an office and a million. The Karin Kuruma (Armored) is an absolute must-buy, otherwise you won't even be able to beat NPCs. After that, you can grind the "Blow Up III" contact mission repeatedly to make money, or run CEO Headhunter—though there might not be any better choices. Hard-grind up to 2.2 million to buy the Kosatka; this has the highest priority. Once you buy the Kosatka, search YouTube/Bilibili for "Hanmufang"—if his tutorials don't teach you, I lose. Then you'll have the ability to print infinite money. After that, you can buy whatever you want while playing through other heists. This period is the most fun, the self-growth stage. Then, when you realize there are no missions on the map you haven't played, no corners of the map your footprints haven't touched, you've pretty much entered retirement mode. If you make a bit of money on Cayo Perico and then don't want to grind it anymore, you can also search up "Don't Fuck with Dre" (obsoleted now, look it up if you're interested). If you don't want to run across the map, search how to do job teleports. Once you mod/hack, the game gets boring as hell, though it's worth noting that modding is pretty much risk-free as long as you don't spawn money. Offline and online are completely different, basically two separate games. I suggest finishing the offline story first. Nothing more to say, I gotta go study microcontrollers. Hope you have fun in Los Santos. As for me, I'm heading out first! I'm still "alive" though, feel free to leave a comment if you have questions.

Though I guess at the end of the day, it'll just mean we players who stick to genuine copies take a total loss for nothing, just like what happened with the 2018 WeGame version of Monster Hunter: World. The game got pulled from the store, a bunch of players trying to support domestic industries insisted on not getting refunds, and in the end the money just got swallowed by Tencent, while probably getting thoroughly mocked by some real-life piracy-defending elitist assholes. Gaming belongs to the ninth art. Any masterpiece of a game inherently embodies the author's ideas and philosophy. Amidst the collision and blending of various ideological cultures, foreign reflections on the future and all sorts of bizarre fantasies are simply unacceptable to the SARFT and the Ministry of Culture. But hey, if the bureaus won't accept it, the real question is whether the gamers can accept it? As things stand right now, due to all sorts of factors surrounding Steam and consoles, domestic games can still rake in a mountain of cash by putting out total garbage. They know that as long as the game's quality is barely passable, and they design some "micro-operations" so players can flex, alongside all sorts of horny character art, and cringe-ass character models and dialogue, they can trick people out of their money. The plot of the game itself has to be absolute nonsense, completely lacking in depth, superficial and easy to understand. It's best if they stir up a ton of drama, good and bad alike, just to cause a public outcry—take *Tower of Fantasy* as a classic example, you guys must have eaten up all that gossip, right? At the same time, pump out some ads and run a promo campaign. Production like that makes way more money than a game where you actually sit down and seriously craft a plot. Even though a lot of people in China seem to know about Steam now, back before *PUBG* came out, you could walk down the street and barely anyone had even heard of Steam. Actually, China's real-name verification system is already way ahead of foreign countries; both UnionPay and WeChat Pay require an ID card, so why the hell haven't they rolled out a rating system yet? Foreign rating systems are agreements between major gaming companies. If that were brought to China, well, what's the first company that comes to mind? Tencent? NetEase? You know what I mean by how greedy those fuckers are. And right now, the Ministry of Culture and the SARFT hold absolute veto power over whether something gets approved, with zero relevant laws or regulations actually determining if a game passes censorship or not. There was this domestic single-player game developer once that made a Wuxia game and submitted it for review. Since they were a domestic studio, they knew the censorship system inside and out, so before submitting it they stripped out all the blood and dismemberment effects, and turned all the corpses black. But even then it still failed censorship because the review board said that after the player-controlled character kills someone, having them serve a ten-day prison sentence could easily cause negative social impacts. Later on, through round after round of modifications, it eventually turned into a Wuxia game where all you could do was ride horses. Meanwhile, in Tencent's *Moonlight Blade*, after you slaughter human enemies you don't have to face a single consequence, you can just keep right on massacring them. Doesn't that cause an even bigger negative social impact? Yet *Moonlight Blade* got approved. Why does this happen? Tencent is raking in millions every day, they can afford the fees, they can keep trial-and-erroring forever, whereas that small studio had practically no money left after finishing the game and just flat-out died on the spot. So the development of Chinese single-player games isn't about how good your production standards are, nor is it about whether your marketing hits the mark; it's about whether you can afford to pay off the right people first. The original intent of the damn Great Firewall was good—it was meant to block the export of Western ideology, consolidate public opinion dominance, and reduce the invasion of harmful culture. But unreasonable policies have made it hard for domestic games to develop. And precisely because of this reason, a lot of people just take this shit for granted—whether it's blocking foreign websites, censoring games, *Baozou Dashijian*, or the current Steam China version, or being fed a bowl of lukewarm shit by WeGame and various mainland-released home consoles. So many things have been castrated, banned, and wiped out: *StarCraft II* easter eggs, *PUBG's* blood color, that *other game 5* content, Bilibili's philosophy section, plus *World of Warcraft*, *Baozou Dashijian*, and all that other stuff. So much, so much of it, and we can never go back. In our memories, they left behind a brilliant and dazzling mark, because these are the things we love and cherish. They say they want to maintain the online environment, but do they know how we feel? Do they understand our pain?! Now that I think about it carefully, has the purpose of the Firewall strayed from its original design? The Wall was meant to block corrupt culture, but now, it also blocks out excellent games, allowing certain corrupt domestic capitalists to un-fucking-abashedly suck the blood of every single gamer. The Wall has been weaponized by certain people to reap exorbitant profits, and this country's gaming market has been turned by certain groups into a breeding ground for corruption. Policies desperately need to be reformed, or there will be endless trouble down the line. I know saying all this is probably nine times out of ten useless, just consider me venting. Some things have been bottled up for too long, and if I don't say it, my chest feels heavy. As an ordinary gamer, I love Steam, I love the joy Steam brings. A one-size-fits-all ban is quick, but it treats the symptoms rather than the disease. It's about time China's gaming industry policies were reformed. Lots of us just silently take the abuse and endure it. When they blocked foreign websites and censored games, we complied. And what was the result? Facebook, Twitter, and Google got replaced domestically by Tencent, Baidu, and shit like that. Now those giant corporations have occupied massive territories of the domestic gaming industry. Following WeGame, Perfect World, and the fake Steam platform, now the official Steam China version is about to drop. I'm sure you can all imagine just how fucking hideous Steam China's greedy mug is going to be. ------ Reposted from the internet
