translation_en: A friendly suggestion to China: The internet is full of games that scam elementary school kids out of their allowance, and you don't crack down on them. Web pages everywhere have ads with broken Mandarin, and you don't crack down on them. Games with official websites selling hacks, and you don't crack down on them. You're cracking down on AAA games? Violence? Pornography? Look at the images in web ads all over the country; every single one is more exposed than Steam, yet you don't care at all, and instead you mess with Steam. If you have so much time and leisure, why don't you do something about the Chinese film industry? It's more deformed than Lu Benwei. Look at your CCTV, then look at other countries' BBC—what a gap. The cultural confidence you built up yourselves has been stomped back down by yourselves. Why? Because instead of reforming your own management methods, you drag a massive platform down into the mud with you. Even though many Chinese gamers just use Steam as a game launcher, at least it gave people a sense of copyright awareness. Just as things were finally making a bit of progress, you're going to beat us back to square one. Are you encouraging everyone to play pirated games? Not even talking about so-called democracy, why can't there be a rating system? A rating system could solve most of these issues. Is this fun for you? You "experts" are seriously big-brained. Everyday you pull this useless shit—why don't you just cancel the internet altogether, and make it so normal people aren't allowed to use it? Organise some slogan-shanting and go farming every day??? Or just go straight back to primitive society. What I genuinely care about is if the games I bought become unplayable, who am I going to ask for a refund? Perfect World, or the state? But I guess in the end, it'll just mean we players who insist on buying legitimate copies take a total loss, and then we'll get mocked hard by some smug bastards who play pirated games in real life. Big-brained indeed. "Amazing, my country," haha. Emperor Qin, this prosperous era is just as you wished. Some people and their friends grew up playing Legend and CS back in the day, and none of them went around hacking, slashing, and committing crimes. Nowadays, bratty kids watch Pleasant Goat and try to roast other kids—is that really the fault of games and anime, or is it the fault of irresponsible parenting and schooling? Everyone knows the truth in their hearts. Have you abandoned the goal of sticking to socialism for 100 years like this? What is the Chinese Dream? Study hard, get the fuck out of the country. Gaming belongs to the ninth art. Every major masterpiece inherently contains the author's thoughts and philosophy. But given our country's currently closed-off values, foreign reflections on the future and bizarre fantasies simply cannot be accepted by the SARFT. As for domestic games right now—due to various factors involving Steam and consoles—you can still make a ton of cash just by making garbage. They know that as long as game quality is barely passable, and they design a bit of "micro-manipulation" to flex with, along with all sorts of horny character art, and all kinds of chuunibyou modeling and dialogue, they can scam people out of money. The game's plot has to be nonsense, without any depth; it needs to be shallow and easy to understand. Productions like this make way more money than games where you seriously think about the plot and gameplay. Steam might seem well-known in China now, but honestly, before PUBG came out, if you walked down the street basically nobody knew what Steam was. In fact, real-name verification in China is already ahead of foreign countries; UnionPay and WeChat Pay both require an ID card. So why is there still no sign of a game rating system? Because right now, whether something passes censorship is entirely up to the Ministry of Culture and the SARFT—there are no relevant laws or regulations to decide whether a game passes review. There used to be a domestic single-player game developer that made a wuxia game and submitted it for review. Because they were a domestic developer, they knew the censorship system inside out, so before submitting it they removed blood and dismemberment effects, and all corpses turned black. But even then it couldn't pass. The censors said that the player character in this game could just serve ten days in prison after killing someone, which would easily cause a bad social impact. Later, through endless revisions, it basically turned into a wuxia game where you can only ride horses. Meanwhile, Tencent's *Moonlight Blade* has zero consequences after killing human enemies; you can just keep on slaughtering. Doesn't that cause an even bigger social impact? Yet *Moonlight Blade* passed review. Why does this happen? Tencent makes a fortune every single day; they can afford to pay up, whereas that small developer had pretty much no money left after finishing the game. Therefore, the development of Chinese single-player games isn't about how good your production standards are, nor is it about whether your marketing is on point—it's about whether you can afford to pay the fees first. And what do the relevant Chinese departments claim their basis is during censorship? It's the so-called mainstream ideology of society, the core socialist values. What does this kind of thing resemble? Ancient monarchs would always find a statement consistent with legal authority for their power: the Mandate of Heaven, "I am the True Dragon and Son of Heaven, all my power is bestowed by the heavens." And the core socialist values serve this exact same purpose as a tool—giving their illegitimate, legally unjustified power and acquired benefits a seemingly reasonable pretext. Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Macao are Special Administrative Regions; their social, economic, political, and cultural systems are all different from the mainland. Has everyone ever thought about why that is? Actually, it's very simple: the crying baby gets the milk. Take Hong Kong, for example—if they had been under the mainland system when they were handed back in '97, they would have had massive strikes and student boycotts, bringing the normal operation of society to a halt. Plus, there were many eyes at home and abroad watching Hong Kong at the time, which is why they are a Special Administrative Region. And what about us mainlanders? When they blocked the foreign internet, we endured it. When they censored *World of Warcraft*, we endured it again. We have never once spoken out for our own rights and interests. And now they are stepping it up even further—the Steam China version is about to come out. At best, it'll just be a Chinese-version store where the current Mainland region's payment methods and low-price regional discounts get transferred over. If we silently endure this time too, then what about after? I'm afraid we're going to turn into North Korea's Kwangmyong network. Many people treat these things as if they're only natural—whether it's blocking the foreign internet, censoring games, *Baozou Dashijian*, or now the Steam China version. But what are the facts? Europe has terrorist activities happening on Instagram and Twitter, but did they just simply build a firewall to block these social media apps? No, they fought a cyber war against those terrorists and drove them off those platforms. If they can do that, why can't the CCP? Is it just because building a firewall is cheaper? Are our rights and our spaces for entertainment and relaxation worth less than the cost of fighting a cyber war? Do Chinese people just have to compromise and swallow their anger while foreigners get to protect their rights? Please spread these words far and wide. Speak up for your rights and for Steam! I don't know which kind of "being represented" is better: is it the kind they talk about when they censor and ban *World of Warcraft*, *Baozou Dashijian*, and other free media, social apps, and single-player online games—claiming it's the will of the people and gamers? Or is what I'm posting today representing the interests of Steam players? But I know that everything I'm saying comes from the bottom of my heart, straight from the soul, spoken with a mixed bag of emotions after going through all this bullshit. I'm speaking with a clear conscience, whereas they aren't necessarily doing the same. I hope everyone spreads these words. I know it's nine-tenths likely to be useless, but how can one not cry out just because their voice is small? As an ordinary resident living in China, who loves Steam and loves the joy Steam brings, this is all I can do. Thank you everyone. Actually, being a docile subject has zero benefits and only drawbacks. Because if you show obedience, the amount of things they need to provide you with becomes even less—once you've expressed submission, why would they give a damn about your needs? As for so-called rioters, the regime has to provide a lot more just to maintain its rule and appease the public. That's just how it is domestically: when they blocked the foreign internet and censored games, we submitted, and what was the result? Now the Steam China version is about to drop, because they assume that since you submitted before, you'll just keep submitting no matter what. Whenever I think about the First Amendment of the United States and how Steam, as a platform of free speech, allows me to speak out here, while the CCP is rolling out a Steam China version to take all of that away, I am filled with a whirlwind of emotions. Honestly, the things I want when I speak out aren't much. I'm not delusional enough to think that capitalism will magically make life better or anything; you still have to put in the work yourself, you still have to grind for a dozen years to buy a house and a car. All I want are fewer restrictions and controls, and for the government to respect the rights of citizens. But even something as simple as that is so hard to come by. A hundred years ago in Beijing, Qing dynasty subjects helped foreigners scale the ladder to climb over the wall; a hundred years later today, foreigners are helping Chinese people scale the ladder to climb over the wall. translation_en: A friendly suggestion to China: the internet is full of games that scam kids out of their money and walk away, and you don't crack down on them. Webpages full of games with awkward Mandarin pop up everywhere, and you don't crack down on them. Games that sell hacks right on their official websites, and you don't crack down on them. But you're cracking down on AAA games? Violence? Porn? Look at the ads plastered all over Chinese websites—every single one of them is more exposed than anything on STEAM, and you don't give a damn, yet you come after STEAM. If you have so much time to spare, why don't you manage the Chinese film industry? It's more deformed than Lu Benwei. Look at your CCTV, then look at the BBC. What a gap. You crush the cultural confidence you built up all by yourselves. Why? Instead of reforming your own management methods, you drag a massive platform down into the mud with you. Even though many Chinese players just treat STEAM as a game launcher, at least it gave people some awareness of buying genuine games. Just when we're finally making some progress, you're about to beat us back to square one. Are you encouraging people to play pirated games? Not even talking about so-called democracy, why can't you just implement a rating system? A rating system could solve most of these problems. Is this fun for you? You "experts" are truly fucking brilliant. Every day you pull this useless shit—why don't you just ban the internet altogether and stop letting normal people use it? Organise some rallies to shout slogans and farm fields every day?! Or just straight up regress back to primitive society. What I actually care about is that if the games I bought become unplayable, who the fuck am I supposed to ask for compensation? Perfect World, or the state? But at the end of the day, it'll probably just mean us players who insist on buying genuine games take a total loss, only to be thoroughly mocked by some real-life piracy-loving elitist assholes. Brilliant. Fucking awesome, my country, haha. Emperor Qin, this prosperous age is just as you wished. Some people and their friends grew up playing Legend of Mir and CS when they were kids, and none of them went around hacking, slashing, and committing crimes. Nowadays, some brat watches Pleasant Goat and tries to roast other kids—is it really the fault of games and anime, or is it the fault of irresponsible parenting and schooling? Deep down, everyone knows the truth. Have you just abandoned the goal of upholding socialism for 100 years like this? What even is the Chinese Dream? Study hard, get the fuck out of China. Gaming belongs to the ninth art. Any major masterpiece of a game inherently contains the thoughts and philosophy of its creator. But given our country's currently closed-off values, foreign reflections on the future and their wild, countless fantasies are simply unacceptable to the National Radio and Television Administration. As things stand, between STEAM and console restrictions, domestic Chinese game developers can still rake in a fortune just by making utter garbage. They know that as long as the game's quality is barely passable, and they design a few flashy, show-off "micro-operations" inside the game, along with all sorts of lewd character art and cringe-inducing character models and lines, they can scam people out of their money. The plot of the game itself has to be nonsense—it can't have any depth; it has to be shallow and easy to understand. Productions like that actually make way more money than games where you genuinely put effort into the story and development. Even though STEAM seems to have a lot of awareness in China now, before PUBG came out, if you walked down the street, hardly anyone even knew what STEAM was. In fact, real-name verification in China is already way ahead of foreign countries. Both UnionPay and WeChat Pay require an ID card, so why haven't they rolled out a rating system yet? Because right now, whether something passes censorship is entirely up to the ultimate discretion of the Ministry of Culture and the NRTA. There are no actual laws or regulations that determine whether a game passes review. Back in the day, a domestic single-player game developer made a wuxia game and submitted it for review. Since they were a domestic developer, they knew the censorship mechanism inside out, so before submitting it, they removed all the blood and dismemberment effects, and turned all the corpses black. But even then, it still failed the review. The censors said that the player character in this game killing someone and only serving ten days in prison could easily cause a negative social impact. Later on, after endless revisions, it basically turned into a wuxia game where you can only ride horses. Meanwhile, Tencent's Moonlight Blade lets you slaughter humanoid enemies without facing a single consequence, letting you just keep on massacring. Doesn't that cause a much worse social impact? Yet Moonlight Blade passed review. Why does this happen? Tencent makes a daily fortune; they can afford to pay up. That small developer didn't have much money left after finishing the game. So the development of Chinese single-player games isn't about your production standards, nor is it about whether your marketing is on point—it’s about whether you can afford to pay the bribe first. And what do the relevant Chinese departments claim their basis is when reviewing? It’s so-called "mainstream social values." It’s "core socialist values." What does this kind of thing feel like? Ancient monarchs would always find a statement that sounded legally and theologically sound to justify their power: the Divine Right of Kings, "I am the Son of Heaven, and all my power is bestowed upon me by the heavens." And the core socialist values just act as a tool for this exact purpose—giving their illegitimate, legally baseless power and acquired benefits a seemingly reasonable pretext. Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Macau are Special Administrative Regions. Their social, economic, political, and cultural systems are completely different from the mainland. Has anyone ever thought about why that is? Actually, it’s very simple: the crying baby gets the milk. Take Hong Kong, for example. If they had been handed the mainland system when they were handed back in '97, they would have launched massive strikes and boycotts, bringing society's normal operations to a halt. Plus, there were many eyes both at home and abroad watching Hong Kong back then, which is why they are a Special Administrative Region. And what about us mainlanders? When they blocked the foreign internet, we endured it. When they censored World of Warcraft, we endured that too. We have never once spoken up for our own rights. And now it’s getting worse and worse. The China version of STEAM is about to drop. The best-case scenario is that we just get a Chinese storefront, and all the existing mainland payment methods and low-price region perks get transferred over to it. If we silently endure this time as well, what happens after that? Are we just going to turn into North Korea's Kwangmyong network? A lot of people treat all these things as if they're completely natural—whether it's blocking the foreign internet, censoring games, *Baozou Dashiji*, or now the STEAM China version. But what are the facts? Europe has terrorists operating on Instagram and Twitter. Did they simply build a firewall and block these social media apps? No, they fought a cyber war against those terrorists and drove them off those social media platforms. If they can do that, why can the CCP not do the same? Just because building a wall is cheaper? Are our rights and our places for entertainment and leisure worth less than the cost of fighting a cyber war? Do Chinese people just have to compromise and swallow their anger while foreigners get to protect their rights? Please spread these words far and wide. Speak up for your rights and for STEAM. I don't know which kind of "representation" is better: the one they talk about when they ban and censor World of Warcraft, *Baozou Dashiji*, and other free media, social apps, and online/offline games, claiming it's the will of the people and the players; or the things I'm posting today, which actually represent the interests of STEAM players. But I know that everything I'm saying comes from the bottom of my heart. It's heartfelt, spoken with a complex mix of emotions after experiencing all of this. I am speaking with a clear conscience, whereas they might not be. I hope everyone spreads these words. I know that nine times out of ten it won't do shit, but how can you refuse to cry out just because your voice is small? As an ordinary resident living in China who loves STEAM and loves the happiness STEAM brings, this is all I can do. Thank you, everyone. Actually, being a docile subject has zero benefits and only drawbacks. Because if you show obedience, the things they need to provide you with become even fewer. Since you’ve already expressed total submission, why would they give a shit about your demands? On the other hand, the so-called "rioters"—for the sake of their own rule and to appease the masses, the things they end up providing are bound to be much more. You see this all the time domestically: when they blocked the foreign internet and censored games, we complied. And the result? Now STEAM China is about to drop, because since you submitted before, they figured that if they launch it, they launch it, because you'll just keep on submitting. Whenever I think about the First Amendment of the United States and how STEAM provides a platform of free speech that allows me to speak out here, while the CCP is about to roll out STEAM China and strip all of that away, I get a wave of mixed emotions. Honestly, the things I want by speaking out aren't much. I'm not delusional enough to think life will magically get better under capitalism; you still have to work hard yourself, you still have to grind for a dozen years just to afford a house and a car. All I want are fewer restrictions and controls, and for the government to respect the rights of its citizens. But even something as simple as that is so fucking hard. A hundred years ago in Beijing, Qing dynasty subjects helped foreigners set up ladders to scale the walls; a hundred years from now—wait, a hundred years later today, foreigners are helping Chinese people set up ladders to scale the wall. *(Let this post spread far and wide)*

translation_en: Actually, writing this review makes me a bit conflicted. First, because I used a cheat once back when I first started playing (on my previous account). I was level 35, had nothing, and just cheated in some cash, and ended up getting banned. Honestly, I'm a bit ashamed of that. Second, the game price dropped to 112 RMB the very second day I bought it... which feels kind of unfriendly. Anyway, figuring I've played around 500-600 hours (total), I'll write a guide for new players! Don't end up running around like a headless chicken like I did when I first started. When you first enter the game, use Quick Job via your phone. After that, you can steal a car or rob a store. When you have a job available, you'll automatically teleport into the session, saving you from having to dodge the cops. For jobs, you can do more races. Heists might be a bit too hard for you when you're just starting out, so you can do some PVP or racing—you still get a decent payout even if you lose. Once you have some cash, don't go buying guns (if you really want one, an SMG is a decent choice). When you've gained some experience, you can start doing heists. Note that before doing a heist, you can go to a store and buy some snacks, and use the M key to open your inventory and eat them to heal when necessary. (Body armor is optional because your level isn't high enough right now, buying it won't do much good.) The most important thing for you in a heist crew is not to die, because dying might drag your teammates down. When you're playing, just follow behind the others, don't stress too much about your kill count, and try not to die more than twice per heist, otherwise it's a restart. Once you have some money, don't go buying garages and cars. Don't buy any apartment under 200k, they're useless. Save up to buy a 200k apartment, the kind that lets you host heists. This is when your first heist is coming up. Don't rush to accept it. Join a GTA V Discord/group and find a high-level player willing to carry a noob. They usually don't take a cut, so you can set your cut to the maximum. Passing this mission for the first time gives an extra bonus, so you'll get around 300k once you finish it. At this point, don't get all excited with that much money and blow it all on impulse. You urgently need to do the next mission, the Prison Break. The finale of this mission is a bit tricky. Go to a group and look for a veteran who can do the Kuruma glitch (the Kuruma is a car, I'll mention it later). Of course, this is a 4-player heist, so finding someone who doesn't take a cut isn't that easy (though it's best if you can). Once you finish this mission, combined with your previous cash, you'll have around 500k to 600k. At this point, you have two choices: First: Buy the ultimate mission vehicle, the Armored Kuruma, priced at 520k. Second: Buy the Duke O'Death, priced around 660k to 670k. The Duke O'Death can block missiles, while the Kuruma can only block bullets, but the Kuruma is faster than the Duke O'Death. For the best value for money, the Kuruma is the way to go. Now, go back to doing heists. Things get a lot easier once you have a Kuruma. Knock out the Humane Labs Raid and Series A Funding real quick. For the Pacific Standard, just like I said, try to find a veteran for every finale and see if they want a cut. By the time you finish the Pacific Standard, you'll have close to 2 million. Don't rush to buy a facility to do Doomsday. Doomsday is brutal (unless you have 2-3 experienced veterans who are pros and on call, do not attempt it lightly). In my opinion, this is when you should buy a bunker—buy the most expensive one you can afford, meaning within 2 million. After that, buy supplies to fill up your stock. Don't start doing research right away, worry about that later. Once your stock is full, only sell to Los Santos. Oh yeah, by this point your stock will require multiple vehicles, so you'll need a few good buddies (this game proves that having good friends is the most important thing). If you successfully deliver everything in one go, 2 million is easily in your pocket. Do this a few times until you hit 10 million. Also, bunker supplies generate kind of slowly, so I suggest doing missions in the meantime. By this time you'll be around level 70-80. You can go buy some cars, an office, or a hangar to keep doing cargo and import/export missions. (Nightclubs are not recommended, I feel like they don't make much money.) At this point, you're no longer the clueless noob you used to be. You can even host lobbies and carry other noobs in groups, and you might even see your own shadow in some of those fresh players (though honestly, making money in GTA V is kinda...). translation_en: Leaving aside offline mode, here are my thoughts on the online environment as a player with 1000+ hours. First off, as a completely legit player who has never cheated, I gotta say that modding money is actually fine because in-game items are way too expensive! If you think getting money will get you banned, just look at the god-mode griefers blowing up sessions, and you'll realize money drops are really nothing. Plus, if you're the kind of player who likes to grind honestly, you might as well mod yourself 100 million. Why? Because first you need an office, a biker clubhouse, a facility, a bunker, and a night club. And I'm not even talking about office garages and warehouses (by office garages here I mean vehicle cargo warehouses, not your private car parking), plus the biker counterfeit cash factory, weed farm, meth lab, etc.—I won't list them all. If you want to experience all this content, don't you need modded money? You basically have to buy all of it to truly experience the game. At this point, some people will say "just do heists." You gotta know that unless you have a fixed crew, you'd better stay away from random matchmaking. If you host yourself, you'll spend two hours matching and five minutes playing. The endless quick-restart loading screens during missions will also slowly drive you insane. So to sum it up, modding 100 million really isn't a big deal. To be honest, I modded money too, but I don't advocate doing it too early. If you've just started playing, don't mod money yet; you should experience the various jobs and missions first. Wait until you feel like grinding missions no longer covers what you need, and then consider modding money. Take me for example, I only modded money after level 60. I still remember the feeling of grinding missions with my bare hands without any help, saving up over 1 million to buy my first armed vehicle, the Buzzard, and showing it off to my friends. And what about level? Since the money is modded, you don't need to mod your level. You still want to work hard for something yourself, right? Next up, let's talk about cheaters. Whether you cheat or not is your own business and I can't control you, but I'm begging you cheaters, please don't ruin the normal game experience for other players, alright? I don't object to you cheating, but I seriously don't get it when you use cheats to trap people in cages or blow up the session. We're all just playing a game, can't you guys be a bit friendlier and help out new players or those who need a hand? You get the joy of helping others, and you make friends from all over the world, what's not to like? Of course, there's another type of player. They don't cheat, but they're pros at ruining other people's game experience. These are the sweaty tryhards. They only care about one thing in public sessions: killing players! They probably think this game is some kind of competitive esports title. Every time they kill a player, they get a high that lasts for ages. That's my summary of the current online environment. Of course, there are good players too. They're helpful, have a great attitude towards noobs, and won't just abandon you if you don't know how to do something; they'll patiently teach you what to watch out for in the game and how things work. If you run into a player like this, don't let them go—hold onto them for dear life. After all, players like that are rare, practically an endangered species. Seriously, in this game, it's really hard to find a peaceful lobby where everyone is friendly and helps each other out! Either the bottom left corner is spammed with who killed whom, or the right side is spammed with money drop ads, or people are screaming at each other in chat. Anyway, if you want to sell cargo or source cars in a public lobby, you can only resort to lagging yourself into a solo public session. These are my thoughts on public online sessions as a 1000+ hour player. If you ask me how I usually play, it's pretty simple: I just chill in invite-only sessions, fly planes to check out the beautiful scenery of Los Santos, drive cars down country roads to soak in that mountain vibe, or hit the highway and feel the thrill of speed. Occasionally I'll hop into someone else's mission to have some fun. As for public sessions... well, let's just say the only time I go into a public session is when I'm completely by myself. And the only reason to enter a public session is to sell cargo and source cars. Hey, what can I say, I'm just a peaceful player.

translation_en: Today I finally decided to retire. After playing for over 5 years, this game is a total time thief! (Half in a good way, half in a bad way). Lately, with the mod restrictions and all, the reputation hasn't been great. Honestly, if you don't have friends to play with, I wouldn't recommend the online mode if you're buying it now. I'll write more about that in detail below. If you're only gonna play offline, I think the story is satisfying enough for a single player! I don't remember much anymore, but the story alone is probably around 30 hours, and with completionist stuff you can get 60 hours or more out of it. Besides the fact that playing it yourself makes advancing the story more fun than just watching it on a let's-play, it's got close to 30 hours of content. So even if you think "it's a bit much to pay full price just for offline...", you might want to consider picking it up on sale. Now, this review is mainly about the online mode. And it's not a review of recent events, but a look back across 5 years of playing. Like I said at the start, the online mode in this game is probably mind-numbingly boring unless you have friends or someone to play with. I honestly feel like there are zero beginners who play solo for years. That's because when you're low rank, you've got weapon restrictions, no way to make money, low stats, insanely priced cars and properties, griefers, etc... Without at least a mid-ranked player showing you the ropes, it's pretty much unplayable. On the flip side, if you do have friends to play with, most of these issues easily sort themselves out as you go. If you get hooked, you can easily play for 1,000 or 3,000 hours (including the time you spend playing solo). As for the online content itself, I'm sure other people have reviewed it in detail so I'll skip it. Up to this point, the review is for people considering buying the game. From here on out, it's an online review that's probably a bit biased, so if you're thinking of buying it, this part probably won't be very useful. Over 5 years, I've played with all sorts of people. Survival, deathmatches, heists, and all that—overall, it was so fun I lost track of time! It's definitely a game that's super fun when you're messing around and having a blast with friends. A time thief in a good way, for sure. However, as much as I played with friends, I also played alone a lot. As other reviews point out, whether you're solo or in a crew, most of the money-making methods in this game feel like absolute grinding chores if you don't pay-to-win. Despite that, prices are through the roof, and unless you spend hours and hours grinding for cash, you'll never get the vehicles or properties you want. I think I have a higher tolerance for that kind of tedious grind than the average person, but it breaks your spirit whether you're solo or even in a crew. This cycle of stopping playing for a while because of that, and then coming back to it after a long time, was pretty much the standard for me. No matter what method you use, this part of the time spent is abso-fucking-lutely miserable. A time thief in a bad way. There's another issue you just can't ignore. Honestly, I don't really want to write about past events here now, but I really wish they hadn't balanced the in-game economy around the absurd amounts of money floating around when cheating (not just glitches) was rampant. The cheaters got what they wanted and stopped playing, honest players got stuck with ridiculous market prices, and the devs ended up losing those honest players. I still think it was a choice where nobody except cheaters won. From that point on, it became a game where only cheaters, massive whales, or absolute no-lifes could keep playing continuously. While cheaters are to blame for starting the whole thing, the devs are also heavily at fault for completely fumbling how they handle punishments, including this recent mod situation. I'm not playing anymore, but I hope false bans on honest players decrease from here on out. Even though this review sounds mostly negative overall, there were actually a lot of fun times. They'd occasionally hand out bonus cash or run sales, so I spent 5 years playing with various people with the mindset of "it's fun when you play it every once in a while." Because of that, it's hard to put into words what specifically was fun, but I hope it gets across that playing with a crew is the best part of online. I bought both the PS3 and PC versions, but I still feel like I got way more than my money's worth out of it! It really lives up to being the number one game in the world, I think. Even so, I've decided to hang up my boots today. It was the most fun I've had in the 5 years, a fitting and super enjoyable finale, and I'm totally satisfied. If a sequel ever comes out, I'd strongly want to play it. That's about it. Thanks for reading.

translation_en: A friendly suggestion to China: The internet is full of games that fleece kids for their money and then disappear, yet you do nothing. Web ads for games filled with dodgy Mandarin are everywhere, yet you do nothing. Games with official websites selling hacks, yet you do nothing. But you crack down on AAA games? Violence? Porn? Look at all the skin-baring ads on domestic websites, every single one of them more exposed than anything on STEAM. You don't manage any of that, but you come after STEAM. If you've got so much time on your hands, why don't you manage the Chinese film industry? It's even more deformed than Lu Benwei. Look at your CCTV, then look at the BBC. The gap is massive. You step on and crush the cultural confidence you built up yourselves. Why? Instead of reforming your own management style, you drag a major platform down with you. Even though many Chinese players just use STEAM as a game launcher, it at least gave everyone a sense of copyright awareness. Just as things are finally making some progress, you're about to drive us back to square one. What, you're encouraging people to pirate games? Never mind about so-called democracy, why can't you just implement a rating system? A rating system would solve most of these issues. Is this fun for you? You "experts" are seriously retarded. Every day you pull this useless crap, why don't you just ban the internet altogether and stop letting normal people use it? Organise some slogans and go farming all day long??? Or just straight up regress back to primitive society. What I actually care about is if the games I bought become unplayable, who do I go to for compensation? Perfect World, or the state? But I guess it'll just end up with us players who stick to genuine copies taking a total loss, only to be thoroughly mocked by smug pirates in real life. Retarded. Awesome job, my country, haha. Emperor Qin, this prosperous age is just as you wished. Some people and their friends grew up playing Legend of Mir and CS as kids, and none of them went around hacking, slashing, or breaking the law. Nowadays, brats watch Pleasant Goat and roast other kids—is that really the fault of games and anime? Or is it the fault of irresponsible parenting and schooling? Everyone knows the truth. Is this really how you stray from the goal of upholding socialism for 100 years? What is the Chinese Dream? Study hard, get the fuck out of the country. Games belong to the ninth art. Any masterpiece of a game inherently embodies the author's ideology and philosophy. But given China's currently closed-off values, foreign reflections on the future and diverse, bizarre fantasies are simply unacceptable to the State Administration of Radio and Television (SARFT). As for domestic games right now, factoring in STEAM and consoles, you can still make a ton of money just by making garbage. They know that as long as the game's quality is barely passable, and they design some flashy "micro-operation" mechanics for flexing, along with all sorts of lewd character art and cringe-inducing character models and lines, they can scam people out of cash. The plot of the game itself has to be nonsense—it can't have any depth; it has to be simple and easy to understand. Productions like that make way more money than a game where you actually put serious thought into the story. Before PUBG blew up, even though a lot of people in China seemed to know about STEAM, if you walked down the street, hardly anyone actually knew what it was. In reality, China's real-name verification system is already ahead of foreign countries; UnionPay and WeChat Pay both require a national ID card. So why is there still such a long delay in introducing a rating system? Because currently, the power to decide whether culture passes review rests entirely with the Ministry of Culture and SARFT. There are no relevant laws or regulations to determine whether a game passes review or not. Back then, a domestic single-player game developer made a Wuxia game and submitted it for review. Since they were a domestic developer, they knew the censorship mechanism inside and out. Before submitting, they removed blood and dismemberment effects, and turned all the corpses black. Even so, it still failed the review. The censorship body said that the player character in this game could just serve ten days in prison after killing someone, which could easily cause a negative social impact. Later on, after endless revisions, it turned into a Wuxia game where you could only ride horses. Meanwhile, Tencent's Moonlight Blade lets you slaughter human enemies without facing any consequences whatsoever, you just keep right on butchering. Doesn't that cause an even bigger social impact? Yet Moonlight Blade passed review. Why does this happen? Tencent rakes in cash by the day, they can afford to pay the bribes, whereas that small developer had basically no money left after finishing the game. So the development of Chinese single-player games isn't about your production standards, nor is it about whether your marketing hits the mark—it's about whether you can afford to pay up first. And what do the relevant Chinese authorities claim their basis is during censorship? It's the so-called social mainstream, the core socialist values. What does this kind of thing resemble? Ancient monarchs would always find a statement that sounded legally and theoretically sound to justify their power: the divine right of kings, "I am the True Dragon and Son of Heaven, all my power is bestowed upon me by the heavens." And the core socialist values are simply acting as that kind of tool, giving their illegitimate, unlawful power and acquired benefits a seemingly reasonable pretext. Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Macao are special administrative regions; their social, economic, political, and cultural systems are all different from the mainland. Has anyone ever thought about why that's the case? It's actually simple: the squeaking wheel gets the grease. Take Hong Kong, for example—if they had adopted the mainland's system back at the '97 handover, they would have launched massive strikes and school boycotts, bringing normal social operations to a halt. Plus, at the time, many eyes both domestic and international were watching Hong Kong, which is why they are a special administrative region. And what about us mainlanders? When they blocked foreign websites, we endured it. When they censored World of Warcraft, we endured that too. We have never spoken out for our own rights. And now things are getting worse and worse, and a Chinese version of STEAM is about to come out. At best, we'll get a dedicated Chinese store page, and all existing mainland region payment methods and regional pricing discounts will be migrated over to it. If we silently endure this time, what about next time? Are we seriously going to turn into North Korea's Kwangmyongnet? A lot of people take these things for granted—whether it's blocking foreign websites, censoring games, *Baozou Dashiji*, or now the Chinese version of STEAM. But the reality? When Europe has terrorist activities happening on Instagram or Twitter, do they just simply build a firewall and ban these social media apps? No, they wage cyber warfare against those terrorists and drive them off those platforms. If they can do that, why can't the CCP? Is it just because building a firewall is cheaper? Are our rights and our spaces for leisure and entertainment worth less than the cost of waging a cyber war? Do Chinese people just have to compromise and swallow their suffering while foreigners get to protect their rights? Please spread these words far and wide. Speak up for your rights and for STEAM. I don't know which version of "being represented" is better: the one they claimed when they blocked and censored World of Warcraft, *Baozou Dashiji*, and other free media, social apps, and online games—saying it was the will of the people and players—or whether what I'm posting today represents the interests of STEAM players. But I do know that everything I'm saying comes from the bottom of my heart, spoken from genuine inner feelings, with a bitter mix of emotions after experiencing all of this. I am speaking with a clear conscience, whereas they certainly aren't. I hope everyone spreads these words. I know that nine times out of ten it won't do anything, but how can we stay silent just because our voices are small? As an ordinary resident living in China, I love STEAM, and I love the joy STEAM brings me. This is all I can do. Thank you, everyone. Actually, being a docile subject has zero benefits and only drawbacks. Because if you show obedience, the things they need to provide you with become even fewer. If you've already expressed your submission, why would they give a damn about your needs? As for so-called rioters, the government has to provide a lot more in order to maintain its rule and appease the populace. We see this domestically: when they blocked foreign websites and censored games, we complied. And the result? Now a Chinese version of STEAM is about to be forced on us, because since you showed compliance, they figure that if they release it, they release it, because you'll just keep on complying anyway. Whenever I think about the First Amendment of the United States and how STEAM provides a platform for freedom of speech that allows me to speak out here, while the CCP is about to launch the Chinese version of STEAM and take all of that away, a complex mix of emotions hits me. Honestly, what I want by speaking out isn't much. I'm not delusional enough to think life under capitalism is magically better; you still have to grind through your own efforts, still have to slave away for a dozen years just to buy a house and a car. All I want is fewer restrictions and controls, for the government to respect the rights of its citizens. But even something as basic as that is so damn hard. A hundred years ago in Beijing, Qing dynasty subjects were helping foreigners set up ladders to climb over walls, and a hundred years later today, foreigners are helping Chinese people set up ladders to climb over them.

translation_en: To start off, the game's single player campaign is fantastic, absolutely no complaints there. This review is about the online. Rockstar failed miserably at creating an online version of GTA. By introducing the Shark Cards system, they turned the game into Pay to Win. By adding things like Battle Tanks, rocket launchers, and those abominable flying bikes and cars with homing missiles attached to them (WHAT IS THE POINT/NEED FOR THIS?), they gave trolls the perfect weapon to troll and grief. A single player with any of these weapons is capable of trolling an entire lobby, ruining the immersion, the fun, and the enjoyment of the game. But these items are expensive, but wait, back to the Shark Cards, which combined with the trolling tools, create an innovative system never seen before in the gaming industry: Pay to Troll, a system where you swipe your credit card and earn the right to troll and grief other people's gaming experience (something frowned upon in the entire online gaming community, and usually punished by the company itself with automatic kicks from matches, temporary bans, and so on). But we do have a defense against these trolls, which is Passive Mode. HOWEVER, Passive Mode COMPLETELY prevents you from playing, you can't do anything other than walk around the map (though you can still be killed by explosions, NPCs, and other things (yet you can't fight back against any NPCs, because you can't equip any weapons)). Then we have the businesses. Because of Shark Cards, it's extremely difficult and tedious to make money in GTA. Your nightclub loses popularity faster than it gains it while you do the tedious and time-consuming nightclub promotion missions, MC business supplies are extremely expensive and yield little to no profit, and CEO special cargo makes you pay more the more you buy (Yep, only in GTA you pay 2000 for 1 crate, 8000 for 2, or 18000 for 3). Then we also have the best money farm in the game, according to the community itself: The vehicle warehouse. In it, you do 40 missions to deliver 40 cars to YOUR warehouse for YOUR company, with cars that sell for up to 2 million. But does that money go to you? No. You get a maximum of 40k PER car that YOU stole, YOU sold, YOU stored in YOUR warehouse under the name of YOUR company. The rest vanishes. Disappears. Then we have the various missions, where players often quit in the middle of them, screwing over everyone else, who sometimes wasted hours of their own time trying to wait for the mission matchmaking to fill up. Missions that, despite being interesting and fun, pay extremely poorly for the time spent doing them, which causes fewer players to want to play them. Did I mention the absurd loading times? From the moment I click "Launch GTA Online" on Steam, it takes 8 to 12 MINUTES to get into a match. Then you try to join a mission, go through a loading screen to enter the mission LOBBY, and if someone leaves/drops from the lobby while the mission is launching, get ready to wait another 5 minutes for ANOTHER loading screen to get back to the game map (which will probably be different from the previous one). Oh, but I want to play CO-OP with a friend. Cool, first you have to log into the online game (8 to 12 minutes), find your friend on your friends list, and hit Join on their session, which takes another 2 minutes. At this point, you have to go to the Quick Job option (ironic little name), and select to join with friends in the session (No, you can't choose if you have more than one), and hope, almost PRAY, that the game puts both of you in the same match (which, incredibly, doesn't happen as often as it should, and if it doesn't, both of you will end up in DIFFERENT sessions, having to repeat the Join Friend process). With almost 100 hours of GTA ONLINE, you'd expect me to already have a bunch of different stuff, various businesses, different ways to make money, but so far NONE of the businesses I bought (MC Clubhouse, Nightclub, Document Forgery, Office, Cargo Warehouse, Vehicle Warehouse) have even come close to paying for themselves with the moneymaking options available to me, let alone started generating a profit. Ironically, the best option so far is to register as a VIP (or CEO if you have the office, though it makes ZERO difference to the money earned), whose only prerequisite is having 50k in the bank account (something any beginner can get with the few starting missions). Yes, after 100 hours in the game, I'm still doing the exact same thing to make money that I did when I first started, because all the other methods take way too long and usually result in a net loss. All this while trying to dodge trolls. That reminds me, you *can* play in a solo session, free of trolls, griefers, and kids: Invite Only. But you can't run your businesses, company, supplies, buying, selling, or anything else other than VIP work. And even those are limited, since for many of them you need associates playing in CO-OP with you (which almost never happens), or players in the session who aren't part of your organization (which doesn't happen in Invite Only, usually). In the end, you find yourself forced to put up with trolls and griefers if you want to play more than 15% of the Online content. There are still plenty of issues, I could write a book, but I can stop right here. Rockstar is going to release Red Dead Redemption 2 and its Online mode soon enough. Pray that they manage to make sure the game isn't what GTA Online is.

translation_en: This is a genuinely good game, the offline story alone is worth the price. I played through the offline story three times before I even touched online. Then I happily discovered..... what the fuck is this, these are clearly two totally different games! Even though online has no story and no special abilities, it has so many sweet cars, so many customized weapons, so many armed vehicles, so many properties...... none of which are in the offline game! So, is it fun? Of course it is! Setting best times on all sorts of jobs, figuring out faster ways to beat them, watching video guides online and then trying it out yourself, messing around with friends, and then messing around so hard you break your legs. It's super fun! How could a game made with this much care, with zero pay-to-win bullshit, where every single item can be acquired just by playing, not be fun? How could it not be appealing? Before I knew it, I had 700+ hours on the clock, pretty much "graduated" from it. But along the way, this game has made me feel more and more cold and disgusted. When normal players first jump into online without an experienced player showing them the ropes, they hit a massive period of confusion. They don't know what they're supposed to do, and everyone they run into seems to want to stomp on them and kill them a few times. After that, they either quit playing or start going down the wrong path—buying money on Taobao, getting cheats, and shit like that... Buying money and levels is whatever, it just devalues the in-game currency and kills the market for leveling and boosting services. But buying actual hacks straight-up kills the game; give it a week or so and they won't even be interested in playing GTA anymore. I've run into hackers bullying noobs (noobs who just came back from Taobao). At first, they use normal tryhard tactics like the MK2 Oppressor. When they realize the noob can actually kill them sometimes, they straight up turn on teleportation, godmode, explosive bullets, and miniguns?!?! The noob is a Taobao customer, they have no fucking clue what a hacker looks like, and afterwards they just say, "Man, I didn't realize I was fighting a hacker for so long," how fucking sad is that? On the other hand, even if you don't run into hackers, these "noobs" sitting on nine-figure balances have no idea how to spend their money. How do I mod the Deluxo? Where are the Oppressor missiles? Why doesn't my sniper have thermal or explosive ammo??? Stuff like that. With zero clue about how the game is actually played, what fun is even left in the game? Not to mention there are more and more griefing cunts nowadays, I only dare to play in solo sessions now. Any session with 16 or more players is guaranteed to have a cunt, and I'm talking about the all-powerful type who can trap you in cages, spawn-kill you, attach weird models to you, and fly or clip through the ground. They mess with anyone they see, acting like the whole fucking world is in their hands. I don't know if these people are having the time of their lives, I just know that this game has gradually lost its appeal to me and started making me sick. Whenever I think of GTA Online, I don't have happy memories—just total disgust with the game's environment. Don't give me that shit about Chinese players just having low standards, crows are black all over the world, and hackers sure as hell aren't only Chinese. Some friends tell me, if someone plays by themselves and doesn't affect others, that's just using a trainer, because not everyone has enough time to grind and progress. I can barely accept that point of view, that way of playing. Just treat it like a single-player game, whatever makes you happy, right? But using cheats specifically to target other players, using godmode and explosive miniguns to PvP, attaching random models to other players and blowing them up over and over—I honestly don't fucking get it. Aren't you worried your mom's gonna get run over by a car and sent flying fifty meters? All of this is just the current state of the game, caused by the low standards of a handful of players. Honestly, I could accept it. What society doesn't have scum? What truly makes your heart go cold is Rockstar's sheer inaction, letting this chaotic game environment run wild, letting people advertise and sell hacks and money drops right there in the game. Honest players' reports never get a single response. That's the real reason that makes you want to give up on this game. Is GTA Online actually just a game meant for hackers, and honest players are just something Rockstar doesn't want? So, I don't recommend this game. This genuinely amazing game, one of the evergreen classics on Steam, I do not recommend it. I absolutely do not recommend it to those of you who love games and play them seriously. I don't want your expectations and longing for GTA to turn into ultimate disgust. Beautiful things are best admired from afar; don't peel back that whitewashed surface to see the maggots crawling all over the inside.

translation_en: I really love Michael De Santa. Even though he's a hypocrite, he had to sell out his crew for the sake of his family. On top of that, his son doesn't understand him, his wife cheats on him, and his daughter hates him, yet he still loves his family. When Franklin has problems, he can talk to Lamar; when Trevor has problems, he either takes down whoever's giving him trouble or goes with Ron and the others to beat those people up—anyway, his reputation is already ruined. But Michael is different. He betrayed his brothers for his family, and he couldn't even talk about it. Plus, he can't go crazy like Trevor, because his family would hate him even more. On top of all that, he still has to mentor Franklin and guide him in the right direction. It's even more impossible for him to tell Franklin that he looks at him like a real son—like family. translation_en: [h1][i]MASTERPIECE[/i][/h1] [h1]Revvin` up your engine 点燃你的引擎[/h1] [h1]Listen to her howlin` roar 倾听机器轰鸣[/h1] [b]GTA V is a very special game to me. It was the first game I ever bought on Steam, and to some extent, it's the exact reason I started getting into Steam and the digital gaming industry (yeah, it's just that attractive). Unlike most players, I bought it mainly for its rich single-player campaign, and honestly didn't pay much attention to the online side of things. Lots of critics and players rated this game super high (an IGN 10/10 masterpiece), and the more I played it, the more I came to appreciate GTA V's impact and standing in gaming history.[/b] [h1]◼ Visuals [/h1> GTA V first launched on the PS3, and only later came to PC and other consoles like the PS4. Even though it's a PC game released back in 2015, its graphics are still pretty damn stunning. A lot of the physics effects are super realistic, and the character, vehicle, and building models are all extremely detailed. I still remember the explosions, gunfights, and getaway scenes from the prologue; the realistic graphics and rich, thrilling gameplay have stuck with me to this day. Cruising down the highway in a Pegassi supercar under the scorching sun, the visuals brought by the realistic motion blur and light reflection effects made me completely forget about the main story missions and just lose myself in it. The game also puts a lot of love into small details—like characters running noticeably slower on sand than on regular ground, pedestrians panicking or calling the cops when you pull some crazy shit on the street, characters still having scars after respawning from the hospital, and being able to visit "all sorts of websites" and "shop online" in the game, etc. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1627891414 Though I gotta point out one little detail the game didn't get quite right: pedestrians' behavior on the street during rainy days is kinda weird (do the citizens of Los Santos seriously love standing in the rain, aren't they scared of catching a cold?). Thanks to its one-of-a-kind graphics and jaw-dropping optimization (easily some of the best optimization you'll ever see in a AAA port), GTA V lets players get an amazing sensory gaming experience without needing a high-end PC! [h1]◼ Content [/h1> Here I'm mainly talking about the single-player story mode content and experience. GTA V is an urban crime game with massive freedom. The game gives players a huge map to explore, plus a diverse range of vehicles similar to the real world like submarines, speedboats, sports cars, and planes, letting you rule the land, sea, and air. What's most unforgettable and immersive are the various system settings the game provides—like clothing stores on the street (offering all kinds of outfit combos), barbershops (crazy hairstyles), various racing events (bicycle races, street races, powerboat races, triathlons, etc.), movie theaters (you can actually watch movies, though there seem to be only two, and one of them is pretty philosophical), buying various properties (garages, taxi company, bars, smoke shops, etc.), and collecting and modding all kinds of rides. There are just countless activities to do; players can ditch the main story (or play it after beating it) and just mess around to their heart's content, experiencing the colorful criminal life of Los Santos. On top of that, interacting with NPCs is super fun, like randomly triggering petty theft events on the street, sticking up stores, or taunting gang and biker members and getting into fierce firefights with them. The game's story mode is packed: 69 main missions, 59 hobbies and pastimes, 58 side missions (strangers and freaks), 60 random events, and 30 other activities. It's crazy easy for players to rack up hundreds of hours of playtime. Various main and side missions also feature gold medal challenges, making the game even more challenging. The game uses a three-protagonist system that weaves their stories together, and the character writing for all three is a massive success. Personally, I think Michael is the most deeply fleshed out. Their backgrounds are also super symbolic: a young Black guy lost and desperate for a shot to make it big; a middle-aged white guy with a seemingly wealthy yet miserable life, suffering through it all; and a psychotic, violent maniac who wants to be an American yet still has your back even if you screwed him over. The game's story is full of satire towards police agencies like the FBI and CIA, and of course, it completely mocks capitalist societal issues and the ugliness of human nature. By comparison, the protagonists are just pawns, and the game uses them to deliver biting commentary and satire on politics. I can't articulate the deeper, more professional meanings of the game, but as long as you experience it with your heart, you'll find that GTA V's story is brilliant and profound. [h1]◼ Online Mode [/h1> GTA V's online mode basically counts as a DLC. The content is super rich, and on top of covering all the recreational activities from story mode, it introduces various multiplayer races, multiplayer heists (continuing the heists from story mode with basically the same workflow), biker clubs, CEO work, and all sorts of clubhouse and cargo delivery activities. Online mode has a player level system tied to unlocking weapons and gear, and grinding active events and double-XP missions speeds up the leveling. The online content lets players genuinely experience how a criminal goes from a total nobody to a big shot. Player-on-player kills in the same lobby are definitely a thrill, but it easily devolves into getting steamrolled by high-level gear and just gets boring. Crews were originally meant to make player characters more vivid, but they don't really serve an effective purpose in actual online gameplay. I feel like if online mode's activities centered around the "Crew" rather than pushing the "individual," it would make online mode way more fun and exciting—like crew cargo runs or crew turf wars. Even though there's tons of stuff to do online, most online content lacks necessary guidance for new players, and the overall leveling path and money-making methods are missing proper hints. That’s definitely something that needs improvement. Thinking back to when I first played online, I was completely lost on what to do, flying solo and just blowing up cars to make cash and rank up. It was only later, through strategy guides and forums, that I slowly figured out online's mechanics, the M menu, and the phone's advanced features. Overall, if a player lacks patience or doesn't have buddies to play with, they'll probably lose interest in online mode pretty damn quick. [h1]𝑻𝒉𝒆 𝑪𝒐𝒐𝒍𝒆𝒔𝒕 𝑴𝒊𝒔𝒔𝒊𝒐𝒏 ----- 𝑻𝒉𝒆 𝑫𝒐𝒐𝒎𝑯𝒆𝒊𝒔𝒕 𝑮𝑻𝑨 𝑶𝒏𝒍𝒊𝒏𝒆[/h1> https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2022873372 Personally, I think the funnest part of online mode is the Heists, because heists are the soul of offline mode after all. But online heists still have a lot of differences compared to offline. Offline heists are crafted with insane detail in level design, storytelling, background, and cutscenes. By comparison, online heists lean way more into co-op play, and the background story and narrative are relatively rough, a bit underwhelming, and hurt the immersion a bit. But considering it's online content, overall the heists are still made with genuine effort and pack a decent challenge. [h1]◼ Final Verdict [/h1> [b]All in all, GTA V is an absolute classic, a rare gem of a game that shows players the infinite possibilities of high-freedom open-world games. But for obvious reasons, you still need a VPN/accelerator to play this game normally, though that minor flaw doesn't hide its brilliance. I miss the days of grinding GTA V, and I still catch myself imitating Lamar's slangy English every now and then.[/b] [b]Postscript: March 22, 2020[/b] Through all the stumbling, setbacks, and months of hard work—plus the help of some warm-hearted, legendary veteran teammates—I finally unlocked the "Criminal Mastermind" achievement. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2031208117 GTA Online is honestly such a brutal grind. Early on you're forced to rely on random heists and solo missions to scrape by, but if your level is too low you just keep getting kicked from lobbies, which makes a new player's cash grind painfully slow. That's one of the reasons why money glitching is so rampant. I was super lucky to have a kind friend carry me through the early days, running the Doomsday Bogdan Problem with me whenever he had time. I'm genuinely so grateful to him, and it gave me a much better online experience. The Criminal Mastermind achievement for the Doomsday Heist has become a precious memory of mine. Sometimes I look back and can barely believe I actually pulled it off. A mediocre player like me really had to rely on constant practice plus getting carried. I even quit for a bit during the process, but deep down I still wanted this achievement because GTA V holds such a special place in my heart, so I couldn't just let it go. Later, when I finally had the time to go for it again, I studied the guides inside and out, practiced repeatedly, and my own skills improved. But starting that first official run was still nerve-wracking as hell, haha—the feeling was pretty much like taking an exam, kinda embarrassing. Luckily, with the enthusiastic help of a few veteran friends, we overcame all the crazy obstacles (shitty net) and finally pulled off this ultimate challenge! [b]To you guys, my friends—9527, Old W, OldD, Little C, and the rest—maybe you'll never see this, but you're definitely worth remembering.[/b] [h1]Thank you Rockstar for pouring your heart and soul into this masterpiece. Can't wait for GTA VI.[/h1]

translation_en: A friendly piece of advice for China: The internet is full of games that scam kids out of their money and leave, but you do nothing; web ads for games with broken Mandarin are everywhere, but you do nothing; games with official sites selling hacks, and you do nothing. You go after AAA games? Violence? Porn? Look at the web ads all over the country—every single one is more exposed than anything on Steam, yet you turn a blind eye and come after Steam instead. Why don't you have the time and energy to manage the Chinese film industry? It's more deformed than Lu Benwei. Look at your CCTV, then look at the BBC—what a gap. You trample on the cultural confidence you built up yourselves, and why? Because instead of reforming your own management methods, you drag a massive platform down with you. Even though many Chinese players just use Steam as a launcher, it at least gave people some concept of buying genuine copies. Now, just as we're making a bit of progress, we're being beaten right back to square one. Are you encouraging people to play pirated games? Not to mention so-called democracy, why can't you implement a rating system? A rating system could solve most of these issues. Is this fun for you? You "experts" are seriously brilliant. Every day you pull this useless crap, why don't you just ban the internet altogether and stop letting normal people use it? Why not organize a bit of slogan-chanting and farming every day??? Or just go straight back to primitive society. What I actually care about is that if the games I buy become unplayable, who do I look to for compensation—Perfect World, or the state? But I guess in the end, it'll just mean we players who insist on buying genuine games take a total loss, and then we'll get properly mocked by all the real-life piracy snobs. Brilliant. Fucking amazing, my country, haha. Emperor Qin, this glorious era is just as you wished. Some people and their friends grew up playing Legend and CS back in the day, and none of them went around hacking, slashing, and committing crimes. Nowadays, bratty kids watch Pleasant Goat and roast other kids—is that really the fault of games and anime, or is it the fault of irresponsible parenting and schooling? Everyone knows the truth in their hearts. Have you strayed this far from the goal of 100 years of socialism? What even is the Chinese Dream? Study hard and get the fuck out of this country. Gaming belongs to the ninth art. Any major blockbuster inherently contains the author's thoughts and philosophy, but given our country's current closed-off values, foreign reflections on the future and bizarre fantasies are simply unacceptable to the SARFT. As for domestic games right now—due to various factors like Steam and consoles—you can still make absolute crap and rake in mountains of cash. They know that as long as game quality is barely passable, and they design some micro-management features to let players flex, along with various lewd character art and chunibyo character models and lines, they can scam people out of money. The plot has to be garbage, with no depth, plain and easy to understand. Productions like this make way more money than games where you seriously puzzle over the plot and mechanics. Steam might seem well-known in China now, but honestly, before PUBG came out, you could walk down the street and hardly anyone knew what Steam was. Actually, real-name verification in China is already way ahead of foreign countries; both UnionPay and WeChat Pay require an ID card. So why still drag your feet on introducing a rating system? Because right now, the final say on whether culture passes censorship lies solely with the Ministry of Culture and SARFT; there are no relevant laws or regulations determining whether a game passes review. Back in the day, a domestic single-player game developer made a martial arts game and submitted it for review. Since they were a domestic studio, they knew the censorship system inside and out, so before submitting, they removed blood and dismemberment effects, and turned all the corpses black. Even then, it failed review. The censors said that after killing an NPC, the player character only had to serve ten days in prison, which could easily cause a negative social impact. Later on, through endless revisions, it turned into a martial arts game where you could only ride horses. Meanwhile, Tencent's Moonlight Blade requires zero consequences for slaughtering human enemies; you just keep on butchering. Doesn't that cause an even worse social impact? Yet Moonlight Blade passed review. Why does this happen? Tencent makes a killing every single day, so they can afford to pay up, whereas that small developer had no money left after finishing their game. Therefore, the development of Chinese single-player games depends neither on your production quality nor on whether your marketing reaches people—it depends entirely on whether you can afford to pay the bribe. And what claim do relevant Chinese departments base their censorship on? The so-called social mainstream, the core socialist values. What does this kind of feel like? Ancient monarchs would always find a statement of claim for their power that sounded legally and theoretically sound: the Mandate of Heaven, "I am the True Dragon," and all my power was bestowed upon me by the heavens. The core socialist values act as a tool for this exact purpose: to give illegitimate, unlawful power and acquired interests a seemingly reasonable justification. Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Macao are Special Administrative Regions. Their social, economic, political, and cultural systems are completely different from the mainland. Has anyone ever thought about why that is? Actually, it's simple: the crying child gets the milk. Take Hong Kong, for example—if they had been handed the mainland system during the '97 handover, they would have launched massive strikes and walkouts, bringing society to a complete halt. At the time, many eyes both domestic and foreign were watching Hong Kong, which is why they are a Special Administrative Region. And what about us mainlanders? When they blocked the foreign internet, we endured it. When they censored World of Warcraft, we endured that too. We've never spoken up for our own rights, and now things are getting worse. The China version of Steam is about to drop. The absolute best-case scenario is that a China-only store launches, and all existing mainland payment methods and low-price regional discounts get migrated over there. If we silently endure this time, what about the next? I'm afraid we're going to turn into North Korea's Kwangmyong network. A lot of people treat all of this as if it's completely natural—whether it's blocking the foreign internet, censoring games, *Top Funny Media* [Baozou Dashijian], or now the Steam China version. But what are the facts? When terrorists are active on Instagram and Twitter in Europe, do they just simply build a firewall to block these social media apps? No, they fight a cyber war against those terrorists and drive them off those platforms. If that's the case, why can't the CCP do it? Is it just because building a wall is cheaper? Are our rights and our spaces for entertainment and relaxation worth less than the cost of fighting a cyber war? Do Chinese people have to compromise and endure while foreigners get to protect their rights? Please spread these words far and wide. Speak up for your own rights and for Steam. I don't know which version of "being represented" is better: the one they claim—that blocking and censoring World of Warcraft, *Top Funny Media*, free media, social apps, and standalone online games is the will of the people and players—or the things I'm posting today, which represent the interests of Steam players. But I know that everything I'm saying comes straight from the bottom of my heart, spoken from genuine emotion and with a cocktail of complex feelings after experiencing all this shit. I'm speaking with a clear conscience, whereas they certainly aren't. I hope everyone spreads these words. I know 9/10 times it won't do shit, but how can we stay silent just because our voices are small? As an ordinary resident living in China who loves Steam and loves the joy Steam brings, this is all I can do. Thank you, everyone. Honestly, being a docile subject has zero upside and all downside. Because once you show compliance, they need to provide you with even less. Since you've already expressed submission, why would they give a damn about your needs? As for the so-called rabble, the government has to provide a lot more just to maintain its rule and appease the populace. We see this right here at home: when they blocked the foreign internet and censored games, we complied. And the result? Now the Steam China version is about to drop. Because you always show compliance, they figure that if they launch it, they launch it—after all, you guys will just keep rolling over. Whenever I think about the First Amendment of the United States and how a platform for freedom of speech like Steam allows me to speak out here, while the CCP is rolling out a Steam China version to strip all of that away, I get a cocktail of complex feelings. Honestly, when I speak out, I don't want much. I'm not delusional enough to think life will magically get better just because of capitalism; you still have to work hard, and grind for a dozen years to buy a house and a car. All I want is fewer restrictions and controls, and for the government to respect the rights of its citizens. But even something this simple is so hard to come by. A hundred years ago in Beijing, Qing dynasty subjects helped foreigners set up ladders to scale the walls; a hundred years today, foreigners are helping Chinese people set up ladders to scale the wall. ------ Reposted from the internet
