translation_en: I hope everyone takes a moment to read this review before buying the game, it will help you immensely. I bought GTA 5 back in 2015 for 189 at full price, played for over 1,500 hours, and got banned yesterday. Absolutely tilted. I hope everyone thinks twice before buying the game, Rockstar's ban system does not accept appeals. Getting banned is a big fucking deal. If they won't let you play, it doesn't matter how fun the game is, you can't touch it anymore. Don't think that just because you play honestly and legitimately there's no way you'll get banned. Let me give you all a quick rundown of Rockstar's ban system: 1. Most of the time servers are constantly dropping connection, which results in hackers running rampant everywhere. Vicious cheats include things like one-shot killing all players with a single button (advanced cheaters can even frame other players—the system might show someone else killed you when it was actually the cheater), model trapping (like attaching a giant windmill or UFO to your character, making you unable to move an inch. These models usually require restarting the game to remove, and a restart takes about five to ten minutes. Also, if your PC specs aren't great, the physics engine calculations after being model-trapped will exceed your hardware's limits and the game will straight up crash), wiping your game money (no matter how much cash you have or how you got it, everything gets zeroed out, and your bank shows it as medical expenses), and dropping money bags (lots of newbies run over to pick up money bags as soon as they see them, resulting in bans due to abnormal data). 2. Extremely harsh. At certain specific times, usually right before a major update rolls out, Rockstar's cheat detection system suddenly starts actually working. Operating on the principle that it's better to wrongly execute a thousand than let one escape, this leads to massive waves of false bans (like right now). Hacking, money modding, getting banned—fine, nothing to say about that. Exploiting glitches to get illegal game currency? Okay, I admit I used glitch methods before, nothing to argue about there. But during a ban wave, even if you just got model-trapped by a hacker, played in the same session as a hacker, picked up money bags, weapons, or specific vehicles spawned by a hacker (please note, these are things completely out of your control), or even just because you played too well and people suspected you of cheating, or someone else cheated and framed you and then you got mass-reported by multiple people, any of these can get you banned. Oh right, people in China have a habit of downloading security software on their PCs. Using memory-clearing functions while the game is running (commonly known as clicking the "boost ball") also carries a chance of being flagged as a cheat and getting you banned. Yes, a strict ban system can purify the gaming environment, but this kind of blatant intermittency—either doing fuck all and leaving legit players in deep misery, or being so overly nitpicky that innocent clean players catch strays—makes for a truly terrible gaming experience. Fine, you say cheaters will get banned eventually, justice delayed is not justice denied, but the gaming experience of us legit players is genuinely being violated. Being brutalized by hackers is already a reality, the damage is already done, what the fuck good does it do to ban their accounts later? Furthermore, Rockstar has never given you any compensation for getting violated by hackers. 3. Irreversibility. Like I said, Rockstar does not accept appeals for bans. If they say you're banned, you're banned. There's no such thing as getting the penalty reversed. Once you're banned, they wipe your data too. Doesn't matter if you're a noob who's played for a few days or a veteran like me with thousands of hours, it doesn't matter how much of your assets were legitimately earned versus illegally obtained, everything starts from scratch. Having said all this shit and criticizing Rockstar's ban system, the game is actually still really fun. The various cool-looking sports cars, yachts, and fighter jets in GTA Online give you endless motivation to grind and make money (the so-called "liver-destroying" grind). That's why many players can play for one or two thousand hours without getting bored. But nobody wants their criminal empire, built over hundreds or thousands of hours, to vanish into thin air because of some tiny slip-up—a slip-up that is often completely impossible to prevent. Oh right, even if you're a whale who spends real money, the moment Rockstar thinks you're cheating, you're getting banned just the same, it's just that the game currency you bought with cash won't be deleted. On the Tieba forums, there are players who dumped thousands of RMB into the game and still got banned. To be fair, GTA 5 is a monumental masterpiece that defined an era. I admit writing this review has some venting involved, but every single word above is true, I'm just deliberately picking out the ugly truths to talk about. Below, I'll give everyone a few more tips on how to prevent getting banned: 1. Obviously, don't cheat, don't ask people to mod money for you, and if you see money bags on the road, do not pick them up. If you accidentally pick one up, you need to turn yourself in to Rockstar. Google the specific methods. 2. Do not exploit any glitches, regardless of whether it involves illegal game currency. Replaying the finale glitch (job warping/curfew glitch), getting special outfits, or glitching specific vehicles all violate the online terms of service. If you don't want to get banned, don't touch them. 3. Steer clear of hackers when you see them. If you run into one in a mission, quit the mission (go to the pause menu and find a new session). If you run into one in a free roam lobby, switch sessions. Signs of a cheater include: a level over 400 (most veteran players who started in 2015 are mostly around level 200-400, anything higher is likely modded), a K/D ratio over 10, wearing extremely, extremely weird outfits (the kind that give off an interdimensional glitch vibe), or things appearing in the session that shouldn't possibly be there (like a UFO spawning on the road, a giant metal cage trapping your house, or iron cages spawning inside your garage), or the kill feed showing one single person killing everyone in an instant. 4. Play less during ban waves. As mentioned before, there are truly tons of false bans. Staying offline is the safest method. Keep an eye on the GTA 5 Baidu Tieba; during ban waves, there will be lots of threads discussing it. 5. If you've ever played a pirated copy or used cheats in single-player, make sure to clean out your game directory completely, ideally doing a full reinstall. That's the only way to be safe. Also, don't click the boost ball. Don't click the boost ball. Don't click the boost ball. 6. The most profitable legitimate way to make money in this game is running heists. However, using special methods lets you skip the tedious setup phases and endlessly replay the final heist finale (commonly known as "doing the heist replay glitch") to get massive amounts of cash. The replay glitch carries a chance of getting you banned, whether you're the heist leader hosting it or a crew member participating. Therefore, aside from not doing the glitch yourself, you also need to prevent yourself from "getting caught in someone else's replay glitch." If your friend keeps quitting and restarting the game every ten to twenty minutes, and then sends you invites to the heist finale on a loop, there is a very high chance they are doing the replay glitch. Do not accept their invites; cherish your account. 7. As an online multiplayer game, GTA 5 is only really fun when played with close homies. Go to Tieba to find a crew, join player groups, make posts looking for people to carry you, and try to stay out of public lobbies as much as possible, especially during ban waves. 8. The above suggestions can only lower the risk of getting banned. If you get banned for no fucking reason, maintain your dignity and don't turn into a bitter asshole who resorts to cheating to ruin the game for others. Also, new players shouldn't go looking for money drops, because it completely ruins the game experience and strips away all the fun of GTA 5. I hope everyone plays cleanly, stays away from cheats, and prays they don't get arbitrarily banned by Rockstar. Upvote me to the top, thanks.

translation_en: There are as many ideas of how to play Grand Theft Auto as there are players in the world. Don't believe the fairy tales that GTA is only needed to chase hookers with a chainsaw — if it were that simple, Saint’s Row would have put Rockstar North out of business a long time ago. In Grand Theft Auto V, you'll be watching cartoons and doing yoga. You'll also have to kill and rob, but not by choice. Namaste. As is well known, the action of GTA IV and V takes place in a new reality where there was no Claude, no Tommy Vercetti, and no CJ. It turned out almost like J.J. Abrams' Star Trek reboot or comic book reboots: the names are the same, the places are the same, but everything else is different. Therefore, returning to Los Santos is somewhat deflating. Redesigned for the new generation, the city has kept some external features, but overall has become completely unfamiliar. For example, of the old Grove Street, where Carl Johnson and his gang lived in the story of San Andreas, only a musty courtyard remains, and its former inhabitants seem to never have existed. Now the purple Ballas live here, and if you manage to show up here on foot, the guys will jump you as a whole neighborhood. An entire era in the history of San Andreas was simply erased, and the state itself was rebuilt from scratch. Out of three cities, only Los Santos remains, but it has transformed and grown so much that it finally looks like a real city. INTERESTING FACT: references to GTA IV are encountered at every step: sometimes fleeting mentions ("There was this guy from Eastern Europe in Liberty City, but he kept his head down..."), and sometimes even characters. And the fact that they forgot about the events of San Andreas might actually be the right call. After the madhouse that CJ's story ended with, Los Santos should have been left in ruins. The entire territory (the city itself is the size of the new Liberty City from GTA IV, plus the surrounding countryside twice that size) is, for once, open right from the start: no excuses like "bridges are closed due to a terrorist threat." And everywhere, absolutely everywhere, you can stumble upon something interesting. First of all, this is what distinguishes GTA V from its genre peers — the sandbox here is so vibrant, well-thought-out, and unpredictable that you can get mixed up in some shit at any minute. Bandits steal purses, motorcycles, and cars (and you can help the owner get the stolen property back), cops are having shootout with street gangs and rednecks (participating is totally allowed), forest deer run out onto the road (a good deer is a roadkill deer), accidents happen at construction sites, people curse, fight... Every, every single second something is happening somewhere. These aren't just decorations (since you can intervene in any random event), nor are they Potemkin villages thrown together just for you — Los Santos gets along just fine on its own. GTA is no longer just territory you have to drive through from point A to point B according to the plot, occasionally breaking for mass murder when you get bored. Having gone through the thorny path of evolution, Rockstar has achieved an almost ideal game space, creating a real ecosystem with almost no rules and conventions. And on top of that, very beautiful and cozy. It has never been so pleasant just to drive down the highway in GTA. Some Gerry Rafferty is playing on the radio, cars are rushing past in a solid stream, trees and some shacks, the sunset peeks out from behind the mountains, the car bounces on road bumps, and you even feel the wind resistance — not a game, but a happiness generator. The last time it was like this was in last year's sunny Forza Horizon, but that's still a narrowly specialized racing game. So, you could say GTA V has no competitors in happiness generation. When it became known that GTA V would have three main characters instead of one, many had doubts — back in the day, Rockstar could barely handle even one. But the doubts are gone — this is the best thing they could have come up with to diversify the game. In essence, it turned out to be three different GTA games that not only coexist, but also complement each other. Franklin is a typical righteous "nigga," with a clear system of values and a hyperbolized sense of gang loyalty. He's young, inexperienced, but surprisingly sensible, boosts cars to order, and dreams of a big score. He doesn't like to take risks unnecessarily, but he's ready to do anything for his friends. Michael is a hardened robber who has retired and lost himself at the bottom of a bottle. Unlike the previous heroes, he has long since settled into adult life: a mansion in Vinewood, a garage full of cars, an unhappy wife, a daughter hanging out with porn moguls and lustful showmen, and a post-pubescent son who does nothing but smoke weed, troll people on the internet, and play the local equivalent of Call of Duty. And Trevor... Trevor is just a psycho (he even has a doctor's note to prove it). He lives in a dirty trailer, cooks methamphetamine, screams profanities for any reason and none, wipes out bikers, and at the first opportunity punches people in the face (and women, women too!). Completely out of control, insolent, quarrelsome, and socially dangerous. Just like in previous parts, the main storyline in GTA V is tangled and disjointed — but this is no longer perceived as a flaw, but rather as a distinguishing feature of the series. But the routine has decreased by an order of magnitude — mainly due to the fact that you can switch between characters. When, say, Michael has to lay low, we switch to Trevor, who has another slaughter or crazy stunt on his agenda. You don't have to think about the mandatory races or the infamous flight school from San Andreas — everything that used to look like tedious "filler" is left in GTA V at best as optional stuff. Even the obsessive dating from GTA IV has stopped being obsessive. No more "Nico, let's go bowling!" with hurt feelings if you refuse. Want to invite partners for a hangout? Go ahead. As a reward, you'll get an adorable episode with, say, Michael and Franklin getting totally wasted. But no one will demand anything from you. Few games treat additional content the way GTA V does. Knowing full well that many players won't notice even half of the side activities, secrets, and cute little details, Rockstar built a real paradise for explorers. You are reminded that scuba gear exists in the game during a single story mission, and you can easily miss that moment. But if you don't miss it, you'll discover a whole underwater world with its own secrets, valuable loot, and biting sharks. Flying by helicopter for another errand, it's hard not to notice another curious place and mentally make a note to "drop by in my free time." It's even harder to resist not dropping by during work time: there's so much going on around that it's almost impossible to focus on just one thing. At home, the TV plays shows and cartoons (we'll talk separately about the satire, of which there's really a lot in GTA V, because the local jokes are simply impossible to retell), and the local internet has dozens of interesting pages. Besides, you can mess around with yoga in the yard, and if you don't like it, run over to the nearest tennis court, say. Mini-games like yoga have almost no practical value: they improve character stats, but this has a minimal impact on the course of the game. But the main thing is that such activities exist, and they are entertaining. So let them be. To make life in Los Santos even more like real life, Rockstar tries to instill a sense of private property in players, and in places it even works. Each character has a personal car: Trevor has a redneck and eternally filthy pickup truck, Franklin has a cheap "boy racer" sedan resembling a Lancer and a stolen green motorbike, and Michael has something like a prestigious Audi A6. Only these cars are worth upgrading: they won't go anywhere and will always be with you. Tuning the engine, transmission, and other things is expensive, and a random car can easily disappear if you don't put it in the garage (and sometimes even from there) — money down the drain. You can also invest money in real estate, like in Vice City, or play the stock market.

translation_en: -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Note: Cheating is bad in every way and should neither be practiced nor tolerated by any real gamer. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Other reviews talk about tons of modders. With this review, I want to present the perspective of a formerly honest player who turned into a cheater exclusively in GTAV. I am aware that this goes against the rules. Nevertheless, I believe that this report is also important for forming an opinion before making a purchase, and therefore I want to publish it. It's been a while since I started playing GTAV. After really only a short time in singleplayer, I immediately switched TO GTA Online and was overwhelmed. You don't often see a truly large repertoire of content in one game, plus continuous free updates (which actually came and keep coming). However, this pretty facade completely fails to hide just how poorly thought-out the game is. I don't want to get into bugs, since they never really bothered me. It's more about Rockstar's gameplay policy itself. Because somehow they try to force players to buy these Shark Cards by practically hiding all content behind a paywall. Either you grind yourself to death and therefore have no fun playing, or you hand them a bunch of cash to buy the content (which actually shouldn't be the point, because making progress by unlocking things is supposed to be fun). I played GTA Online for barely 150 hours the way it was actually intended (without really having fun, because grinding was pretty much all I did). Only to look back and realize that my progress was pretty meager. On top of that, new updates kept coming with genuinely interesting content at the time, which I actually wanted, but I never even came close to having enough spare change. Until a modder simply spawned a bunch of cash for me without me asking. I was initially overwhelmed by the situation and didn't know how to evaluate the action, because cheating is inherently a bad thing. However, the result was an enormous amount of fun in the following hours of play, because for once more was going through my head than: "hey, that car is cool, so first I'll grind 10 hours or more for it." Eventually, though, when I had spent all my money, I lapsed back into the endless grind. I got the feeling that Rockstar, with GTA Online the way they planned it (meaning without cheating), had simply made a very weak and boring game. I wanted to have fun again. I wanted to get money again. I didn't want to grind that money forever in-game (at least not as long as the "gameplay" intends). I didn't want to buy Shark Cards (I had already shelled out 50€ for the game). I became a cheater. So I looked up a mod menu on the net and installed it. Everything worked wonderfully and I got my fun back. It sounds unbelievable, but for me, real fun in the game only started at that point. From then on, I shaped my own gameplay. Whenever I thought Rockstar simply gave me too little for completed missions, I gave myself more money. I never affected other players with my mod menu. I just wanted to "fix" the gameplay for myself. After around 100 hours, a player must have watched and reported me. They were right to do so. I broke the rules. I've now been banned in GTA Online for just under a year. However, the reason for this review is not the fact that I was banned. The reason is, [b] that Rockstar's GTA Online gameplay strongly tempts you to cheat. [/b] So strongly that I couldn't resist and I hope that many other players out there are stronger than I am.

translation_en: [h1] Zero[/h1] I remember first touching GTA back in elementary school, don't really remember clearly though, just that the first one I played was SA. At the time I was genuinely blown away by Rockstar's open world. Hand on heart, I wasn't playing a game, I was playing a world! Afterwards I played VC, GTA3, CW on and off, plus some modded version of GTA called something like Wild City, and then finally I played GTAV. The only one I never played was IV because my PC back then couldn't run it 23333. [h1] One[/h1] Maybe I should get to the point. GTAV's first impression on me was that the graphics were really good, that's what I thought when I first saw the trailers. After actually playing the game, at first I couldn't really accept the three protagonists thing. What the hell? Three people?! But as I kept playing, the storylines actually ended up intertwining!! I just have to quote this: "Three men and a dog are totally invincible!" The plot truly twists and turns, it's deeply satisfying! In one word: awesome, extremely awesome! The Easter eggs are also super rich, totally worth replaying. The Director Mode is an innovative and user-friendly innovation, you can pretty much just do whatever the fuck you want. Whether you can install mods is the key to how long a single-player game will last. Today, I, Iron Man, am gonna wear the Hulkbuster armor to commit arson, murder, and pillage in Los Santos! Today Trevor is gonna grow some hair! Get a skin smoothing filter! Whitening! Crossdressing!!! Modding is so fucking fun! [h1]Two[/h1]Next I gotta talk about the online mode that you both hate and love. Let me tell you about the first time I played online: Who am I? Where am I? What am I supposed to be doing? As soon as I log on, they humanely give me a pistol with 36 bullets to defend myself? Whatever, let's steal a couple cars first? Huh? Why do I have a wanted level? Run for it first! What the fuck? The cops online are so goddamn persistent! Come on! Let's go! Who's scared of who?! And then I died 2333. Lonely and helpless, I was lost on the bustling, wide streets of Los Santos, when suddenly a unique sports car drove towards me not far away. My first instinct told me it was a player, I finally found one of my own species!! But I vaguely felt something was a bit off. Why was his speed still that fast??? I gotta dodge. And then I died. Not long after, I saw a few colored dots on the map chasing each other, so I drove the Karin Sultan I'd just stolen not long ago to find them, and then I blew up. Turns out they were fighting! Through dying over and over again, I finally learned the laws of the online world. Of course, it's not all people like that—thanks to those high-level players who carried me through missions and taught me how to make money. Little by little I got my own place and knew what to do next: [b]The Fleeca Job[/b], my first decent heist......... [h1] Three[/h1]The online mode requires investing a lot of time and energy to play. This time, you are the protagonist, and you have to commit crimes in a civilized manner rather than mindless slaughter. We've all become CEOs, leading our own MCs, forging documents, selling guns, cooking drugs, robbing banks—all this money is earned with blood and sweat. Maybe this is the fun of online gaming: doing missions with a few friends, helping each other out, surviving to the end to get what everyone deserves. This is the true essence of GTAV co-op missions. In recent years, the trend of the times seems to favor games where individual glory is greater than everything else. There's a widespread lack of cooperation awareness among players, everyone wants to show off their own abilities, leading to frequent failures in co-op missions and a downward trend for co-op games. Major developers have made various modifications and innovations to ease this situation (mostly domestic devs, won't mention them). Overwatch ultimately compromised and added Deathmatch, and GTAV's Doomsday Heist prep missions don't even need a 4-player squad to start. Even though the current trend favors the individual, I believe true gaming lies in team spirit. [h1]Four[/h1]As for money glitching and mod menus/cheats, there's not much to say—after all, any game is gonna have cheats, trainers, and whatnot. I think money glitching isn't wrong; the prices are so high and mission payouts are so low, how long would it take to buy some luxury items? Maybe what I'm saying is wrong, but think about it from another angle: as casual players, we don't have that much time to grind, we still have things we must do, running around for a living. In my view, as long as money glitching isn't taken too far, you can still experience the fun of the game. [spoiler] For casual players [/spoiler][b] I neither advocate nor oppose [/b]money glitching behavior. Cheaters/modders are a bit too much though—they ruin lobby order and go on random killing sprees. You might think it's super fun, but have you ever thought about how the people being bullied by cheaters feel? No! You're just here to cause chaos and disrupt this harmonious Los Santos (wink). Cheaters are our common enemy! To build a harmonious and beautiful Los Santos, we need everyone's effort! (Big wink) [h1]Five[/h1]Thanks to Rockstar for giving us a world! Looking forward to the next GTA! [h1]If GTASA was where our dreams began, then GTAV is the continuation of our dreams.[/h1]

translation_en: Foreword: If all of this is too much reading for you, you can just scroll down to the bottom of the review and read my conclusion. I am only using rough numbers in this review that might deviate, but not really enough to make my review a lie. GTA 5 Singleplayer: Has an interesting story, good gameplay, great graphics for the time it was released, and has moments that make the singleplayer really great. Here and there there were some problems regarding mods in SP (just look it up if you're interested), but all in all a solid game. GTA Online: The actual part of GTA 5 / Online, I'll divide the whole thing into Pro and Contra and rate it with points. Pro: - You have your own character (multiple can be created) and fully customizable with the given means [2 points] - The multiplayer is extensive with many vehicles, weapons, game modes, missions, and free DLCs that are released every now and then [5 points] - I've already had several days where I had a lot of fun with random people in the game or with friends, no matter if we earned money, did stunts, or just beat each other up [4 points] That's roughly the positive stuff about GTA Online. Contra: - Over the years, the game has evolved more and more into a paywall-like grind. [-10 points] -> Grind factor: New content costs more dollars + Rockstar or Take Two Interactive reduce the rewards received after missions and the like. -> Paywall with combined grind: 1.25 million to access certain missions (Doomsday Heist), 2.5 million to access certain missions (Import/Export missions), 1.2 million to access certain missions (Bunker and Gunrunning). >>> Now, as an example, I'll go into an import/export mission: I have to steal a car, worth 2.7 million dollars (X-80 Proto), which is guarded by 10 bodyguards, one of them has a key to the car, I get rid of the guards and steal the car, then get chased by a helicopter and an armored car, I arrive at the vehicle warehouse, repair the damage incurred at my own expense let's say 5,000 dollars and then sell the vehicle worth 2.7 million to a specialty dealer with elaborate tuning which costs another 20,000 dollars, during the sale I again have pursuers who damage my car so the value is reduced again by about 5,000 dollars. So I get 100,000 dollars for stealing and selling the vehicle minus 30,000 dollars from the costs incurred, so 70,000 dollars. That is relatively little considering that I did about 70% if not more of this sale myself. Add to that the fact that I can't choose which car to steal, but the game assigns it randomly. So I don't even get a guaranteed 100,000 dollar commission, but only 30,000 or 62,500 dollars, and then you have to keep in mind that you can't just do these missions all the time, but after a vehicle is sold there is a cooldown of 11 minutes. Not only do the missions repeat all the time and I am constantly chased by something that is just annoying, I also have to wait for the missions. - But that's not even the climax, there are vehicles worth 4-6 million, to buy the vehicles naturally you can also use microtransactions. Whereby the word microtransactions could also be changed to macrotransactions. For 100 USD (real currency of course) you can buy 8 million dollars, which means that a single vehicle in a game that STILL costs 60€ without discounts, a single vehicle alone would cost 75 USD? You'd think I was buying DLCs for Train Simulator. This makes GTA Online the absolute definition of inflation, which makes me extremely sad because a great game lies beneath such a pile of garbage. [-6 points] Total sum: -5 points Conclusion: Point 1: NEVER buy Shark Cards in GTA Online because you are simply supporting this ridiculous business model with it. Point 2: The basic idea of the game is good and also fun, the business model in turn ruins the entire gaming experience, you'd think it was a Free 2 Play game with paywalls and waiting times, I haven't mentioned everything here either because that would just take too long, but this review should just reflect the current state of the game, especially since the Battlefront 2 scandal the gaming community should really take a look at what the current gaming industry is mutating into. Many thanks to everyone who read the review to the end. I hope it was a help for you to make a decision about the game.

translation_en: Pros Feature I Status Graphics I ✓ Gameplay I ✓ Enjoyable I ✓ Design I ✓ Recommendation I ✓ 2-Player I ✓ Audio/Music I ✓ 9/10 Cons -Waiting on loading screens pisses everyone off, of course -Frame drops happening from time to time Story: ******THERE ARE SPOILERS******* The game starts with a bank robbery mission that took place in 2004. The failed robbery set in the city of Ludendorff, state of North Yankton, is carried out by Michael Townley, Trevor Philips, and Brad Snider. After taking the money from the bank, during the fight with the cops, Brad is killed by Agent Dave Norton. Dave also shoots and injures Michael. Although Trevor wants to keep fighting the cops instead of leaving the team behind, Michael tells him to escape. Trevor manages to escape by taking a civilian woman hostage. In the next scene, Michael's funeral appears. However, the person buried is actually Brad, and Michael is alive, watching the funeral from afar while smoking his cigarette. Michael Townley enters the witness protection program with his family in the city of Los Santos, state of San Andreas, and starts living under the alias “Michael De Santa”. And the game continues in 2013. Franklin Clinton, working as a repo man for a car dealership along with his best friend Lamar Davis, receives orders from his boss to repossess the car of Michael's twenty-year-old son Jimmy, who bought a new car but is late on his loan payments. While Franklin is taking the car and heading to the dealership, Michael appears in the back seat. Realizing that his son is about to fall victim to a loan scam, Michael orders Franklin to crash the car into the dealership, and Franklin crashes into it. After this incident, Franklin is fired from his job but becomes friends with Michael. Catching his wife Amanda in bed with her tennis coach, Michael, along with Franklin, chases the tennis coach all the way to his mansion and destroys the mansion out of great rage. However, the mansion belongs to Mexican drug lord Martin Madrazo, and Madrazo, getting very angry at this, demands Michael to cover the expenses of his mansion. Michael decides to rob a jewelry store with the help of his old friend Lester Crest and pay off Madrazo's debt with the money they'll make from this robbery, and they pull off the heist. Trevor Philips, the only survivor of the Ludendorff robbery, gets news of this robbery and realizes that the person who pulled it off can be none other than his old friend Michael, whom he thought was dead; later, he tracks Michael down in Los Santos and confronts his former partner. The characters' personal lives start getting out of control. Trevor's unexpected reappearance causes Michael to exhibit reckless and unstable behavior, which leads to his family leaving him. Over time, Michael earns the enmity of Devin Weston, a wealthy billionaire entrepreneur and venture capitalist. As events unfold, Weston starts bearing a grudge against Michael and vows revenge. Franklin is bothered by what Harold “Stretch” Joseph, a traitorous gangster who joined a rival gang while in prison and repeatedly attempted to kill Lamar to prove himself to his new gang mates, is trying to do to Lamar. Trevor, in his struggle to solidify his methamphetamine market in Blaine County, has entered into a war against the San Andreas branch of the Lost motorcycle club, numerous Latin American street gangs, rival meth dealers, government-backed mercenaries, and the Triad gang led by Wei Chang, one of the top figures of the Chinese underground criminal underworld. In order to undermine the IAA, the rival of the FIB, Michael is forced by two FIB agents, Dave Norton and Steve Haines, to carry out a series of operations alongside Franklin and Trevor. At Haines's instruction, they attack an armored convoy carrying an IAA funding source and rob a bank that holds the payroll of every corrupt cop and public servant in Los Santos. When Haines reaches the point of facing an inquiry for his illegal activities, he forces Michael and team to infiltrate the FIB headquarters and delete all evidence against him from the files. Seeing this as an opportunity to eliminate the pressure Haines has been putting on him, Michael deletes Haines's file while simultaneously removing the evidence of his own past activities. Michael and Trevor do a job for Madrazo, and Trevor wants to get paid for their services to Madrazo, but instead he kidnaps Madrazo's wife, which puts his and Michael's lives in danger for a while and causes him and Michael to flee the city and go into hiding. After Trevor returns Madrazo's wife, the trio starts making plans for the biggest heist of all time: robbing the gold bullion reserves from the Union Depository. Upon returning to Los Santos, Michael patches things up with his family and they start living together again. However, Trevor finds out that Brad, one of his partners in the Ludendorff robbery, is not in prison as he thought, but was killed and is buried in Michael's grave. Trevor thinks he was betrayed by Michael, and this leads to disagreements among the group, posing a threat to the plans they made for the Union Depository heist. While Michael and Dave Norton are caught in a Mexican standoff taking place between the FIB, IAA, and private security firm Merryweather, Trevor arrives at the scene and saves Michael. He explains his reason for saving him despite everything is that he doesn't want anyone other than himself to kill Michael. Although Trevor doesn't forgive Michael, he agrees to part ways with Michael after carrying out the Union Depository heist as planned. The trio of Franklin, Michael, and Trevor successfully pull off the Union Depository heist. After a while, Franklin is pressured by Haines to kill Trevor, and by Weston to kill Michael, driving him to an impasse. Franklin has three choices: kill Trevor, kill Michael, or let them both live and face his own enemies. The player decides which choice will be carried out. If Franklin kills Michael or Trevor, he cuts ties with the remaining character and returns to his old life. Alternatively, if he kills neither of them, the trio withstands all pressure and joins forces, setting out to kill Haines, Stretch, Wei, and Weston. After eliminating all their enemies, the trio stops doing business together, but they maintain their friendship. translation_en: GTA Online has barely anything to do with GTA V anymore! The reason for this is the many recent updates that keep making the game more unrealistic and nonsensical. The gangster vibe that defined the series has been replaced by tons of unrealistic and unfair content. The worst thing about GTA Online, though, is the community, which feels like it consists of 10% hackers, 40% kids, 45% money- and kill-obsessed idiots, and 5% normal players. Rockstar has only itself to blame for this terrible community: 1. For example, when you do a vehicle cargo source mission, every other CEO in the lobby gets tasked with stopping the theft for a comparatively tiny reward. This pits players against each other even more and ensures that nowadays, in EVERY vehicle sale or source mission, 20 random players try their absolute hardest to ruin your mission, even though it gains them NOTHING since they aren't even CEOs. For example, when you're trying to sell your stolen vehicle, some ASSHOLES wait 20 minutes outside the warehouse just to deny you an $80,000 profit. And literally for no reason, since they don't even get anything for it. 2. Because of all this ridiculously expensive OP content lately, like the Oppressor, hackers and people with hacked money get an extra advantage, because even with CEO missions it takes forever to earn $5,000,000. Especially when you are CONSTANTLY hunted down by these Oppressor kids. Hackers and rich kiddies are therefore completely overpowered in EVERY well-populated lobby and can make the game an absolute hell for any normal player with complete impunity, FORCING them to switch lobbies, where only the next batch of idiots is waiting. 3. Because of all the unnecessary and annoying kills by the aforementioned "people," even the normal players I run into seem to have an instant panic attack because they think I want to kill them, and they shoot me on sight. Because of this, playing in a public lobby basically means playing entirely by yourself and avoiding everyone else out of fear. I've never encountered such a broken community, and the online mode only makes sense if you play with real or Social Club friends you know a bit better and who are reasonable. Actually, the online mode is way better than the story, and you could easily just ignore the useless content (which is difficult because of the INCREDIBLY annoying in-game ads), but I can play for a maximum of 2 hours before I want to smash my hardware to pieces because of hackers and rich spastic kids abusing this crap. There are also very frequent crashes during the endless loading times, which wouldn't even be a problem if you could at least play decently afterwards. Besides, I'd really appreciate it if my 25 supercars, some of which cost $2,500,000, could actually go faster than roughly 220 km/h, which wouldn't be an issue in terms of implementation and hardware demands since it works without any problems in story mode using Franklin's ability. Conclusion: If it wasn't for the terrible community and the OP content, GTA Online would be by far the best game on the market (and has been for almost 5 years now), but right now it's just a mix of an exaggerated physics sandbox and an infuriating generic shooter, and for a €60 game from Rockstar, I definitely expected a lot more fun. In the end, you just get pissed off at other players... Edit: Meanwhile, the game just gets worse with every update. On average, I can only play for 1.5 hours before the servers / connection to the server drop or just glitch out (e.g., "required catalog files could not be downloaded" or something similar). The old problems haven't been fixed either, they've just gotten worse! Since I can barely play the game anymore, I should honestly get my money back! It feels like Rockstar is slowly shutting down servers or something. GTA V: 9/10 GTA Online: currently a 2/10 at most I really hope things change soon, because the game used to not deserve bad reviews at all!

translation_en: Gta Online: What started out as a REALISTIC game... where you accompany your character on their journey doing missions and earning money to buy a nice apartment, has lately turned into a game about ABSOLUTE megalomania. For example, back then the Adder (Bugatti Veyron) was the most popular and expensive car in the game, and whenever you saw someone driving it, you knew they were rolling in dough. Unfortunately, that changed, cars got more expensive, and real estate got more and more ridiculous. Nowadays, if you join a server, you pretty much find the following: You're standing somewhere... maybe looking at your phone first, wanting to bank the money you have. You hear a bang... what happened? Another player runs you over for no reason and shoots you dead before you can even get back up. Since the update, it also happens extremely often that you get killed by one of the new FLYING motorcycles, or simply wiped out during a mission by an orbital satellite. Such a shot is of course very expensive... around $500,000... but that's no problem for most players. About 95% of the players didn't earn their money honestly. They were given money by modders or multiplied it using exploit methods. It's really sad that such a decent game has turned into such an unrealistic and unfortunately broken game full of modders and idiots. As for Rockstar's anti-cheat measures, they have failed across the board. You see more people with player levels in the high hundreds than ever before, and players who want to earn their money honestly are doomed to grind missions in solo sessions just to keep up with the others.

translation_en: [h1] Los Santos, the city where dead men come back to life [/h1] [u] Player since PS3 [/u] Los Santos, how I've missed you since San Andreas, and man, what a great comeback. [h1] STORY [/h1] The game doesn't have the seriousness of its predecessor, GTA IV, but it's not bad. A good story, not one of the best (nothing beats GTA IV in narrative) but it has a lot of action—just saying the prologue is a bank robbery and you can already imagine the rest. [h1] GAMEPLAY [/h1] This Grand Theft Auto features the ability to play with 3 characters and switching between them during a mission is awesome, each with different skills (shooting, driving, flying). First-person mode was also added on Next-gen and, even though it's super disorienting, it looks great. There's also the option to do heists in different ways, either stealthy or all-out guns blazing; it doesn't change the ending, but it can change how much cash you pull off. The physics aren't as realistic as GTA IV's, but it holds up well. [h1] GRAPHICS [/h1] When I played it on PS3 compared to the PC version, it looks like ass, but it was mind-blowing for the time (2013). How the old-gen handled the game was incredible, and now with PC... it's just wonderful. With the settings on High (High, not Ultra) it looks really pretty, I can only imagine Ultra would look super realistic. Not to mention mods—MVGA, Redux, NaturalVision, etc.—it's a visual treat (and of course, a nightmare for lower-end PCs). [h1] ONLINE [/h1] The reason I have over 300 hours. Super packed with activities, from a street race to breaking into government facilities to steal data on a potential nuclear strike... awesome. The downloadable content (DLC) is, thanks to Rockstar, totally free. Of course, vehicles, weapons, etc. will cost GTA dollars, but hey, everybody already knows that, and there's nothing a bank heist can't fix. What impressed me the most is how online changed. I remember those times on PS3 when we were all hyped for the Beach Bum DLC, the Business DLC, DLCs where they only added new vehicles, new weapons, and the occasional piece of clothing for your character, and then... boom! Rockstar finally brings heists to online, and from then on, GTA Online went through major changes (for the better), basically turning into the Fast & Furious franchise (from street racing to flying cars, you get it?). If you're thinking of buying it 2 years after its PC release, don't sweat it, the content in the game will give you tons of hours, and Rockstar isn't slowing down—they'll keep dropping new content (unless, of course, the rumors are true and this is the last DLC). [h1] SOUNDTRACK [/h1] Incredible. Hearing "We were set up" while you're in a Survival mission is awesome. 20 radio stations in the game with a huge variety of tracks for all tastes, from the first trailer song, "Ogdens' nut gone flake", to a station with exclusive songs like "Speedlines miracle masterpiece", "Welcome to Los Santos" and more tracks that would take me like 2 paragraphs to list. [h1] MODS [/h1] Remember that shitshow when they shut down OpenIV and banned mods? Yeah, it was awful, and Rockstar learned their lesson: don't touch mods. It's something that defines us as PC Gamers, something console players can't do—modding the game. And GTA has the most mods by far, from community-made vehicles to graphical mods that demand twice your PC's specs. [h1] FINAL CONCLUSION [/h1] My 4th favorite GTA. Hey, it's not the best, okay? (In case you're wondering, #1 is San Andreas, followed by GTA IV, and #3 is Vice City. Absolute masterpieces). [u]Pros: [/u] -A huge, living map, from the city to the woods and an ocean full of mysteries, unlike GTA IV where the only nature is Middle Park lol. -Plenty of missions (70 main and 30 side). -A super complete Online mode. -Free DLCs -Mods (just don't go online if you install any mods, you'll get banned instantly). [u]Cons: [/u] -If you're expecting a deep story like GTA IV's, you won't find it here. -Toxic people online who just go around killing everyone for no reason (I mean bro, you're just chilling cruising the street in your newly stolen ride when some asshole in a tank shows up and wrecks your shit). -Aside from toxic players, there are mod menu users who use them for evil (wiping out the whole server with out-of-nowhere explosions, forcing your character to do... weird things). Basically Rockstar's anti-cheat sucks. 8/10 [h1] WELCOME BACK TO LOS SANTOS WE MISSED YOU LAST TIME [/h1]

translation_en: Tips from a noob with 1000+ hours, let me give you guys some advice. Shark Cards and starter packs are totally unnecessary. Once you get online, leach off free-roam jobs. Once you hit level 15, go to a clothing store, find the utility vests - heavy utility vest (forget if that's the exact name, check the top racks, bottom few items). This vest (the turtle shell) lets you take way more hits in missions (though your movement speed drops while wearing it). Save the outfit at the store counter, then go to the ammu-nation and buy the Special Carbine. Aside from the MKII, I think it's the best assault rifle in the game. For pistols, wait till you unlock the AP Pistol—hands down the best gun to use from inside a car. Don't buy the Homing Launcher, you can't afford to run it, ammo costs too much. Buy sticky bombs instead; they're cheap, highly effective, and you won't cry when you use 'em (just remember not to run around with a sticky bomb in your hand, if you get hit it'll blow up). Once you're geared up, join some heists. No one's expecting you to carry or top the damage charts, just stay back and play it safe, don't die. And don't go begging for a huge cut either. You're a clueless noob who can't do shit, demanding a massive cut right off the bat is just repulsive. Grind until you've got around 700k, then buy an apartment. Get the cheapest one in Eclipse Towers (they all have the same functionality, the expensive ones just look a bit nicer). Then wait for Lester's call, do the Fleeca Job. On the Fleeca finale (last mission) when you're drilling, don't just jam the mouse forward, push it in slowly. If the drill starts getting hot, ease off. Once you finish Fleeca, go buy the Kuruma—the Armored one from the bottom of the Southern San Andreas Super Autos website. Don't buy the wrong one, the standard version isn't bulletproof. (Once you have the Kuruma, don't go picking fights in free-roam, high-level players will chew you up and spit you out. The Kuruma is bulletproof, not blast-proof). For a daily ride, grab the ęlergy RH8 from Legendary Motorsport. It handles way better than the trash Banshee, and it's free. Don't upgrade the RH8 to the Retro custom—the handling gets a lot better, but the top speed tanks. There's also the Schafter V12. For supercars, get the Zentorno (even if these aren't the absolute highest performance, they're the best bang for your buck). For bikes, I recommend the Pegassi Bati 801—great handling and cheap. The 801RR track version is the same as the standard, just comes with a livery while the stock doesn't. When riding the 801, remember to lean back/wheelie (Numpad 5, or Left Ctrl if you don't have a Numpad). Pop a wheelie and that speed shoots straight up to 120. Get all the heists done ASAP to unlock the Pacific Standard replay glitch. Hit up Tieba or various chat groups to find a squad; random lobbies are a waste of time and too risky. When you're hosting, remember to set the outfit option to "Player Saved Outfits" so you can wear your turtle shell vest. You can buy a MC Clubhouse, just get the cheapest one. MC businesses make shit money, you only want the clubhouse so you can spawn bikes with zero cooldown, plus it gives you 10 bike parking slots. For CEO stuff, buy two large warehouses, then buy the Buzzard attack chopper. It's cheap, handles well, and has homing missiles. Grind crates by alternating between the two warehouses. It's fast money, but mind-numbing. When your warehouses are full and it's time to sell, make sure to lag yourself into a solo public lobby (instructions on how to do that are at the bottom). Get a friend to help you sell; never sell in a populated lobby because griefers are everywhere, and if your cargo gets blown to shit, you've lost your entire investment. Trust me, once you've done everything I just listed, you're already a seasoned veteran and don't need a newbie guide anymore. Hope you have a blast in the world of GTA Online. Also, to all the cheaters crying about ban waves: stop fuckin' whining. You know damn well what you did. You get banned and then run around claiming it was a false ban. I've played for over 1,000 hours, how come I've never been banned once? Let me explain the ban waves: starting around April 2017, there was a massive ban wave. If a single byte of your account data was out of whack, you'd get banned (didn't matter if you were actively modding or just got caught up in someone else's money drop). Things calmed down quite a bit after September. If you received hacked money, Rockstar would usually just do a balance correction (just don't spend more than your original legitimate balance before they do). Getting mod-models forced onto you or getting bombed by hackers won't get you banned, but don't stick around acting cocky. If someone drops a modded object on you or starts griefing you with hacks, switch lobbies immediately. If a modded object gets stuck on you, you have to restart the game completely, otherwise changing lobbies won't clear it off your character. If you're terrified of your cargo getting blown up, open up a network throttling software, find GTA, limit the speed to 1KB, and tab back into the game. Drive around the streets for a few seconds and the lobby will empty out until it's just you. Then tab back out and remove the speed limit. Using this method too many times in one day carries a small chance of getting you banned, so use at your own risk. The Nightclub generates passive income, but the payouts are way too low. The upside is you don't have to mess with supplies or deliveries, but the startup cost doesn't match the returns. Newbies can decide for themselves, veterans do whatever. The nightclub also adds extra garage space which you can pick when buying, but you can't park cars on the first floor. The first floor is strictly for DLC special vehicles—you can only park the After Hours DLC special vehicles there, and so far (no clue how future vehicle drops will turn out, won't comment on that) their actual utility is pretty much zero. Think twice if you're buying it for practical use; check out the older vehicles instead, they're way more useful. Not sure if another ban wave is hitting, but it's always best to force a solo public lobby before inviting your friends when going online. Rockstar will ban you the second they detect anything abnormal with your data (cheats or no cheats). 2018.07.29

translation_en: I want to give a heads up to players who are on the fence. If you only want to play single-player and online isn't your main focus, don't hesitate and just buy it. The game content of GTA V won't disappoint you. However, if you want to play the online portion, you need to mentally prepare yourself for the cheaters in public lobbies and wrongful bans by the devs. Right now, if you get banned, your online character gets reset. Basically, they completely wipe all your online character data and appeals are not allowed. And the chance of a wrongful ban is very high. You'd better make sure you turn off programs like FPS counters and CPU temperature monitors when you play GTA V. Content-wise, this is a great game. I've had a ton of fun playing GTA V with my friends. But even though we tried our absolute best to avoid public lobbies and nobody was cheating, we still got wrongfully banned. Last year I nominated GTA V for BEST GAME, this year I'm nominating GTA V for BANNED FOR NO REASON

translation_en: Hey cuties reading reviews, if you like the following stuff, this game is for you: RPG, open world, Los Angeles city and nature, gunfights, street racing, vehicle customization, flying planes, riding bikes, driving speedboats, steering submarines, all kinds of low-to-high-end criminal activities, dogs, animal roleplay... Yup, I happen to like all of them (* ॑꒳ ॑* ) . Rockstar's single-player games always guarantee good gameplay, and as a hardcore nostalgic fan of the GTA series who finished this in one go, I am totally satisfied (•‾⌣‾•). Missions with just the right difficulty, smooth handling for land, sea, and air vehicles, a reasonable and immersive plot, funny dialogue that fits the characters... Simply put, it's a game worth your money and time. Buying GTA V also comes with a free, continuously updated online game called GTA OL. Yep, you heard that right, totally free, paid DLCs are not a thing here. Don't hesitate if you haven't bought it yet, full price isn't a rip-off, half price is an absolute steal ヾ(*´▽‘*)ﾉ . As a lifelong single-player gamer, when I first heard about online GTA, I actually wasn't having it. Because you can't just tell me to play and make me play right away. First, I can't afford to pay to win; second, I don't have the grind in me (manual smiley face); third, I have PvP anxiety {{(>_<)}}. I remember it was a cold, quiet morning when I finally made up my mind to try out the freebie. With trembling hands, I clicked on the Online mode, clutching the Shark Card I bought in a bundle with the game, feeling all nervous inside. I always heard those bastards talking about heists and robberies, afraid I'd get blasted into a crying mess the second I logged in and lose all my stuff ಥ_ಥ ... ...... ...And then? Well, then I played another 1000 hours (｡ŏ_ŏ) . This is the first time I've ever experienced the joy of online gaming [spoiler] (actually I've never played online games before ==)[/spoiler]. I love teaming up for heists, I love leading newbies to steal cars and cargo, I love all kinds of out-of-the-box PvE and PvP jobs, I love ambushing noobs in lobbies to boost my K/D, I love buying things and customizing things, and most of all, I love any mission where I can fly planes \(≧▽≦)/ (Hangar missions are super fun)! As for modders/cheaters, if I can't beat 'em, I can at least avoid 'em (actually, getting my model glitched sometimes was pretty hilarious, gotta admire their rich creativity and imagination). I met some buddies, joked and bullshitted together, banded together to collect rare cars (lining up a bunch of hearses, modding their horns and colors the same, and cruising downtown, or driving four hearses to rob a bank in a mission 23333); we put on the cutest little dresses and went to the mountain to take photos with the female ghost (ಠ_ರೃ pity I lost all screenshots before reinstalling my system); over and over again, I carried groupmates through the Criminal Mastermind challenge; fought shoulder-to-shoulder in survival mode enduring 10 waves of attacks; grinded the Pacific Standard till we puked on double payout days... When we didn't feel like committing crimes, we'd set up a match of tennis, darts, parachuting, golf, or ride the Ferris wheel at the amusement park... and still had an absolute blast. ...... ...And then? Well, then my buddies all went off to play PUBG Σ(っ °Д °;)っ . Left without any friends, I had no choice but to quietly grind out all the achievements and retire early while my criminal empire was booming. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Just heard the news about the Dec 12 heist update, rising from the dead for a bit. Rockstar ID: collychang, feel free to add me and play together. Also welcome to join my retired veteran club, QQ group number: 618175569. Thanks to GTA Online for continuously breathing life into Los Santos, I really, really love this land (╭￣3￣)╭♡

translation_en: Just happened to glance at it, and it looks like this review made it to the store page's featured tab for a month. Since someone in the comments is accusing me of money glitching, I'm updating my full review to address it. If you have any doubts about my experience, please head over to this portal and read [b] [u] [url=tieba.baidu.com/p/5586116518?pid=118576804330&cid=0&red_tag=1587799214#118576804330] My Story [/url] [/u] [/b] [h1] About GTAV [/h1] Just how good of a game is GTA5, how much heart the dev team put into it, and what kind of developmental history this series has... please look that up on Baidu yourselves. After all, I personally prefer to introduce things through my own experiences. The first time I ever laid eyes on GTA, I wasn't even in elementary school yet. In an internet cafe run by a relative, under the dim lights, I watched the older kid sitting in front of me play a game that looked super interesting—even though he seemed to just keep dragging people out of cars and getting in himself. I asked the network admin, "What game is this?" The admin told me it was Grand Theft Auto, turned down my request to try playing it, and opened up *PopKart* for me instead. Even though my parents were strict and I didn't get much exposure to various games, whenever there was an elementary school sports day or field trip, classmates would bring their beloved handheld consoles, which naturally included the well-known PSP. Terms I couldn't understand at the time kept popping up in my classmates' discussions, but that didn't stop me from being a quiet spectator. I saw some kids even writing down stuff called "cheat codes" all over a scrap of paper. ↑L↓R←L→R — that's the only cheat code I still remember and have actually used myself, seemingly the tank-spawn code for *Vice City*. In middle school, I saw CJ from *San Andreas* on a classmate's phone, and watched a friend fly helicopters and glitch out motorcycles on a PSP. How fun, with so many weapons to choose from, and such a huge map to roam around in... but why does the car break so easily? And hey, what does that "hooker" thing you guys keep talking about mean? The final fragments of memory, swept along by the passage of time, gradually faded out of my life. Until I saw GTA5. Well then, let me see what kind of story you're going to tell me. Payment successful. Right after opening the game, my mental journey went something like this: Robbing a bank right out of the gate? Intense! Damn, this opening feels just like a blockbuster movie! Whoa, stealing a car, and looks like a convertible too? Awesome! Huh, character special abilities? Oh, the black dude. Wait, are you—Brain Accelerator?! Before I got into GTA, the three words I heard most often were "Pacific Standard," which apparently was online mode stuff? Since it had multiplayer features, and I couldn't stand being lonely, naturally I wasn't going to miss out. So after some pigeon pulled me down the rabbit hole, I spent the next few hundred hours in online mode. GTA certainly didn't disappoint. A map so big it felt a bit overwhelming, all kinds of vehicles, standard American English, and meticulously crafted character animations and expressions made me feel a genuine sense of admiration for the dev team. As someone who values story, one afternoon I finally made up my mind to try out single-player mode, only to get hit with a dose of reality not long after starting: [spoiler] When Franklin goes to visit Michael for the first time, Michael tells him he should have studied hard and gotten a degree when he was young, so he'd have the chance to become a bourgeois who exploits others with a legitimate excuse. [/spoiler] Thanks, that's way too real, but I'm playing a video game here, uwu. Personally speaking, GTA is undoubtedly a work deeply steeped in social realism. The character dialogue, plot setup, and all the little details we see on the streets are meticulously designed, and we can often feel the game's satire of real-world society. Alas, my life experience is limited, so I can't fully grasp all the messages the creators wanted to convey. But whether it's the fleshed-out character personalities or their behavioral choices when facing adversity, it all oozes an air of "authenticity." And as a renowned open-world game, nobody forces you to do anything. You can spend all day wandering the streets, exploring Easter eggs hidden all over Los Santos and Blaine County, or calling friends to hang out, go to the movies, and drink together. How fun GTA is depends entirely on how much time you're willing to invest in exploration. Strip clubs, a wide selection of guns, military bases you can freely infiltrate... GTA provides elements of sex and violence that players will almost never experience in real life to the maximum extent, while simultaneously making us realize that becoming a "real" criminal has an extremely high barrier to entry and requires corresponding criminal knowledge. A bit of rationality makes it easy to see that all the heists in the game come with meticulous planning and preparation, and a single mistake at any step can lead to total failure. Yet in the real world, plans changing faster than you can keep up is the norm, and this life of living on the edge and getting rich overnight isn't suited for ordinary people—you can't reload a save in life, and someone who takes a bullet cannot heal themselves just by eating a few snacks. I don't know what the aesthetics of violence are, but I don't think games containing bloody and violent content will necessarily trigger criminal impulses in people in the real world. Whether you're an emotional person or not, I hope you all remember this: [b] Violence cannot solve all problems; that's why Trevor is busy all day yet still fails to get rich; But a voice and influence are won through capability, and the core of solving problems can often not avoid a clash of hard power; this is why Lester keeps looking for execution-capable partners; Therefore, when you cannot reason with people, you must have violent means to ensure your own safety—if you can't even do that, what are you going to use to protect your loved ones? However, human strength has its limits. When suppressed by an overly powerful force, you should also possess a strong enough inner resolve, taking shame as courage, to have a chance at making a comeback—this is the choice Michael had to make to secure a comfortable life; Oh right, to a certain extent, people who are economically affluent and independent possess true freedom. [h1] About GTA Online [/h1] Since I'm a loyal online mode player, I naturally can't just gloss over this mode. After face-sculpting and choosing the tutorial, players visit Los Santos as Lamar's homie, starting from the bottom as a low-level thug. Please figure out the rest of the story on your own. Personally, I think the storyline of online mode is also interlocking and meticulously designed. As for timeline issues, let me give a clear answer here: 80% of online content takes place before or concurrently with the single-player mode, and DLCs starting from *Gunrunning* basically take place after the single-player story. When you eventually become a veteran player, you can pay close attention to the character dialogue during heists or everyday crate sourcing and selling; you might just discover something new. [spoiler] For example, is it really money that you're robbing out of the Fleeca Bank? [/spoiler] My own story is pinned at the top of this review, so I won't ramble too much, and I can't really tell the story with pictures and text here anyway. The online mode and its accompanying DLCs indeed make GTA's replayability even stronger: a wide variety of vehicles, officially pushed events, and custom jobs made by players keep the gameplay diverse; players can race, fight, play PvE safely with friends, or even live a peaceful, passive retirement life. Multiplayer heists start testing a player's individual skills and have become the main source of income for most players, but the 4-player team requirement often results in capable players getting dragged down by teammates. Therefore, *The Doomsday Heist* released in late 2017 was probably tailored to player requests, set up as a 2-3 player mode to kick off missions, largely avoiding the awkward situation of having to scrape together four stable teammates just to do missions. Content like *Import/Export* and *Gunrunning* adds business systems that require a large one-time investment for long-term financial returns, allowing players who are willing to grind theoretically to easily realize their tycoon dreams. Overall, though, the design philosophy of online mode seems to include a heavy dose of "encouraging player conflict." Compared to single-player, not only have the cops become lazier, but ordinary players trying to make money seem to face extreme system friction. [spoiler] After all, OL mode isn't a charity; looks like they want everyone to buy Shark Cards. [/spoiler] When hardworking players complete public session deliveries or Special Cargo missions, the whole session gets a system notification, and players are told that disrupting others' production activities rewards them with cash and RP. In reality, the damage caused to others by griefing far outweighs the tiny reward we get from it, but certain players whose sole purpose is venting and destruction will use this as an excuse to go on a killing spree against others. Theoretically, I shouldn't interfere with other players' freedom, but I still hope newbies jumping in won't go around picking fights, while always staying vigilant against anyone approaching them; at the same time, knowing how to use Passive Mode will help avoid the vast majority of disputes. In fact, due to game ballistics and other reasons, coupled with technological suppression, [i] high-level players can easily suppress low-level players in combat effectiveness. [/i] In a game with extremely high freedom and massive content, bugs are naturally unavoidable, but at the same time, practically omnipotent "modders"—cheaters—are even more in their element. They possess the power to blow up the entire lobby, apply gradient color skins to all vehicles, make pies falling from the sky no longer a dream, use restricted weapons and vehicles, and apply model morphs to you... Meanwhile, cheaters have even spawned a sub-industry: money drops. From what I understand, a relatively fully-featured cheat menu costs around 100 RMB. Meaning when these cheaters sell in-game currency at 50 million per 5 RMB, they only need to find 20 players who don't want to spend time on the game to easily experience a free cheat menu. If things keep going this way, they can even make back the money they spent on the game. I've seen people say that money-droppers and cheaters, if they don't actively ruin other people's gaming environments, aren't committing much of a sin. What I want to say is that cheats and money drops are ultimately just a means for law-breakers to profit. Most people who say with their mouths that they won't ruin the game environment can't handle getting slighted, and if they really get stomped by pure skill, what they'll resort to doing is anyone's guess. In the end, Rockstar—who made a good game—doesn't recoup enough funds, while the developers and users of third-party software laugh all the way to the bank. Most importantly, this vicious cycle does nothing except further ruin an already toxic gaming environment. So, if you truly support this game, buy Shark Cards. You can still live a peaceful life with no worldly desires, but the impact of your actions on the game will be positive. Lastly, allow me to rant about Rockstar's anti-cheat measures. Four words: [b] Heartbreaking [/b]. Trying to make money peacefully is not only hard, but it's a massive grind and even requires help from others. We don't use those means that violate the Terms of Service, yet we never get any corresponding protection. Cheats have all sorts of features—not only can they blow up the lobby, but they can also prevent you from reporting them. As a result, today's reporting system is practically useless, and justice never seems to be served. Not only that, they can just casually drop a tiny bit of money on you and report you, easily getting your account banned by R*. Bans nowadays are different from the past: no appeals, character resets. For normal players, this is practically a devastating blow, whereas players who were already money-dropping or cheating don't care all that much. The most ridiculous thing is that some players who used to drop money past 2.1 billion, causing their game functions to break, actually play the victim and beg R* to help them clear out their "excess" money. Even more ridiculously, R* actually grants their wish and gives them zero punishment. Without knowing R*'s banning mechanisms, I advise all players: 1. Do not report modders, because it's useless; 2. Don't curse at modders when you see them; switch lobbies immediately, because they have 100 ways to mess up your data; 3. No matter if it screws over your teammates, the moment you spot someone cheating during a mission, quit immediately; 4. Do not do money drops. Unless you feel you're really too poor to afford Shark Cards, don't have much time to spend on the game every day, already know the gameplay of all missions and heists inside and out, have mastered cargo sourcing and car stealing, don't want to do repetitive labor, and are mentally prepared to further ruin the gaming environment and get banned. I really hate players who buy ranks and money yet think they're hot stuff, running around like headless chickens everywhere. Lastly, answering questions about online mode live, including heist strategies, etc. Questions are welcome. That's all for now. Further content will be updated later. --- *Content from the day of the ban:* Logged in in the afternoon with no friends, logged in at night and caught a permaban. I'll still try submitting an appeal. I'll post the proper review whenever it's done writing / [u] [b] False bans definitely exist, but GTA really is a good game. Solo players have it way harder when it comes to earning cash and leveling up. Doing business solo takes a massive amount of time and effort. If you're hauling cargo (for god's sake, stop doing that shit), after selling a certain number of crates, the game will give you more than one vehicle. You can sell in smaller amounts, but what's the fucking point if you miss out on the bonuses? So what is a solo player supposed to do then? Biker clubs? Most of those missions are designed for two or more players. How about the bunker? The bunker is pretty much the same deal as crates, except if you wait too long and stock up too much product, there's no way you're moving it with a single vehicle. translation_en: GTA is one of the greats, truly one of the biggest in the video game industry, and with all its quality, how could it not be. I’m going to skip the obvious, this game is incredible; a good story, well-implemented mechanics, sound and graphic quality ahead of their time (still being a great work worth seeing today), but if you look at and read the reviews, all of this works great in story mode (except for graphic quality and sound, obviously, we’re talking about the same game)... now, Online... I’ll be honest, at this point I have mixed feelings; it’s very good but very bad. Let me explain: First the bad, 3 words: PAY TO WIN. If you aren't clear on those 3 words, I think you'll get bored very soon, because if you want to fully enjoy the game, you have to buy a shark card from time to time. Let me tell you, the prices of cars and weaponized vehicles (to put it one way) are excessively exaggerated. Everything costs a fortune, and to make decent money, you have to dedicate at least a whole week to it (okay, maybe I'm exaggerating. I think 9-hour sessions for 5 days is more accurate. Yeah, 45 hours to get 1.5 to 3 million depending on the businesses you have, more than that... difficult). You see, money is what rules the game, and that's fine, I enjoy Online mode and the number of activities you can do and the players you get to meet, plus the market is currently like that and it works. Maybe PAY TO WIN is the worst thing in this life, but nobody forces you to buy it and you can get everything paying or not from your own wallet, and for me that's totally fine even if it costs you more time (and a lot of it, but I'll get back to time again), but there is nothing hidden or exclusive. The problem lies in a pretty big part of the community; if players played fair, I think Online would be one of the best experiences in its category, but it’s not like that and it never will be. The platform is super vulnerable with the excessive use of MOD MENUS and the amount of Hackers you run into. Most of them dedicate themselves to annoying people and doing whatever they want; from chasing and killing you endlessly to ruining your businesses, modifying the map, or crashing your game. They are super obnoxious players who have nothing better to do than mess with others. Players who haven't even played 50 hours and are level 300+, with every vehicle in the game and bank accounts with a ton of zeros. Look, this is where it pisses you off and you ask yourself, why bother playing fair? But you still do anyway. You want the experience, but these guys ruin it, although I must admit, not all of them are like that; the other half are low-key and just enjoy the game. I suppose those players are just taking back what's theirs, their time, and once again I emphasize the insane consistency and time the game takes from you to have money and be an established player. I played GTA Online for about 400 hrs, reached level 108 and had the Bunker business, the Office which I used for car export, the hangar, and as my latest acquisition, the Cocaine business which I got around level 100, and that was it. I had a modded Insurgent and a Savage and that's about it. Meanwhile, other players of similar levels had nothing left to buy because they'd already bought everything. See? Anyway, I've rambled on. The good stuff is obvious. GTA Online is not a bad game, Rockstar does its thing and protects its interests like any company to pay its employees and develop the great games they bring us... but Rockstar, come on, don't overdo it, you're abusive and you don't respect your legit players. To wrap it up, I got banned. And I admit it was totally justified; I injected 20 million. I did this because all the things I mentioned... just overwhelm you. My intention was to compensate for my time in GTAO, nothing more, nothing less. Even so, after the ban I submitted a ticket to respectfully ask for "forgiveness" for my loyalty to their game, which was denied. Now I'm stuck with a banned account for a month and my stats wiped, and honestly, I don't plan on playing again after investing so much time into a game that rewards hackers 24/7 instead of the small minority that plays fair. I think if you intend to fully enjoy this game, you need to know that you'll need friends to play with, otherwise, it's very hard to last without getting bored. I say this because everything I just mentioned, I lived it. As a verdict, the game is good and worth it. I recommend it if you want to play with friends and have a good time. If you play fair, stay fair and nothing will happen. You'll get pissed off many times because of Hackers, but if you manage to have patience, you'll get through it. But based on my experience I CANNOT RECOMMEND IT. Thanks for reading and your comment is welcome, this way we open up dialogue and share points of view.
