translation_en: An absolute record... 385 hours at the time of writing this review... if a year ago someone had told me I'd spend this much time in Grand Theft Auto V, I would've never believed it. But, unfortunately, it's true. I've wasted 385 hours of my free time, and I'll easily waste another 15. Why?... Look... Didn't the game hook you? Well, you already forked over your hard-earned 2 grand [rubles], and you gotta make that money back somehow! The answer is simple - play. You have nothing else left to do. Take my case, for example: Up until level 50 in online, I was getting my ass kicked. I had little money, few guns, zero skill. But, having finally hit that cherished number 50, I unlocked all the joys of GTA. I don't know how it happened. I just decided I needed to change something. I changed my haircut, my clothes, my playstyle. I realized you gotta be more selfish, and never help anyone. Kill or be killed. That's how players stroke their egos. Get used to it. I also got the combat machine gun, which became my second wind. This is your first rush weapon. Your first killing machine. You don't need anything else at this stage. That comes later, when you're level 100, with sick guns and a stilt house, you'll be more precise, patient, stealthy. But for now, you're a trash-tier noob, and all that's gonna save you is sheer firepower, in the form of the combat machine gun. Until you unlock the Heavy variant, this is the most lethal piece of shit that shoots at medium and long ranges in your weapon wheel. That's how I got into GTA, with a machine gun and a biker helmet on. How you'll do it, God only knows. So you can't afford to relax. Now, the details of GTA (Online) gameplay as a list: 1) You'll be creating your "senpai" for a long time. It'll take a while before you make a character you actually like. I made mine around level 55, with the release of the "Independence Day" update. I still play as my badass wolf in a suit to this day. For the record, I'm level 104 already. Only after creating this "outfit" did I truly fall in love with who I'm playing as. 2) Most cheaters are your ticket to the world of fun. Sure, there are those who ruin the whole session, but you can easily escape those by hopping to another one. Most hackers will gladly share a couple dozen million bucks with you, which will make your life way more interesting and spare you the endless grind on missions and heists. Believe me, having 3 houses with fully upgraded sports cars, 10,000 rounds of ammo for almost every gun, and the ability to buy whatever your heart desires at any moment is way easier than grinding your dick off for some Coil Brawler that costs 800k, and spending your whole evening farming the money to buy it. 3) Heists aren't shit, but playing each one more than 3 times is almost impossible. You start puking bile. They'll fuckin' annoy you to no end. 4) I realized what I got for my 2000 rubles. I watched GTA change for the better. Every update brought a ton of pros, fun, and seriously improved the "base" of the game itself. For example, "Lowriders" introduced the ability to not give a fuck about shi...shitty races and customize your ride based on your character's level instead. Now you don't have to trade wins in races with each other just to get turbo tuning. Now, the main thing - the question of buying it, and a few more details. What makes Grand Theft Auto 5 so unique after all? The answer is: the game has everything that can hook ANY gamer. Love racing? - GTA 5. Love 3rd-person shooters? - GTA 5. Love 1st-person shooters? - GTA 5. Love open worlds? - GTA 5. Interesting story? Co-op? Customization of everything and anything? - GTA, FUCKING GODDAMN, 5! and blah... blah... blah. GTA is like an elite hooker. Expensive, but everyone walks away satisfied. There's not a single person who wouldn't find something to like about this game. So much has been packed into it that everyone will find entertainment in the world of GTA to suit their taste. That's all I wanted to say about the most hyped blockbuster in the gaming industry. It's genuinely worth buying. It'll be able to surprise you, trust me! P.s. Lastly, I want to note that I didn't cover the story mode of GTA 5 because I think it's amazing. Playing it, you genuinely feel those 2000 rubles spent. The characters are great (except Trevor. He's interesting, but personally I find him repulsive. Michael is love ^_^), the world is magnificent and very alive (unlike online), all the missions are super gripping and very interesting. I don't remember a single bad mission out of the 70 story ones. And that's an indicator of quality. Well, that's it! If you read up to this point - you're a hero! Happy New Year everyone, and as usual... SEE YOU ON THE BATTLEFIELD! Good luck!

translation_en: [h1]GTA V is an insanely good game, and IGN giving it a perfect score is totally deserved[/h1] It's been out for so long and I only just thought to write a proper review. It probably doesn't mean much now, but I still hope anyone who sees this realizes what a masterpiece worth buying it is. I totally recommend grabbing a copy. Rockstar really cares about this game too—it comes with official Chinese, the translation quality is awesome, and they actually paid attention to the mainland Chinese market. Even though some people might look at it as a gray-market import, as long as you're a legal consumer, you're an official, legitimate player regardless of local authorization. The story mode's plot is amazing. Just like GTA IV, it's split into biographies for 3 characters, except in GTA IV the other two characters' stories were released as DLC expansions. The plots are all interconnected, and things you don't fully get in the main game can be completely understood through the expansions. GTA V's story mode is really long, and it has extra mission requirements that add to the gameplay. This feature was already in *Grand Theft Auto: Episodes from Liberty City* (specifically *The Ballad of Gay Tony*), except back then, if you missed an optional requirement, you had to wait until you beat the game and pull out your phone to retry. Just like GTA IV, you can still run into strangers or acquaintances on the street to chat or get missions. Los Santos in GTA V is crawling with luxury cars, and each of the three protagonists has their own specific unique vehicle. Even if you lose it or blow it up, it'll just respawn right by their safehouse. The GTA series' garages are back. Unlike GTA SA where you could only store 2 cars, in GTA V you can store as many as you can physically cram in there. GTA V also has vehicle and weapon customization. It costs a decent amount of cash, but protagonists in the GTA series always end up rolling in money by the late game. When your health runs out and you pass out, instead of GTA IV's penalty where they take 10% of your total cash for medical bills, it's a flat $5,000. And when you get busted by the cops, they don't confiscate all your weapons anymore—just all your ammo. Of course, that's because weapon modding is so expensive in GTA V. The cops in GTA V are way more aggressive than in previous GTA games. Brutally murdering just 2 people will get you 1 wanted star, and resisting arrest bumps it up to 2, where cops will start shooting on sight. Killing a cop under any circumstances instantly bumps it up to 3 stars, and the police can deploy helicopters to hunt you down or take you straight out. But when cops take you down, you just end up at the hospital instead of getting arrested, which is pretty unrealistic. GTA V's cops are tougher than in any previous GTA game, and the wanted levels last longer. There are tons of random events in the game, like helping pedestrians out of jams, or helping robbery victims chase down muggers to get their wallets or cars back. You can also hold up cash transport vans, though they don't drop that much money—obviously to keep players from depending on that to get rich. ...... GTA Online is mind-blowing, the biggest in history. The devs cracked down on mods multiple times specifically to keep players from using them to ruin game balance. Even though the top players in some races are obviously cheating, and certain lobbies support custom player-made content (which boosts the game's longevity so it can have the lifespan of a regular MMO), the Heists update is current-gen exclusive and lets you rake in massive cash. On top of that, the devs keep running events to keep the game playable. ...... Ever since GTA 3, the GTA series has been about an ultra-realistic sandbox version of the real-world US, creating a fictional city based on American ones. GTA V's Los Santos is a modified Los Angeles, featuring the desert topography and climate of the American West, the Mediterranean vibe of the West Coast, and a bustling, miniature-LA-style downtown. The city itself is smaller than GTA IV's, and the whole sandbox map isn't as big as GTA SA's either. It doesn't have the amusement facilities of GTA SA, nor the heartwarming detail from GTA IV where paramedics would actually try to comfort and revive injured people lying on the street. But when it comes to game details and city recreation, it's an absolute peak. From its release on Xbox 360 and PS3 on September 17, 2013, to the next-gen console versions on November 18, 2014, Rockstar kept a low profile and quietly worked on the next-gen versions. They cared the most about the PC platform, which wasn't even announced until 2015. Initially listed on Steam for early 2015 back in late 2014, it got pushed to mid-January 2015, then changed to March 24, 2015. The pre-order bonus was $500k in single-player cash, $1M in online cash, and a copy of GTA SA. But then it got delayed yet again to April 14, 2015. On launch day, the PC servers were in pretty good shape and the optimization was surprisingly good. But later on, a massive influx of players and huge online updates made the network performance worse and worse. Combined with some game bugs, it caused constant stuttering. However, based on player feedback, Rockstar basically fixed this issue by September. That said, severe frame drops during explosions and car crashes still happen—they weren't there on launch day (April 14), but at least driving and gunfights stuttering are clearly gone. The stuttering was a bug caused by the game's unstable CPU utilization, where it would suddenly drop, making the graphics card think the game was closed and it could take a break, which tanked the framerate to 0 and caused stutter. This issue was unique to the PC version. It also happened when hitting ESC to bring up the in-game menu, where CPU usage would plummet and it would lag hard. Now this issue is mostly fixed—not completely, but mostly, so it's not nearly as laggy anymore. GTA V's CPU usage in game menus is pretty high. Testing on an i7-4720HQ, CPU usage in the main menu is over 60%. With the framerate capped at 30fps, ingame it's over 40%; capped at 60fps it's around 60%; uncapped it's over 70%. To be honest, the recommended CPU is an i5-3470, and that's cutting it a bit close. Running the game uncapped pushes CPU usage past 90%, while turning V-Sync on drops it to around 60%. The recommended GPU, the GTX 660, using the recommended graphics settings with V-Sync on (since the game uses triple buffering), will cause framerates to tank and lock to 30fps in certain areas, ruining the experience, so you basically have to leave it uncapped. GTA V is super demanding on VRAM and texture settings, and even more demanding on GPU power. I ran a quick test on an i7-4720HQ + GTX 970M + 16GB RAM using recommended settings with V-Sync on, and it held a mostly stable 60fps. But cranking shadows up to "Very High" drops it further. Grass effects, soft shadows, and MSAA are total GPU killers—turn them up even a bit and you're screwed. Soft shadows use Nvidia's tech and look super realistic, but the GPU tax is insanely high. To run those settings, you really need a GTX 970 or above. Story Mode Score: Incredible plot, 9.6/10. Online Mode Score: Servers in some third-world regions need work, but overall it's a pretty solid MMO, 7/10. Soundtrack: Might be slightly less unique compared to previous titles, but overall it's fantastic. The radio stations are the best in sandbox gaming history—tons of channels, easy to switch between them, though changing weapons while driving is still kind of a pain. There are a lot of Spanish stations, probably because of the Mexican immigrant population. To be honest, compared to English, that Mexican Spanish always sounds like the language of a more backward group (no offense intended), 8/10. Overall Score: 9/10.

translation_en: [h1]Buy and play it when everyone else is playing.[/h1] If you're only looking at the single-player, it might be fine to buy it when the price hits rock bottom. But considering that the true charm of this game undeniably lies in its online mode, I recommend buying it early on when a lot of people are playing so you can enjoy it together. [h1]The Pros: Single-Player[/h1] [+] Graphics: A game that makes you despair over your PC specs and consider upgrading. [+] Characters: Three characters with three distinct personalities, especially the psycho Trevor and his neck tattoo (Cut Here...;;). [+] Story: The three-perspectives-in-one story was impressive. Of course, the back-and-forth system allowing you to switch between the three at any time also makes things a bit chaotic and kind of ruins the immersion. [+] Cheat O-Matic: A godsend for someone like me who really hates grinding for money through the stock market or chores. [+] Working girls: Enjoy a sleazy game in a sleazy way. [h1]The Cons: Single-Player[/h1] [-] Various bugs and errors: There was a huge uproar from launch when it wouldn't even start, and even now there are users who still can't run the game due to countless, inexplicable errors. [-] Graphics: High specs and VRAM requirements for its time of release, insanely long loading times, frequent errors, frame drops, random crashes, etc. [-] [strike]No cloud support for single-player save files: People who assumed it was supported because it's a recent game had their mentalities shattered after formatting their PC[/strike]. [i](※ Rockstar Social Club now supports save file cloud syncing.)[/i] [h1]The Pros: Online[/h1] [+] Graphics: You can experience the great graphical feel of the single-player mode right in online. [+] Contact Missions: Fun at first because there's a good variety, and the co-op mode feels like mini-heists. (On the other hand, it gets boring if you grind them endlessly for levels.) [+] Heists: Needs no words. This is the core online content of this game. Experience 4-player full-party co-op raids just like instance dungeon raids in an MMORPG. (Warning: Doing this solo with randoms will completely shatter your mental state, so I recommend playing with Korean users who speak the same language. The world never goes the way you want it to.) [+] Ramp hunting and rare car collection: Finding the 50 stunt jumps and hunting down rare cars gave me a whole different kind of fun in this game. Recommended. [+] People: The most important part of an online game. There are many people I got to know because this game served as a connection, and I liked that it created lots of interactions with Steam friends that weren't there before. [h1]The Cons: Online[/h1] [-] Social Club, servers, and network: Frequent server disconnects on weekends, insanely long loading times, bugs where chat doesn't work or isn't visible—I still can't call the network, servers, or Social Club good. [-] Hackers: It's true that the game is rampant with various mods and cheats, but it's pathetic both ways—hackers acting like assholes even in online mode, and Rockstar failing to issue harsher penalties. [h1]Final Thoughts..[/h1] GTA Online V was my first experience with the online mode. Up until previous titles, I only ever touched the single-player. When I first played San Andreas, I realized that my favorite genre is "open-world third-person action/adventure," and ever since then, I became a fan of Rockstar's delightfully cracked charm. Personally, I feel the core of this fifth installment is online and the Heists, rather than single-player. Actually, I chose Steam to stay away from online games (MMORPGs) due to my personal circumstances, but this game forced me right back into playing online anyway, chatting with people over voice comms until late into the night, getting sleep-deprived and dozing off at work. It's been a long time since I felt the joy of online gaming like this. As expected, the ultimate fun is playing together, and among that, I think cooperative play (co-op) rather than multiplayer (PvP) is the real deal for me. Over 600 hours of playtime that never would have happened with just the single-player.. Just for that, I don't feel like I wasted a penny, so I recommend this game!

translation_en: I've been a severe gaming addict for years, as well as having anger issues. Ever since I got into GTA, I've found my true self again. When I first bought it, I just wanted to enjoy a violent open world, but I never expected that this violent game would bring me peace. Every time I start playing online and begin slaughtering other players, I immediately get forcefully kicked from the session and turn into a white cloud floating above Los Santos. At that moment, I can look out over the entire city. Oh god, I've never seen such a beautiful city! Behind me are falling raindrops, hurtling down towards Los Santos just to splatter their broken bodies on the ground. As I'm admiring the rain in Los Santos, the rain god somehow packs away his playful tricks. The dark clouds behind me disperse, and sunlight breaks through the bustling layers of clouds. The shadows of the buildings in Los Santos intersect, and the lights of cars flow through the streets. Before long, the sunset fades and the bright moon hangs in the sky. At this very moment, Los Santos is as quiet as a bride-to-be, yet her heart is throbbing with fiery anticipation. I start to deeply blame myself—why did I want to taint this beautiful city?! No matter when I log into online mode, Rockstar keeps me floating in the firmament. It's as if they are protecting me, protecting a closed-off and broken heart that has been locked away for years from sinking any further. For the first time ever, I leave the computer not because I'm being chewed out by my parents, but by getting up from my gaming chair on my own, walking over to my parents, and saying: "Mom, Dad, can you take me out to the countryside?" My parents' expressions shift from apathy and disappointment to surprise. They look at me with overflowing joy, because I, who used to shut out the world outside, actually took the initiative to leave this virtual world and embrace nature! Thanks Rockstar, for making me stop wasting my life.

I've always waited for something like this, something that would hook me and not let go, something I could boldly play for days without thinking I wasted my time. I feel like the core of the whole atmosphere rests on the shoulders of the characters and the plot, and that's where the perception of the game grows from. And that's strange, because all around us is a huge world that holds so much interesting and new stuff. Although, looking at it from another angle, it's totally normal since the main characters immediately become like family to you. The only things that haven't changed in this game since San Andreas are the lampposts; everything else looks quite updated and pleases the eye—beautiful landscapes, flora and fauna, memorable characters, and a magnificent atmosphere. It's always nice to come back to this game after work, and for that alone, it deserves respect. The graphics in the game are simply top-notch, looking attractive and decent even on minimum settings. Of course, on high settings the picture is just gorgeous, just like the game itself. Excellent optimization; it's been a long time since I've seen that in newly released games. It's very nice that the developers tried hard and made a game for the people, and not just for personal enrichment like many do nowadays... Most of us could write at least 10 volumes about Grand Theft Auto V. I suppose there's just no point in doing that, since you and I already know how high-quality this game is. And I wrote this review purely out of respect for the developers. It makes me very happy that there are still developers who bring goodness to their loyal fans. Even for 2k [rubles], this game is a gift, a gift to loyal and happy Grand Theft Auto fans. *[i]Written for you by the [url=http://steamcommunity.com/groups/bestgoodgames]''Best & Good Games''[/url] community (subscribe if you liked this review)*.[/i]

translation_en: Check out [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/26214428-%25E9%259B%25BB%25E7%258E%25A9%25E7%258B%2582%25E7%2586%25B1%25E6%2584%259B%25E5%25A5%25BD%25E8%2580%2585/lists/] Gaming Fanatics [/url] for more game reviews, info, and guides. Alright. First of all, as a hardcore fan of the PC version of the GTA series for 14 years (2002–2015), I'm giving this game a positive review! For old-school fans of the GTA series, the PC version of this AAA masterpiece is something I've been waiting for ages. This game leaves you with mixed feelings of joy and sorrow, and after playing for 200 hours, I can finally write a proper review. I'll stick to my own style for this, writing it very seriously and pointing out all the pros and cons I can think of. [h1]Graphics[/h1] This is a next-gen game from 2013. Playing the PC version in 2015, the graphics are still stunning. While they are no longer top-tier, they are at an ultra-high HD level. The overall color tone of the game is very pleasing to the eye and looks super comfortable. Car and gun models are on point, and character models are good too, though face modeling still feels a bit lacking. Rockstar's perennial Achilles' heel has always been their terrible foliage. In part 5, herbaceous plants saw a massive improvement, but woody plants still scream heavily overlaid textures at first glance, which feels totally out of place in an HD environment. The water is gorgeous, and the tactile feel and texture of the water bodies are great. There are many kinds of water effects in the game, including sea water, river water, and lake water, and their depths vary. Deep water areas and shallow water areas have distinct vibes, unlike other games where almost all water shares the same texture. Overall, the portrayal of water in this game is exceptionally stellar. Rain and night scenes are full of great details, but the rendering isn't strong enough. Rain and night scenes look very realistic, and the road puddle effects and raindrops hitting surfaces are well-done, but compared to other games, it lacks that post-rendered beauty. [b][u]Replay Value[/u][/b] Actually, the single-player mode of GTA 5 isn't as perfect as people might think, because it cut a lot of great settings and details from previous titles. For example: the body shape system, RPG/stat-building system, gang system, homie mechanics, personal bodyguard feature, martial arts schools and gyms, girlfriend system, and fun mini-games (like arcade machines and billiards). They also cut minor details, like leaving the car running when you get out in GTA 4 (in GTA 5 you can only keep it running if you bail out while moving), pedestrians using umbrellas, and other atmospheric details. In this game, when you ride a motorcycle, your clothes don't even blow in the wind—yet *Vice City*, released twelve years ago, portrayed that detail vividly. Especially, the number of enterable buildings has decreased. But why is it still an awesome AAA masterpiece? Because while it cut a lot of classic settings, it added even more interesting elements. If you feel the single-player mode isn't exhilarating enough, the Online mode will give you a refreshing experience. The map size is 7.2 times larger than GTA SA, and the rich variety of online missions and game modes keeps the replay value of the GTA series firmly at the top of the sandbox game throne. The interactions with players, NPCs, and the developers give you a truly immersive feeling of roaming around a sandbox world. I won't spoil what specific things were added—you have to play it to find out. At the end of the day, if they hadn't cut those classic settings from VC, SA, and 4, GTA 5 would have been even more powerful. (Some players might be very unhappy with Rockstar's servers. This review only discusses game content and won't evaluate the servers.) [u]Follow-up update:[/u] The Online mode of this game has been consistently updated with high replay value; clocking 1K+ hours is no problem at all. [h1]Music & Sound Effects[/h1] It maintains that classic GTA flavor: cool BGM, in-car music where you can add your own custom radio station, and a mix of pedestrian NPCs with voice acting from all over the world (you'll hear English, Russian, Cantonese, Mandarin, etc.). Sometimes you can hear Chinese people speaking Mandarin on the street. However, the sound effects in this game aren't as good as the previous titles because vehicle engine sounds are mostly identical, and weapon firing sounds are pretty much all the same. Also, the theme music for this entry isn't as distinct and full of personality as past games, and they even removed the background music that played upon successfully completing a mission. [h1]Combat Experience[/h1] It also sticks to the classic GTA style: guns, cars, boats, planes—you can fight anytime, anywhere, using any vehicle. The GTA series has always focused primarily on gunplay, with melee combat taking a supporting role (Sleeping Dogs went the exact opposite way and innovated its own style). So, how are the shooting feel and driving feel? Praiseworthily, the driving feel is fantastic; every distinct vehicle has its own handling difficulty and feel. Among games in the same genre, you could say the driving feel is the best. The shooting feel is just average—neither good nor bad—lacking that heavy, visceral bullet-tossing-meat impact found in GTA 3 and VC. Moreover, the game's "combat exhilaration" (you could also call it immersion) isn't ideal. What exactly is the combat experience? Let me briefly explain it here. When we play games, it's easy to notice that some titles make combat extremely thrilling and deeply immersive, whether the enemies are tough or weak, whether the fight is a struggle or a total mowing-down of enemies—even if the physical impact and shooting feel aren't that great. Maybe it's paired with a fitting BGM, or maybe the environmental atmosphere is super gripping. In short, after a fierce battle, it leaves the player with a satisfying, exhilarating combat experience! That feeling is what we call combat exhilaration. But in other games, after a fight, you might feel the enemies are too punishing and BS, or the combat strategy is too monotonous, or it feels too much like mindless mowing. Anyway, some games leave you without that tense and thrilling feeling after combat, even if the hit feedback and shooting feel are decent, making it rather dry and boring—meaning the combat exhilaration is terrible. Well, the combat exhilaration in this entry just doesn't feel as tense and exciting as GTA VC, GTA SA, and GTA 4. [h1]Vehicles & Weapons[/h1] The GTA series has always strived for diverse vehicles. Back in the day, GTA SA's 186 vehicles were shocking, and this year's GTA 5 features over 300 vehicles, which can honestly dazzle a player. To this day, there are still many vehicles I can't remember, and even plenty I haven't driven or simply never seen. The weapons are also dazzlingly diverse, making it the most weapon-varied entry in the GTA series. However, what disappointed me is that the vehicle engine sounds are all pretty much the same, giving off a lazy, phoned-in vibe. Many cars share the exact same engine audio, unlike older titles where every car had its unique engine sound that you could instantly recognize just by listening with your eyes closed. The driving feel, though, can be said to be the best among similar games. One neat feature in this GTA is that vehicles don't flip over as easily as in previous titles, and even if they do flip, it's very easy to right them. But there's one thing about the driving feel that drives me nuts: the car momentum is way too high, and it always feels like you're driving on ice—meaning compared to previous titles, it's easier to "slide out." The handling isn't quite top-tier. Also, it removed the SPAS-12, a brutal weapon included in every past GTA title, likely for balance considerations in the Online mode; part 5 only has one fully automatic shotgun. [h1]Game Story[/h1] GTA 5 is set in 2013, completely breaking away from the gang warfare present in all previous titles. In single-player mode, gang wars are almost nowhere to be seen, and gang events are brushed off lightly in the plot. Because the three main characters aren't gang members, but rather a car thief and high-level organized criminals. The storylines of the three protagonists intersect, offering strong interactivity that previous games never had. Plus, while half of the protagonists in the GTA series are unmarried, one of the main characters this time is not only married, but a lot of effort was put into writing his family drama. Overall, the story is the most unique in the GTA series, feeling very fresh, and the endings are diversified rather than sticking to a single linear path like before. But what left me a bit disappointed is that you no longer get that passionate, hardcore gang-versus-gang turf war vibe from playing the older GTA games. Hopefully, in a GTA 5 expansion or GTA 6, they can blend the contemporary plot style of GTA 5 without losing that 80s/90s gangster aesthetic. [h1]PC Port Optimization[/h1] Needless to say, Rockstar probably felt they did PC players dirty with GTA 4, because GTA 5 is absolute god-tier optimization. Even a GT 630 can run it smoothly on low settings. Unfortunately, high-end players wanting to max out all settings at 1080P and maintain a stable 60 FPS will find it isn't easy. Graphics: ★★★★★ (2014) Sound: ★★★ Shooting Feel: ★★★ Driving Feel: ★★★★ Melee Feel: ★★ Replay Value: ★★★★★ Story: ★★★★ Details & Settings: ★★★★★ Optimization: ★★★★★ Combat Exhilaration: ★★★ Content Richness: ★★★★ Overall Score: 9.3/10

translation_en: Well, a few days after finishing the game, I'm finally gathering the strength to summarize my thoughts on this much-anticipated installment. I’ve played every GTA since Vice City, and whether you like it or not, you end up comparing these games. For anyone whose first GTA experience is this, or who even played GTA IV, I think this turned out to be a pretty perfect GTA game, since GTA IV was the worst in the series—I honestly don't even get why it's IV and not, say, San Andreas. But let's forget IV's shameful failure. GTA V has clearly improved a lot, definitely in terms of graphics, but I think the characters' personalities and behavior are also much better, and the cutscenes give the game an almost cinematic feel. As an old-school GTA player, it was very strange to control three characters here, and even see events from three perspectives and live our weird lives. At first I didn't like it, but then I got more and more into the characters' viewpoints. But how much of our own life do we actually have, how much can we shape it? Well, this part of the game turned out pretty bleak. Let's start with the fact that we can barely customize our characters again; I get that they wanted to create three different lifestyles, but why couldn't they be customized more beyond a few hairstyles and lots of different colored clothes? [b]That massive idea from SA where you could even change your body weight and muscle mass is once again not in the game![/b] Then I have this huge sense of emptiness, not feeling like I'm getting ahead either financially or in terms of power by completing missions. We don't even always get money for them now, which is fine, but sometimes I feel the rewards are way too low. [b]Just like in GTA IV, you still can't buy buildings or stores that unlock new missions![/b] Yet that was also a huge idea in the older games. Back then, you really felt like you were slowly taking over the whole city. The buildings here, however, just give you income and occasionally a few tiny missions. A really bleak execution. Basically, as I progressed through the whole game, I didn't feel like I had any impact on the city; I didn't get buffer, I didn't get cooler, I didn't become anyone's boss—basically I just became a richer guy in the big city, but nothing more. Where is that old GTA feeling? To sum it up: This GTA installment became very flashy, everything is supercharged, everything is prettier and punchier, but the devs once again failed to clear the bar they already reached back with Vice City or San Andreas. Pros: - Gorgeous graphics - The city and countryside feel very alive, adding animals to the game adds so much to this! - Very good character development, cinematic cutscenes - Good jokes - Mid-mission autosave - Multiple endings Cons: - Terrible memory requirements and poor memory management, - memory leak - (the game easily maxes out 8 GB in downtown traffic) - Nothing surprising about the story, it's a "we've seen it before" category. - The player doesn't feel like they're actually gaining more power as they progress - I feel it's a bit too easy, we rarely need to buy weapons and ammo - They once again left out great ideas from VC and SA (buying buildings for missions, and freer character customization) - Somehow that GTA mobster vibe from VC and SA is just missing.

translation_en: 'The game we\'ve been waiting for is out after 1 year and 6 months!' Yes, the game we are talking about is GTA V. Before playing, your PC needs to be powerful and you need 60 GB of free space. While downloading the game takes hours or days, there's nothing else you can do except go crazy with excitement in front of the screen. Also, it's not the same as the Playstation 3 or XBOX 360 versions and has extra features (e.g., FPS mode), and the difference from the Playstation 4 and XBOX One is the Editor Mode. Looking at the map, it's a really huge map and half of the map is city and half is countryside. (Actually, the countryside takes up more space :D) Aside from that, we're on an island anyway, water, sea, and air everywhere. Since the map is so big, wide, and diverse, there are tons of vehicles. (What the author is trying to say here is that there aren't just city vehicles, and that's why off-road vehicles are also very diverse.) Also, air vehicles like Jets and Helicopters are fun in their own right. There are many scenarios and non-mission activities we can do in the game. To give examples of these; going to the movies, mountain parachuting, riding a bike, and so on and so forth. By the way, the Easter eggs are also very diverse; on the map, there are 4 UFOs (1 in the water, 3 in the air), 1 ghost, 50 spaceship parts, Master Chief (those who play Halo know), a frozen Alien, and also there is a money case among the corpses in a fight between a mafia (or similar). (There are no money cheats in the game, and this money case yields 25,000 Dollars. No joke.) You can research and see many Easter eggs like this yourself. Aside from that, the game has its own stock market. In harmony with the missions we do, the share values of companies go up and down in this stock market. The stock market mode is only available in story mode. -The paragraph below contains spoilers!!- To touch upon the storyline without making it too long, the story revolves around 3 characters. Our 1st character is Franklin. He is black (I'm not being racist, please) and you can tell this from his conversations too. Our 2nd character is Michael De Santa, he (used to be) a hardcore criminal. Until his whole gang was killed by the cops. Taking advantage of this situation, Michael steps into a new life with his family by entering the witness protection program (making a deal with the FIB) (I won't even mention the troubled family members) and accidentally(!) destroys the mansion of one of the biggest mafia bosses in the city, and therefore gets into trouble with the mafia. To fix this problem, of course, you need money, and Michael returns to crime. Our 3rd character is Trevor Philips, he is a bit out of his mind (a bit is an understatement) and also one of the gang members Michael thought was dead. Trevor used to be a pilot in the army, but was kicked out because of psychological problems, and because of this, Trevor blames the army and still loves flying. Trevor sees a crime news story in Los Santos, and hears one of the witnesses say something in an interview (a quote from Michael). This quote doesn't leave Trevor's mind, he realizes Michael is alive, and goes to the city. Things get very, very complicated. Also, the war and fight between the IAA (CIA) and FIB (FBI) is reflected in our storyline. -Spoiler is over for your information- We've touched upon the story and the gameplay, what's left? The best part is left. ONLINE!! Yes, online is really fun, GTA V is fun as it is, and just imagine playing GTA V with other players. If you want, you can race, get the police on your tail and drive around the city like a maniac, do CO-OP Heists (there are 5 Heists, they'll probably improve this in the future because only 5 Heists gets boring after a while, man), DeathMatch mode (team, solo, you can choose what weapons are available), a mode where you fend off waves of enemies (I don't remember the name of the mode), and activities like robbing convenience stores. Activities like golf that are available in Singleplayer are also available Online. There are practically infinite levels Online. Well, what is this level good for? There are some special weapons, vehicles, and vehicle upgrades, and these are only given to those at or above that Level. Some cars are unlocked after Heists. For example, vehicles like the Armored Kuruma (an armored, 4-seater, fast vehicle) or Insurgent (This vehicle has a machine gun or a closed-top version. It's an armored vehicle. You could also call it the vehicle the soldiers and police use, commonly referred to as the scorpion). Apart from that, there are upgrades unlocked by winning Races (coming in 1st). You need a High-End house to do Heists. These high-end houses range between roughly 300,000-500,000. These houses also have a garage, you take the cars you buy out from here. Also, if it blows up, there's a contact in your phone book named like Mors Mutual, if you call them, they give you back any vehicle of yours that blew up. But of course, you have to get insurance. You do that at the mod shop too. It's automatic for cars bought from the internet. If you can't find anything to do, go to the city and kill two or three guys (not NPCs, real players), those guys will keep you busy for a while :) [h1]Pros[/h1] - There are 3 characters in the story and the storyline is really fluid. - There are tons of activities in the game as I touched upon. - The game is long, Online is even longer. - There is a huge variety of vehicles, weapons, upgrades, houses, and clothing combinations. - One of the rare games that genuinely deserves 179 TL. (It was 179 TL when I wrote the review, but they raised the price before the summer sales, then put it on sale -.-) - Also, there's a point I forgot to touch upon. There are many options when doing a Heist. In Singleplayer, you can choose your gang members, and whether to do the robbery stealthily or by rushing in. In Multiplayer, there are many missions in a Heist. For example, one holds the hostages, one blows the safes, and the other hacks the system. [h1]Cons[/h1] - Bugs... (Some bugs can be funny, but a bug is a bug.) - FPS drops. My rating: 95/100 I know it was a long review, but bro, this is GTA V. It's a pretty long game. I tried to cover everything in this review, I'm glad if it was helpful. Also, this can be considered my first written review, my other reviews weren't this detailed. If I made mistakes, write them in the comments and I'll fix them. Bye :) Review Date: 08.06.2015 (Yeah, it's a bit late)

translation_en: [h1]Saving the Best for Last[/h1] [h1]Introduction[/h1] For me, the summary of GTA V is two peak moments I experienced. One is crashing a plane into another plane during a mid-game mission, fighting the guys inside, stealing the plane, and then jumping out with a parachute to watch it crash so I wouldn't become fish food for military jets, all while feeling emotionally invested. The other is driving an off-road buggy in the desert, spotting a road going up a mountain, spending 5 minutes driving up there, and then getting chewed out by a group of hikers. And them telling me they almost get run over by perverts driving ATVs every time they go for a hike. I could go on like this for years; GTA V is packed with moments, both big and small, that make up San Andreas. The city of Los Santos and its surrounding area feel like a living, breathing world where anything can happen at any moment, and it actually is. You are given a conservative, darkly funny, exciting story along with a world you can explore forever. And the fact that it's a step up from the previous game in the series is easily proven by the fact that there isn't a single gameplay element in the game that wasn't improved. The cover system is more familiar and auto-aim for gamepads is more precise. Car physics are buttery smooth so you can experience all kinds of moments, and you get a different driving experience depending on the terrain and climate. And Rockstar has finally beaten its greatest enemy: the checkpoint system. You no longer have to drive the same long way five more times. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=804352501 [h1]Subject[/h1] GTA V is also a contemporary satirical commentary on modern America, especially the post-financial crisis era. The commentary covers all bases: millennials, celebrities, the right, the left, the middle class, the media... Even other modern games haven't escaped Rockstar's sharp tongue. One of the important side characters plays a game called "Righteous Slaughter" in his room until evening, screaming curses at people with his headset never coming off and a "contemporary" tattoo on his neck. No matter how basic this might seem as a foundation, the entire game is packed with eye-opening messages just like this character. GTA San Andreas had a theme that exposed greed, corruption, hypocrisy, and the abuse of power. GTA IV was literally an assassination of the American dream. When I saw the $30 price tag, I thought, "Hmm, a bit pricey, buying this is pretty pointless." I originally bought it just to add another game to my library, thinking it'd be totally fucking useless. But the moment I logged into the game, I realized I was wrong. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- This is a whole new world. Here you can be a moody, eccentric psycho killer, or you can be a hero holding onto your own personal code, walking through this sin-infested, gore-soaked city. The moment you buy the Kuruma, cops and the law probably won't hold any restraint over you anymore. Come on, this is the world of Los Santos. Here you have cursing and deception, glory and humiliation, a glamorous city paved with blood and tears. Law and humility are total bullshit here; cash and bullets are the sweet-ass treasures. Come on, shoulder your Stinger and roar at the cowards sitting inside their Armored Kurumas. Come on, you and your buddies in the Insurgent pickup, declare your challenge to this city. The skies are never short of roaring Hydra kings, and the Rhino on the ground will bare its iron cavalry fangs. The challenges here take courage and wits; the partners here need trust and communication. I am strong because I am fearless. I am fearless because I have you guys by my side. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- It took me 2 weeks to go from level 1 to 90, and a week to go from the Fleeca Job to Pacific Standard. The three of us always lacking a fourth, dragging random people in from the L4D group. It wasn't until we cleared the Pacific Standard Heist that I actually started enjoying doing missions—in other words, doing missions without using the Armored Kuruma. "Doing missions in an Armored Kuruma? Then what's the fucking difference between you and a lazy piece of shit?" Without the thrill of instantly dropping to low health, without the heart-pounding rush of sprinting for cover through a hail of bullets, playing GTA relying entirely on a moving iron fortress to spray enemies down gets pretty damn boring. translation_en: Actually, Rockstar has started shifting their game development focus since GTA 4. Their attention is no longer solely on building city models and maintaining high freedom, but increasingly on character development and narrative performance. GTA 5 takes this to the absolute extreme. The main storylines of the three protagonists intertwine and lock into each other step by step. Several major missions in the main plot are carried out by all three together, allowing players to switch between them on the fly. This is a brilliantly structured writing technique, both in terms of literature and filmmaking. The ultimate result is that it tells a story with an incredible sense of immersion. For me personally, I used to give up on all previous titles in the series, including GTA SA, once I reached a certain point because I could never really immerse myself in the plot, and sometimes I just felt lost and overwhelmed by the open-endedness. But with GTA 5, after spending 70 hours completing the main story, I still wanted more. That's the difference. In terms of character development, Trevor is probably the most memorable character in the entire GTA series. The other two protagonists also vividly display their respective personalities. You could say it gets a full score for character building and plot construction, but the thematic depth of the story barely passes. All in all, it's like a Michael Bay popcorn flick—super fun and thrilling while you're playing it, but without much substance. Also, the sudden shift in two of the final ending choices feels a bit tacked on just to fill the quota. When it comes to the sandbox modeling, it's also a case of a few flaws spoiling a masterpiece. The game map is about the same size as GTA SA, but the detail level is vastly superior. The white clouds drifting in the blue sky, the clear crosswalks on the ground, the bustling traffic during the day, the neon lights at night, scaling from mountains, rivers, forests, deserts, and overpasses down to small details like billboards, graffiti, shops, interior home furnishings, and cigarette butts—it almost perfectly recreates a real world. In terms of specific gameplay, it brings together the vast majority of the series' elements, letting players wander through a lifelike city again and again after beating the main story. The only drawback is that there are too many buildings on the street you can't enter. Many places you can enter during main missions, but they get locked up afterward. So if you're just strolling around, there aren't many places to explore, and you can't interact with many NPCs. In this regard, it's not as good as Ubisoft's games. Maybe this is a bit harsh, but after all, this is GTA. Fortunately, it's rumored that the next generation will fix this issue, along with the technical difficulties of infinite random encounters. Word is that they'll also integrate Online and single-player, allowing players to write and publish their own random plots and missions, which is definitely something to look forward to. One thing that must be emphasized is the god-tier optimization. The game's modeling, graphics, and lighting effects are extremely realistic, but it doesn't force players to have high-end specs. If you're willing to accept lower settings, even old machines can run it smoothly. My computer is a laptop I bought five years ago, with only 512MB of VRAM and 8GB of RAM, which doesn't meet the minimum system requirements at all. But after forcing it to run, it could still handle it despite some stuttering, and in the 80 hours of gameplay, it never crashed or froze once. Before this game, I simply couldn't have imagined that. Another thing you could call perfect is the game's physics engine. Basically, every realistic effect the players and the developers could think of has been made. There are tons of videos online like "100 Realistic Details" or "GTA 5 MythBusters," so you can check those out yourselves; I won't list them all here. As for the controls, airplanes, submarines, and vehicles are all much better than in previous entries in the series, though flying is still a pain in the ass and could be simplified even further in the future. Finally, regarding the Online mode, it's another case of minor flaws. The transition cutscenes are well done, but the tutorial is a bit unclear. Heists are very tense and emphasize teamwork, and the peer-to-peer network structure makes players rarely feel any lag. However, because of this very structure, it's hard to get a full squad together for Team Deathmatches, races, and a series of other activities. Generally speaking, it's suitable for rounding up friends, but not for public lobbies. Plus, there are quite a lot of mods and cheating in Online nowadays. Regardless, it's still a very successful part of the game for enriching gameplay variety and replay value. +2 Plot architecture and character development +1 City sandbox creation +1 Rich gameplay +1 Realistic physics engine, astonishing attention to detail +1 God-tier optimization +1 Online mode +0.5 Decent official Chinese localization -0.5 Weak plot depth -0.5 Extremely annoying vehicle recovery mechanic, worse than our great country [T/N: referring to strict insurance/impound systems] -0.5 Plane controls are absolute torture Overall verdict: 11/10 Beyond a masterpiece. No matter how you look at it, spending 180 RMB for at least nearly a hundred hours of high-level gaming experience is absolute value for money.

translation_en: [h1] 2 years of waiting and [strike] 2000 [/strike] 1999 rubles [/h1] Absolutely everyone with a decent PC and good internet (the game is ~60 GB) has already managed to test this game out. Some have already played it on previous and next-gen consoles. And some, like me, waited 2 years and stubbornly didn't play or watch anything related to the game just to enjoy the gameplay on PC. Of course, Rockstar said there wouldn't be a PC version and everyone needed to rush out and buy consoles, [i] but we knew... [/i] Finally the game is out, but it didn't go smoothly. Issues with Cyrillic characters in usernames, issues connecting to Rockstar Social Club, endless loading screen issues, issues for laptop users, and problems, problems, problems. Many of these have already been fixed with patches, but a bad aftertaste remains. [spoiler] And owners of laptops with Intel+AMD graphics still can't launch the game [/spoiler] But none of these problems ruined the magnificent Grand Theft Auto V. Compared to the console versions, the graphics on PC look much better, shooting has become more convenient, and consequently, handing out headshots has become much more fun. Rockstar even polished their video editor for PC, which used to record and cut video back in GTA IV. But we didn't get to enjoy the exclusive feature for long, as the editor is coming to PS4 as well. Many of my acquaintances and friends play exclusively GTA Online. I decided to check out the story first, and only then have fun and pull off heists in Online. And I didn't regret it. The story here is simply magnificent. Compared to GTA IV, where you'd get bored somewhere in the middle of the game, in GTA V it's always interesting to follow the plot. Even optional side missions are memorable for their epic and cinematic feel. All of this was made possible thanks to the three main protagonists, whom you can switch between not only during missions, but also in free roam, thus following the action from their perspectives. Each character also has their own traits and special abilities (shoutout to Lost Vikings): Michael is a good shot but a poor pilot, Franklin is a good driver and runs fast, but struggles with shooting, and Trevor is just Trevor, and that says it all. You get attached to each character and don't want to part ways with them. Well, and the final missions are so cool and memorable that there's no point talking about them, you have to see them for yourself. Lastly, I'll say that the police in GTA V have become much more dangerous and brutal than in previous parts of the series. At the slightest sign of trouble, they start shooting to kill, constantly block the road, and try to take the player down by any means necessary. [h1] Pros: [/h1] [list] [*] Wonderful graphics (even on minimal settings) and optimization. [*] The story, especially the endings, some of which can plunge you into depression for a long time. [*] The unique three-character feature, which sets GTA V apart from its predecessors for the better. [*] Dangerous cops and military who don't die from one or two shots from a puny pistol. This makes the game more interesting and somewhat more hardcore. [*] A huge selection of weapons to cause absolute mayhem. [*] Realistic nature and weather conditions. A large variety of wild animals you can actually hunt. [*] Great soundtracks on the in-game radio stations. [*] Abundance of vehicle modifications and upgrades. [*] Facial animations. [*] Michael and some of his missions are very reminiscent of Max Payne and his adventures from the third installment of the eponymous game. [/list] [h1] Cons: [/h1] [list] [*] A lot of issues upon release. Gradually being fixed by official patches. [*] Poor car physics. After GTA IV, where cars swayed and deformed realistically, the vehicles in GTA V are painful to look at. Even from the hardest impact, cars will only get scratches and minor dents. [*] Not enough hairstyles for the main characters. [*] Crazy pedestrians who constantly run each other and the player over with cars. [*] Controls for planes and helicopters on the keyboard are not very convenient. [*] Lacking the ability to eat and restore health at fast-food joints (Burger Shot, Cluckin Bell, etc.). [*] Civilians die from any injury. Even from a punch, a stun gun shot, or two body/leg shots from a pocket pistol. [/list] [u] Verdict: 9/10 [/u]

translation_en: [h1]A game with compelling both online and single-player campaigns![/h1] Playing about 50% of the single-player campaign, I felt that the main quests and side missions—which beautifully capture the distinct personalities of the three protagonists, Franklin, Michael, and Trevor, and the people around them—are harmoniously well-balanced. Also, using the money earned from quests to buy real estate like cinemas or taxi companies to generate regular income, not to mention the fun of stock market investing, shouldn't be underestimated. Needless to say, the voice acting for all the characters and the scene direction are superior to other games in the same genre, so you can enjoy the feeling of watching an omnibus movie tied to each character. It strongly feels like care was put into the story of the GTA series, which wasn't considered all that important until now, so I think it will appeal plenty to single-player campaign users who aren't necessarily into online. As mentioned before, not only the main quests, but all the character-specific sub-missions are equally fun and there aren't too many of them, which is also worth praising because you never get the feeling that you're doing them just for the sake of it. For PC users who didn't play it on consoles first, I'm sure that even if you only play the single-player campaign, you'll fall head over heels for GTA 5 and it's well worth the price. As for the online mode, there's a slight sense of being overwhelmed by the sheer scale of the numerous missions, but the feeling of building up your own avatar—buying a house, a car, a tank, and so on—gives it an even higher level of fun than the single-player. Above all, the 5 Heists (The Fleeca Job, The Prison Break, Humane Labs Research, Series A Funding, and Pacific Standard) are the absolute highlight of online play because they involve 2 or 4 players working together in co-op, and you get a pretty sweet financial reward from them. Also, getting stronger by acquiring weapons with the income you earn as you rank (level) up, disabling passive mode, and killing other players is secretly quite satisfying. Raising your shooting skill through deathmatches or shooting range practice, unlocking upgrades through races and stunt jumps, as well as mid-to-early game addictive features like fist-fighting other players, arm wrestling to build strength, or swimming/running to build stamina are also quite engaging. Unlike single-player, online's charm is that because you're playing with other users, there's a variety of fun beyond the predefined missions—like raiding military bases with friends you've made or playing assassination games in the session. However, while it's heavily optimized for low-end PCs, the occasional crashing and lagging issues on high-end graphics cards are something that needs improvement moving forward. (Of course, it's worth praising that a game this hot is handling traffic stably in terms of online/servers.) Since GTA 5 came out on consoles 2 years ago, console players might dismiss it as an old title, but I dare say that even as a 2-year-old work, the game's overall polish and the fun you can get from it are just as good as—or even better than—recently released titles. The fun you get for just 60,000 won transcends its value, so I strongly recommend it. 9/10

translation_en: [h1][b]The game that best fits the term Massive Open World[/b][/h1] [b]Auto-Thief God 5[/b] The sequel to the most infamous game of the era. This installment sends players to Los Santos, a fictional city modeled after LA. The game opens with a bank robbery from 9 years prior, spearheaded by Michael and Trevor, two of the main protagonists. But the heist goes wrong; crew members die off one by one, and in the end, only Trevor manages to escape. Cut to Michael's funeral amidst a priest's prayers that seem to rub salt in the wounds of his past life. Not far from the service, a mysterious man appears who looks suspiciously like the guy lying in the grave. Time passes to the present day, where young Franklin, a car thief and another of the game's protagonists, happens to steal a car belonging to Michael—the man who supposedly died 9 years ago. From here on, players must step into the shoes of Michael, Trevor, and Franklin, navigating lies, betrayal, the criminal underworld, and friendship to survive the insane events that are about to unfold. [b][u]Pros[/u][/b] + Telling the story through 3 characters is fucking awesome. Each person's perspective always has its own reasons, and most importantly, it's fun and extremely engaging. + A massive world packed with jaw-dropping details. If you thought 4 was detailed, 5 is many times more detailed than 4. From various events like playing tennis, golf, hunting, triathlons, street racing, the stock market, extreme sports, to random events all over the place. + Aside from dedicated racing games, GTA V probably has one of the best driving systems out there. The car chases in this game are genuinely fun. + The Online mode is fun and refreshing, sticking to the open-world format of the main game while adding missions scattered across the map for players in the server, ranging from basic competitive modes like DM, TDM, CTF, and Racing, to co-op missions like heists, prison breaks, and vehicle thefts. + All the characters are interesting, even the supporting cast. + FPS Mode (Shooting fans will definitely love this). [b][u]Cons[/u][/b] - Even though the various activities in the game world are detailed and fun, they lack challenge and good enough rewards, making a lot of activities boring after just one try. - Many missions should have been cutscenes instead of making players play through them and get bored. - Several side quests lack engagement and are just not fun at all. - Movement sometimes feels quite clunky, especially in fast-paced action scenes like gunfights, getting out of a car while being chased, or even climbing. translation_en: People don't talk about it much, yet it was one of the major selling points for the PC version of the game: I am talking about the FPS view, obviously. According to Steam achievements, 2.9% of players (who own the game on Steam, obviously) have played for 15 hours in first-person view. I think that's really low, especially considering all the work that went into it. So I'm going to share my experience with it. I currently have 80 hours of playtime and I've played almost exclusively in FPS view. I've obviously compared as many things as possible with the 3rd-person view. [b][u]The FOV[/u][/b] Personally, I don't get what people are complaining about. As a huge FPS fan, I usually play with a horizontal FOV of 105-110. By setting the FOV slider in the options to the halfway mark, I feel completely comfortable, whether it's during gunfights or driving. [b][u]Driving[/u][/b] Really excellent! You get a great driving feel, fantastic visuals, and top-notch immersion. Quite a bit of attention went into the details, especially the sound which changes depending on whether you're in FPS or 3rd person, inside a closed interior or a convertible, etc. The character's hand textures are super detailed so they look good up close. Plus, the vehicle interiors are well-crafted. Crashes have a really heavy, very impressive impact, with details like your character's head snapping down if you hit something head-on. You completely lose your sense of orientation when you crash and start barrel-rolling or whatever. So the immersion is executed really well here, giving a real impact to crashes that might seem almost trivial in 3rd person. A few downsides though: [list] [*] The mirrors only reflect very vaguely (they're super pixelated, even with maxed-out graphics), which is a shame seeing as the mirrors work perfectly everywhere else in the game. [*] Compared to the 3rd-person view, you end up with overall massively reduced firing angles in FPS view. For example, in certain vehicles it's impossible to shoot backwards whereas you can in 3rd person, and generally speaking, the horizontal and vertical angles are reduced too. [/list] This is my biggest gripe. It's not really a flaw of the FPS view itself, since the firing angles actually make sense, but rather that the 3rd-person angles make zero sense. The FPS view suffers from this difference in firing angles compared to the 3rd-person view, and it's especially unfair when playing online—you're at a huge disadvantage against other players. [b][u]Flying[/u][/b] Always loving to fly in games, I was hooked by the possibility of playing in first-person view, knowing the keyboard controls are pretty straightforward. Unfortunately, I ran into a few issues: [list] [*] The viewing angle: The problem is that to fly you need both hands on the keyboard (you can also use the mouse to control, but I find it less intuitive). So in that case you lose the ability to look around, restricting you to a pretty limited view. [*] Vertical landing: You can't see what's directly beneath you, making it impossible to land in tight spots. [*] The vibration, especially in smaller planes, is way too violent. It's not pleasant at all to fly those kinds of planes; you feel like you're about to stall any second. [/list] Because of these flaws, I generally end up flying in 3rd person. Only fighter jets and commercial airliners are free from all of these issues (you can't look around freely, but almost the entire screen looks outside) and are therefore really the only air vehicles that are fun to fly in FPS view. [b][u]On Foot[/u][/b] Movement is very immersive, footsteps sound great, and camera movements are pleasant. Even after hours of playing straight, you don't get motion sickness like you might in games like Arma, which have way too exaggerated head bobbing (by default). All the character animations were reworked so you can see them in FPS view, and it's pulled off very successfully. [b][u]Shooting[/u][/b] The game offers 2 shooting options: one with a dot crosshair and the weapon slightly offset, and iron sights (you scroll the mouse wheel to switch between modes). The aiming movement is a bit clunky and clearly not very enjoyable for someone like me who's used to much faster-paced games. However, I think it fits the game well, as it tries to give the character a certain heaviness (in movement, etc.). Personally, to aim more precisely I don't use iron sights (which is a bit contradictory). All weapons shoot completely straight with zero spread, so the crosshair is just essential for landing headshots. It's a shame, but it makes gunfights more enjoyable. So, that's a big summary of my experience with this famous FPS view. Thanks for reading my wall of text, hopefully it convinces players who are still too hesitant about this view to give it a try, even if it hurts a bit for the first few minutes or hours.

translation_en: Every new installment in the [b]Grand Theft Auto[/b] series is a celebration. The fifth part came out a year and a half ago and, as is tradition for [i]Rockstar Games[/i], initially on consoles. I had to patiently wait and gracefully deny myself from watching any videos or screenshots other than the official ones. But as it turned out, we didn't wait all this time for nothing. On PC, the project came out looking way better and heavily improved. After the frankly clunky port of [b]Grand Theft Auto IV[/b], the fifth part is like a breath of fresh air — it's wonderfully optimized and cleaned up of bugs. I already liked the game engine in the fourth part, but that it (as well as the developers' skilled hands) was capable of such gorgeous visuals, I could never have imagined. While in the fourth part water looked more like jelly, here it has become some of the most beautiful I've ever seen. Nature is pretty much the same deal; if [i]Niko Bellic[/i] couldn't run around nice slopes in thick grass, the protagonists of the fifth part can easily have a picnic on a picturesque Pacific Ocean shore. And what about the rain and puddles after it in the game? It's something unbelievable, especially at night and during a heavy thunderstorm. The game itself has become much more elaborate, overgrown with tiny details, and equipped with new features. For the first time since 2001, the developers decided to change the familiar third-person view to a first-person one. Now you can even drive a car in first-person, just like in good racing simulators. The main character learned how to swim back in [b]San Andreas[/b], but it's in the fifth part that this idea was truly developed. Now you can not just swim, but fully explore the ocean depths with or without scuba gear, or even in a scientific submarine. Furthermore, for the first time in the history of the [b]GTA[/b] series, animals were introduced to the game (aside from birds). Cats, dogs, coyotes, cows, killer whales, sharks, and even deer that you can hunt have appeared. Even [i]Niko[/i]'s primitive phone has turned into a powerful smartphone for each of the characters. From it, you can now not only make calls and send texts, but also browse the internet, take photos, take selfies, save your game, and check the time. Everyone probably already knows about the three protagonists instead of one. The idea is great and the execution didn't disappoint, but as someone who's been around since the very first part, I'll probably stay loyal to the system where there is one protagonist and everyone else just revolves around them. Since I've written about this, I need to go over the points that seemed controversial to me. Well, how can I not, right? The spawning algorithm for cars on the roads is not very clear. While the insanely expensive sports cars can somehow be justified by the millionaires living in mansions behind the [i]Vinewood[/i] sign, the American classics darting back and forth just leave you dumbfounded. Such rides should be very rare, yet they drive around almost in herds. The main highlight of the game was decided to be heists involving three or more characters at once. This is of course very cool, but because of this, the geography of the missions suffered — the game map is huge, with plenty of interesting places, but due to the elaborate "heists," they are completely untouched by the plot. And I'll highlight the biggest downside for me separately. The [b]Grand Theft Auto[/b] series has always been famous for its subtle humor and satire on real life, but the humor was selective and didn't interfere with serious things in the game. In the fifth part, something clearly happened, and the humor noticeably took over. In almost every cutscene, mission, or dialogue, the developers try to crack jokes. Maybe I'm missing something, but that's exactly why [b]Mafia: The City of Lost Heaven[/b] still remains #1 in this genre for me. You can talk about this game a lot and for a long time. About the little things, like the dog named [i]Chop[/i] taking a dump by the pool, about global things, like the deep tuning of almost every car and similar features. All because there are practically no projects of this scale, and to this day, [b]Grand Theft Auto V[/b] is the most massive and detailed sandbox and simulation of a huge metropolis life. And I am sincerely glad that major [b]GTA[/b] games come out once every few years instead of every year like it happens with [b]Call of Duty[/b]. P.S. Hats off to the developers for the great band [b]Tangerine Dream[/b], which wrote several musical themes for the game. Movies with their music became iconic, and some outstanding. Their solo albums are no less famous. Edgar Froese passed away earlier this year, so [b]Grand Theft Auto 5[/b] can be dedicated to his blessed memory.

translation_en: It's Grand Theft Auto V, not much to say here, a cult game that has finally made it to PC after almost 1.5 years. + An interesting storyline centered around heists, alongside which the story of the main characters also unfolds, revealing their personalities and relationships with each other. The plot of Grand Theft Auto V can be compared to a really solid TV series, like "Breaking Bad" produced by AMC. In GTA, the three heroes also go all in, losing their minds, all for a big score, watching it, and even more so taking part in it all yourself, is just unforgettable. I think Rockstar deserves high praise for something like this. + The presence of various side quests, collectibles, random events, all of this contributes to an even longer playtime in Los Santos and its surroundings. + The presence of a video editor, which you can use to shoot decent machinima, make jaw-dropping screenshots that you can totally use as your desktop wallpaper, thankfully the game allows for it, there are plenty of picturesque locations here and just very beautiful spots. + Quality optimization, although with a fairly high level of resource consumption for your graphics card. But despite even this, on my graphics card with 2 gigabytes of VRAM, going over the limit by almost 450 megabytes, the game runs relatively smoothly, around +60 frames in the city and about +37 - 50 outside of it. Unfortunately, to see this game in all its glory, you'll need a very powerful computer with a setup of two or three graphics cards. — Rockstar Social Club, all these publisher DRM technologies, a massive festering boil on PC gaming. Some owners of retail versions of the game couldn't even launch it, simply because the stupid Social Club couldn't find the game folder or save files. And a number of other issues, all stemming from the SC as well. Grand Theft Auto: Online deserves a separate comment. To my regret, a lot more ideas could have been implemented in this sandbox; in reality, we have a hodgepodge of Test Drive, Battlefield, Max Payne 3, wave-shooter games, similar to the survival mode from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3 or Killing Floor. You'd think how cool it is to have all this under the hood of one game, but! It's implemented here in such a simplified form that it even gets a bit disappointing. Why, say, couldn't they add the ability to set up additional fortifications in survival mode, place some remote turrets, call in reinforcements, and everything else that exists in any game of this genre? In the end, we just sit on 1 out of 5 or 6 maps, shoot through 10 waves of enemies, and that's it. The deathmatch mode, I must say, is very similar to the multiplayer of Max Payne 3, which is very good, and if you switch to first-person mode and pick a map with vehicles, you get Battlefield. Unfortunately, I dropped PvP modes a week later due to the sweeping influx of kids with godmode, knowing Rockstar's policy towards these "people", you realize that no one is going to ban them. The game, with a budget of +$160 million, whose developer skimped on a coherent character editor, is hard to imagine it was even simpler on the previous-gen consoles. The character editor has so few settings that you will constantly run into clones of yourself during the game. Only about ten types of hairstyles, the inability to adjust your hero's body parameters, height, weight—even Saints Row 2 had that figured out. Could a developer as talented as Rockstar really not implement this in the Online mode, where players have spent and will spend hundreds of hours? I find it hard to believe. GTA Online also has a built-in level editor for deathmatches, races, and other modes, but there isn't one for survival, and "that's sad." You could explain this by saying users would farm XP there on unbalanced maps, but what's the point of such excuses when you can already run into people with +4000 level who got it with a single click in Cheat Engine? Dumb as fuck. GTA Online doesn't have the most ideal netcode; if you have crappy internet, everything will definitely lag in Free Mode in the thick of the action. Overall, everything is great, the game will give you long hours of the campaign. But the Online mode is crawling with retards with trainers and other cheats, so you're better off playing it on current-gen consoles, maybe there are fewer of them there. Definitely worth the money, one of the best sandbox games, if not the best.

translation_en: This review is only about the Online part. Not really a review, just sharing some random thoughts. After endless stuttering, reconnecting, disconnecting, and crashing, I finally busted out the good old VPN magic to smoothly connect to R*'s servers. My naive ass thought I could finally have fun playing with Los Santos residents all over the world, but I was seriously too young, too simple, like a tender little lamb. After finishing the tutorial, I was around level 3. I ran around the session looking for the other three players, tailing them like a creep (Grand Stalk Auto V?), but these three big bosses kept running all over the place completely ignoring me. Fine, if you big shots won't let me ride your coattails, I'll go find someone else. Right then, I got an invitation. Wow, a Heist! I clicked join while thinking, "Hmph, watch me totally flex my skills in front of you big shots." Once I joined the lobby, I was dumbfounded. Among the list of other players who were level 70 or 80, my level 3 tag stuck out like a sore thumb. Don't panic, we've got game sense and skills, true hardasses fear nothing. Stumbling and bumping along, I arrived at the mission location over a minute late. The big shots were already going toe-to-toe with the enemy in a fierce firefight. I hatched a plan, slammed the gas pedal, barreled straight into the enemy camp, jumped out of the car, and started blasting. That was just what I expected to happen. Amidst the astonished gazes of the big shots, I was riddled with bullets and died. Mission Failed. Did I mention that my flying car also ran over and killed a teammate? Dejectedly quitting the mission, I decided to calm down, do things steadily, and keep a low profile. Yeah, for a beginner, heists and shit are way too hard, so let's start with a race. Afterward, under the gaze of the top 7 players (8 in total), I slowly drove my car with popped tires right into the river. DNF. Nah, I figured flight school—uh, air races—should be pretty simple. Throughout the whole race, I did my best to scatter pieces of my airplane across every corner of the track. Flying planes is way too hard, let's just ride bikes instead. Yet 20 minutes later, I was still stuck on the first hill, unable to jump up. The other racers and I were definitely not riding the same kind of vehicle! Ah, why is this game so hard?! Let's pick up some guns and do some manly stuff. Versus mode, 2v2. I got teamed up with an orange-haired wave-perm chick. Seeing the opposing team's matching crew IDs, names, and mafia outfits, I wondered if we walked into a sweatfest. I wanted to tell her, "Girl, let's play it safe and just hide, don't feed the enemy too much." Yet this chick was fiercely wild. She charged straight up, shot at the enemy's gas barrels, and blew them twenty meters away. So bold. Girl, do you need a girlfriend? So the girl laid down the DPS up front while I cowered behind cover, kill-stealing and mooching scraps like a coward. In the end, our side actually took the lead. Finally, my first victory in life! After the match ended, I desperately chased after the girl on foot, welcoming the dust kicked up by the tires of her pink sports car. But she didn't say a word, stuck her middle finger out of the car window at me, and drove off into the sunset. If I were straight, I definitely would have fallen in love. Alright, after all that fooling around, I was pretty much level 5. Time to buy a house, get a sports car, and live that decadent sugar-daddy life. After buying the apartment and the sports car... yep, I was broke. Even the pre-order bonus money was basically gone. I stood in front of the floor-to-ceiling window of my luxury mansion, looking up at this fickle and noisy world, then looked down at my empty-ass wallet, and smiled with satisfaction.
