translation_en: I've never written a review or comment for games or under videos before, but I feel like I just gotta let out everything I have to say about this dumpster fire that I’ve put 2k hours into. Devs, you're absolute fucking morons, greetings from 80% of the PUBG player base, I hope you dumbasses actually read this review and a lightbulb goes off in your empty heads. Let's start: 1. Cars - I don't understand what kind of moron is in charge of car physics and driving in general in PUBG, but he must only know about car physics from 2000s games or doesn't even own a car. Driving feels like sliding a piece of cardboard across asphalt, and don't even get me started on the suspension—it literally doesn't exist. Hit the tiniest bump and you and your whole squad fly into the stratosphere. And that eternal bug where you pick up a teammate, park a meter away from them, and somehow the car still runs them over and does damage or even knocks them out. 2. Cheaters, and Chinese cheaters. Yeah, yeah, these are two different categories that are equally annoying and that the devs do absolutely nothing about. Let's start with regular cheaters: brainless scumbags who've achieved nothing in life except playing with software. Then there are the hardcore sweaty nerds who got tired of just wiping everyone with pure skill and decided to blatantly mock not just the players, but the devs themselves, showing how completely helpless they are against cheats. They run around in FPP while playing TPP, level 25-45, absolutely shitting on four squads single-handedly left and right. 3. The "anticheat" - yeah, I'm putting that in quotes because it simply doesn't exist. Players have to track down cheaters themselves based on their actions, and even after you point out to this pathetic excuse of an anticheat that *this* is the guy ruining the game for everyone, what does it do? It slaps him with a temporary one-day ban, after which this little shit either comes back with a fresh burst of energy or just makes a new account without bothering to wait out that embarrassing one-day review period. And if by some miracle you actually manage to ban the bastard permanently, don't get too excited—he'll just make another new account and ruin the match for everyone all over again, since it's F2P now anyway. 4. Bugs - it feels like the game hasn't left early access after 6 years. At the time of writing this, I'll just list a few bugs I can remember off the top of my head: "Unite" signs and other text floating in mid-air next to the wall they're actually supposed to be on; crashing into invisible obstacles in a car; that fucking annoying settings menu popping up when you're trying to type something in chat. 5. Skins - skins are a literal slap in the face to the players. For 500-900 G-Coins they offer such absurd skins that it'd be shameful to sell them even for 100. Weird-ass themes directed more at kids, even though PC PUBG is mostly played by adults. And probably the weirdest thing is the blatant sexism towards male characters—somehow all the decent-looking clothes always go to the female models. 6. Progressive weapon skins - this is an absolute joke. First you gotta waste a fuckton of coupons just to roll the base legendary skin, and then don't forget you need just as many materials and blueprints to actually level the damn thing up through its 10 tiers, or else drop another fuckton of cash trying to get what you need out of crates. Why can't they just let you level up the "legendary" skin by getting a certain number of kills, or drop blueprints and materials for that same kill count?! 7. Free-to-play version - oh, this is the biggest mistake for an already sinking ship. You made it free to keep player numbers up, but you actually just got an even bigger mass exodus of players thanks to cheaters and your sheer apathy. I honestly think PC PUBG is headed for the exact same fate as PUBG Lite, where eventually it'll just be nothing but cheaters and absolute zero player counts by Steam standards. 8. Macros and whatnot - so many people play either with full cheats or at least with software like macros to control recoil on things like the Beryl. The funniest part is there are even YouTubers who proudly use these macros on live streams, but the devs don't ban them permanently for one simple reason: *someone* has to stream this piece of shit to keep inexperienced players interested. You report the guy, he just logs into his alt account and plays on that until his main gets unbanned. It's basically a cheat, but they only get banned for two or three days, which is complete fucking nonsense to me. 9. Chat - the most crippled, useless chat ever. Here's how it works: when you're in the lobby, you can type to someone saying you're waiting for them or something, but the person you're messaging can't reply with normal text or type anything out—they only have pathetic pre-set one-word answers. 10. The Zone - a lot of people have noticed how weird the zone behaves. It feels completely bugged; people can camp in the exact same spot for 20 minutes and the zone will literally keep pulling to them over and over, completely ruining the game balance. Players just can't push them, and then the campers get the win from inside the zone. 11. Packet loss - this is out of control. How can you be so completely checked out towards the people who support your lazy asses??? Ever since the last three updates, massive packet loss started happening and nothing is being done about it. Every update just brings more tacky-ass skins and missions nobody gives a single fuck about when the game is in this state. Personally, my packet loss spikes up to 70-75%, and a lot of other people have the same issue. In a normal match, it's usually sitting at 15-20%, which means hits don't register, you're constantly rubber-banding back to where you ran from five seconds ago, etc. 12. Bots - another braindead feature they came up with: bots in level 300-500 lobbies. Not only are they completely useless at those levels, but I'd rather have a match start with only 80 real players instead of random-ass bots spawning out of nowhere and ruining the gameplay. How many times has this happened: you're tracking down some little rat, you finally find him, line up your crosshairs, and suddenly a fucking bot spawns right in front of you out of thin air and starts shooting at you, completely giving away your position—all to the benefit of the rat who either kills you while you're dealing with the bot, or goes right back to hiding while you're distracted. 13. Ranked mode - FPP only. Why can't we have TPP ranked? A lot of people want to play ranked in third-person, but for some reason, it just doesn't exist. 14. Matchmaking - absolute fucking garbage. It's completely broken in both ranked and normal matches. Why not make matchmaking actually make sense, so newbies play with newbies and level 300-500 sweats play against each other? 15. The Lobby - yeah, you change the lobby background, but you don't change the actual concept. Sometimes matchmaking takes forever, and there is literally fuck all to do in the lobby. Why not design something actually fun to do while waiting for a game? 16. Maps - such a weird decision with the map rotation. For some reason, they always rotate the other four maps, but they never touch Erangel or Miramar—which, by the way, literally everyone is fucking sick of. There's no map selection, and sure, people will say the player count isn't high enough anymore, but I'd rather wait longer or have fewer players on the map than get stuck playing Miramar 5 or 6 times in a row instead of picking my favorite map. 17. Game mechanics - the game feels super sluggish movement-wise. The character runs like a snail, the leaning left and right is just as clunky—it seriously lacks any kind of snap or responsiveness. 18. The absolute brainlessness of the dev team - why not make the game paid again, at least for ranked? For example: TPP and FPP ranked are only for players who bought the game. That would at least solve the cheater problem for ranked, while keeping a free-to-play version with ranked locked. Let the people who want a cheat-free experience play the paid version, and let the cheapskates play the free one and deal with whatever dumb luck they get—meaning cheaters and other clowns. 19. Maximum smooth-brained decisions regarding item usage - for example, you can use bandages and pop an adrenaline syringe while driving a car, but you can't use a medkit even though it uses the exact same syringe animation. Or when you're flying in the plane towards the zone, you can't use bandages, medkits, or energy drinks, even though your character's hands are completely free. 20. And of course, the thousands of reviews written in bulk that are forever ignored!

translation_en: I'm a banned PUBG player. After graduating from high school, I got hooked on watching mobile game streams. Back then, there was this "Paratrooper No. 1" who would hot-drop every single night. I really loved the vibe of them playing: a group of people chatting, laughing, and having a good time while gaming. I remember when the game first came out, knocking someone down didn't mean an instant finish, giving the winning squad a chance to revive their teammates. Nowadays you'd call that "martial virtue." I wanted to fight alongside my buddies too, so I found out about this platform called Steam, and PUBG cost 98 RMB. On July 12, 2017, I bought the game at an internet cafe near my house. I didn't know anything at first. Whenever I saw someone playing PUBG, I'd deliberately sit next to them, ask to team up, and get them to teach me how to play. When my game kept lagging, they told me I had to get a UU Accelerator. Even though I was broke, I clenched my teeth and bought a monthly card. Fresh out of graduation, I didn't have many friends willing to shell out 98 for a game, renew monthly accelerator cards, and go to the net cafe every day to play. So my teammates were all randoms from the net cafe. We had this tacit understanding not to smash windows when looting, and we'd communicate whether to fight or run. Even though I sucked, as a disciplined medic, they were still willing to carry me. In my freshman year, my laptop couldn't handle the game anymore, so I generously lent my account to a friend. But my friend lent my account to his cousin. At the time I thought, "Fine, there's nothing valuable on my account anyway, playing on it will at least pad my total hours." With that kind of mindset, I painstakingly sent verification codes to his cousin from my email every single time. At first, it was still under control, since I was involved in every login. But later on, things changed. For some reason, Steam stopped sending me emails, and other people didn't need my approval to log into my account anymore. (I didn't find out until much later when I started trading CS:GO skins that there was this thing called Steam Guard Mobile Authenticator.) I don't know when exactly it was that people stopped playing on my account. But when I wanted to queue up for PUBG with my friends at the net cafe, what stared me in the face was a line of English: **you have been banned!** I finally understood why people stopped playing on my account—it must've gotten banned for cheating. I went to confront my friend, and he said he didn't know anything about it. (Yeah right, his cousin got his friend's account banned, how could he possibly have the nerve to tell him?) Later, on June 10, 2021, I paid to appeal the account, but unfortunately, it didn't work. I guess whoever used it was rage-hacking, because Support's attitude was so hardline there was zero room for resolution. Every time I see other people playing PUBG nowadays, I get sad and nostalgic. Nostalgic for the joy that drifted away from me, nostalgic for that naive boy who's long gone. I fucking despise cheaters. I am a literal victim of cheating. Because it wasn't their own account, they didn't give a shit, and the consequences fell entirely on the account owner. Because of the PUBG ban, I'll never be able to get through the green-trust verification on the CS:GO Perfect World platform, and that single recorded ban just keeps stinging me. What I can't go back to is the youth worth remembering, what I can't go back to are those carefree days of my prime. The game is a great game, but after everything is said and done and people have drifted apart, you still gotta look forward.

translation_en: [list] [*][h1]A fun yet deeply regrettable Battle Royale[/h1] Nobody can deny that PUBG is genuinely fun, which also makes it probably the most regrettable game of all time. The gaming experience is completely ruined by cheaters, and it genuinely affects every single player. Cheaters stunted the game's growth; without them, you can only imagine just how popular it would have been. CS and Dota 2 could barely count on one hand the number of times they hit 1 million concurrent players, while a few years ago PUBG pulled off the miracle of hitting 3 million concurrent players day after day, a record that will likely be hard to beat even in a few years. [h1][quote=] [table] [tr] [th] Welcome to follow the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/38287879]NetEase UU Curator Cultivation Program[/url][/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] Find quality games, squad up with friends, and get free UU time cards here [/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] Remember to use UU to boost the Steam community and games _(:з」∠)_ [/th] [/tr] [/table] [/quote][/h1] [*][h1]Gameplay remains unchanged, with more elements and maps introduced[/h1] The biggest difference between PUBG and traditional FPS games like CS is that you can race cars and boats in the game. If you're a beginner or your aim is just so-so, and you can't beat people in a gunfight or out-sneak them, you can still get your gaming thrills from driving. You don't necessarily need to play the standard way of reaching the final circle and getting a chicken dinner, or constantly racking up kills, to have a lot of fun. After years of continuous updates, PUBG has brought bigger changes and more maps. Yet Erangel and that epic, soul-stirring theme song from back in the day are still unforgettable after all this time. PUBG back then was pure—it was all about gunfights or going for the win. Rain and fog maps made the people who loved them absolutely adore them. Those who hated them would just dodge the map, but I was one of the people who liked the rain and fog maps. The devs really shouldn't have removed rain and fog maps; it just reduced the fun of the game. For newbies, rain and fog could reduce that feeling of panic, increase a sense of inner security, and bring players an alternative immersive experience, so there was really no need to remove them. Also removed was the snow map, which I played a ton back then—ever since the snow map got deleted, I haven't played it since. Things like these that gave players a good gaming experience were all removed, which is pretty speechless and leads players to quit the game. Either don't release them in the first place, or once they're out and quite a few people like them, you shouldn't remove them. Back then there were only so many skins, and things like the white miniskirt and black miniskirt were worth a lot. Now there are tons of outfit changes in the game, and there are no longer any skins that valuable, nor does anyone chase after those expensive skins anymore. Maybe the in-game store skins bring in decent revenue nowadays, but what players still like more is that old model—not too many skins, free trading, where everyone wanted them yet very few people owned them. Nowadays any player can afford any good-looking skin, but they've also become common, anyone can own them, and there's no sense of scarcity left, nor can you tell who the rich players are anymore. Of course, many of the fun new elements in the current version are indeed very creative, such as manual mountain bikes, self-AEDs, drones, and tactical gear. The introduction of these elements still leads the genre. They are innovating and haven't stopped moving forward. [*][h1]Conclusion[/h1] As a player, the biggest wish is of course to permanently solve the cheater problem once and for all, but that's like a pipe dream and impossible to achieve. Players are helpless, and I'm sure the development company is quite helpless too. I hope the relevant cheat developers will stop breaking the law and instead do something law-abiding and contributional to humanity. Sure, you made money, but at the cost of how many people's gaming experience? Do you really have to be so devoid of morals? Anyway, the game is free-to-play now, and PUBG is still a good game. If you haven't played it yet, you can come and give it a try. [/list]

translation_en: A note to veteran players: This game is always changing. Just trust the saying: buy early, enjoy early; buy late, get a discount. After all, PUBG Corp making this decision means they're following market trends. They're looking at the game's future, not at old players' nostalgia. Nobody is right or wrong, it's just whether you can accept it or not. Between the criticism and the influx of new players, PUBG Corp clearly chose the latter. So I guess just take a wait-and-see approach, try looking at it from the developer's perspective, and also from a player's perspective. Maybe that way you can get something out of it to make up for the annoyance of the game going free-to-play. But if you're just here to hate for the sake of hating, you can completely ignore everything you just read—feel free to just keep scrolling that mouse up! A note to new players: Congratulations! You're in luck! Whether you're totally new to this genre or jumping over from another game, you can now experience the pioneer that made the battle royale genre explode in popularity for free. Welcome to come and experience what makes this game so appealing! However, I need to give you a heads-up on a few things first. First, this game has been out for a long time. The players who've stuck around have survived everything from actual hackers to human-aimbot-level players, so they've got serious skill. Don't get discouraged if you occasionally get matched against these guys—that's totally normal! Nowadays, with bots around, it's not like every single match will give you a terrible experience. Compared to the past, it's way more friendly to beginners, and the addition of the training grounds clearly makes the early learning phase much more comfortable. Second, for players in Taiwan, the game has always had terrible connections to foreign servers. The chance of you peeking your head out and pulling it back only to still get shot is very high, because the people on the other end are usually mainland Chinese or Southeast Asian. Their geographical locations are closer to the servers, so their internet being better than yours is totally normal. Third, character movement in this game is actually relatively less responsive compared to other battle royale games, so it takes time to get used to. The timing for pulling out or switching weapons, reloading, vaulting through windows, and climbing walls all have brief animation recovery locks. The smoothness of picking up items, opening doors, and getting into cars—all of the above are tied to the stability of the server you're connected to in that match. So sometimes when things feel janky, you just have to get used to it. These are just the things that come to mind right now. Of course, there's still a lot you need to jump into the game to feel for yourself, so go explore on your own. I guess... that's kind of the essence of this game.

translation_en: This was my first PC game. For the first 30 hours, I died instantly every single match. I figured out the gameplay on my own, watched tutorials to adjust my sensitivity, and played all by myself every day, enduring the endless quick deaths. Later on, I slowly coaxed my friends into playing it. Back then, I was still a newbie, and watching my friends' wacky plays at the start made me feel like I was looking at my past self. A full squad of 4 good friends, our mics filled with laughter and cheers—we even got noise complaints from the neighbors. But that period was the happiest time I've ever had playing this game. Time slowly passed, and those 4 friends from the squad rarely came online anymore. I also gradually stopped opening the game that used to bring me countless moments of joy. Seeing the game update over and over again, yet having zero motivation to log back in myself, I slowly realized what this game gave me: maybe it was the intense thrill of the final circle, nerves strung so tight I could vividly feel my heart beating fast, a rush of pleasure flooding my brain; or maybe it was when we wiped the last guy in the final circle, and my friends' voices came through the headset shouting, "Holy shit, nice!" then heading back to the lobby to keep enjoying the happiness that belonged only to the four of us. Now the game is going free-to-play, and I hope more people can experience this joy, instead of zero-cost cheating that ruins this beauty.

translation_en: Played it back in '17, hopped over from H1Z1 at the time. PUBG had just come out back then, and the reason this game blew up was entirely because H1Z1 got huge. Players found out about H1Z1 through all sorts of channels, joined up, and a ton of people transitioned from H1Z1 to PUBG. I bet you anything a lot of people found out about H1Z1 and PUBG through Neihan Duanzi. What stuck with me the most was watching Americans on YouTube swearing in broken Chinese—"Cao ni ma" and "Wo ai ni". Back when I first started playing PUBG in '17, there were hardly any cheaters and the gaming experience was top-notch. The lobby music, the English UI, the engine sounds and the sound feedback of bullets hitting vehicles, plus the gun sounds—man, I miss it all so much. I'm an IT major, and my home PC was decent—nah, you could say it was damn good. I grabbed a 1080 Ti right when it came out in '17 just to play PUBG. What really sticks out in my memory is when my friends didn't have PCs at home, so we'd pull all-nighters squading up at this internet cafe. That place had a coffee maker and a promo where playing PUBG got you a free cup of hot coffee. No cap, back then our regular squad of four would stack up a whole table's worth of coffee cups by the end of the night. I also remember the net cafe had a PUBG leaderboard for daily kills, weekly kills, win counts, and rating points. We took top three every single week, ending up as the monthly cafe champs. That net cafe had pretty high specs for back then, but to play PUBG you still had to crank the graphics down to super low, and it would constantly disconnect, and sometimes you couldn't party up and were forced to play solo. But that didn't kill the urge to play at all—we still had an absolute blast. Finally, right there at that cafe, we watched more and more players jump into PUBG, some coming from League of Legends, others from all sorts of random games. Back then everyone sucked, there were snake-in-the-grasses everywhere, and gunplay wasn't nearly as sweaty as it is now. The whole internet cafe would just be echoing with loud-ass shouts of "revive me, revive me!", "let me pop a medkit, the blue zone's gonna kill me", and all those classic PUBG lingo, hahaha. In a blink, I've gone from a kid to a dad of two, and watched PUBG fall from its peak straight to rock bottom, sharing the exact same fate as H1Z1—both ruined by cheaters. There were a couple of seasons where I didn't even log on once; getting utterly depressed and walled by hackers will do that to you. Plus, once you have kids you gotta hustle for a living. After all, free time is fleeting, and whenever I fire up the PC nowadays I might still play a match or two. Because of love, there is persistence. There's a nice saying: "Love rises in the east and sets in the west, romance is undying to the bitter end." Maybe that sums up me and PUBG. Whenever I run into a cheater teammate, I'll quit without hesitation and queue up for the next match, 'cause letting hackers ruin your mood just isn't worth it. A clean gaming environment takes all of us to maintain. People who play dirty will get what's coming to them sooner or later, one way or another. Everyone's just here to play a game and unwind, don't let it chain you down. Finally, wishing all you players out there a winner winner chicken dinner, PUBG.

translation_en: A story about an unexpected encounter and a silent stranger. My first game always loads for ages. I only load in just as I'm already falling after jumping out of the plane. Usually, a couple of other guys are falling near me. Though maybe those are just AFKers? This time, there were 9 such bodies circling around me. Diving down, I saw a car. A brilliant idea popped into my head: run all these poor bastards over. Landing, I climbed into the whip. It was an old minivan, the kind hippies usually drive in movies. It's slow, but sturdy. As I drove closer to the site of the upcoming Carmageddon, I heard the roar of a second engine. My first thought was either lag, or someone just decided to drive past. I was wrong. The second car didn't drive past. It started running the poor bastards over too. Me and the stranger in two cars were squishing the AFKers. After running over the last one, I got stuck in a ditch. The driver of the neighboring car tried to ram me. But stopped next to me after the first attempt. Probably thinking it was pointless, or maybe because he got stuck in the ditch right next to me too. I got out of the car next to his car. I tried to initiate contact using the sign language of mutes in video games. For example, a jump means "apple," and crouching twice means "I am friendly. Don't shoot me." So that's what I did, crouched a couple of times. Started waiting for his reaction. I thought he didn't understand me. I was ready for him to show some kind of aggression towards me. I looked at him, he knew I was waiting for some kind of reaction from him. He slowly got out of his car. Looked at me one more time, then crouched a couple of times. Yeah, he answered me, even if with a bit of an accent in the language of the mutes, but contact was established. After that, we ran down the road together, leaving our cars behind. We ran, maybe because there was no trust between each other. Whoever stops first gets a fist to the face. Maybe that's what we both thought, maybe I was the only one thinking that. But my thoughts were scattered by the sounds of gunshots. Someone was shooting at us. While we were running, someone opened fire on two targets. Pretty predictable. Two unarmed people running along the road make a good shooting gallery target. We got lucky, we didn't even get hit, we got away. Reaching a small cluster of houses with a motorcycle nearby. Whether out of mistrust and a desire to ditch each other, or maybe because we were far from the zone and time was running out, we both hopped on the bike. One was the passenger, the other the driver. We rode down the road until we ended up in some sort of township whose name I don't know. We scattered into the houses. Scavenged through the trash for gold that would help us survive. I found a UMP among all this junk. Time was running out and everything in the houses had been looted, it was time to get back to the transport and relocate. The thought crept in to ditch him and drive off. But thinking about it again, I decided to wait. About 30 seconds later, he showed up. I aimed my SMG at him, he aimed his shotgun at me. The moment had come that could destroy our fragile friendship, all it would take was for one of us to click the left mouse button. Nothing happened. We both put our weapons away behind our backs and got on the motorcycle. That's when I realized I could trust him. We rode down the road. The wind was blowing through my hair and I was waving my gun left and right. Me and my companion were speeding forward. But as it usually happens, this couldn't last long. Because sooner or later, one of us still had to betray the other. After all, only one survivor was supposed to remain in this bloody and brutal game. In a game where you can't trust anyone. But we managed to break those rules, we were like Katniss and Peeta from The Hunger Games. It was pure idyll between us, but it had to come to an end, sooner or later. And then what none of us expected happened. We were betrayed by the motorcycle. Motorcycles are the most treacherous thing in the game. You never know for sure whether you'll die trying to get on it, or if it will just bump into something on the road and flip over? Or maybe it will actually decide to work normally and get you to your destination? Who knows with these bikes. Dying on the road, I died with a smile on my face. I was glad for this death. Neither of us had to make the hard choice and shoot the other in the back. The last seconds of this round I thought about that and hoped he was happy with this outcome too. We never exchanged a single word with each other. What's sad is that in the next reincarnations of our avatars, the chance of us being in the same game is very low. Even if we do end up in the same game, the chance of running into each other is even lower. But even if we met, one of us would just kill the other without ever knowing that this was the exact same "silent stranger."

translation_en: Few games manage to travel the path that PUBG has. A cobbled-together game with a billion bugs and server issues managed to blow up worldwide. But over time, both the game and the players changed. Those early days when the game first came out were so much fun. Nobody knew how to play, complete chaos reigned, and everyone played however they saw fit. But eventually, for obvious reasons, a group of people emerged who studied the mechanics, tricks, and other things that the average casual player didn't care about. Gradually, the anarchy disappeared, a meta emerged, and player behavior became pretty monotonous. And right here, a problem appeared that the developers never solved and, apparently, never will. Right now, there are no new players in the game. Yet that is precisely what gives a game a long life. You can milk money from the core player base all you want, but it starts looking more and more like an exclusive club for regulars. Look at Counter-Strike. New players always show up there, and the low ranks are just as much of a mess as they've always been. Jump into casual matchmaking and you'll find the exact same squeaking school kids that were there when the game came out. Meaning, some people come into the game, others leave. That's why it stays popular: both veterans and newbies can find something to do. But PUBG doesn't have that. It can't hold onto a new audience, and the old one is shrinking. Honestly, when was the last time you even randomly stumbled upon this game anywhere lately? The hype around it is gone and the player count drops every month. Sure, you could mention PUBG Mobile and how it has a huge audience, but mobile gaming audiences don't really count for much. From a financial standpoint, though, it's a colossal success. All sorts of cosmetics, battle passes, and other garbage bring in a massive amount of profit, I'm sure. In the end, it's hard to give this game a straightforward review. It depends a lot on the angle you look at it from. If you look at it money-wise, it's a genius idea that brought in mountains of dollars. As a game — well, it's fine too: one of the best in its genre. But what to do about the players... Of course, there's the "genius" solution for all newbies: "spend a hundred hours of your life learning the game," but who needs that? Realizing the current state of affairs, new players will quietly ride off into the sunset pretty quickly. And the veteran players have been spinning in their own world for a long time now. The hype era for this game is gone for good.

translation_en: PUBG was the game that led the Battle Royale craze that took over the gaming world back in 2017-2018. At that time, the rise of cheaters in popular games like CS:GO and the backlash against recent updates drove players straight into PUBG's arms. Me and my friends were part of that crowd. Back then, despite its flaws, bugs, and optimization issues, we had an absolute blast playing this game. We didn't have to wait to find a match, and matchmaking was based on rank. Everyone was playing it, and it was heavily advertised. Streamers were constantly playing it live, making videos on YouTube all the time, and we'd just open them up and watch. Because of the hustle and bustle of life and starting my career, I stopped playing the game back then. Now, I thought I'd play this game I loved so much again. I no longer have the chance to play this game with my friends. I queue up for a normal match and everyone is a pro. The second I lift my head up, I'm dead. I queue up for ranked squad and my English isn't good enough. I get flamed. I queue up for solo squad, and the game turns into a game of hide and seek. Since I'm good at hiding, I make it to the top 10 without firing a single bullet and then die. But even if I really want to, I can't queue for solo matches. No one plays solo. I tried queuing solo in ranked. I waited 15 minutes and finally quit without finding a match. This just shows that the player count is in the gutter. Yet I want to queue solo in ranked. I've always liked the game's graphics. But I know I play games with much better graphics at higher FPS. You need a good rig to play comfortably. With a system that you can't really call bad, I can't break 80 fps. Most of the time I'm playing around the 60 fps mark. In a situation like this, I realized I'm now trying to force myself to play a game whose logic and atmosphere I love, while just suffering through it. The game hasn't added much since I last left it. Maybe that's why it's not played as much as it used to be. Not much has been done to retain players, things that needed fixing weren't fixed. Finding a match is one pain, optimization is another. Even though most of the bugs were fixed, it wasn't enough. The crowd still keeping the game alive is hardcore, professional players. Grenades exploding right in my face and getting one-tapped in the head from 300 meters away taught me that. I said earlier that we broke away from CS:GO and came to this game. Right now, while I still see CS:GO as a playable, successful game, I can't say the same for PUBG.

translation_en: First of all, I gotta say I'm a veteran PUBG player. I still remember back in 2017, watching livestreams on my phone every single day. As an FPS-only gamer, PUBG's fresh and innovative gameplay deeply hooked me. After watching streams for a few months, I figured out how to buy the game, how to play it, and that's how I got into Steam. Since I didn't have a place to play after buying it, I was constantly hitting up friends, hunting for internet cafes, specifically ones with high-end specs. I racked up about 800 to 1,000 hours in internet cafes. Let's not even talk about how much cash I dropped back then—I was just a low-level clerk, wasn't married yet, and didn't dare ask my family to upgrade parts of our home PC. But it taught me how to build my own rig. I5-7500, 1060—saved up on food and drinks for months, downgraded my cigarettes to Hongtashan, and built it myself. Played another 1,000 hours or so. By that time, there were already tons of cheaters, and getting constantly wrecked. But you know what? I've got pretty high resilience. Cheaters would abuse me a thousand times, and I'd still treat PUBG like my first love, just kept right on playing. Back then, you could still trade PUBG items on other sites, and I got totally addicted to unboxing and playing the market, flipping items inside the game. In 2019, life took a few turns—got a promotion, got married, played a bit less. Whatever came out in the game, I bought it: weapon skins, outfits, battle passes. Early 2020 hit with the pandemic, and I built myself another PC. This time, at least I didn't have to scrimp and save. i9-10900K, 2080Ti, went all out. Played comfortably for a good six months. Right on cue, I had a business trip, so I had to find an internet cafe, log in, play a match, check in, and done. Seemed like a chill, simple routine. But things didn't go the way I thought. On October 6th, when I got home and got ready to sit down for a game, I noticed my Steam was asking for a verification code. I kept entering it, but it was always wrong. Turned out, surprise surprise, my Steam account got hacked. Rushed to recover it, got the account back, but a nice little VAC ban came right along with it. This was like a bolt out of the blue, left me depressed for half a month. Looked it up online, searched Douyin, people said you could appeal a false ban, so I started spamming appeals. Kept at it for two months until my heart was completely dead. Just like that, my 2,786-hour PUBG journey came to an end. Even though I got banned, I still recommend this game to everyone, because it holds way too many of my awesome memories.

It doesn't matter if you launched anything or not, if it finds a file on your PC — not necessarily a cheat, just any modification not even related to PUBG — you can get BANNED without warning and without explanation. I don't know what they're thinking with an attitude like that, but I've drawn my conclusions. This company was a dumpster fire and it stayed a dumpster fire. translation_en: I've spent 1000 hours on this game and I do not recommend buying it. I sat in this project for 3.5 years, dropping in from time to time for 50-80 hour sessions to see what new stuff they added, and managed to watch it grow up. I caught the game's renaissance in its second year of life, when the marketplace economy was thriving and it was genuinely improving from a technically barely playable state into an optimized, adult project with fine-tuned balance and an in-game store that didn't shove its selection down your throat. Back in 2018 it was a great tactical-leaning shooter with unique gunplay that I haven't seen anywhere else. Moreover, the game let you make actual cash off of it by regularly dropping new cases that cost 350-450 rubles a pop at launch. A lot of people paid for their internet bills that way just by playing their favorite session game. Playing the hell out of it was fun and gave a real profit. The studio even managed to deal with the flood of cheaters that infested the servers during the first year and a half by introducing report systems that actually worked, which earns them a little extra karma. But then the red flags started, the first of which was shutting down trading in-game items between players, and consequently on third-party sites, which tanked the prices on the marketplace. This was followed by the introduction of a battle pass and a rework of the old map. Even back then, it was clear what the devs meant when they talked about their intentions to overhaul the in-game economy and their new approach to supporting the game. But even after copying the cash-cow formula from competitors, they still gave you the chance to complete simple challenges to earn a paid key, which had the potential to pull you a skin that could cover the cost of the game itself. Unfortunately, it seems the devs thought they were over-saturating the already dead marketplace and removed this type of reward for your no-life grind. Every half-year, things got worse. During 2020, the game got flooded with skins that you can't get through any means without paying, which makes their market prices sometimes mind-blowing, while the only case where you can get at least $1.5 drops maybe 2-3 times a year if you buy them every Wednesday. Right now the game looks like a straight-up 50-hour f2p game that begs you at every turn to buy some new festive stockings for your character, yet it costs as much as something like Control on a discount or Battlefield, which will give you a way higher quality experience and positive emotions for that money. Gameplay-wise, the shooter hasn't evolved for a year and a half. New weapons and features are dragged out kicking and screaming, and all the developers' resources are thrown into drawing newer and newer skins that drop every 3 months. Yeah, they finally started giving us new maps, but in terms of scale and fun they look like stripped-down scraps compared to the big, well-crafted Vikendi or Sanhok, which took a year to make and on which I spent my last hundreds of hours, ignoring these attempts by PUBG Corporation to copy Warzone's successful mechanics, which just don't work on the technical ecosystem of an outdated 2017 game. To sum it up: You should buy this battle royale dinosaur if you've got buddies there to run around with for a hundred hours and then quit. I can pretty much guarantee you'll regret the money spent (I didn't have to, I made my money back many times over back when the market was alive). But if you're just a random player who values their time and the quality of the product they're buying, don't even look in this direction. You're better off trying whatever has been buzzing for the last two years. Nowadays the genre has way more interesting and progressive entries across the board. P.S. Years later, I'm genuinely going to miss the cozy runs across huge, diverse locations with emotional gunfights, when the game gave you the feeling of a totally unique match every single time. Erangel, you'll forever be in my heart <3

I always agreed with that. I've been playing this game for a long time, picked it up not long after it first came out. I used to play H1Z1; if it wasn't for too many cheaters, this game wouldn't even be able to surpass it. But the release of this game also sealed its decline. How happy it made you just to kill one person. Even many players, afraid they wouldn't survive long, basically stayed in the blue zone looting supplies, just terrified that a sweaty player would rob the loot they worked so hard to collect. I wouldn't call myself a super hardcore pro player, but I could still rack up a lot of kills every match. Later on, this game blew up. More and more cheaters and profit-driven subhumans found their joy in ruining this game. At first, you could still outwit cheaters, but later on, there were just more and more of them. What broke my heart wasn't the people using cheats, but the fact that the game publisher did nothing over and over again. Feeling helpless, I had no choice but to play with high ping on other servers. When I first came to the new server, I was so happy to meet many foreign friends. But I also ran into unpleasant stuff—every time I said hi and people asked where I was from, when I replied "I FROM CHINA," there would be a hint of disdain. I immediately realized that a lot of people from our country really do go to other servers to cheat, which makes people despise Chinese people. Our country has plenty of talented people; I don't want foreigners to always say "CHINA Hacker," but there's nothing I can do, and I fucking hate cheaters too. Now, it's almost 3 years since this game came out, and I've noticed that legit players are gradually decreasing. In most final circles, we're fighting against cheaters; there really aren't many legit players left (not saying there are none at all). I basically only played this game with real-life friends. Gradually, their hearts broke over this game too, and slowly my real-life friends stopped playing it. I didn't know what games to play, so I just kept sticking with it and playing. When too many people report you, it triggers random reviews for no reason. Although the ban isn't long, it's not short either. If this keeps up, will I eventually get permanently banned? If you're going to ban me, just ban me permanently so I can remove this game from my library. It would actually feel more relieving. I've spent some money on this game and I have an inventory. Although it's not a huge amount, it's not a little either. It was all ground out through my own hard work. For several seasons, I maintained a 3.0 KD. Whether I'm a cheater or not, the stats don't lie. Therefore, I hope your company completely fixes this anti-cheat system. And every time, the in-game store updates ridiculously fast, while I haven't seen you improve optimization or the anti-cheat system at all. It just makes the vast majority of us players so heartbroken. I've seen way too many unjustified bans in other reviews; if you keep going like this, going bankrupt is just a matter of time. Better watch yourselves, Bluehole. One last thing: I hope legit players keep playing clean.

translation_en: I'm usually way too lazy to write anything about games on Steam, but I've finally reached my breaking point. 1000+ hours in flight, let's go. I'll start with the positives: - interesting gunplay - interesting positional gameplay in the late game - still pretty much one of the best in its genre (though that's subjective, of course) AND NOW FOR THE CONS, HELL YEAH: - Russian servers are hell, they're just a fucking shithole: - Chinese cheaters. In every other ranked match during the late game you get sprayed down by a Beryl from 300 meters, headshot every single time by a Mini 14 whose fire rate in the hands of the Chinese equals an AR, a grenade thrown right into a house where you weren't even moving, and so on, and so on, and so on. When you get killed, watching the replay is especially cool when you see the guy tracking you through walls, houses, and foliage, or headshotting everyone in your squad in a couple of bursts. How the fuck are you actually supposed to rank up on RU when there are real cheaters in literally every other match? Though one day in the afternoon I set a personal record of getting wiped by cheaters in 5 out of 5 matches. You'd think there's a solution to the above—just don't play ranked, but who the fuck wants to play normal matches when half of them are bots? With the Chinese, you can partially solve the problem by using a VPN and playing on EU. But the ping difference is 5-8 vs 45-50, which is fine if you're from the western part of Russia, yeah. But what are the guys from the Urals, Siberia, etc., supposed to do? That's a rhetorical question. And honestly, there are Chinese players on EU too. It's just that instead of running into some "huilu-tv" cheater in every single match, you'll run into one every third or maybe fifth match. - The community. Sometimes listening to voice chat, you feel like 1/3 of the players on RU servers are hardcore [slurs] (05/dag and other such wonderful tags that tell you right away you won't have a teammate), and Kazakhs—oh yeeeeah, this game will make you hate those guys. Dudes with the tag kz, beka, aleke, and thousands of others, using a cheap-ass 200-ruble microphone that farts louder than your grandpa, and as the cherry on top, they definitely have screaming in the background because a true Kazakh will play from a PC bang. With a ping of 90-100, usually doing complete and utter bullshit. And that's fine, but when there are two of them on your team and they spend half the game babbling in their own language and clogging up all comms—that's where the joy is (no). - Optimization. Running a 2700X and a 2070, and I still get FPS drops down to 70 frames on some shit like Miramar. Seriously? So for this game, for comfortable gameplay, you need a rig costing 90k+ rubles? Yeah, about thaaaaaat... So long story short: on the one hand, you have a potentially decent game, but in its current state, it's being killed by its own devs. Because the anti-cheat and optimization issues have been around for 2 fucking years, 2 FUCKING YEARS. And for a somewhat normal experience, you need a fairly expensive PC, a VPN, and ideally your own squad, because playing on RU with randoms is like playing Russian roulette with half the chambers loaded. Without that, there's literally 0 point.

translation_en: I don't know how many people will see this, but every little bit helps. If you guys value your accounts, please avoid buying this game as much as possible; if you've already bought it, do everything you can to NEVER log into your Steam account and run this game at internet cafes or other public places. I used to see a lot of people saying they were falsely banned, and I thought it was just Bluehole's own fuck-up. But after I logged into the game at an internet cafe in Shandong Province on July 28, 2020, and played for about three hours, in the early morning of July 30, 2020, I logged into my Steam account because I couldn't sleep, only to shockingly find that PUBG was currently running. Since I had Steam In-Home Streaming enabled on my PC, I used that feature to take remote control of the game. When I looked at the remote streaming interface, I found that my account was being used by some unknown person while cheating. When he realized I had taken control of his game via streaming, he quickly cut the game connection, and I didn't react fast enough to even take a screenshot of his computer. That night (early morning of July 30), I changed my Steam password, mobile authenticator, reset all my bound devices, and even disabled Family Sharing (which I used to share games with my friends). I didn't finally fall asleep until 4 AM. But when I woke up the next day, I faced a hard truth: I was definitely not the only person who had experienced this. My account was banned about two days later. If I hadn't had Steam streaming enabled, or if I hadn't been suffering from insomnia and opened Steam that morning, I wouldn't have even realized any of this happened. I would've been like most people, cursing Bluehole for being incompetent and handing out random bans. Meanwhile, my Steam account would still be floating out there, facing even bigger risks—and I'd be totally clueless. I actually don't really like battle royale games, but I've played plenty of multiplayer competitive games. I can put my hand on my heart and swear that I have never, and will never, use cheats in multiplayer games. Because, like most normal people in this world, I hate this kind of behavior that disregards fair play, destroys other people's gaming experiences, and brings shame upon oneself, one's family, and one's country. But actually, that's not even the main point I want to make. My account has already been banned, and I've already removed this game from my Steam library. If anyone doubts the story I've told, I can provide my Steam login history—it is the one and only piece of evidence I have. Ultimately, I want to emphasize again: if you guys value your accounts, please try your best not to buy this game; if you already own it, do everything you can to never log into your Steam account and run this game in internet cafes or public places. I hope everyone who sees this can enjoy our games and our lives.

translation_en: [quote] [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/36579661-Setna/]Before you start, follow my curator page where I have my other reviews.[/url] [/quote] Yeah, the wheel has turned, it's time to settle the score, PUBG. Yep, I'm finally writing a review for this game that I've been playing since its beta. Grab your coffee, sit down, and let me tell you at length what this game is all about. In my first years of university (about 4 years ago), game keys were being handed out to streamers (and later to players). Even though it didn't look like much in the Twitch world at the time, the genre was super interesting so people were curious about Battle Royale games. H1Z1-style games were already pretty popular among streamers, and PUBG's development team included people from the H1Z1 team. This created the impression among players of the aging H1Z1 that a new and better game was coming. Well, I thought it would be like that too, not gonna lie. After grabbing one of the distributed game keys along with my roommates, we started playing. We started playing alright, but the game was running at 10 FPS and 200 MS. Fortunately, they fixed these issues within 5-10 days, and we started playing the game getting between 30-40 FPS. The developer team, turning the game's beta phase into a very good marketing tool, saw the audience's potential and after a while released the game into early access on Steam. My friends and I bought the game at full price and started playing. The game was seriously full of bugs and had very severe performance problems. For months, with my PC featuring a 1060 6GB graphics card, I got around 50 FPS from this game. But it was fine because it couldn't get any worse than this, and the devs were making serious money, meaning they had plenty of budget to develop the game. After all, you gotta spend money to make money, right? Wrong. Wrong, and it was never like that. Thanks to the tons of money they made in a short time, the devs got huge egos and instead of improving the game, they started thinking: "How much more can we milk the players? What can we do to make players spend more money?" Time had marched on and they still couldn't fix the game. Instead of improving it, they removed foggy and rainy weather, cutting back on the game's variety. But they did bring a new map, and well, since they couldn't fix the performance issues, they figured the theme of the new map should be a desert. Why? Because there's no grass, no trees, so performance is artificially high. Around this time, Epic Games' production Fortnite came out as a competitor to PUBG. PUBG didn't care about this game at first, but Fortnite being free, having pretty good optimization, and very few bugs pushed people to play Fortnite. Fortnite, increasing its player count over time, forced PUBG to improve. But guess what happened? Despite all the tons of money they made, instead of improving the game, the devs put out a statement: "Did you ask us?" Yes, the developers actually said Epic Games didn't ask us for approval while making Fortnite. Who the hell are you that this guy has to ask you? You're the guys who abandoned H1Z1 yesterday because you couldn't handle it, and before that Arma 3 DAYZ because you couldn't handle that either—where does this impudence come from? Who the hell would ask your permission for anything? No, and when the 1.0 version of this game launched, they were like, "Uh, well, the game is actually still like early access, please don't be mad." What happened? You were acting all badass and suddenly you turned into, "I'm a little pastry UwU." No one has pissed me off in the gaming world as much as the developers of this game. Oh, and by the way, you heard right, PUBG isn't the first half-assed game this team made. Let's get to the point—we kept playing because we were making serious profits by getting crates and stuff from the game and selling them on the community market. I personally doubled the money I spent on the game during the time I played, and my roommates did the same. Recently, I wanted to log in and see how much the game has changed. translation_en: How I regret wasting 1000+ hours on this piece of shit! Let's start with the pros of the game (there are none...) :) The first pro is the shooting and gunplay. The gunplay here feels nice; you have to control recoil and spread, you need to lead your targets and calculate bullet ballistics (which actually exist here). Shooting at long distances can be pretty tough. The second pro is the variety of weapon attachments, which you constantly have to scavenge for, and which can heavily affect your shooting and therefore the outcome of the match in certain situations. Actually, it's hard to call this variety a pro, because the attachments in the game are divided into two categories: good ones, which make shooting comfortable, and bad ones, with which not just anyone can manage to properly kill enemies purely on skill. The third pro, for myself personally, is that I actually made a very nice profit off this game. Roughly speaking, from all the cases and skins I sold, I made about 9-10 thousand rubles. Let's subtract the 900 rubles I paid for the game and the 2400 I spent on battle passes. That leaves me with around 6500 rubles in net profit from this game. So I guess you could say I didn't lose money on it. Now onto the cons of the game, there are way more of these than the pros... The first con is the god awful optimization! Over three years, the developers (if you can even call them that) haven't been able to optimize the game so that it doesn't lag even on top-tier PCs. Personally, I currently get between 70 and 110 fps on any settings, while ultra-high settings somehow lag a little less..., but there are still constant stutters and fps drops. The second con is the disgusting graphics on any settings. They could at least polish the graphics and optimization with every update... but nah, they'd rather add more skins! The third con is the massive amount of bugs. I see no point in going into detail here. Let's just say it's completely normal in this game to get stuck in textures, jump out of a vehicle at full speed without pressing any buttons, reload your weapon multiple times yet still end up with 0 ammo in the mag. You can easily fall right through the textures. You could write a whole book about the bugs in this game. The fourth con is the awful gameplay. Matches last 30-35 minutes on big maps and 15-25 minutes on small ones, out of which you'll spend 90% of the time running from the zone and looting, and the rest of the time dying to rats who sit in corners of houses and lie in bushes the entire match getting just 1-2 kills... The fifth con is way too much reliance on RNG and luck! You hotdrop before the enemy, but they get lucky and find a weapon first; the zone spawns miles away from you and you have no vehicle; you can easily get killed by the red zone; the enemy has a better position than you, or better weapons or attachments, etc. In any of these scenarios, you have a 99% chance of losing. The sixth con is the atrocious netcode. I've had countless times where I shot an enemy, but they didn't take any damage at all even though you could clearly see blood squirting out of them. Or when you get killed behind a wall. Situations like this happen all the time! The seventh con is the huge number of cheaters and macro users. The developers claimed that with every update the anti-cheat gets better and there are way fewer cheaters, but that's bullshit! Yeah, cheaters do get banned, but there are still tons of them. The eighth con is the developers' mediocre attitude toward the game. They do everything they can to milk more money, while making zero effort to improve the game and completely giving zero fucks about all its major and significant problems! This con pretty much sums up the entire review because it's the most important one, and that says it all. My advice to you: don't play this dumpster fire, don't waste your time on this game (if it can even be called that). Go play other, actually good games instead. The game is simply dying. Compared to its competitors, it just looks pathetic and laughable. If you disagree with my opinion and keep playing THIS, I feel sorry for you, but it's your time. Draw your own conclusions! Thanks to everyone who read and upvoted this review!

The players who only play competitive don't even bother trying these updates, and they probably never will. translation_en: Even someone like me who's not into the Battle Royale style (last one standing wins) gotta admit I got hooked on this little game for a few hours, cause it really grabs you and it's pretty competitive, with up to 100 players having to fight to the death on an island until only one is left, the winner. The coolest part is that there are different game modes: solo, duo, squad (up to four people) in both competitive and casual across five different maps (two desert, two forest and a snow one). Although there are a lot of sweaty players who've been playing for years, your chances of winning depend on luck and skill, in the time I played I managed to get second place three times, including in my first match, so anyone can end up doing well by being careful and drawing as little attention as possible. A cool point is that even though the maps are huge it's very easy to find weapons and gear, pretty much everywhere has ammo and survival items, you don't gotta kill yourself searching to find something useful, putting a bigger focus on combat although it still requires exploring for better resources for anyone who wants even better odds of winning... and as everyone knows as the match goes on the area keeps shrinking until it closes into a small circle in the center of the map, and that puts on a lot of pressure and makes every match frantic and stressful cause you're constantly spinning around and paying attention to any nearby noise or gunfire, also having to always keep moving while being careful not to get spotted while running to the safe zone of the map. It's really cool, and there are even some vehicles scattered around the environment for quick travel, but the downside is the engine noise catches the attention of any nearby enemies, making you an easy target. There's also the option to play in both third person and first person, and I honestly thought it was way better as an fps, cause the gameplay feels stiffer in third, but I got a headache from constantly whipping the camera side to side all the time, which made it impossible for me to play for very long sessions. Another point a lot of people complain about and it's true is regarding graphics and performance, sadly the game is poorly optimized and often suffers random fps drops and stutters during the match, and that ends up messing things up sometimes since every second is crucial between life and death for every competitor. So I recommend PUBG to anyone who's really a fan of the Battle Royale style or really likes competition and pvp (player versus player), but it's good to test it first to make sure you won't have major performance issues and can play without getting a headache, making it worth checking out on a free weekend or using the refund system if needed (remembering that in this case you gotta test it for up to two hours and nothing more than that).

translation_en: Today I saw this game on the Steam front page again, so I'll share my personal experience and advice. My PUBG account got banned exactly a year ago today. I bought the game in late 2018 because it was super hyped at the time and all my friends knew about it, but very few actually owned it. Driven by desire, I asked a friend to buy it for me. After that, I went to the internet café every day to play PUBG. Whether I died immediately upon landing or came in second, I never complained, because that's just how the game is: "survival of the fittest." Running into cheaters was the same—they just have no parents, never got a proper education, or to put it simply: scum of society. I also spent a little bit of cash on it just to try and roll for skins I liked (tears of an unlucky bastard ;-;). But after I got into CS:GO, I stopped playing this much, though I'd still occasionally hit the training grounds to keep my feel for it. Plus, it was the first game I ever bought, so naturally I cherished it immensely and never even thought about hacking. Until I checked out some skin-unboxing site and entered my Steam account info on it. A few days later, when I logged back into Steam, I saw the words "You have a Steam Support message" at the top. I clicked it, and in big bold letters it said, "You have been permanently banned by the developers of PUBG." In that exact instant, I was totally dumbfounded. I stood frozen in place for about a minute, my brain completely blank. When I came to, those words were still just sitting there, cold and indifferent. My first reaction was to appeal, but to this day they've never given me a clear response. A friend next to me asked if I lent my account to anyone, which I figured was impossible since our crew is as tight as it gets. Then I opened my QQ mail and a bunch of Steam verification code messages popped up—at least a dozen of them—and the hidden IP address countries showed CN (I've been living in Korea these past few years). That's when I realized my account had been hacked. I immediately changed my Steam password and added the Guard authenticator, but no matter how much I racked my brain, I couldn't figure out how I got hacked. That whole day, food tasted like cardboard and I couldn't sleep. Then I stumbled across a report saying some phishing sites pretend to be skin-unboxing websites to steal people's accounts. It all clicked, but there's no cure for regret in this world! Today is the "one-year anniversary" of my PUBG account ban. Everyone, you gotta be careful with unboxing sites and random links in Steam comments. There's a high chance they're scams. Report them the second you see them, and absolutely do not click on them, absolutely do not go in, absolutely do not!

translation_en: It's one of my favorite games. However, currently with over 850 hours played, and having just reached the game's 3rd anniversary, I feel obliged to say that I find it disrespectful on the part of the company to have profited so insanely much at launch, with millions and millions, and the game is still like this: -Most bugs have been cleared up, but with every update, it gets bogged down with tons of lag. -You can't say there are many hackers nowadays. I've only run into 3 or 4 since I started playing. But the ban system is trash. A friend of mine got his steam account hacked and when he recovered it, he had a permanent ban in the game, and there are barely any ways to communicate with the developers and fix the problem, thus losing a fair player and a gaming buddy for other players. -The microtransactions are an insult. €10 for a t-shirt, who comes up with prices like that? Plus the same loot box system as Overwatch but worse: about €2.5 to open a box, with a very high probability of getting 40-cent items. Haven't you made enough money already? Even so, the passes are okay, I bought one and I'm satisfied with all the rewards (even though it takes a while to reach level 100). I think it's the most honest thing in the game regarding in-game purchases. -Game optimization feels like it's never going to reach a comfortable spot. What bugs me the most is that the menu buttons are sluggish and the whole menu itself could be more dynamic. In-game, I have no issues. -Sometimes, it feels like the company is shifting its attention from the game to trivial stuff. The fantasy battle royale? Okay, funny, but all of us players see that and get disappointed seeing the time and effort dedicated to that instead of looking at their game's flaws. All in all, it has to be said: This game is a work of art. Despite all the useless crap that keeps getting added whether it's for profit or not, the important thing is that if you have a decently powerful PC you are going to enjoy a unique gameplay experience in the battle royale genre. Honestly, no game has made me feel so alive in a free-for-all situation against so many players. Plus, a parkour system was added which it desperately needed, and they have constantly been working on new weapons and new maps, meaning new experiences within the game. I highly recommend it, although you should wait for a sale to buy it, and know whether or not it's worth buying stuff inside the game. Even with its bad stuff, it's still a unique shrine to war survival.

translation_en: Haven't played in a while, time to state the obvious and talk some armchair bullshit. PUBG was never killed by cheaters, nor by COD Warzone, but by the devs, the players, and the streamers. The core of Battle Royale is SURVIVAL!!!!!!!!!! Use any means necessary to survive, stay alive, and if you make it to the end, you win!!! Battle Royale was never about getting as many kills as possible. What is a "Battle Royale"? First you're supposed to *flee*, and when you can't run anymore, *then* you fight back, okay?! If you drop in and run around the whole map looking for people to kill, what kind of Battle Royale is that? That's just CS, alright... A results-driven mindset has made the gaming taste of the vast majority of Chinese players genuinely low, rock-bottom low. In the minds of many: As long as I get the final win, the fun along the way, the immersion, the interaction—all of that completely doesn't matter. When a minority of high-skill players realized that running around looking for kills could shorten match times; When streamers realized that a 30-kill game seemed to get them more gifts; When the developers realized more and more people leaned towards this optimal solution to winning the game and started compromising... That's when the game started to lose its flavor. Everyone forgot why this game was so fun in the beginning. Because over 95% of those "noobs" in your eyes—even though their aim is trash, their movement is clunky, and their game sense is terrible—still had a chance to win! Even if they died right off the drop, they wouldn't feel too frustrated, because they believed that in the next match they'd still have a chance, even if that chance was no more than 5%. For a noob, losing 20 games in a row doesn't matter; if they win the 21st, the previous 20 are just water under the bridge. When everyone else is going to Pochinki to bash each other's brains out, I can go to a remote corner and still loot up. When everyone is running around the world looking for gunfights, I can drive straight to the center of the circle and lie prone waiting—even if not a single person walks by, isn't that nervous, fearful feeling also a form of game fun? If I get lucky, lying prone in the destined circle, isn't there hope of watching two dogs fight and then scavenging the scraps at the end? Yet this hope was jointly destroyed by the developers, the minority of players, and the streamers. For the game to reach the state it's in today, anyone can be criticized. But you hardcore gunplay-meta players have no right to talk. Are the devs stupid? Of course they are stupid. But from the moment technical streamers started mass-cloning this playstyle, the dead end for this game was already sealed. For a game meant for everyone, when its gameplay becomes increasingly homogeneous, and when its optimal solutions become fewer and fewer, it gradually devolves into a circle-jerk for a minority. And looking at the developers, what did our fucking dipshit Bluehole do? They kept emphasizing hardcore mechanics, adding more and more tactical weapons. Are you guys planning to drop a close-quarters urban map for CQB next? Are you sure you're making a Battle Royale and not Rainbow Six? Just wait and see, I don't think this game will survive the year. Dying along with it will be a bunch of completely generic streamers. Time to bash Korea while we're at it. Koreans and Chinese are like two biological specimens when it comes to making and playing games. Chinese players go straight for the result, completely skipping the process, which is why they love using cheats. Koreans have a terrifyingly small worldview yet possess this baffling, honeyed self-confidence, so the stuff they make, no matter how polished, can never be grand. Of course, these two countries happen to be neighbors, and trade the most games with each other—it's fucking hilarious... Finally, it's not like I'm looking down on players who only found out about Steam because of PUBG. You registered a Steam account back then for PUBG, and 3 years later, the most expensive game in your library is still PUBG, with a total of no more than 5 games. You haven't even heard of Epic and Origin, you don't even know how to register for a Battle.net international account. You watch a COD stream and immediately start comparing it to PUBG. Whenever you guys play a game, you *have* to find an opponent for yourselves—either I kneel, or you kneel. Whenever you do something in a game, there *has* to be a clear, positive feedback loop. You probably can't even fathom how a game like *Animal Crossing* got popular. It's not that you're not interested; it's that they wouldn't even deign to talk to you. You guys are even qualified to talk about games? Honestly, fuck right back off to TapTap and stay there!

Right now there's nothing more normal in this genre. Fortnite or Apex don't count. They're totally different games with different mechanics that just don't click with me personally. Let's move on to the flaws of this game. 1. Randoms. Everybody says that Dota or CS have the most fucked up players. The most brain-dead ones inhabit random squads. I haven't seen this many degenerates in any other game. How does this manifest? Very simply, with examples again. PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS is a survival game, the goal of the game is to win the round. But in the heads of 99.9 percent of people, the goal is to drop under the plane, preferably at school or apartments, take someone down with them to the lobby and start a new match. Why the hell are you playing squads if you just need to shoot stuff? Go play solo, they made a deathmatch mode for you, no need to play in squads. The point of the game is to survive and win matches, not to die at the very beginning. Even if half of the four survive after a skirmish, that's already not a full squad, your chances of winning drop. That is extremely fucking stupid. Even if you place a marker on a remote town that you can easily fly to just by holding ctrl, or drive to in a car, in response you hear on voice chat, "nah that's too far, why would we need that, let's go to Pochinki..." Gulls, that's what I call people who just steal loot from enemies you killed. Just imagine, you have an empty backpack, you kill an enemy with a single shotgun, you have nothing, but the enemy had loot. And then on the horizon your teammate appears and just takes absolutely everything from the enemy you killed. In moments like that you want to kill not the enemies, but your teammates. The only thing that stops you is a week-long ban for teamkilling. Whoever kills gets the loot, if there's anything extra you just need to voice it. Team play is completely absent with randoms, everyone plays for themselves. What's so hard about pressing the middle mouse wheel when you see a spare gun? What's so hard about gathering attachments you don't need in your backpack and sharing them with teammates when you meet? Meds are a whole separate story. You say on voice chat, guys do you have a first aid kit? In response, nah no. A squad skirmish starts, two go down, the squad gets wiped. You start looting them and find 5-8 first aid kits on the guy who said he had no extra meds. Most people drop a quick marker on the compass, but don't say where the enemy actually is. There's a village in front of you, you ask on voice chat, where exactly is the enemy? In response, I just dropped a marker! It feels like they think they're playing with mind readers. And as for throwing a smoke on a knocked teammate, that's just straight up sci-fi. You try to get into the zone quietly from the blue, and you get these special specimens who start shooting at an enemy with low HP. Voice chat is something else entirely. You constantly run into people with typewriters instead of keyboards. Constantly people who have the TV on in the background, a dog barking, a baby screaming. What stops you from putting voice chat on a push-to-talk button? You run into music lovers, because apparently in a game where you need to listen to every sound around you, you just can't play without your favorite track... There are so many degenerates who will cuss you out right off the bat for no reason. Good thing there's a report for insulting, plus the option to mute this subhuman. 2. Cheaters. There are extremely many of them in this game. Everyone in the comments blames everything on the Chinese, that's partly true, but from personal experience, cheaters can be found among anyone. Any Vasya, Petya, and Seryozha too, can easily visit certain resources and pick out specific software for themselves. Anyone can buy a private cheat and run around the map tearing everyone a new one with an aimbot, knowing who is where from a kilometer away. And I'm not even talking about macros, which especially gifted individuals don't even consider cheats. Every second person in this game uses a recoil control macro, and it seems like they don't even get banned for that. The game has a report system that works every other time. A minimal amount get banned, while the rest keep running around with privates just like before. Moreover, a new account or key can be bought for pennies on trading platforms. I used to constantly send videos where they belong, but now I don't see the point, reports only. In terms of anti-cheat, the game is dead. Statements from certain characters about cheaters being more common in TPP and on Russian servers are complete absolute nonsense. I'm a veteran TPP player, I ran all seasons from the third-person perspective, this new season I'm playing FPP, mostly on Europe, and the result is the exact same. Back then the online was over two million, now it's 500-600 thousand. People simply left the game because the anti-cheat doesn't work. 3. Survivor Passes. It's clear all this is done so as not to let go of the audience, to give people something to do in the game, plus profit from sales. But you get this feeling that the latest pass was made without any soul. The skins aren't pleasing to the eye, I won't even mention the AK wrapped in, let's say, wet rags. And this is the reward for level one hundred... In my opinion, the best ones were Event Pass: Sanhok and Survivor Pass: Wild Card.
