translation_en: Pubg is dead already, I planned to change my review long ago but the Steam store page was bugged these past few days and wouldn't let me. Now that PC 1.0 is out, I'm gonna write a proper review for the game. 1. Replayability: Because the mode is fresh, the replayability is pretty high. It brings back that initial tension and thrill of gaming, especially in the first 100 hours—your hands would literally shake in the final circle, and getting a chicken dinner got you super hyped. Squads and duos offer completely different experiences. Squads involve all kinds of tactical coordination: covering fire, flanking, feints, baiting, rifle cover for snipers, etc. Pushing houses especially feels like a tactical squad game. How long this game lasts depends on the person. At least for me, with 400 hours played, I feel like I could play another 100 and not get bored. 2. RNG: A lot of people say this game relies too heavily on luck, but once you play enough you realize that resource spawns are actually fixed for a certain period or patch. For example, right now the steel mill (cemetery/factory) has a super high chance of spawning a 98k. Back then the school always spawned big guns and high-tier loot, but now the school has turned into a poor zone. My advice to newbies is to get familiar with one place first—like the steel mill I mentioned. My route is crystal clear: first target is the roof, eye the gun spawn spot and land. If someone else lands first, skip the roof, the containers by the entrance have a high chance of spawning a weapon. Inside the back of the containers, or if not there, the building behind the containers definitely will have one. 3. New map: The desert map. A lot of people say loot is too spread out, and the cities are so huge they'll drive you nuts, and I feel the same way. But looting time is still enough, and the new patch made the first safe zone bigger. Still, I really don't like the new map. It's fine for solos, but in squads getting a win is kind of tough. Maybe it's just because I'm not familiar with it yet. 4. Optimization: The optimization in the new patch is actually alright. My PC is from five years ago: i5 2500, GTX 760, 12GB 1333 RAM, everything on very low and a stable 70 FPS. But the servers are truly trash. When player counts are high at the start, severe rubberbanding happens, lagging back 1-2 minutes every single match. Especially on Asian servers, JP/KR servers are way too bad. 5. Cheaters: Still severe, but maybe because of the big update and leaderboard reset, I've run into fewer cheaters lately. PS: Cheater TV, I really want to learn Snake Brother's 15x M4 full-auto tracking a moving car point-blank. I bought the game in June, the optimization was trash back then and I didn't leave a negative review. From July to September the game blew up and concurrent players surged from 200k to 1.5 million, causing servers to shit the bed every day, and I still didn't leave a negative review. In October cheaters were everywhere—aimbots, wallhacks, speedhacks, teleports, player-sucking, godmode. Getting bullied by all these fatherless bastards and I still didn't leave a negative review. When Bluehole partnered with Xunyou and Tencent, I didn't leave a negative review either. Because I knew Bluehole was trying their best to improve everyone's gaming experience, they just have a small team and might genuinely lack the capability sometimes, but at the end of the day they were trying. BUT!! In December I gave my very first negative review! Why? Because with all this video evidence of Lu Benwei cheating, the official devs actually chose to stay silent? Cover for him? Why does my SKS have breath sway the second I scope in, but Lu Benwei's can stay stable and not shake for that long? As the biggest streamer on Douyu TV right now, he's setting the example for cheating, yet the official website chooses to turn a blind eye. I am fucking furious! Until the cheater Lu Benwei gets banned, this negative review stays.

translation_en: You can complain about Playerunknown's Battlegrounds just like about many other games where we play "The Hunger Games"—that the optimization could be better, that there are cheaters, that the balance could be better, that we could use more guns, or anything else that comes to mind. Let's not forget that the game is still in "Early Access," and the whole world is playing it, and you can't deny its phenomenon, which took this genre of games to a new level. I resisted buying this title for quite a long time myself, thinking: "meh, everyone is playing it so much it makes you want to puke," and then I bought the game and nearly 200 hours later spent on crawling, sneaking, hiding in bushes, and shooting more or less accurately, I honestly admit—the game has its charm. You don't get it right away, because at first glance the gameplay is repetitive, you know, we fly to some spot on the map and try not to die and not let ourselves be killed. However, after your umpteenth match, passing the exact same little house for the nth time, you think to yourself: "oh, that's where I had a firefight with this tough bastard last time" or "that's where I ran in without checking my surroundings and took a shotgun blast to the head." Every match, supposedly the same, is a separate story in itself, written by the players themselves in this death sandbox. A separate element is playing together with friends, hours of laughter from good or totally botched plays, terrified screams in your headsets when an enemy pops out of nowhere, or yet another flip while riding a motorcycle together. "Are we jumping here? It should be empty," followed by running into 5 opposing squads and trying to wiggle your way out of the situation. This is very brief, but playing with friends makes this title a completely different experience that we live through. Playing solo, you listen to every single sound because it might be an enemy, and playing with friends, it's not that easy. Because even when you neutralize an enemy, usually his buddy is lurking in a bush somewhere nearby. That's it in a nutshell. With a clear conscience, I recommend it to anyone who likes to shoot and feel a bit of adrenaline, because this game delivers both. PS beware of the red zone and silencers.

translation_en: I particularly don't really like writing reviews for games that are in Early Access, so I'll write this review as a preview/informational piece on the current state of the product, and when the game is released I'll update it with the proper changes. First of all, from personal experience I'll say that this review will probably be heavily criticized and attacked by haters and fanboys, because generally people who like the product tend to ignore the negatives and defend it with every possible argument, even if some are completely baseless. In this case, I ask that you please act seriously and be polite when facing criticism; it's fine to defend a product you like, but as a wise old man I know always says... "Analyze a review, it will help someone else just like it helps you." Playerunknown's Battlegrounds is an action Battle Royale sub-genre game created by Brendan Greene (popularly known as "PlayerUnknown"). The game has been gaining massive popularity over the last few months thanks to streamers and content creators, apart from the fact that it's extremely fun... For anyone who has never played a Battle Royale game or has no idea how this type of game works: Battle Royale is a sub-genre very similar to Hunger Games, where we have a huge map and a large number of players (more specifically 100) compete against each other to decide who will be the victor or victors (in case you're playing team mode). — What? Is that it? — Basically yes. The game is quite simple, you literally drop onto the map and your only objective is to survive (besides blasting the enemies away hehe). I confess that initially I had a strong prejudice against games in this sub-genre, because I was one of the people who bought the infamous H1Z1 on pre-order and ended up bitterly regretting it even before playing, however, after a lot of insistence from some friends I was convinced to play these games and ended up getting addicted... The fact is that these games are fun machines, because just like most MOBAs, they are dynamic and fun. It's practically impossible to play the exact same match twice, the challenge is always there and winning is always rewarding. Now, the real reason I don't recommend buying this game in its current state is the terrible optimization. Frankly, it's sad to see a game with so much potential fall short on one of the most important aspects of PC gaming... The hard truth is that the game is a lot of fun, but completely slapped together, not to say something worse... PUBG is obviously in Early Access, which means the product is unfinished, there are hundreds of problems to be fixed and it seems the developers aren't giving it the proper attention... On the game's Steam store page there is a small questionnaire with the following question: — "What is the current state of the Early Access version?" — and the answer is: — “The game is stable.” — No fucking way! You just have to play it for 5 minutes to realize the product is completely unstable... You could even use the argument that the game is in Early Access, so we shouldn't complain about the optimization, but the thing is there are hundreds of other games in Early Access that don't slack on optimization, plus, it's been 8 months since the game was ''released'', there's no excuse for them not having optimized it yet. And another thing, considering this is the product's main problem, how the hell did the developers have time to add cosmetic items (crates) and microtransactions? Why didn't they optimize the game instead of adding clothes and weapons? I'll tell you... Priorities... Priorities... Priorities... Or maybe because they just don't have the competence to optimize it... The store questionnaire also states when the game will leave Early Access, I mean, supposedly states... — “Players, Today I want to update everyone on PLAYERUKNOWN’S BATTLEGROUNDS progress through Early Access. Over the past few months I have done a lot of interviews, and in many of them, I said we hoped to be out of Early Access six months after we first launched. I’ve come to realize that restricting the window to a specific month could hinder us from delivering a fully featured game and/or lead to disappointment within the community if the launch deadline is not met. So, we have decided that we are going push the full launch back a bit from the initial six-month timeframe, but want to assure you that we are still planning a full release before the end of Q4 2017. We will continue to push weekly and monthly updates until full launch as we want to ensure that the game we release is the best version possible. This is why we’re giving a launch window rather than an exact date. We hope this makes sense, and appreciate your understanding.'' — So basically they changed the release date, which was scheduled for 6 months after the launch month (March), to an indefinite date that will possibly be at the end of 2017. That says a lot about what's going to happen to this game... I imagine PUBG will leave Early Access symbolically... It'll leave, but it'll still be completely fucked up. The only way to actually optimize this piece of crap is to remake the game from scratch (just like the Rust developers did). It's obvious the developers don't know shit about programming, it makes no sense for a game with last-gen graphics to have this mediocre performance... For comparison's sake, even on a high-end rig it's hard to hit 60fps; the game using 10-11GB of RAM, 7-8GB of VRAM and failing to maintain 60fps at 1080p on a GTX 1080 is sickening. Aside from the optimization, there are other serious issues: [list] [*][b]Texture Loading:[/b] Textures and buildings take a long time to load and that hurts a lot in a competitive game, for example, you just hit the ground but the buildings haven't loaded yet, so you can see nearby enemies walking through the map; [*][b]Map Loading:[/b] On an SSD map loading is fairly fast (which was to be expected), but I've had cases where on a regular HDD the game didn't even load, it just froze and I got stuck on an infinite loading screen; [*][b]Crashes:[/b] I had a few, can't say exactly why, since they happened randomly on two different computers; [*][b]Cheaters:[/b] Like every multiplayer game, this one has them too. For as little as I played I shouldn't have run into cheaters, but unfortunately that wasn't the case. Lately the number of cheaters has been increasing a lot, even more considering the game gets more popular every day, not to mention the price is considerably low; [*][b]Physics:[/b] In games where we have cars and objects (items) we can interact with, it's essential that the physics have at least some fundamentals, but in this case it was totally left by the wayside... It's common to see flying vehicles, players, items and projectiles clipping through walls, floating bodies and buildings, etc. Anyway, it's a show of bugs that often mess up your game. [/list] After at least a dozen matches played, you can establish a baseline and say beyond a shadow of a doubt that the game is addictive, fun and rewarding (literally, since you get crates by playing), but unfortunately PUBG falls very short in terms of software and I can't recommend it in its current state. The tip I leave here is NOT to wait for optimization, because I think it's practically impossible for it to ever arrive. translation_en: So, PUBG has officially been released in the state they managed to "finish" it on the test servers. The early test updates noticeably boosted FPS, and warps and stutters during gunfights almost completely vanished, but just a few days later they "fixed" this—Russian players are once again dealing with the old problems. On top of that, a new fun feature was added—rubberbanding: when your character constantly gets pulled back. An enemy running after you with a frying pan in their hands will definitely catch up and bash your skull in. For this same reason, when dropping with a parachute, players flying right behind you will end up landing earlier. Average ping to the London servers is 66ms, Ireland 88ms, Frankfurt 53ms. They also didn't fix the game crashing without an error, or the long menu loading times. One of the new jokes—closer to the end of a match, three out of four squad members got a "network lag" spike. Top loot, 3 circles left until the final zone, and this bullshit. We didn't wait for it to unfreeze, just restarted the game via ALT+F4. After restarting, the game didn't offer to reconnect to the unfinished match. Just go fuck yourselves, guys, try again, dammit! And a new type of cheats—getting killed through a concrete wall. There's no one in the room, yet a bullet flies in and boom. Shooting. Apparently, PUBG runs on the principle: whoever has lower ping is right (deals more hit damage). The netcode problem has not been solved at all. An enemy who takes 5-6 bullets from an SKS or AKM keeps living, running, and smiling. It feels like more than half the shots simply aren't registered. Meaning, locally the game shows a hit with blood splatters, BUT! 1-2 hits on you is an almost 100% guarantee you'll end up dead or knocked out. In addition, they changed the ballistics in some incomprehensible way. When watching replays, we found a hilarious sight. This is a whole song in itself. A player with a Kar98k and an 8x scope aims LOWER than the head—hits the head, aims HIGHER than the head—hits the head again. HOW IS THAT EVEN POSSIBLE?!!! If you watch your squadmates shoot, they have the exact same problem as you. No matter how you aim, half the shots seem to go straight to devnull. UPD: On Asian, South, and North American servers, stutters and warps happen much less often. Apparently, European servers are running at their maximum capacity, shooting is slightly better. Graphics. Nothing really changed with the release. BF3-BF4-BF1 gives me 150-180 FPS on Ultra. In Pubg on below-medium settings, it's 45-75 FPS (2K resolution, 1ms matrix response, 16GB RAM, Core-i7 5930K 4.4GHz, GTX980SLI 1400MHz). Physics. When parachuting next to a house, get ready to lose 50% of your health because your parachute caught on an invisible roof. STILL NOT FIXED after release! Cutting the parachute during a phantom snag is still impossible. The Zone. No comment: didn't find a vehicle—you're gonna play as a homeless sprinter. While you're running, the zone will gobble up all the meds you were lucky enough to find. The remaining loot will go to a cheater near the end of the match with an 85% probability. After the release, they increased the zone damage, especially after the 2nd-3rd circles. And the exact same cheaters and macro users, although their number has dropped noticeably (for now) (on January 18th in squad games it's an infestation of cheaters again. Trash players fighting for the right to sell more crates and buy themselves acne cream and instant noodles), but in the leaderboards, the top spots are once again filled with weird names like qw-iuh9812g1fskdf. Summing it up, I can say that instead of being fun, the game has turned into a total nerve-racking chore. But campers will definitely love it. UPD December 11, 2018. Uninstalled the game. Cheaters in 10 matches out of 10. Magic bullet, WH, Maphack (loot), they've stopped banning these scumbags. Loot and weapon balance is completely broken. PUBG is the best way to throw your money down the drain. Actually no, the best way is to buy the game, play one or two matches, see for yourself, and request a refund. Maybe mass refunds will motivate the devs to somehow change the situation with cheaters. Although, considering this piece of shit has already been ported to all platforms, they've already made the bank on PC that they were aiming for.

translation_en: *Edit Nov. 5, 2017: Even after the anti-cheat measures, I ran into wallhacks and aimbots... Death to cheaters. On top of that, since Nov. 2, the KR/JP servers have been lagging to an unplayable degree. Honestly, with the server issues constantly popping up during Early Access and the severe cheater problem, I almost feel a bit sorry for Bluehole, but hang in there, I'll wait to some extent. I'm rooting for you.* *Edit Nov. 1, 2017: Following the anti-cheat update on Oct. 27, it looks like another update is rolling out on Nov. 2. I haven't played enough to judge how effective these measures are, but judging by Twitter and other sites, cheaters are still running wild. That said, it's clear Bluehole sees cheaters as a problem, which gives me some hope for the future. I'm sure a lot of users are rooting for you, so hang in there, Bluehole...* ------------------------------------------------ This is a game that makes you paranoid because there are way too many reports of cheaters. The game itself is amazing. Even though there's only one map right now, you just keep playing to get that chicken dinner. It's that kind of highly replayable game. Also, I think the fact that Solo, Duo, and Squad all offer different kinds of fun is a really nice touch. And looking at the roadmap, even though the development speed is like a turtle's, they are steadily making progress, so I can wait patiently. Considering that it exploded in popularity right during Early Access, I was prepared for at least this much. Up to this point, I would definitely recommend this game. I'd want to say, "Go buy it." However, cheaters are ruining all of that. I started about a month ago and I'm a casual player who plays maybe 2 to 3 matches a day, but I've run into cheaters several times. Let me introduce you to three cheats I've encountered: Speed hacking, aimbot, and Divine Punishment (what I like to call it). You can probably guess what kind of cheats they are just from the names. As ridiculous as it sounds, I can still tolerate speed hacks. That's because if you get good enough, there's still a chance you can take them down. But I cannot forgive the other two. They completely kill your motivation. If you can imagine how it feels when an entire moving squad gets instantly headshot-deleted by an enemy the size of a bean, only for a super-fast enemy to immediately show up to loot your stuff... Or how it feels when you're proned on the second floor of a house where enemies can't even see you, and multiple bullets rain down straight through the roof into your head... I seriously don't get it. In this game, if even a single cheater is in the match, that match is ruined. And due to the nature of the game, the better you are at surviving, the more likely you are to run into cheaters, wasting 30 minutes of your time. There is no way I can recommend a game that makes you sacrifice 30 minutes for the sake of a cheater. And above all, there are so many reports of cheaters that it leaves you terrified of the invisible ones. When I see the kill feed filled with headshots by the same person, I find myself doubting, "Is that a cheater?" When I'm chugging energy drinks and sprinting, but an enemy far away drops me with a few headshots, I find myself doubting, "Is that a cheater?" I really hate myself for becoming like this. In a normal game, when I lose, I want to hone my skills so I don't lose next time, but in this game, my motivation is killed by thoughts like, "Well, if there are this many cheaters, any effort is just a waste of time." I want to ask Bluehole if they really think users can enjoy a game in such a paranoid state. Let me just say one thing: if you watch pro gamers stream, skilled players look like cheaters, so even if the kill feed is full of headshots from the same guy, there's a chance they aren't cheating. However, that's just not the mindset we can have in the current state of the game. If you didn't run into cheaters, it would have the right amount of tension and be amazing, though... Lastly, for anyone thinking of buying it now, I recommend waiting to see how Bluehole handles things. Considering that other major blockbuster games are coming out one after another from October to December, this isn't a game you need to force yourself to buy right now. Given how terrible things are right now, it won't be too late to get it even after it leaves Early Access. Even for Early Access, leaving the Chinese players—who are the root of the problem—completely unchecked is way too extreme. This isn't racism or anything; it's simply because every single cheater I've ever met was Chinese (or Taiwanese). PUBG is the ultimate bait being eaten away by cockroaches. That's all for this very long review. Thank you very much for reading this far. *(※If the situation ever improves, I would gladly edit this review at that time)*

translation_en: First, let me start with H1Z1. My first experience with battle royale was H1Z1 two years ago. Back in the beginning, there were no cheaters, no Red Army, and the game wasn't that popular yet. The game was normal and really fun back then, so I recommended it to my friends and even gifted copies to two of them so we could play together. After they played 6 matches with me, they said the game was boring. Fine, I figured the game just wasn't for their taste. In the blink of an eye, two years passed, and I had also quit for a year and a half. Then that well-known article came out: "China No. 1." And then a hilarious thing happened: those two friends I originally gifted the game to suddenly hyped up a "great game" they found, told me they bought it, and asked me to play with them. What the fuck? They had even forgotten the game accounts I gave them back then! Now they're reverse-hyping it to me and bought the game all over again. (I've realized that a friend's sincere recommendation isn't worth shit compared to some viral marketing account. From now on, I'm never recommending games to anyone again.) I know what the environment was like back then: streamers leading bunches of the Red Army, screaming "China No. 1" the moment they get in, fucking around in the game under the banner of patriotism, ruining game balance, and shitting on other players' gaming experiences. A bunch of people got banned back then, and those people cried, "We weren't even cheating and we got banned!" Don't they know that malicious teaming is even more disgusting than hacks? This directly made me move some games from my wishlist to "Ignore," like ARK and RUST. (Combined with streamers leading squads to raid foreigners' bases.) Actually, I get how those people feel—they just want to chat with foreigners. (I can understand that feeling; when I first played CS:GO, but I communicated normally. The longer you play, the more you realize that chatting with foreigners on Steam is completely normal.) So I really grew to resent H1Z1. Time flies, and PUBG was released. Actually, I had been following it for a long time, just sitting on the fence because I was worried shit like the Red Army would show up and ruin my gaming experience. After watching from the sidelines for 2 months, I noticed it seemed pretty normal. Plus, with friends hyping it up—the number of people pushing this game on me was 10 times that of H1Z1—I finally caved and bought it! The game is actually pretty fun: looting with your heart in your mouth, happily stripping boxes, the intense final circles, especially the first time you get a chicken dinner, which was so tense I almost choked. Dying doesn't kill the gameplay either; you just click to start the next match right away. If you run into a cheater, you just chalk it up to bad luck and queue up again. I had a lot of fun playing with friends. Then the Nuomi incident happened. The number of cheaters skyrocketed straight up, and the gaming experience became absolute trash. At first, I was naive enough to think there was no Red Army anymore, but later on I ran into them a few times. Honestly, I hate the Red Army even more than cheaters. Cheating is an individual action, but what the fuck even is the Red Army? Later, people told me that reporting malicious teaming gets people banned even faster than reporting cheats. Sometimes when I see reviews of people claiming they got banned without cheating, I assume it was probably for malicious teaming. Now I can't even play anymore; 4 out of 5 matches have cheaters. Streamers openly run speedhacks on stream, and while streaming, they even have the nerve to say the game is boring. Some streamers claim they have great aim and game sense, and when suspicious cheating moves happen, they immediately make excuses like "the streamer is a pro player" or "I'm not short on money, why would I cheat?" and so on. Now when I watch PUBG streams, my reaction to the streamer is just: "This streamer seems pretty normal, I'll follow." Actually, once you watch enough esports, you know that everyone eventually gets ratted out and killed by a camper, but some specific streamers are always driving around honking horns, get shot at, whip around and dump a whole mag, and just slaughter their way to a chicken dinner from start to finish. My first thought after watching is: sorry, we are definitely not playing the same game. Lastly, let me ask if the devs are ever going to fucking do anything, or is this just part of some money-making supply chain? It scared me so much I went and re-watched [spoiler]Extra Credits' Video Game Industry[/spoiler].

translation_en: [b]Foreword:[/b] For a long time H1Z1 sat alone on the throne, despite being unfinished, buggy and purely profit-driven. But thanks to upcoming competition from other Battle Royale/King of the Hill games, even that's starting to shift and updates are actually rolling out. PUBG is now available in Early Access and has already blown past everything else. At first I was skeptical, expecting just another game riding the coattails of the Battle Royale/King of the Hill hype train, ending up unfinished and flooded with microtransactions. I was wrong. My first impression is currently based on the Early Access version from Oct 11, 2017 after roughly 250+ hours of playtime, experience from about 200 hours of H1Z1, and testing out Fortnite. I'll update this review if there are any major changes. [b]Game Principle:[/b] As is standard in Battle Royale/King of the Hill, you drop onto a huge map along with 100 other players, pick an area where you want to land and loot houses to gear up with weapons, medkits and other equipment. On a map that continuously shrinks due to a lethal energy field, you try to survive without getting killed for as long as possible, fight others and ideally be the last one alive to win—meaning you're the "King of the Hill." The zone where the game ends is always random, just like (more or less) the drop spot. Every now and then certain areas get hit by artillery strikes that you should watch out for, while planes drop supply crates at various locations. You can play Solo, Duo, or as a Squad (a team of 4), with each mode having its own leaderboard and stats. It's played in 3rd person, but you can switch to 1st person if needed. In the meantime, 1st person-only servers have been added where 3rd person is disabled. [b]Content:[/b] - Currently there is one large map (8x8km), another one with a desert setting of the same size is almost finished, and a third has been announced. - Loot boxes & skins, stats & leaderboards, custom matches & fun modes. - Solo, Duo & Squad, each in third or first person. - 30 firearms (pistols, submachine guns, assault rifles, machine guns, sniper rifles, shotguns, crossbow). - 7 ammo types (9mm, 7.62mm, 5.56mm, arrows, ...). - 38 attachments (scopes, silencers, flash hiders, stocks, extended mags, ...). - 4 grenade types (frag, flashbang, smoke, molotov). - 5 melee weapons (everything from fists to a frying pan). - 6 consumables (bandages, energy drink, pills, med-kit, adrenaline, ...). - 9 vehicles (2/3-seater motorcycle, buggy, jeep, car, boat). - 3 weather effects (sunny, thunderstorms with rain, dense fog). [b]Maps:[/b] [u]Map 1:[/u] Name: Erangel Setting: Rural / Eastern Europe Size: 8x8 km An abandoned Russian island in the Black Sea, featuring meadows and fields, forests and mountains. There are cities of various sizes, smaller villages, bridges, a military base, ruins, a bunker system, a power plant, and many other little things to discover. [u]Map 2:[/u] Name: Miramar Setting: City / Desert Size: 8x8 km Map 2 is located in Central America / Mexico and focuses on urban areas as well as villages, slums, and canyons. Map-exclusive weapons & vehicles. [u]Map 3:[/u] Name: Unknown Setting: Snow / Europe Size: 8x8 km Map 3 is located in Europe by the Adriatic Sea. Alongside forests, it's supposed to feature a snowy mountain region and a warm coastal region. [b]Graphics & Sound:[/b] The graphics are nice thanks to Unreal Engine 4, but given the map size and player count it's obviously no Crysis. To me, it compares to Day-Z. I'm blown away by the massive draw distance without popping textures, the dense vegetation, weather effects, and explosions. Window panes, doors, fences, and small wooden shacks are destructible. The buildings aren't just empty shells like in H1Z1; they offer more variety in shape, color, and interior furnishing, which makes the whole map feel even more believable. The rain sounds good, and the thunderstorm is the best I've ever seen in a game, both visually and sound-wise. In the fog, the map vanishes under a thick white veil that reduces visibility to 20-40 meters. The audio also feels somewhat muffled, which conveys a sense of isolation. You can also find the odd blurry texture here and there, plus UE4 has an issue rendering hair—it tends to look pretty ugly. Weapons, explosions, vehicles, everything sounds believable, but the distance at which footsteps can be heard feels unrealistic to me. You can approach a house almost silently and get into position, but if someone takes steps on a wooden floor on the 3rd floor of a house, you can pinpoint them from outside another house away. [b]Controls & Options:[/b] The control options leave almost nothing to be desired. Sensitivity can be adjusted separately for each zoom level, and keybinding is extensive. The developers keep adding new control options, too. In general, the menu offers tons of settings for graphics, HUD, FOV, and the ability to choose for many keys whether their function stays active by "holding" or "toggling" the key (crouching, going prone, free-looking, ...). [b]Hardware Requirements:[/b] Weaker systems are currently struggling massively. A lot of optimization is still needed, though it's questionable how much more performance they can squeeze out. The issue isn't getting good FPS, but keeping them stable in all situations. At the beginning I played on "High", but the FPS drops from around 100 to less than half were obviously an issue in a firefight. That's why everything is set to "Medium" now, even though more would be possible. System 1: Core i7, GTX 980, 16GB RAM: 70-100 FPS on "Medium" System 2: Core i5, GTX 770, 8GB RAM: 50-70 FPS on "Low" [b]Differences from H1Z1:[/b] While the map size, artillery strikes, supply crates, and zones work very similarly, there are changes in many areas. Whether these are always an upgrade is a matter of taste. - Only 100 players instead of nearly 200 in H1Z1. - Jump timing from the plane can be freely chosen, plane flight path is always different. - In Duo & Squad it's temporarily possible to revive downed teammates if they haven't been "finished." - No more jumping out of fast-moving vehicles without taking massive damage. - Vehicles can no longer be rendered unusable by doing things like taking the keys, etc. - No crafting bandages etc. like in H1Z1; instead, all weapons can be fitted with attachments. [b]Pros:[/b] - Fast, skill-based matchmaking. - Content amount. - Graphics. - Map design. - Sound design during rain & thunderstorms. - New additions like the revive feature, inventory, etc. - Surprisingly polished for EA. [b]Cons:[/b] - Hardware requirements / optimization. - Only 100 players instead of 200. - Price. - Footstep audio / enemy positioning. - Microtransactions (keys) getting added soon. - Laggers from other regions. - EA bugs (fall damage, connection issues, lag, vehicle physics, collision detection, FPS drops, ...). [b]Conclusion:[/b] Rightfully the new top dog, and I don't think I'm going out on a limb by claiming this will be the genre's leading title for the next few years, one that's practically impossible to bypass. Feels like H1Z1 2, a sequel that's been spruced up and comes with more content, features, and detailed improvements. The price is steep, but fair—if not for the loot box/key system. 19.90€ would have been fine, too. For an Early Access game, it's already very good—far from an alpha, it's a solid beta. I'm optimistic based on the updates and minimal flaws and excited for new maps and weapons. Highly recommended for any Battle Royale/King of the Hill fan—provided your PC is powerful enough!

translation_en: First of all, this review was written on October 6th and does not reflect possible changes the game might undergo after that. I took into account the current details of the game, which is still in early access. PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS is the result of years of waiting by the battle-royale fan community. Expected as the ultimate successor to [i]H1Z1: King of the Kill[/i], PUBG was envisioned as the future masterpiece of Brendan Greene, considered the great mastermind of games in this style. After much anticipation, it was released to the public in early access in March 2017, with its actual release scheduled for the last quarter of 2017. [h1]Concept and Existence[/h1] PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS (PUBG) is a battle-royale style game built on the Unreal Engine 4 (the same engine as ARK: Survival Evolved), developed by PUBG Corp. and published by Bluehole (the same publisher as TERA Online). In it, you are dropped onto a gigantic island where you have to fight against 99 other players (if playing solo) in order to be the last survivor. As time goes by, a blue zone that drains health points closes in on the map, making it smaller and smaller, forcing players closer together and eventually fighting for survival with the weapons and tools they've found so far. [h1]Gameplay[/h1] PUBG has third or first-person gameplay, depending on the server you choose. The game is divided into servers, with a dedicated server for South America, but without ping and/or nationality restrictions. Upon dropping onto the island without tools and/or weapons, your objective is to try to arm yourself as quickly as possible (by looting houses and/or sheds) to defend yourself in a potential early fight. Depending on your game strategy, you can look to fight and eliminate enemies at the beginning of the game while they are vulnerable, or you can choose to drop in a more distant area, gear up, and only seek out fights necessary for your survival, leaving most of the action for the end of the match when the map gets smaller and players find each other more easily. [h1]Community[/h1] The game's community is the standard for any shooter. Since there is no in-game text chat, any and all communication with players who aren't your friends is done through an in-game voice chat system, which you can also mute if you want. Therefore, there isn't much room for toxic players, unless you're playing solo and decide to queue duo or squad with randoms. These players can be toxic if you make a mistake and/or can attack you on purpose just to ruin your experience with the game. In these cases, you can report them and the ban system seems to be effective. Actually, there's even room for a lot of fun with the voice chat system during the wait times, moments before you get thrown out of the plane. The game puts you in a lobby with all the players in the match and many play music or tell jokes there, providing some fun pre-game moments. [h1]Game Details[/h1] Since it was made on a new engine, a more optimized game with more fluid gameplay was expected, but what you see is the exact opposite. Even on high-end PCs, the game seems to run with stutters and a low frame rate, making gameplay quite difficult. The UI is sluggish and poorly optimized, and throughout the game, there is an immense feeling of input lag. Even above 60 frames per second, the input lag feels gigantic. In practical terms, the game still feels very new and raw, with zero polish. The available weapons are poorly finished, unbalanced, and don't have much differentiation (except for the excessive recoil of the AKM). Loot in the game is poorly distributed and sometimes way too scarce or way too abundant (depending purely on a poorly optimized RNG, random number generator). The game still offers no sense of reward, despite "BP" points, which you can save up to buy random drop crates within the game. There is no progression in levels or ranks, no skill-tier differentiation—in fact, there's no skill tier at all, since you can be killed by a player who spent the whole match hiding and clearly has a worse skill level than you. Besides the lack of progression, the game could also lean into cosmetic and/or customization details so that every player could create their own identity and/or be known for it. However, cosmetic items are still lacking (which is fairly justified by the game's young age), and the few that do exist are heavily overpriced. Even with such items, the lack of an in-game "identity" makes PUBG feel more like an arcade game than anything else. There is practically no difference from playing against slightly smarter bots. On top of all that, besides the excessive and clearly noticeable input lag, the game's netcode seems to go from bad to worse. Many hits don't register, compounded by the fact that the South American server suffers terribly from packet loss (evidenced by rubberbanding during the game) and/or unexplained crashes. In my view, in its current state, the only advantage and "appeal" of playing PUBG right now is the "unexplained hype" it receives. The only motivation to play it is the fact that "everyone is playing it," so it's not hard to find matches and have something to play with your friends. Even this "unexplained hype" somehow makes sense, given the growing number of bots in the game "farming points" in matches to spend on crates and resell them later on the community market. In these 100 hours I haven't seen issues with cheaters/hackers, but I've heard about them and seen them on streams. As it seems to me, having such a massive player base right now, the chance of running into them in a match is still slim, but I'd like to see how the company handles them once the hype dies down. [h1]Conclusion[/h1] With easy and interesting gameplay, but bogged down by poor optimization and poor execution of its entire design, PUBG seems to suffer from its greatest asset: unexpected and unexplained hype. The game seems to have suffered from a massive injection of players way too early, which sets expectations way too high and makes the delay in implementing necessary tweaks way too long, despite how recently it was released. Therefore, I don't recommend the game in its current state, though I might completely change this review over time if the necessary tweaks are made. For now, I'm afraid the game is nothing more than another "[i]DayZ[/i] or [i]Infestation[/i] that knew how to invest in the Steam market, attracting bots that mask the true player engagement in the game." [h1]Rating: 6/10[/h1] [b]Pros:[/b] [+] Guaranteed fun moments if played with friends [+] Hope for improvements soon given the developer's competence [b]Cons:[/b] [-] Low range of visual customization [-] Inflated market, excessive presence of bots [-] Poor local performance optimization [-] Poor weapon and loot balancing [-] Poor execution of rules and ideas in the game [-] Server issues, such as lag and packet loss

This is my perspective, don't feel attacked and if you want to offer constructive criticism or have the urge to discuss things with me and maybe others, then don't be shy and do it! (As long as it stays objective and informative, insults/hate speech will be deleted!) At the beginning I'll present the positive and negative aspects of the game for me, followed by a (hopefully) short conclusion and at the end personal wishes for future updates. + Weapons: Large selection of weapons, which can all be very strong based on different scenarios. + Map: Nicely large, many towns with loot and potential urban combat (smaller map already on the way as I've heard, Gj!) + School: Action. Action. Action. + Duo/Squad: Reviving possible, not like in H1Z1. (If the enemies don't finish you right away) + 2-seat motorcycle: Simply fucking awesome - fast, agile, small. <3 - Vehicle physics: Touch a stone slightly and your car does 4 flips and explodes. Touch another moving vehicle and both explode almost instantly. - Community: If you have voice chat enabled (whyever), you meet 3 types of people: 1. Complete idiots just spamming some shit through it (music, weird noises, catchphrases etc.) 2. Toxic kids who start abusing other players' mothers in every conceivable position every time they die. 3. "Normals" who drop a quick GG WP during an "exciting" firefight (win or lose) and then bugger off. (These are very, very rare unfortunately, most players belong to the 1st and 2nd type) - Loot distribution: I understand why the loot is distributed randomly. But for the most part the distribution is fucking garbage. If I drop at a huge building (mansion, police station), I expect at least 2-3 weapons there, and not an empty building with grenades and backpacks, just for some enemy from the neighboring building to show up with an AKM etc. and execute you. (Or when you have to run to the zone and don't find a single car on the way, while in another area 10 vehicles spawned right next to each other... feelsgoodman). - The zone: I HATE the current zone structure. The first zones usually don't matter that much. You hardly have any trouble getting in on time anyway (it's not that bad if you sleep through the first 2 zones, just drink an energy drink and run through, the damage isn't all that high yet). In the midgame you can actually ignore them by playing well... but in the lategame... wow. It's very simple: Either the zone is for you or against you. The zone decides about victory or defeat for the most part at the end. I've caught the worst zones - zone at the enemy team, my squad has to run across open field while the containers had cover. No chance unless the enemies are complete aimlets. Or: Prison 1vs1, the zone right on the slope, one player stands up top, the other player stands at the bottom and the zone shrinks on one of them, leaving the other no chance to get there. Why not just take the position of all players from Top 20 onwards and calculate the center point so that the zone spawns there? Maybe even only from Top 10 onwards, but something has to be done there! The game has even more RNG than Hearthstone! +/- Bugs / Crashes: I understand that it's an Early Access game and therefore usually won't be bug-free. That's why I'd like to view this point neutrally. The game just has a few bugs - sound bug when diving, glitching through windows that haven't been shot out, getting stuck with the parachute (so you hit the ground a few seconds later, which could decide victory or defeat in active drop areas), random crashes in the loading screen and reconnect failing due to some error. I just hope that before the game leaves Early Access and is officially released, these bugs (and maybe others I forgot) get fixed. Conclusion: All in all I'm torn - the game is fun (especially with mates), but currently has too many problems to give the game a thumbs up. But PUBG is definitely the best KotK game and I'm looking forward to further development. What I wish for: Improved physics, less RNG - improved zone, better optimization, more weapons (flamethrowers, traps, tripwires etc.), bug fixes, more maps. Sorry for the slightly longer text. Thanks for reading and maybe see you on the battlefield soon!

translation_en: Another battle royale, pff. Awghmrmuch. That was precisely the opinion I formed when PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS (PUBG) was released to the world. I had bad experiences with H1Z1 and therefore didn't feel like playing another battle royale at all. But! There is always and everywhere some "but", and this case is no exception. Immediately upon release, PUBG became a massive phenomenon. Absolutely everyone was playing, streaming, recording, and translating it into real life. So I simply couldn't escape it and, whether you want to or not, you end up watching some video of it. I think this could suffice as my classic review introduction and I could finally dive into the core of the problem. Or... It's not actually a problem, but you surely know what I'm getting at. :D The game is still in early access and costs 30€ which is not exactly cheap, but trust me, even for this kind of cash the purchase is worth it. For this price you get an incredible battle royale that combines the best of games from these genres, while adding simple elements also from DayZ and Arma3. As if that wasn't enough, it combines all of this with its own elements and all of this together makes PUBG clearly the best battle royale there has ever been so far. (I apologize if someone thinks otherwise, but in my opinion - yes, this is my subjective opinion - that's just how it is.) As for bugs and optimization, the game is still lagging behind here, but I believe it will keep getting better and better, if only because of regular updates and the promise that the game will leave early access around January 2018. I believe in this and I think they will seriously try to do it, if only for the reason that BlueHole was some "noname" studio until now and they will want to fight the competition. If you are transitioning from H1Z1 to PUBG, I think that as far as bugs are concerned, you will be grinning from ear to ear. + regular updates + weapons - a huge variety, you can find SMGs, ARs, and SRs here, and with further updates more keep coming + weapon attachments - you can add attachments to every weapon (extended mags, scopes, stocks, and much more) + various game modes - so far we only have two modes to choose from and those are FPP and TPP (first-person perspective and third-person perspective) + solo, duo, squad - don't have friends? Don't despair! You can play solo and you don't have to be afraid that a group of multiple players (who do have friends :D ) will play against you, because in solo everyone goes purely for themselves! And if you do have some friends, you will also be pleased that you can play either duo (you will always play against teams with a maximum of 2 players) or squad (instead of two players, there are four). + airdrops - you will find both "common" items here and things you cannot get otherwise + various weather on the map - sunny, sunset, rain, fog. All of this can be found in PUBG so far, though this weather stays for the whole duration of the game, it's not like the rain would suddenly change into fog in the middle of the game. - optimization - it can be understood, the game is in early access, but despite that, it could be a hair better - bugs - despite the fact that they are getting fixed, there are still bugs here that persist for a longer time and some can even cause a loss (unable to get into the zone, etc.) - one map - so far there is only one map in PUBG, but according to info a second one is already being worked on, though it's not yet known when it will be finished and when it will get into the game. - lengthier game - when God forbid it happens that you make it to the end (Winner, winner chicken dinner!), the game can take up to an hour. For someone it might not be much, but towards the end it's more about sneaking and camping, so it's more of a waiting game, but that's part of it too. Well, and in conclusion? I'm finishing writing this at 1:00 AM and I've had just about enough, so if there are any mistakes here, I deeply apologize. :D And now back to the game - whether you are a loner or have a bunch of friends, go for it! 9/10

translation_en: Back in the day I was still playing CrossFire, saved up 50 bucks by scrimping and saving for half a month, and bought the Blade character. I was so damn proud. Waking up during class, half-asleep, I kept hearing the word "Blade" floating around in my deskmates' chat. Suddenly I perked up and joined the bullshitting circle, wanting to flex just a bit with this half-month's worth of effort. "Who the fuck is still playing CF, we're talking about the Blade Dancer from LoL. Let me tell you, LoL is super fun, let's hit the net cafe at lunch and play a few rounds." Perhaps that was my first time experiencing the tie between gaming and socializing. To have a say with the majority, you gotta do what the majority does. When getting along with people, talking about common topics is probably one of the easiest ways to close the distance. And discussing trendy things within those common topics gets twice the results with half the effort. In the gaming circle, almost no one plays games all by themselves, completely isolated. Play games, add friends, look for like-minded people, and maybe grab a "cultivation group" link on the side—pretty much every modern gamer does this stuff. After that, you enter the stage where gaming binds with socialization. PUBG's massive success, personally, I think rode on the coattails of two bandwagon trends. The first one was that universally known article, *Global Toxic Trash is in This Filthy Game*. Even though the author stated they'd never played the game, just watched a video, and even mixed up the survival and battle royale nature of the game in the post, it didn't stop a bunch of players who had never seen this kind of game mode from developing a deep interest in it. During that time, a bunch of classmates who had never even heard of Steam started learning how to buy games with real money, going further and further down the "China No.1" road. After a long time, the flaws of H1Z1 gradually showed: outdated graphics, poor gunplay, too many hackers, terrible gaming experience, and players dropping the "classic three insults" upon meeting. Anyway, having read the article, the whole world knew those three words—say them first, then shoot. Right then, PUBG showed up: H1Z1, but high-spec. After all, the iPhone 8 was out, time to think about tossing the 7 aside. The second bandwagon was live streaming. PUBG's gameplay meant there were tons of unpredictable factors in the game. All kinds of hilarious and thrilling gaming experiences meant that even streamers who weren't top-tier could pull in massive audiences. "Watching this streamer play makes this game look so fun, I gotta try it too." "Let me tell you, I played that PUBG yesterday, it's so fucking fun, you should buy a copy and I'll carry you to a chicken dinner." Word spread from person to person, creating the spectacle where PUBG still hasn't fallen off its pedestal to this day. Back to the game itself. The game is still in Early Access, so there are unpolished areas. And because the player base is so huge, even though the devs are trying their best to fight cheaters, the number of "hackers" is still pretty high. On top of that, the game optimization is garbage, and random bugs pop up occasionally. But as a shooter, the actual shooting feels pretty damn good. The gameplay takes the essence and discards the dross from all past generations of battle royale games, and the various tactical terrains and buildings also show the developers' careful consideration. All in all, 7.5/10

translation_en: Now that I actually own this game, I'll share my little experience so that — hopefully — in the future, I can help anyone who might be in my shoes. First off, you don't know what the hell to do, since it's a cool game that's trendy, but it costs a whopping 30 bucks and it hurts to spend that on something you won't use. After carefully looking at the requirements, game reviews, and even talking about it with friends, etc., my premeditated decision was to buy it to test if I liked it and if it ran well for me [i](mostly the second part, because I'd watched a lot of gameplays and stuff and knew I'd like it)[/i]. If not, I would've refunded it (without hitting the 2-hour mark). The big problem was that ever since that moment I haven't been able to stop playing. As I said before, and I insist, I've read a lot of the reviews here, specifically the negative ones, which are the ones that give you reasons not to buy it. And the vast majority talk about two problems: [b]lag and bad optimization[/b]. Right, first, the [b]lag[/b]. Simple explanation: it's true that it exists, but not in every match. If you've got a halfway decent connection (I have 100MB[i][b]*[/b][/i] if I'm not mistaken), it'll run fine. Maybe you'll lag out in a few matches, but that's just what you get for playing with 99 other people from the rest of Europe (or the world). It's something you have to understand and accept, it's not that deep. Without going too far, today, by accident, I played a match on the NA server and had zero lag. Second problem, [b]bad optimization[/b]: honestly, it's true, the game isn't well optimized. I've got a GTX 950M and 8GB of RAM[i][b]*[/b][/i] and I have to play with most settings on low. By this, I don't mean I've got a total beast of a rig and should be playing on Ultra, but simply that I shouldn't need to pedal a bicycle to make it run either. On the other hand, you have to keep in mind that this is a [b]game in development[/b] [i](one of the key points that helped me make my decision)[/i], meaning they'll very likely improve this issue with every [i](weekly)[/i] update, since right now it's the most serious flaw and fixing it could bring in huge profits for the devs (since more people would buy the game). On a personal note, though, and I admit I'm a pretty easy-going person, playing with almost everything on low isn't a problem for me since it doesn't affect gunfights. Though obviously, I would've preferred to play with higher graphics. [i][b]*[/b] I put my own specs here to help you compare them with yours.[/i] Moving on from that, and starting to talk about the good stuff, having low graphics doesn't matter because your focus from the very first second is maxed out, along with the tension and of course the enjoyment [i][b]*[/b][/i]. Anyway, it doesn't matter what I write, you have to check it out for yourself and I'm sure your opinion on this game will be way better than any words I can write here. If not, just ask my 26 hours in 3 days. I highly recommend buying it, it's an absolute blast and it's only going to get better. [i][b]*[/b] I've also read that this game is only worth buying if you're gonna play with friends. [b]TOTAL BULLSHIT[/b]. What's more, a lot of people (myself included), will probably enjoy it more playing solo, making their own calls and plays. An absolute masterpiece in every way.[/i] When buying, if you're not sure, I recommend making the same choice I did: buy it and try it out, and if you don't like it or your PC can't run it, refund it[i][b]*[/b][/i]. [i][b]*[/b] I'll leave an article [b][url=https://support.steampowered.com/kb_article.php?ref=6695-QIKM-7966&l=]HERE[/url][/b] that shows how to do a refund, for those who don't know.[/i] [b]PS:[/b] Keep in mind that this game will probably get more expensive as time goes on. When it's finished, they'll release it on consoles, where it'll end up costing double. Look at [b]ARK[/b]. This is my review and I hope it helped you out. If it did, don't forget to mark it as [b][i]Helpful[/i][/b] to help others who are in your shoes. Thanks for your time!

translation_en: A few things you need to know before starting this game: 1. Back in 227 AD (the fifth year of Jianxing in the Shu Han dynasty), Zhuge Liang, the outstanding politician, strategist, and military commander of our country's ancient Three Kingdoms period, left chicken-diners with an ancient motto: "Clinging to life in troubled times." 2. The previous sentence means that in this game, surviving is what matters most, even if you have to live like a dog. 3. That ancient motto has a second half: "Not seeking fame among lords," which means if you haven't found a suppressor for your gun, don't shoot first, otherwise it's no different from telling everyone: "I want that chicken, shoot me!" 4. The three philosophical questions for battle royale noobs: Who am I? Where am I? Who the fuck just shot me from the shadows?! 5. Knowing how to get kills isn't a sufficient condition for winning, because even if you rack up 98 kills, you might still end up second, and the guy who killed you gets the chicken in the end. 6. Don't think a gas mask lets you survive a bit longer in the blue zone; it's just a cosmetic. 7. If you see an untouched airdrop inside or near the zone, don't think you're getting closer to your dreams—it's probably a massive trap. 8. You might not see a single person from start to finish, and you won't even know who killed you. That's totally normal. 9. Get into the zone as early as possible. Get in late and you're just a delivery boy. 10. Camping like a coward isn't shameful, as long as you outlive the very last guy. 11. Buildings mean: a natural bunker, rich loot, and countless people squatting in corners waiting to rat you out. 12. If you see a corpse lying next to a crate, put a couple of bullets into it before you loot, and don't ask me why. 13. Even though the frying pan is strapped to your back, it doesn't mean the bullet that hit you came from behind. 14. Don't just yell "Car!" the second you see one, because it could mean two things: there's a car to drive, or there's a car driving right at you. 15. Even though vehicle noises are already loud enough, you might as well lean on the horn to let everyone know you've arrived. 16. New cars are generally on the road; a car out in the open fields either has blown tires or is a trap waiting for you. 17. When you're aiming at someone through a window, someone is also aiming at you through the window. 18. When playing in a squad, keep a certain distance from your teammates. Too close and you'll get wiped out together; too far and they won't make it in time to revive you. 19. You still need to practice your aim a bit. Even if you can't kill the enemy, at least try not to team-kill. 20. You gotta be super careful running through wheat fields; you might just step on a snake in the grass. 21. Little bushes frequently contain people squatting in them to take a shit. 22. The most terrifying moment in this game has got to be looking through your scope and seeing a face filling up your entire screen. 23. Sitting in a car doesn't mean you're safe. While it might occasionally block a bullet or two, if it gets blown up, it turns into your coffin. 24. If you're unlucky enough to get into a face-to-face melee brawl with an enemy, going prone and begging for mercy might just save your life. 25. There are three beginner modes to choose from: garbage collector, delivery boy, and dying right off the plane. ========== That's it for now, I'll add more when I think of them ==========

translation_en: [h1] Detailed High-Win-Rate Guide and Practical Tips for "PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS" [/h1] [b] Early Game: [/b] First off, let's talk about choosing a landing spot. I usually jump to fixed vehicle spawn locations or slightly less crowded areas. My most frequent drop is the houses at the left bridgehead of Rozhok, [strike]the garage is guaranteed to have a vehicle[/strike]. There's one habit I recommend everyone build: remember the flight path of the plane at the start. This lets you roughly figure out where enemies are distributed and where to go once you get a car. The safe zone usually spawns about 30 seconds after you land [strike](the safe zone timer starts when the last person lands)[strike]. If nobody else drops with you, you can loot the houses near the car a bit and wait for the circle to appear. If someone drops with you and you're pretty confident you'll find a gun first, go for it; otherwise, just run straight for the vehicle. Dying right off the bat means missing out on a chicken dinner, or costing yourself two or three top-five finishes. There's no point risking it for a single kill. Try to grab a car and get out of there as fast as you can. I also advise noobs against dropping in big cities. Stuff takes forever to load when you hit the ground, and you usually get around ten people dropping into a single major city. Not only is your looting experience a nerve-wracking nightmare, but playing at 20 FPS will teach you some hard lessons. (So far, the only card I've seen handle big cities at a stable 80+ FPS is the 1080ti). Anyway, the way I see it, this game is really just about 20 or 30 players anyway. My strategy is to land, grab a car, head to somewhere empty to gear up in peace, and only really start fighting when the third circle starts closing in. Let me list a few good spots to head to after getting a car. Depending on the plane's path, there are about five places I usually choose: the container yard in the top left, the shooting range, the steel mill in the bottom right, Kameshki, and the lighthouse in the bottom left. (The shooting range and the two small bomb shelters above it can guarantee you're fully equipped with guns, though meds might be a bit scarce. The lighthouse area lets you loot up and then camp the bridge roadblock for easy delivery kills, plus there are boats on the coast for fast, long-range travel so you don't have to worry about flipping a car. I won't bother mentioning the other three—they're definitely loaded). [b] Mid Game / Looting: [/b] Now for some personal tips: don't pick up any more bandages once you have 10. As for weapon preference, the order is M4, SCAR, AK. (M16 can't take attachments, so only use it early game; swap it out for an M4 or SCAR as soon as you find one). I won't even mention the 98K and SKS—use them if you're good with them. For scopes, 4x and red dot are the obvious go-tos. Let's talk about the 8x: I personally advise against using it within 500 meters, especially on moving targets. As for the 15x, if you're lucky enough to actually find one, figure it out then. By the time you're ready for the second blue zone to close in, there are probably about 50 people left. At this point, you have two choices. First, if a large group of enemies is outside the second safe zone, you can drive to the edge of the circle, find a outhouse or guard shack, and wait for delivery boys. (I once waited in an outhouse for three delivery guys, and two of them died in just a couple of random shots; a lot of people still aren't scared of the first two zones). Second, find a spot right in the center of the safe zone near a large open field and go prone/hide out. Since the final safe zones are mostly open areas, you can claim the advantageous position early. After hiding through the third blue zone, there are around 20 people left. Do NOT drive at this point. Try to path along the edge of the blue zone, flanking toward the back of the safe zone. Don't just right-click a random spot on the map and run straight there. (Beginners should get into the habit of right-clicking the map to mark where you want to go, thinking through your route before you move, and keeping track of the general terrain along the way instead of looking at the map every two steps). Remember that your path should always go from one piece of cover to the next, unless it's completely open. While running, hold down Alt to look around in all directions. [b] Final Showdown: [/b] Now for the final showdown. First off, there are two major no-nos. First, don't shoot every time you see someone, especially when trying to hit a distant moving target with a red dot. If you know you can't kill them, why give away your position? Second, remember—and this is crucial—that this is a third-person game! The perspective you see from is not the angle your gun is firing from! Also, when scouting, keep your character safely behind cover and use the camera angles on either side to look around. Make good use of Q and E! Also, while high ground gives you a wide field of view, reverse slopes are much safer. The steeper the reverse slope, the less the person coming up it will expose their entire body to check your position. A bit more running and there will only be a dozen or so people left. At this point, it's super important: when you hear gunshots, don't panic. Use the reverse slope to flank them, closing the distance to guarantee the kill. People aren't sprinting around as frantically right now, so even if you spot a moving target really close by and they haven't seen you yet, just wait a second. Let them run up to a tree and stop to scan for other people, then blow their brains out. No need to rush—wait for the recoil to settle, tap once more, and they're dead. (If you have a 4x and you hear they don't have a suppressor, try *not* to loot their box! If the situation allows you to loot and you like to crouch, you need to get used to doing irregular movements with WASD. Going prone makes you harder to spot, but if someone *does* see you, you're basically dead, because people at this stage are usually close by and most of them have 4x scopes). Once you take this guy down, you're basically in the top ten. Open your map, scroll to zoom in, and check where the buildings are in the next safe zone and what the terrain looks like. High tension often makes people forget the blue zone countdown, so watch your timing closely. This is super important. Since the end game is mostly open ground, even if you manage to outrun the blue zone, you'll just expose yourself to people already holding down positions, and they'll farm you like their own son. If you've got time to spare, keep creeping along the edge of the blue zone. Try not to shoot anyone in the distance unless you have to; giving away your position right now is fatal. All you're doing right now is surviving. If you can outlast one more wave of the blue zone, congratulations, you're in the top five. At this point, definitely remember which direction gunfire came from and keep an eye on the kill feed in the bottom left. Now it all comes down to your eyesight. When there are four or five people left, knowing your position and figuring out where enemies are coming from is way more important than getting kills. I don't know if my way of handling this is good or not, but I generally prioritize securing my own position and safety first, and always make sure my back is clear. Then I watch where the enemies are, using the sound of gunshots to figure out whether distant shots killed someone close by, or if close-range shots wiped someone else out. When it's down to the final three, if you spot someone from behind cover, carefully consider whether you even want to kill them. If you kill him, it becomes a 1v1, but now the other guy knows where you are while you have no idea where he is. That instantly puts you at a 50% disadvantage. That is no exaggeration. So when there are three or four players left—especially three—let the other two fight it out while you play it safe. That's why people can rank in the top 100 while having trash-tier KDRs. Personally, getting kills isn't that important when the goal is to win. Sure, other people might get 7, 8, or 10+ kills a game, but even though I usually only get 3 or 4, I feel like this playstyle makes getting a chicken dinner way more consistent than shooting everything that moves. [strike]That wraps up this detailed guide, hope it helps out all the players out there![/strike] Anyway, those are just my personal thoughts. Everyone has their own playstyle and weapon preferences—this is just how I play and what works for me, not gospel!

translation_en: [url=https://www.senscritique.com/jeuvideo/Player_Unknown_s_Battlegrounds/critique/136108418]Check out my review on SensCritique ![/url] You have to be extremely wary of trendy games. They can be either extremely good or terribly disappointing, and generally they lean more toward the bad side of the scale. With its hideous name, PUBG sits right in the middle of the road. It has good qualities, but it's boring. The current phenomenon that is the battle royale is a genre where dozens of players are dropped onto a large map and have to quickly find gear and weapons to take out the many enemies in the surrounding area. In the end, there can be only one. No, this isn't Highlander, but very often it's just some camper. Before each match starts, all players (about a hundred per game) are grouped together on an island for a minute while the game loads. The weapons in the game are laid out on tables so you can get familiar with them. If I have one good piece of advice to give you, it's to disable voice chat unless you want to enjoy the auditory garbage spewed by your future enemies... Then comes drop time. All players are in a plane flying over the map, and it's up to you to choose when you want to jump. Because you're going to have to use a parachute to reach the spot on the map you want to get to. You've finally made it! But you might not be alone! The race begins; you need to find weapons fast so you can defend yourself in case your neighbor decides to beat the crap out of you. If you're lucky, you'll find good weapons, giving you an advantage at the start of the match, but make no mistake—generally you'll have to make do with a handgun and a shotgun or a crossbow. They're weapons and they kill, no problem there, but if your opponent is luckier than you, fighting with arrows against an assault rifle isn't great... Of course, the map is packed with attractive locations that practically guarantee high-end gear, but you'll almost never be alone there. It's up to you to decide which approach you prefer! A low-profile start to loot in peace, or an offensive rush? A few minutes after the plane passes, a white circle is randomly defined somewhere on the map. That's where the combat will take place because after a few more minutes, a blue zone will gradually close in until it reaches the white zone. If you stay outside the blue zone, you'll take continuous damage until you die. Little by little, the white zone will shrink, with the blue zone catching up shortly after, and so on. Natural selection having done its work, there will usually only be ten to fifteen players left at this point. In such a small patch of the map, deaths happen very fast and the end of the game approaches rapidly. Watch out, because a red zone will randomly appear on the map. Don't go in there. Because a bombing run is about to happen... You should also know that throughout the match (which lasts about thirty minutes roughly), a supply plane will occasionally fly randomly over the map and drop a supply crate which very often contains some really good gear. But it's a coveted prize among players, and you'll almost certainly have to fight a battle to get the precious contents. PUBG provides an immense and varied playground. Cities, all kinds of buildings, fields, forests, and so on—everything is there to offer a realistic map that allows for different survival tactics. Make no mistake, the "safest" tactic is to move slowly while staying hidden as much as possible. Some people win matches by letting everyone else kill each other off and then taking out the last player still alive. In any case, this game is both gripping and stressful. Gripping because the concept works, you want to do better, to get that #1 chicken dinner, and stressful because throughout the match you have to pay attention to everything around you, checking that there isn't a guy hiding behind a door, another one lying in the grass, or someone at a window ready to blow your head off... That's where the boring part comes in. Sure, the more you play, the more experience you'll gain and the easier it will be to survive longer, but the luck factor is omnipresent and it can shit all over you whenever it feels like it, stringing together matches with crappy loot even after more than five minutes of searching, where you'll take a single bullet without even understanding where it came from... If losing pisses you off, don't play this game. Seriously. Fortunately, you can play in teams! This is a very important point of the game because playing solo gets boring really fast, as I mentioned just before. You can play in groups of two, three, or four. This completely changes the dynamic because even though you'll need to get enough gear for everyone, above all you can play by using tactics specific to your squad. Plus, you can also play in third-person or first-person view, and once again, that completely changes the game! In third-person, it's easy to see without being seen, surprise people while keeping an eye on everything thanks to the camera. In first-person, the stress is through the roof. Is someone behind you? Or behind this wall? You'll naturally pay way more attention... Be aware, however, that the servers don't mix the different playstyles. If you play duo, you'll only face pairs of players, same for a four-player squad. If you play in third-person, you'll only play against people using the same camera view. This prevents any imbalances, and that's a good thing! It's also important that I touch on ballistics before finishing this review... A lot of modern shooting games have far-from-realistic ballistics called hitscan. You put your crosshairs on the enemy, you shoot, and you hit, simple as that. Distance and gravity aren't factored in. In PUBG, it's not like that at all. You have to factor in the distance between you and your opponent, adjust your weapon's zeroing, or aim higher/lower if you haven't. Just like when an enemy is running, you have to lead your shots a bit—basically calculate the bullet's trajectory to make sure you hit. In short, we have a title here that dominates its genre, one that manages to appeal to everyone by offering a great gaming experience, which can quickly turn out to be a time-sink despite its often redundant aspect that will sometimes make you want to never touch it again before coming back to it anyway because, fuck, it's fun. Since this game is still in early access, its optimization isn't quite a success yet and it's not free of some recurring bugs. That should improve over time. It's possible this review will evolve along with the game.
