translation_en: I’ve played quite a lot of PUBG and got the hang of it by now. But this review of mine might not actually be about the game itself—it’s about the players. I just want to talk about the different levels of skill among PUBG players. Level 1: No gun in hand, no gun in mind. These guys are probably total newbies who just bought the game. Most of them are humble, serious, and trying their best. This bunch is easy to spot—they admit they’re just starting out, they love the game, and they’re grinding hard to get that chicken dinner. Level 2: Gun in hand, no gun in mind. These players fully understand how the game works and have started getting the hang of some strats and mechanics. Though still a bit rough around the edges, they no longer need a veteran to carry them to a win, and they can even dish out some advice to Level 1s. Even though their game sense and aim aren't fundamentally flawed, you can tell they're not totally effortless and smooth with it. A lot of the time, they don't even realize when their positioning or judgment calls are mistakes. This type of player is pretty picky about guns and scopes. Most of them love a fully-kitted M416 with a 4x scope, the more ammo the better, and running low on meds really messes with them. Same goes for hardware—they demand the best mechanical keyboards and mice, and the monitor has to be big enough. They usually have a restless mindset, think they're absolute god-tier players, and always love to boss people around or give unsolicited advice in squad matches. Level 3: Gun in hand, gun in mind. You could call these guys pros. They've got the mechanical skills down, though with a bit of roughness and cockiness. They're usually ranked in the top 10,000, can pinpoint enemy locations easily, basically never die in the early game (landing and getting sent back to the lobby), and airdrops are pretty much guaranteed for them. But sometimes they get overconfident and don't look at the details objectively. Solo and duo wins are just everyday life for them, and they're pretty harsh when it comes to squadmates, though when they're in a good mood they'll carry some noobs. Players at this level have basically split into distinct playstyles, like the hot-dropper, the rat (snake/LYB), the wilderness survivalist, etc. Players at this level aren't that picky about guns anymore. Whether it's an AK, Groza, SKS, or Mk14, they handle them all well. They aren't super picky about scopes either—lots of times they can win with just a red dot. Their need for meds isn't desperate either; just having enough is fine. The hot-droppers have insane aim. Even with just a red dot or holo sight, they don't lose engagements with enemies 300 meters away, and in close-range fights within the same match, they're practically unmatched. If they get their hands on a 98K or something similar, it's like giving a tiger wings. 1v3s and 1v4s happen all the time. But they have a hard time calming down to analyze their positioning or battlefield movements, and often get tunnel vision, putting themselves at a disadvantage and missing out on the win. The wilderness survivalists might not have as good of aim as the hot-droppers, but they're still plenty deadly. These guys know how to conserve their strength and maximize the advantages of terrain, time, and psychology. Sometimes they don't even use a single magazine of ammo or a single med kit the whole game and still win. People often confuse them with rats, but that's not true—they just know the exact right moment to fire and the safest, most secure routes to take. They usually suffered terribly back in Levels 1 and 2, dying in every corner of the map, which is how they forged their extraordinary game sense. The rats (LYBs) might not always win, but when Lady Luck is on their side, getting a chicken dinner is as easy as taking candy from a baby. You can find them in literally any corner of the map, sometimes holding nothing but a silenced P1911 and 15 rounds of ammo. Both the wilderness guys and the hot-droppers have taken Ls from them. These guys are like vipers, delivering a fatal strike the moment you let your guard down. Usually, by the time you die, you don't even know where the bullet came from. Level 4: No gun in hand, gun in mind. These guys have basically lost all desire to win at this point and don't care about rank. Sometimes they watch PUBG streams, or complain in group chats about the servers acting up again. They probably don't play PUBG in front of people much anymore, maybe playing CS:GO or Rainbow Six Siege instead. They're way less picky about guns and attachments, trying to live by the rule that "less is more, simple is complex." When playing around others, they pretty much only use one gun and rarely get into serious gunfights. But they never stop learning, constantly researching all sorts of techniques and strats, and even studying things unrelated to the actual game. When playing with friends, they rarely give orders, and their firing rate is so low you'd almost think they're griefing or afk. Don't for a second think they can't do anything—they just don't feel like playing with you. They're sick of the praise, the worship, and the questions. They're waiting to cross paths with an equal opponent or someone they can actually talk to on their level. Then, after casually pretending to be nonchalant and chatting for a bit, they finally show their sharp side. Level 5: Not killing. This you could call the unity of man and gun... If the previous type is a hidden martial arts master in the city, this kind of person has lost all bloodlust. They don't need bloodlust to defend their status and skill, and they've moved past the whole concept of high-tier or low-tier gear. That doesn't mean they don't understand it, just that they have a relatively more objective, correct philosophy in their heads. Just having them there is enough. If the previous level was forged through time, this level can only be forged through an immense amount of gaming experience, knowledge, and extreme skill. Almost everyone in the community knows who they are, and everyone respects them. They're probably not young, and very few people have ever actually teamed up with them. But anyone who has played in a squad with them will say, "That guy is insanely good"—though you have no clue *just how good* they actually are. The strategies, skills, knowledge, and fine details involved are probably way beyond your comprehension. And Level 2 players are the ones who love saying, "I just played a match with this guy."

translation_en: The game is pretty good for now, and if you have a group of friends, there's practically no chance you won't have fun. However, do I recommend it? I don't right now. Because the game is currently being way overhyped by its developers. It's always hovering in the top 3 on the Twitch popularity list, and people see this and buy it. "Whoa, if Jahrein is playing, it must be good," "Damn, the streamer is having so much blast, the game is awesome," they thought, and bought it, but it didn't turn out that way. The player count skyrocketed thanks to these ads, and PUBG shot up the charts everywhere. And right now, we're the ones paying the price for it. Updates keep coming, but the game isn't actually getting better, optimization isn't being fixed; updates are being pushed for the things that are needed the absolute least. There's no visible difference—why? Because with or there being an update or not, there are thousands of people playing the game. Right now, it looks like nobody gives a shit. That's why I don't recommend buying it unless you have a high-end PC. Of course, this opinion might vary from person to person, but it looks like it's going to stay this way for a while. Please don't be fanboys for any game. Every game must be criticized, otherwise it can't progress. I wrote the pros and cons above. It pays to be objective. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Update coming about 1 month later: My review was right to some, wrong to others. But it's certain I got a lot of backlash, maybe because their favorite streamers were mentioned in the sentence, or maybe it didn't make sense to them. But I wasn't bashing the streamers, I was just giving examples. Speaking of the game, the number of huge problems from before has decreased. An average graphics card like a GTX 770 can now run it normally. Of course, it might differ on laptops. But in any case, if you're using 8 GB of RAM, you might run into some render issues. Houses might load a bit late, etc. That's why my advice is to use more than 8 GB of RAM, you'll be much more comfortable. You won't be sitting there waiting for houses to load while other people are looting. Another issue that seems minor but ruins your mental state is audio bugs. Sitting camping in a house, and suddenly a vehicle sound comes from the heavens somewhere. Of course, there is no such vehicle sound. Only you hear that sound. Your teammates hear jack shit. Whether you call it a secret message or think you're the chosen one, I don't know, but that vehicle sound you hear can make you run around in circles inside the house. It's so annoying that it sometimes makes you wonder, "Have I lost my mind?" If you have the budget and have friends to have fun with in the game, buy it and enjoy it. I specifically mentioned having friends because I personally get bored playing alone. Whether you like the game or not is subjective, people can even play H1Z1 if they want, that's up to the individual. What hooked me and made me love the game is that its mechanics are very close to Arma 3, and teamwork being extremely important genuinely appealed to me. I'll leave the September update here for those who want to check it out; http://pubg.tamgame.com/news/view.do?page=1&idx=1559

translation_en: [h1] [b] [i]Record-breaking[/i] [/b] sales figures and, content-wise, a [b] [i]record-breakingly[/i] [/b] double-edged game! [/h1] [b] What's it about? - Tried and tested, but nothing new [/b] The gameplay loop is pretty simple. Up to 100 people jump out of a plane, land, and scavenge for weapons, ammo, helmets, bulletproof vests, or medical supplies—just like the good old DayZ days—so they can dish it out and take a beating. Every few minutes, the play zone shrinks, as is well known from various Battle Royale games. So you're forced to move, you inevitably run into enemies, and the last person alive wins. Alternatively, you can compete against other duos or squads as a duo or squad (1-4 players). There's also the option to play in First Person only instead of 3rd Person. [b] - Fast-paced [/b] First off, it has to be said that the game is very fast-paced. Depending on luck and player skill, rounds last anywhere from a brisk 10 seconds up to a maximum of about 45 minutes, and then it's over. So it's perfect to just jump into a quick round even if you're already on your way out the door. It's also great for quickly putting a botched round behind you and trying your luck again. The addictive factor is definitely there! [b] - Skill and luck [/b] The new, shrinking play zone has ruined the match for plenty of players over the course of a game despite good equipment, or catapulted them into the top 10 despite lousy gear. In principle, it's an aspect that can provide a certain element of surprise and balance between skill and luck. But the tendency is probably the same as with red lights. You always get screwed by this crap yourself, while other people never do. However, this feeling is driven by other annoyances in the game, not by this mechanic itself. [b] - Variety: Weapons and attachments [/b] There are plenty of weapon classes and weapons within them. In my opinion, just enough to keep things organized while still offering variety. The same goes for weapon attachments like flash hiders, scopes, or extended magazines, which are easy to find sorted by weapon class. New weapons are also implemented into the game every now and then, and when it comes to weapon balancing, you have to emphasize that it's always been pretty decent so far. That's by no means a given, hence a "thumbs up"! UPDATE: 09/04/2018: Shotguns, however, are now basically completely useless in some cases. Their damage is relatively pathetic even at point-blank range, and on top of that, their fire rate is garbage. [b] - Crates [/b] Yeah, yeah... the good old crates you might know from CS:GO. Some of them offer virtual clothing items that are purely cosmetic, purchasable exclusively with in-game currency earned through good placements, hits, and kills at the end of a round. The thrill of opening such a crate and hoping for the big score is something everyone should know from the lottery booth at the fair. Since the in-game currency has no other use, you can cross your fingers and go for it as soon as you've earned enough. The prices are currently tiered as follows: 1st crate 700 BP, 2nd crate 1400 BP, 2800 BP, 4200 BP, 5600 BP, 7000 BP. The price doesn't go higher than 7000, and every new week you get reset back to the first tier. A fair system. For comparison: with a win and a few kills or hits in a single round, you can easily rake in 400+ BP to your player account. UPDATE 09/04/2018: Meanwhile, there are also weapon skins—likewise purely cosmetic—and crates that require a paid key. [b] - Bugs, glitches, crashes, and performance [/b] UPDATE 09/04/2018: The game is no longer in Early Access, bugs have been reduced, higher FPS is possible, and crashes are extremely rare. Yet various other little flaws still occasionally reduce the gameplay to utter absurdity. Bullet drop and hits are sometimes visible via dust and blood, and other times they just aren't. Reliable feedback on whether or when you actually hit something is thus not consistently possible. Sometimes, just like a year ago in the Early Access phase, you get hit while in cover, or you shoot out of cover only for your own projectiles to stubbornly get stuck in the object you were using for protection. At times, the damage dealt and received also raises questions. An SR + headshot through a T3 helmet always takes me down, while the reverse often results in simply nothing happening at all. How can something like that happen so regularly? Even the killcam (glad it exists!) is sometimes so asynchronous that its usefulness is merely rudimentary. The exact same problem already existed in Early Access when spectating teammates. Embarrassing. Also, the load time for the first round after starting the game is so long that you simply get chucked out of the plane before you're even done loading. How this title can be associated with the ESL and e-sports is a mystery to me. A fun game maybe, but in my eyes still not competition-ready, despite the release. The development process out of the Early Access phase HAS to keep going from here! [b] - Hackers and other anomalies [/b] Sure, it's hard to impossible to prove that you were just taken out by a hacker. But various YouTube videos clearly show that it's not far-fetched to say they exist. And it's more than unlikely that no one has ever been in a situation where they couldn't quite explain what the hell just happened. How many of these more than shady situations—which happen en masse—are genuinely attributable to a hacker or just a game bug remains a mystery. The fact is, however, the built-in killcam sheds very little light on the matter. Completely regardless of whether it was hacks, bugs, or your own shitty play that brought your character down, the salt levels caused by this are at times [b] [i]record-breakingly[/i] [/b] high, provided you actually care about playing well. Because even if you don't give a crap about stats or winning the match and are just playing a casual round for fun, unfairness—no matter the cause—gets on everyone's last nerve eventually. To counteract the claims of some people who deny there are hackers in PUBG, here is an official statement from the developers: Playerunknown tweeted on 13/09/2017: "[i].@TheBattlEye has now banned over 150,000 cheaters from @PUBATTLEGROUNDS, with more than 8,000 banned in the last 24 hours alone! GG WP[/i]" BattlEye itself announced on 04/02/2018: "[i]We have banned over 1,044,000 PUBG cheaters in January alone, unfortunately things continue to escalate.[/i]" [b] Conclusion [/b] At the end of the day, you oscillate between addiction and frustration, and end up quitting the game mostly because you just can't take it anymore. So if you're looking for a heavy-duty salt shaker for the upcoming winter, you'll find it here for currently 29.99€, though you should probably consider whether you'd rather invest that money in a physical snow shovel or simply wait a bit longer. Because maybe, by the time the first snow falls, the game will actually be one thing: [b] [i]record-breakingly[/i] [/b] frustration-free to play and therefore genuinely worth its money. Honestly, I think the game will never be finished. Purely from watching it(!), I'd sooner recommend Fortnite to players interested in Battle Royale, provided you're willing to master its building mechanic alongside the classic shooter elements.

translation_en: First of all, I want to clarify that I've been playing since it started in Early Access. I think it's a great game with a huge future. It's true that it lacks optimization, but despite a lot of reviews from smart-ass know-it-alls and haters you see around here, the game is infinitely better than it was a few months ago. The dev company is working really hard to fix the game; in fact, the latest update has added and improved a lot of things, like the option to lock the game at 60 fps, for example. They've added quite a few vehicles and more are confirmed, they've also thrown in a ton of new weapons, and it's known that they are working on 2 new maps (there are already images of one of them on social media). Another important thing is that if you read that there is a lot of LAG on the servers, and those reviews were made around August 3-4, 2017, you need to know that with the new update they detected a bug causing that LAG and they are already working on fixing it. Another issue that pisses people off quite a bit in the reviews is the new paid crate, and I want to make a few points clear for those people: 1. They put those crates out to raise money for the tournament taking place at Gamescom. 2. They've added two other completely free crates. 3. The paid crate can be bought with in-game money, and even if you don't want to buy the key to open it, you can sell them on the Steam Market and, as of right now when I'm writing this, make at least 3€ per crate. In short: The company is rolling out constant updates, both to add new content and to fix the game. In fact, after releasing the latest update, they've pushed out two 500mb patches to fix issues that had popped up. Does it still lack optimization? YES. Do they work hard to improve and fix the game? ALSO YES. This isn't the typical company that abandons Early Access halfway through after getting rich. They really listen to the community, you just have to read them on Twitter. Don't let yourselves be fooled by the bullshit and the hate over the crates, they are working their asses off. AMAZING GAME with a huge, huge future.

translation_en: PUBG is currently still in development and there is room for improvement here and there. Despite this, you can safely jump on the train for what looks to be the game of the year. It's very addictive whether you play solo or as part of a team. Together with 99 other players, you start in a transport plane flying over the approx. 36km² large island, Erangel. After landing with a parachute, you fight to become the last survivor and thereby the winner. Since no one starts with anything other than their bare fists to defend themselves with, it is crucial to secure weapons, gear, and supplies. Your first weapon might be something as simple as a frying pan. By exploring the island, you'll find pistols, submachine guns, shotguns, rifles, or light machine guns, all of which come in many variants. For these weapons, there is also a sea of attachments, such as scopes and magazines etc., that increase your chances when you run into one of your opponents along the way. If you take down one of the other participants, you can loot his/her gear. In true Hunger Games style, crates are also continuously dropped by parachute onto the island. These contain particularly good weapons or armor that everyone wants to get their hands on. The entire island is available from the start of the game and you can get around faster if you can find a motorcycle, car, or boat. As time goes on, however, the survivors are squeezed together into an area that gradually gets smaller until a winner is found, which typically takes 30-40 min. If you die, you're out. However, the auto-match feature quickly finds a new game and you are back in action in under 2 min. Apart from the lack of a dedicated jump/climb function (under development) when a fence or window needs to be cleared, all basic functions are in place. Lag can occur at the start of the game. Servers etc. will eventually be financed through microtransactions of cosmetic clothing items that only have visual significance. Playerunknown's Battlegrounds is a MUST HAVE :)

translation_en: It might be the beginning of the end for MOBA games. Unlike you sweatlords dropping in with Level 3 vests, we casuals getting fucked by divine intervention are happy just wearing a green cuck hat. 98 for the game. 30 for the VPN. 600 for internet bills. That's what I paid for this game. And now those crates are selling for 17 a pop. Broke players play PUBG, rich players ship loot. Ten minutes of looting, one second of delivery. 700 crates, nice, a white hat. 1200 crates, nice, a red hat. 2400 crates, nice, a white hat. 4200 crates, nice, a red hat... Wait? It resets next week? Then why the fuck did I open 4200?! I remember my first time jumping from the plane, pulling the chute immediately, and just floating and floating before I even hit the ground I got fucking beamed. Dead on landing. SOLO mode 99/99. DUO mode 49/49. SQUAD mode 28/28. Every time I saw that dead-last rank, I'd reflect on myself, and then queue up for another match just to jump last and fight dead bodies. Even then, I still somehow got killed by a zombie who just revived. Finally, I accepted my true calling: a delivery boy. As long as I can run someone over with a car on the road, what more could I possibly ask for? When my teammate and I were cowering in a corner with pistols, shaking at the sight of the Level 3 gigachad across the road, the red zone arrived. O(∩_∩)O Haha, thank god, we got blown up. Do you want to eat chicken or do you want to kill people? I want to kill people! Hell yeah! Fishing, car traps, phantom tanks, besieging a point to kill reinforcements, camping airdrops, setting up a toll booth! Putting a medkit at the warehouse door and managing to kill three people with just a crossbow. Blasting the tires of a Jeep outside the blue zone, camping behind a tree inside the zone, watching some clueless noob get in the car and panic because it wouldn't move, and just casually popping them with the SKS. I still remember that body of water that had me spaced out. "That's where I first dropped, pretty right?" Lele (my squadmate) said. Staring at it, time seemed to stand still. "Looks nice?" "Yeah." "Looking nice doesn't do shit!" Riding a motorcycle with my homie, speeding around like we owned the world, until we did some aerial acrobatics in a death spiral and someone sniped us right out of the air. On top of the power grid with an 8x AKM, 800 meters away, I one-tapped a shelter-rat's car tire, and oh—Lele instantly got knocked by a KAR98K. A streamer threw a grenade that blew a motorcycle out of a wall, and I threw a grenade that blew the motorcycle straight to hell. Crouching by the staircase with a shotgun, staring at the doorknob for 5 minutes, finally someone shows up, one shot, one kid down. After killing some rich guy in a skirt, I excitedly put the skirt on and felt like I was playing a whole new game. After turning into a crate, Lele braved a hail of bullets and fulfilled his wish to wear the skirt out in public. Final circle, never moved since landing, two airdrops right on my face. Ghillie suit, M24, 15x scope. Still couldn't beat a two-man pinch, bitter about taking second place. Doomsday circle stuck in Z-town, safe zone in S-town. Survived four blue zones and even wiped a squad of desperate players during the third blue zone. Thank god we found a Dacia, but no sooner had we gotten in than Lele collapsed at my feet. "Don't revive me, just go!" "I'm not leaving! Take my meds!" My downed teammate agonizingly pulled out a medkit and pain killers. Caring for my teammate, I got in the car and drove off without looking back. Not even 50 meters later I had to heal, falling short by 0.5 seconds. White-kill finally died outside the zone. At that moment, I was less than 50 meters from Lele and under 3 kilometers from the safe zone. Fuck, the zone shrunk again. Staying alive is tough. Of course, even if I know I can't beat someone, I gotta shoot my gun just to fire a warning shot. Kill one, break even; kill two, turn a profit. Die on landing, change your outfit to switch up your luck, and go again. Whenever I get dropped in, I always miss that carefree minute in the lobby, missing the AWM and Thompson sitting on the tables. When I drove a speedboat back there, the faces were gone, but the peach blossoms still faced the sun. The tables were still there, but who knows where the AWM went. Tearfully used an AKM to kill someone who didn't even get on the plane???? Left in the boat without looking back, didn't even leave a single bandage. Didn't even get to taste a single bite of radiation. Climbed mountains, ran through sunsets; crossed broken bridges, swam across streams. All just to see you, to lovingly pack up my Level 3 backpack and hand-deliver all my gear to you. If you're kind, you might even get a green cuck hat. Long-distance express delivery, please remember to sign for your package. Butterflies don't know the malice of human hearts, birds don't know the vicissitudes of the world, and flies don't bite seamless eggs. There's no road longer than your feet, and no gun farther than the AWM. Once you grab a crate in the lobby, your path of no return is set, and all that's left is snake-crawling and slaughter. Gunfights in the wilderness, hiding from red zones in outhouses, sniping from high towers, going crazy by airdrops, underwater assassinations, tearing up the highway. Patience in a room, lurking in wheat fields, relentless struggle in torrents, looking down from a high tower, running across hillsides, gazing into the sunset, and struggling outside the safe zone! All for survival, for those uncontrollable, continuous gunshots fired into the sky at the very last second. WINNER WINNER CHICKEN DINNER! ——————————————————————————————————————————— I am two ugly divider lines ——————————————————————————————————————————— "Duoduo, do you feel like Bluehole let you down so much that they deleted your review?" "Nah." So I'm dusting off a review from half a year ago. Someone left a comment saying: With so many hackers, haven't you been bullied enough? Change it to a negative review. Yeah. After an update a while ago, the game lagged like crazy. Both my friends and I were lagging hard. Looked it up and found out turning off the replay feature fixes it. I was so upset—isn't that just shielding the cheaters? Without replays, how am I supposed to know if the guy who killed me was actually hacking? Over the summer, the entire summer, I didn't run into a single hacker in low-tier lobbies. But after school started, after the game blew up, I ran into them every single day. I bombed the college entrance exams, and I discovered PUBG during my lowest point. My friends accompanied me in the game, helping me through the toughest times, letting me still laugh every single day. Games aren't everything. After school starts, I have a lot of things worth doing, a lot of things worth loving. Every week, I still call up my scumbag friends to happily drop in and die on landing a few times on a weekend afternoon. When chilling, we shoot each other in the back; when in crisis, we block bullets for each other (though the happiest part is probably crying tears of joy while looting boxes). I am a person who is easily satisfied, yet hard to satisfy. Winning just one chicken dinner a week is enough to keep me happy for a long time, but I am far from satisfied with my current status. PUBG is just a game to me, but more importantly, it's a weekly one-on-one connection with my friends. No matter how far apart we are, there's still a chance, a time, to open our hearts to each other and fight side by side. People in the community speak well and are fun, people are interesting, and the girls are gorgeous. I super love talking to these gorgeous friends. Lonely people immerse themselves in games, painful people immerse themselves in games, but games bring relaxation and joy, and gamers are not lonely or in pain. Some people make a living off games and find success through games, but most of us don't. Therefore, I hope my friends don't adopt a sadistic mindset where they derive joy from making other players miserable. Games aren't everything for most of us. I know the world is big, way bigger than Erangel. I know survival is hard, harder than Pecado. But we can't always lose ourselves in games. Maybe once I get a girlfriend, I'll take her to climb mountains, run through sunsets, cross broken bridges, and swim across streams, experiencing the romance of Erangel with her. Or maybe years from now, on a lazy afternoon, I'll call up my friends again for some bloody, satisfying slaughter. I still recommend this game to my friends in the community. At the very least, for me, it brought me way more moments of deep emotion. (I still have no idea why Fen and Lele's aim was so fucking accurate when they shot at me.) Happy 1st Anniversary to PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS in advance. Just as the scenery in Jiangnan is at its best, falling blossom time brings me across you again.

translation_en: A game I didn't really know I'd been waiting for for a long time. It's got everything you need in it: - A well-done "action" side. Gunfights are believable, weapon sounds are spot-on. You often feel outmatched against more experienced players, but it all comes down to practice, and once mastered, certain rifles can be deadly. - A "strategic" side. You have total freedom in how you approach a match: You can play super aggressively or just hide in a corner waiting for an inevitable clash, but either way you have to carefully anticipate your every move so you don't end up out in the open getting blasted by a smarter sniper. You're still limited by the play zone that shrinks as the match goes on, and you have to keep a close eye on it or else you'll take damage (and usually die as a result). At the start of each match, you have to choose your spawn point on the map: go to a crowded town and risk dying in an early fight, or choose to start in a less populated area with potentially worse loot? Because you start every match "naked" and victory naturally depends on the gear you scavenge. - Management too, then: Choosing your weapon based on what you need, gathering ammo and upgrades, picking up body armor, helmets, backpacks, upgrading them... PUBG is a game that keeps you on edge the entire match. You're always on the lookout for the tiniest footstep that gives away the presence of an enemy/victim. You're always wondering if crossing an open field is gonna be your death warrant. You open doors cautiously, you only rush in critical moments. The stress is there from start to finish, and finishing in the top 10 is a reward you savor with pride. PUBG is a good game in my opinion, a game that knows how to plunge the player into a dangerous and merciless world, but one you gladly jump back into after getting run over by some random passing 4x4. Update: I'm back after almost 200 hours of playtime, and my experience doesn't match the reviews I'm seeing in the recommendations at all. Sure, sometimes the game crashes, sometimes there are cheaters but REALLY VERY FEW, sometimes the servers lag and the game isn't super well optimized, but I genuinely have fun with it, and as long as you play with a friend or friends, the game is truly excellent, just like I said in my first review. So it's gotta be one of two things: either my PC is an absolute beast (which it kinda is), and I'm fabulously lucky not to run into too many issues, or the community and especially the people leaving reviews are super salty, and get bent out of shape over nothing, like, I think, a good chunk of the gaming community these days. So to you game owners, rethink your priorities if the second option sounds right to you: would you rather bitch like everyone else and spew your toxic hate in the comments, or queue up another match with some friends and have fun? Yeah, the devs are a bit slack right now, but you bought an Early Access game, knowing the risks and uncertainties that come with it. You signed up for an unfinished game with an indefinite development timeline. Be patient, and just ask yourself why the game is so popular right now, and almost always ranks in the top 5 games on Twitch. Have fun, that's the most important thing, the updates will come, for sure.

translation_en: The game costs 98 RMB, but actually you also need a 30 RMB monthly subscription for the accelerator. I'm currently using Panda and it works great. This game is nicknamed "Courier Simulator" or "Running Simulator". If you want to play PUBG happily, go to the Southeast Asian server. The ping is playable and you can connect without a VPN. Most players there are complete cowards; sometimes you'll drop into Pochinki and realize you're the only one there. But as more and more players from the Asian server move over, it might turn into a server full of camping rats too. If you think camping is boring and want to play a proper shooter with straight-up gunfights, go to the NA or EU servers. The players there are fierce and aggressive, and they love running toward gunshots. By the time the first circle starts closing, half the players are already dead. If you want to play a horror game, go to the Asian server. I've been scared so badly that I jumped out of my chair a few times. Even if a door is closed and a house is fully looted, you still need to loot carefully—peek around the corner to make sure nobody's there before you open the door. If you want to hone your skills, I recommend playing solo on the Asian server. Once you come out of there, you'll be battle-tested. What haven't you seen of those Western tricks? I suggest not playing too like a coward. Otherwise, if you camp until there are only 20-something people left, and you get randomly shot without having killed a single person, your gaming experience will be trash. The game doesn't have an aim-practice server. If you want to practice your gunplay, go to the NA server and specifically drop at Pochinki, Rozhok, Sosnovka Military Base, or School. Grab a gun and go kill people. Once you can make it out of those places alive, it means your shooting skills are up to standard. Even though it's a survival game, I suggest everyone go out there, hunt people down, and take gunfights. Campers are not only bored out of their minds themselves, but they also ruin the gaming experience for others. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Holy shit, so many upvotes.... I'm flattered. The main arguments everyone's having are about PC specs and campers... As for PC specs, you honestly don't need an 8,000 RMB rig. The game's optimization is way better than when it first came out, and the hardware requirements have dropped. Graphics aren't even the main thing in this game anyway, as long as it's easy to spot people. Regarding the camper playstyle, to each their own—different types of players just have completely different mental processes: Chinese players: 1. I'm poor, I'm gonna camp. When someone walks by, I'll kill them and get rich. 2. I'm stacked, I'm definitely not running out to take gunfights and play courier. I'd better keep camping. NA players: 1. I'm poor, I'm going out to hunt someone down so I can get rich. If I die, whatever, I'm broke anyway. 2. I'm so stacked, it would be a waste not to go out and kill people with this much gear. I'm going to find someone to frag.

translation_en: I feel like the most amazing thing about this game is how it masterfully creates the illusion—and actually scatters those moments throughout the match—where every single participating player thinks, "Maybe this time, I could actually win (get the chicken dinner)." In a lot of popular FPS and TPS games, beginners probably stand almost zero chance against mouse-wielding veterans when it comes to aim and gunfights, and I'm sure there are quite a few people who steer clear of various titles for that exact reason. But in this game, besides pure skill, there's a huge element of luck involved not just with weapons, attachments, and healing items dropping, but with movement as well. Maybe I'll find a better weapon or scope before the higher-ranked player does, and if that happens, maybe I can take them out from a long distance where their gunfire can't reach me. Maybe my location will be in the next safe zone, and I can ambush some sweating pro player who's frantically running in. Maybe a pro player will just walk right past me while I'm terrified and proned out in a potato field, letting me catch them from behind. Maybe a fight between pros will break out nearby, and I can finish off the survivors like a total vulture... Countless "what ifs" like this exist throughout the game, and it's designed so that players naturally feel that way. It's fantastic that the gameplay isn't set up as "aim is absolute power, so new players and bad shots can turn right around and go home," and I think it lets beginners feel a glimmer of hope too. If I had to compare it to something, it's like "a lottery ticket where you can raise your odds of winning depending on what you do." Yet at the same time, of course, it doesn't just turn into a pure RNG fest; there are plenty of moments where good positioning and good aim genuinely matter. It's tough for a beginner to win the final showdown purely on luck, and likewise, it's just as tough for a veteran to constantly rack up wins purely on skill. That balance is just too exquisite. If anyone reads this review and feels like "maybe I could actually enjoy this," please take the plunge and give it a try. After playing, you can't help but think about the "what ifs"—"what would've happened if I did that back then?"—and before you know it, you find yourself heading right back to the battlefield to test out those "what ifs." Asking yourself "what if I had done that..." even gives you a sense of how it connects to human life itself. It totally makes sense why it recorded the highest concurrent player count in Steam history—it's that fun and deep.

translation_en: [h1] PUBG-BUGG?-BADG?[/h1] [u][i] For this review, I've written down all the negative points from various reviews and I'm going to go through them one by one. These addressed points should result in a good and clear review. [/i][/u] [spoiler] My own opinion! I'm happy to read about your gameplay experiences in the comments, unless it's obvious trolling and not meant seriously.[/spoiler] [olist] [*] Price [*] Bad optimization [*] Server lags [*] Clunky controls [*] Cheaters [*] Repetitiveness [*] Luck-based game [*] Campers & circles/zones [/olist] [u]Let's get to the price:[/u] When it comes to the price, I think what's important is how high the potential maximum playtime is. I think €25 is fair, but not less. The developers are doing an exceptionally good job in my opinion. That means they're constantly putting out patches that fix bugs, add game content, and optimize the player experience. If things keep going this way in the future, nothing should stand in the game's way. So I'm pretty sure that with continually arriving content and game optimizations, you'll get a high amount of playtime out of it. Unless you just personally don't like the game. But I'm not assuming that. The publishers are future-oriented, and therefore €25-30 is neither too much nor too little for a game like this. [u]Let's get to the bad optimization:[/u] Here I agree with most people. Engine-wise, the game doesn't seem to be optimized well enough yet. Even the best setups have FPS drops or just low FPS overall. Still, I don't see "bad game optimization" as that huge of a problem. Because right now, you actually only have advantages if you put your graphic settings on the lowest preset—for example, to spot enemies better or just get more FPS. That still doesn't change the fact that the game definitely needs to be optimized, especially in the high graphics range. And for people who might only be able to play on "Very Low", I recommend [url=https://reshade.me/]Reshade[/url]. Tutorials for it are on YouTube. Check it out yourselves. And in case anyone is asking whether Reshade is banned: [url=https://www.reddit.com/r/PUBATTLEGROUNDS/comments/64eb64/it_is_ok_to_use_reshade/]Reshade yes or no?[/url] [u]Let's get to the server lags:[/u] Anyone who has been playing PUBG since the beginning knows how much the server issues have improved. Back then you constantly had disconnects and were getting rubberbanded all over the place. To be honest, I don't get it when people today still say they have lag. Maybe you occasionally experience minimal lag. Even on the NA or AS servers, I have practically zero problems. [u]Let's get to the clunky controls:[/u] Often I've seen people wishing the controls were just like CS:GO or Overwatch. I think many don't realize we're talking about a semi-realistic shooter here. Anyone who has played Arma 2, 3, or even DayZ knows how good the controls are compared to other games. The fact that this or that action feels sluggish is only because, as mentioned above, we're talking about a realistic shooter. I find it more something you have to get used to rather than clunky. For some it might be hard to deal with, for others not. Just play a bit and you'll get used to it. [u]Let's get to the cheaters:[/u] I've been playing PUBG for a solid month and a half now, and I think I've run into a hacker maybe once. Otherwise, I've never felt like I encountered one. Here too, I think people often claim there are too many cheaters out of frustration and their own failure. Here's a link to how well the publishers are cracking down on hackers: [url=http://www.pcgamer.com/pubg-cheaters/]What is being done against cheaters?[/url]. I'm not saying there are no hackers. But I am sure that good action is being taken against them. Saying the game is plagued by hackers is just ridiculous to me. [u]Let's get to the repetitiveness:[/u] [quote=author]The game is so boring. You just wait in a house and then you fight at the end. If you lose, 30 minutes were a waste of time.[/quote] [quote=author] Always the same thing... you jump out of the plane and loot, wait, and win or lose. [/quote] Yeah, at the beginning you jump out of the plane and try to find the best possible loot wherever you end up landing, to then hit the road or not. Here I agree with people... yes, the basic gameplay loop is pretty much always the same. But every single round is different. After all, you don't always land at the same spot (the plane path doesn't allow for that), you don't always find the exact same weapons right away, you don't always run into enemies at the same locations, you don't always find the drops in the same spot, and you don't always get the same circles (zones). Those are reasons why I think the game isn't repetitive at all. As I said at the start, the core gameplay loop stays the same, but every round is a completely new round in itself. Plus, you decide your playstyle and whether you go the whole game without running into enemies and hide in houses, or roam and look for fights. A good comparison for the same gameplay loop is League of Legends (I'm assuming pretty much everyone knows League of Legends). [u] Let's get to whether PUBG is a luck-based game:[/u] Yes, of course you need luck to find the best weapons or the best gear. Weapon spawns and car spawns have been adjusted now and aren't always the same anymore. Back in the day, 30 people would drop in Rozhok just to get the car in the garage... thank god it's not like that anymore today. Here I don't understand people who say the game is luck-based while at the same time calling it repetitive? Doesn't that contradict itself? How your luck affects the gameplay experience is something I'll discuss in the next point. [u] Let's get to campers & circles/zones:[/u] With the last patch, campers are now being punished. The zones are no longer dead center, but can also spawn way out West at the end. Meaning if you aren't camping and you're in the middle of the circle, and the circle suddenly spawns way out West, you'll have an easy time getting there. The exact opposite goes for the camper... they figured they could stay in a house in the East to ambush everyone, but now they've got problems because they have to move. Of course, there are campers who were in the West from the start and got lucky. I think the problem isn't campers themselves, but the Third-Person View. After all, you can just lie behind a tiny rock and see everything (or in the tall grass right now). But there are solutions for this too that have already been announced. First-person servers are supposed to be coming soon. Of course, there will still be campers there... but I don't think it'll work out well for them—you'll get punished way too often for camping. I've often read that the circles and zones are placed so terribly and campers almost always win. I can't really argue against this. If you have the ultimate position and the circle spawns on you five times, your chances of winning go up rapidly. Still, it must be said that even something like that can be outplayed with skill. Here I have an example of a streamer who is perfectly inside the circle and has a long bus in front of him, allowing him to look around it using third-person and just wait for the other guy to come out and slaughter him. But he decides against the perfect position and sprints out into the worse position to fight the guy anyway. Here's the clip: [url=https://clips-media-assets.twitch.tv/25771031536-offset-21118.mp4#t=0]Clip[/url]

translation_en: [h1]Playerunknown's Battlegrounds[/h1] This is a "Battle Royale" game. Meaning you drop onto a map alone, with a buddy, or in a 4-man squad and search nearby buildings and other structures for weapons, meds, backpacks, and anything else that might help you survive. It is a really formidable rival to H1Z1:KOTK. You can see this in things like Steam sales numbers, staying on the bestseller list, and player reviews. The goal of the game is to be the last person or team standing. Achieving this rewards you with "points" which you can use to buy crates containing cosmetic items. You won't find the same push for crates here as in H1Z1 where you have to spend real money. The developers promised to leave Early Access within 6 months, and you can really see it! Loads of updates, even up to 1.5 GB, which not only fix a ton of bugs but also improve optimization. At first, I didn't play this game often because of the FPS and massive stutters that made it really hard to play, and my rig isn't even old. However, the latest optimization update changed everything! Averaging 90 FPS and the game runs better and better! The 30 euro price tag might turn some people off. Trust me, it's better to pay those few extra euros and get a way better game than H1Z1, which I have close to 2k hours in across different accounts (friends played dirty). When we don't have anyone to play with in Duo or Squad mode, we can always queue with random people, just like in Counter-Strike. In solo lobbies, you might want to turn your headset down a bit because the players are, how should I put it... loud. On the other hand, I have never encountered rudeness or insults from the people the game matched me with in my squad. Tips, tactics, etc. Really cool people! I hope there will be more like them in all games. ________________________________________________________________________________ [b]Pros[/b] +Weapon variety and attachment system +No push for cosmetic items (crates) +Gameplay mechanics (Knockdowns in Duo/Squad mode) +Massive amount of updates +No jumping out of vehicles going 100km/h like in H1Z1 (Here, it results in damage for the person getting out) +We can choose where we want to jump from the plane +Lots of vehicle types +Large player base +Nice, clean GUI. Health bar and an indicator showing how close you are to the safe zone and how close to the gas. It also shows how much time is left until the gas releases, etc. [b]Cons:[/b] -Optimization - It's getting better, but still needs some work, like in any Early Access game. -Jumping / Physics. (A vaulting system for walls etc. is supposed to be added, it's not there yet) Meaning: If you see a wall you should be able to vault over, your character won't do it. -Vehicles can rarely behave weirdly (I managed to fly a few hundred meters away just by clipping a motorcycle). [b]Summary[/b] In my opinion, Playerunknown's Battlegrounds is currently the "king" of Battle Royale games. It's really worth spending that 30 euro, hell, it might turn out that when the game leaves EA it will be more expensive (like ARK). You can spend long hours playing it with friends as well as by yourself. A must-have title for Battle Royale fans. Highly Recommended!

Created by the founder of H1Z1 himself, this game of the same genre was bound to be compared to H1Z1. I have to say Battlegrounds is very successful, making hundreds of millions in sales within a few months and ranking #1 in sales for over a dozen consecutive weeks. As someone who played both H1Z1 and Battlegrounds, I'm writing this review to guarantee fairness and objectivity. ―――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――― The success of Battlegrounds is no accident; it has many advantages. (1) A wide variety of vehicles. All kinds of cars and boats, and they are more realistic. Compared to H1Z1 where you can jump out of a moving vehicle anytime, jumping out of a moving car in Battlegrounds will kill you. Much closer to real life, a very good feature. (2) More freedom in gameplay. In H1Z1, you can only drive or run, but in Battlegrounds, you can also swim and even dive. Compared to H1Z1's random parachute drop, Battlegrounds lets you choose for yourself, making it much more open and free, which isn't a bad thing. As for firearms, you also have many guns to use, paired with different attachments, which makes H1Z1 look quite inferior. (3) More user-friendly settings. Speaking of this, I have to mention walking quietly (sneaking), which allows you to sneak up behind enemies more carefully. At the same jogo, Battlegrounds also has lean-left and lean-right mechanics, and throwing weapons gives you a predicted trajectory. This is very user-friendly and awesome. ―――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――― However, I have to mention that there are also quite a few flaws. (1) Optimization issues. Severe frame drops, but since this game is newly born, we can look forward to future optimization. (2) The appearance issue that many people complain about—characters are always hunched over. (3) Due to certain reasons, hitting people sprays green blood, and the bullet holes on bodies are also green (I'm begging you, if all else fails, just change it so no blood sprays, it's so gross). (4) The "naked" meta. Since gear doesn't matter much, many people choose to run around naked. I especially have to mention shoes—for the sake of footstep audio, a lot of people go barefoot. Excuse me? ―――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――― Lastly, some suggestions from me. Regarding specs, the optimization isn't actually that terrible. I'm on a laptop with the following specs and I can tolerate it: GTX 950M, i7-4720HQ, 16G RAM, 128G SSD. This game is definitely worth a try. For me, switching back and forth between H1Z1 and Battlegrounds is truly thrilling. ―――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――― In the end, what I want to say is that comparing games is fine, but blind hating is just mindless. I hope people don't get a sense of superiority from playing a video game. Thanks for reading.

translation_en: Good "Battle Royale" mode game (everyone against everyone or groups against groups with no weapons, gear, or vehicles at the start). Made by "PlayerUnknown", the creator of this game mode and co-creator of H1Z1. Unsatisfied with the final result of H1Z1 and the lack of attention from the development team, he decided to make his own standalone game. And here we are. +Possible player combinations: Solo(1), Duo(2), Squad(4) -> There is a "filler" to complete multi-player modes (Ex: 3 players in the same group plus a random player) +Map shrinking system is random and each new circle can be anywhere in the safe zone. +Fast matches, around 30~40min. +Large map, but not big enough to stop you from running. +Infinite run (there is a run bar that when it hits zero only decreases your speed a little bit). +Good movement in a middle ground of realism (with realistic limitations that weren't in H1Z1 and were in excess in Arma). +Vehicles are a good resource, but very loud and not that fast (like they weren't in H1Z1). +Abundant vehicles (Unlike Arma) and without removable internal parts that prevent them from working (unlike H1Z1) +There is plenty of customization possibility (to improve weapons, like: scopes, grips, stocks, and firearm muzzles). +There is a lot of "Loot" (item scavenging on the map), without any terrain distinction (the military base won't necessarily have a higher percentage of weapons), what happens is that certain places have more "loot spawns" (places where items will spawn on the map), making the amount of weapons higher. +Item rarity system and "Care Package" (special armaments that drop by parachute on the map) -Game still in Beta -The shooting system leaves a bit to be desired, there are few people I've seen mastering the art of shooting from afar (+80mts) due to bullet travel time. There are two types of shooting: first and third person. [b]First Person[/b] Good for very close or very far away fights, but it has very bad weapon movement on screen, being very sensitive to any movement. [b]Third Person[/b] Good for medium-distance fights, but there is huge inaccuracy and a lot of ammo is wasted. I must say this game reminds me more of Arma's Battle Royale, despite obvious differences, which pleases me and my friends a lot (even those who don't like Arma, nor its hyper-realistic style). Furthermore, it allows freedom for the playstyle the player wants, with all of them being viable, noting that your opponents are players too. Despite being a beta game, it is well polished, besides having a large number of people playing. The gameplay is good and fun is guaranteed for those interested in this game mode. The game is suggested for groups or solo players, every team size has its challenges and perks. In my view, the points I highlighted are essential for this game mode and, after trying several games that fell short, I can say that I'll be sticking with the Battle Royale mode in Playerunknown's Battlegrounds, making it my permanent game in this mode from now on. Just out of curiosity, I'll put the common combat progression in a match here: Close Range(0min) > Medium Range(10min) > Long Range(20min) EDIT: After the release of two crates, I can state that the game is infested with hackers, I don't know how long it will take for a company with no track record like Bluehole to deal with this. But know this: every new crate release comes with a large number of hackers on the servers, mostly Chinese ones (which makes me think: why does the game allow you to choose servers to connect to? A player with 400+ ping doesn't seem good for them or for other players. This simple limitation would cut out 90% of the hackers). [b]I still love this game, despite the frustration of dealing with hackers almost every match, which is why I'm keeping the game recommended, despite the blunders of the company behind it.[/b] As a final thought, I'd like to say that you always have a chance to kill a hacker, you just have to learn how to play against them, which my squad has become professional at doing (remember, an aimbot can't kill an entire squad aiming at the hacker all at once).

translation_en: [h1][i] The definitive battle royale game [/i][/h1] [h1]Pros[/h1] ＋[b]Frying pan[/b] ＋Shrinking play area ＋Self-paced gameplay ＋Great gun handling ＋Great sound design ＋Rating system ＋Active feedback and updates [h1]Cons[/h1] －Meh gun balance －Still has server lag －Lacking optimization －Cheaters [h1]Playtime[/h1] [i]1 to 40 minutes per match[/i] [h1]Recommended buy price[/h1] [i]Full price[/i] [h1]Things to note[/h1] [list] [*]If you run into any launch or in-game issues, you can fix them [url=http://forums.playbattlegrounds.com/topic/25335-faq/]here[/url]. [*]For optimization tips, refer to [url=http://cafe.naver.com/playbattlegrounds/44883]here[/url]. [*]If you have a gamepad with vibration connected, your controller will vibrate every time you take damage, so please unplug it. [ /list] [h1]Recommended for people who[/h1] Want a game they can dive into for short bursts like LoL or Overwatch [h1]Not recommended for people who[/h1] Like survival games with long prep times like DayZ [h1]Personal thoughts[/h1] I fucking hate survival games. It takes forever to loot, you're just scrambling to stay alive, and once you die or win, you hit that post-nut clarity of "why the hell am I playing this again?" But I seriously cannot get sick of this game. This is the first time I've played a survival-type game for this kind of length. (Right now, H1Z1 and Battlegrounds are the main reps for these short-match battle royale games, but I never bought H1Z1 so please understand I can't compare them.) http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=960791903 [i]Even if your aim sucks, as long as you've got good game sense, you can get a win with just 1 kill.[/i] The goal of this game is to kill other users until you're the last one standing as the play area closes in within 40 minutes. Even if you don't know the rules, it's simple and intuitive—grab a weapon, fight people, and head to the safe zone—making it easy for anyone of any age or gender to understand. Along the way, you can control your own pace throughout the match: loot moderately, camp out in a safe house, and move slowly when the zone shrinks; or drop into a loot-heavy city or military base packed with other players to have a bloodbath right from the start. Also, something that blew me away the whole time I played was the distinct feel of each gun. I was impressed by how attachments change the feel—like gunshot sounds, noise reduction from attachments, recoil control—while still not being hardcore like Arma. On top of that, every sound a player makes—gunshots, suppressed gunfire, switching firing modes, reloading—can be heard from all directions, making sound whoring feel almost like playing Rainbow Six Siege. Because of that, even though matches are short, it feels super immersive and puts you right in the thick of the action. Also, normally you get that post-game burnout and quit, but having a rating system gives you a great reason to keep playing, and thanks to ratings, the skill gap between the 100 players isn't that huge, so you're always playing with people at your level. http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=960792025 [i]If your PC specs are shit, wallhacks turn themselves on. -0-[/i] I don't have any major complaints about the gameplay itself, but it's a bit disappointing that some guns are so much worse than others that people don't even bother picking them up and just leave them. Some people might force themselves to use those garbage guns because they like how they feel, so I hope they tweak the balance a bit. Also, while optimization and netcode have gotten a lot better through repeated patches, I don't think it's quite ready to shed that Early Access tag yet. Random network errors and sudden lag still need work. Lastly, maybe because of the huge player base, I'm seeing quite a few cheaters. They ban cheaters every week, but they're still around, and in a 100-player lobby, a cheater's impact is overwhelming. I'm hoping they get faster at dealing with hackers. http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=960791601 [i]You can even pull off sneaky lurk plays like this by using flipped cars or boats.[/i] This game completely fucked up my daily routine for a while—work -> home -> PUBG -> sleep -> work. I'm so hooked that even as I'm writing this review, I want to fire up PUBG. I've gotten this addicted even with an exhausted body after work... Setting gameplay aside, it's just great to see a proper game made in Korea doing so well globally. I hope this inspires game companies to put out games with actual gameplay instead of gambling garbage. I hope they polish it well during Early Access and it has a long run. I'm genuinely hyped for the finished version of Battlegrounds. Highly recommended.

translation_en: You've probably heard and seen a lot about PlayerUnknown's BattleGrounds, but if you still haven't taken the plunge to try it out, I'm here to tell you what you're really missing. Don't let the trees stop you from seeing the forest, because the essence of this game is deep inside, and I'm going to sell it to you if you keep reading. You can also find the review here: http://akihabarablues.com/impresiones-con-playerunknowns-battlegrounds-para-steam/ What does PlayerUnknown's BattleGrounds have that it keeps selling units on the only platform that currently exists, and that it's also right in the middle of Early Access development? Apparently, it doesn't offer anything out of this world. I'm sure you've seen its mechanics, its environment, its gameplay, or its style in other games, and that's really the case. It doesn't invent anything. It doesn't innovate in anything. I'd even dare to say that many things it does, it does quite a bit worse than other similar games. But if you try it, you can't help but appreciate it because it does offer you gaming sensations that are maybe harder to get in other games. PlayerUnknown's BattleGrounds is a pure and hardcore survival game. There's a single map in the shape of a huge island, and you are dropped from a cargo plane along with the roughly 100 players that make up the match. The goal is to be the only one alive out of all the players in the match. You can play solo, in pairs, or in squads of 4, but never mixed. That means if you choose solo, everyone else will be solo, just like if you do it in duo, all rivals will be in duo, and ditto with squads. The plane will cross the map randomly at the start of each match and you choose when to jump with a parachute. If you don't do it yourself, the game will drop you at the very end before it finishes its route. All players arrive on the map under equal conditions. Without any gear and with just the character skin you have selected. Glide as much as you want with the parachute and as soon as you touch ground your life is in danger. Anyone can come and wreck you with punches, so the first thing will be to check around you if there are other players. Once that's done, we need to gear up as best as possible. For that, we have to search buildings of all kinds that are scattered across the map. In them you'll find many types of weapons and ammo. Attachments for these like grips, quickdraw mags, scopes, etc. As well as protective gear like bulletproof vests or helmets and other clothes for the character that do nothing other than modify the appearance. We'll also find healing items (medkits, bandages...) or items to boost our stats (Energy Drinks, painkillers...). We must gear up as best as possible and always with the fear and care that we can be surprised by another player and that if they end our life, they can feed on our loot. Gearing up is very important in PlayerUnknown's BattleGrounds, but if you don't do it fast, it's going to be the least of your problems. The game will progressively reduce the war zone to force players to move and avoid "ultimate camping". That play zone is marked as a white circle that will get smaller every so often. If you aren't in that zone, a larger zone in the shape of a blue circle will slowly shrink until it reaches the white zone. If it catches you outside, you'll be losing health until death. You'll be able to run, swim, drive a vehicle, heal to recover the health that being outside the zone is taking away from you, and even juice up on vitamins to make it, but if you don't do it fast you'll end up dead. At this point, three big problems/needs arise for us to advance in the match. First, gear up well. A primary weapon like an assault rifle with a good scope and grip, plus a secondary like a pistol with a quickdraw mag for example. With a melee gadget like a crowbar or a pan (please nerf the pan XD). Grenades, both stun and frag, and healing gear, all you can. Backpacks to carry all this and a helmet plus bulletproof vest as a complement. Second, always stay in the play zone. If we are very far from the zone don't wait around to move, even if you are poorly geared it's not going to do you any good if you are outside the zone because you are going to die fast without using any gear. Grab a vehicle as soon as you find one and start progressing toward the zone with it to gear up with caution. Keep in mind that moving in a vehicle makes noise so others are going to know when you are approaching. Third, and maybe the most important, try to control the rest of the players so they don't kill you. Try not to expose yourself so they see you, and if possible, see the rivals yourself first. You're going to have no choice but to move no matter what, but just like you, the rest of the players are too, and you can use this factor to your advantage. All your actions make noise and it's the only non-visual way to know the enemy's location since they are never going to show up on the map. If you walk, run, or crawl you can be heard if, for example, you do it on the second floor of a house and there's someone downstairs. Vehicles are the loudest. If you intend to search a house, keep in mind that someone might be there and hear you arrive. If you manage to be around the safe zone, it's relatively easy to reach the last 30 players of the match, and if you reach that point, your position and everyone else's is crucial in PlayerUnknown's BattleGrounds. You already know what the game is about. And now you'll ask yourselves, what does PlayerUnknown's BattleGrounds have that those who play it love it so much? For me, its main virtue is putting the player into an authentic Russian roulette and making them believe they can come out unscathed from all this. That poses to you that, despite always being on the same map and in the same way, you are never going to have two identical matches and that you as a player are going to grow and do better each time. Naturally, the luck factor also counts for a lot, but far from making you resentful about it, it livens up the fact that all players are on equal terms, and that encourages you that you can move and tip the balance in your favor. All of this makes it so from the moment you put a foot on the ground you are in tension, constantly thinking about where to go and how, and constantly getting resources. The fact that it's you, or your duo, or squad, against ninety-odd other players under the same conditions is what makes you feel powerful. Very few games can offer you these sensations, and even fewer in this way with such great balance. And you feel like you are so close to getting a good result that when you get taken down, you can't stop trying again. Plus, the game finds matches relatively well due in large part to the high number of players always in the game. And the game has sold, I think I'm not wrong, three million digital copies in quite a short time and considering it's an Early Access. And it is one in every sense of the word because the game is far from finished. Graphic and physics bugs are aplenty and it's rare when the game doesn't crash one out of every five matches, especially if you're in the company of other players. It's without a doubt the big "but" of this game, the doubts about when it will be finished. They said it wouldn't be in the Early Access program for more than 6 months and far from announcing a definitive release date they have ventured to announce, at past E3 2017, that the game will have new maps with different themes and that it will also make the jump to consoles, specifically on Xbox as an exclusive. It scares me because like I say, the game doesn't seem finished and I hope they aren't biting off more than they can chew. I hope they know how to polish PlayerUnknown's BattleGrounds like it deserves and it doesn't die of success, because it is truly very worth playing it, don't just stick to the vibes of watching it because it's very different from playing it.

translation_en: [h1] BETTER THAN H1Z1? [/h1] If you ask around which of the two games (H1Z1 vs. PUBG) is better, you'd probably expect a relatively even result, with PUBG likely being slightly ahead. However, this review is going to be about my opinion and that's clear-cut. In my opinion, you can't go wrong with PUBG. I'll tell you why... [b] What makes PUBG so special? [/b] For those who don't know PUBG: PUBG is a survival game where you jump out of a plane onto an island and try to gear up as best as you can to survive in the end as a team or solo. Airdrops as well as the safe zone, which does more and more damage, turn a quiet situation into a firefight that can last for minutes. What makes the game special in my opinion is that it's not about "the better shooter wins" — the game can't just be won through "aim," but also through tactically smart approaches. You can play the game in many different ways and everyone can kind of find their own "middle ground" :D. While one person wants to intercept every airdrop, the other person can avoid every fight. Another special feature of the game is that you feel — or have to feel — constantly watched. [b] Long-term fun? [/b] As long as you like the game, it'll be fun enough that you'll lose track of an hour or two playing it. While some other games get repetitive (i.e. you don't feel like anything new is happening, rather it's always the same = it gets boring), with PUBG the firefights might be similar, but every battle has its own unique twist. I'll explain why: Just like in many other survival games, in PUBG you have to spend a lot of time on foot or in a vehicle and therefore don't have a base to defend. And since a shootout can start every second no matter where you are, every rock, every tree, and even every cornfield can become a final hope and a lifesaver. [b] Conclusion: [/b] In my opinion, you can't go far wrong with buying PUBG. If you decide to buy the game, plenty of exciting fights await you soon. Have fun! If this review wasn't enough for you, feel free to check out the videos about the game on my YT channel: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCn2RPvMl1SKocjZWKA54Q1w
