translation_en: [h1] A true battle royale that makes H1Z1: King of the Kill look like cheap trash [/h1] I've been playing since the old Arma battle royale mod days all the way through H1Z1. I wouldn't call myself a battle royale expert or a pro, but I've developed an eye for where a game is heading and how its ongoing development is shaping up. Right now, the game it's being compared to the most (especially in Korea) is definitely H1Z1. Since they come from the same director, that's kind of to be expected. However, the big difference is that while PLAYERUNKNOWN wasn't the main director for H1Z1—only serving in more of an advisory role—he's leading the development as the lead director for BATTLEGROUNDS. To put it simply, here’s how it stands out compared to H1Z1. [h1] H1Z1: King of the Kill vs PLAYERUNKNOWN's BATTLEGROUNDS [/h1] The biggest difference is the weight of the controls and gunplay. H1Z1 goes for super lightweight controls. You can't really call aiming and shooting all that difficult, and the overall game feel is pretty casual (since the game's roots were basically a lightweight version of DayZ anyway). BATTLEGROUNDS, on the other hand, has relatively heavy controls and gunplay. It’s not quite on ARMA's level, but if you jump into the game expecting the same controls and gunplay as H1Z1, you might need a bit of an adjustment period. But far from being a detriment, this heavy feel faithfully multiplies the tension and the thrill of firefights, which are the core points of the battle royale genre. The gunshots sound impressive, and the hit feedback is decent. There's also bullet drop, so sniping or mid-to-long-range engagements require quite a careful aim. Also, while H1Z1 still has a very small weapon variety even after being out for a long time, BATTLEGROUNDS has a solid amount of weapons—not just picking up whatever, but enough that you'll have fun finding the gun that fits your hands best as the match progresses. Considering it just started Early Access, this is a positive green light. There are also a handful of weapon attachments so you can set up your weapons to match your playstyle. To sum it up, unlike H1Z1 which is obsessed with peddling skins and has long since parted ways with improving gameplay, this game is helmed directly by the father of the battle royale genre. Because of that, its fundamentals are much more polished and solid than H1Z1's. Looking at its internal elements, it's safe to say it doesn't fall behind in a single area. (Ah! Well, it might have a few fewer underwear color options than H1Z1. :) ) To add information compiled from the weapon, attachment balance, and new patches released in May 2018: the difficulty of running ARs has gotten quite a bit higher compared to before. At the same time, a bunch of attachments were added, which widens the range of choices based on how you run your weapons. While this recent patch made the difficulty even higher compared to H1Z1, H1Z1 doesn't look like it can even compete with PUBG anymore, so I won't be mentioning H1Z1 in future updates. + Added user feedback (from overclasskr): I enjoy playing both games. I can't agree that H1Z1's gunplay is super easy at all. I do think H1Z1 has light, casual shooting while PUBG feels heavy. But H1Z1 has its own unique style, so calling it easy? Aiming, bullet velocity, bullet drop, leading shots—you need all of these and a lot of effort just to reach the level of a high-ranking player. [h1] PLAYERUNKNOWN's BATTLEGROUNDS is in Early Access, should I buy it? [/h1] Since it's currently in Early Access, there are a few lacking areas. I wouldn't call them major issues, but the current problems are: 1. High GPU usage even though the graphics aren't mind-blowing. In other words, it needs better optimization. The optimization isn't trash, but it's not at an acceptable level either. There are frame drops when playing in some big cities, and the performance relative to the graphics is a bit disappointing right now. However, since the first developer diary offered concrete solutions and teased patches for this, we can expect improvements here. +++++ Optimization updates after the 1.0 official release +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++ Since the official release, optimization has progressed to an acceptable level. Even with a pretty potato PC, you can run it on lowest settings without any issues. Compared to the terrible optimization during Early Access, it's a massive leap forward. If you have a GPU around the 1060 level and a CPU from the i5 onwards, you can definitely run it. 2. Server optimization is needed: You see some ignorant reviews saying, "Ah, game's unplayable cuz of server lag, gg," but that's not true. It is true that server lag happens when 96 players are connecting at the very beginning of a match, but this gets sorted out during the match lobby countdown or within a few seconds of hitting the ground. However, the ping spikes that happen very intermittently do need improvement. Considering it's made by the Korean developer Bluehole, it's a bit disappointing that ping in the Asia region is somewhat high. (Though it doesn't stop you from playing.) 3. Minor bugs exist: There are no game-breaking bugs that stop you from playing. The game is so stable you wouldn't believe it's an alpha version, but a few minor bugs stand out. Typically: 1) A bug where you make hit sounds and scare yourself even though you weren't hit and your HP didn't drop. 2) A bug where the UI doesn't pop up when you need to return to the main menu after a round ends (you have to force-quit the game). These need fixing. [h1] PLAYERUNKNOWN's BATTLEGROUNDS Review Summary (Written Mar 27, 2017, Updated Feb 2018) [/h1] PLAYERUNKNOWN's BATTLEGROUNDS has solid enough fundamentals that they could slap his nickname on the title and release it. The minor details inside the game show just how much preparation went into Early Access. The tension and fun of the battle royale genre itself are rock solid, and I'd say they've elevated the game's quality a notch higher by properly mixing in heavier, semi-hardcore elements. If you enjoyed H1Z1, this is a game worth buying and playing, and in my personal opinion, you'll enjoy it wayyyyy more. translation_en: Because of the nature of the game, it gets compared to H1Z1 a lot, and I even saw some ignorant people claiming this game ripped off H1Z1. I couldn't just let that slide, so I'm writing a Steam review for the very first time. According to a developer, 'Brendan Greene', the creative director of the Korean game company 'Bluehole Studio' that made PUBG, is the creator of the Battle Royale mode, having first created it in Arma 2. Back in the day, H1Z1 only had a survival mode, but seeing how popular the Arma Battle Royale was, they signed a licensing deal with Brendan Greene, which gave birth to the current H1Z1 title, 'KING OF THE KILL'. Early on, H1Z1 KING OF THE KILL even featured "PLAYERUNKNOWN", the pseudonym of Bluehole's creative director. By the way, the full name of this game is PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS. It's kind of like how "Tom Clancy" is attached to titles like "Tom Clancy's" The Division or "Tom Clancy's" Rainbow Six. In other words, this game is a superior version of H1Z1. Comparing it to FPS games, if you want to keep enjoying a casual Battle Royale like Sudden Attack, you can stick with H1Z1. But if you want to experience a realistic and weighty Battle Royale mode like Battlefield or Arma, you should buy this game right now. Plus, since this game is made by the creator of the Battle Royale mode, it can be updated without being restricted by licensing issues, giving it infinite potential for development compared to H1Z1, which was made through a licensing contract. Evaluating the in-game aspects, the massive graphical leap compared to H1Z1 is the first thing that stands out. You can tell they put a lot of effort into the sound, especially: differences in footsteps depending on the terrain, echoes indoors, the sound of bullets whizzing past, ricochet sounds, unique gunshot sounds for each weapon, the sound of casings dropping when reloading (I was blown away by this), realistic vehicle engine noises, and so on. If you play this game with a headset or earphones, the fun is doubled. However, that doesn't make it a flawless game with only pros. Even though it's Early Access, the poor optimization (you aren't even guaranteed 60 FPS with a GTX 1070; the frame rate is unstable) is definitely one of the issues this game needs to solve first. On the flip side, the director guaranteed that optimization, above all else, would be his top priority to fix, and during the 1 month of closed beta tests, optimization visibly improved week by week, so it seems worth trusting and keeping an eye on for a while.

Put the milk in a pot along with the cinnamon stick and vanilla over medium-high heat. As soon as it starts to boil, remove from heat, cover the pot and let it cool and infuse for about 30 minutes. The goal of infusing it is so it picks up way more flavor than if we remove the sticks right away. Let's prepare the caramel: Put the sugar in a small frying pan or saucepan over medium heat, along with the 4 tablespoons of water and the lemon juice. Stir a bit with a metal spoon so it starts to dissolve (caramel gets so hot that the ideal thing is to use metal tools). Take out the spoon (leave it resting in a bowl or similar), and wait without stirring until the caramel starts to turn golden. Take it off the heat and be very careful, do not touch it at all because it is at a ridiculously high temperature and can cause severe burns, sorry but you won't be able to taste-test it like I usually recommend with everything. Heat the 40 ml of water in the microwave practically until it boils and pour it little by little into your caramel and stir it with a spoon. The goal is to get a caramel that doesn't harden even in the fridge when we let the flans rest, so if you see that it hardens in the saucepan, try adding more hot water until it stays fluid. Pour the caramel into the 6 molds. In a bowl, crack the 4 whole eggs, and for the other two yolks we need, crack the two eggs in another bowl letting the egg white out and the yolk straight into the rest of the eggs. Heat the oven to 160ºC with top and bottom heat and place an oven rack in the middle where we'll later put the tray with the flans. Beat the 4 whole eggs along with the 2 yolks and the sugar for the flan with a whisk until the mixture is smooth, but don't overbeat it so there isn't too much foam. Strain the milk and pour it into the bowl with the eggs and sugar and mix it all together. Pour the mixture into the molds and place them on a deep oven tray. Fill the tray with water until it covers the molds halfway and put it in the oven at the middle height. Let it cook in a water bath in the oven for about 45 minutes. Take them out of the oven, and when they've cooled down, put them in the fridge and let them chill for about 3-4 hours.

Countless times, my best friend and I pulled all-nighters until 3 or 4 in the morning, blindly rushing B together only to die to an AWP. I still remember how our favorite thing was to buy Bizon submachine guns and rat in A site on Dust II. I'd tell everyone that we were the most in-sync Bizon warriors. Even when we got tilted out of our minds getting tased on Nuke, we'd reset our mentalities just in time to queue up for the next match. When we were winning, we’d do challenges you couldn't possibly dream up unless you had severe brain damage, like knifing five chickens and then getting three kills with a pistol. When we were losing, we'd encourage each other or just hurl abuse at each other. Even after blaming each other and taking a ten-minute break, we could still keep playing. Four or five years ago, when we went on massive losing streaks, we’d write "breakup letters," but the breakup never lasted more than 3 hours. Our story is too long, impossible to fully express our deep friendship in just a few words. But at 2:17 AM on September 17th, Beijing time, you called me. You told me a lot of things, but I just cursed you out, yelling at you asking if you were out of your mind for calling me at 2 AM. September 17th, 8:43 AM. I got a call from your mom. She told me you were gone. I didn't believe it. This had to be fake, you were just pranking me. 1:34 PM. I had already called you on voice chat 30 times. You didn't pick up a single one. At 8:33 PM, I stood by the riverbank, staring off into the distance in silence for a long time. I went to the snack street we always went to, and bought your favorite grilled starch sausages. Just like something out of a script, the boss asked me where the tall guy who used to come with me was. I stayed silent. I bought two sausages. I ate one, and left the other behind. Before this, you came across a video about the death of a friend or family member. We used to joke that whoever goes first, the other will eat the most at their funeral. But tomorrow is your funeral. I'm sorry, I don't dare to go. I'm too much of a coward, I don't dare to see you. I'm afraid you'd make fun of me. I guess our friendship has come to an end. I remember when you were dating someone, you spent 600 on a meal to treat someone and they called you poor. I spent 200 treating you to three meals and a bunch of snacks, and you called me Daddy. Now I've accepted the fact that you've left me. I’ve watched Coco three times, and now I finally get it. Death isn't the end, being forgotten is.

translation_en: [h1] So fucking great. [/h1] Under the "perfect" blessing of CS2's subtick, latency issues are magnified infinitely. The issue of asymmetrical player perspectives—already quite noticeable in CSGO—truly shines in all its glory in CS2. In the players' eyes, everyone can transform into a steamroller running people over without ever letting go of the W key, completely ditching counter-strafing, while all covers and walls are utterly useless in the face of lag. In this update, players need to constantly calculate and compensate based on their own ping and the opponent's ping, just to accurately predict the enemy's actual position on the server during a firefight and adjust their shots, while praying that their own bullets get registered by the server a split second sooner to save their pathetic lives—just like in those games where you have to lead your shots, predict movement, and factor in bullet travel time.[i][u] Even if your ping is only 10 and the opponent's is only 8, it doesn't change the fact that you still have to predict this tiny little variable—you even have to make even more precise predictive adjustments for where the enemy "actually" might be, while your reaction window is made even shorter. Doesn't that sound just fucking fantastic? [/u][/i] I gotta say, CS2 is truly amazing, raising the realism of a competitive game to heights that no other game can ever hope to reach. Other games only simulate realism within the game code, [u][b]whereas in CS2, the "sense of realism" brought by needing to predict due to network latency directly impacts everything within the match from outside the game [/b][/u]. It's a major, industry-shaping, truly trans-generational innovation! No other game company has ever achieved such fucking awesome realism. The "sniping realism" of Sniper Elite is worthless by comparison, and the so-called "hardcore" nature of Escape from Tarkov pes in comparison. All those pre-programmed realistic prediction mechanics in other games are just game mechanics, but the "realism" mechanic of our CS2—that is thoroughly tangible reality! [h3] Utilizing the impact of real-world network latency to simulate the mechanics of predicting bullet drop and enemy positioning in the game—isn't that way more realistic than other games that just rely on code to simulate so-called realism? [/h3] As expected of Valve, who emphasized right when they dropped the CS2 promotional video: [h2] "CS is a realistic competitive game" [/h2] [h3] This split-second of "tangible lag" can instantly decide the life or death of every player—isn't this precisely that hair-trigger tension of a real battlefield? [/h3] Anyone who ever says CS isn't realistic enough from now on, I'm gonna teach them a proper lesson. You can say any past CS game isn't realistic enough, but you can't say CS2 isn't realistic. [h2] Real-world phenomena being able to tangibly and precisely affect everything that happens in the game—isn't that the most "real" "realism" of all? [/h2] [spoiler]You better fucking be happy.jpg[/spoiler] [spoiler]Thanks a fucking lot, CS2.[/spoiler] PS: By the way, [b][u]remember to adjust your graphic settings like resolution first before adjusting your screen refresh rate[/u][/b], otherwise every time you change the resolution, your refresh rate will automatically reset to 60hz by default. [i][u]Just imagine enduring 60hz screen tearing while watching yourself stutter and teleport around like Rayquaza, only to watch others with zero ping run-and-gun headshot you (without wallbanging) and kill you behind cover, right down to the death cam animation being completely torn apart[/u][/u] — this kind of "unprecedented" experience is truly exclusive to CS2.

translation_en: Never again. The game that witnessed my youth. From figuring it out all by myself, to classmates nearby, good brothers from all over the country online, and childhood playmates—even in a new environment you could still find all sorts of topics related to CS. 2212.6 hours. You clearly could have used this time to study hard and top the exams, go to the gym to build an aesthetic physique and pick up chicks, chase the girl you liked like a total simp, or even work a part-time job and save up a decent chunk of change. But you resolutely chose to play CS:GO, pulling all-nighters with the bros, fully locked in. Staring at the screen, sometimes grinning like an idiot, sometimes fully focused and tense, yet you don't regret a single second of those 2,000+ hours. To you, CS:GO was the best game in the world! From when Danger Zone first dropped back in 2018, you slowly opened that unfamiliar "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive" icon on your older brother's PC, stumbling and fumbling your way across this new continent, starting out slowly with bots; rushing home from school in 2019 to open Casual immediately and playing every day until your mom got furious; 2020 when the pandemic was spreading and everyone was panicking—for you, that was the best time, grinding CS:GO 25 hours a day, and you started making many friends through the game, real-life classmates, and online bros who were closer than actual brothers; going back to school in 2021 meant you had less time to play, but you'd still skip breakfast to save up for a 1,700 RMB Ultraviolet Butterfly Knife, adding a new skin every week. On days you couldn't play at school, you and your classmates played LAN CS 1.6 on the ancient school PCs in the computer lab. Unfamiliar yet familiar, you never got tired of it. On weekend nights, you'd queue up on schedule with a few regular bros you'd been playing with for a long time, hopping on voice chat to watch matches together. You'd often bottom-frag, tilt, and talk trash. When a female classmate you liked needed to borrow money to make a dream come true, you decisively sold off your expensive skins, getting nothing in return but the label of a clown. Your friends made fun of you for it, but it was still your favorite era. Come 2022, you and those regular bros had less time to play together. Someone mentioned "companionship is only for a certain stage," and you brushed it off, but you'd still queue up together from time to time. Now in 2023, you're in college, with a broader perspective, more social connections, and a girlfriend. Your energy for CS:GO is slowly fading. You've faced many problems: a warped market, the girl you like not understanding the game you love, good bros gradually losing touch, your own skill dropping off. You've started avoiding CS, but you'd still occasionally open the game up for a match, only to realize this game has already become a part of your life, and CS:GO is ushering in its continuation—CS2. Everyone said tonight would be CSGO's final night. You played a simple matchmaking game on Inferno, your most familiar map, and figured that was enough. Yet when you look back, the good bros have either moved on to Valorant or quit the game; some found new queue partners and grinded to Supreme/Global, while you're still stuck in the stinky B+. Looking at DMA cheaters everywhere, prodigies, smurfs, the expensive and warped market, and TikTok clickbait streamer kids who've never even played the game—you feel so powerless to protect this purest passion. That's when you remember: back then, it all just felt like ordinary days. You will never again have those beautiful times like you did with your good bros. You have to admit, you love this game; it has already become a part of you. It's a story, it's youth, an end, yet also a beginning. Goodbye, CS:GO. You don't know how much longer you'll be able to play this game, but whenever you think of it, you'll be reminded of every little detail of your youth, these people, and those events. Perhaps, that is the most precious thing of all.

translation_en: [h1]It's the early morning of September 28, 2023. CS:GO is coming to an end, and CS2 is about to drop.[/h1] I'm sitting at my PC, thinking about what I should say right now, but I type and delete, delete and type. "One Last Kiss" is looping in my headphones, and a bunch of things flash through my mind. When I try to think about them properly, I can't quite remember, leaving this hazy feeling. I try to ask myself: [b]Why did I first open CS:GO?[/b] ————A friend recommended it. I played CS:GO for the first time at an internet cafe. [b]How were these 1,018 hours in CS:GO spent? Did it make you waste your time?[/b] ————I could've used these thousand-plus hours for a lot of things: learning something I've always wanted to learn, spending more time with friends and family. But I played CS:GO instead. In CS:GO, I made a lot of friends. I used to grind maps and utility until I forgot to eat and sleep. I've had ace highlights, pulled off clutch comebacks by myself, tasted the misery of griefing teammates, and dealt with the annoyance of losing streaks from time to time...... Anyway, I feel like this was a very meaningful period of time, not a waste. Of course, looking at how much time I spent, I still think it's a bit of a pity. But if you gave me another chance, I guess I'd still resolutely choose CS:GO. [b]Did playing CS:GO actually make you happy?[/b] ————Even now, I can't really say whether playing CS:GO counts as happy: at the very beginning, playing with friends and knowing nothing, I'd get mad because I couldn't get kills; once I actually started getting the hang of it, I'd get mad because the teammates I got matched with sometimes weren't human; nowadays I just play for the sake of playing, I don't practice my aim anymore, and the last time I opened CS:GO was almost a month ago. It seems like as long as I play this game, getting pissed off is inevitable, but I'll still fire it up and play again and again. [b]Do you really like CS:GO?[/b] ————I wouldn't say I love it, nor would I say I hate it. Even though I prefer single-player games and aren't really down for multiplayer games, in my heart, no game compares to CS:GO. Beyond the game itself, I love everything related to CS:GO—like cool gun skins, pro players with great personalities. I'd get happy over getting a new skin today, feel smug when my favorite team G2 won, and I've got a habit of checking CS:GO pro scene news and tutorial videos daily. Just like going to school or work, CS:GO has become a part of my life. Even though I don't really like the game itself, the experience of playing CS:GO is still an extremely special memory that I'll never forget. I don't know if staying up late here thinking about all this is any use, and I keep reminding myself I've got study and work tomorrow and need to sleep early. But I also feel like this is a summary of this chapter of my experience, of my life. I really cherish the game CS:GO, and I should give it a proper, decent goodbye as it leaves. Actually, no need to stress about tomorrow either; besides studying and working, there's the new CS2 to chill and play. [h1][b]CS:GO, I love you more than I'll ever know.[/b][/h1] [h1][b]Goodbye, CS:GO.[/b][/h1]

translation_en: Back in my freshman year of college in 2020, following the Rush B trend, I bought a laptop and downloaded Steam. You could say it was the first game on my Steam account. At first, I didn't play on any third-party platforms, just messing around and laughing with strangers in casual mode—sometimes using the Zeus, sometimes the P90. Back then I couldn't move for shit, didn't know how to counter-strafe, and had zero utility knowledge. I played straight through the National Day holiday, eventually got my service medal, and started buying cheap skins on Buff using my phone. I remember spending 2 bucks on an AK-47 Safari Mesh; that was my first skin. Later, following some dude in my class, I started playing on 5E and FACEIT/Perfect World. Slowly, I learned some basic utility, though my movement, counter-strafing, and spray control were still garbage. I started watching streamers like JZFB, Donggua, and Lao X. Actually, I watched Lao X the most; I only watched Donggua to learn how to swear. I almost forgot to mention buying a knife. I didn't know much about skins back then, so I bought a Huntsman Knife Forest DDPAT for a little over 500 RMB. Later, saving up bit by bit, I moved on to a Bayonet, a Talon, and a Ursus. Around that time, I bound jump to the scroll wheel and messed with my viewmodel settings. I grinded in Perfect World C+ for a couple of seasons, then made it to A. My playstyle gradually got more aggressive, and the competitive drive started taking over—I started flaming my teammates. Once I hit A rank, my average damage was around 90, and my rating was about 1.2. Later on, I felt like skins were whatever, mostly just renting them to mess around with, so I sold off my entire inventory. Sometimes I'd drop back down to C+ just to chill and smash some noobs. My friends gradually lost their competitive drive too, and hitting S rank didn't seem that important anymore. Oh yeah, I forgot to mention—since the laptop I bought back then was only 60Hz, I ended up buying a GPW2, a PC, a keyboard, a 165Hz high-refresh monitor piece by piece, and later upgraded to 380Hz. I've got over 1,600 hours on it now. My FPS journey actually started back when I was in the first grade of elementary school at my childhood friend's place in Chongqing. Back then, it was 2008, the era of CrossFire and DNF. I really miss those times. Three or four of us crammed around one computer desk, heads bumping together just trying to get a good view of the screen. Back then, it was two lives each in knife fights or sniper battles. I remember someone shouting, "You guys get two lives, I get three because it's my computer!" When I played Zombie mode, that transformation sound was so terrifying that I'd be scared walking home alone at 11 or 12 at night. Thinking back, it's pretty funny. Now, PC specs keep getting better and there are more games than ever, but friends have less and less time to play. It feels like I can never get back that initial, most carefree, burden-free time. I'll be turning 22 after Chinese New Year—will I still have time to play a match with friends in the future? Will my friends even have time to show up? As an FPS gamer, I sincerely hope everyone can truly enjoy these times. Gaming has somehow become an indispensable part of many of our lives. Even though it's hated by many parents and criticized by society, I feel like it's a precious gift that somehow makes up for an incomplete childhood. I don't even know if this is because CS2 dropped, but either way, consider this the review I finally owe to this game. Youth doesn't last forever, so don't grudge the money for drinks by the bed.

I just knew that when a match ended, you'd drop cases, graffiti, and skins, and bit by bit I started understanding the maps. Back then I was also mute, playing without a mic. I remember our squad name: the Crayon Shin-chan squad, playing together the whole winter break. Homework didn't matter to me anymore because I had people to play games with. There was this snow map where we challenged ourselves to finish the match using only Deagles, and we did it. That was also my very first challenge in CS:GO. We played official matchmaking every day, but... Laoye went to high school and rarely played with us anymore. Xituo had to focus on his studies and classes, so we rarely played together either. That long heartfelt message that was super popular early that year, I wrote it to my internet friends. I poured my heart out, writing a full wall of text to them. My real-life insecurity and low self-esteem—in front of them, I could show confidence and be totally open. In the summer of 2022, my mental illness... well, you could also say it was because of two of my internet friends, we started playing together less and less. Last online 7 weeks ago. Last online 7 months ago. Jiaxin and Luan brought their classmates into the group for me to meet: Liu, Xu. We played CS:GO Prop Hunt until we knew it by heart. Our whole group played together every day. By 2023, a lot of the fun from back in the day was gone. I only cared about improving my match stats. My slump lasted more than a just day or two; I didn't touch my PC for a whole month. Back then I treated my PC with a 960 graphics card like an absolute treasure, playing with internet friends all day long. Now I've got a PC setup worth tens of thousands, yet very few games actually interest me. Lethargic, combined with taking meds every day since last year. This game is a pretty damn good memory from my youth. I met a lot of people, it was my escape from reality, and it's the competitive game I've played the longest.

translation_en: Today when I opened the game, I glanced at my playtime and realized I've somehow hit a neat and exact 1,000 hours in CS:GO. Of course, my history with the CS series goes well beyond 1,000 hours. [spoiler](Come to think of it, CS:GO even shares the exact same birthday as me.)[/spoiler] My very first exposure to CS was back around 2010 at a friend's place. Back then, the graphics of 1.6 already looked super realistic to me, and compared to all those side-scrolling 2D or top-down 3D games, the first-person perspective was practically unbeatable for immersion. The various weapon stats and data in the buy menu felt like opening the door to a world of military hardware. The workshop maps with all their diverse, culturally and naturally rich designs also sparked endless daydreams about their real-world inspirations—scenery from all over the globe. After '09, CF became huge, and CS—which I had almost forgotten about—came back into view through the online version, CSOL. Compared to the original, it added a bunch of awesome modes and well-crafted story maps. [spoiler]During those years when Zombie Scenario was popping off, it even sparked a trend among classmates to write fan-fic "novels."[/spoiler] CF and CSOL were in fierce competition back then, and my gaming friends were "taking sides," accusing each other of "cloning," and arguing over which game was better. These so-called "arguments" didn't make our bonds worse; if anything, they made our friendship stronger. After some heated trash-talk, we'd just keep laughing and fighting together across both games. Around 2015 or 2016, thanks to the hype around MSG/KZ and hide-and-seek, I accidentally noticed CSGO, which was just starting to take off. Back then, playing this game before the Perfect World server existed meant using a US Visa card on Steam to buy it, though I honestly forget how I finally managed to sort out my account. [spoiler](It was my very first Steam game too 🤣)[spoiler] I only remember that shortly after getting my account sorted, I witnessed a historic moment for CN CS:GO. TyLoo, who had been silent for so long, used a brand-new playstyle—[spoiler]Rush B / Ganla[/spoiler] "urban management squad" style—to pull off upset after upset, beating the world #2 Liquid (featuring s1mple) and world #1 LG, before narrowly losing to NAVI, making a massive splash on the world stage. [spoiler](What's pretty funny is that TyLoo's English name lets foreigners pronounce it something close to the Chinese "Tailu".)[/spoiler] Soon after, CN CS also ushered in its own spring: the Perfect World national server launched, professional clubs and teams popped up like bamboo shoots after a spring rain, and domestic teams TyLoo, Flash, and VG each secured three team stickers. At that time, the international scene was also a free-for-all: the three-time major champion cosmic squad fnatic, the Golden Five betting steamrollers VP, the international homies overlords SK, the galactic battleship old-man-fun FAZE Clan... they all had distinct personalities and it was a hundred flowers blooming. CS back then had a charm kind of like soccer; aside from the exquisite performances on the server, the behind-the-scenes gossip about the players was also deeply nostalgic and moving. More than just watching others play and perform, the fun I got from gaming with my friends myself was 100% real. Playing cat-and-mouse with the computer teacher during IT class, running 1.6 competitive matches and CSOL solo bot biohazard with classmates. Back when I first started playing GO, I was grinding aim practice with my buddies on a shitbox PC [spoiler]one frame for smooth play, two frames for esports[/spoiler], learning utility, and running some basic strays [spoiler]like throwing two mollies for a spicy barbecue on Banana, or quick-pop flashes on Banana. Basically all Banana stuff (not really)[spoiler], and the sense of accomplishment and joy from that was incomparable. Five-man queues in the dorm, appreciating each other's brain-dead plays. My most memorable ace has got to be the time I clutched out the round for the whole team with a Desert Eagle on A-Site. Playing Operation missions with newly joined friends, only to get completely disoriented by countless flashbangs and getting utterly farmed by endless bots. These gaming experiences were nothing short of a great remedy against the heavy pressures of those times. After 2020, my focus shifted more toward life and work. Tides rise and fall both inside and outside the game, changing with each passing day. Looking back, it’s already become one of the most important vessels for holding onto friendship and the passion I once poured into it.

translation_en: I'm an older man, 57 years old. Unfortunately I had to face the worst pain a father can suffer: the loss of my son in a traffic accident. After that fucking event, my life became a sea of loneliness. My wife left us years ago and now I only had my grandson, a ten-year-old kid. At first we didn't understand each other, it was constant fights and arguments, but it was in the middle of that storm that we discovered csgo. My grandson taught me how to play it, and what started as a simple distraction became a window to escape our pain. Playing that little shooting game with my grandson became more than just a simple hobby. It was a ticket that helped us rebuild our bond, to find moments of happiness in the middle of uncertainty. Together, we laughed our asses off, shared stories and felt less alone. In this virtual world, my grandson and I found a refuge where the memory of his old man, my son, didn't hit us as hard. We'd dive into the shootings in the desert, as a symbol of our unity and strength in the face of adversity. It was as if every brick fit with our emotions, and through that creation, we found mutual comfort. Sometimes, while we were playing, a quiet tear would slip from my grandson's eye. And in those moments, I would hug him, reminding him that we weren't alone, that we would always be right next to each other to face any challenge that life threw at us. So, dear friends, csgo became more than just a video game for us. It's a tool that helps us heal, to find a little peace in the middle of uncertainty. It teaches us that, even in the virtual world, you can build bridges toward love and hope. I thank you for giving me this space to share our story. And to those who are going through difficult times, I tell you to never underestimate the power of a game, of a simple virtual connection. Sometimes, it can bring comfort, company and, above all, a reminder that you are never alone. Hugs

Bigos recipe: Bigos 3 kg sauerkraut 20 dag pork fat 50 dag pork neck 50 dag beef cutlet meat 30 dag regular sausage 20 dag smoked bacon 5 dried mushrooms tomato paste sweet paprika powder 1 heaped tablespoon majoram allspice bay leaf 4 large onions Boil the sauerkraut twice in a big pot, drain the water. translation_en: Borscht is the cultural heritage of Ukraine, our pride, and the culinary symbol of our country. Remaining indifferent to this thick, rich soup is simply impossible. There are countless recipes for borscht, and almost every housewife has her own. Some like borscht with beans, some cook it without cabbage, and some make it with mushrooms. Quite often, borscht recipes are carefully passed down from generation to generation in families, and some are even kept strictly secret. Classic Ukrainian borscht Water – 1.5-2 l. pork or beef on the bone – 400 g potatoes – 4 pcs. (medium) beets – 2 pcs. (small) carrot – 1 pc. onion – 3 pcs. (medium) fresh white cabbage – 300 g tomato paste – 2 tbsp. l. sunflower oil – 4-5 tbsp. l. citric acid – a pinch salt, bay leaf, herbs – to taste. First, we cook the broth. Pour 1.5-2 liters of water into a pot. Add the meat and put it on medium heat. Skim off the foam before it boils. As soon as the broth boils, cover with a lid and simmer on low heat for an hour to an hour and a half. Meanwhile, we prepare the base (zasmazhka). Peel the beets, carrots, and onions. Grate the beets on a coarse grater, and the carrots on a medium one. Dice the onions. Heat oil in a frying pan over medium heat, toss in the onions and carrots, and fry for 5 minutes. Then add the beets (you can sprinkle them with citric acid or drizzle with fresh lemon juice – this way the borscht will be truly red). Fry the vegetables for another 5 minutes, add tomato paste, mix, and fry everything for another 5-7 minutes. And now we cook the borscht itself. Take the meat out of the broth and, while it cools, throw the shredded cabbage into the broth. After 5-10 minutes, add the julienned potatoes. Separate the meat from the bone and dice it. Return the meat to the borscht, salt it, and add the zasmazhka. Mix the borscht, add the bay leaf and finely chopped herbs, cover with a lid and cook for another 5-7 minutes. Serve borscht with sour cream and herbs.

translation_en: Cherry Vareniki INGREDIENTS For the dough: 500 g flour (plus extra for kneading) 250 ml milk 1 chicken egg 1 tbsp sunflower oil ½ tsp salt For the vareniki: 400 g pitted cherries 1-2 tbsp sugar 1 tbsp semolina 1 pinch of salt STEP 1 Prepare all the ingredients for making cherry vareniki. Remove the pits from the cherries. You can also buy frozen pitted cherries and just thaw them. STEP 2 Measure out 500 g of flour and pour it into a large bowl, add ½ tsp salt, 1 chicken egg, and 1 tbsp sunflower oil. STEP 3 Then pour in 250 ml of milk. STEP 4 Knead the dough. It should turn out elastic, not sticky to the hands, and not fall apart during the cooking process. STEP 5 Add a tablespoon of semolina to the pitted cherries. The semolina will absorb the excess cherry juice, keeping the vareniki juicy without the juice leaking out when you bite into them. Also add 1 tbsp of sugar. STEP 6 Roll out the dough to a thickness of about 2-3 millimeters on a cutting board or work surface. Use a mug or a glass to cut out circles in the dough. STEP 7 Place a little filling on one edge of the circle and gently press down with the other side. Pinch the edges of the dough well so the filling doesn't leak out during boiling. Shape vareniki from all the dough circles. STEP 8 Shape vareniki from all the dough circles. Boil the vareniki in boiling water over low heat for about 3-4 minutes after they float to the surface. STEP 9 Boil the vareniki in boiling water with a pinch of salt over low heat for about 3-4 minutes after they float to the surface. Then put the hot vareniki into a bowl and sprinkle with sugar. This will add sweetness and prevent the vareniki from sticking together. Cooking is easy!

translation_en: [h1]An Undying Romance and Classic[/h1] First of all, I'm super happy to announce that I've finally graduated~! I finally solo queued to Global Elite on my 911th win. This is literally a once-in-a-lifetime moment......... T_T CS truly has an indescribable charm. Ever since I was a kid, it was one of my biggest introductions to shooter games. I remember starting with 1.6, then 1.5, and only much later did I find out there were even earlier versions like 1.2. But the most nostalgic version of the classic era for me was the one with the reverse knife grip. I was actually a bit sad when CS:GO's 20th-anniversary lazy asset flip didn't use that one. Though I guess the Bayonet is a lot more widely recognized nowadays, huh. Playing against bots as a kid, I could have an absolute blast all by myself. Cops and robbers, both sides having various operators and characters, and weapons with their own unique traits. Hearing the bots call out "affirmative" and "roger" to each other on the radio was just so immersive. Besides, what little boy doesn't like guns? I remember my favorite map was assault—the warehouse. Back then, I didn't know that many English words, but I just knew that "assault" meant *that* map, lol. I loved its ventilation ducts, the armored vehicle right next to the CT spawn, the silly hostages and the electronic sliding doors outside their room, and that little squeaky door in the warehouse you could push back and forth. Then there was the Boeing 747 map. I remember it being super dark, but the layout of the plane was so interesting. Playing in the pitch black of an unfamiliar environment was actually pretty terrifying, even with a flashlight you could turn on whenever you wanted. So whenever I played that map, I *had* to buy NVGs to have any fun, hhh. Oh, and `iceworld` plus another map whose name I forgot, the one with lava in the middle. Simple, brutal, just made for fighting, and I loved playing that too. I never got into *Condition Zero*. To this day I only know of it, haven't actually played it yet, hhh. I *did* play *Source*, though, and I super loved its graphics and physics engine. They were just amazing. I don't know why I have such a thing for ragdolls with volume and physical effects. For a while, I spent whole days blindly figuring out how to mod various weapons into my Source, "shopping" on foreign forums, especially modDB, lingering there for hours on end. Actually playing with them in-game wasn't even a quarter as fun as hunting for them, hhh. Later on, I also played various versions of *Half-Life*, which was incredible. And then I found out about *GMod*. Got totally addicted for quite a while, obsessed with finding all sorts of mods, posing ragdolls in different ways, and making up plots and stories for them based on my wild imagination. Then, *GO* showed up. I still remember how back in the early days of GO, the T's all had pure white hands—that gave it a very distinct vibe. The gunshots and weapon performance from back then have long since blurred in my memory. The most impressive thing was probably the sound of a Zeus combined with an AWP cracking like a plasma whip. When GO came out, I never would've thought we'd get to play such a high-end CS. The graphics and models were so refined, yet the gameplay remained uniquely and endlessly charming. This time, GO finally had official matchmaking like a standard client game, so naturally, I joined in. I didn't play the first few years, but it came out around 2012, and now it's been over 10 years. I've played on and off for almost 10 years now. Time really flies without you noticing. I remember when I first started playing, I was a total blank slate when it came to hardware or settings. I recall using an in-game sensitivity of a dozen or something, and a cheap-ass no-name mouse, so I was probably playing on several thousand eDPI. But sometimes I still did pretty well. For a period, I met a group of Filipino friends in matchmaking and played with them for a good half a year—that's also a very special memory. For the first few years, I bounced around Double AK and could barely make any breakthrough. Then, I don't know when it started, I wanted to push past my limits, so I went looking for all kinds of ways and knowledge to get better. I learned a lot about sensitivity, config settings, and hardware stuff, and I started doing aim practice. Slowly, I made it up to Sheriff. Through all these years, I've played on and off. Often, I'd play other games, but in the back of my mind, I never forgot to practice certain fundamentals. I played PUBG for a long time, R6 for a bit, Apex for ages, and a bunch of COD titles too. I really love competitive games, though I also play plenty of other single-player or multiplayer genres. Every now and then, I'd pick CS back up, play for a bit, feel like I hit a wall, and put it down again. This repeated many times. Until recently—I've been super busy lately, rarely playing games, and not even enjoying them as much as before. I prefer to spend my free time on other hobbies. But the last couple of days I had more free time, so I just fired something up to play casually, and I never expected to hit Global Elite just like that, hahahaha. My placement rank immediately put me at Supreme Master First Class! I remember the last time I had a rank, I was only a Sheriff, so I honestly didn't expect to place so high. Then I went on a smooth win streak for a few games, and before I knew it, I ranked up to Global Elite. That instantly reignited my passion—I was just one step away from Global Elite! This is the highest rank I'd dreamed of getting years ago. Back then, the highest I could reach solo queueing was Supreme, and anything higher was just hitching a ride to Global with transient stack buddies. I had never actually hit Global on my own before. So for the past few days, it's just been grind, grind, grind. Endless aim training, learning new aiming concepts and principles, trying to fix and strengthen the weak spots in my plateaued mechanics. There were wins, losses, and moments of getting completely rolled into the dirt by high-tech animals. Usually, I'd perform well in the early rounds, but as the game went on and my form dropped, my leaderboard placement would slide to the middle or even dead last....... In every post-match screen after that, I watched the ranks of both teams creep closer to the very top—either Supremes or Globals. I could feel my Elo rating was right on the threshold, and my excitement grew more and more. Every single win had me anticipating that crisp "clink" rank-up sound effect, hhh. But sometimes I didn't want it to happen *that* match, because ranking up without utterly dominating first somehow felt a bit less satisfying, hhh. And then, amidst the ups and downs, during one particular post-match screen, the *clink* sound effect and animation suddenly flashed on screen. On my 911th win, I finally achieved the highest rank I had dreamed of many, many years ago: Global Elite. And whether the system just pitied me this time or not, it gave me opponents and teammates with low enough ranks that I actually managed to pull off this promotion while completely dominating the lobby. Right at that moment, I was genuinely happy. But I knew this feeling wouldn't last long; emptiness would be waiting for me soon enough. High-tier joy doesn't come from this. But at least I finally made it here, and looking back on it from time to time will still make me happy, hhh :) CS will always have its indescribable charm, and Valve will always find a way to create interesting things. I used to always complain about GabeN: how come he's making so much bank and not putting out any new games? And just like that, right as you're talking, he drops a game-changing VR headset and *Half-Life: Alyx*. Just like that, right as you're talking, he drops a high-performance, highly compatible handheld console. So Valve isn't slacking off; they're always biding their time, ready to astound the world in a single move! I love CS. I love Valve~~~

translation_en: When it comes to competitive shooters, CS:GO has pushed the genre to its absolute limit, leaving later games with no choice but to either take inspiration or pivot to battle royale. Its hyper-competitiveness also creates a steep barrier to entry. If you don't sink hundreds or even thousands of hours into hardcore studying, you'll just reap endless frustration and failure in matchmaking. After 600-plus hours, the cost of going any deeper is just too high. I know that if I want to rank up further, I have to study maps and refine my aim, but I just don't have that kind of time and energy to burn. It forces you to rethink what gaming is all about. Why did we start playing in the first place? Maybe what we really need is just an outlet to blow off some steam, a place to chill and chat with others. That's why I like non-prime casual—everyone's just messing around and chatting, purely to unwind, win or lose. High-intensity sweatfests are just draining. You gonna grind aim maps for hundreds or thousands of hours just to see some stupid rank number go up? That definitely wasn't why I started gaming. Maybe what we actually need is just a place to connect and chill, and it doesn't even have to be a specific game, it could be anything. And just like that, thinking back to when I was a kid playing Plants vs. Zombies, I decided to sell my CS:GO skins and quit for good.

To make the charlotte we will need 4 small apples, it's better to choose sour varieties. Peel the apples from stems and seeds, slice them thin. 2.To make the dough, sift the flour with baking powder. Set aside for a moment. 3.Crack chilled chicken eggs into a deep bowl and beat with a mixer, gradually increasing the speed. Add granulated sugar. It's best to flip the warm charlotte onto a wire rack and let it cool, this way the cake will turn out more even. 8.Using a fine sieve, dust the finished fluffy charlotte with powdered sugar and, cut into portions, serve. 9.Homemade apple charlotte will be a wonderful addition to evening tea time with the family. translation_en: I'm not a professional reviewer, but I can help you make and cook French onion soup. Ingredients: 1 kg regular onions - 5 large onions 80 g clarified butter - just under half a block 3/4 cup dry white wine 500 ml beef broth 5 medium cloves of garlic herbs and spices: a teaspoon of thyme, half a teaspoon each of salt and pepper, a flat teaspoon of sugar, 2 bay leaves Crouton ingredients: half a long wheat baguette 2 tablespoons of mild olive oil 50 g Gruyère cheese or another Parmesan-type cheese I'd recommend you use a 250ml glass I also added broth to the onion soup Soup: 1. Prepare the onion soup in a single vessel, preferably a thick-bottomed pan. Put about 80 g of clarified butter in the vessel. Wait for the butter to melt and heat up. 2. Add the peeled and sliced onions to the butter. During caramelization, the onion shrinks a lot and becomes super soft. 3. Set the burner to medium power and fry the onions for about 20 minutes. Stir every 3-4 minutes with a wooden spoon. And so for 20 minutes. 4. After about 20 minutes, the onion will brown, release more liquid, and shrink further. Add ♥♥♥♥♥♥ [if you write "pe.pper" it censors you XD] as well as the garlic pressed through a garlic press and the thyme. If you have fresh thyme, use it instead of dried. Mix the onion and continue frying, not forgetting to stir it in the pot. 5. After 10 minutes, pour in 3/4 cup of dry white wine. Reach for a good wine with a deep flavor. You can replace the white wine with Vermouth, which is a flavored wine. It additionally contains herbs and spices. Vermouth is often sweetened with sugar or caramelized sugar (for color). 6. Finally, pour in at least another 500 ml (two glasses) of rich beef broth. With this amount of broth, the soup will be quite thick. So you can pour more broth... as you prefer. Generally, beef and vegetable broth is best for onion soup. However, if you only have chicken broth or only vegetable broth, you can use it. Beef and chicken broth works great. It is very important that it is a rich stock. 7. Finally, cover the pot with a lid and cook the onion soup for the last 30 minutes on low burner power. The soup should only gently simmer. After the last 30 minutes of cooking, the onion soup is ready. You can serve it immediately, or after cooling, put it in the fridge and serve 2-3 days after cooking. However, it is most delicious baked with croutons. Croutons: 1. Cut the long wheat baguette crosswise into thin slices. Spread each slice on both sides with mild olive oil. Heat a large, thick-bottomed pan. Place the pieces of baguette on the heated pan and toast until golden brown on both sides. 2. Pour the onion soup into a convenient baking dish. I recommend cast-iron pans and pots. 3. Place the croutons in the dish with the soup, and grate Gruyère cheese on a coarse grater. Swiss cheese is very tasty and super healthy. It's a cheese made from cow's milk with a delicate, slightly nutty flavor. translation_en: I know I've got nearly 3000 hours in this game, but unfortunately I have to leave a negative review. Let me start with when I started playing CS. I started playing when it was more popular, back in 2015, and back then the game was genuinely evolving. Meeting a cheater was like finding a needle in a haystack. The later you played, the worse it got; the devs successfully fucked up literally everything. First off, they started changing maps to be even worse than they were before, but that's a minor detail. At the end of 2018, everyone who bought CS got slapped right in the face because the game went fucking free-to-play. And why? Because the game was starting to die and started attracting a horde of cheaters and smurfs. Overwatch stopped being cool and appealing because every single overwatch case is just some dude spinning on a spinbot like shit swirling down a flushing toilet. People without prime shouldn't even bother launching the game without cheats, because you won't get a normal match. And even if you buy prime, you still won't get one because you'll immediately run into a little smurf or a cheater who bought prime and 30 PLN cheats and is rubbing his hands together thinking he's a god at the game. The anti-cheat is a masterclass in utter bullshit; ever since the anti-cheat was created, absolutely nothing has changed—COMPLETELY NOTHING. For the people who bought CS before it went free-to-play in 2018, the devs gave us cases and blue skins worth a 5 PLN candy bar at Biedronka just to show how much they don't give a fuck about us. You can't even play the battle royale mode either, because as soon as you load in, some guy has a spinbot and starts blasting you. I don't know what kind of brain-dead idiot you have to be to cheat in that mode. It's 2022 and now we're reaching a whole new level of retardation. Updates started rolling out where the AWP has 5 bullets instead of 10. How the fuck can an AWP have 5 bullets, for Christ's sake, that's completely unrealistic. Then they decided that—well, people say the M4A1-S is too OP—so the devs decided to fuck that gun up so badly that now you can't hit anyone at a distance because they ruined the long-range damage. The rank system this year is one big fucking joke; you win 12 matches and don't rank up, but the moment you lose 3 matches you derank, and to get back to the rank you had you have to get so fucking tilted trying to do it. If you don't have a premade squad, it's not worth playing because every match has Russians screaming their lungs out and making it impossible to play, and getting info in this game is rule number one. I forgot to mention that reports don't do shit against cheaters, so it's not even worth reporting them, total waste of time. Gaming belongs to the ninth art. Any major masterpiece game inherently contains the thoughts and philosophy of its creator. But given our country's currently closed-off values, foreign reflections on the future and their bizarre, numerous fantasies simply cannot be accepted by the SARFT. As for domestic games right now—factoring in STEAM and consoles—you can still make a ton of cash just by making absolute trash. Their social, economic, political, and cultural systems are all different from the mainland. So has everyone ever thought about why it's like this? Actually, it's very simple: the crying baby gets the milk. Take Hong Kong for example: if back at the 97 handover it had been the mainland system, they would have gone on massive strikes and student walkouts, making society unable to function normally. And at the time, many eyes both domestic and international were watching Hong Kong, so they became a Special Administrative Region. And what about us mainlanders? When they blocked the foreign internet, we endured it. When they censored World of Warcraft, we endured that too. We've never raised our voices for our own rights and interests. And now they're escalating things—even the China version of STEAM is about to come out. The best-case scenario is that a China-version store comes out, and the existing national server's payment methods and regional pricing discounts get transferred over to it. If we silently endure this time, what about after this? I'm afraid we're going to turn into the North Korean Kwangmyong network. A lot of people treat these things as only natural, whether it's blocking the foreign internet, censoring games, Top Funny Media, or now the China version of STEAM. But the reality? In Europe, there are terrorists operating on Instagram and Twitter. Did they simply build a firewall and block these social media apps? No, they fought a cyber war against those terrorists and drove them off those social media apps. Since that's the case, why can't the CCP do it? Just because building a firewall is cheaper? Are our rights and interests and our recreational entertainment spaces worth less than the cost of fighting a cyber war? Do Chinese people just have to compromise and endure while foreigners get to protect their rights and interests? Please spread these words far and wide. Speak up for your own rights and interests and for STEAM. I don't know which kind of "being represented" is better: the kind they claim when they ban and censor World of Warcraft, Top Funny Media, and other free media, social apps, and single-player online games, saying it's the will of the people and gamers; or whether the things I'm posting today represent the interests of STEAM gamers. But I know that everything I'm saying comes from the bottom of my heart, straight from the soul, spoken with a mixed bag of feelings after going through all this bullshit. I'm speaking with a clear conscience, whereas they aren't necessarily doing the same. I hope everyone spreads these words. I know nine times out of ten it won't do shit, but how can one not cry out just because the voice is small? As an ordinary resident living in China who loves STEAM and loves the happiness STEAM brings, this is all I can do. Thank you everyone.

translation_en: This is my second review, and it's quite long, so please bear with me, gentlemen. Point 1: Skins. You can trade on IGXE, Buff, and the Steam Market. But compared to Steam, Valve is a bunch of greedy bastards, the market tax is way too high, and Buff's cash-out fees aren't low either (can't be helped, NetEase wants to make money, nothing you can do about it). IGXE had some drama before, so their reputation took a hit. As for cases, I advise all new players: do not open cases. If you're just starting out, I suggest buying a few cheap weapon cases and opening them just to learn your lesson. Actually, opening cases in moderation can help you kick the "see a case, open a case" habit (look up Global Elite sliding around to see what I mean). The CS:GO market is heavily influenced by public opinion and skin speculators, so don't buy things thinking the price is gonna drop. I seriously don't recommend renting skins; don't let a little bit of vanity cloud your judgment. Point 2: The Game (might be a bit long) 1. To those people who say "if you suck, go play casual," I honestly want to curse you out. Let me put it this way: 100 games of casual don't even compare to 7-8 competitive matches. Saying that is genuinely misleading people. So what if you suck and play competitive? If you're trash, your rank will just calibrate to Silver 1, does that affect you? Or what, are you the kind of loser who can't even get out of Silver 1? Newbies only need to play about 10 games of casual, after that, stick mainly to competitive. I hope that in the future, those of you who say "if you suck, play casual" stop pushing your subjective views and misleading newbies. It's just a game, so what if you lose a competitive match????? 2. I advise those of you who kick people just because they suck or accidentally hit you, using it as some petty revenge. Let me spell it out: what the fuck is the point of kicking people in official matchmaking now? It doesn't even give you a bot replacement anymore. Are you guys who vote to kick even using your brains? Dead players still have their uses, kicking one person instantly puts your team at a disadvantage, is that useful? 3. Whether your teammate is trash or whatever in a clutch, call out footsteps if you hear them, call out info if you have it. You can complain if there's multiple of you, but wtf is the point of just one person whining? You can talk a bit during a clutch to help your teammate relax, not screaming "what the fuck, cnm" after every single sentence. Don't be bored and kick a teammate just because they had a terrible round. Let me tell you this: the moment that kick prompt pops up, that struggling teammate's combat effectiveness drops through the floor, and the chances of losing go way up. You think you're playing 4D chess with reverse psychology, but in reality, you're not caring about anyone else's feelings at all. Please trust people. (There are plenty of these morons on the Pela/B5 platform, even more than in official matchmaking). Summary of points 2 and 3: Don't deal with toxic tryhards. When you see the kick prompt, just default to F2, never F1 (unless that motherfucker is genuinely griefing). 4. Map understanding and utility (Newbie guide) Map understanding can't be learned from so-called YouTube guides, it only comes from game sense (not the cheating kind) and racking up hours. For example, how many people actually understand how to use the Zeus? Whether you're good with the Zeus comes down to map knowledge and game sense. Too many people have no idea where to position themselves with a Zeus. Holding an angle in the alcove on Inferno A-second-floor spiral staircase with a Zeus and expecting to zap someone—what the fuck are you smoking? The moment the enemy swings wide or has decent crosshair placement, either you whiff, or they spot you first and you're dead before you can even click. To those getting zapped, I can only say: play more. Getting trolled once is whatever, but getting trolled a few times just means you're genuinely trash. You can learn utility whenever, just learn the commonly used ones. Leave the fancy high-end anti-rush flashes for newbies to learn later, you don't need to copy major streamers. Once you hit a certain rank, you'll naturally learn how to throw those nades. 5. Ranting on platforms (The fanboys of Pela/B5 are just like CXK brainwashed stans, completely intolerant of anyone pointing out their platform's flaws) PBA/Pela section: Pela's 128-tick servers, wow, right, so high-end. Everyone says it feels amazing. Bro, in official matchmaking when I see an enemy, at least I know roughly how many bullets to burst before stopping. Pela sometimes catches me completely off guard: I hit the guy in the head and saw sparks fly twice, hit his body 3 times at super close range, and I shot first. The end result? He didn't get headshot and I died. Ping 30, packet loss 1-2%, and what blew my mind was that the var value (directly tied to server quality—the shittier the server, the faster it spikes, which also messes with your local game FPS) spiked into the yellow way faster than in official matchmaking. What the fuck is wrong with your servers, Pela? Are they made of shit? And you see this shit all the time. As for their anti-cheat, let me ask you: do you think getting VAC'd (machine detection, un-appealsble) or OW'd (overwatcher ban, potentially appealable, assuming it's not a blatant spinbot) costs more, or getting banned by their PWA anti-cheat? First off, players need to realize one thing: the fact that Pela bans so many players just shows that their initial client-side anti-cheat is basically window dressing. Since you don't need Prime to play there, the barrier to entry for cheaters is way lower. So when it comes to banning efficiency, official matchmaking's anti-cheat is no different from Pela's. Aside from having matchmaking that's like 0.1% better than official and a slightly larger player base, I literally can't find any other pros. Pela anti-smurf? More like Pela anti-newbie, hahaha. 5E section: Let's cut 5E some slack and start with the pros: their servers are currently the best out of all platforms compared to official. Bullet registration is crisp, var barely spikes, and gunfights feel the best. But what the fuck, you piece of shit 5E, cheaters are literally everywhere. Who are you putting on a show for with that anti-cheat? If you don't want to make a proper anti-cheat, just hire human reviewers instead. And what's with using plugins to automatically ban anyone who does a 180-degree spin and gets a kill? That's treating the symptoms, not the disease. B5 won't even mention it, never played it. Official matchmaking is 64-tick, gunplay doesn't feel as good, and the matchmaking system is pretty garbage. 6. Community servers There's tons of variety, I'll go through them one by one: Prop Hunt: x93 Surf / Zombie Escape: Fys (Fengyunshe), ub, exg, x93 (seems to have fewer people now), zed (Zombie Paradise). {Zombie Escape community culture is pretty chaotic right now, all community forums have a lot of drama. If you want to get into this scene, I only recommend it if you already have prior forum experience. If you've never touched a forum in your life, I strongly advise against trying it. If you don't know the commands, ask the commanders and OPs. Hope you have fun.} KZ Parkour, Surf, and Ice Skating: You can look in the in-game community browser for servers with the "KZ" tag. The skill ceiling for KZ is insanely high, requiring immense game sense and extremely rich experience. Newbies can try it out though. Jailbreak (barely see anyone playing this anymore) Point 3: Thoughts on CS:GO As a hardcore competitive traditional FPS, it's done remarkably well. Even though Valve often slacks off and fixes bugs slowly, the game optimization is actually solid and bugs are few. I hope CS2 comes out a bit later—sharpening the axe doesn't delay the work of cutting wood—and I hope Valve does a better job.

translation_en: Quit after 800 hours. The game is good, the community is absolute trash. As a 5-year vet, when I bought this game at full price for 48 RMB five years ago, I never expected it to turn into this dumpster fire. Maybe 800 hours isn't really enough to get good, and some people even say you're only out of the tutorial at 1000 hours in CS:GO, but my 800 hours over these five years give me enough grounds to speak on the game itself, the environment, and the player base. Valve matchmaking puts Gold Nova 4 against Silver 4, VAC is useless, and servers constantly fail to connect. Never played 5E so no comment, and too scared to touch it anyway. Perfect World C/C+ lobbies are an absolute circus: smurfs, people forced to smurf because they deranked, griefers running it down feeding, headshot gods, timing demons, absolute bots who don't even know how to walk, don't know how to pre-aim or crosshair placement, can't spray and just dump bullets straight up, brainlessly spamming F while getting flanked, playing slower than molasses, too scared to swing or trade, mutes, solo-flank warriors, zero comms or teamwork, and guys with a god complex talking shit to everyone... It's either you serving time in prison or the enemies doing it, and close, hard-fought wins or losses are getting rarer and rarer. It feels like there's no fairness on any platform. All the time you spent grinding aim maps, learning utility, all your hard work gets chipped away every single round by your opponents, and by your teammates. People online always say anything below Perfect World rank B is just about raw aim, well excuse me for having zero CS talent, I just suck! But neither MM nor platform environments give players who actually invest time and effort into this game any kind of proportional positive feedback. Playing awp deathmatches in primary school computer labs, then messing around on CSOL, getting into CSGO properly in high school, and now sitting at 800 hours—I've been playing CS for 10 years. Lately, after picking CSGO back up these past few months, doing 1000 aim_botz flicks and 1000 bots a day, hitting 100 max KPM on 100 bots, and getting 88 on 500 bots, practicing my util, my game sense isn't terrible, I can play with the team—sorry I can't carry every single game with a 1.8+ Rating, and I might occasionally drop to a 0.5 or 0.6 when I'm off my game. I don't have a stable stack, and I mostly solo queue. Serves me right, serves me right! The game is a good game, but I do not recommend solo queue players to start playing. CNCS? NetEase BUFF! The macro environment is all about money, and the younger generation is full of toxic social Darwinists and bootlicking wannabe-capitalists. Some players even need to constantly update their weapon skins just to stay interested in the game, scalpers keep pushing skin trading into the spotlight, and for some people, CSGO has become an investment portfolio rather than a competitive game. Under traditional differential mode genetics, everyone in public lobbies is self-centered and fights their own battles, making teamwork virtually non-existent. Premade stacks form little cliques and use in-game voice chat like mutes. The exam-oriented education system has bred tons of ends-justify-the-means result-orientated people who use third-party cheats as a "shortcut" to win. As older CS players gradually quit or become casuals, restrictions on minors gaming, combined with CSGO's utterly toxic environment, are bound to scare away any newbies trying to get into the game. Does CNCS even have a future?

translation_en: I recommend CS:GO for the shooter that it is, but not without first making it clear that playing this game requires being mentally prepared, especially when you reach a high level. And I don't mean having your mind ready to win matches, I mean having it ready to be aware that the community is riddled with players who aren't entirely legit. translation_en: In a saucepan, heat the heavy cream with the sugar and the cinnamon stick. Stir the mixture until the sugar has melted. The moment we see it start to boil, remove it from the heat and let the mixture cool down a bit. When the cream is lukewarm, beat the eggs in a bowl. Add the cream to the eggs and mix well. It's necessary to strain the cream when adding it to the eggs just in case any little bits of the cinnamon stick came loose. Set aside. Prepare the caramel in a small saucepan. To do this, add the water and then the sugar. Put the saucepan on the heat and wait until we see it take on a golden hue. Turn off the heat and pour the caramel into the chosen molds, whether they're individual ones or a single large one. Baking and final preparation of the cream flan: While the caramel is being prepared, we preheat the oven to 180°C. Pour the flan mixture into each mold and place the molds in a baking dish with water. Put the dish with the flan molds into the preheated oven. Bake at 180°C with top and bottom heat, no convection, for about 25 minutes. In case we are using a single large flan mold, the time would increase up to 45 minutes. In any case, we can check if the flan is ready by poking it; if the knife comes out clean, the flan is perfect. Remove the tray from the oven and let the flanes cool down to room temperature before putting them in the fridge. Nothing better than a classic dessert like a flan to finish off a meal or for an afternoon snack.
