translation_en: Sometimes, I find myself wondering, why do we play CS? Why? Let me tell you a story. Because I liked a hardcore, extremely niche FPS game, I started a group chat. At first, there were only 9 people in it—besides me, everyone else was an admin. Then, through our slow promotion and accumulation on Tieba and Steam, the group gradually started to grow. That day, I was just planning to drop some usual harmless banter to farm some activity in the group, and the topic randomly jumped to the "beggar's edition" of Rainbow Six, where you have to no-life the grind like crazy just to unlock all the operators. Then, this dude piped up and said that grinding was the one thing he had in abundance, though playing a dozen games a day was making him feel a bit tired. When he was on his PC, he’d keep his phone right next to it to play mobile games. To play games, he bought five phones and three computers, and his PCs hadn't been turned off in nearly two months. He put two computers in his office and would play games on them whenever the boss wasn't around. Making 5,000 kuai a month, he’d only keep 300 for himself and blow all the rest on Tencent games. He had to go to work a bit after 6 AM every day, but he’d often game until 5-ish. Because of all this, his girlfriend, whom he was actually about to marry, broke up with him. At first, we thought it was completely unbelievable, didn't even know where to begin roasting him. When we asked him why, he first said he just liked playing games, and then mentioned he felt like he was poisoned or something—the first thing he thought of every time he woke up was rushing to grind the game. Then we started talking about how domestic mobile games use crazy pay-to-win tactics and all sorts of disgusting events just to boost user retention. These so-called games don't offer any real relaxation or entertainment; once you take these mobile games as your life's goal, you become their slave. You aren't playing the game, the game is playing you. These practices that exploit human psychological weaknesses are truly sickening, just like preying on a gambler's urge to win back their losses. After that, the topic looped back to this guy, and we started urging him to quit gaming, pay more attention to reality, stop pouring all his money into Tencent, or save up to go traveling—road trips were best. Then he dropped the bombshell that he used to crash his car because he was on his phone while driving, so he switched to riding a bicycle. But after buying a phone mount for his bike, he ended up playing on his phone and flipping down a flight of stairs, landing him in the hospital for several days. We, who had just been trying to advise him, fell dead silent after hearing about his "legendary achievements" and didn't even know where to start the roast. Someone helplessly remarked that only military service or Professor Yang could save him. If the story ended here, it would just be another cliché example of media propaganda claiming that "video games ruin people." But the twist was unexpected: he said he used to be in the military. He started talking about his past—serving in Xinjiang, holding the rank of second lieutenant as a platoon leader. But disaster struck on his very first patrol leading a unit, and 3 people died. He could never forgive himself, and afterward fell into severe depression. The military doctor said he was no longer fit for military service, so he was honorably discharged with deep regret. He slowly recounted how he had led a squad out on patrol, never expecting a huge freight truck to come hurtling straight at them. At the time, he noticed something was off with the truck, but he didn't pay enough attention to his teammates' warnings, and disaster struck. He felt like he had killed his own comrades—out of the three of them, the youngest was only 18. When his comrades' parents came to the base and saw their sons, it utterly shattered his heart. So he took his severance pay and some of his own savings, scraped together about 100,000 kuai, and handed it to his comrades' parents, lying to them that it was the official death compensation. After being discharged, he cut off all contact with everyone from the military; he didn't even dare have any contact with them. Every time he saw his own parents, he couldn't help but think of what his comrades' parents looked like when they came to the base, and then he couldn't stop blaming himself. He said with heartbreaking grief that he wished it had been him who died instead. That vivid, lingering memory constantly tortured him. Right after being discharged, he did a lot of stupid shit to try and "free himself," but seeing his devastated parents made him give up. At this point, another group member spoke up about his own military experience. Back in 2002, there was an incident where his platoon was sent out, not knowing the explosion was a terrorist attack. In the end, he was the only one who survived, and he watched with his own eyes as a comrade was blown to pieces. He said being a special ops soldier really isn't anything glamorous; when you first become one, you feel all high and mighty, but gradually you realize *you're* the real sinner, because you've killed so many people, your hands stained with human blood with no way to seek redemption, leaving you completely lost. His tone was slightly teasing as he tried to get the other guy to let it go. To be honest, just hearing it made me feel completely shocked. I don't know how he climbed out of that shadow, or if he even ever did. Maybe time dulls everything, or maybe even a decade later, he’s still jolted awake from nightmares by the tragic deaths of his comrades. Only those who have experienced war can understand how precious peace is—much like how the German and American soldiers walked out of their trenches on Christmas Eve to celebrate together and exchange gifts. I probably didn't fully understand these truths before, obsessed as I was with all sorts of war games, feeling entirely clueless about the psychological confusion, fear, guilt, and madness of the characters in *Band of Brothers*, *Hacksaw Ridge*, or *The Pacific*. But coming into contact with these stories somehow connected the scattered, lurking shadows in my own mind. It reminds me of a movie directed by Ang Lee, *Billy Lynn's Long Halftime Walk*. To be honest, the movie doesn't have any grand scale, nor does it have a thrilling plot; it even looks like some low-budget indie film. But ordinary people probably struggle to understand the movie's depiction of the sense of loss felt by soldiers wondering where they belong. Not every hero needs to be burned alive, and not every soldier has to sacrifice themselves to plug a machine gun nest. On the battlefield, redemption is always far more precious than slaughter. And behind the heroes, out of reach of the spotlights and flowers, there are even more unsung "heroes" and less glorious realities—a truth that we ordinary, mundane folks might never understand. This made me think of how I once saw a video mentioning that many US soldiers in the Middle East suffer from a psychological condition called Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). To effectively treat them, experts use electronic devices to constantly replay the traumatic scenes right before the patients' eyes. I remember how for the patient in the video, they replayed the moment he was driving a Humvee armored car when an RPG suddenly struck the vehicle in front of him, the instant explosion flipping that Humvee straight up into the air. To be honest, certain experiences can never truly be replicated through secondhand text, video, or audio to make you feel the real thing. We can never fathom what those nameless heroes felt at the time, and we'd better pray we never get the chance to find out. But when they are at their most psychologically vulnerable, when they leave the military, they don't just magically vanish from this unfriendly world. I hope more people pay attention to this issue so that, at the very least, after their trauma, they can feel that the world they have left to experience isn't entirely made of slaughter and loss. After learning about all this, honestly, it's hard not to question the meaning of life. Ordinary people fight over trivial interests in this world just like ants fighting over a dry leaf, hurting each other over mere scraps. Deception, hypocrisy, apathy, indifference, jealousy, hatred—can these really withstand the test of real life and death? Are they genuinely worth fighting over? Is there truly any point in crying, laughing, getting angry, or feeling joy? When there are people out there risking their lives and fighting tooth and nail for responsibility and duty, aren't we wasting our lives away like parasites, doing a massive disservice to them? What the hell is the point of this dogshit life of ours anyway? So, why do we play CS? Because we only have to face a virtual electronic world, wildly venting our violent desires without having to bear the consequences; because we don't have to experience the agony of parting of life and death, nor face the daily dread and anxiety; and above all, because we don't have to make a choice—the choice to become the kind of soldier General Patton talked about. That soldier might be you, and your ultimate destination is to be killed by the very last bullet in the final battle, because you were the last one standing, and once you die, the war ends and no one else has to sacrifice themselves. Otherwise, if you survive the brutal struggle among your own kind, you will spend the rest of your life carrying blood-stained hands, trapped in confusion, pain, and a lifetime tormented by illnesses and nightmares—just like the people in the story. Peace does not come easily. Cherish your games while you can. May the scenarios in games never become reality in the real world. Salute to all the brave soldiers fighting on the front lines of counter-terrorism.

translation_en: Cheesecake recipe ingredients: Cheese mass: 1 kg semi-skimmed curd cheese twice ground, bucket curd cheese or 20% quark 250 g sugar (= 1.25 cups) 3 teaspoons vanilla sugar 100 g butter (or margarine) 7 eggs (size M) 2 tablespoons potato starch (= 30 g) 2 tablespoons wheat flour (= 30 g) Optional: grated orange peel approx. 2 handfuls of raisins a few drops of flavoring Additionally: powdered sugar for dusting Preparation method: Line the bottom of a 26 cm springform pan with baking paper, then clamp the rim. Separate the egg yolks from the whites. In a small bowl, mix the starch with the wheat flour. In a mixer bowl, beat the soft butter with sugar and vanilla sugar until light. (The sugar won't dissolve, the mass will only become creamy after adding the yolks). Continuing to mix at highest speed, gradually add the yolks one by one. Reduce the mixer speed to medium and gradually add the cheese, followed by the mixed flour. (Now you can add the grated orange peel, flavoring or raisins and mix until combined). Separately, whip the egg whites until stiff and gently fold them into the cheese mass with a spatula. Pour the cheese mass into the springform pan and smooth the top. Bake in a preheated oven for about 60 minutes at 170°C (top-bottom heater). Turn off the oven and let the cheesecake cool with the oven door slightly ajar. Leave until completely cool. Put the cold cheesecake in the fridge for a few hours. Dust the cheesecake with powdered sugar or pour chocolate glaze over it. Enjoy your meal!

translation_en: This game takes a long time to get into, but it's a super interesting shooter that's definitely not easy. As the current torchbearer of practically the founding series of FPS shooters, it has a high entry barrier: map knowledge, gun recoil and spray patterns, the specific mechanic where you need to stand still to actually hit your shots (maybe I just play fewer FPS games, but it feels like CS is the only one that requires counter-strafing), utility usage, and so on. Personally, I also think the game's balance is better than a lot of shooters on the market (especially certain famous domestic giant companies). The game is free. If you played CS:GO before 2019, you get Prime status for free. Everyone in the game uses the exact same weapon stats—there are no skin stat boosts. The vast majority of weapon skins, stickers, and music kits can be traded on the Steam market. A lot of people slowly fall down the rabbit hole starting from borrowing a teammate's knife _(:з」∠)_... Official matchmaking runs on 64-tick, while third-party platforms have 128-tick servers, ensuring the razor-thin margins between high-level players—undoubtedly a blessing for players into high-tier competitive play. Also, this game is easy to turn you off when you first start. After all, getting one-tapped out of nowhere without even seeing a shadow is both terrifying and ruins the game experience, or jumping around trying to regroup with your teammates only to suddenly get tased or knifed in the back by a rat is super embarrassing (lol). But fun can also be built on other people's startle-induced freakouts. Once you gradually figure out the patterns, learn the map bomb sites, learn how to pre-fire, peek, and check corners, the game slowly gets interesting. You can one-tap the enemy's head, wait for some little dumbass to expose their ass to you, and soak up praise from your teammates in voice chat... All in all, CS:GO is an exceptionally good shooter. As long as you spend time learning and understanding it, you'll be able to enjoy a ton of fun.

translation_en: Unfortunately V/\lve made the game a living hell for anyone who plays well and just wants to mess around/kill time in casual matches. First, there's that 'mute' bot, which basically works in a completely broken way, like a Facebook report bot, except the reports aren't reviewed by anything or anyone—it just relies on the 'goodwill' of players not to report for no reason (Yeah right), which has brought misery to a lot of friends and strangers out there who live muted for absolutely nothing. In other words, just another example of how this 'bot' works completely automatically and takes into account nothing, absolutely nothing other than the number of reports. Worth mentioning that this type of report is extremely dangerous, because if you get banned for 'Griefing' 'forever', it's like getting VAC banned, the game becomes completely useless, including the community market. Early this morning as I write this, after playing CS:GO since the Beta, having a lot of fun and making several friendships (many of which spilled over into real life), I'm quitting the game for good. Anyway, I don't even know what else to say. Except that I don't recommend it to anyone, because there's no justice, freedom, or the fun of years past left here. Just leaving a short story here from someone who has always been a fan of this series and played it since 2001, having been through a lot and "lived" through a lot in it. What a damn shame.

translation_en: [h1]A Time to Live and a Time to Die[/h1] [i]Paleozoic Era.[/i] Thirteen-year-old me, along with a bunch of other slackers, is discovering for the first time a whole world outside the doors of a local LAN club. A vibe of its own rules inside: a dimly lit, smoke-filled room has only fifteen setups for aspiring cyber-athletes, but it's packed to the brim with a crowd of standing lookers-on. A grumpy warden, getting ten rubles from each member of our little gang, nods toward the free PCs, where the friendly face of a guy with a fan screwed to his case is already visible. It's hard to imagine how much time [strike]and money[/strike] we spent on [b]Counter-Strike 1.6[/b], swimming in the pool on [i]fy_pool_day[/i] or storming the impregnable warehouse walls of [i]cs_assault[/i], but one thing's for sure – those were wonderful days, full of joy and healthy rivalry. [i]Mesozoic Era.[/i] The internet finally reaches my dreary five-story apartment block. By that time, Lord Gaben is already serving up something called [b]Counter-Strike: Source[/b] on a silver platter. My buddies and I, of course, poke it with a stick for a few hours, but don't really get the appeal. Instead, we head back to 1.6, trying to shoot a flying grenade out of the air with an AWP, while simultaneously getting hooked on a mod that combines the shooter we're used to with elements of [b]Warcraft 3[/b]. [i]August 21, 2012.[/i] [b]Counter-Strike: Global Offensive[/b] comes out. I don't give a fuck – I'm a Dota player. [i]1 hour in CS:GO.[/i] Three years later, it becomes obvious that our sweaty 4k-god stack is hardly going to get picked for The International, and Valve's new brainchild finally makes its way into my library. More experienced friends, who have already logged a couple hundred hours in the game, smugly try to teach a calf just coming out of suspended animation how to walk again. The gunplay is a blast, the remastered maps straight from childhood are sweet candy, the Skype vibe is fire, the community is... um. Well, anyone who’s been through the [b]Dota[/b] school isn't afraid for their mother anymore. After figuring out which button is responsible for jumping, the two of us dive headfirst into calibration. We get completely destroyed by anything that moves, and anything that doesn't move, we move. In the end, we sew a few stripes onto our shoulder boards and stay on the digital battlefield for a long time. [i]1000 hours in CS:GO.[/i] Time flies, our chests get covered in medals for service to Gaben, whales stop being associated with marine mammals, and we start using basic nade throws. But the novelty effect evaporates somewhere, and we need some kind of push to bring back the old colors. And that push turns out to be the removal of Dust 2 from competitive mode. Faced with the new [i]de_inferno[/i], my old laptop starts pumping out a humanly comfortable 24 fps, and we migrate to hostage maps. Yeah, I'm aware they're a textbook definition of the word "imbalance." But, firstly, who are we to question the opinion of the Greatest, and secondly, nobody canceled a tear of nostalgic sorrow while loading into [i]cs_assault[/i]. [i]1700 hours in CS:GO.[/i] On another happy weekday morning, along with a "sick note" for skipping my first class, I catch a double headshot while standing in my spawn. Round after round, twisting all moral principles up their ass, a horde of bloodthirsty spinbot-killers rushes at me. Turns out Gaben decided that our wholesome community didn't have enough choice trash and put the game on F2P rails. Which, with the current performance of the [b]VAC[/b] system, basically makes cheating legit. Luckily, by that time we had new hardware, and [i]cs_assault[/i] and [i]cs_militia[/i] were removed from the map pool, [strike]though they could've replaced the latter with [i]cs_politia[/i][/strike], so we move over to [b]Faceit[/b] with a clear conscience. And – oh, wonder! Here you have 128 tickrate, a proper anti-cheat, and players who actually want to win. And Valve, the little indie studio, once again fails to match the original quality of the project they themselves released. [i]2500 hours in CS:GO.[/i] Turns out that changing your PC doesn't magically increase your skill, and age takes its toll on priorities. Some of my friends hang up their mice for good, turning their Discord status a gray, lifeless color forever. The rest of us from the old guard try to cling to *something* just to stay a bit longer in the game we once loved. You'd think the release of [b]Valorant[/b] would motivate the developers to show at least some initiative, but all the gentlemen at Valve could manage was to release [i]de_ancient[/i], having previously locked the trains away in an abandoned depot. The main work of "beautifying" CS:GO still rests on the shoulders of weapon skin artists and thoroughly fucking tired blue-collar workers hanging and rehanging doors on [i]de_dust2[/i] over and over again. [i]The last hours in CS:GO?[/i] There's just two and a half of us cripples left, who really ought to be retired. A couple of times a week, coming home from a real office, we perform the exact same hated ritual, bringing a virtual office to life. There’s no joy left, no competitive spite – they've been replaced by the most terrible feeling of all: indifference. The developers, failing to fix bugs, turn them into features, and failing to balance maps, scrap them right along with the bots, since AI is an insanely complicated thing. You don't need to see me out, I can find the uninstall button myself. [h1]A Sad Conclusion[/h1] Unfortunately, over time, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive turned into a stagnating swamp for me. Yeah, the developers didn't break everything that was already working just fine, but they never once dared to stray from the straight-as-an-arrow, narrow path. Maybe I'll come back someday, but only to try and find the emotions lost over the years with my friends. Some might find this speech childish babble. Like, if you didn't make it to [b]HLTV[/b], you basically never played. Well, you young level-tenners, this wasn't written for you anyway! Though you're always welcome in the comments. Oh, wait... translation_en: 106 hours in, started playing back in 2018, and compared to most pros I'm still a total noob. But even noobs have noob fun. Calling your friends to get online with you early in the morning, all sorts of wild, retarded plays flying everywhere, basically playing while laughing your ass off, and occasionally pulling off a sick play to flex on your homies. Lose the match, your fault, your friends chew you out; next game it's their fault, you chew them right back. Win the match, you get MVP, your friends are screaming "LETS F***ING GOOOO" over and over again, a bunch of dumbasses singing the MVP anthem, sometimes laughing until tears stream down your face. But then the more you play, the more you realize your friends' aim is better than yours. You start grinding your aim, going from watching pro matches every day to actually hitting the servers. Crosshair placement, pop flashes, counter-strafing, jiggle peeking, holding angles—your accuracy gets better and better, headshot rate consistently above 50%. You start getting really slick. The comms in your headset change from "Watch this, if I don't kill him I'll do a handstand and wash my... nah forget it, you guys are baiting me" to "I got entry, throw smokes and push!" As enemy after enemy drops, you're cheering, going wild... Right at that exact fraction of a second, when you hear the MVP music kick in: "D-d-d-d-d-drop the bass..." What blasts through your headset isn't just Blitz Kids, it's that familiar cheering, the sound of five dumbasses footstep-spamming all over each other. Back in spawn, I finally realized, I wasn't the only one feeling it. "Hahaha, you dropped the AWP? Just singing instead?" "Who gives a shit about an AWP? I've never laughed this hard, I'm jumping." They're back, everyone's back, and sitting here in front of my PC, my soul got hit with a deep tremor. It was a 4-2 crucial buy round, us five dumbasses won, didn't buy rifles, just Zeus taser-only, didn't buy a single piece of utility, all five of us squatting in one doorway. Nobody even called that strat out, but we just shared this telepathic understanding—it was the exact same tactic the five of us used on our very first day playing CS:GO against bots together, playing 15 matches with just tasers, laughing so hard we couldn't stop. After getting zapped three times, the enemy team just typed in chat, "Are you guys retarded? Bunch of 12-year-olds." "Fun." Now I finally understand the true meaning of gaming—it's something you just get, you can't really put it into words. But I'm telling you, whoever is reading this review, remember: an ace will never, ever beat playing with a full stack of five. Never!

translation_en: Just in case you've been living in a village in Uganda for the last fourteen years and have never heard of the series, the first Counter Strike was developed back in 1999 by two guys named Minh Le and Jess Cliffe. Initially, CS was just a mod for the game Half Life, but the mod became so fucking successful that Valve decided to buy the rights and turn it into a real game. And besides that, unlike what a lot of companies do, instead of Valve giving the creators pocket change and calling it a day, both of them were hired to lead the game's development. One fun fact that I think most people who play CS don't know is that the voice that says "Terrorist Win" is actually Jess Cliffe himself. And yep, to this day both of them still work at Valve. Well, Jess works there, Le left to work on another game called Tactical Intervention. In 2010, after several versions of the game, Valve released Counter Strike Global Offensive, which was basically meant to be the definitive CS. The game doesn't have a storyline or anything like that. Aside from the offline mode against bots, CS is a game totally focused on online strategy and competitiveness. The 2 main game modes are the bomb defusal mode: Where the Terrorist team needs to plant a bomb, and the Counter-Terrorist team needs to prevent that bomb from being planted. And the hostage rescue mode, where the Counter-Terrorist team needs to rescue a hostage and the Terrorist team needs to prevent that from happening. Both of these modes can be played in either casual or competitive mode. What do you mean, Paz? Like most online games, CS GO has a matchmaking system. In this system you can choose the mode you want to play, but you can also choose between casual and competitive matches. The difference between the two is that casual mode is made for casual players, there's no ranking, you can leave the match whenever you want, basically, it's for anyone who just wants to have fun. In competitive mode, on the other hand, you can't leave in the middle of the match, you have a sort of ranking, and you encounter much better players who are a lot more serious to play against and with you. One really cool thing they added in GO that's brand new to the series is a weapon economy system. Holy fucking shit, Paz! But isn't the game paid? Yes it is, man, but here's how it works: Every time a match ends, random players get weapons, or even random weapon cases. The weapons are yours to keep, you can use them, trade them... Do whatever you want. But as for the cases, you'll need keys that you can only get by actually buying them. Ahh Paz, but what if I don't want to spend money? Well, then you can make money. All the items you get from playing can be sold on the community market, and the money goes right into your Steam wallet. Exactly for this reason, a lot of people open cases; in one of those, you might find a weapon worth 80 cents, or 800 bucks. Ohh Paz, so I'm gonna quit my job and get rich just playing CS all day long. Ahhhh, that ain't gonna happen. Simply because no matter how long you play, you can only drop up to 8 items per week. And before anyone asks, no. The weapons with skins don't have any functional difference whatsoever compared to the others, so don't worry. Actually, the game's balancing, as usual in the Counter Strike series, is really good. Practically all weapons are good, but of course, once you learn how to master them. The gameplay in CS is something I personally think is amazing. Because here's the thing: At the same time the gameplay is simple, it manages to be complex. Let me explain. In CS you run (the character is always running), walk slowly, crouch, shoot, and aim with weapons that have scopes. That's basically all you do. So, you pick up the game and in half an hour you've learned everything you need. But to be a good player, you're gonna have to know the maps, learn all the spots and shooting angles on the maps. You'll have to learn which weapon you're good with, you'll have to learn how to control weapon recoil and spread. And you'll have to learn the small mechanics, or better yet, the "tricks" of the game that make all the difference. For example, you can put out a molotov with a smoke grenade. You can punch holes in a door with bullets, but to destroy one you'll need a grenade... And so on. The game has a built-in voice system, so generally people talk a lot during matches. In competitive, this is used to map out strategies and use callouts. "Ahh Paz, what the hell is a callout?" Callouts are basically nicknames that people give to certain areas of the map. For example, on the map DUST 2 there's an area people call "catwalk" (fundo). In 99 percent of the lobbies you say that, people will already know where it is. This is so you don't have to say, I don't know: Look, there's a guy in the hole, near the T-spawn gate, to the left of bombsite A. Instead, you just say: Look, there's a guy in cat. It's way simpler. In casual, things change a bit. Usually people use voice chat just to fuck with each other, trash talk... Complain about the team... Anyway, it's non-stop trolling. There was one match, man, I shit you not, I'll never forget it. Check this out, one guy died and insulted another like this: "Oh you son of a whore, your mother's right here in my bed." And the other guy replied: "Bro, my mom died 6 months ago." Then the guy answered back: "Who gives a fuck! She died from how much I fucked her, that bitch." Man... That was kind of messed up, but at the time I cried laughing. The game's graphics are really nice. Like practically all Valve games, CS GO uses the Source game engine. I can define this engine in 3 little words: beauty, lightness, and stability. That's Source. The game's sounds are very well crafted, if you have a good headset and you're one of those guys who likes to play listening to enemy footsteps, you'll do very well in this game. The connection is good. Aside from the official servers, there are the famous community servers, the ones loaded with mods, custom sounds, etc. And now, time to touch on that sad subject, the scum of the gaming community: cheaters. So, as of the recording of this video I have exactly eighty-eight hours of playtime and I haven't run into absolutely ZERO CHEATERS. translation_en: It was the summer of 1999. A friend dropped by and said a PC bang just opened up in the neighborhood where you could play a badass mod for Half-Life. I’d beaten Quake ages ago, but multiplayer was a blast. An hour cost 5 rubles back then, and the computer science teacher was the god of the school because he decided who got to play today and who didn't. There were about 12 PCs in the room, and there was always a line on the weekends. Anyway, I'm getting sidetracked. So when regular Quake got boring, someone brought in mods—Quake Ninja, which was hilarious, then the Team Fortress 1 mod with capture the flag, the spy playing dead, and the engineer with OP turrets. If you died, you had to wait until the round ended, no respawning, and you'd get so invested in your teammate, peeking at where the enemy was and feeding him info, which led to everyone shouting, "STOP SCREEN-PEEKING! WHY THE F*CK ARE YOU PEEKING?!" There were plenty of IRL fights in PC bangs because of that. You had to whisper info and pass it stealthily.) The version of the game back then was a beta, nowhere near 1.0; shots went straight to the crosshair with no recoil, silencers on the pistol and M16 couldn't be removed, bunny hopping was wild, and sniper rifles had crosshairs, which made them OP because shots always landed dead center so you could run around without even scoping. I remember already tinkering with mods and bots at home back then, learning how to create them, mapping out their paths from scratch, actions, even general chat and reactions. That's why when I installed Steam about 10 years ago, I bought CS:GO right when it came out. I don't have the urge to play now, plus I'm too old for this kind of game, my reaction time isn't what it used to be (back then I played with a 10-12 sensitivity on a ball mouse). Maybe one day I'll sit down to play again for the nostalgia, but nothing more. I'm too old for this sh*t. Thanks, CS, for a fun childhood.

translation_en: As soon as the news of Japan's surrender was announced, a Chinese radio announcer hurriedly started broadcasting: "We have just received word, the Japanese Emperor has accepted the Potsdam Declaration..." By this point, he was too emotional to continue. Then a second announcer took over: "Japan officially..." But he too started crying and couldn't go on. A third announcer, holding it together, continued: "Japan has surrendered!" Then everyone broke down crying together, making it impossible to continue the broadcast. Finally, they opened the window, pointed the radio microphone outside, and said, "Come listen to the cheers outside..." Firecrackers were going off everywhere, and it had become an ocean of joy. When the Central News Agency in Chongqing received the news of Japan's surrender, they immediately wrote huge characters on the wall: "Japan has surrendered!" The reporters from the Central News Agency didn't even have time to print newspapers, so they simply rode their bikes everywhere, shouting out loud to tell everyone: "Japan has surrendered! Japan has surrendered!" Every time I read this passage, my eyes well up with tears, and I think of Du Fu's poem: "Suddenly outside the Sword Gate, news comes of the recapture of Jibei; upon first hearing, tears drench my clothes. Then I look at my wife and children—where is their sorrow? I carelessly roll up my books, wild with joy." I hope we will forever remember this war and remember Japan's atrocities, and at the same time, I hope Japan stops visiting the sinful Yasukuni Shrine. It was really hard to find people to play with consistently (whether due to schedules or just my sole focus on winning). So my purpose in playing was pretty simple: just to win. But in the last month or two, after countless discussions, negotiations, and even shouting matches with teammates, I finally started feeling exhausted and numb. As a player whose only goal is to win, endlessly trying to cooperate with four other players who had completely different motives wore me down to the core. I finally started feeling like a machine—a CS:GO machine—rather than someone playing for fun. I've decided to let myself off the hook. There's more to life and happiness outside of CS:GO. But this review is for other players. So, as a veteran CS:GO player, my advice is this: if you can find good friends to play with, that's obviously the best—the joy of climbing ranks together is the ultimate high. If you're a solo player, I hope you have a strong mental. The most important thing a solo player needs to train is their mindset, and make good use of platform tools (like strict solo queue features). And if you're a beginner who just started, or someone with only 400-500 hours, I hope you'll communicate a lot in your future games. Honestly, the greatest joy in this game is actively communicating, coordinating tactics, and striving for victory with four complete strangers. Be a positive player. I rarely write Steam reviews, but let this one be the final chapter of my Counter-Strike journey. Though I'll probably still keep up with CS:GO esports, just like how I've always been an armchair viewer for LoL, lol.

translation_en: Why Valve's competitive shooter has actually gone to shit and become unplayable garbage without decent updates, and has become more depressing than appealing. Counter-Strike: Global Offensive has long been among the top 5 most popular games on Steam and periodically breaks online player count records. However, many fans often admit their hatred for it and regret the time they wasted. After a thousand hours spent in Valve's shooter, I decided not to stay on the sidelines and tell you what the fuck is wrong with it. Toxic community! CS:GO, like any team game, requires players to work together smoothly. Ideally, teammates should plan their actions, share info about what's happening in their field of view, offer prompt solutions, and figure out the opponents' tactics. Reality is much more depressing — in competitive mode across almost all ranks (and especially most often on Silver and Gold Nova), there's a high chance of running into at least a few toxic players on your team. They can hate on literally anything — your bad shot in the back, a losing streak in rounds, or just the weather outside — after which the verbal hate in chat starts, with mandatory mentions of your parents and trolling. For example, a teammate starts intentionally team-killing or deliberately staying at spawn. As a rule, peaceful negotiations asking them to act normally end in failure. In particularly severe cases, after a bad firefight (let's say you're left 1v1 against an enemy), you can simply be vote-kicked from the team. Cheaters and abusers! Cheaters have always been a pain in the ass in CS:GO. Neither Valve's anti-cheat nor the Overwatch system (where users review suspicious moments themselves and hand down a verdict on a player's fairness) solves the problem on a global scale. Cheaters often use "private" software that's hard to detect at the system level, or easily create a new account after getting banned. Based on experience, the aforementioned removal of free Prime status hasn't really changed the situation in competitive mode. Just the other day, the enemy team had a sus character who guessed literally all of our moves. After analyzing the match demo, my teammates and I made sure he was definitely using a wallhack. Filing a report didn't really help — a week has passed and the player still isn't banned. Valve is doing almost nothing! The third point stems from the first two: Valve isn't taking any large-scale actions to improve the atmosphere and globally combat cheaters. For example, nowadays in other competitive games like Overwatch or Rocket League, users are chat-banned for a careless curse word, and permanently banned for repeat offenses. In CS:GO, the communication moderation system barely works, and to avoid catching negativity, you either have to just turn off all chats or put together your own team of five friends. The game still has a bunch of exploits, and people at the highest level aren't even shy about using them. In September 2020, a major scandal broke out when it turned out that dozens of esports team coaches used a bug that allowed them to freely move around the map and see enemy positions. Another vulnerability was found in early summer 2021 — through certain actions, you could see where enemy players were, and the official anti-cheat didn't notice the exploit being used. In general, Valve has a really hard time communicating with the community. In May 2021, the company released a video statement saying that, quote, developers gather feedback by analyzing forums and comments, and almost never publicly announce upcoming changes. Presumably, this is a safety measure in case a planned update is suddenly delayed or ships without a previously announced feature. Many disgruntled users in the comments under the video noticed that the company tactfully stayed silent about cheaters and issues with false VAC bans. Smurfs and imbalance! If Valve is at least trying to do something about cheaters, the situation with "smurfs" is way more depressing. In every second or third match, you're bound to run into a player (by the law of shittiness, always on the enemy team) who plays way better than everyone else. He hits headshots, reads you like an open book, and completely demotivates you — someone who just logged in to have fun after a hard day at work — from even trying to fight back. These players aren't cheaters, they play fair, they're just way better than the rest of the users at that rank. They "boost" other accounts (usually for money), raising them to mid or high ranks. At the same time, smurfs technically aren't breaking any rules, don't use forbidden software, and even chat politely. Except their main account reached Global Elite ages ago, and right now they're playing with you at Silver 3. Smurfs have become one of the main causes of imbalance. One strong player easily carries the whole team, while much lower-level opponents sometimes simply refuse to keep playing out of sheer frustration (and a wild urge to uninstall the game forever). At the same time, CS:GO has a unique property of giving you incredible feelings when you manage to win a fair game. And moments when, say, you clutch (staying the last teammate alive and beating two or three enemies) give such a rush of emotions that you want to experience these moments over and over again. But your chances of getting negative emotions in the game still remain much higher, and it doesn't really look like the developers are ready to change anything globally.

translation_en: 1 hour: What the fuck are the AK and M4? Why does running and shooting spread bullets everywhere? Trash game. 10 hours: Trash game, flashed so hard even the minimap went white, what the fuck, I can't even walk around. 100 hours: P90 and MP5 are so fucking awesome, I can still use the big awp. 200 hours: What the fuck, you pay-to-win assholes, can you even win without skins? 300 hours: My knife can spin, needle doesn't poke, I feel like I'm good at competitive again. 400 hours: Placement matches are fucking brutal, this guy's a cheater, that guy's a cheater, I'm gonna puke. 500 hours: What the fuck are utility grenades, why are they so complicated? 600 hours: What the fuck is international matchmaking, why is everyone in this rank hitting one-taps? 700 hours: The fly head takes off its mask and it's actually clever little Pharoh, holy shit buy the operation pass, I'm gonna throw my money away today, whoever stops is a dog. 800 hours: Fuck, besides the AK and Negev, aren't all the other guns just useless sticks? 900 hours: Accidentally checked my report count for cheating, suddenly felt like I might actually be getting into CS:GO; yet zero-level alt accounts with default skins are dumpsters on service-medal accounts, a 10-year veteran is somehow 1800 Elo on 5E, and level 1 accounts are going on rampages in mid-tier 5E, B5, and Faceit lobbies. Was all my time wasted? 1000 hours: If I had used these 1000 hours to study, I might be in grad school; to work, I might be a team lead; to live, I might have my life completely sorted out; to date, I might be celebrating my 2nd anniversary with a girlfriend. But... isn't the reason we enter gaming worlds to catch a breath from the hustle and bustle of competitive real life? As long as there are winners and losers, cheaters won't ever stop, so what is the point of the game? It's to tell yourself that life is short, and I always have to persist in doing something. No matter what that thing is, just remember: You don't need to be great to start, but you have to start to be great! The hearty gunfights relieve the exhaustion I face in daily life, and the foul-mouthed shouting of teammates from all over the country, while vulgar, precisely reflects our country's rich and colorful folk culture. It constantly reminds me of how vast our motherland is, and how many places I haven't been to yet, how many things I haven't done yet, and the person I love is still waiting for me to press on. I once replayed a music kit song 200 times in a single day; maybe the MVP anthem doesn't play in-game every single round, but in my heart, it never stops playing! (Side note: Newcomers getting into the game don't necessarily need a spinning knife or thousand-dollar skins, but a music kit is an absolute must: Hotline Miami, Desert Fire, Inhale/Exhale, Invasion, High Noon, 8-Bit, Chill, EZ4ENCE, Gun Embraced Taco Truck, Dominant, It's Me, Take a Dive—these are the ones I suggest newbies shouldn't miss out on.)

translation_en: I remember back in 2017 when I first got into this game, shortly after the Chinese server launched. I was still a minor, didn't have my ID bound, and couldn't afford to spend over 90 bucks on the game back then, so I could only play offline with bots. Soon after, I bought the international version on Taobao. Dust II was the map I played the most against bots, and it's still one of the maps I'm most familiar with. I started exploring casual mode, watching game streams, learning pop flashes, spray control, and gamesense. When I first opened competitive mode, I was super nervous holding angles, my heart pounding, too scared to talk, obediently listening to my teammates' callouts. Later on, I got more and more familiar with the game. With only around 200 hours under my belt at the time, I was tearing it up in competitive and dropping top frag every single match. After graduating from middle school, I got into an ideal high school and scored a huge stack of red envelopes (cash gifts) from family and friends. I bought my very first knife: a Flip Knife | Doppler (I remember people saying the flip knife was the best for quick-switching with the AWP back then, and the AWP was my best weapon). Later I traded it for a 0.46 float battle-scarred Hand Wraps | Mint Kimono. Ngl, Mint Kimonos look so damn good, even though they were battle-scarred they were still pretty decent. I got bored of the flip knife pretty quick, so I traded it for a Damascus Steel Talon Knife. Man, was it shiny. That was the first time I found out you could spin the talon knife with F+R. I found my own kind of happiness in the world of CS:GO. Soon my high school life began, and I started doubting whether I could keep playing. Coincidentally, I met someone I had a crush on around that time. Chatting day and night made me fall in love. I figured if I was going to date, I probably needed some cash. Clinging to the resolve to study hard in high school and my romantic ideals of love, I ended up selling off all my favorite inventory. But reality is cruel—if I had succeeded, maybe I wouldn't be writing this review. My high school life was an absolute trainwreck; I lost the relationship and I lost at life. Maybe I really am just an AWP: at my peak I could flick-headshot and clutch the round, but when I'm at rock bottom, I'm just a 4000-dollar price tag, a sniper missing mid-to-long... In the summer of 2021, I came back to this game. My old bros had already improved by leaps and bounds—it used to be me carrying them, but now they were carrying me. I slowly scraped and clawed my way up from 1500 Elo to 2000, and bought back skins I liked, but I just couldn't find that original feeling anymore. So I kept trading and trading; a 7-day trade hold was the speed at which I swapped out skins. But that feeling of falling in love at first sight? I couldn't find it anymore. Yeah, and the old me isn't coming back either. You can run it back when you lose a game, but you don't get a second chance when you lose at life. Countless times, I've reminisced about what was going through my head when I put those skins up for sale on BUFF. I guess I'm just too damn sentimental. Now, I still love this game. It doesn't just bring back memories of when I was young and reckless; it's also my emotional crutch. Maybe life is just like this game, full of endless regrets. And you—you're like the defuse kit 4 seconds too late, a 4700-dollar economy, the one HP left after getting dinked on a peek, a bomb plant missed by 0.1 seconds, the regret of getting headshot right after pulling off a spray transfer quad-kill. I love CS:GO.

translation_en: Step-by-step brownie recipe Ingredients 200 g baking chocolate 4 eggs 3 tablespoons flour (80 grams) 9 tablespoons sugar (120 grams) 90 g butter or margarine 50 g walnuts 1 tablespoon instant coffee (can be decaf) (3 grams) Prepare the chocolate batter Melt the chocolate together with the butter or margarine, add the coffee, mix, and set aside. Separate the egg yolks from the whites and whip the whites until stiff peaks form. In a bowl, beat the yolks with the sugar, add the chocolate mixture, and mix. Add the walnuts and egg whites Add the walnuts, mix, and add the flour. Once everything is mixed, all that's left is to add the egg whites, folding them in carefully. Pour everything into a well-greased rectangular baking pan or one lined with parchment paper. How long does the brownie need in the oven? Bake at 180°C (350°F), preheated, with convection or fan for about 25 minutes. You have to be careful not to overcook it since the brownie should stay moist on the inside. And that's it, all that's left is to serve and enjoy this delicious chocolate brownie. For example, with homemade ice cream and some walnuts on top, it's absolutely delicious. Some tips for making a perfect brownie. What chocolate is best for brownies? It's best to use good quality baking chocolate with a high cocoa percentage. Ideally, chocolate with 70%-80% pure cocoa. The chocolate should be melted together with the butter, over low heat and keeping an eye on it, and it's even better if you do it using a double boiler (bain-marie). Baking time: The brownie must be baked for the indicated time, because ideally it shouldn't end up dry, but rather a bit moist. Although it can vary from one oven to another or depending on the size of the pan, it will be roughly 25 minutes at 180ºC. Make sure the batter has a crispy top layer and that when you poke the center with the tip of a knife, it comes out slightly damp (never raw). How to get the crispy chocolate crust on the brownie? To do this, we must beat the egg yolks well with the sugar, making sure the sugar dissolves properly. As we explained above, once the yolks are mixed with the chocolate and butter mixture, fold in the stiffly beaten egg whites very carefully without beating. This is how we get that delicious crispy chocolate layer on our brownie. Brownie with or without walnuts? Although the original recipe doesn't have walnuts, in the US they do add them, and we personally like them better with walnuts than without, since it adds some texture to the dense brownie batter. How to serve the brownie? Like we said before, it's delicious with vanilla ice cream. We should let the brownie cool down slightly when we take it out of the oven, but it can be served warm alongside the ice cream.

translation_en: At first CS was really fun, but right now the game is in a phase where normal people can't play it anymore without having to commit themselves to a psych ward afterwards. In this review, I want to list a few points that make the game absolutely unplayable for me. 1. Matchmaking. Sometimes at the end of a match when I see the ranks, I wonder if the people at Valve even play their own game. We play as a five-stack, one is Gold Nova Master, 2 are MG1 and 2 are MG2. Unfortunately you get completely steamrolled because the enemy team is playing with 2 MG1s, an MGE and a DMG player. But it's totally fine, the fifth guy on the enemy team is Gold 2, so it's balanced, that's definitely gonna be an even match. 2. Smurfs. They are of course unavoidable and still better than cheaters, which I'll get to, but by now you can be sure to have at least one smurf on the enemy team in EVERY SINGLE GAME who completely steamrolls you, drops 45 frags, and at the end turns out to be a Gold 4 player. I now have the feeling that there are so many cheaters and smurfs in circulation that the whole ranking system is completely down the toilet. If you find a game where there's no smurf on the enemy team, and all opponents are really MG1, they get completely rolled, but you just can't rank up if you get crushed in every 2nd game by someone who is actually at least 4 ranks above you. 3. CHEATER FORFUCKSAKE. It's just terrible. You play the first half 10:5, think the game looks good. Well, tough shit. The guy from the enemy team with 200 hours on record and 2 hours in the last 2 weeks, who was wiping the floor of the enemy leaderboard for the first half, realizes that the game isn't any fun when you don't hit shit and just get your ass kicked. The guy then multiplies his kills by five in the next 10 rounds and just hits you with some shady running flick headshots. Strangely enough, he also knows every time where you're coming from, stops checking corners, and only checks the one where someone happens to be standing. Those get prefired nicely. But VAC is a good system, thanks Valve. I mean how sad is it that during the WarmUp you first have to check all the opponents' profiles, and you want to throw up because you see that one of them already has a VAC ban on his profile, two of them are Steam Lvl 0 with no info, one has 10 pages of comments under his profile insulting him as a hacker and the last one of the bunch has 400 hours played. That really puts you in the mood to play. Sometimes I wonder what's so hard about coding a decent anti-cheat program, especially when you own one of the biggest, if not the biggest FPS game in the world. Then I remember that we're talking about Valve, and an anti-cheat system would not only COST money, but also NOT MAKE ANY MONEY AT ALL. And that really doesn't fit into corporate policy. Wouldn't surprise me if at some point there's a subscription service where you can play clean matchmaking for 10€ a month. What are Trust Factor, VAC and so on even for, if NONE of them work?! Just buy the anti-cheat tool from Faceit or something. How can it be that Valorant has had a working anti-cheat program since day 1 and CS:GO has been on the market for over 10 years and still doesn't have one? People should think about that. 4. Randoms. The game has reached a point where you're almost forced to play as a 5-stack, because anything where you have more than one random is a less secure gamble than Russian Roulette. And don't even think about solo queueing, you can actually just walk up to the nearest wall outlet and stick your fingers in it, the chances of it being A. fun and B. coming out unharmed are significantly higher there. In a solo match, after 5 rounds at the latest, you reach the point where self-mutilation becomes incredibly attractive. Or you go crazy and scream at all your mates yourself, even as a person who is normally the definition of calmness, only to realize that the probability of them understanding English is about as high as getting struck by lightning while teaching a guinea pig how to do long division. Apart from a "SHADDAP PIDAR BLYAT" you won't get anything back. Provided your mates even have a headset, which is only the case in the rarest of instances. The probabilities with random mates are about as high as opening cases, except in that case you pay with your soul: A Rare Special Item corresponds to a mate who actually hits something and isn't close to brain death, a Rare Special Item in StatTrak would then be a smurf. Anything lower in quality than pink is then mates who, for example, have spontaneously unbound their E key, go 0/0/14 after 14 rounds (yes, I've had to witness that too), scream toxic bullshit the whole time and do team kills, or our beloved AFKs. But that last case isn't even bad anymore, because everyone gets 1000 dollars if someone leaves. Unless you kick someone because he's trolling. Then you don't get 1000 dollars. Who the hell came up with that, who the hell approved it and thought "well, actually a good idea" and who the hell then also put it into the game?! (Valve please please please I just want my bots back, by now I don't even care if the bot commands absolutely don't work and they only listen on the 10th ping (props for that btw again)) 5. Questionable Updates To keep this point short: What did we want? Better bot commands, meaning the bots *actually* listen to commands. What did we get? Bots have been removed. What did we want? A new, exciting and varied operation. What did we get? Fang fking rat premium. What did we want? Working anti-cheat. What did we get? Free2Play and bootleg PUBG in crap: Dangerzone. What did we want? Comebacks of old, legendary maps. What did we get? Rat maps that are in the Active Duty pool for 2 weeks because nobody gives a fuck about them afterwards. And Ancient, where, in the best case scenario, the shaders of pig-ugly are bugging out, and in the worst case scenario your rig crashes. Thanks Valve, thanks for nothing. Conclusion Due to the perhaps a bit too detailed points, the game is barely playable for me anymore, and drives me up the wall every time. I'll probably still play it when we get a 5-stack together again, and otherwise only 99damage and Faceit, but otherwise I'll probably switch to Valorant. The game totally sucks in terms of things like movement and aim (compared to CS), but it's worth it to me not to constantly play against cheaters, and lose a piece of my will to live every time I hit "Accept". With the newest CS update, the only way to still get drops, XP and Prime (which is basically a must-have, because you don't want to subject yourself to Non-Prime in any parallel universe) is to buy the Prime upgrade, and you're better off burning that roughly 15€. So better keep your hands off, or you'll soon find out what true regret is. Addendum: Valorant also sucks ass, I guess I'm fucked.

translation_en: [h1]Having racked up 3870 hours, it's about time I wrote a review for this game, don't you think?[/h1] (UPD: At the time of writing this review, Prime status could be obtained for free). When I first got here, the game cost around 500 rubles, and I was totally fine with paying that. To get Prime status in the game, I had to reach level 21 ([u]pretty much like now[/u]). Although back then Prime didn't cost anything, people using prohibited software weren't encountered all that often, only in rare cases. As for Prime back in those days, it just opened the way for you to play with more experienced players. Back then you could safely count on the fact that your team's victory depended solely on your overall teamwork and each player's individual skills. You understood that when you were losing a game, you were losing it fairly, along with your team, because the enemy team surpassed you in some criteria. (Or maybe they were just super lucky, okay you got me=*). You could often be skeptical about whether your enemies, just like your friends, might be messing around with something banned. -->A lot of time has passed since those days, I've seen a lot of players, both good and bad, and ideal... Even those who shouldn't be talking to people at all, let alone playing a game where everything depends on teamwork. Where do I put myself? I don't know. That's for the people who play with me to decide. The ones who keep playing with me after all these years. For almost 6 years of playing, I've changed a lot. In some ways for the better, and in some ways for the worse... I can't even say which way more. But I think everyone I've ever crossed paths with had a big influence on that. I picked up a lot of good stuff from someone, they taught me something, I taught them something. Someone taught me not to trust people, and to treat them how they deserve. I'd continue with this topic, but after all, this is a review of a game, not my worldview maturation arc)) -->Now, many years later, everything I talked about at the beginning makes no sense at all. There are so many people using prohibited software now that they've become the absolute plague of this game. Skepticism is completely gone, one lucky random shot through smoke is enough to catch a report. The game became free, even, strange as it may sound, for those who once bought it. They just don't get any privileges over those who downloaded it a month ago and got free Prime without any problems. Yes, Prime can be bought, it costs twice as much as the game used to cost. But what's the point? Why sell something you can get for free? I believe the game can be free, but Prime - absolutely not. Cheaters don't take a loss, getting a free premium account that gets banned after a while. They can just create a new one. VAC doesn't justify itself at all, some people play with prohibited software for several months and feel just fine. Even those using spinbots don't always get banned within a month. Don't even try to tell me otherwise, I'm an experienced guy, I keep track of the ones I've reported in the past, and I get really sad when I see a player who was using a spinbot quite a long time ago and still hasn't been banned. It gets especially painful when your friends betray you by getting VAC-banned. And especially if they do it several times, and you keep playing with them, hoping for their empty promises, because you're very attached to this person and don't want to lose them. I had a friend like that... Until after yet another ban I told him to fuck off. This guy turned out to have no honor or dignity, acting like a pig by betraying his friends yet again. Constantly promising that it wouldn't happen again, that he'd changed, that he wasn't using any software anymore... In the end, when he got another ban, I cut ties with him once and for all. He didn't even say anything sensible, just made up bullshit excuses that, just like him, weren't worth shit anymore. But the main problem here is that there are still people who keep playing with him. Yeah, you can forgive one mistake... But when this person completely doesn't give a crap about his friends... Anyway, another problem with the game is its community; some people think that playing on the same team as a cheater is normal, even great. Some people are toxic as hell, and in my opinion, they should also get a full account ban and have no access to the game. The problem is that the community doesn't depend that much on the developers, rather, the community depends on the community. And yet, the developers managed to influence the community by making the game free. After that, loads of little kids flooded into it who previously didn't have the money to buy it, and school kids are a whole different story. Very often it's them who become cheaters, not understanding the main point of the game. Plus, this game can ruin the immature minds of 10-year-old boys who plunged into the world of adult, not always polite uncles. -->I'm not going to discuss the game mechanics, it's pointless, everyone already knows everything. In this review, I just wanted to share a part of the journey I've been through and what bugs me the most. If you judge the game by my review, it should be negative... But I made it positive. Why? Probably because I didn't rack up all those hours in this game for nothing... And I keep playing it after all these years. During this time I've found and lost friends, made enemies... And I think that's wonderful. If VAC starts working the way it should, the cheater problem will disappear, and cheaters are, once again, the main sore spot of the game. And I sincerely hope that the developers, who have huge sums of money, will be able to use them for good. I'm not going to make a pros and cons list; I look at this review a bit differently. Lastly, I'd like to give the game a rating... 5 fair players out of 10 in a single game. If VAC becomes amazing, I'll gladly give the game an 8/10. *(UPD: Several people have already been unhappy that I allegedly fell out with a friend because of the game. Specifically for them, I want to emphasize why exactly I stopped talking to him: Firstly, I didn't mean it as a fight, I just stopped talking and communicating with him. Secondly, the main reason for this wasn't cheats, I forgave him for those several times, but the fact that this person simply cannot be trusted. He constantly lied to us, made false promises, and played the act of "Ah, all cheaters are pieces of shit, but I'm not like that." In my opinion, those who put on that kind of act are the most vile people. Even spinbotters are better in that regard, at least they cheat openly. And the behavior of this "friend" can easily be counted as betrayal, and I hate traitors most of all. I became friends with him playing CS, and I parted ways with him playing CS. Regards, Fair Ildzhar.)* The end, I guess.

translation_en: Reviewing a masterpiece like Counter-Strike GO is like reviewing two different games. One review is about the game itself, the other is about the game's community and the environment created by it. Starting with the second point (and the easiest): the CS community is a problem, and I don't just mean the asshole behavior of most players, because brother, the CS environment has been like this for almost two decades, so if you're getting into playing it, you can't plead ignorance of that fact... The problem here is twofold, the first and most serious being the constant hacks, and the second is that CS has become an absurdly predictable game, and the massive pixel-holding done nowadays by 5 out of 10 players is perhaps irrefutably proof of what I'm talking about. This is made worse by the lack of map reworks, which means that jobless kids who spend 8 hours a day playing end up heavily contaminating the gameplay and driving other players away (not just casuals, but even those who play for an hour every day). On the other hand, "rework" is practically a curse word for CS players, just look at the flood of negative comments the game gets whenever they release a new mode or rework a map. The standard CS player is terrified that the developer will kill the soul of the game, and I understand part of that fear, although in the medium term, the lack of certain targeted overhauls will result in the slow and agonizing death of the game. As for the game itself, CS is a masterpiece, and most likely the most relevant FPS in gaming history. As mentioned before, there is obvious wear and tear in the game mechanics, especially when comparing CS to more modern games, as well as some limitations on utility and even movement, but those two points are also responsible for the game's charm. Such is my affection for CS that before corona, since 2016 my friends and I would get together in person every Thursday to play our "Weekly CS." The next day, everyone went to work exhausted, but it worked better than anti-anxiety meds. These social events with friends that games like CS manage to provide are precious, rare, and rarely properly valued. Overall, CS is the bread and butter of FPSs; it might not be your favorite dish, but it holds a special and lifelong place in your heart. Rating: 8/10

translation_en: **As someone who was getting close to depression, I'm really grateful for everything this game has brought me.** I've thought about suicide and even tried it, but I was pulled back every time. Even though this game has a lot of cheaters, terrible optimization, bans people for no reason, can make you super depressed, and takes a ton of time to practice—just like that, I met some super great friends in the game. I say some, but it's really just a few, and I met my best friend on a map called Dust2. Back then I hadn't been playing long, and my rank was Silver 3. The rain was pouring outside the window, and looking at the time, it was already 10 PM. I decided to play one match of my favorite CS:GO and get ready for sleep. Because at around 400 hours I had hit Gold Nova 3, I was a bit scared to play once I ranked up. I decided to queue on 5E, clicked on my most familiar map, Dust II, grabbed my default T knife, and picked up my most practiced P90. I can say for sure I wasn't planning on winning that match; I wanted to go to sleep halfway through because my teammates were different from usual. My 5E Elo was around 1200 back then, and I was getting slightly annoyed. It was my teammates' encouragement time and time again, instead of constant condemnation, that gave me motivation. "Can't win? It's fine, bro, next game." "Ah, too bad we didn't get the kill this round, but whatever, we'll bounce back next round," instead of "You're so shit with that M4, why the fuck are you playing this game?" The five of us pulled off a comeback from 7:13 to win 16:14. And I met a super great best friend who acts all proud and loves to show off, but is actually good to you, comforts you, and sticks by your side. My life was at a low point back then, and I wanted to leave this world countless times. I cut off reality and only lived on the internet. I wanted to leave this world over and over, but I kept getting pulled back. I love this atmosphere, I love CS:GO, I love everything about it! Even though I suck at playing, the game's optimization isn't that great, it hands out random bans, it's poorly optimized and makes you depressed, but I just fucking love CS:GO! Even so, I still practice every day. High-intensity daily practice got me to Global Elite, and I met more foreign friends as well as some high-tier players from back home—some former pros, active players, and some foreign high-ranks too (we don't talk much now because of the language barrier, maybe). But even when we don't talk much, heart-to-heart connection is still there during ranks, I could always understand what they meant~ What CS:GO brings me isn't just fun; more than that, it showed me the motivation to keep living. A lot of people ask why I practice so desperately. I can't answer them; I can't say I view CS:GO as my reason to live, because in their eyes, someone who says that is mostly just an idiot. But only people who can genuinely play CS:GO can understand and appreciate these things. My hours have gone from 400 to 1,348, going from Silver to Gold, then AK, then Global Elite, and now just a washed-up Supreme. I don't see this game as just a game anymore; I only know that it gave me the motivation to keep living. **I can't judge it too much. There are cheaters, the optimization is trash, the game makes you depressed, and you need to practice your aim, but I will forever love the friends I'm with and this game called CS:GO~**

When I had played for dozens of hours and figured out the real gameplay, and when I decided to seriously play with my friends, I changed my name to [u]GK Major[/u] [spoiler]GK is GodsKiller, just a chuunibyou phase www[/spoiler] Later, because of that whole Anomaly/Shroud equivalent drama in China, whenever I joined a game my teammates would joke, "GK, NMLGB." Truly caught strays just lying there. That was when my truly happy CS:GO entry-fragger [spoiler]madman[/spoiler] career officially began. An Inferno regular who only used SMGs, a high school counter-strike trainee named GK Major who couldn't save the world, was born. And in that brief counter-strike life, I met a lot of interesting people and made many friends. [u]Jing Jiujiu[/u], who promised to play PUBG with me later because his hardware wasn't good enough... [u]Wen[/u], a NetEase Cloud resident a year younger than me who invited me to play in Sichuan... [u]Xiao Beiye[/u], a genius high schooler who hit Global Elite in his freshman year of high school...... And my real-life good friend Ergou. I was GK[spoiler]GodsKiller[/spoiler]Major and he was GK[spoiler]GouKing[/spoiler]Admiral. I used the P90, he used the MP7. I bought a bayonet, he bought an M9 [spoiler]Man, I miss the days when you could buy a butterfly knife for 700 RMB[/spoiler] and so on. Like-minded friends, we all used to laugh out loud together in the game, turned into fake friends, had arguments, and eventually made up. And now? Some are forced by life, some had their accounts hacked and VAC banned, some drifted apart because our paths diverged. We went our separate ways for all sorts of reasons. I still remember Jing Jiu telling me about his graffiti, his dreams, his city, his future. I still remember me and Ergou, two GKs holding down the top two spots, banana double-boosting. I still remember Beiye saying my voice sounded nice, carrying me in Wingman and APEX. I still remember an opponent saying I was cheating, me saying "u mad bro," and then him actually starting to cheat. I also remember discussing the future of life with Wen late at night, promising to visit each other's cities in the future, and birthday gifts we sent each other. Reality is truly cruel. Sometimes I often think, since parting ways is inevitable, why did fate make us cross paths in the first place? Is this a trick of fate, or a growth we are bound to experience? [h1]People are sometimes connected to each other, with even the meaning of life intertwined; people are sometimes scattered everywhere, to the point where even each other's names are forgotten.[/h1] But clearly, the high school version of me didn't think about any of this. My brain was only filled with what to eat for breakfast, what to eat for lunch, what to eat for dinner, and what game to play at home this weekend. Calling me a high-spec Denji wouldn't be wrong at all. But the happiness in the game filled the pain in reality, whether it was the stressful and muddy future, or the unfindable fragments of the heart. Put on the headset, grip the mouse, a little bit of the emptiness inside is filled, the pain in reality slowly fades away. Winning a 1v5, praise from teammates, compliments from friends—it's as if time stops right there, the world focuses on you. I even thought, maybe the meaning of my existence is right here? Wanting to share this joy with the whole world, only to look back and realize there was only myself around me. 50 hours Silver IV, 400 hours Gold Nova IV, 600 hours Distinguished Master Guardian. I never thought about going pro, because I knew I didn't deserve to, but what I got in the game was an incomparable sense of achievement that the version of me in reality—labeled as a [b]loser, trash, stupid dog[/b]—would never experience in a lifetime. Even though I know now that this isn't right, what can I do? The impossible high expectations given by teachers and family. The pressure generated from internal competition among friends and classmates. And me? I only had the happiness bestowed by the gaming world. I have to say, education in China is truly garbage to the extreme, reminding me of a quote: the gaokao only filters out poor students, not scumbags. It really is like that, riding on their good grades and wielding the power given by teachers, carrying out inhumane exploitation against the "losers" who weren't as good as them [spoiler]Why use the word inhumane? Because I was the victim[/spoiler] Finally, after going through the hardships of the gaokao, thinking that breaking out of the cocoon meant the pain was over, and that I would finally start a free life in a new place and end this dogshit campus life—the result was just the beginning of another tragedy. [h1]Growth and Divergence[/h1] Perhaps the choice of university already decided the divergence from others. Growing along with age were also the ever-expanding conflicts. Different values, morals, and worldviews ultimately led to the creation of alienation from others. Maybe the conflicts existed from the very beginning, but fighting in the gaming world kept us from discussing them further. After all, growing up means having to think about future directions, and then during arguments, words we never thought we'd say all came pouring out, resulting in bonds built over years turning to ashes in an instant. Finally, my thoughts exploded after looking at one VAC record after another in my friends list. Former friends, former ideals, the wonderful future I once yearned for, along with CS:GO which symbolized that wonderful yet dogshit youth, vanished completely along with the music kit that recorded that wonderful yet dogshit youth. In the end, I sold [u]BlitzKids[/u], the music kit that recorded 986 MVPs and symbolized my youth and dreams. [h1]These homeless emotions have now turned into text to write this messy review.[/h1] The me who used to huddle in a room looking dead can actually write something like this now, huh? If you see this...... If you still remember an uninteresting guy who used to be called GK Major http://music.163.com/song?id=28017977&userid=133897090 Then, let's end it here.

translation_en: I am asked every now and then whether people should buy "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive". Personally, I really like it, but it's not for everyone. Anyone who has the spare cash and just wants to try it out is warmly recommended to do so. Anyone who is unsure should think about it first. That's why I'm approaching this review the other way around: Who is CS:GO NOT for? 1) For level-uppers and perk lovers There are no unlockable weapons, no perks or variable weapon skills. You buy your loadout every round and can do so from the very first minute of the game. It's not for everyone, but in return, it guarantees a very balanced playing field with a focus on individual skill. Small downside: There are weapon skins that allow you to "personalize" your weapons. You either find these randomly at the end of a match or can buy them in the community market (or trade them with other players). There are also season passes every now and then, so-called "Operations". Leveling up is possible to some extent there. 2) For loners. It is a truly tactical team shooter. If you want to have fun for a bit longer and more professionally, you need to be able to act as a team. That means: Help your team by calling out where you've seen enemies. Your money isn't your money, it's the team's. If you have enough money and someone asks you if you can buy them a weapon (of course this isn't a blank check for everything), then do it. Hold the position entrusted to you. You lose as a team and you win as a team - simple as that! 3) For people who care endlessly about their K/D. This actually ties into point 2). It's a team shooter and no matter how many enemies you defeat, ultimately what counts after the rounds is whether you won the most or not. Your K/D has no influence on that (holding positions is more important than just blindly running around fragging). 4) For people who only want to play a single round within a certain amount of time. Counter-Strike has always been characterized by its round-based nature. You get money round after round and, within a time limit, have to either plant or defuse a bomb (rescue or guard hostages, etc.). Not everyone likes that, but it increases the tactical quality. 5) For quickscopers and SMG-snipers. Sure, exceptions prove the rule, but unlike many genre peers, you shouldn't go into close combat with a sniper rifle or snipe across the map with a submachine gun here. Why? It rarely ever works because it heavily relies on weapon range and recoil. 6) For realism lovers. "The crosshair doesn't sway with the sniper rifle - totally unrealistic!!" Yes, that's true, and there is also no "down-the-sights" aiming. In my opinion, though, it's not about being the most realistic shooter (especially since that's never possible anyway, and all the ones that try are still wildly unrealistic in so many places because otherwise it just wouldn't be fun to play). It's about your skill, your team, and balance. ________________ So, whoever read this far might have just wanted to check if they fit into any of these categories. Those who aren't discouraged yet can look forward to an exciting team shooter (Man, the way you sometimes sit in front of your PC when the bomb has been planted and it's down to a 1vs1... ;)) that includes a few nice, classic game modes (Bomb Defuse, Hostage Scenario, Arms Race [get a kill, get the next weapon], Deathmatch, Battle Royale, 2vs2, and tons of community servers with various features) and runs on almost any PC. It doesn't come with a half-assed single-player campaign, it's cheap, equally suited for casual and competitive players, and has a huge community. So it's a recommendation from me, with the caveat that not everyone will like it! :-)
