translation_en: [h1]A game you love and hate at the same time[/h1] [b]Love:[/b] 100 hours in, it's the game I've played the most on STEAM. Currently [b]hovering around Official Matchmaking Gold Nova 3, 5E Play 1300-1400[/b], it's really fun. When I first started, everyone was running and gunning, with any gun, just running and gunning. A [strilke]fucking[/strilke] bro told me you can't run and gun (except for SMGs), so I tried playing SMGs, and I gotta say, the UMP is truly the GOAT. Later on, after playing more, I started getting into rifles like the AK and M4, but I still prefer playing with the AWP. Even though I suck a lot of the time, pulling off sick plays is still super exciting, and every time I play a clutch my adrenaline spikes and my heart goes pounding. Every time my bro watches me play a clutch he's like: "Don't stress, don't stress." Winning a 1v3, 1v4 or even 1v5 feels amazing, I guess this is the charm of esports. [b]Hate:[/b] Why does a fair competitive game have so many cheaters? Back in Silver I'd only occasionally see a cheater, and every time I ran into one I'd let loose a torrent of abuse, saying every dirty word in the book. If the cheater was on our team I'd TK him to kill him (got banned 5 or 6 times for killing cheater teammates) and hop on the mic to flame him. Once I hit Gold Nova, there were seriously so many cheaters, 4 out of 5 matches had them. I went from cursing people out, to being sarcastic, to just going numb, feeling nothing anymore. Cheaters became a totally normal thing in my eyes. Even though I still get super pissed, what's the point? Cursing out their family in front of a cold screen isn't actually gonna get their family cursed. I'm numb. When the enemy starts spinning I even ask my teammates if we have any cheaters, and when both the enemy and our team are spinning I'll save up to buy my teammates auto-snipers. Seriously, as long as everyone is spinning, it turns into another kind of fair. One match the whole enemy team of 5 was spinning and 4 guys on our team were spinning, I felt like I was completely useless, could only save up to buy them guns. I'm a hypocritical piece of shit, I simp for cheaters, but only when the enemy has cheaters. If the enemy doesn't have a cheater and someone on our team turns hacks on, I'll still TK him to torture him. I can't take it anymore, go play 5E (not an ad for B5, Perfect World platform is fine too), fewer cheaters, and it plays more comfortably. But it still sucks, I want to grind Official Matchmaking ranks, I want to get medals, but whatever, you queue in and it's all cheaters. Ran into 5E with a placement of 1400, dropped to 1300 later because I played like shit, and now I'm just hovering there. [b]What I want to say:[/b] Can't rank up, I'm too bad. If you're bad, just practice. To break down CSGO ranking into details, it's basically [b]aim[/b], [b]gamesense[/b], [b]util[/b]. Gamesense is something you gain from day-to-day accumulation. Pros like s1mple have 20k+ hours of hard work paying off, my 100 hours doesn't even compare, so starting with aim and util is the best breakthrough. You can practice both aim and util in the Workshop, and I'll recommend a few maps I think are useful. [i]Aim:[/i] 1. Aim Botz-Training (It's a really good map, I go in and tap 1000 heads every day before playing Official Matchmaking, I believe day-to-day accumulation yields results) 2. FAST AIM/REFLEX MAP-TRAINING[DUST2] (Enemies run at you in this, I can practice shooting while moving) 3. Training Center1.5c (Super useful map, has a lot of content inside, explore it slowly. I use it to practice reaction time) [i]Util:[/i] For this part I genuinely recommend all of Yprac's maps, you can practice util, check angles, crosshair placement, you can practice anything inside (I go to Bilibili to find tutorials and practice them in the free practice mode inside the maps) Map names: Yprac xxx (English name of the map) For example Mirage: Yprac Mirage Guide 2021/4/8 Edit: Yprac's regular angle-clearing practice and stuff is seriously useful, can quickly get you familiar with common T or CT spots, and takes your pre-aim to the next level! [i]Gamesense:[/i] For this part I usually like watching pro player DEMOs. I recommend stanning a pro player you like and learning his gamesense, aim, util, etc. I personally like ZywOo, I'll watch his DEMOs before eating, sleeping, or when I have free time, you can learn a lot of things. Recommending a few uploaders who post DEMOs, I don't know much about the pro scene either, can only recommend the ones I follow (Bilibili uploaders): 1. CSGO Machine (Lots of people like him, but I haven't watched him yet, I'll recommend him anyway) 2. CSGO-DEMO (Standing out for being chill, focuses the whole match on one player, skips the footage after they die, makes it easier to pay attention to a pro player) 3. CSGO Highlights (I checked and a lot of the DEMOs seem to include all sorts of big and small match DEMOs, if you don't want to slowly search inside CSGO you can just look in this uploader, they're all match recordings with live casting) 4. Bu Tai Zheng De Wai Wai (This little missy doesn't have many followers, but every single video is packed with dry knowledge, worth watching and studying repeatedly. Recent videos like the four types of peeks, rushing, fast clearing Mirage A-2nd floor, etc. (The little missy's voice is friggin' adorable)) 2021/3/20 It sucks, stuck in Official Matchmaking Gold Nova 4, dropped back down to Gold Nova 3. Clawed my way back to Gold Nova 4 just yesterday. Feels like practicing aim still does a lot, but lately I seem to have hit a plateau? (I'm a trash tier player) Feels like I can't win aim duels, the more I play the more I lose my groove... 2021/4/7 Feels like I'm not as confident anymore, don't dare to take direct duels, started caring about KD Rating. Lately I want to try taking confident gunfights, don't want to always stand at the very back when the whole team is rushing banana. To get stronger you just gotta take the fights. 2021/4/8 Insane, yesterday right after typing the stuff above I went and played a 5E match, actually managed to run wild and destroy in a 1500 lobby. Been practicing peeks lately, feels like learning util threw my aim off a tiny bit. Gotta be confident, you gotta dare to take the fights, family! 2021/4/20 300 hours now, currently trying out B5, played 4 matches so far, lost one, went on a rampage in one. 2021/4/24 B5 placement 1015 rating, 5E 1600 rating. Feels like B5 is too hard to play. 2021/5/29 Grinded B5 up to 1400, rating is 0.93. 2021/9/4 Lately playing 5E non-prime, currently 2400, rating 1.21.

translation_en: A friendly suggestion to China: The web is full of games that scam schoolkids out of their money and just run away, but you don't crack down on those. Every time you click a webpage, it's full of games with broken-ass Mandarin, but you don't crack down on those. Games where you can literally buy hacks right off the official website, and you don't crack down on those. You're cracking down on AAA games? Violence? Porn? Take a look at the banner ads all over domestic websites, every single one of them is more exposed than anything on STEAM, you don't give a shit about any of that, but you come after STEAM. If you've got so much damn free time, why don't you go regulate the Chinese film industry? It's more deformed than Lu Benwei. Look at your CCTV, then look at the BBC, what a gap. You stomp out with your own feet the cultural confidence you built up yourselves. Why? Because instead of reforming your own management methods, you drag a massive platform down into the mud with you. Even though a lot of Chinese gamers just use STEAM as a launcher, it at least gave people some awareness of buying legit copies. We finally made a little progress and now we're getting hammered right back to square one. Are you encouraging everyone to play pirated games instead? Let alone talk about so-called democracy, why can't you just implement a rating system? A rating system would solve most of these problems. Is this shit fun for you? You "experts" are seriously big-brained. Since you spend every day messing with useless crap like this, why don't you just shut down the internet entirely and stop letting normal people use it? Why not just organize everyone to shout slogans and farm fields every day??? Or just straight up regress back to the primitive society already. What I actually give a shit about is if the games I buy become unplayable, who the hell am I gonna get compensation from? Perfect World, or the state? But I guess at the end of the day, it'll just mean us players who insist on buying legit copies take a total loss for nothing, and then get thoroughly mocked by some condescending real-life pirate fanboys. Big brain moves, seriously. Good job, my country, haha. Emperor Qin, this prosperous age is just as you wished. Some people and their friends grew up playing Legend of Mir and CS as kids, and none of them went out chopping people up or committing crimes. Nowadays, bratty kids watch Pleasant Goat and roast other kids, so is it really the fault of games and anime? Or is it the fault of irresponsible parenting and schooling? Everyone knows the truth in their hearts. You're just gonna abandon the 100-year goal of socialism like this? What even is the Chinese Dream? Study hard, físico-out (flee the country). Games belong to the ninth art. Any major masterpiece inherently contains the thoughts and Dao of its creator. But given our country's currently closed-off values, foreign reflections on the future and all sorts of bizarre fantasies are simply unacceptable to the SAPPRFT. As for domestic games right now, due to STEAM and console factors and all kinds of other things, you can still make an absolute killing just by churning out garbage. They know that as long as the game's quality is barely passable, and they design some "micro-operation" flexing mechanics inside the game, along with all kinds of horny original art, and all kinds of chuunibyou character models and lines, they can scam people out of their money. The plot of the game itself has to be convoluted and devoid of depth, simple and easy to understand. Producing crap like this actually makes way more money than games where you seriously put thought into the plot. STEAM seemed like it was known by a lot of people in China, but in reality, before PUBG came out, if you walked down the street basically nobody knew what STEAM even was. Actually, real-name verification in China is already way ahead of foreign countries. UnionPay and WeChat Pay both require a national ID card, so why still drag your feet on rolling out a ratings system? Because right now, whether something passes censorship is completely up to the arbitrary final say of the Ministry of Culture and SAPPRFT. There are no actual laws or regulations that determine whether a game passes review. Back in the day, a domestic single-player game developer made a wuxia game and submitted it for review. Since they were a domestic developer, they knew the censorship system inside and out, so before submitting it they stripped out all the blood and dismemberment effects, and even turned all the corpses black. But even then it still couldn't pass review. The censors said that the player character in this game could just serve ten days in prison after killing someone, which could easily cause a negative social impact. Later on, through round after round of changes, it turned into a wuxia game where you can literally only ride horses. Meanwhile, Tencent's Moonlight Blade lets you slaughter human enemies without facing a single consequence, letting you just keep right on butchering. Doesn't that cause an even bigger social impact? Yet Moonlight Blade passed review. Why does this happen? Tencent rakes in cash by the day, they can afford to pay up, whereas that small developer had pretty much no money left after finishing the game. So the development of Chinese single-player games isn't about how good your production quality is, nor is it about whether your marketing is on point—the first thing that matters is whether you can afford to pay the bribe. And what do relevant Chinese departments claim their basis is when reviewing things? It's the so-called social mainstream, the Core Socialist Values. What does this kind of thing feel like? Ancient monarchs would always find a statement consistent with legal authority to justify their power: the Mandate of Heaven, "I am the True Dragon," and that all their power was bestowed upon them by the heavens. The Core Socialist Values serve this exact purpose—a tool to give themselves an illegitimate power and obtained benefits that lack legal basis, wrapped in a seemingly reasonable statement. Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Macao are Special Administrative Regions; their social, economic, political, and cultural systems are completely different from the mainland. Has anyone ever thought about why that is? Actually, it's very simple: the crying child gets the milk. Take Hong Kong, for instance. If they had been handed the mainland system back when they were handed over in '97, they would have gone on massive strikes and student boycotts, completely grinding normal societal operations to a halt. Plus, back then, plenty of eyes both domestic and international were watching Hong Kong, so they became a Special Administrative Region. And us mainlanders? When they blocked the foreign internet, we endured it. When they censored World of Warcraft, we endured that too. We've never raised our voices to speak up for our own rights. And now they're escalating things further—even a Chinese version of STEAM is coming out. At best, we're just gonna get a Chinese store, and the payment methods and regional low-price discounts we currently have on the international store are gonna get ported right over to it. If we silently endure this time, what about next time? Are we seriously gonna turn into the North Korean Kwangmyong network? A lot of people just treat all this bullshit like it's a matter of course—whether it's blocking the foreign internet, censoring games, *Baozou Dashijian*, or now the Chinese version of STEAM. But what's the reality? In Europe, when terrorists are active on Instagram and Twitter, do they just simply build a firewall to block those social media apps? No, they fight a cyber war against those terrorists and drive them off those social media platforms. If that's the case, why can't the CCP do it? Just because building a firewall is cheaper? Are our rights and our places for entertainment and leisure worth less than the cost of fighting a cyber war? Do Chinese people have to just compromise and swallow their shit while foreigners get to protect their rights? Please spread these words everywhere. Speak up for your rights and for STEAM. I don't know which kind of "being represented" is worse: the kind where they ban and censor World of Warcraft, *Baozou Dashijian*, and other free media, social apps, and single-player online games and claim "this is the will of the people and the gamers," or whether the things I'm posting today represent the interests of STEAM gamers. But I do know that everything I'm saying comes straight from the bottom of my heart, spoken with a mixture of a hundred different bitter feelings after experiencing all this garbage. I'm saying this with a clear conscience, whereas they definitely can't say the same. I hope everyone spreads these words. I know it's nine times out of ten useless, but how can we stay silent and not cry out just because our voices are small? As an ordinary resident living in China who loves STEAM and loves the joy STEAM brings, this is all I can do. Thank you everyone. Actually, being an obedient subject has zero benefits and only drawbacks. Because if you show obedience, they need to provide you with even less. Since you've already expressed your total compliance, why the hell would they give a shit about your demands? As for so-called troublemakers, the regime has to provide them with way more stuff just to maintain its rule and appease the populace. That's just how it is domestically: when they blocked the foreign internet and censored games, we complied. And the result? Now a Chinese version of STEAM is about to drop, because since you acted like compliant sheep, they figure if they launch it, they launch it, since you'll just keep right on obeying. Whenever I think about the First Amendment of the United States and how STEAM as a platform for freedom of speech allows me to speak out here, while the CCP is about to roll out a Chinese version of STEAM to rip all of that away, I get a flood of bitter and complicated emotions. Actually, what I want when I speak out isn't much. I'm not delusional enough to think that capitalism automatically makes life better, you still have to work hard yourself, you still have to grind for a dozen years just to buy a house and a car. All I want is a few less restrictions and controls, and for the government to respect the rights of its citizens. But even something as small as that is so damn hard. A hundred years ago in Beijing, Qing dynasty subjects were helping foreigners hold the ladder to climb over the wall, and a hundred years later today, foreigners are helping Chinese people hold the ladder to climb over the wall. translation_en: I think everyone already knows what Counter-Strike is and what it's eaten with (shit). But I have my own personal opinion about this project: 1. First and foremost — personally for me, this is the most nerve-wracking game I've ever encountered (sometimes even worse than Dota 2), I've raged harder here than in the Donbas. 2. Despite the first and foremost, it drags you in like a swamp, because you see an imaginary potential in yourself when you actually carry matches for armless teammates. I won't lie, there are good players too, usually not on your team, but still, they exist. 3. At any suspicious death you blame the enemies for cheating, that's a fact, even though sometimes you pull off VAC moments yourself, after which you sit there in shock at yourself (never used cheats and still don't know and don't want to know how it's done). 4. There's a charm to playing with friends. Then you get to hear your whole team burning up in Discord, or everyone praising each other if the match is going your way. Also, importantly, if you're left alone to clutch, a little party starts among your friends in Discord. 5. The weirdest ranking system in the entire gaming industry. Either you carry, always sitting at 1st-2nd place on the scoreboard and you don't get ranked up even for a win streak of 5-10 games, or you don't log into the game for a month or more, then you come back, start a game, play like an absolute piece of shit while being at the very bottom of the scoreboard, but you somehow magically win the match anyway, and you instantly get ranked up (that's a little life hack for those who want to rank up, tested on myself several times). 6. There are more Turks and Poles than people on the planet. But lately I've started noticing them less, and thank God for that. I have nothing against them, but I mostly ran into toxic ones. Bottom line: a typical online team shooter that has both negative and positive emotions. Why are the negative ones first? Because there are more of them.

translation_en: Dazhu has been playing CS for fourteen years. He met Cuihua while playing CS 1.6. That was ten years ago. Cuihua was the exact match of his dream girl, her braided hair falling all the way down to her waist. Dazhu would often have a secondhand cigarette hanging from his mouth and sneak glances at Cuihua. Naturally, as the only girl playing CS in the shady internet cafe, Cuihua was surrounded by pros, and Goudan, the king of fast-zooming, was universally acknowledged as the number one in the cafe. Goudan would often drag Cuihua along to play against the others in the cafe, which of course included Dazhu, and Dazhu was more than happy to suck up to Cuihua, jumping around repeatedly and trying his best to stick his head into her graceful bullet trajectories. Naturally, Dazhu's K/D was at the bottom year-round, and his super-jump bullet-fishing moves were mocked by the little kids in the shady net cafe. Yet Dazhu wasn't sad; seeing the smile on Cuihua's face when she headshot him made him feel like it was all worth it. One day, Dazhu had just sneaked out of the shady net cafe. Seeming to be in a good mood, he wasn't in any rush to go home. He squatted down against a corner of the wall, casually picked up a cigarette butt, and stuck it in his mouth. He reminisced about Cuihua killing him over and over, and about the sneers and jeers from the brats watching around them. He let out a chuckle, took a deep drag of the cigarette butt, ground it out on the floor, and patted his pants as he got up to go home. Right then, he saw Cuihua and Goudan coming out of the net cafe, holding hands like they were super close. Dazhu's eyes went slightly bloodshot, his brain stopped working, and he tiptoed after Goudan and Cuihua. Not long after they walked away from the net cafe, Cuihua linked arms with Goudan. Blood rushed to Dazhu's head, but he didn't flip out; he figured he might have misunderstood Cuihua, so he didn't take any action. Soon after, Goudan took Cuihua and turned into a place called "Happy Tun Hotel." Dazhu let out a sigh of relief. So they were going to watch TV. Time flies, and five years later, on this particular day, while Dazhu was showing off his movement, a brat behind him asked why he was still playing CS. CS's graphics and textures were totally blown out of the water by CF. Dazhu felt like his sense of superiority had been beaten to a pulp, but switching to CF just because of that was way too lame. He considered if there were any other reasons to transition into a great CF player, and later realized there were none. He still curled up in the corner playing his CS, moving from net cafe matches to platform matches. He played his rank up, higher and higher, higher and higher. He even spotted Goudan's ID in there: |x|FastZoom|x|Batian. Typical Goudan, Dazhu thought. Another two years passed, and Dazhu had climbed to a ridiculously high rank on the platform. Cheaters or no cheaters, his movement ensured he never took more than 2 bullets in a single round. Many people still sticking with CS had vaguely heard of this movement king who moved around effortlessly amidst a hail of bullets. Dazhu was getting ready to pull another all-nighter. At three in the morning, Goudan suddenly walked into the net cafe, dragging along a woman dressed up like a demolition turkey. Her smoky eye makeup and teased pink hair made Dazhu a little nauseous, but he knew this was the most popular look in the hood. Goudan scanned the room and naturally spotted Dazhu in the corner. He walked over happily and said to Dazhu, "Why are you still playing CS? Come on, go pick up chicks with your big bro!" Dazhu looked at the turkey next to him and naturally felt a bit scared. "Big Bro Goudan, you go have fun, I'll play a couple rounds of CS." Goudan spat on the ground and said bitterly, "Such a loser." He went to the counter to pay for five bucks of net time and sat down right next to Dazhu. Dazhu felt a bit awkward and wanted to make conversation. "Big Bro Goudan, how come you're online so late?" "Done working, came out to stretch my legs and chill," Goudan said impatiently. The turkey chick behind him had a cigarette hanging from her mouth with a whatever expression. "Play a couple rounds?" "Alright." Dazhu invited Goudan, and the two of them opened a room on the platform to party up. Two rounds later, Dazhu was still in first place while Goudan was dead last the whole time. Goudan slammed his keyboard with a smack—"What a piece of shit game!"—and left in a huff with the turkey chick without even logging off his PC. Dazhu logged off his PC and spent a buck-fifty to buy a bottle of mineral water. "My fucking life is so damn good," Dazhu thought to himself. A week later, the CS platform ran a survey, and Dazhu filled in his info, hoping to win something. Things gradually took a turn for the better; he won a Valve mega-bundle and could finally play genuine games. Dazhu saw that the newest CS in it was CS:GO, and felt he could finally match the graphics of those CF brats. The next day, based on the info he provided, a manager from the platform reached out to him. He asked Dazhu if he wanted to play pro, and Dazhu said, yes. Dazhu really wanted to. He kept thinking about making money, because deep down in his heart was hidden something that could be called a dream. Over the next few years, Dazhu played in a lot of tournaments. He was also turning 25, and his reflexes and aim couldn't keep up with the youngsters anymore. Today was his last match, and also his first time playing abroad. He felt this international tournament wasn't any different from playing in the shady net cafe back in the day; he just wanted to take this massive prize money and do that one thing he had always wanted to do. Stepping onto the stage, he rubbed his hands together, as if he saw Cuihua sitting across from him in the shady net cafe all those years ago. He took a deep breath, looked up, and saw the $1M banner for the major championship winning team. It seemed he had faith and a decision in his heart. translation_en: I thought about it for a long time, and finally decided to write a review. Maybe it's a bit long, but if you've had the same experience as me, I hope reading it can bring you some warmth. (I want to say first, I'm still a student, still in school, that's right, I racked up over 300 hours in three years. Some people say I'm coming on here playing the victim, believe it or don't, I didn't cheat, I don't flame, a clean player, flame all you want.) In October 2016 I started my CS:GO journey. Back then, 56 RMB was a few days' food money for me as a student. Back then, there were no more than ten people playing this game in any net cafe. Now it's been three and a half years, from the old versions of dust2 and cache to the new ones, from dying on sight to clutching 1v5 turnarounds, from a total newbie to learning how to throw utility, hold angles, and gamesense, and slowly learning how to awp. This game kept me company through the lows in my life, bringing me happiness time and time again. But all of that changed after April 27th. On the 27th at 7 AM, an email from Valve support woke me up from my sleep. I was VAC banned! I was shocked. Three and a half years of playtime, and I have never used any cheats, hacks, or any third-party plugins. I was at a complete loss. Because of this, I searched Tieba, Zhihu, Baidu, Bilibili looking for any way to fix the problem, and then I submitted a support ticket following the methods online. The entire day after I submitted the ticket, I kept thinking about why on earth I got VACed. I checked my last matchmaking game, it was on April 4th, my score was terrible and we lost. Could it be that playing casual and deathmatch for two months would get me banned? On the night of the 28th, I found a group on Tieba full of people who were false-banned in March and April. I joined the group and shared my experience with everyone, comforting and encouraging each other. I think CS:GO means a lot to me, not just the skins in my inventory—those things are one of a kind to me—but more importantly, that time that money can't buy. I know I'm not the only one who got false-banned. People on Tieba call us fatherless, call us kamikazes, say we definitely cheated. If you were also false-banned, and you know for a fact you didn't cheat, don't give up, ignore other people's trash talk. You can join our false-ban group. In the group there are friends with inventories worth anywhere from tens to tens of thousands whose accounts were false-banned. We will share our experiences with you and offer you warmth and help. If you need to, you can leave a comment under this review and I'll reply. Good luck.

translation_en: After over 12,000 hours that I've been allowed to spend with the games in this series over the last 12 years, it's finally time to give a verdict on the least old installment. CS:GO has already been behind us for almost 8 years and I've spent a few thousand hours with this game, some more and some less enjoyable. I don't regret it either. I think the game itself is very well made and Valve is still working a lot on the game. I really like that it's directly designed for competitive play. Back in the day (with CS 1.6 and CS:S), it was quite annoying when you had to count the rounds during a PCW or ESL match, switch the team manually after halftime, and restart the match with zBlock. This is no longer necessary since the game handles everything. It's also cool that there's a direct deathmatch and gungame mode. Although with the predecessors and dedicated servers, that was also very good. I must admit that in all that time I only played on "official" servers by Valve and never on dedicated servers. Therefore I can't say anything about that area. CS:GO plays very well and anyone who already knew the predecessors didn't have a hard time learning this game. The basic principle has always stayed the same. Gameplay-wise you absolutely cannot complain about the game. In itself, CS:GO is the embodiment of what I always wanted in a Counter-Strike title. But now we come to the part that bothers me extremely and why I am very torn about whether I recommend this game or not: As already criticized in a few other reviews, you notice that Valve has gotten extremely greedy for money in recent years. I'll quote a review here that hits the nail on the head: [quote=de_SIRt-sToRm] Those cocksuckers at Valve are only out for the money anymore [...] You can get skins for weapons by earning cases and you have to buy the keys for big money, mostly there's nothing but crap in these cases and way below the value of a key, and to top it all off, Valve even makes more money through the Free to P(l)ay system where Prime status no longer has to be laboriously earned and activated with a mobile number, but can simply be bought for the price that CS:GO costed before! [/quote] By making CS:GO Free 2 Play, they gave the game the coup de grâce. Just for fun, I made a new account and checked what the game would be like as a clueless beginner. It's a disaster. CS:GO has had a hacker problem for many years, but ever since it's Free 2 Play, they don't even try to hide their hacks anymore. As soon as they lose a round, the rage settings for the aimbot are loaded and the match can be written off. If I were starting CS:GO completely fresh and had no clue about it .. I would delete the game after 2 or 3 matches and never touch it again. To come back to the skins: In itself, I don't think the whole thing is fundamentally bad. Back in CS:S, I sometimes had skins too to mess around a bit with that kind of stuff. Back then you downloaded the skins from gamebanana.com and inserted them via models/materials. But you notice that Valve wants to squeeze as much money out of the players as possible with it. For my part, apart from free skins you sometimes got, I've never had any because I don't see the point in paying money for something like that. Why some people even pay a few hundred bucks for a rare knife is a mystery to me. But if someone thinks the cash is worth it to them, go ahead. Nobody is being forced, after all. What do I want to say in conclusion? For experienced players like me or many others, CS:GO is an absolute must and it's also super fun to follow the pro scene (ESL Pro League, CS:GO Majors, Intel Extreme Masters, Dreamhack and whatever else is out there) and I'm glad that Counter-Strike is still holding its ground right at the top of eSports to this day. But if I were a bloody beginner in this area, I would keep my hands off the game. There are better alternatives. As a beginner, it has become completely unplayable, especially due to the massive hacker problem.

For example, playing Dust 2 as CT, the enemy team had two players holding A-Long during the last full buy round and liked to play an A-Plaza AWP. Another example: if you know the enemy team likes to rush, have everyone coordinate their holding spots, and once you lock down a site where someone gets a kill, go push that side. Instead of dying in silence, or blaming your teammates for being noobs, actively call some simple strategies to dictate the pace. This not only boosts morale, but some good opening strategies can win you a lot of crucial rounds. 2. "Why does the enemy's VIP/mid AWPer always manage to kill me? When you start thinking like this, you've already lost half the game, or deep down inside, you don't even want to win anymore. "We all have bad days" is my favorite thing to say to console teammates who are beating themselves up over mistakes. Everyone has times when they're not playing well. Maybe you aren't actually worse than him, it's just that today, after finishing a hard day of work or school, your aim is genuinely a bit trash. At times like this, you have to calm down and use weapons you're good at besides the AWP (and of course, not the Desert Eagle either). Even though this post is aimed at average players, I still want to say a couple more things. In the current map pool consisting of 7 maps, CT side double AWPs have become mainstream for pro teams trying to win critical rounds. Generally, pro teams split duties between a primary and secondary AWPer (like everyone's familiar with f0rest and bot allu, or JW and olofmeister). However, running double AWPs on the T side is pretty rare (if you're gonna forcefully bring up exceptions like Fnatic running 5 AWPs or NiP running 5 AWPs, I can't really argue with that, but I'll just say those are rare edge cases). Not only does it slow down the tempo, but it also lowers your margin for error, and if you play even slightly poorly, you'll just feed the enemy team economy. Take Inferno as an example. The enemy team tries to hit A at the start of the round, putting a ton of pressure on A. Your co-site B player rotates to help A. Here's an incorrect example: you're holding B alone in a clutch, hiding near the sandbags, sitting there completely silently without looking at anything. This puts your teammates at a massive disadvantage. So the correct play here is to use two-way / multi-directional cover to handle the clutch. For instance, the triangular box (Triple Box) is arguably the most broken piece of cover on Inferno. Strictly speaking, it's a three-way cover because you can also peek through the gap in the middle. If you don't have smokes or flashes, you can stand quietly behind Triple Box without rushing to shoot, while immediately calling for rotators. Wait until you hear footsteps approaching (trust your headset to tell the difference between running on Banana, jumping on Barbecue, and footsteps about to check Triple Box). If you don't get it, put yourself in their shoes: what's your clearing order when you first run onto B site? After getting one kill, **do not** wide swing, overpeek, or re-peek. If someone aggressively pushes you, switch to the other side of the multi-directional cover to deal with the next guy (the goal is to always expose yourself to only one gun at a time). If you don't mess up your aim, you can kill the guy showing his side and the other guy who's just realizing you're at Triple Box, successfully pulling off a 1-for-2. translation_en: Not a game for everyone, if you're faint of heart and play games to actually have fun, you should scroll past this. For kids, it's mostly an excuse to show off, 1v1 you, and shit on you based on how many skins you have and what your rank is. For the older crowd, it's a reason to challenge you to a fair fight because (oh gods) you dared ask this drunken animal to stop screaming in voice chat so you can actually hear footsteps, and next thing you know he's triggered, has already doxxed your address and is buying a ticket to your city. The community dictates most of it, and unfortunately this isn't a game it can be proud of. Every time you get a kill, some zoomer goes absolutely apeshit in voice chat screaming that you're a cheater and "How the fuck did you kill me?". You also very often run into people who judge what kind of person you are based on your skill—maybe I'm phrasing it wrong, but I think you get the point. The second you miss a shot, a torrent of non-stop swearing and insults comes your way (this happened in my first 10 hours, pretty vivid memories). However, I did like the competitive matchmaking system itself. The balance of power on both sides is roughly equal; it's one of those games where how much you spent on microtransactions doesn't matter nearly as much as how well you can actually play. I got my rank at Gold Nova Master and now I'm Distinguished Master Guardian. If you know how to keep your cool and a clear head, love competitive games, and are looking for something that isn't pay-to-win, but rather "you learned, so you earned the right to win," then I definitely recommend it. If you take everything to heart, I wouldn't recommend it because you'll get dragged and put down faster than you can even get your rank. If there was a 10-point rating system, I'd give it an 8/10 because, for instance, some servers don't have enough resources for smooth gameplay, and there are some bugs too (in rare cases hits don't register or packets just get lost). On rare occasions it also throws you into lobbies with way too high or way too low ranks—and that's just rating the game itself. The game fulfills its purpose, and that purpose is simple: to give people a chance to compete on a level playing field with equal chances to win.

translation_en: It's hard for me to answer the question of whether CS:GO is fun or not. Repetitive and outdated gameplay rules, boring sound design and graphics, and a pitifully small official map pool. It lacks innovation, and I've wasted decades of my life playing as T and CT. It's not fun at all; I once played against bots for four hours straight and skipped a whole day of KZ, just so I wouldn't die like a total noob. Spending thousands of hours in deathmatches, aim training, and jump servers has just numbed me. The number of competitive maps can be counted on one hand, and matches just cycle endlessly through these few maps. I've spent half an hour perfecting a single smoke grenade lineup, and spent entire afternoons and evenings running maps and practicing coordination. I often smash my desk and slap my thighs when my aim goes to shit, and I still vividly remember the time I got so pissed off at a mistake I smashed a mouse. I hate losing; I've abandoned matches just because we lost a single round, and I've flown into rages at my teammates during games. However, I don't always lose. When we took third place in an offline tournament, or beat our opponents in campus league scrims, I was insanely happy. When I grew stronger through the grind of aim training and KZ, I felt immense pride. Even just successfully throwing a smoke grenade sends a wave of excitement deep through my heart. Maybe that's the magic of CSGO. I've suffered and been pissed off, but I've kept going for the moments of happiness and fleeting joy. So, I really can't tell you if CSGO is actually fun, nor can I be sure if you'll like it. But once you dive deep into it and feel its charm, it becomes a game that stays with you for years, or even a lifetime. Aside from cash, the prize for that offline tournament included a mouse—a white SteelSeries Kinzu V2. It's the exact one I smashed, and I still keep it to this day.

translation_en: I remember the days when we'd gather with friends at school during computer science class and set up five-on-five matches in Counter-Strike 1.6, time flying by unnoticed. Back then, nobody thought that a regular competitive game would grow into something bigger and turn into a total circus where cheaters are the norm, nice weapon textures are a high status symbol, and regular players turn into clowns. I understand, of course, that most players don't have any specific goals in mind when they log into this game, just coming here to relax and have a little fun, but what's happening in the game right now is a downright toxic circus. I'd like to share my opinion on this matter. [h1]Gameplay:[/h1] I remember the release day of the new Counter-Strike: Global Offensive very well, I was a freshman in college and I remember that day clearly. By then I had more or less mastered Steam as a gaming platform and bought the game on release day, and to my luck, didn't start playing it right away. As I understand it now, it was for the best, because many of my friends who started their journey in this dumpster at that time deeply regretted it later. At the initial stage of its life, the updated competitive shooter featured a light and quite pleasing-to-the-eye picture. It seemed like all the best parts from the previous installments had been taken and improved, plus a little something new added. True, I didn't pay much attention to it back then, most of the maps were memorized like the multiplication table, and everything around me looked slightly different. The first major update called "Arms Deal" dropped in mid-2013, introducing weapon skin collections to the game. Since that day, the competitive and, most importantly, classic game we were all used to started turning into a clown show with brightly colored guns. Over the past few years, CS:GO received minor updates in the form of patches, content updates with new skin drops, UI changes, and even its own battle royale mode. In a word, on the inside, the game remained in the exact same state as on its release day and visually hasn't changed at all. All the content added by the developers are the so-called operations with various missions and replenishing the arsenal of cases with different skins. Well, following the established tradition, this game is wildly popular in esports, which constantly supports its promotion in real life, attracting new players with wide advertising and great accessibility, especially since the game recently became free-to-play. For the rest, the game is supported by its huge gaming community with YouTube content and marketplace prices for items. As the saying goes: As long as the Valve spins, the money wins! For most players, buying an expensive item in this game is something prestigious, a way to show off what a high-roller they are to a large audience, while for others it's a genuine way to make money. Well, the evil corporation Valve (sarcasm) just gets to bathe in cash. Otherwise, it's a typical competitive and, most importantly, team-based shooter where tactics and teamwork decide everything. Just like all other similar games, nothing new can be said here. As for the ranked mode, or as the locals call it "MM", it has long since strayed from its name and nowadays it's nothing more than a battle between cheaters and sweaty tryhards. Generally speaking, Counter-Strike: GO is a game where it's considered normal to grind to Global Elite with cheats and then show off in front of everyone like, look what a pro I am! Long story short, any competitive drive gets lost because of this, and that's why it's easier to run around on some community server with a good admin than to waste your nerve cells (which, by the way, don't grow back) on some half-witted kid playing with third-party software. There are thousands of them in the game right now, and due to the lack of a functioning anti-cheat system, they feel quite comfortable. Which Valve apparently doesn't give a damn about, since people keep buying cases and keys! [h1]Technical side:[/h1] As I mentioned above, the main problem of this game is cheaters. The game features an automated cheat detection system called Valve Anti Cheat, or VAC for short. In reality, it's only automated on paper and apparently can only ban players using already exposed, free software that's in its database, while it's completely unable to detect paid stuff. It's rare that during a game against a cheater, they get disconnected and sent to the permanent ban-hammer zone. In most cases, these morons last anywhere from a week to half a year and, you know, feel quite at ease. Sure, you can spam reports on their profile, but right now it's ineffective because most reports are thrown out as a precaution against almost everyone at the start of a round, making it apparently much harder to track down the actual rule-breaker. You'd think it's long past time to simply abandon this system and resort to more effective protection tools like Easy Anti Cheat and BattlEye. But no, they have to invent something new and stubbornly insist like a ram that their system is unique and works like clockwork. Instead, they introduced the so-called Overwatch system, where players are given the opportunity to act as this very patrol and hand out their own verdict to a potential violator. In short, the more verdicts against a single person from such "investigators," the higher the chance that the VAC system will automatically issue a ban on that player's profile. The principle of this system is simple: a player watches a recorded demo and leaves their verdict (vote) at the end of the replay. Many people hand out guilty verdicts on innocent people just for fun, causing them to get permanently banned. My friend already had a case like this when, because of his genuine skill, he got banned via the Overwatch system. After that, he simply dropped this game and looks like it's for good. That was the happiest sound of a holiday."[/h1] [code]This review was written on 2019-11-30 as a nomination for the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/steamawards/nominations?snr=1_4_autumnsale__autumn2019-SteamAwards]2019 STEAM Awards[/url] [b]"Labor of Love Award"[/b]: This game has been out for a while now. The game team is well past the delivery of their creative offspring. But they are great parents, continuing to nurture and support their creation. Even after all these years, right up to today, the game continues to roll out new content. Your nomination: [b]Counter-Strike: Global Offensive[/b][/code] How good is this new-era, now-free CS? No matter how refined my review, it can't sum up its stormy journey over the past twenty-something years. Four words: [b]a classic with endless replay value[/b], I think that's enough. If you still ask me, what else is there? Then I can only answer you— [list] [*][h1]It's not my favorite, but it became my memory[/h1] [/list] First is [url=http://music.163.com/song?id=60263&userid=1470527593]that song[/url] that was being passed around in the forums back then: [code] I'm hiding in B site, sniper rifle in hand Hoping to snipe a few T's planting the bomb You're walking closer, I hear two sets of sounds I'm caught off guard, left staring like a clown I should've been at A site, shouldn't have been at B Seeing all of you, coming to sandwich me That way it'd be way easier for me to counterattack Give me the power to blind scope! He must really love to snipe, outdoing me too Killing me only took a single second, it's true He must really love to snipe, way better at sniping than me Not like me out here, blind-scoping randomly Can't even kill an enemy~~~ [/code] And back when there were no virtual discs, "Half-Life" was a mandatory install on every PC in the net café—years later I found out its real name was "Half-Life"—[url=https://bbs.nga.cn/read.php?tid=16252662&fav=7d32549b]Ban Shuai Qi[/url]. And I found out that symbol wasn't the Chinese character "入", but the Greek letter "λ"—Lambda. The game also spun off from a mod, and versions started upgrading bit by bit: CS1.3 → CS1.5 → CS1.6. In the first few years of the new century, there were internet cafés dedicated purely to playing CS. I still can't forget the name of one, called "Apollo Concentration Camp". With the external speakers blasting, playing CS there was exceptionally satisfying. Even the people standing around waiting for a terminal would watch with burning blood, thoroughly hooked. It wasn't until college, seeing those CS gods among my classmates, that made me understand the bittersweet realization of changing an ID name from "Who do I fear" to "I'm afraid of death". [b]All that happiness, looking back in memory, seems so simple and pure...[/b] My scattered memories more or less dissolved into this video I bookmarked a few years ago: [url=https://www.bilibili.com/video/av723116]Counter-Strike [CS] Ragic's Farewell Season, Uploader: Call Me Old Zhang[/url] Finally, let me share a [b]true story[/b]. *[Wine glass]* In 2003, in middle school, one weekday after class, a few classmates who constantly hung out at net cafés invited me and my deskmate YJ to go to the aforementioned "Apollo Concentration Camp". Although I was a netizen who had been hitting the web for at least five years, I had a good habit of studying hard on weekdays and not going to net cafés. This good habit stemmed from my allowance not being enough; I'd save up bitterly and painstakingly just so I could afford to go surf and play for an afternoon during the holidays. YJ was different. He was a good student who ranked in the top twenty of the class and had never been to an internet café, harboring endless curiosity about everything inside one. As night fell, I watched them walk into the net café. The joy on YJ's face was something I had never seen before in the classroom... The next day, YJ was dozing off in class. I poked him, he woke up a bit, and continued dozing off, repeating the cycle... It was like that for several days of classes, his demeanor looking entirely like a devout believer worshipping a Buddha on the podium. It wasn't until he got caught during our head teacher's class that I found out he had been pulling all-nighters at Apollo Concentration Camp playing CS for several nights straight. Even after things got so serious that his parents were called to the school, he still snuck off to keep playing. During the holidays at the net café, this former computer newbie's CS skills had gotten so good he was actually bossing me around and pointing fingers. What surprised me even more wasn't just that, but what I couldn't believe was that this game actually had such a huge pull on him?! His gaming skills went up, but his grades never made it back into the top forty. Later on, I felt like YJ didn't have as much energy and spirit as before, and he was struggling a bit to keep up with his studies, but that drive to thoroughly figure things out never left him. Then came high school, and I ran into him a few times. That good-student vibe was completely gone. For the past ten years or so, we've never met. If there's still a chance, I just want to ask if he still plays CS? I'm guessing YJ is probably still playing this classic game. Maybe right now he's online in CS:GO, playing his most familiar Dust II or Inferno, and bossing people around... Chatting about all this, I just wanted to vent a bit: [b]This labor of love didn't start in 2013, but in 2003, or even tracing back to the end of the last century.[/b] *Welcome to leave a thumbs up, correct mistakes, and share in the comments...*

translation_en: 2022.07 update: Almost going into my second year of grad school. Reading this review lets me see my old, super gloomy self. Having 400 extra hours played is pretty fucking ironic, hahaha. Now I feel like CS:GO's mechanics are just what they are—there are always ups and downs, no permanent victories, and no permanent throws. Keep a chill mindset, find that a man's romance within this brutally straightforward game mechanic, and pull off miracles (thinking you're gonna lose and throw, but ending up clutching and carrying)! 11.17: Just your average postgrad entrance exam dog, studying for a Juris Master (Law for Non-Law Majors). Probably fucked this year, feels like time is totally not enough, yet I'm still out here getting anxious about wasting time 233333333 Nah, a game is just a game, and CS is true love. But getting sucked into it doesn't feel good. Happy times go by real fast, and soon it's time to say bye-bye. To the replies calling me a smoothbrain: objectively speaking, this game is genuinely fun. If I add up my time on CSOL and CS 1.6, 3000 hours probably wouldn't even be enough. After all these years, CS is still the only thing that genuinely keeps me hooked. Even now, I still occasionally watch throw compilations, watch JZFB's 2018 reruns, and videos by SAKULA (I actually just bought some luosifen from his shop), Dongguaqiang, and Laixuebeng. Because I genuinely love it, I hope CNCS can take off (though I don't really know much about the esports side of things). When I wrote this review, it was obviously super subjective—it's a review after all, and I added my own perspective. The reason I gave it a negative review wasn't because the game is bad. I just hope everyone develops some other hobbies. My own reasoning was honestly pretty naive and ridiculous; if people get addicted to online games, well, obviously I can't stop them from getting addicted to other shit, right? As an old-school Gold Nova veteran with a fragile ego, dealing with real-life misfortune and then getting randomly flamed in-game and getting shit on for no reason, it's understandable that I needed to vent, especially since it resonated with some friends. I've seen some comments before saying: if you have to speak this cautiously in the virtual world, your real life must be pretty pathetic. Exactly, that's me. Anyway, it's not like I'm never playing again after the exams. After all, I haven't even played high-tier lobbies yet, I'll be back (ignore my playtime from last week). Lastly, a huge thanks to the friends who came to wish me well. Seriously, thank you, you guys are the best. ------- I'm a college senior, and late at night I wanted to write a real review for this game. This is a game that's kept me company for 3 years and brought a ton of joy to me and some of my friends. Just like college life in the 80s, I really loved playing CS in the dorms or at internet cafes, queueing up with a few bros for a few competitive matches on Dust II, Cache, Inferno, Mirage, Overpass, and some maps that only came out in 2017 like Insertion, where you rescue hostages on an island. I used to suck, but the more I played, the more used to it I got. The standard tactics on the Perfect World servers were second nature to me by then: A2, B2, leaving one guy mid, either out-gunning or getting out-gunned, leaving the odd man out to play the clutch. I've played over 1,200 hours. How a competitive round plays out, where the enemies are gonna pop out from, which spot is the weakest—I've known all of that by heart for ages. While I wouldn't call myself a god, at least I won't drag the team down, and a lot of the time I can step up as the "key player." But what's the price? If you add up all that time, it's more than a whole month of sitting in front of the computer playing without eating, drinking, or sleeping. Precious college life can be spent in many ways. Some people throw themselves into their studies and reap rich rewards, some improve themselves by joining clubs or student unions and end up achieving something. But most importantly, it's about finding someone with similar values to accompany you. Some netizens might be laughing right now, saying playing CS doesn't get in the way of anything, you can have a booming career, a great relationship, and a fun game all at once. To that kind of person, I can only say you still haven't gotten addicted to that degree. Years pass by, you go in circles, she left me, my classmates turned out more successful than me, and the choice between grad school and finding a job is waiting for me. I chose the former, and the experience of studying for the entrance exams was pretty painful. It was loneliness—unprecedented loneliness and anxiety. When I had no one to talk to and felt like giving up on myself, I'd choose to boot up CS:GO again, including just now. After a match, the loneliness and anxiety were still there, because this was just escaping reality. CS:GO has a medal system; every 40 ranks you can trade for that year's uniquely shaped medal, and every trade levels up its color. I ended up getting the 2018 blue medal. Because I'd play CS:GO in the school dorm or pull all-nighters after getting off work. Of course the hours are gonna be high. The existence of the medal system already proves that there's a certain mechanic at play here that gets you addicted to playing this game. Just like League of Legends—why is it that after playing all night and feeling totally empty, you still play again the next day? It's a mechanic where you can beat the other side, and the opponents are real people, and you're better than them. When your teammates praise you, when your name is at the top of the leaderboard, you've proven yourself on some level: I'm still pretty strong at playing such a good game. But CS:GO strips that feeling away real quick. If you don't have a strong premade stack and just solo queue, the quality of your teammates and opponents is all over the place. Because of certain things, you'll feel like your gaming experience is absolute shit: 1. The enemy suddenly gets super sweaty, and you can't even tell if they're hacking or not since they're in the same rank anyway, though smurfs are pretty obvious. The most disgusting thing is when they suddenly play like a completely different person, or they're just impossible to kill; 2. Your teammates don't cooperate, or even troll and flame you. This isn't super common on the Perfect World servers, but it's regular occurrence on international servers, complete with discrimination. Russians, Southeast Asians, Japanese, Koreans, etc., will easily flame you, threaten to kick you, or even spew enlightened takes like "stand with [Hong Kong]." There's nothing you can do about this kind of stuff, and even if you report them, you never hear back; 3. You see some people with gorgeous skins, knives, gloves, unique inspect animations, combined with pro players' flashy plays, and you follow the trend and buy them. Some people say CS:GO is an investment game because your money goes into skins whose prices fluctuate, and you can even get back more than you originally spent after selling them. But trust me, the ones who ultimately lose money are the ones opening cases and playing the market. Gaben and the major marketplaces are never gonna take a loss. And those case-opening websites, the ones with ads at the beginning of JZFB's Bilibili videos—those are all traps. Make sure you don't lose your head over it, best thing is just not to touch them at all. If you don't even have a normal source of income, doing this shit is just burning your parents' money. I'm getting really tired typing this. After I finish writing this, I'm uninstalling the game and going to sleep. I have no idea what this review can accomplish, since CS:GO hardly brings in any new players anymore anyway. I really hope everyone, including myself, quits these online games—except for CS:GO. I'm not that old, and people who play CS aren't gonna be ancient either. Just hoping that whoever sees this can put down their mouse, go achieve their ideals, care for their family, and embrace their life. Seriously, if you guys think I sound like a total dumbass, feel free to give it a funny award. If you look down on it, I hope you continue playing this game well and become a DouYu night-owl streamer like JZFB and Donggua. You get to make money while gaming, how great is that? 2019.10.18 64 days until the 2020 postgrad entrance exam.

translation_en: CS:GO, a breakthrough in PvP shooters! After around 3,000 hours of playtime across 3 accounts, I honestly have to say that this game entertained me a lot during my youth. It was the first game I ever played on PC. Back then on my old laptop with 20 FPS and laggy internet, I started my CS:GO career! Over the years, I kept getting better and eventually switched to a proper PC. In CS:GO, you have the option to step into the role of either a terrorist or a police special unit and fight for your respective side. To put it simply, terrorists have to plant a bomb or hold hostages, and conversely, the special unit has to defuse the bomb or rescue the hostages. The game is updated regularly and, thanks to the huge community market, has an extremely large selection of weapon and character skins. Graphically, the game isn't quite up to date anymore, but that doesn't matter since gameplay is what matters most. After all is said and done, you unfortunately have to say that, like so many shooters, it has a massive problem with hackers and cheaters, which personally led me to put the game on the shelf for a while. Personally, I think the game is basically very well made and I have nothing to complain about, except that they really need to overhaul the VAC anti-cheat. Btw., I would completely remove the "Overwatch system" or significantly raise the rank requirement, because many "inexperienced" players can vote there too, and in my opinion they can't really tell what cheating actually is. All in all, a very nice game! :3 👑 [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/43242924/]More game reviews[/url] 👑

Ingredients: Milk - 400 ml Water - 150 ml Eggs - 2 pcs. Sugar - 3 tbsp. Salt - 0.25 tsp. Flour - 200 g Vegetable oil - 2 tbsp. Butter for greasing - 50 g 1. Pour milk and water into a bowl, add sugar, salt, and mix well. 2. Add eggs, whisk thoroughly. 3. Gradually add sifted flour while constantly whisking, the flour should be fully incorporated with no lumps. 4. Finally, pour in the vegetable oil, mix. The batter should look like very runny sour cream. 5. Heat a skillet well, preferably one with a thick bottom. Scoop up some batter with a ladle (about 1/3 of a ladle), pour it into the skillet and, tilting the skillet in circular motions, spread the batter evenly. Fry for about 15 seconds, until the edges are golden. 6. Pry up the edge of the pancake with a knife or silicone spatula and flip it over (I flip them with my hands, it's not scary at all and not hot). Fry on the other side and, also prying up the edge, remove from the skillet. 7. Grease the hot pancake with butter. Fry pancakes using all the batter and stack them up. (From this amount of batter I get about 50 pieces.) 8. Serve with any syrup, condensed milk, melted chocolate, or whatever your imagination allows. Bon appétit!!

translation_en: Either Faceit or suffer Cons: 1. 7-day trade ban 2. VAC anti-cheat is complete garbage 3. You can play MM solo and get matched against a full party of tryhard esports nerds... By the time you grind to a Prime account, you've already been ass-fucked in every hole by cheaters and toxic freaks. Also about cheaters and why you need to move to Faceit and forget what MM is: closer to the LEM-Global ranks, there are more cheaters, even on Prime... You buy Prime, you grind to Global, and your rank gets wiped out in a couple of games by cheaters. The closer you get to those ranks, the more of them there are. Again, where is the anti-cheat? Globals on Prime are spinning like helicopters. 6. They push out some useless updates instead of fixing bugs and broken, laggy maps... NO, let's drop a new OPERATION instead. 7. With every such useless update, you lose FPS : D 8. Also about the community: TONS of squeakers and toxic dumbf*cks. A guy sounds 19-20 years old, yet acts like a complete retard. They blast music in voice chat, talk absolute nonsense, hurl insults — in short, they're toxic. I won't even mention the Poles; every single match with them is kur.wa mother this and that. 9. Complete nonsense with regions: you can get thrown into a lobby with Poles who have 200-500 ping while you have 20, or vice versa. 10. Sometimes there's weird rank balancing — though more rarely — when a full party of Sheriff-LEMs gets matched against a full party of straight-up Globals. 11. You can wait for a match for over an hour. 12. Smurfs. When a guy with a Gold Nova badge plays like a Level 10 Faceit player. And there are so many of them. 12. Boosted accounts... People who boost their accounts using the same smurfs, boosting services, cheaters, etc., and then go play solo at high ranks with zero skill, dragging down normal games for everyone else. Usually, these boosted players are kids who saved up their school lunch money to buy a boost. 13. Valve only cares about squeezing out more cash instead of taking care of players, fixing bugs, and making an anti-cheat. 14. Back to the community. Especially when you play with Poles, you carry the game, they kick you in the last round, and then you get a 7-day ban for getting kicked too often. 15. You frequently run into toxic players, and you keep getting kicked? You get a ban for getting kicked too much! And who gives a crap if there's a rage-hacker on your team right now! God forbid you say the skin is trash, you'll hear the entire lore of your family tree. 19. BIG-BRAINED TEAMMATES — when a defuse kit is literally a step away from your teammate, he starts defusing the bomb without it and runs out of time. When a squeaker at the bottom of the scoreboard with a 3-20 score tries to teach you how to play. 22. You get banned for no reason because the system can mistakenly VAC-ban your account, you write to support, and bots reply. You will never get a real human in support. If you have any other problem, a bot answers again, and proving you're right is practically impossible. 23. A girl joins the random lobby — horny squeakers instantly stop playing the game and just try to "conquer" Madame. 24. Don't play for a while — your rank expires. 25. Incomprehensible rank progression — who knows how many matches are left until a rank-up or rank-down (shall we compare it to Dota again? :D) 26. Win 10 matches in a row — no rank up; lose 2 matches — ranked down. 27. Skill or skin?) When a guy's inventory costs a few months' salary, but he's dragging at the very bottom. 28. I just love toxic teammates, especially when they shoot you, throw grenades at you, including flashes, and straight-up throw games... Finally, the Pros: 1. You can learn Polish and English within a few days. 2. A massive variety of community servers and game modes. 3. You occasionally get free skin drops after an MM match (not always, and usually junk, but still). 4. Good-looking skins (some cost more than your dad's salary at the factory). There's nothing to do in MM... Better move to Faceit or just play other modes for fun... Why am I comparing CS and Dota even though they're different things?) They have the same developer. Basically, things that could be done equally well in both games just aren't done — CS has been abandoned. While Dota gets GOOD AND NEEDED updates, CS sits in the corner smoking and dropping useless sh*t. It used to be a game, but it's dead now. Gabe, thanks. 4/10

translation_en: As soon as I got into this game, I bought a Factory New Dragon Lore because I'd heard ages ago that it was the best skin. Whenever I pulled it out in-game, those foreigners would make sounds of amazement, which really satisfied me. At first, I didn't play well at all—my positioning, counter-strafing, and utility were garbage, and sometimes I'd even run and gun with an AK. I grinded it out on North American official matchmaking servers, practicing day and night so that the Dragon Lore in my hands wouldn't fall into enemy hands. Maybe it was just some innate talent for FPS games from childhood, but in less than half a year I hit Global Elite. It was a tough journey, with tons of cheaters flooding the official matchmaking. Later on, I realized the only reason I hit Global was thanks to those "cheater friends" of mine. I didn't mean to queue with them; newly arrived in America, my English wasn't very good, and I just happened to run into a few guys who played well. Back then, my naive self thought they were genuinely god-tier—after all, CS:GO is a game where miracles happen. It wasn't until the end, when I got a VAC ban and checked my friends list, that I figured it out. Later on, once my rank had reached the absolute peak, I started getting into skins. Stepping into the skin trading scene for the first time, I realized that the Dragon Lore wasn't actually the best; above it were gem knives, StatTrak Howls, StatTrak Fire Serpents, and even higher up were top-tier Case Hardeneds and 4x Kato '14 Holos. Right, I'm someone who chases the peak. I played through gems, Howls, Fire Serpents. I started chasing Case Hardeneds and Katos. Compared to the former, the latter were practically one-in-a-million. I spent big bucks buying quite a Case Hardeneds from other people; it wasn't worth it, but as long as I liked it, I didn't have any complaints myself. People around me called me a big baller, and that feeling of being surrounded like the stars around the moon was intoxicating, I couldn't get enough of it. Later on, I wanted more people to know me and to integrate into a bigger circle, so I went to a community called MAX+. I made a post showcasing my inventory and priced things according to what I paid for them. Who would've thought that this single move would plunge me into an endless abyss. A lot of people started mocking and verbally abusing me, utterly vile stuff, calling my beloved inventory trash. Yeah, I know a part of them was just jealous, but I never imagined human jealousy could be so strong. From a fucking video game, they managed to psychoanalyze my family background and tear down my character. No, this wasn't what I chased in the beginning. I thought people would judge a person's worth by their game skill, not their inventory. But reality is just like this: play well with no inventory and you're just "cheating and hacker"; have an inventory and you're a "good player." Nah, even if you roll up in front of me with a StatTrak FN 4x Titan Holo #661, you're still dying to a single accurate bullet. Skins don't give any stat boosts. Skins can be traded; only skill and ability stay with you forever. Bullshit. You know deep down that skins don't give boosts, yet you still act like a bunch of lapdogs to the skin whales. Yeah, exactly as you see it, I've quit the game. I sold off all the inventory I used to treat like absolute treasure. My CS:GO career ended with the New Year MAX+ community tournament, where my team, Central Command, won with an absolute 16:1 domination. That curtain call was pretty decent; the people who used to spew filth at me had to watch as I taught them a lesson. A game is just a game; it won't treat you differently just because your skins are expensive. Only raw skill is the true meaning of this game. I want to say a few words to those of you still playing CS:GO: 1. Buy fewer skins, don't open cases. Buy what you like, don't gamble your luck. (I've probably opened over 5,000 cases and never made a profit.) 2. Play on third-party platforms instead of official matchmaking. (When I went back to China for the holidays, I got clapped by Silvers in Asian official matchmaking—you adapt to whatever level you're playing against, or just toggle if you have no shame.) 3. Don't talk trash. 4. Don't cheat. A clean environment needs everyone to maintain it. At the end of the day, I still hope everyone has fun playing. Maybe one day I'll return to this game. Thanks everyone. Peak play compilation: https://www.bilibili.com/video/av49875938?from=search&seid=16118794434668357096 *** **Update - April 17, 2019:** Many people are curious about why people flamed me, so let me tell the story. Once upon a time, on BUFF, there were two Factory New Specialist Gloves | Mint Kimono. One was mine, and one belonged to a guy named Riven. Suddenly one day, right underneath Riven's Mint Kimono listing, there was a line of text: "Look at the trash index finger on the one above, looks practically Field-Tested." Of course I was pissed off reading that. How can people step on each other just for money? Demeaning others to prop yourself up is super toxic. So I fired back: "Yeah, yours is the best, right?" That was the setup. Immediately after that, I went to MAX+ to make my post. My original intention in posting was just to find more people who liked Case Hardeneds, because being in America, I had very little contact with the domestic community and didn't know anyone. All of a sudden, out of nowhere, some guy popped up under my post and said, "Your Mint Kimono's index finger has flaws." Right, maybe my Mints really did have issues; even though they're Factory New, flaws are inevitable. But hunting me down to my own post just to shit on me was seriously out of line. It was Riven, the same guy I was beefing with on BUFF. What I didn't expect was that they had a clique on MAX+, what people call the "big ballers." Haha, the vibe of my post was originally super friendly, but right after he showed up, tons of unfriendly comments flooded in. After all, I only had one mouth, and being new to MAX+ I didn't know anyone. Swayed by the public opinion, I got slapped with all sorts of labels. Most people didn't even know what was actually going on, just parroting whatever others said, and I instantly became the bad guy. And nowadays, that's just the vibe—netizens love drama. Once you get hit with the labels of flexing wealth and looking down on the poor, you're gonna get swarmed by salty haters. Right after that, LOU—the guy with an inventory full of Kato '14 Titans—stabbed me in the back. At that point, my friend couldn't stand him kicking a man while he was down, and posted the chat logs between me and LOU in the community. It was the chat where I tried to buy out his entire inventory for 750k RMB as a bundle, only for him to flake on me. In the logs, I told him, "That's fine, I can have someone meet you in person in Shanghai for the trade, or you can send me a photo of your ID so I can verify who you are, and I'll wire you the money first." In the end, LOU still wasn't comfortable with it, and he canceled the deal. Seeing the logs of him flaking getting leaked, LOU naturally felt he lost face, so he made a post mocking me, saying I was just some punk living off his parents' tuition money trying to act cool. Actually, I run some businesses in North America—a used car dealership and entertainment venues—and I've been financially independent for a long time. But collective slander is a powerful thing; I couldn't exactly drag out my whole net worth to prove myself. Still, the people who actually know me know how much I hate being called a rich second-generation kid. Even though my parents are very wealthy, I've hated living in my parents' shadow since I was a kid. When I went abroad, I asked my parents for an extra ten thousand US dollars, used that starting capital to work my way up step by step, and yet an inspiring story like that ends up with this kind of outcome. To be honest, the money spent on playing games and buying skins is just like buying toys—if you like it, you want it, and if you have the means, you buy it to play with. You can always sell it anyway, it's not like you're losing that much. I just wanted to meet more people to play games with, where the hell is all this salt coming from?! **Summary:** A bunch of brainwashed lapdogs hopped into a personal feud, and in the end, the lapdogs won the verbal battle. They protected their fragile self-esteem by using their keyboards to defeat a so-called wealthy-flexing, poor-shaming piece of shit rich kid. Hahahaha. Lapdogs are everywhere, it's just a matter of numbers. *** **Update - July 19, 2019:** I haven't played this game in over four months, and my mindset has chilled out a lot. I still chat with friends I used to play CS:GO with, tell stories, and the group even organizes tournaments. I'm just like before, acting as a spectator referee. Every time I scroll through Douyin I see CS:GO videos, and it seems to be getting more and more popular, but every time I just swipe past them. Sometimes I can't help but scroll back up, and seeing those familiar scenes always leaves a bitter taste in my mouth... The old me used to be just as passionate as them. *** **Update - February 26, 2020:** A year has passed since the MAX+ incident. Over this past year I've matured a lot, losing that arrogant hot-headedness and becoming a lot more grounded. I bought some low-tier skins, just enough to get by and play. CS:GO is getting more and more popular, and my high school classmates from the international department have slowly started getting into the game too. Now we're all studying abroad, which means I'm no longer a lonely gamer—I found my squad. Drawing on my gaming experience from a year ago, I'm pretty much the leader of our little team. After finishing classes every day, we get to play together at night, which has given me renewed hope for this game. These few hours are the happiest part of every day for me in America. They're all newbies, lacking the tight coordination of my old teammates. And after not pulling a trigger for nearly a year, I've lost my peak-form edge too. For a fleeting moment, I felt like I really couldn't go back. The final competitive match before I quit last year let me put down my gun without any regrets: a 2v4 clutch, one AK, three headshots, and an AWP shot like JW possessed me, getting a kill outside the scope. Haha, every time I think about that, the aftertaste is amazing. But a good hero doesn't dwell on past glories, I won't ramble on. My official matchmaking rank, unplayed for a year, was hidden. But when we five-stack, it's painfully obvious that our opponents are starting at Double AK/Sheriff level upwards, which is super unfair to my four Silver bros, and pretty unfair to this boomer gamer either. So I had someone help me derank a bit. While there's a bit of smurfing involved, that wasn't my original intent—I just wanted to experience the fun of the game with my friends. Besides, this isn't a one-man game; it requires all five people on the squad to grow together, and I'm more than willing to start over from scratch. The feeling of coming back is so damn good. I still love this game. **Typical Team Dynamics:** Inferno: "What the fuck, Cui Futong[spoiler]—the physically challenged, hearing-impaired, creepily-behaved 6th man of the team[/spoiler]—I told you to rotate, are you fucking deaf? Connector is wide open, they're flanking us, why are you still tucked away on A site?!" "I, I, I, I'm scared." "F1, F1, hurry the fuck up, stop talking, just vote-kick him for a bot."
