translation_en: He is a Global Elite in CS:GO. His skills are top-tier, his game sense exceptional. P90? Ever heard of a reverse rush ace? AK47? Everyone who's seen him calls him chinaScream. AWP? 360 no-scope headshots are a walk in the park. Negev? He could drop MVPs every single round using a steering wheel. Desert Eagle? 5 bullets, 5 headshots, and he doesn't even need to spam smokes like Happy. Countless people have fallen under his crosshairs, countless people used to call him a hacker, but he knew it was his true skill. Because aside from himself, no one knew how many hours he spent practicing his aim, no one knew how many bots he deathmatched alone to train his game sense. Going from a negative K/D ratio to over 3, almost touching 4—only he knew the sweat and tears behind it. He had a 100-match win streak in competitive mode. Yet he couldn't stay immersed in games forever. Pushed by his parents, he finally got a girlfriend. He also got a job. Now, coming home late every night, exhausted from work, he stopped playing competitive mode altogether. And his match history froze at that 100-game win streak. Every day after coming home, he would only play CS:GO for an hour—only by playing with his "comrades" could he cast away the stress and misery of the day. His girlfriend never understood why he locked himself in his room every night, laughing and chatting. Since their place had two computers, one for each of them, she had no idea what he was actually doing. Usually, he wasn't all that nice to her, mostly because he wasn't much of a talker, and neither was she. But the way he silently looked after her when she fell sick, and made sure her heavy coat and umbrella were ready when the weather turned cold, made her feel deeply cherished. Just like that, a few months passed. Until one day, she learned that because of work, he had to work overtime continuously for a month—he couldn't come home at noon, and he wouldn't get back until midnight. She specially took a month off work to take care of him. After all, her salary wasn't much, and her heart genuinely ached for him. Every day at noon, she brought him lunch, and at night she waited until 11:40 to start cooking, waiting on him hand and foot until bedtime. Yet she remained endlessly curious about the laughter coming from his room every night; she wanted to know why. Finally, one day at noon, she turned on his computer and found only one game installed on the desktop—CS:GO. Driven by curiosity, she opened the game... A month later, he opened CS:GO for the first time in forever, only to notice something was off—his rank had dropped from Global Elite to Silver I. He checked his match stats and saw that his most recent games were all losses. His K/D ratio had plummeted from 3.8 to 1.2. He knew his account was only used by him, so all of this could only have been done by her, cooking away in the kitchen. "Did you do this?" He pointed at the Silver I icon on the computer screen. She looked a bit nervous, rubbing the hem of her shirt with both hands: "Y-Yeah, I did it..." "Why were you messing with my computer?" She caught a hint of seriousness and tension in his tone—he was usually exceptionally gentle with her. "Because... because I wanted to understand you... I also wanted to make you happy... I didn't want you to only be happy when you're with your friends." By the end, her voice was so quiet she could barely hear it herself. "Ah!" She was startled by a sudden movement—he had pinned her against the wall (*kabe-don*), using his left index finger to lift her chin: "Does that mean you've met all of them? Chatted with them?" "Mhm... mhm..." She looked a bit flustered. "How many competitive matches have you lost?" "About 100 games, I guess..." She lowered her head as far as it could go, feeling as though the stinging pain of a slap across the face was coming next. "Did you get flamed really hard?" She was a college graduate, of course she understood words like "noob", "f*ck you", "fucking noob" coming from foreigners' mouths, let alone local insults. She wasn't one to give up easily; she wanted to fight back and prove she could play, but helplessly, she couldn't even see the enemies before she died. Every time she lost, she would secretly cry for a bit to vent the emotions building up inside her. Thinking of this, she nodded. "Want to play and prove to them you can do it?" "Yes!" Against all odds, she yelled it out exceptionally loud. "Alright then, I'll teach you." Just like that, he started training her in CS:GO, teaching her how to aim, helping her learn the maps, teaching her everything he possibly could. At the same time, their relationship grew better and better. He changed his ID to NoobTeam No1. She made her ID NoobTeam No2. Every time, he would only use 50% of his actual skill, letting her be the main character. Finally, she successfully ranked up to Double AK (Distinguished Master Guardian). Until one day, she asked him: "Where'd you get this knife? It looks so cool!" "Oh, this? I unboxed it!" "How do you open them?" "Remember the cases that drop after matches? You just buy keys and open them. Like this. But it's all RNG though." "Oh! Is that how it is? I've got over a hundred cases here, let's open all of them!" Just like that, the two of them opened cases and blew their entire life savings. "Welcome to Counter-Strike Derank: Global Opening!" That was reportedly what the two of them told the bank teller while withdrawing their very last savings.

translation_en: When I was a kid, the two of us would happily skip class to go to the net cafe and play CS, carefree, as if we didn't have a single worry in the world. A guy in the class bragged about his CrossFire skills every day, and to show off how loaded he was, he bought her an axe, stealing her away from me. Just like that, she left for CF, leaving me all alone. After school, the gloomy sky had started to rain. Upon finding out she went to play CF, I was practically having a mental breakdown. I walked home in the rain, only to get splashed with mud all over by a bicycle. The one riding the bike was that guy. "Country bumpkin, keep playing your dumbass CS!" he yelled, and then sped off. There was neither joy nor sorrow on my face, but I felt like shit inside. I cried the whole night. ----- Eight years later, she had grown tall and attractive, but seemed to have given up on her studies and was playing in some net cafe CF league. She lost a few matches in a row, a few beads of sweat hanging on the tip of her dainty nose. Her little-skid teammate next to her was playing on a Private Second Class account and didn't even have a single piece of RMB gear. They were gonna lose this round. I saw her, walked over and sat down, and chased the little kid away. She was too focused and didn't even notice me. Four people were already dead on the field, leaving only me as a SAS holding an AK-74. Clutch time. I peeked out, one-tapped an enemy who stuck their head out, and then kept spraying to take down the enemies coming from a crossfire. After that, I used my movement to dodge Fire Kirin bullets and one-tapped him with the Glock's 12 bullets. I picked up the Fire Kirin and secured them the round win. She took off her headset, looked at me with eyes full of surprise, and asked, "Where have you been all these years? You've gotten so good, I've always been waiting for you in CF." CS:GO features new maps, characters, and weapons, and delivers updated versions of the classic CS content (de_dust, etc.). In addition, CS:GO introduces new gameplay modes, matchmaking, leaderboards, and more. 'Counter-Strike took the gaming industry by surprise when the unlikely MOD became the most played online PC action game in the world almost immediately after its release in August 1999,' said Doug Lombardi at Valve. 'For the past 12 years, it has been one of the most-played games in the world, headlining competitive gaming tournaments and selling over 25 million units worldwide across the franchise. CS:GO promises to enhance CS' award-winning gameplay and deliver it to players on the PC as well as next gen consoles and Macs.'" She burst into tears, and came with me to CS:GO. And then she went broke opening cases.

I'm not even going to talk right now about how pathetic Danger Zone is (because it looks like it was thrown together overnight on someone's knee), I'm just going to talk about the cheaters. Now that CS is free = an influx of an absolute shitload of cheaters. You might say, well, free-to-play players don't have Prime and you won't be playing with them. MY ASS. Prime can be obtained in two ways. 1 - buy it, 2 - reach level 21 and link a mobile number. Meaning to get Prime you have to DO THE EXACT SAME THING AS BEFORE, EXCEPT FOR FREE, BECAUSE YOU DON'T HAVE TO PAY 500 RUBLES FOR A NEW COPY AFTER GETTING BANNED. HOW'S THAT FOR CHEATERS, BOYS? P.S. I review every suspicious match and, trust me, every 5th game had cheats in it, and now it's going to be even worse. UPD 06.08.2019 I decided to play Danger Zone because the ranks actually work normally there, the rank icons look cool, anyway, it's playable. A week into playing Danger Zone, cheaters showed up there who are cheating so blatantly it's fucking insane. I haven't seen such impudence in a long time. Just when it seemed like there was at least some reason to play this dumpster fire, a week later that reason is gone too.

translation_en: Back when we were kids, the two of us would happily skip class to go to the net cafe and play CS, carefree, as if we'd never had a single worry in the world. But after starting middle school, everything changed. A guy in our class bragged about his CF skills every single day, and to show off how rich he was, he even bought her a butcher axe, stealing her away from me. Just like that, she left for CF, leaving me all alone. After school, the gloomy sky had already started raining. Upon finding out she went to play CF, I practically broke down completely. I walked home in the rain, only to get splattered with mud by a bicycle. The guy riding the bike was him. "Country bumpkin, go keep playing your dumbass CS!" he yelled, and sped off into the distance. There was neither joy nor sorrow on my face, but it hurt like hell inside. That night, I cried the whole night through. ----- Eight years later, she had grown tall and attractive, but seemed to have given up on her studies and was playing in a CF net cafe tournament. She had lost a few matches in a row, a few beads of sweat hanging on the tip of her dainty nose. Her elementary schooler teammate next to her was playing on a Private Second Class account and didn't even have a single RMB cash shop item. This round was a guaranteed loss. I saw her, walked over and sat down, chasing the kid away, while she didn't even notice me because she was too focused. Four people were already dead on the field, leaving only me, a SAS holding an AK-74—clutch time. With a quick peek, I headshot the enemy sticking their head out, then kept spraying to mow down the enemies coming to pinch me. After that, using my movement to dodge Fire Kirin bullets, I headshot him with the Glock's 12 bullets. Picking up the Fire Kirin, I won them the round. She took off her headphones, looked at me with eyes full of surprise, and asked, "Where have you been all these years? You've gotten so good, I've been waiting for you in CF this whole time." I looked at her, expressionless, and said: "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO) expands upon the team-based action gameplay that it pioneered when the franchise launched 12 years ago. CS:GO features new maps, characters, weapons, and delivers updated versions of the classic CS content (de_dust, etc.). In addition, CS:GO will introduce new game modes, matchmaking, leaderboards, and more. 'Counter-Strike took the gaming industry by surprise when the unassuming mod became the most played online PC action game in the world almost immediately after its release in August 1999,' said Doug Lombardi at Valve. 'For the past 12 years, it has been one of the most played games in the world, headlining competitive gaming tournaments and selling over 25 million units worldwide across the franchise. CS:GO promises to expand on CS' award-winning gameplay and deliver it to players on the PC as well as next gen consoles and the Mac.'" She burst into tears, came with me to CS:GO. And then blew all her life savings on case openings.

translation_en: First time buying CS. I've been playing CF hosted by Tencent before. As an FPS veteran of 10 years playing as a total newbie, here is my review of CS:GO: 1. The most direct difference is how fast the game launches and how you find a match. CS:GO is way faster to boot up than CF. Finding a match uses a matchmaking system, but the load times into the game are a bit slow. 2. Once I got into a match, the experience was totally fresh and different from CF. The detail of the graphics, the realism of the guns, the shooting sound effects, movement, jumping, and other controls feel much closer to real human movement, unlike the stiff animations in CF. At first, it took some getting used to, but the more I played, the more I realized this is truly a masterpiece among competitive FPS games. 3. As a player going straight from CS 1.6 to CS:GO, the shooting feel compared to CF is really a love-hate relationship. I love the realistic shooting feel, but I hate that it's too realistic. Forget about shooting while moving; even when standing still, you can visibly see the bullet flying out of the animation, yet it strays off the spray pattern == getting totally wrecked. 4. The thing that confused me the most was the loadout inventory. I clicked in and kept looking for "Where's the backpack? Where's the backpack? Where's the backpack...". Then it dawned on me that it's not about picking a backpack, you just equip weapons directly. After studying it for a long time, I finally figured out how weapon loadouts work. Of course, without the support of RMB (real money) weapons, everyone's guns are the same, with at most skin differences, which really made me happy. After all, as a poor office worker, for CF's 888 RMB artifact bullshit, I'd rather get wrecked and face unfairness than bring myself to buy them. 5. Let's talk about my favorite mode when first getting into CS:GO. Since I'm not very good, I found out I can't do jump-shots or quick-scopes in CS:GO, or maybe I just don't know how. I haven't touched turn-based modes yet; I'd just grief my teammates and get totally destroyed, turning round-based modes into a spectator sport of watching others play. Finally, I chose the team deathmatch mode with random instant respawns (I forgot what it's called again). I've never experienced such a hyped mode. Random respawns, random weapons, running through a few maps made me realize the true essence of CS:GO: the lighting for indoor and outdoor environments is crafted with exceptional care. Running on max settings, it's genuinely hard to spot CTs hiding in dark indoor areas. Let me mention CF here: even indoors, it's still bright, the whole game just looks like a background was slapped on top. Comparing CS:GO's lighting changes and realistic street scenes with CF's spotless streets and identical indoor/outdoor lighting textures, I realized that not listening to my classmate's suggestion to play CS:GO back then was a huge mistake. 6. The game quality shown in the small details forces me to admire it. CS:GO is truly a well-deserved classic of competitive FPS games. The scope blurring then clearing up when zooming in, the crosshair blurring when moving while scoped—compared to Tencent's CF where scoping in just instantly high-def magnifies the texture, and moving while scoped looks like a scrolling image interface, CF is truly a cash-grab game. The smoke from shooting, the visual feedback of bullets hitting models, and the more realistic reload animations all relentlessly flex their exquisite craftsmanship. CS:GO is the best FPS shooting game I've ever played, period. The moment I picked up CS:GO, I was already at an age where I'm working hard just to survive, yet it managed to give me that same passion, that same love, that crazy obsession for FPS games I had back when I was a kid. It's not like I'm playing this game just because people say CS:GO is a classic; it's simply because I accidentally saw on Steam that CS:GO was free now, then Perfect World took over publishing, and then after doing a trusted account verification, I could play for free without spending a dime. 7. This review has no malicious intent to disparage CF for comparison's sake; it's just a truthful statement of the differences between the two games. As for why I compared it to CF, well, why not? Because I'd been playing CF since middle school until I picked up CS:GO. Now, CF and Tencent's WeGame have vanished from my computer, and I don't even know why. CS:GO probably has to take the blame for that.

translation_en: As one of the big three traditional competitive games, CS:GO continues the CS spirit. Born from a mod just like them, while WoW and SC have gradually faded from the spotlight, it's comforting that despite having relatively few Chinese players, CS:GO is still a rare gem. Precisely because it's competitive, beginners have to spend a ton of time learning the basics like movement, recoil control, callouts, and utility. As a Gold Nova scrub myself, I haven't even really bothered to learn smokes, HEs, and flashes. Many CS 1.6 players have transferred their memories over to CS:GO. Just like me, a lot of people dropped this game for a bit due to the PUBG hype or LoL hype, but after getting getting pounded by cheaters and gods, coming back to CS:GO made me realize it's still just as purely mesmerizing.[spoiler] Definitely not about skin betting and trading; the game has practically turned into a trading and gambling simulator. [/spoiler] Fair competition is CS's biggest defining feature, and at first it was pretty much its only purpose, which makes it boring to a lot of people, but that's also its greatest strength. Actually, though, what I really want to talk about is the vibe within the Chinese CS:GO scene. When you deeply get into a competitive game, naturally you care a lot about matches, especially matches featuring Chinese teams. We don't have the dominance of Dota, we don't even have the competitiveness of LoL, and nowadays just making it onto the world stage in CS:GO has become extremely rare. Major tournaments and certain streaming platforms are flooded with match-fixing and gambling. People no longer care about when Chinese CS:GO will return to the days of wNv when CSERs were so proud; instead, it's like Chinese CS only has hope if you can win money off it. When LoL loses, people can still flame them and be utterly pissed off about the defeat. Meanwhile, all I can do is bang on my keyboard here with wet eyes. December 11, 2005, is a date worth remembering—it brought a massive surprise to Chinese CSers. Even now in CS:GO, I still deeply miss the 1.6 era. It's a symbol, a legend, a story. The wNv of today has turned into TYLOO. And only xiaoJian and zZk managed to become top-tier casters after grinding it out in the CS scene. Listening to Major casting and watching TI matches are the happiest moments; there are many figures who can represent Chinese Dota, but there is only them to represent Chinese CS.[spoiler] I was just born at the wrong time; by the time I got into 1.6, wNv had already disbanded. [/spoiler] TYLOO's decline is jaw-dropping. I hope TYLOO can foster a good environment for pro players and set an example as the big brother of Chinese CS. We don't demand legends like coldzera, s1mple, niko, or olof—we just hope five young players will step up. This is, and always will be, a team game. We can wait, but to quote 117: Where is the road leading to the future of Chinese CS:GO? Dedicated to this text: paying tribute to those who led Chinese CS forward, and commemorating the days we've walked together over the past dozen years.

translation_en: [h1]"This is extremely funny. Here I go. I'm playing Counter-Strike, right? The whole time I'm playing Counter-Strike, I'm not even having fun, I swear to God, it's intense... I get tense, I get pissed off at everything and everyone all the time, I go out of my mind... And then, after I stop, I'm like: 'Man, I want to play some CS.' Even right after the stream, I'm like: 'Man, what the fuck, I love Counter-Strike, I want to play some Counter-Strike.' That's it, [Counter-Strike] is a game you hate but miss all the time."[/h1] [i]Jason "jasonR" Ruchelski, in 2016, on how he feels about Counter-Strike: Global Offensive.[/i] Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO) is an online first-person shooter developed by [i]Valve Corporation[/i] and [i]Hidden Path Entertainment[/i], serving as a sequel to [i]Counter-Strike: Source[/i]. It is the fourth main title in the franchise and, in terms of gameplay and public success, is considered the true successor to [i]Counter-Strike 1.6[/i]. [h1]Concept and Existence[/h1] CS:GO was initially developed with the primary goal of just being a port of [i]Counter-Strike: Source[/i] for that generation's consoles, but as it took shape, Valve saw the opportunity to release it as a full game and expand its gameplay. In it, you take on the role of either the counter-terrorist police forces or the terrorist forces themselves. There are several game modes, the main one being the competitive mode, where you and 4 teammates fight for the most rounds won in a match of up to 30 rounds. During the first 15, you'll be on one side (counter-terrorist or terrorist) and your objective, along with your team, will be to strategize planting and detonating a bomb at one of the two [i]bombsites[/i] if you're a terrorist, or stopping the 5 terrorists on the other team from doing so if you're a counter-terrorist. The round also ends if one of the two teams is completely wiped out in the process. [h1]Gameplay[/h1] CS:GO was developed on the [i]Source engine[/i] by [i]Valve Corporation[/i]. Highly acclaimed for its great performance even on lower-end systems, the game has fluid and very fast-paced gameplay, rewarding players who have good movement control, solid strategy formulation, and above all, fast and precise aim. Official servers (known as [i]matchmaking[/i] or simply [i]MM[/i] servers) run at 64 [i]ticks[/i] per second, which is considered average among today's games. To put it into perspective, one of the most acclaimed games of the year, [i]PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS[/i], has servers running at 16 [i]ticks[/i] per second, while most private CS:GO matchmaking servers run at 128 [i]ticks[/i] per second. This means the [i]hitreg[/i] on official servers isn't as precise and faithful to the gameplay as on private servers, but it's undoubtedly much more faithful than in other well-known games on the market. On these [i]MM[/i] servers and in competitive mode, you will be thrown into a match with 4 other teammates against 5 other people, theoretically all 10 people being of the same skill level, using a "rank" system created by the game itself. As you get better at the game, you rank up, going from the lowest, [i]Silver I[/i], to the highest, [i]The Global Elite[/i], theoretically playing with and against better players. [h1]Community[/h1] Unfortunately, like any major global [i]FPS[/i] game, CS:GO suffers from a toxic and sometimes overly immature community, lacking a regulatory body for it, at least on its official servers. At times, especially in competitive matches, insults (some even racist) go unpunished even when reported. The game has a dedicated South American server but [i]apparently[/i] has no nationality and/or ping filtering (except when ping is excessive), which leads to many Spanish-speaking Latinos who don't speak Portuguese ending up in matches with Brazilian players and vice versa, making communication difficult since there's no common language (and both, most of the time, aren't proficient in English). Furthermore, despite having a relatively effective [i]anti-cheat[/i] system, the [i]Valve Anti-Cheat (VAC)[/i], the game's low price means that when many are caught using illegal programs and get banned, they just buy CS:GO on new accounts and keep using those programs, ruining the whole experience and gameplay for legitimate players. [h1]Game Details[/h1] Besides the competitive mode, which is the most played, the game also features Casual mode (which has rules and formats similar to competitive, but without a ranking system), [i]Deathmatch[/i] (a fast-respawn format where your sole objective is to eliminate as many players from the opposing team as possible), Arms Race (similar to deathmatch, but with only a few weapons unlocked, giving you a bigger and better arsenal as you get kills), among others. Its most important [i]update[/i], [i]Arms Deal[/i] in August 2013, added Valve's biggest trump card to CS:GO: customizable [i]skins[/i]. In it, you get cases containing [i]skins[/i], or paint jobs, for your weapons. However, to open them, you need to buy a key (which costs R$7.79 each in Brazil), giving you a chance to get a paint job from a varied pool of different rarities. With a somewhat inflated market, CS:GO only achieved true commercial success after the introduction of this system, driving a multi-million dollar market of skin sales and gambling. These paint jobs, while offering zero gameplay advantage from any angle, bring a bit of personalization and customization to a game that was already a classic, making it much more appealing to the general public. [h1]Conclusion[/h1] CS:GO is currently the third most played game on the [i]Steam[/i] platform and the most played shooter in the world, so it speaks for itself. A classic perfected and polished by its developer, the game specializes in rewarding those who grind for self-improvement and pays off for those who play well, currently standing as a high-value [i]esport[/i] with massive room for good players. For casual players, Valve's matchmaking servers are more than enough to guarantee hours of fun (and frustration) in the pursuit of self-improvement, while for [i]hardcore[/i] players, unfortunately, the experience can be a bit ruined by [i]cheaters[/i] frequently found in higher [i]ranks[/i] (a problem currently being mitigated by the high availability of private matchmaking services, though often at a monthly cost). Without further ado, I recommend the game to everyone, whether you're a seasoned shooter veteran or someone who has never fired a single bullet in their life. [h1]Rating: 9.5/10[/h1] [b]Pros:[/b] [+] Guaranteed fun moments, whether playing [i]solo[/i] or with friends; [+] Frequent updates and operations; [+] Relatively effective, though slow, anti-cheat; [+] High replay value for veterans; [+] [i]Skillwise rewarding game (SRG)[/i]: A game that only favors those who play well; [+] Clean graphics, intuitive interface; [+] Great performance even on modest setups; [+] Customizable skins. [b]Cons:[/b] [-] Cheaters/hackers in higher ranks; [-] Somewhat toxic community (though easily avoided).

translation_en: Screw this game. After crossing the 1k hour mark, I looked back and saw everything from a different angle. At first, everything was fun: friends, fun ratings, sleepless nights on community servers, a sea of fun. Sweaty MM matches were balanced out by the taste of victory, cool clutches, aces, and other sick moments. After a hard and sometimes ass-blasting match, I’d just go hop onto my favorite community server where familiar, cheerful, and simply good guys hung out 24/7. Absolute chaos, madness, and sodomy. About half a year into the game, I moved up to higher ranks [spoiler] (Sheriff) Please don't beat me :( [/spoiler] That's when I decided to play without a party. Grinding ranks solo, can you imagine? I always considered myself a calm person, but what went down in there was totally unacceptable! Let's go in order. 1) Toxic players who miraculously made it to mid-ranks, or simply put, griefers. Well, everything's clear here, the guy has no intention of playing from the very start. He wants only one thing. To ruin the game for everyone and enjoy watching his teammates burn. The worst is when he's not alone. It used to happen that you want to squeeze in a quick ranked match before bed, and boom, the game drops four Poles into your team. It’d be fine if they actually knew how to play... Nope, you're not in a fairytale, baka, instead they start messing around completely. And if you try to say anything to them, you'll most likely get shat on just because you're Russian. [spoiler] There are adequate Poles, I won't argue, but I (at least) ran into them very rarely. [/spoiler] 2) A serious and quite painful topic for me. Cheaters. This is just something else! Want to play with a friend and chat on Discord? Well, up yours. Enjoy facing some vegetable with wallhack. Fine, wallhack, you can still try to pull through on pure skill, communication with the team, and other crucial skills. But most of the time, these freaks run with a whole pack of cheats! Can't win with just a basic wallhack? HE TOGGLES AIMBOT! They often don't roll solo so they won't get kicked. [spoiler] The funniest thing is watching two such retards battle it out. [/spoiler] 3) What's that? Servers in Russia? What for? Seriously though, people living in the central-western part of Russia can play without any problems. But damn, there were so many complaints from guys in the Far East... The average ping for those guys starts at 100. I could list a few more reasons, but I really don't feel like it. Bottom line. Just to mess around, play with friends, make a little money – go for it. Past that, it's total fucking madness. After 1.3k hours I realized to hell with it. I'd rather go read a book. Goodnight, sweet prince. Upd. The last 1.5k hours were played on Faceit. Most of the complaints above are no longer relevant. You can actually enjoy this game. Play in a party. Play for fun.

(Distinguished Master Guardian is way higher than Gold Nova 1). This happens until you have won a whole 10 games. After that, you will have your own rank. But watch out! And if you win because you pretend to be a weak player, that is deceit. Yet this cannot be proven and is therefore nothing that can be banned. I don't recommend the game because it has many severe flaws, is unfair to newbies, doesn't ban hackers fast enough (partly 2 months is an exaggeration, even though it's mostly 1 month, which isn't any better either) and you constantly just hear kids. translation_en: [h1][i]“I'm not triggered! I'm not triggered!”[/i] (c) Nemagia[/h1] [i]Counter Strike: Global Offensive[/i] is one of the three pillars that the [i]Valve[/i] corporation stands on today. Once an innovator in video games, they've become a miserly knight who gave up on everything and only occasionally invests in sketchy gadgets. But let's not forget about the tournaments. The previous installment, [i]Counter Strike: Source[/i], came out a hundred years ago, but people still haven't forgotten about it even now. A game of the people, what can I say. Journalists all sing the same tune: [i]"CS is outdated, time to move on!"[/i] I agree with them, but [i]CS:GO[/i] can't be called a bad game, people like it, nobody is forcing me to play, so why not just let it go. But I'm not writing this review about how I dislike the mechanics and gameplay. I'm taking a stand against [i]Valve's[/i] policy of not giving a shit. Let's start small – the human factor. [i]CS:GO[/i], like its step-brother [i]Dota 2[/i], is a veritable breeding ground for bile. Nowhere else will you find an audience more aggressively hostile toward one another. And it's not directly the developers' fault, only indirectly. Take one of Dota's arch-enemies, [i]LoL[/i], for example. You don't see that kind of sodomy over there. Skins seem like a simple weapon texture. And it would be fine if you had to earn them, like in [i]Call of Duty[/i], by getting N headshots or something like that, but no, you only get them for free by leveling up. And the higher the level, the slower the progress to the next one. And after all that, there's a 99% chance they'll just hurl some worthless junk at you for pennies—well-deserved, maybe, but it messes with your head. For everything else, be so kind as to buy it on the marketplace or spin our roulette wheel by buying keys and cases. I actually bought the game, I didn't download some F2P mutilated scrap. The worst part is that [i]Valve[/i] has turned these skins into idols. They release collection after collection. Just take a look at the [url=http://steamcommunity.com/market/listings/730/Sawed-Off%20%7C%20Wasteland%20Princess%20%28Factory%20New%29]Sawed-Off | Wasteland Princess[/url]. Nowadays, people are asking 90-200 rubles for this disgrace on the market. Look at the [url=http://steamcommunity.com/market/listings/730/AUG%20%7C%20Akihabara%20Accept%20%28Factory%20New%29]AUG | Akihabara Accept[/url], going for 2300-20000. Is this a joke? And all those stickers, too. Why not add rhinestones, sparkles, and gold skins so you can feel like a gay African dictator. Weapons deal death; the paint job on them should serve as camouflage or be intimidating, not laughable and pathetic. At least the gloves look like gloves, but I don't think they have long left either. I would've just left [i]Counter Strike: Global Offensive[/i] alone and only logged in to drop a new case. But in light of recent events, even I, a neutral person, am getting burned. And it's not because of the recently announced [i]Artifact[/i], whose appearance was just a matter of time, but because "Counter-Strike" is launching on the Chinese market with an F2P model. Meaning they're figuring out ways to verify identities and digging through Chinese legislation instead of creating a normal anti-cheat or remaking the old one so it works like clockwork, without doing showy purges of half a million scumbags every six months. And that's not even mentioning the service issues. [i]Valve[/i] is just starting to lose active players in "Counter-Strike," and that's food for thought. But they won't think about it and won't change a damn thing, because [i]Dota 2's[/i] charts have been crawling downward for a long time. You might call me a mom's little rebel, but if all of us together tank the rating, they'll listen to us just like [i]Paradox[/i] did back in the day, and no review charts will save them. P.S. If you don't know what to write in a review, or you're too lazy, you can just put a period and make it visible only to yourself. UPD: Now CSGO is just free, and we were given a prime account. I understand the people who are insanely pissed about the money they spent, but you need to look past your own stinginess, don't lower yourselves to Gabe's level. The ship is burning, cheaters are infesting everything, and Valve is just raking in money on an escalator. UPD2: Playing on non-prime accounts is pure punishment. Instead of improving the anti-cheat, Valve decided to divide the player community into 2 classes: the conditionally rich and the conditionally poor. So the former can feel better, the latter were thrown to the wolves as fodder for cheaters. As a result, animals with accounts created yesterday come into lobbies and wallbang people, or use full-on aimbots. The response from ordinary players has been paranoia—people kick anyone who looks suspicious. And the privileged part got screwed over too.

translation_en: So, I've played this [strike]devil's[/strike] toy for 1,029 hours (where, according to the csgo-stats service, the time spent in matches is 624 hours). And now I want to share my unasked-for opinion with you. If you wanted to buy this game and start playing it seriously, and were wondering: is it worth starting or not? I can answer right now: DON'T YOU DARE! If you're still burning with desire, you'd better read all the cons of the game that I'll list below first. [h1]Cons of the game[/h1] [table] [tr][th]Aspect:[/th][th]Description:[/th][/tr] [tr] [td]Cheaters – the very thing that causes millions of law-abiding players' asses to burn on a daily basis.[/td] [td]Yeah. There are just A FUCKTON of cheaters in the game. I have at least three friends in my friends list who use cheats. Not even paid ones, but free ones. And did they get banned, you ask? I answer: NO. They've been playing just fine. For months now. I won't disclose the players' nicknames, whose fault is it that the system allows the use of third-party programs? Clearly not theirs. And how do you like the prospect of playing knowing that the opposing team can turn on cheats at any second when they start losing? Yes, there are third-party services like FaceIt, ESEA, which have their own anti-cheat systems (by the way, ESEA has the best protection). But that's not it! Why should I pay a monthly subscription to services that have nothing to do with Steam's official competitive mode? Paying someone just so you don't play against cheaters – meh. Why wouldn't Valve make their own NORMAL anti-cheat like these services? Unclear! Okay, they introduced Prime accounts. But the catch is that Prime access can only be enabled (!)after 70 won matches(!). How does it even help? It doesn't, because it just asks you to link a phone number to your account. And after that, you'll only play with those who did the same by providing their phone number. But the thing is that it DOES NOT help at all. There are services on the internet where you can order a virtual sim card for Steam (!) for just 2 rubles(!). Meaning your Primes [b]DO NOT SAVE YOU FROM CHEATERS[/b]!! VALVE, stop milking money from us! STOP! What the fuck are cases? What card games in Dota 2?! Why are you giving such a massive zero fucks about regular players?[/td] [/tr] [tr] [td]Among the few adequate players, there are many people with a shithole personality.[/td] [td]Get ready for the fact that if a team, where besides you there are 4 English-speaking people, suddenly finds out that you're Russian, they will now address you like this: "Hey, cyka bliet', come here!". And it's no wonder. Here's a situation: there are 4 Russians and one English-speaker in the team. Guess on the first try what language they will communicate in? In Russian, of course. Obviously, the guy can't listen for 30 rounds straight to people whose language you don't know. And they're discussing something there non-stop, laughing. Are they laughing at you? In 5% of cases, the player just blocks communication with all "teammates" and plays the rest of the game in silence (by the way, it's almost impossible to win like that, you can't carry 16 rounds all by yourself), and in the other 95% of cases, such a person snaps and at the start of the round buys a shotgun and [strike]like Kurt Cobain[/strike] shoots [strike]himself in the face[/strike] right in the face of any of the guys talking. The system kicks this player and issues a ban that prevents you from connecting to the competitive mode. Such a ban lasts from 30 minutes to 7 days. Of course, after such cases, there will be a biased attitude towards every Russian. And here's another situation: there are 2 Russians, 2 English-speakers and you in the middle. Neither side understands each other. And they start insulting each other in their own language from the very first round. And it will be like that until the very end. You, of course, knowing both languages, can try to make peace between them, but you need unreal charisma for that, because every other person in this game has such a GODDAMN high opinion of themselves. And I will now try to convey their logic so that you understand it better. Let's take Petka Ivanov, the scumbag – this is our hero for the following situations. So Petka rushes 1 against 5 terrorists, playing as counter-terrorists. He does this like 10 times, letting his team down. Because of this, the score is 10-0 in favor of the enemy. And you know whose fault it is according to Petka's logic? Of course – [b]YOURS[/b], because you didn't cover/didn't help/didn't cheer him up/didn't pray for Petka/didn't light a candle for him in church, etc. Okay, say you got a smarter Petka. He doesn't rush, he sits in one place, holding the angle against the enemy. But it's not that simple. He can't hit his shots. Who's to blame here again? That's right! You! Why?! Because you didn't cover him/didn't distract all the enemies' attention to yourself/supposedly got in his way, etc. Admitting his mistake for once — I have NEVER heard that in all 624 hours of playing matches. It seems like the only ones who know how to admit their mistakes and apologize for them here are me and like one and a half other people who are destined never to end up on the same team as me.[/td] [/tr] [tr] [td]NOT EXACTLY equal conditions.[/td] [td]Besides your personal shooting skill, there is another factor here – hardware. If the opponent is superior to you in this factor – consider you've lost. No matter how well you aim, no matter how ideally you get along with the team – you can't beat hardware. If the opponent has: a more powerful computer, better headphones and a more expensive mouse – consider you've lost to this opponent. Hardware is fine, you can BUY it even if you're a schoolkid. But there is something you can't influence in any way. It's your location. "So what?", you ask. I answer. Ping. Or rather – latency. The servers you play on are NOT located in Russia. If a person who lives in the exact same city where the server you're playing on is located plays against you – they will have a clear advantage over you, because unlike you, their latency will be lower. It's fine if the ping differs by a couple of units, but in my situation, it's worse. I live in Siberia. My ping in every game is at least 70, if a person plays against me whose max ping is 5, it's absolute hell. Imagine you're gunfighting with such a person, and you run out of ammo, you reload and step behind a wall, you've hidden, but in the last second you get killed (AND YOU ARE ALREADY BEHIND THE WALL), but not for the opponent. What you see on your screen happens with a delay. For you – your corpse falls already behind the wall, but for the enemy – closer to the exit from behind the wall (I explained it poorly, but I hope you understand what I mean).[/td] [/tr] [tr] [td]Many things are slightly out of your control.[/td] [td]You can get high on drugs and play better than anyone in the world. The stars in the sky just have to align in such a lucky way that you get into the server closest to you with a good team of 4 people, against total idiots who don't know how to shoot at all. This will apply to only one match. After that, you'll have bad luck for 2 months. (Everyone's experienced this, I don't know what it's connected to)[/td] [/tr] [tr] [td]Unstable, laggy game client.[/td] [td]The game won't output more than 150 fps if you have some sort of i9 processor, 32gb of RAM, two "Titan" graphics cards and an SSD, on the contrary, it will even sometimes drop down to 100 fps. I know by hearsay, but the thing is that the majority of the community has this problem. Everyone complains that the game crashes, lags and stutters. I have an average computer, the game is on minimum settings, and the game lags WHEN 3 ENEMIES ARE SPRAYING AT ME POINT-BLANK! FPS can drop even when you just get headshot – there can be a 0.5-second micro-freeze. And also... Here, when you press Esc – you lag not only for yourself, but also for the enemy, which many people take advantage of. It's fucking impossible to hit such laggers.[/td] [/tr] [/table]

translation_en: I didn't have much FPS experience before, so it took me a month of playing to finally hit Gold 3. I've clearly learned that the overall quality of people in low ranks is pretty low, which seriously ruins the gaming experience. A lot of the time, my mental energy goes into dealing with teammates yelling and cursing. However, I've stuck to the principle of cooperating well when I get good teammates, and just focusing on playing my own game when I get toxic flamers. That's how I've managed to smoothly get this far. (Before I go on, I want to say this isn't a bait review. Most foreigners I encounter are actually pretty friendly. Of course, if you really hate foreigners in this game, it's just because certain individuals said things that you found most repulsive.) The one time I got so angry my whole body was shaking was when a friend and I played Mirage for the first time. He wasn't even familiar with the map, and I had only played it once or twice. After my friend went 0/5, a foreigner started flaming him and brought his country into it. (Honestly, I'm really trash and screw up a lot of the time. When teammates say I'm bad, I just laugh it off because it's the truth, and I actually feel grateful when nobody says anything. When he said my friend was trash, my friend had nothing to say either because he really didn't play well—but you have to attack the whole group of Chinese people?!!!!!!) Since the opponents were playing pretty fiercely and we were down 2-9, and all 4 teammates were Chinese while this guy kept typing abuse, I chose to vote kick this foreign player. As a result, the foreigner kept cursing out China, saying things like "Would you guys win without me?" After yelling back and forth for a bit, I just stopped paying attention to him. (I really hate bringing countries and race into this stuff. If someone plays poorly, you can call them trash, that's pretty 'normal'. But their country...... I have my own national pride and won't allow others to insult it, though I don't really care to talk about being 'patriotic' or anything like that.) During the vote, one of the Chinese teammates actually said, "Are you guys playing any better than him?" (At the time, my kills were the same as the foreigner's, just with 2 points less.) Hearing just that one sentence made me so mad my hands were shaking while typing. Let alone the fact that his skill level was about the same as mine (someone who's only played this map once or twice), even if he really was super good, so what? (He reminded me of something often said by brainless keyboard warriors: people like this would be the first to turn traitor if a war broke out.) But my bro totally saved my face by coming back from 0/5 to top frag. In the end, the foreigner was 3rd place, and the two of us were 1st and 2nd. That fellow Chinese player shut up after a while, but the foreigner kept right on flaming. I'm already pretty used to running into foreigners like this, so I just kept playing well and let the scoreboard slap him in the face. What I really couldn't understand, though, was why Chinese people like that even exist. With the foreigner cursing Chinese people, and then having a negative vote among the 4 Chinese players—that situation just made me feel so ashamed. Of course, people like that are just a minority, and this incident was a one-off. Compared to the hundreds of matches I've played, the odds of that happening are really low, and I've only ever seen one spinner. Still, I hope that towards friendly people, we can get along better. After all, people with terrible mentalities in games—the kind who see someone playing slightly better and immediately suck up to them, unbothered even when someone hurls racial slurs because their desire to win is all that matters—that has nothing to do with race. PS: 1. If you think there are too many cheaters and you hate foreigners, try 5E Arena. 2. Encourage your teammates more. Play well and say "nice", lose a clutch and say "nt" (nice try)—how hard is that? But you can help your teammates regain their confidence; no matter how bad they are, your yelling won't make them any smarter. Once the mental boom hits, you've already lost more than half the game. At least being in the same rank as you says a lot. Maybe nobody has ever yelled at you when you made a mistake, which is why you think you're always right. 3. Rank is just an official standard used to put people of similar skill levels into games together. It's best not to treat it as a vanity metric, and don't obsess over winning and losing just for the sake of ranking up, as that will ruin your entire gaming experience. 4. If you lose, it's because you didn't perform better. Who knows, if you handled a few clutches differently, the result might have been completely different. If you don't think like that, you might find yourself getting very exhausted playing this. At the very least, don't expect your teammates to save the world for you. What we need are pleasant surprises, not high expectations followed by disappointment and cursing. 5. Most low-rank players don't have extensive FPS experience, so their skill levels fluctuate wildly. You'll often find a teammate who plays like an absolute god in one match—making you suspect they're a smurfing pro—only to add them as a friend and find out in the next game that they play even worse than you. So do more map practice in the Workshop to stabilize your skill level. 6. I once saw someone say that Chinese people on worldwide platforms are actually quite restrained when it comes to their personal conduct. I strongly agree with this; I can feel that everyone in a foreign environment hopes to improve outsiders' perceptions of Chinese people's conduct through their own actions. 7. Because of my love for this game, I've come to deeply realize the responsibilities one sometimes has to shoulder, the responsibilities your teammates help you carry after you mess up, the expectations your teammates have of you in clutch situations, the fact that everyone can step up and handle things on their own, and the tolerance and encouragement teammates show you when you're playing poorly. This is a game that can help people grow.

translation_en: THE LEGENDARY COUNTER-STRIKE, COMING FROM BEYOND THE YEARS AND REDEFINING MULTIPLAYER GAMING, IS BACK BEFORE US WITH A BRAND NEW FACE. THE MAIN ACTOR OF ALL-NIGHT INTERNET CAFE SESSIONS LOOKS LIKE IT'S GOING TO GIFT US TIRED EYES ONCE AGAIN. When the first Half-Life came out in 1998, it quickly became a massive phenomenon in the gaming world not just with its amazing gameplay and intense atmosphere, but with many other features as well. Unlike the hardware madness of that era which was on the rise and required every gamer to refresh their computer components every 6 months, the game engine of the first Half-Life could run even on low-end systems. Because the game engine was flexible in terms of optimization, provided good graphics, and delivered very, very solid game mechanics, it became very popular among indie developers too. As a result of this, two buddies named Minh Le and Jess Cliffe created a Half-Life mod called Counter-Strike. This venture, which definitely had no commercial purpose, changed multiplayer gaming forever and made a horribly huge contribution to the concept of professional gaming. In fact, Minh Le was later hired by Valve. The huge success of Counter-Strike also served as an inspiring story for indie developers. In the passing years, brands that fundamentally changed multiplayer gaming like Modern Warfare (MW) and Battlefield (BF) came out, but a classic is always a classic. NEVER WITHOUT A TEAM! Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS: GO) applies almost identically whatever used to make us prisoners to CS back in the day. Extremely exciting gameplay, realistic weapons, and team play... All these components form the nervous system of CS: GO. Even though there isn't a groundbreaking innovation in the game, the reinterpreted maps and new modes are quite addictive. Even though players still organize tournaments via CS 1.6 and Source, we reckon that GO's policy of spreading to more players will make the game popular. And in our opinion, GO turned out to be a rendition closer to 1.6 than Source. For instance, beginners or those who haven't played in a long time can dive straight into the action with the Classic Casual mode. This option literally lets you warm up to the game and its mechanics. For example, in this option FF (Friendly Fire: your teammates being able to take damage from your weapons) is directly turned off and you can buy weapons automatically. This option lets you adapt to the game much quicker. The Classic mode is just the CS we know. The two new modes we encounter in CS games, Demolition and Arms Race, ensure that extremely exciting and high-level matches are played. In Arms Race, your weapon changes as you wipe out opponents, and therefore every new frag means a brand new challenge. After every death, you respawn immediately. (Of course, let's remind you that you take no damage for 5 seconds after spawning. No life for Spawn Campers!) In the final frag of this mode, you fight knife-to-knife and try to leave an epic signature at the end of the match. In Demolition, your weapon changes at the end of each round you win, but you don't respawn when you die; you have to wait for the rounds to end. As you can understand from the name of this mode, in each round terrorists try to plant a bomb and the special forces try to stop them. Aside from this, we can count the overhaul of classic maps among the innovations. Seeing classic maps like de_dust and cs_italy with brand new graphics is quite nice. Of course, all character models and weapons have been overhauled too. Even though it has no effect on gameplay, it makes the game look good cosmetically. Even though Global Offensive is a rendition close to 1.6 that tries to please both new and old players, especially the Classic mode has gotten quite difficult. When you dive straight into the game without getting used to it in Classic Casual, you'll notice that aiming and especially landing headshots, which is the golden key to success in CS, is harder compared to 1.6. Honestly, the fact that the game's hit feedback is a bit lacking has an effect on this too. In 1.6 you could rattle and feel every single bullet sinking into your opponent's body, but in GO that feeling has slightly disappeared.

translation_en: [h1]After years of trying CS:GO and now CS2, here is my review:[/h1] Since 2017 when I last wrote a comment about CS and I think things have changed, boy have they changed. Since the days of the R8 Revolver in CS:GO and cheaters out the ass, the game has gone through massive changes (maybe not so much with the cheaters, that's just luck). The things the game had to go through to become CS2 have been really rough sometimes, like how the game literally couldn't be updated anymore. CS is one of those games where you're gonna need someone or need to watch someone to understand it fully. Now in CS2 there's a short tutorial that helps you learn the basics, but actually playing it with some competence might take many hours. That's always been a problem with CS games, how steep the learning curve is, especially at the start. So if you have the patience to try a game for about 20-100 hours and catch nothing but bullets to the face, only to later realize you're dealing with one of the deepest and most entertaining games in the world, this is gonna be your game. Now upon the release of CS2 things are a bit rough around the edges in some aspects: performance, specific issues with cheaters on the new leaderboards, and very poor balancing in PREMIER mode. However, it has the platform to improve, the new engine, a Bible's worth of community feedback—if they don't do it, it wouldn't be for lack of information, it would just be Valve being Valve. This is the best time ever to get into CS; many mechanics have been simplified (for convenience, not for ease), the ranks have been reset, and the experience looks and plays better than ever. Dedicating my life, at least my early years, to this game has been one of the best things I've ever decided to do. There are several places where you can find info about CS2, my channels are a place where you can do that too. Play CS2, it's not perfect, highly recommended.

translation_en: Of course I recommend this game! An edit almost a year later, I almost forgot about this review... I play a lot less CS:GO now, and I barely mess with skins anymore (Dota 2's Legend of Dota is way more fun, though). I feel like I bear some responsibility here because this review can now only serve as partial reference, especially the trading sites and price estimation stuff. The price estimates might not be accurate anymore either, so please head over to the forums to ask. The rest of it is mostly still fine, though. ————————————————————— I just found out Valve banned both IGXE and skinsjar's bots for alleged gambling... My heart goes out to my friends who had items on IGXE. This ban was way too unreasonable, dropped out of nowhere without any prior warning or official statement, using suspected gambling as the excuse (meanwhile, OPSkins is totally fine). If IGXE still can't unban those bots, casual players like us are the ones getting screwed over. Anyway, everyone shouldn't buy or sell on IGXE for now; the safety of your own money is what matters most. There's not much we can do at the moment, so let's just wait and see how it plays out. Still, I wouldn't recommend buying on OPSkins, the taxes are way too high. Even if one IGXE dies, a bunch of LGDXE, TYLOOXE, and VPXE will definitely pop up in its place, so you don't need to worry about not being able to sell your stuff later. Wishing good luck to everyone whose items got swallowed up. ---------------------------------------------------Another update----------------------------------------------------------------- Some Workshop maps and authors that might help: Map for farming StatTrak kills, requires playing with a friend or a smurf account: "TGS—Best Stattrak Map" -by whiskeyo Recoil control practice map: "Recoil Master" -by Mr.uLLetical All-weapon practice map: "Aim Botz-Training" -by Mr.uLLetical Crosshair placement / prefire practice map: (the Inferno one is genuinely hard) "Prefire Practice X (X=Dust2/Inferno/Cache/Mirage...)" -by Yesber Specific smoke grenade tutorials: "X (X=inferno/dust2/mirage...) training" -by Dolnm Map for when you buy a new gun and want to see what it looks like to take screenshots and send them to your buddies: "Live skybox, screenshot" -by Reminiscences There's also an even better map specifically for screenshots that has filters and depth of field effects, but unfortunately I unsubscribed from it. If anyone knows it, feel free to mention it in the comments. =========================Update Divider====================================== Negative reviews are just for grabbing attention. This is a great game—it has nostalgia, competitiveness, and is fun to watch, with massive replay value. Anyway, with so many positive reviews, they don't really need mine, and writing a negative review makes it easier to get noticed, hehe. Below are some tips and insights I've gathered from playing this game; you can try reading through them, they might be somewhat helpful. First off, the 48 RMB price has discounts. Both the Christmas and Summer sales give a 50% discount. I bought this game for 24 RMB myself, so it won't rip you off. Next, once you hit level 3 in casual mode, you can play competitive mode. At level 21 you get Prime status, which cuts down on cheaters significantly. In my 450 hours of playtime, I've only encountered one obvious cheater—some anime profile pic getting headshots in casual mode. Before level 3, I suggest playing active duty maps to prepare for competitive, and avoid Dust 2 because it was undergoing a rework and future versions would be different. (Correction: It's been reworked ages ago, but competitive mode has the most cheaters and rage-quitters.) To practice unpopular guns or just for fun, I recommend playing hostage maps as T—you have a bigger advantage. In competitive mode, you MUST use a mic and wear headphones! You MUST use a mic and wear headphones! You MUST use a mic and wear headphones! If you don't use a mic and headphones, you're basically being irresponsible to your teammates and not playing with a competitive mindset! You might as well just play casual mode. Furthermore, the game has a Perfect World (国服) client, but right now there are tons and tons of cheaters, so I don't recommend playing on the national server. If you run into teammates in competitive mode who ruin your gaming experience, you can choose to report or block them (hit Tab to open the scoreboard, then right-click). Don't teamkill, idle, or rage-quit—the penalties are very heavy. You can use the same method during warmup to check which country your teammates are from to figure out what language to communicate in. If you run into Russians or people from the Philippines, I suggest muting them right away (they are annoyingly loud). The Russian phrase "cyka blyat" is trash talk and also a meme. You need to win ten matches to get your rank, and ties count too. If you don't play for a month, your rank disappears, and you'll get it back after winning one match, but you'll probably rank down (Latest edit: I used to be AK rank, didn't play for a few months, won one and lost one while placing 4th and 3rd respectively, and dropped to Gold Nova 1). ECO means not buying any utility or guns that round. Here is the real meat and potatoes: Once you've played this game for a certain amount of time, you might want to buy some game skins—unlike skins in Honor of Kings or League of Legends, all skins can be traded multiple times (Latest edit: though around 2018 they added a 7-day trade cooldown, I think, and the market is sluggish). When you don't want the skins anymore, you can sell them for a price close to what you bought them for, or even make a small profit. In other words, you can totally use that 48 RMB as small-time reseller capital to make enough for skins or even gaming peripherals. IGXE and OPSkins are the mainstream and best skin trading sites. If you want to buy skins worth more than 5 RMB, please don't buy them on Steam because Steam charges a seller tax, making prices about 10% to 15% or even higher than IGXE, so IGXE will save you a lot of money. The key part is that you can withdraw cash to Alipay. Skins under 1 RMB are actually cheaper to buy directly on Steam. Buying low-market-ratio items on IGXE and selling them on Steam lets you achieve a "top up 1 RMB, get 0.25 RMB free" effect, commonly known as "hanging the knife" (挂刀), though it has a certain learning curve. Currently, IGXE is hit by Valve's big purge, and some skins can't be retrieved. It's best not to do skin trades on IGXE right now. If you have skins locked up in IGXE, please just sit tight and wait for good news... Good luck. CS.MONEY and SkinsJar are two skin-to-skin trading sites with a small tax (3%-5%). If you have a bunch of low-tier cheap skins, you can consider swapping them for a big-ticket item on these sites. Sometimes you can score some good stickers or low-float items. SkinsJar's bots were recently banned by Valve due to suspected gambling—they're probably dead for good... Everyone should go to CS.MONEY or CSTrade to swap items instead, or Tradeskinfast works too. Metjm and CSGOLa: These are skin wear and sticker checking websites. They are super useful. I recommend experienced folks use Metjm—it checks wear quickly, provides clear resolution images, and can check wear values on various Doppler knives. CSGOLa has a similar effect, but without a premium membership, checking wear is very slow. I suggest players who aren't very familiar with stickers or case hardened patterns use it to check sticker prices, whether stickers have been scraped, case hardened patterns (patterns, commonly called P1, T1, blue mags), and how to change the gun names into Chinese using codes. Max+ and the pinned threads on the CS:GO skin trading Baidu Tieba (though most are scammers now and there's no active moderator). Max+ is an app for discussing skin trading insights, and you can also talk about Dota 2 and other games, plus it has news push notifications. The Tieba pinned threads have some solid info, and people usually sell big-ticket items there. There are also plenty of hardcore experts who understand metaphysical items like Case Hardened. NEVER touch the Max+ skin prediction section; it's too hard to stop once you start. DO NOT TOUCH THE FOLLOWING WEBSITES OR SOFTWARE!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! CS:GO's built-in cases, Farmkins (case opening sites), CS:GO Reaper (commonly called coin-flipping), niugame (domestic prediction sites), Max+ prediction section. Don't think you're actually that lucky and can get rich quick relying on these. You'd be better off playing Bitcoin instead. All those people claiming they made a fortune opening cases or coin-flipping are just shills. I've seen way more people lose thousands or even hundreds of thousands of RMB on these sites. I lost around 1.6k RMB myself. By the way, "bocai" (菠菜) just means gambling/betting. Next is some experience regarding buying skins. Some trading terminology (well, terms I guess): Most importantly, no matter who it is, unless they are a real-life friend, be very cautious about cash-first trades or borrowing skins! Or just straight-up refuse! You must use a trading site or a trusted middleman! I consider myself lucky; I only got scammed out of three days' worth of takeout money. Before trading, make sure the other person isn't a level 1 or 2 alt account, and check if they constantly change their name—frequent name changes usually mean a scammer. "Fang" (方) / "Yuan" (缘): Swapping skins for skins, leaning towards item bartering. If there's a price difference, people usually make it up with keys or nametags. It's usually done directly through Steam trade links, bypassing trading sites. Since there's almost always a price difference to make up, it's a bit more of a hassle. CS:GO players usually call it "Fang," while Dota 2 players call it "Yuan." "ZhiFang" or "ZhiYuan" means no price difference to make up. "Pan" (盘): Exchanging money for items via a middleman (zhongjie) or a legitimate trading site, such as IGXE private trades. "Pan" usually refers to the seller's asking price, while "co" is the buyer's offer. "Dao" (刀): Bargaining/haggling. People buying and selling skins on various forums have explosive tempers right now, so if you're not buying, don't haggle. If you do haggle, do it ten RMB at a time, otherwise the seller might chew you out to death. "NBK": Commonly called "N", 1N = 10 RMB, a Max+ exclusive term. Regarding the specific value and prices of skins, I'll just mention a few absolute basics. Judging prices by wear is generally: Factory New (FN) > Minimal Wear (MW) > Field-Tested (FT) > Battle-Scarred (BS) > Well-Worn (WW). Well-Worn is sometimes more expensive than Battle-Scarred and sometimes cheaper, but try to avoid buying Well-Worn skins. Don't buy Factory New or StatTrak (commonly called "StatTrak" or "counters") for every single skin—it's super not worth it. For example, buying Factory New vs. Field-Tested for "Desolate Space" or "Blood Sport" has almost no difference besides brightness. You can check the skin section of the Max+ app to see what a skin looks like under different wear conditions before buying. StatTrak weapons can easily be farmed to 100k kills with friends using a Workshop StatTrak map, which makes it totally meaningless. StatTrak knives are even more so. Next is estimating the price of sticker-applied guns. Since stickers lose value once slapped onto a gun, sticker combinations from 2015 onwards with four of the same sticker are usually priced at 1.5 to 2 times the sticker's price. A mix of different stickers is usually calculated at 0.15 to 0.2 times the total sticker price. For 2015, four of the same sticker is usually counted as two stickers' worth, and mixed stickers are counted as 0.25 of the total sticker price. For 2014, aside from the Katowice series stickers, everything else is calculated similarly to 2015. You shouldn't buy 2014 Katowice sticker guns unless you know skins well, as it's very easy to get ripped off. After calculating the sticker price, remember to multiply the gun's base price by 0.85-0.9 and add them together—that's generally the reasonable price range for a sticker gun. Stickers inside capsules like Enfu are usually calculated as four for the price of one, or not counted at all. As for the Howling Dawn sticker, the 2014 Dignitas Holo sticker, the Crown sticker, and the Lucky Cat sticker, please make a post on the forums to ask for their prices. !!! Note: When buying sticker guns, you must check on CSGOLa whether the stickers have been scraped! Scraped stickers are worthless!! Don't be greedy for a bargain!! Case Hardened AK-47s are divided into Tier 1 (T1), camo, pure blue mag, Tier 2 (T2), blue mag, blue barrel, Tier 3, Tier 4 (gambling trash), etc., with prices decreasing from left to right. PS: There are only four patterns for pure blue mags (the ID number shown when inspecting an item): 502, 579, 587, and 716. If IG sellers claim it's a pure blue mag, they are basically lying to you. I don't remember where pure gold AKs rank, so I won't talk nonsense about them. As for the "Doppler" series knives, they are also divided into Phases (P1, P2, P3, P4). P1 has lots of black and less pink; P2 has less black and lots of pink; P3 has less blue, lots of black, and a hint of green; P4 has lots of blue and less black. You can tell which phase it is using websites like Metjm and CSGOLa. Price-wise: P1 < P3 < P4 < P2. P1 and P3 are usually used as gambling currency and don't look as good. You can roughly tell the phase from Steam and thumbnail icons. (Latest edit: But remember, when buying a flawless Doppler, always ask the seller for a backlit screenshot to check the distribution of dark spots. If there are a lot, they're playing you.) Dopplers aren't necessarily cheap. Expensive Dopplers include Gamma Dopplers and various Gem Dopplers. Gamma Dopplers are also divided into P1, P2, P3, P4, but they are all green: P1 has more black, less green; P2 has more green, less black; P3 has a tiny bit of blue-green; P4 has a tiny bit of light green distributed fairly evenly. As for Doppler Gems... I can't afford those. Regarding Marble Fades, there are metaphysics like red tips, double red, etc.; I suggest heading over to the old Max+ section "Yuwen YW"'s posts to check them out—he knows a lot more than I do, and it seems he has charts for pattern indexes. Different knife types have even more detailed metaphysical traits that cause price fluctuations, like checking the ring color on Karambits or M9 Bayonets; checking the wear and dark band distribution on M9 Dopplers, and so on. I won't go into detail, but remember to compare multiple listings when buying. For beginners, I recommend popular gambling-tier knives: stable prices, huge trading volume, sell fast, and hard to lose money on. For example, Safari Mesh M9s, Safari Mesh Bayonets, and the like. Gut Knives, Huntsman Knives, and Shadow Daggers are not recommended; they are very hard to sell. Personally, I like the M9 Doppler—drawing the knife feels snappy, and the Doppler shades look better than on flip knives. Don't develop "StatTrak-itis" or "Factory New-itis" unless you've decided to buy these skins and never sell them (StatTrak items usually take twice as long to sell compared to normal ones). If your cash flow is tight, don't buy too many (they aren't much more merciful than FGO)... Also, AWP/SSG/etc. Asiimovs—except for the P90, none of them come in Factory New, so stop acting cute in Bilibili or Pig's live streams. I suggest you do not accept friend requests from any foreigners! Just decline them straight up! Changing your name to something without Chinese characters will effectively prevent random teammates—especially Filipino retards—from team-killing and cursing at you for no reason, and it will also stop some scammers (just a suggestion). A lot of foreigners will add you after a match and ask you for a knife or gun, or pretend to invite you to a 4-man stack of foreign players, lying that they can't hear your voice and telling you to download some voice chat software from a certain website. Once you turn on your VPN, struggle to download it, and open it, your Dragon Lore, Howl, Gem knife, Dragonclaw Hook, and Lava Meat Hook will all go GG, regardless of whether you have Steam Guard enabled or not. I'm really not being paranoid; this hasn't happened just once or twice. Earlier, a foreigner played a match with me and said today was his birthday, asking me to send him a gun, and even sent a trade offer directly, picking the most expensive ones. Me: ? Finally, I wish you all a good time gaming~

Newer scam methods mean you have to watch out what you do and what you'd better leave alone. [/b] [b]2. In case Matchmaking isn't enough anymore, there's always ESEA or FACEIT. 3. [b]Summary[/b] CS:GO is like a drug, it ruins you but you can't live without it. translation_en: Back in 1999, I was 19 and transitioned from DF1—my go-to first-person shooter—to CS 1.0. I'd tried a few versions of the CS beta back when it wasn't a standalone game yet. I loved this game series and barely played anything else like CF. In 2017, I turned 37. For 18 years, from 2005 to 2009, a group of like-minded friends and I built a CS:Source clan called "Red Front" into one of the best teams in the country. We even went to Shanghai for the CGS qualifiers, beat a pro team from Singapore, and played against Alex back when they were still on wnv. In online leagues, we played teams from over a dozen Southeast Asian countries and pretty much held our own for China. Years of late-night training and matches blew my weight past 200 catties. My mom was my only family back then, and seeing the worry in her eyes, I knew I was at an age where I needed to step up and take on more family responsibility, so I started losing weight. During the hottest summer in Chongqing, I went from not even being able to do half a sit-up and 0 push-ups, to doing 400 sit-up, 300 push-ups, and running in place for 3 hours every day. In those two months, I dropped over 50 catties. Later, I got into hiking and mountaineering. Seven years after starting the Chongqing Forest Hiking and Mountaineering Group, I founded Senlan Outdoors. Now we have over 1,200 members, and I've made a lot of friends, including my wife. In 2015, I did a 100km full-pack trek across Xinjiang's Wusun Ancient Trail (Wolf Tower C route). A few years ago, I summitted Mt. Siguniang No. 2 Peak at 5,278 meters and No. 3 Peak at 5,335 meters. At the end of July 2017, I did a 70km full-pack traverse of the Aotai line. I only started playing CS:GO in early 2016, playing two matchmaking maps a day. There was a time I didn't play for a bit and deranked from Double AK. My aim is nowhere near what it used to be when I was young—my old 0.25-second reaction time is gone, and now I'm just running on gamesense. This version has a faster pace and relies way more on teamwork. Whether it's the teammates' fault or your own, just do your best. I still believe that cheaters are a tiny minority after all; don't let that small fraction ruin your attitude and principles. I enjoy the process of the game, and whatever happens with wins and losses happens.
