translation_en: Listen up, anyone thinking about buying CS:GO, keep these things in mind! 1: Best stay away from cases! That luck-based shit is just like gambling, once you start you literally can't stop. Unless you think you're some kind of lucky bastard, you're better off not touching cases and just calmly buying skins instead! 2: XP needed to rank up is fixed. No matter what level you are, leveling up always takes a fixed 5,000 points. Every level-up gets you a random graffiti drop (with limited uses) or a skin gun, though they're basically all worthless, and you only get one per week. Once you hit level 40 you can Prestige, reset back to level 1, and they'll give you that year's Service Medal. Like, if you max out and prestige in 2017, you get the 2017 Service Medal. Basically, these medals are just for show. 3: Balance, don't even need to talk about it. Skins don't give any stat boosts, so no need to worry about running into some pay-to-win whales. 4: Both CTs and Ts have their own faction-exclusive weapons, like the CT's M4A1 and the T's AK47. [Mentioning this just to roast a noob friend of mine who kept asking me why CTs can't buy an AK47 and Ts can't buy an M4A1. Honestly, I can laugh at him for a whole year, 23333] 5: Now you can play Competitive once you hit level 2. And placement matches don't make you play 10 games to get ranked, they make you *win* 10 games—you only finish placements after 10 wins. Every 2 wins will freeze your competitive mode so you can't play, using your record from those 2 wins and the losses you had before to evaluate your skill level. Once the freeze time is up, you can keep playing competitive. After you finish your placements, you can play competitive to your heart's content! 6: You gotta be careful around strangers. Some scumbags will add you as a friend and send you links—do not click those links, and don't believe those assholes saying "I'll buy your knife/skins for XXX yuan," none of these guys are good people. [Mentioning this because I've seen people getting scammed on Tieba more than once.] 7: Right now CSGO has two types of servers, Perfect World (PW) and International. The PW server requires an activation code to play (though that might change after the 18th). Go search Baidu for the CSGO Perfect World official site to grab a code. The PW server censorship is pretty harsh, blood turns into oil, terrorists turn into censored symbols, etc. For International server players, I'd recommend NetEase UU and Qiyou for VPNs. If International players want to switch to the PW server, just like doing it in Dota2, right-click the game, hit properties, go to the properties page and click "Set Launch Options", type `-perfectworld steam` into the launch options, hit confirm, and you're good to go. Though International players without a code still won't be able to queue before the 18th. 8: I haven't messed around with skin trading sites much, but just a warning to everyone—small amounts are fine, but stay away from big amounts, shit goes wrong too easily. 9: Now that the PW server is out, to keep noobs from getting scammed as much, let me add a bit to point #6. Let's talk about how scammers actually run their scams right now: basically, anyone wanting to buy your knife or get you to play in a league is 100% a scammer. Some people used to wonder why you shouldn't click links, so let me break it down for you. These are inventory links. If you've got Steam Guard Mobile Authenticator enabled it's not as bad, but if you don't, you are totally fucked. It'll trade your entire inventory to the other person. With the phone it's fine since you can confirm the trade, but players without Mobile Guard are screwed. And don't think having the mobile authenticator means you can just do whatever you want—some hackers already set up phishing sites just waiting for you to slip up. Right now scam bots' favorite method is pretending they need an extra player for a league to trick you. Since those are automated bots talking, let me explain how they usually pull it off: Scammer: We need one more for our league, what position do you play? Noob: ??? Scammer: Alright, got it. Add our team manager, she'll tell you more. [XXX — this is the inventory trade link] At this point, just delete them and don't bother trying to troll them, it's just a bot and it won't reply. ------------Divider------------ There are tons of gameplay tips in CSGO, like grenade trajectories and stuff, which take a lot of practice to get down. Play long enough and you'll realize this game relies heavily on tactics; play even more and you'll start figuring out your own strats. [Though the most classic strat in this game is still RUSH B, the most classic weapon is still the P90, and the most classic map is still DUST 2, 23333] New players should hit up community servers to practice their aim, like deathmatch. Practicing more always helps. Aim is the foundation, but game sense is king! Also, you gotta call out enemy positions in this game, otherwise when you die your teammates have no idea where the enemy is and you'll get shit on easily. You *have* to communicate. [Of course, if you get matched with foreigners and can't communicate, nothing you can do.] By the way, in Casual mode, whether you die and use voice or text chat, only dead people can see and hear you. You can only truly mind-meld in Competitive mode, 23333. Alright, the basics are pretty much covered. You gotta experience the rest of the game content for yourself. I hope more and more Chinese players start playing CSGO!

translation_en: [b] Counter-Strike: Global Offensive [/b] [h1] Introduction [/h1] So after over 850h of Counter Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO) I'm finally writing a review for this game. It's one of the best known and most popular shooters worldwide and is even played in the ESL. But like in every game, there are pros and unfortunately also cons. I'll start with the pros. [h1] Pros [/h1] + It's very tactical and therefore a great team game. + It's a lot of fun playing it with your friends. + Almost everyone has the game, which is why you always find nice people to play with. + There are many nice skins, which however have zero impact on the game itself. [h1] Cons [/h1] - There are many maps that are almost never played, which ensures that you always end up playing the same maps (e.g. Mirage, Dust II, Inferno). - Unfortunately, there are a lot of cheaters who ruin the fun and it feels like they aren't getting any fewer. (Though having a so-called "Prime" account reduces the chance of playing with cheaters). - In my opinion, the ranks are distributed incorrectly. It happens that some Silver players (Silver is the worst) beat Gold Nova players (Gold Nova is sort of average). And then you can understand why some people get mad about why they aren't getting ranked up higher. - Unfortunately, there are many players without a headset or microphone who heavily prevent tactical play, because you don't know where the other guy is going or where the enemies are and thus run right into a trap. [h1] Other [/h1] ~ Unfortunately, there are also "scammers" who try to scam players out of their skins or take their skins using tricks and empty promises. Sadly, it works very often, which is really sad. However, there are ways not to fall for it. (E.g. NEVER trade with strangers, NEVER give your skins to anyone). If people message you acting weird with cool skins and stuff, they're mostly scammers. Just block them and remove them as a friend, that's how you keep your skins. [h1] Summary [/h1] Even though there are so many negative aspects, it's still fun to play this game. I give the game 8/10 points. If this review was helpful and you want to see more detailed reviews, feel free to follow our [url=http://steamcommunity.com/groups/-German_Gamer_Community-#curation] review program [/url]

translation_en: [h1][b] Go, rush long, go! [/b] [/h1] That case when the older a game gets, the more it degrades. If I was writing this review like 2 years ago, I'd definitely recommend playing it, but now... Let's break it down. [b] For those who hate reading a lot: [/b] I do not recommend this game under any circumstances. No, seriously. Right now there's a huge amount of other online shooters that actually deserve attention. Take Battle Carnival, even though I don't really like it, but I don't think it's that bad over there. Or better yet, take this money and buy Call of Duty Modern Warfare 2. The single-player campaign there is top-tier, and the multiplayer is the best. [b] And now for those who need a more detailed breakdown: [/b] Let's start with the main thing: How does it play? I won't lie and will say that it plays well. Tactics, maps with their own nooks and paths — all of that is there. The gunplay. Every weapon shoots differently, every gun needs its own approach (except the P90, but more on that in a bit). In short, it's all done well... it would be, if not for a number of problems that won't let you enjoy it. Let's continue with the weapons. P90. Years ago and right now — absolute imba that doesn't need any practice. And nobody fixed it, no. What is this? Oh well, whatever. At the end of the day, nothing stops you from grabbing it yourself and finally turning the game into a total circus. Okay. There's a more significant problem: The game [b] DOES NOT WORK [/b] the way it's supposed to work. And I'm talking about the mechanics. Remember what I said about tactics? Well, that only works at high ranks (and even then, not always). In all other cases you are doomed to play with people who pull off absolute fucking madness. No, seriously... it's just a nightmare. Endless screaming in voice chat, toxic freaks who love to vote-kick everyone, 2 guys who play exclusively for each other and bitch that the team is losing, the MANDATORY guy who shoves his purple skins in everyone's face, the MANDATORY guy who criticizes the OTHER MANDATORY guy for his skins... Br-r-r. And yeah, speaking of the community... You know, I remember very well the time when everyone mercilessly flamed Warface players for being such toxic idiots and talentless hacks with bad taste. Nowadays COD players get flamed the exact same way (doesn't matter which COD, the point is it's COD). So, what was I getting at. Most of these people held up Counter Strike:GO as the ultimate standard. And you know what's ironic? It has sunk to that exact same level. To the level of a free-to-play FPS run-and-gunner. No, seriously. Just think about it: - Microtransactions - Present! (Weapon skins, knife skins, glove skins, graffiti...) - Toxic community - Present! (I thought there were no people worse than in COD multiplayer... how wrong I was. At least those guys had some soul, but here you can sort them by types and classes. Bad shooter, the guy who doesn't give a fuck about tactics, the guy who dies first, the guy who teamkills you for a bad play or something. The -1/0/1 guy... You could make a movie about them.) - Old graphics - Present! (Someone's gonna tell me graphics don't matter that much... and they'd be right. But nevertheless, after a massive influx of people saying they don't play other shooters due to (direct quote) "Bad graphics" (they were talking about Overwatch, Call of Duty and Battlefield), it forces me to point this out.) - Abundance of cheaters - Present! (Cheaters are everywhere and of all shapes and sizes. There are those who literally can't play without them. Total myopia, the whole deal. There are those who toggle them on sometimes in especially tough matches. There are completely brain-dead people who can play well, but specifically play with cheats just for the BAN! THE BAN! Look what we've come to. I wish these people turn back into monkeys as fast as possible and run away deep into the forest. That's where they belong. And the saddest part is that while people actually fight this, they do it very lazily. Alas.) And what do we have in the end? A game that could have been and can be good, but only if it gets rid of at least one of these problems... But no, that's never gonna happen. Because developing the game is expensive and they're lazy, cutting off such a massive cash cow (shit, they don't even design them anymore, they just take the creators' best works and release their designs) is suicide, and the community... the community never changes. They play and will keep playing, screaming their lungs out that this will turn them into esports pros, ugh. Summing it all up, I want to say just one thing: If after all of the above you changed your mind about buying this game, then my efforts weren't in vain. For everyone else... it's great that you have your own opinion. Just wait for the summer sale. Maybe you'll find something that interests you more and costs less. That's how it is.

translation_en: As a Counter Strike player since the 0.7 beta, which was born back in 1999 (long before Steam even existed), if I remember correctly, my review is as follows: [h1][b]Positive aspects:[/b][/h1] - It allows a few lucky bastards to cash in (big time) with the workshop system; in most countries, 30% of each sale goes to Valve and the rest to the creator. - The whole skins, stickers, and other stuff thing has its appeal. (Although it borders on abusive). - It keeps the essence of previous installments and requires good gun-skill to stand out during matches. - It runs on mid-to-low-end PCs, although performance could be improved. - Decent matchmaking and the ranking system is a plus. - There are tons of people playing 24 hours a day. - It allows custom CFGs, which in many cases are useful. - You can watch your last eight competitive matches and download them. It also lets you view other people's matches. - When there are major tournaments they give out drops (weapon cases) for watching them live, most of them sell for a good price, and some cases contain unique weapons like the well-known "Dragon Lore." - Overwatch, an anti-cheat system, way more effective than the well-known VAC, though everyone knows there are totally undetectable "cheats" available to buy on endless websites. - If the miracle happens and a hacker gets banned, the contents of their inventory are completely "blacklisted". [h1][b]Negative aspects:[/b][/h1] - "CS" has been infested with hackers since the holy beginning, and Global Offensive is no exception. (The game is cheap, so people don't give a flying fuck about getting banned). - Too much shamelessness from Valve with the "buy-sell" system for weapons, stickers, cases, etc. The price of keys is an abomination, and unfortunately people keep paying for them. I say unfortunately because the chances of making a "profit" are practically zero. I understand they've created a foolproof system, making enough money to feed the entire world for decades, but they take the piss... they don't even know what else to do to milk money out of their players anymore. Example: Graffitis with 50 charges, stickers you can only apply once... OMG. - The weekly drops are just fucking gross. You spend hours playing just to get rewarded with a crappy 3-cent weapon, or what pisses me off the most, graffitis... - Playing late at night, without a premade and (in Spain), means suffering the mental deficiency of Russian players. I've never seen more "troll" players than the Russians; you try to rank up and these "characters" ruin your day. [h1][b]All in all:[/b][/h1] I recommend it because I've always enjoyed "CS" and it's a tactical game that requires a certain amount of skill, and because playing with friends is fun (except when those "geniuses" ruin your day).

translation_en: At first, when I heard about the Perfect World server launch, I was against it, because you can't just release a server like that out of nowhere. It was like it had special effects added to it. However, I later learned through Perfect World customer support that for us Steam international server players "returning" to the national server, the data is mutually compatible, and account info, weapons, items, etc., are all shared. There's no such situation where your stuff disappears on the international server after data migration. To put it simply, when logging into the national server, you use a "Chinese" IP, and when logging in via Steam, you use a "foreign" IP. If you want to play on the national server, you launch the national server launcher (you can also manually modify the launch options), and if you want to play on the international server, you launch it through Steam. So it's actually really convenient if you have friends playing on the national server who didn't buy the Steam version. Fortunately, national server players can't play on the international server—some people claim they can, but it requires an invitation from an international server friend. Otherwise, those of us who bought the game on Steam would have felt pretty uncomfortable about it, even though it wasn't expensive. Finally, a review of the game itself: Personally, I think this is currently the fairest competitive game out there. Leaving aside CrossFire and A.V.A, I actually really enjoyed playing COD Online, which was published by Tencent. But later on, the thing I least wanted to happen actually happened. As expected, COD Online started releasing stat-boosting skin guns, where whoever spends money is God. But CS:GO? You can spend a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand, but if your skill is bad and you buy a skin, it's still a waste. In CF, you spend tens or hundreds on timed weapons. Here, you can buy skins to your liking anywhere from a few bucks to a few hundred—isn't that awesome? CS has been improving all these years, but it also feels like there's nothing left to improve. Compared to the original 1.5 and 1.6, back then there was no ragdoll system, no 3D modeling, let alone powerful lighting and physics effects. Compared to those games with planes and cannons, this is more direct, simpler, and more competitive. The final verdict on this game in one sentence: Classic, fun, and takes a beating. [h1]Edited on April 22, 2017 at 23:38[/h1] There are recent rumors that the CS:GO engine is going to use Source 2—Dota 2 players should have heard about this. When that happens, the interface will change to a much more gorgeous full-screen main menu, and the in-game physics engine, lighting system, etc., will be upgraded to a higher level. A brand new CS:GO will be presented to us; let's all look forward to its update. 10/10

translation_en: When I was a kid, the two of us would happily ditch class to go to the internet cafe and play CS, carefree, as if we’d never had a single worry. But after entering middle school, everything changed. A guy in class bragged about his CF skills every single day, and to show off how rich he was, he even bought her a battle axe, stealing the girl I loved. Just like that, she left for CF, leaving me all alone. After school, the gloomy sky had already started raining. Upon finding out she went to play CF, I was on the verge of a complete mental breakdown. I walked home in the rain, only to get splashed head-to-toe in mud by a bicycle. The one riding the bike was that guy. "Country bumpkin, keep playing your dumbass CS!" he yelled, and sped off. My face showed neither joy nor sorrow, but it hurt like hell inside. I cried the entire night. ----- Eight years later, she was tall and attractive, but seemed to have given up on her education and was playing in a CF internet cafe tournament. She lost a few matches in a row, a few beads of sweat hanging on the tip of her dainty nose. Her elementary schooler teammate next to her was playing on a Private Second Class account, not even a single RMB item on it. This round was a loss. I saw her, walked over and sat down, chasing the kid away. But she was too focused to even notice me. Four people were already dead on the field, leaving only me, a SAS holding an AK-74. Clutch time. I peeked out, one-tapped an enemy sticking their head out, and continued to spray down the enemies coming to pinch me. Relying on my movement, I dodged a Fire Qilin's bullets and headshot him with the Glock's 12 rounds. I picked up the Fire Qilin and won them the round. She took off her headphones, looked at me with eyes full of surprise, and asked, "Where have you been all these years? You've gotten so good, I've been waiting for you in CF." I looked at her, expressionless, and said, "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO) expands upon the team-based action gameplay that it pioneered when the franchise launched 12 years ago. CS:GO features new maps, characters, weapons, and delivers updated versions of the classic CS content (de_dust, etc.). In addition, CS:GO introduces new game modes, matchmaking, leaderboards, and more. 'Counter-Strike took the gaming industry by surprise when the unlikely MOD became the most played online PC action game in the world almost immediately after its release in August 1999,' said Doug Lombardi at Valve. 'For the past 12 years, it has been one of the most played games in the world, headlining competitive gaming tournaments and selling over 25 million units worldwide across the franchise. CS:GO promises to expand on CS' award-winning gameplay and deliver it to PC as well as next gen consoles and the Mac.'" She burst into tears, and came with me to CS:GO. And then she blew all her savings on opening cases.

translation_en: Having played 5 thousand hours, here is what I can say: Pros: - you can play on Valve servers (Casual lobby) and not play on public community servers (for me, after CSS, this was the main plus). - 5v5 game mode (Competitive), it's totally doable to go solo almost anywhere and rush, meaning you can carry even alone if your team is trash - a huge number of custom servers with various mods (search in the legacy server browser internet tab) - decent shooting with decent recoil (compared to CSS) - Workshop Cons: - cheats and cheaters everywhere and in all ranks, right now cheats cost around 500 rubles (prices for cheats vary and for any taste) and VAC doesn't get issued for months, server VAC protection is currently "worthless" - Overwatch (no guarantee there'll be normal guys in there, often it's schoolkids, cheaters, toxic weirdos) - playing with bunnyhop (it's basically a mini speed hack) or autofire, getting a VAC ban is almost impossible (you might get banned by Overwatch) - a ton of toxic people in both casual and competitive lobbies (partially solved by voice_enable 0) - updates adding a lot of useless junk (arguable for some) - the game teaches you nothing - playing CS:GO won't develop your reaction time - playing CS:GO won't make you smarter, there's a chance to degrade to the general average level of the toxic mob - this game is entirely designed to milk money out of players and grab your attention to the max so you waste your time here, the developers have no other goal - low performance and lags (noticeable on full 64-slot servers, especially on zombie escape servers), which is unforgivable for a game made on an ancient engine that was already ready at least by 2003 when the HL2 beta was out - a large number of bugs (YouTube to the rescue) - the game isn't worth the time you spend on it; it's better to "level up" yourself in something more necessary and useful (everyone decides for themselves what matters to them) - grinding the exact same maps with the exact same goal gets boring - there is no classic game mode like "VIP Rescue", even though it's no less interesting than Arms Race, Bomb Defusal, etc. The only way to 100% (almost 100%) play without cheaters and lags (stutters) is to play on a LAN network on someone else's PC (with all USB ports and internet disabled) sitting in the same room (gaming arena) with the opposing team. At the same time, you'll also be saved from running into a toxic idiot on your team, because in real life, seeing each other at arm's length, people behave noticeably more decently. Do I regret starting to play CS:GO? No, I don't regret it, but right now the game doesn't hold much interest for me and I wouldn't recommend it to anyone.

translation_en: For absolute CS beginners, you need to know that CS:GO is a 5v5 competitive tactical shooter. If you get killed by the enemy, you cannot respawn until the next round starts. Because of this, players must work hard to practice both attacking and defending skills. Naturally, killing all enemy players leads to victory, and a good Terrorist team can cause even more trouble for the Counter-Terrorists by planting the C4 at the right time and place. Before each round starts, both sides have the opportunity to spend the money earned in previous rounds to upgrade their gear so they can snowball their team to an advantage. Unlike other FPS games, the weapons in the CS series are much deadlier, which makes rounds extremely short. Human nature's constant desire to do better drives players to analyze and figure out how to play better than the previous round. Players from the Call of Duty and Battlefield series might find it hard to adapt: Why can't I sprint? Why aren't there any aiming sights to help me shoot more accurately? Old CS players will find CSGO feels like a newly remodeled home where everything is very familiar. Most developers chase trends that CS cares about the least; CSGO is still the same old CS formula. There is no high-tech gear, no wall-hack devices, and no remote artillery support. All players are limited by their field of view and can only rely on the gun in their hands. Hiding and running are the only ways to lower the opponent's hit probability in CS. Killing an opponent brings an immense sense of achievement because you know they aren't coming back, and only playing smarter will keep you from becoming someone else's prey. If a player refuses to check corners, trade kills or create space for teammates, or use utility, a bullet to the head is most likely waiting for them. This unique gaming experience keeps players from giving up easily, even when facing adversity. For veterans who have stuck with the CS series all along, CSGO is very much like CS 1.6 and CSS. CSGO upgraded the graphics, but only made minor tweaks to the core gameplay. So, veterans can pick it up quickly without worrying about any barriers to entry. CSGO introduces the concept of fire, which can mercilessly burn your opponents to death, or at least force them to turn in another direction. Without a doubt, PC remains the best platform for CSGO, featuring the convenience of a keyboard and mouse, along with the Steam Workshop for downloading mods. Plus, Valve, the owner of CSGO, has strong matchmaking capabilities, as proven by their flagship product, Dota 2. CSGO is a sequel with distinct CS colors; the two look very similar, with just a few subtle adjustments. It remains a demanding, skill-based multiplayer game, which hasn't changed, and it's truly great for hardcore professional players who demand a lot. If you can't break your habits from other shooters, you'd better not try it. This is a top-tier tactical strategy game that carries on the legacy of CS. For the new generation of FPS players nowadays, CS is just one of many legends we've heard about. Facing a new generation of FPS games packed with rich multiplayer content like Call of Duty and Battlefield, it's hard to say CSGO has much competitive edge in attracting them. But what this game truly appeals to are those FPS veterans who still reminisce about CS and that glorious era. And from the looks of it right now, this new installment will indeed move them.

translation_en: After not-too-long of a time in the CS:GO community, I'd like to share my opinion here. (I've played more than 150h on my twin brother's acc). So please spare me the explanation or stupid jabs about my low playtime which is currently 11h! Pro: - You can make money through in-game items that do NOT change the gameplay, like weapon skins, cases etc. (This is totally optional and you aren't forced into it) - There are custom servers (community servers / dedicated servers) - There is an active community with lots of Germans around - Compared to the predecessors there are new game modes, whether you like them or not is up to you. - The game gets regular updates that result in a working game and actually make sense - Lots of attention to detail - The community can decide on suspected cheaters themselves with enough matchmaking wins - You can like "Operations" or not (allows new maps and weapons etc.) - Personally I think the graphics are pretty good too - Great in-game mute function - An internal CS:GO profile as well as a player commendation system (friendly, good teacher and good leader) Contra: - Hackers are rarely kicked in matchmaking because they win the game for people - Few maps in the new game modes (workshop maps not included) - Every now and then you run into stubborn cheaters who ruin the game - Some bugs are present, but are fixed quickly (pixelwalk etc.) - Servers run on 64-tick, so some actions aren't registered properly - New recoil patterns annoy hardcore veterans - There should be a regional filter that lets you avoid getting put into a team where only Russian is spoken and you are totally despised, hated and insulted just because of your nationality. Conclusion: I bought the game at full price and haven't regretted it for a second. I've been playing Counter Strike since the 1.5 release and know plenty of bugs and nasty tricks that have finally been fixed here! And therefore I can only recommend Counter Strike: Global Offensive. Thank you for your attention, your time, and I'd appreciate a rating.

translation_en: CS:GO is currently one of the most balanced competitive shooters out there, with zero pay-to-win mechanics. Compared to games in China like CF or CODOL, which are now dominated by all sorts of cash-shop weapons, CS:GO isn't like that. CS:GO has a huge player base, and the skill level is generally quite high. Because of Steam, players tend to be older and more mature; they've all been through the baptism of 1.6 and CSS, so they have a solid foundation, not a ton of noobs. CS:GO carries a kind of dream, really. As a shooter, it has tactics, teamwork, and it's a hardcore game where it's kill or be killed the second you see someone. CS:GO also carries national pride—everyone wants their country to take back its former glory on the world stage. Sure, you might think the graphics haven't improved much, but compared to 1.5, with its lack of ragdoll physics, 3D modeling, and lack of powerful lighting and physics engines, CS:GO is getting better and better in the current environment. Compared to those games with planes and cannons, it's more balanced, simpler, more direct, and more competitive. After trying out so many esports games and coming full circle, I finally chose CS:GO.

No matter what level you are, leveling up always takes a fixed 5,000 points. Every week, leveling up gives you a random drop—either a graffiti [with limited charges] or a weapon skin, though they're basically all worthless, and you can only get one per week. Once you hit max level 40, you can prestige back to level 1, and you'll be given that year's Service Medal. For example, if you max out and prestige in 2017, you get the 2017 Service Medal. Basically, these medals are just for show. 3: Balance—I don't even need to explain this. This is how the system evaluates your skill level based on your last 2 wins and the previous losses. Once the lock time is up, you can play comp again. translation_en: First of all, I'd like to say that this game is pretty tricky to review because it's very iconic and has a lot of aspects where opinions are all over the place and "good" players are divided (don't pay attention to the Kevins who tell you "Best FPS!!!" or "This game is so good!"). I'm going to offer a more or less complete review of the game that will speak to the most hardcore among you, to the real gamers. First off, I'd like to talk about the community and cooperative aspect, which is unique in this new installment that follows the evolution of Counter-Strikes. In previous episodes, when you played CSS alone without caring about those around you and just handled weapons all by yourself, well that's over! Yes, because now we actually discover that CS:GO leans towards an unexplored side of Counter-Strike: cooperation is essential to guarantee optimal gaming enjoyment. And on this subject I have a few important examples to develop: This game is not made for lone wolves, arm yourselves with friends even if they aren't very good, because if that's not the case, the internal communication of the team you play with will be poor, whereas if you end up with your 4 friends on your team the game will already be that much more enjoyable yet more strategic, cooperation is the keystone of this game. As for the community aspect, frankly I'm disappointed, aside from a few good people, the community boils down to mocking assholes and toddlers with screams and rage to spare. If you want good social relations, don't go fishing in the enemy team. Next, regarding the value for money, I take my hat off to them, 14 Euros I find that very fair and above all it allows people strapped for cash to afford an FPS at a low cost, I'm stoked to see players coming from developing countries who really had to fight to get this game. (well, I'm imagining funny things, I know). On the flip side, we'll notice a clear increase in immature players in the community but also a business side regarding the sale of weapon skins and other fancies, a knife is nice but not for 150 euros... On the sound side, the soundtrack is really not bad even though it's short and the menu music gets somewhat annoying the more you open the game. They released a brand new concept, which are music kits that replace the in-game ones (though hey, by messing with the game files, you can put in your own custom ones huehue). As for the graphics, there's nothing to complain about, it's pretty promising. Different modes that are very good, but as soon as you start the competitive mode, especially with friends, it's pretty hard to go back to the other gamemodes, plus there are the community modes which are also a lot of fun like surf, jailbreak, deathrun and others... Overall, (lol best joke ever) the game is really enjoyable to play especially with combat buddies even if they each have their own gaming preferences. Another success by Valve that draws a crowd and will remain a success following in the line of CS. Thanks, thanks to this game, I have these little moments of fun that I've never encountered in other games.

translation_en: "How is your recoil control this laser-focused?" I asked, looking in absolute shock at the gigachad I got matched with solo in Global Elite. "Ah, yeah, well, you see, with recoil control, let's first set the origin of the coordinate system at the first shot, with each round as the X-axis and the deviation distance from the previous shot as the Y-axis. Look at this, the sixth shot deviates by 1.33mm. I remember back then, from 0.1mm to 0.4mm, 0.8mm, 1.1mm, people with actually good recoil control are getting fewer and fewer. People are really just losing it these days, sigh, shooting ain't easy." I secretly jotted down the data, assuming these were six consecutive shots. Then I logged off and plotted a graph using a precision calculator. Turns out, it looked kind of like a logarithmic function, except the point at x=1 seemed a bit off. So I tried raising each data point to the power of e. Well, what do you know. Doing that was an absolute stroke of genius. Except for the point at x=1, all the other points seemed to form a straight line. So I wanted to use the least squares method to calculate the regression line. After some number crunching, I got S(ye^x)=12.2646, S(e^x e^x)=8.662. Thus, b hat= 1.4159, a=-0.29684. So I finally figured it out: (in all expressions below, I'll drop the "hat") y=1.4159e^x-0.29684. The next day, I was planning to ask the AK guy about the seventh shot's deviation to collect one more set of data. But as soon as this Global Elite saw me, he grinned and said, "Young man, wanna guess how much the seventh shot deviates by?" My heart skipped a beat. I thought back to the least squares regression line I calculated last night. I couldn't quite remember the exact coefficients, but anyway, it seemed like... b was around 1.4 something, and a was around -0.3? Screw it, let's just roll with that. My brain started spinning at warp speed. At that moment, time stood still. If y=7, then 7=1.4e^x-0.3, so e^x is approximately 5.2. Oh crap, e^x is about 5.2, then what the hell is x?! I'm not a calculator, how the hell am I supposed to know how to calculate ln?! Right then, I thought of the Mac-... no, wait—Maclaurin expansion of e^x. This... doesn't seem very easy to calculate either.... "Go ahead, kid, take your time, calculate it slowly." After thanking him, I started solving the equation. Expanding it to the fourth power should be about enough, I figured. So I scribbled it out, and got 1.68. I pushed up the non-existent black-rimmed glasses on the bridge of my nose and said proudly, "Based on the trend of your first six shots, this one should deviate by around 1.68, let's call it 1.7." The Global Elite chad nodded and smiled: "Wanna try spraying it out yourself?" "Hard pass." "Actually, this shot didn't deviate by that much, only 1.3. I can tell by that confused look on your face that you've been too busy studying advanced math and skipped Stochastic Processes, hehe. Recoil control after the recent update is a stochastic process; nobody knows what the next shot is gonna do. To be precise, it has the Markov property." "Holy shit, true legends are hidden among randoms. I'm utterly humbled." Got his WeChat. His bio read: CS:GO is my day job, occasionally teaching math. That's when I realized how utterly insignificant I am, worse than even a random pub player. From then on, I studied my ass off.

translation_en: After 2k hours I finally decided to write a review. What we have: Naturally, CS is CS. I remember when I started playing 1.6 in basement computer clubs when I didn't even have a PC at home. Nostalgia, all that. It was unbelievably interesting. Naturally, a lot of water has gone under the bridge since then and the gaming industry has stepped far ahead. 1.6 is morally outdated. Only old-schoolers who don't accept other games in principle, or hardcore fanboys play it. After all, it's 2016, not 2005-2008. Then there was CS:Source, or just CSS. Basically not bad, like a breath of fresh air after 1.6, but still somehow not quite right and something was missing. And then CS:GO came out, immediately winning huge popularity among players thanks to Valve's support, who got really heavily into promoting this game. And what do we have now? A pretty good game, made with quality, lots of maps, a decent engine, almost no bugs, etc. Valve is constantly trying to improve something. Either they change the gunshot sounds, or something else minor. So ideally the game doesn't need anything, everything is smooth and good. And it would seem - everything is ideal, just 10/10 right? Well fuck no! Now about the main problem of CS:GO. Why? Because the whole issue is the fucking community and a million cheaters. Seriously. 10 cheaters out of 10. JUST FUCKING EVERYWHERE. Name me another fucking game where there were this many cheaters? And you won't name one, because this is just rock bottom. Cheaters in low ranks, all kinds of 10-13 year old scrubs with cheats in Gold Novas, cheaters in high ranks, LEMs, Supremes, Globals. Cheaters on the pro scene. Cheaters even in casual publics. Cheaters all around just. The whole issue is a normal anti-cheat. Why don't we see it? Because for Valve, cheaters are a very large percentage of income. You ask why? I'll answer. Take a standard piece of shit with cheats. The piece of shit bought the game, paid Gabe, bought a key, paid Gabe, bought a knife, gave a % to Gabe, got a VAC. Bought an account, paid Gabe for a copy of the game, bought skins again - paid, raised Steam level - bought cards, paid. And so in a circle. Naturally we will never see a normal anti-cheat, and at the same time the cheats themselves have become much more advanced and much more accessible. Now downloading a legit cheat or buying one is dead simple, there are tons of variations, etc. For example, back in CS 1.6 there was one type of aim, the crosshair would just jump across half the screen and it was obvious even to a kid with Down syndrome. And what about now? Now these are cheats where you can configure anything you want. Both the spread, and where the bullet will hit, and what kind of spread this or that weapon will have, and how the WH will work, all kinds of radar hacks, etc. A TON of stuff, seriously. Already now, for example, for me, a person with 12 years of gaming experience, it's sometimes very hard to distinguish skill from a cheat. I have to watch a demo and check every moment 2-3 times. And what will it be like in 2 years, for example? The cheat industry will grow exponentially, Overwatch will only catch the most hardcore freaks. And on the pro scene cheats will be even more widespread. After all, it's much easier to frag left and right with cheats than to learn to shoot yourself. And there have already been many examples in the esports scene. And many scandals with VAC among pro players. In the future the situation will only get worse. Hence the conclusion: Until there is a total fight against cheaters, not just a normal VAC, but making it so that a cheater can't just buy another account—for example, banning by hard drive serial number, or something else—the game won't improve. Right now it's just treading water. They tinker with sounds, some skins, slightly change a few maps, etc. Nothing global. At this stage, playing MM will only cause disgust. Seriously, normal people play it either out of desperation, or those who don't give a flying fuck who they play with. Who couldn't care less that a schoolboy with software is going to fuck your whole team in the ass time and time again, or a cheater on your team will do the exact same thing to the opponent. Bottom line: The game itself is 9/10, provided cheaters are minimized. At this stage 5/10. Don't play with cheats. Don't ruin the game for yourself and everyone else. Don't make the community even worse than it already is. Thanks.

translation_en: After playing actively for a while now, experimenting, sharing with friends and acquaintances in the scene, and observing the communities... the CS:GO ranking system has brought more negative things than positive ones. I'll argue my case in the following paragraphs. I've ranked up many times and dropped down too; I rank up, drop down, rank up, drop down again, and rank up once more, and I've noticed several things: the ranking system has made people sick in a horrible way. It no longer matters if you were or are a veteran player with tournament wins, a reputation for being a fair player (fairplay gg, gl hf, no big mouth, no insulting others), it no longer matters if you were or are part of legendary teams, it doesn't matter if you're actually a good player... now what people care about is THE RANK YOU HAVE. There are people who stop playing with others who have a rank lower than theirs, they even insult them, call them horrible names, and even forget the most basic things in CS (like covering, being tactical, communicating, calling out where you died) to turn into absolute scum who only go after frags to boost their ELO and therefore their rank... they stop playing with lifelong friends or other people "because of their rank", they even refuse to keep playing once they reach a certain rank, seriously? What happened to this game? What happened to the friendships made in public servers? What happened to the clan matches that helped the community grow, what happened to the importance of participating in a tournament (wan/lan)? How sick have people gotten over the rank? Now blessed MM is a war zone of cheats. People getting paid to hop on, hack, and boost other people's ranks, a fake rank that doesn't belong to you and that you aren't, just for the sake of what? An appearance. It's true the game has been growing, but every day teamwork is lost more and more to make way for individualism, just to "rank up" and show off what? What actually gives you a name are your tournaments, your online participations, the way you are... everything else is just a joke. It's true that ranking up is an achievement, we all want it, myself included, but I'm not going to sacrifice real competition for appearances. It's nice to hit a rank, take a screenshot, and get back to playing real CS:GO—there are options: ESEA, Altpug, Fraghype, and leagues like CEVO and more. Otherwise, you're just wasting your time. Of course, this applies to those who still "have the dream" of attending major events; for those of us who already went or did something, it doesn't matter anymore. Let's hope this changes one day and it becomes fun again. Cheers!

Your team in the meantime will be waiting somewhere in the distance admiring the beautiful textures and skins, occasionally giving some info, fake info, then so you can show off even more, they will fall like matches chasing a frag giving you a chance to hit an ACE or lose the round. With each passing day of combat, you will begin to learn the reality that playing so-called mms is just farming rank. If you're good, you're just good, because whether in silvers or globals, it's just retarded FFA 5v5 running around the map and you won't find advanced tactics or full info here, just fucking flame on the way to a rush on A or B. Just as with each passing day you will get to know a mass of talented young players who don't have more than 200 hours played on their profiles and will still be better than you. Their gamesense, anticipation, aim, is sometimes greater than pro players from the top 10 hltv. You will meet them in every match, because there are more and more of them and there will only be more. These talented players in 70% of cases end their careers on these accounts within 1/2 months, when a message suddenly appears on their profile - 1 VAC ban registered. The game developer of course does literally everything, daily updates, new cases, skins, putting bunny ears or pumpkins on chickens, all just so you can finally see that they don't give a fuck, and CS:GO is starting to resemble its predecessor 1.6, where on every server you will find more cheaters than slots on it. Wait! That's not how it is! Valve introduces non-prime and prime! Great! It looks like on non-prime 90% of the matches are cheaters playing against cheaters, and on prime you will find them a little less. Instead of eliminating them, the developer prefers to throw them into another bag. The rank system over time becomes more and more ruined and meaningless, because it is no longer an indicator of anything. Not everyone cheats, but in every match regardless of the level you will meet a complete mixture of skills, at low ranks you will play against globals with golds, and at higher ranks you will play with golds against globals, because you will never get a smurf, a competent player to your team, just some boosted shit. The charm of our beloved game is added by the fact that we have to blow some cash on hardware because otherwise we can forget about any goals. If someone thinks that hardware doesn't play, they are an idiot. A person with normal fps + 144hz monitor might be much weaker skill-wise than you, but if you hover around 60 unstable fps on a normal monitor, they will have too big an advantage over you despite your skills. With each update, the game's fluidity decreases, which is so fucking annoying that you don't even want to play it anymore, because it should be the other way around. If the gameplay itself hasn't convinced you yet, you can think about collecting skins, flexing with them in front of others and showing how fucking awesome you are because you have some pink bayonet and everyone gets a hard-on at the sight of a regular pixelated skin sometimes worth more than your 4 months of income. You can of course make nothing out of nothing, go the path of gambling, but if you get lucky and don't sell it in time, the next day you'll blow everything, because every game of chance is designed so that such a moment will come, sometimes even unrealistic but it will happen 100%. If I've convinced you with my opinion about this game, the whole community, then you can go further grinding your high rank, preferably getting 5 frags per match and looking only for people to carry you, because a rank-up will satisfy you more than your mediocre game with which you won't do shit anyway, because according to you what you have on your profile defines how you play. In the future I will certainly run into you and once again you will make me realize not to play matchmaking with a bunch of retards on 64 tickrate, because the wonderful rank system places you in such a way that if I want to win, I have to hit an ACE every round while additionally playing against magical new accounts, because in my team out of 100 games played I don't have the honor of hitting even once. Fortunately, I don't care about it, because for me winning a tournament, taking a good place, having a lot of knowledge about CS and improving my game every day on ridiculous 50 fps is an achievement, and not some rank that is just a picture.

translation_en: When we were kids, the two of us would happily skip class to go to the internet cafe and play CS, carefree, as if we’d never had a single worry in the world. But after starting middle school, everything changed. A guy in our class bragged about his CF skills every single day, and to show off what a rich baller he was, he bought her a battle axe, stealing the girl I loved right out from under me. Just like that, she left for CF, leaving me all alone. After school, the gloomy sky had already started raining. Finding out she went to play CF practically broke me. I walked home soaking wet in the rain, only to get splattered with mud by a bicycle. The one riding the bike was that guy. "Country bumpkin, go back to playing your dumbass CS!" he yelled, speeding off into the distance. My face showed neither joy nor sorrow, but inside, I felt like shit. That night, I cried for hours. ----- Eight years later, she’s grown tall and alluring, but seems to have given up on her studies to play in CF internet cafe tournaments. She’s lost several matches in a row, a few beads of sweat hanging off the tip of her pretty nose. Her little elementary school teammate sitting next to her is playing on a Private Second Class account, doesn't even have a single RMB cash shop item. This round is a loss. I saw her, walked over and sat down, kicking the kid away. She was too focused to even notice me. Four people were already dead on the map, leaving just me holding an AK-74 as SAS. Clutch time. You saw me jiggle peek, headshotting the enemy who poked their head out, then continued spray-transferring to mow down the enemies coming to crossfire. After that, I used movement to dodge a Fire Qilin's bullets and dropped him with a headshot from the last 12 rounds in my Glock. I picked up the Fire Qilin and clutched the round for them. She took off her headphones, looked at me with eyes full of shock, and asked, "Where the hell have you been all these years? You've gotten so good, I've been waiting for you in CF this whole time." I looked at her, completely expressionless, and said: "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS: GO) expands upon the team-based action gameplay that it pioneered when it was launched 12 years ago. CS: GO features new maps, characters, weapons, and delivers updated versions of the classic CS content (de_dust, etc.). In addition, CS: GO introduces new gameplay modes, matchmaking, leaderboards, and more." "'Counter-Strike took the gaming industry by surprise when the unlikeliest MOD became the most played online PC action game in the world almost immediately after its release in August 1999,' said Doug Lombardi at Valve. 'For the past 12 years, it has continued to be one of the most-played games in the world, headlining competitive gaming tournaments and selling over 25 million units worldwide across the franchise. CS: GO promises to expand on CS' award-winning gameplay and deliver it to gamers on the PC as well as next gen consoles and the Mac.'" She burst into tears and came with me to CS:GO. Then she blew all her life savings opening cases.

Regarding this, I have a few words, please listen quietly everyone.[/h1] To summarize the problems you might encounter in the game: 0. Foreigners beat me 1. Foreigners kick me 2. Foreigners flame me 3. Foreigners insult my country 4. My English isn't good enough to flame back, voice comms are loud as hell, and you want to kick them but can't 5. Disagreements over cross-strait relations and the One-China principle leading to endless arguments with teammates/opponents 6. The enemy is hacking/smurfing and destroying me, can't win, the game is unplayable Summary: This fucking game is not friendly to noobs at all. Yeah, makes sense. First of all, a reminder to everyone to make good use of the in-game report and mute functions. However, is it really because foreign players look down on Chinese players? Are Chinese players the only ones being isolated? Not at all. We ourselves often call Russians "Russians" (Tl/Note: 'Maozi'), and refer to people from Southeast Asian countries collectively as "SEA monkeys." I refuse to believe that these terms carry no derogatory meaning toward those countries. In fact, when a country is large and has a lot of players, it's inevitable to run into unpleasant things like this. As a player fighting in the European servers, I can tell you very clearly that over 50% of European players do not want to queue with Russians. [spoiler] As an aside, although the game is Global Offensive, in reality you can only connect to servers close to your geographical location. That means the "foreigners" most people talk about are actually just players from other Asian countries. Don't assume they're American or British just because they speak English. If you actually want to play with friends in those countries, you first have to set your maximum matchmaking ping to 350, and then endure a 300 ping fight against your opponents. This state of gaming can basically be summarized as: the enemy has already killed the future you, while the current you is still aiming at their past self. Of course, you can also choose to make both you and your friend experience 190 ping, which is a very fun thing to do. Just to emphasize, when the physical distance is far, VPNs are useless. [/spoiler] Why? Because Russians can chatter away in fluent Russian over voice chat with their friends, completely disregarding your feelings as a teammate. Get them excited and you might even catch a nice "cyka blyat" (which translates to our "Saonima") directed at you. Abusing voice comms—especially when we don't understand them, combined with the awful noise of cheap microphones—can seriously damage our hearing and interfere with players from various countries trying to listen for footsteps in clutch situations... Because of this, Russians are infamous on EU servers. Very often you'll see teammates or opponents typing: "We have a Russians, this game is lost"; or when losing, you'll directly see them teamkilling each other in spawn, blaming each other for being Russian... The scariest thing of all is solo queuing and running into a Russian four-stack. When losing, you might hear four teammates squawking away in the spawn room, and even if they occasionally toss you some garbage English callouts, you feel bad just muting them outright; when winning, you still have to guard against them suddenly vote-kicking you right at match point or randomly shooting you in the head... Is that going too far? As for why Asian players hate Southeast Asian players, I think the logic is pretty similar. But man, judging the whole collective based on the behavior of a few individuals is a massive mistake. Yet nobody wants to be the victim, so they resort to broad generalizations. Once you do that, innocent people are bound to get caught in the crossfire. Don't normal Russian players feel wronged by this? Don't ordinary Southeast Asians feel helpless? Impossible. Yet how are Chinese people any different? A group is missing one player, so they decide to four-stack. When the fifth person is a foreigner, do we Chinese kick him? Do we use Chinese in team voice chat without giving a crap about how they feel? If you think you're giving him callouts and he's not reacting, have you ever considered that he might think you guys are too loud and muted you ages ago? Precisely because an individual is in a weak position relative to the group, once the positions are flipped, the previously aggrieved underdog reveals their own vicious side. At the end of the day, the seeds of "evil" planted by other players from our own country transform into the fruit of "evil" that falls upon the rest of our group. The views that "foreigners" in our mouths hold toward Chinese players are just as full of prejudice and inequality as how we view Russians and Southeast Asians, yet all of this is caused by ourselves. The easiest way to completely avoid all this is simply to choose domestic platforms like 5E or B5. The official Perfect World server is out now too; just do the real-name verification and download it for free, and you can easily get rid of the language barrier. As for changing the image of Chinese players ourselves, I don't really want to talk empty words here since I'm powerless to change it anyway. I can only beg international server players reading this review to maintain a friendly attitude in every match, and when there are both Chinese and foreign players in a team, try to communicate in English to take everyone's mood into consideration. That's all. One argument I've seen floating around is: being bad at the game is the ultimate sin. Indeed, many noobs jump straight into competitive without a deep understanding of CS, and even more players get boosted to their ranks. Once they solo queue, their true colors are exposed. They feel like they've tried their hardest, but they have no idea what flaws are in their gameplay. To experienced Chinese players and foreigners, you just suck and are intentionally throwing, so they have to flame you and kick you; while in your own eyes, foreigners are just picking fights for no reason and are unfriendly to China. On domestic platforms, the takeaway is just that the game environment is trash and looks down on noobs. It's a very helpless situation, which is why I always recommend that newbies solo queue their placement matches, and only lend a helping hand when they get stuck in their skill bracket. Not everyone is born good at this game, so I'm asking everyone to show a bit more tolerance toward players who just picked it up. I've carried noobs who went 0 kills in the first half and 2 kills the whole game, so I guess I have some right to speak on this. I still hope everyone can accept my advice... But I also hope newbies will definitely wear headphones to play, and having a mic is even better so you can give callouts to your teammates in time. After all, even if a carry is boosting you, if you act like a deaf-mute the whole time and can't get any kills, even the carry is gonna get pretty triggered... [spoiler]If a real noob plays with me, I will definitely keep my emotions in check. Even if I'm dying of anger inside, I won't let it affect the noob in-game. Usually once the match is over I'm fine, though I might DM them later to talk about their main issues 2333. But seriously guys, please don't just vent your emotions, especially among strangers..... The only time I'm actually fierce is when I'm tearing into our team captain and caller over tactical and common-sense mistakes 23333. Maybe you shouldn't get too close to me if you don't want to see me lose my temper XD?[/spoiler] As for those separatist players shouting "Taiwan No.1"[spoiler] or troublemakers with hidden agendas[/spoiler], our principle should be: if we can't beat them, report them; if we can beat them, crush them and then report them. We just deal with them that way.[b] Of course, just muting them saves time, effort, and keeps your mood intact. [/b] At the end of the day, what we need to do is improve our skills through various channels, queue up as a full team, and if the enemy flames us, we crush them with our skill; if the enemy calls us hackers, we take it as a compliment to our skill and keep working hard. Don't get angry and smash your keyboard when the enemy cheats; report them first as a courtesy, and at worst let them win by a landslide 2333. I also hope everyone competes fairly and says no to cheats! Thanks to everyone who had the patience to read this far. translation_en: Once upon a time, there was a company called Valve, which made a masterpiece called HALF-LIFE. A genius college student spun off a mod of HL called CS. In an era when the FPS genre had no undisputed king, the world went crazy. To put it simply, your internet cafe could lack any game, but it couldn't lack CS. Back in the day. Every day at the internet cafe, I'd only eat a single bread bun for a meal and couldn't even bring myself to buy a bottle of water, because water = one hour of net time. Back in the day. I had the absurd thought of trading a year of my life for god-tier aim. Back in the day. There was news like this: a boy shot someone because of playing CS. Back in the day. There was a tragedy like this: a college student played CS for N days and N nights straight at an internet cafe, and died of exhaustion right there. Back in the day. There were also romances to be envious of—falling in love over CS and walking down the aisle in real life. Back in the day. I thought I was just lighting a cigarette, never imagining I'd never be able to quit. Back in the day. I thought I was just clicking on a game, never imagining it would brand me for life. I remember pulling all-nighters at the internet cafe back then. I played countless games and switched through countless titles. But only CS never changed. It was already a religion. I remember that year the sun was shining bright. I remember that year the sky was still blue. I remember that year the clouds and my youth still had the scent of youth. The me back then hadn't yet shed my childishness. The me back then still loved it deeply. Amidst the gunfire, youth slipped away silently. Unwittingly, the traces of time had also been carved in. Only I know what was given for Counter-Strike—it was way more than just sweat... We used to be noobs, despised noobs. In a hail of bullets, we were the ultimate meatshields. While others raised their weapons in victory, we just cried in the corner. Charging forward time and time again, falling down time and time again. And the abuse hurt our hearts more than bullets. Finally, one day, we made it into a comic. In the comic, we were called trash... From then on, we learned to endure, and we learned what loneliness is. The fallen casings record our defeats. Weird-ass sprays are the best reward we could ask for. Amidst the teasing and cursing, we didn't back down. In the hail of bullets, we understood a spirit called "Courage!" We knew that you gotta have an attitude in life: "Perseverance!" I don't know when we became veterans. All we heard was applause, all we saw were smiles. Opponents turned to ash in the flash of the bomb, VIPs narrowly escaped the jaws of death under the sniper's crosshairs. Sometimes, a teammate's mistake cast a shadow over the whole match, and noobs showing up turned the attack into friendly fire. A grenade flies in from behind, and even if you're lucky enough to become an "angel," you don't forget to say: Aim! No mocking—we all started as noobs. No blaming—who never makes a mistake in their life? Not enough cash? I'll buy you a gun. Enemies coming? Let's all rush them. Leave the most dangerous spot to me, send the weak ones to safety. There's no solo hero bullshit here; tight teamwork is the absolute truth. A team needs this kind of style: "Sincere, united!" As they say, survival of the fittest—hard training is non-negotiable. Look at every single leaf on the branch until tears stream down your face; listen to every sound on the ground until it's deafening. Other people count their days one by one, I count mine second by second. Arriving at the spot instantly: fast; hitting the first shot: accurate. The road to becoming a pro is still long, very long! Victory is exhilarating. Whenever a battle ends, standing on a sea of yellow flowers, looking up at the boundless sky, The sky is clear...

translation_en: Bought CS:GO on September 1st, 2015, and on September 15th, 2016, I finally hit 1,000 hours. Though to be fair, that playtime's a bit inflated, probably 2 to 300 hours of it was just idling. Even today, I'm still a total noob, my aim is trash, my utility constantly TKs my teammates, and my clutch awareness is permanently disconnected. I've been playing FPS games since I was a kid, and the one I played the most before this was probably CS 1.5. Back then, all my older and younger cousins were obsessed with CS. During Chinese New Year, we'd all cram into an internet cafe to queue up and play together. But later, when 1.6 dropped, I didn't get to play much because of school. Then came 2008, and CrossFire officially launched in China. A friend introduced it to me, so I ended up playing CF on and off for the next 7 years. During winter breaks, I'd still go to the net cafe with my cousins to play CF, and because of that game, I started down the irreversible path of buying expensive gaming peripherals... At the end of 2015, Gou-ge (my CF idol!) dragged me into the game. Honestly, I didn't plan on buying it at first because I seriously couldn't wrap my head around why I'd actually have to pay money for a game??? But then he kept explaining it to me and making me watch his streams. In the end, it was actually getting my game account hacked that made me officially jump into this bottomless CS:GO pit. When I first started playing, I still had a bunch of bad CF habits, like jumping and shooting, making noise in a clutch, and always running while shooting. Counter-strafing? WTF is that? Economy? WTF is that supposed to be? ECO? Holy shit! I really didn't understand anything, and I'd totally forgotten all the CS basics. When I first went into official Deathmatch, I thought everyone was so fucking pro! People were getting so many kills! But after playing a few dozen hours, I was pretty much consistently finishing in the top three every game. I got dragged into official matchmaking by czy and the boys—a bunch of Globals carrying a noob like me! I was seriously dogshit. Getting chewed out in clutches: Why the fuck are you making noise?! Why are you jumping?! Who told you to run and shoot?! Didn't I tell you there was someone at XX, are you blind or what?! ???? If you're better than me and point out my mistakes, I won't say shit; in fact, I'm glad. I'm not afraid of getting flamed, I'm just afraid of not improving. That was my mindset when I first started playing CS:GO. Being too eager to improve is genuinely a bad thing. To train myself, I started solo queuing, but I kept getting endlessly farmed because of my own fuck-ups or my teammates, and my mental slowly started to crack. I got impatient and irritable. I could never find that humble attitude of wanting to learn again. When 5E Arena Season 1 dropped, I was solo queuing again, still lingering under 1000 elo??? I started doubting my own abilities, thinking, what the fuck, I clearly have the skill, why the hell can't I climb out of this sub-1000 elo hell? This is probably what they call having ambitions that far exceed your actual ability. After calming down and reflecting for a bit, I started finding map guides to practice utility, watching my own demos, and learning pro players' angles. Every day I was grinding aim, fighting against myself. By Season 2, I was way better than in Season 1. Even though I didn't have much time to play—at one point I was even waking up at 7 AM to grind bots for an hour before going to work—it was seriously insane! Now, I basically don't know shit about Train and Nuke, but for the other maps, I can more or less give comms and throw some basic utility. I gotta respect my own perseverance, even though I'm still trash, managing to stick with it is already pretty good. Actually, when you look at gaming as a whole, the most important thing is having people willing to stick by you, to laugh with you, and cry with you. People come and go. Who's right and who's wrong, I've long since stopped caring. You reap what you sow; just like the people I care about, no matter what decision they make, as long as it doesn't cross moral lines, I'll support them. Win or lose, a game is just a game—you always gotta face reality in the end. Finally, I hope everyone has fun playing this game. After all, with the CS bloodline going strong for so many years, there really aren't many games left that can accompany us for this long!

translation_en: 900. That's how many hours it took for the love I had for this game to truly disappear. How to easily and quickly explain what I feel for CS:GO... after reaching a respectable skill level -> Legendary Eagle Master, or commonly known as the Fancy Pigeon. I've had a fucking gutful. Between the 90% of Russians, kids raging over nothing and teamkilling afterwards, and cheaters... you don't even know what to do anymore. The sad thing about this game is that it had potential. Really... I think 128-tick servers and being separated from the Russians would have been a dream. But you might tell me, "Well RektByPoneY, why separated from the Russians, are you racist?" Well, not even... simply because when you see in game "Мы сделаем разделить" [google translate] you might eventually wonder what this nice Russian wants from you. When he was just saying to go A, but since you don't understand, you make your call for B and your team dies and kicks you because "Foucking knoob suka blyyyat." There you go, I think you're slowly starting to understand why after 900 hours of gameplay you end up fed up. I think if one day they ever think about putting region-separated servers like on "League of Legends" and upgrading their 64-tick servers to 128 ticks, I'd come back. Otherwise I'll just be one more person who got sick of their bullshit, but I clearly won't be the last. Thanks for reading me, and make up your own mind about the game. But my gut tells me it's going to end up pretty much like mine. GL&HF! ps: I want to point out that I have no problem with Russians! Just that we should be separated from them simply because the language demands it. And you might tell me they can speak English, which most of them do, but even so it's still way too common for them to get together in groups of 2-3 and sometimes even 4 speaking their language 24/7, that's just how it is for me. :) Review update from 21-01-18: I'm coming back to my review after over a year to add a few "clarifications." I've been a CS player since 1.6, I've seen all types of players come and go since I started playing CS. The Counter-Strike games are the reason I became a gamer. They're games that brought me a huge amount, whether in terms of emotions or people I met... I have a very strong attachment to the "Counter-Strike" series despite my negative review of this one. I don't think CS:GO is bad... but they could have done so much better, so many things need a rework. The sad thing is that CS:GO has become a cash grab, we lost that competitive game that I personally loved so much. Nothing forces you to spend money, we can agree on that. BUT, if I were a dev and cared even a tiny bit about the game I created, instead of adding a 40th P90 skin I'd try to at least slightly improve the reason the game became so successful in the first place: the competitive side. Still no region-separated servers, no 128-tick upgrade... Nothing new in this game except a 36th case with a €2 key where you'll drop a €0.03 skin. Nah, I'm just being biased, right... there were changes like weapon spray patterns (which frustrated me more than anything else), or new sound effects (OmegaLUL), or map reworks like "De_Dust 2" (which actually isn't bad, but it's not enough to make me come back and play CS:GO). Message to Valve: It is more than time to listen to the community a bit instead of your wallet. Thanks for reading or re-reading me, GL&HF for your future games, Suuuuka! é_è

translation_en: You’ve probably already read a few reviews on the Steam store and heard about how terrible the community is, how the ranking system sucks, and how Valve just ruins this game with every update. Right off the bat, you need to keep in mind that a lot of them are somewhat exaggerated. Sure, if the issues weren't there, the number of complaints would probably be lower, so they aren't completely unfounded either. Counter-Strike: Global Offensive has been one of the most popular online shooters on PC for many years and maintains a high position despite stiff competition. The title is still being developed and will continue to be, because despite the shift to a free-to-play model, it still brings in high profits, largely thanks to the booming market sphere where in-game items are traded. The esports arena is still holding strong and should remain that way even as the years go on. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=632927926 The gameplay is deceptively simple. An unremarkable FPS, but I’m not surprised by people who have over 1000 hours on the clock because this game is insanely playable. It's hard to say what the reason is, but you simply keep coming back to this game from time to time, and even though we're playing Dust II for the hundredth time, monotony just doesn't happen. In the case of CS:GO, the esports aspect is definitely immensely important. There are many interesting titles on the FPS market, but CS still features at the top of popular games. Compared to most, it gives us stronger hits of dopamine when we defuse the bomb in the last second or take out the last three opponents on our own. The game gives us a taste of being a professional player participating in real tournaments. It’s a production where you mostly spend time in competitive matches, learn new tactics, and better skills result in a higher rank used for better matchmaking in competitive matches. Matchmaking is a mixed bag, as you run into all sorts of people. Sometimes you can run into a genuinely solid crew even in the lower ranks, although it’s best to play with friends. That’s the recipe in any online game, and a perfect system doesn’t exist yet. Matches are classic in the 5vs5 variant as well as in the "Wingman" mode, where you play 2vs2 in smaller locations. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=692124914 Aside from tournaments, there are community servers and casual official ones. A Battle Royale mode was recently added to them, which feels tacky and doesn’t fit the game. It might be a nice break from other modes tying into the Half-Life vibe, but aside from trying to attract more players along with the arrival of Free and Prime accounts (after paying or reaching level 21), it makes no sense here. Instead, it showed that CS:GO wasn't built for sprawling maps. Rendering and drawing objects in the distance looks ugly. It would be better if new maps for "Arms Race" or "Demolition" modes had appeared. At least one of the newer modes is "Flying Scoutsman," which is an interesting variation on sniper duels. The sound design deserves absolute praise. The sounds of guns spitting lead or the process of uncocking them are pleasing to the ear. Footsteps and all sorts of noises coming from afar are perfectly audible even on cheaper headphone models. The soundtrack is pretty decent, and if it doesn't suit us, you can buy a soundtrack from an artist of your choice. The visuals haven't seen a noticeable facelift, but CS:GO doesn't need that change. Most people play on low details anyway just to get a higher framerate. Much like cyclists who buy lighter screws for their bikes. Besides, low hardware requirements are one of the factors influencing the popularity of the discussed title. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=752872369 As is always the case with popular brands, they often attract hate for no reason. Sometimes maybe rightfully so, but the flaws are exaggerated. Updates that "ruin" the product—meaning changes criticized by people who don't like anything new. A toxic community and a relatively high population of cheaters are somewhat exaggerated flaws, and you have to remember that the larger the player base, the proportionally larger the community of cheaters or difficult personalities. If by some miracle someone hasn't played CS and likes online shooters, they should definitely try the game out, because it's a solid game that easily lasts for thousands of hours. It has flaws, but perfect things simply don't exist.
