translation_en: Have you ever wanted to get into a verbal fistfight with complete strangers? Have you ever wanted to know how many 12-year-olds have been with your mom? Welcome to CS:GO! Here you’ll learn Russian within a few weeks and memorize the top 100 insults in every language. Within a few matches, you'll know more Russian insults than in your native tongue. Anyone who thinks they can get anywhere with English in this game is gravely mistaken. Conflicts are resolved with teamkills, and if that's not enough, a "Nazi, ♥♥♥♥♥" comes right after. If you fall behind in the first quarter of matchmaking, the first teammate is already abandoning the game. Okay, jokes aside. With almost 1000 hours of playtime, I've seen quite a bit in this game and have some experience with how standard matchmaking goes. Teams: Once even the last funny creature hits "Accept" in the very last second, the teams are chosen. They usually look like this: 1. You 2. Russian 1 3. Russian 2 4. Russian 3 5. Russian kid As soon as someone says "Cy*a" in voice chat—if it's even used at all—you already know: "another fu*king russian in our team..." Since this is a team-based game, the Eastern Europeans naturally realize that English is a no-go. So you might as well disable voice chat right away. With a bit of luck, you'll occasionally get a competent player on the team, but otherwise, it's: keep your dictionary ready. Gameplay: Since the game is so realistic (I mean, I'm deployed in Afghanistan and die from a decoy, easy!), the gameplay naturally has to be built accordingly. While the RPG isn't available as a weapon, every other weapon does that job with flying colors. If you stand behind your enemy and empty your entire magazine because not a single shot hit, and then move a millimeter, they greet you with a 180° MLG spin while mid-air. What happens? You get your face bashed in so hard that you just chill in the corner and your keyboard, mouse, headset, or monitor might end up broken. Then there’s the AWP. If you know how to use it, it's the deadliest weapon you can hold. But hardly anyone can, and yet everyone buys this weapon anyway. Why? To lose it again because not a single shot hit. Rank System: Anyone who thinks that thanks to the rank system they only play with people of equal skill is also dead wrong here. Because for many weeks after a CS:GO sale, the place is crawling with hackers, and I won't even mention smurfs. Then there's Prime Matchmaking, a pointless button that fulfills its function just as well... Skins: Skins are the key to success. Anyone who thinks that cosmetics make them better can walk right out that door and play Call of Duty. If you don't have skins, you're poor, a hacker, or a smurf. If you have skins, you're a 12-year-old lucky bastard who made €500 out of 3 cases and is flexing about it like a total loser. If you have a knife, you're the king of the dust heap. To acquire skins, you once again have two options: 1. Buy the few pixels for insane amounts on the marketplace. 2. Buy keys, FOR €2.30 OR MORE, and open cases where in 80% of cases you're looking at a -98% return. 3. Use your parents' credit card—they'll be thrilled. Conclusion: If you play the game just to have fun, you can't go wrong here. But if you also play to win competitively, you should find a full lobby of friends before starting the game. If you're sick of that and want to play at a higher level, sign up for ESEA or FaceIt. A good alternative to dodge the hackers (WARNING! Pros play there too, who actually... yeah, really know how to play...) Always remember: CS:GO is like Russian roulette, fun until it gets Russian.

translation_en: [h1] If a garden isn't tended, it turns into a dense tangle of weeds. [/h1] [i]Anyone who has ever played shooters knows what CS is. Needless to say, the Counter-Strike series gained huge popularity way back in 1.6, later CSS came out, and now GO. So, after studying the game for years, high-profile events, and a huge wave of popularity, we can give a balanced answer to the question [/i] [b] "Is it actually worth playing?" [/b] [b] This wonderful game has quite a few pros. The developers took the best from previous parts and added various innovations. The core gameplay hasn't changed, it's still the same 5v5 game, old and new maps that got a fresh look. Well, except now modes like "Deathmatch" have been added, and perhaps the most hyped-up mode, MM, or rather Matchmaking, which we'll talk about a bit later. Also, alongside competitive play, they added skins, specific weapon paint jobs for real money, which brought Valve a huge number of new players as well as money. Basically, what we have is the same old Counter-Strike with new perks. [/b] [b]Problems.[/b] [i] There are quite a few problems in the game, but let's take them one by one. First off, I'd like to say that I've spent over 1.5k hours in the game across 3 accounts and I know what I'm talking about. [/i] [b]The community [/b] [i] is a rather sore subject, both for Dota and CS. But is it really that bad? Yes. This is one of the most disgusting communities I've ever seen. A: Over 55% of foreigners are friendly, I've made a lot of cool foreign friends... But there are also those who talk trash to us... This game was never really friendly to us in China to begin with. Q: The most surprising thing that happened to you? A: I got 2 kills spamming through smoke, and the enemy actually accepted it... MP7 rush no brain gets a thumbs up! A: Teammates bickering, they were all good friends, some chose to throw a molly and commit suicide, but there were also those who played it out. I really, really, really, really hope this shit never happens a second time. Q: Did your friends advise you not to play matchmaking? translation_en: After just over 1000 hours across two accounts spent in this game, I'll write my opinion about Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, and about the state of modern online games. Counter-Strike is the greatest online shooter of all time and peoples. CS 1.6 is a legend, I still believe there is no better gunplay anywhere else. CS:S - even though many people don't like it, I played it for about 6 years and was satisfied. CS:GO - skins, ranks, random gunplay, tickrate, cases, operations, money, "fuking rashns". Valve came up with a brilliant scheme to milk cash - skins. A skin is just a set of textures, its stats are the exact same as the standard weapon, only the price can be 5000 rubles, 20000 rubles, maybe even all 100000 rubles or more. The point of a skin is "well, like, it looks cool". Cases - it's a ride of spend 170 rubles, and in return get a skin worth 50 kopecks, brilliant right?! The ranking system. They whine, whine and whine about their rank (which means nothing). They don't play for fun (like it used to be) but to rank up. I reached Legendary Eagle, but very often I wanted my rank to be reset to Silver 1, I had to listen to so much whining that it made me sick. Aggression. Modern online games and the people in them are degrading very heavily. Back in the day there were no ratings, competitive games and other esports crap. People came home from work and played online games for fun, and not to rank up. I remember back in the days of CS:S people just talked during the game, sure sometimes there was some aggression, but nothing like what there is now. There were no "fuking rashns", "fuking americans" and stuff like that. I remember me and my friend would hop on servers with all sorts of Brits, Frenchmen and even Japanese. We were interested in talking with people from another country and they with us. Now you play every match with foreigners, but you can barely have a normal conversation (thanks to f*cking politics for that). Back then you'd join a server, say "Hello everyone", you'd get the same in response (well maybe sometimes a playful "fuck off") and you just play and talk. Now people rarely even type gh and gg, and they play like some kind of robots, just to rank up and drop a one-ruble case. In general, I am completely disappointed in modern online games. The main goal nowadays is money and the degradation of the people. It's a damn shame. 11/30/16. And here comes the moment when CS:GO introduced glove skins. Screenshot this, later they'll introduce skins for grenades, the bomb, defuse kits, you'll be able to paint your nails and get tattoos. Screenshot this, I'm writing this to you seriously.

translation_en: Right off the bat when playing, I run into old acquaintances. Classic maps like DE_Dust, DE_Aztec, CS_Italy, and DE_Inferno got a fresh new look. They're all more realistic, but without losing the layouts and familiar ways to play. The little door on Aztec, for example, is still a very dangerous place. Aside from the classic modes, a new weapon caught my attention. Called the Zeus, it's a single-shot taser. Why bother getting a knife kill when you can unload a few thousand volts into the nearest CT? Two other novelties are the grenades. The decoy grenade is the cheapest on the list and does nothing other than trick the enemy into thinking something's about to explode right next to them. The Molotov, on the other hand, is a bomb that leaves an area of the ground on fire when it explodes, dealing damage to any players who step in it. Pretty useful for small corridors and doorways. Two very similar game modes were also added. Arms Race is a race where the first player to kill an opponent with every weapon in the game wins. With no teams, it's a playstyle along the lines of Deathmatch. Demolition is another similar mode where players start with the best weapons in the game, and with each successful kill against an opponent, they progressively get weaker weapons until the final challenge with the little knife. Another new feature is regarding the bots. Besides being smarter now, while you wait for a match to end, you can take control of one of the bots. Great for anyone who wants to jump into the action quickly and doesn't want to wait around for the game to finish. Very useful in those online matches where the entire opposing team decides to camp. The menus for buying weapons were also simplified. Now instead of 8 categories they dropped to 6: pistols, SMGs, rifles, heavy (heavy weapons like shotguns and machine guns), gear, and grenades. The matchmaking system makes searching for servers a lot easier. At no point did I have to wait more than a few seconds to find a low-latency server within the game mode I was looking for. For anyone looking for a brand new game, CS Global Offensive might disappoint a bit, but for anyone looking for something familiar to spend some good hours playing an upgrade of an old acquaintance, CS:GO can be a fine choice.

translation_en: Have you ever wanted to get into a verbal fistfight with total strangers? Have you ever wanted to know how many 12-year-olds have hooked up with your mum? Welcome to CS:GO! Here you'll learn Russian within a few weeks and master the top 100 insults in every language. Within a few matches, you'll know more Russian insults than in your native tongue. Anyone who thinks they can get anywhere with English in this game is gravely mistaken. Conflicts are solved with team kills, and if that's not enough, a "Nazi, blyat" comes right after. If you fall behind in the first quarter of matchmaking, the first teammate is already abandoning the game. Ok, all jokes aside. With almost 1000 hours of playtime, I've experienced quite a bit in this game and have some experience of how a standard matchmaking game goes down. Teams: Once the very last funny creature hits "Accept" in the very last second, the teams are chosen. They usually look like this: 1. You 2. Russian 1 3. Russian 2 4. Russian 3 5. Russian kid As soon as someone says "Cy*a" in voice chat – if that even gets used – you already know "another fu*king russian in our team..." Since this is a team-based game, those Eastern Europeans naturally realize that English is a no-go. So you might as well just disable voice chat right away. With a bit of luck, you'll occasionally have a competent player on the team, but otherwise, it's time to keep your dictionary ready. Gameplay: Since the game is so realistic (I'm also deployed in Afghanistan and die from a decoy grenade, easy!), the gameplay naturally has to be built accordingly. While the RPG isn't available as a weapon, every other gun does that job with flying colors. When you stand behind your enemy and empty your whole mag without a single shot hitting, and then move a millimeter yourself, they greet you with a 180° MLG spin-shot executed right in mid-air. What happens? You get your face bashed in so hard that you just chill in the corner and maybe your keyboard, mouse, headset, or even your monitor gets broken. Then there's the AWP. If you know how to use it, it's the deadliest weapon you can hold. But hardly anyone can, and yet everyone buys this weapon anyway. Why? Just to lose it again because not a single shot hit. Rank system: Anyone who thinks that the rank system means you only play with people of equal skill is gravely mistaken here, too. Because even many weeks after a CS:GO sale, the place is crawling with hackers, and I won't even start talking about smurfs. Then there's this Prime Matchmaking, a pointless button that fulfills its function just as well... Skins: Skins are the key to success. Anyone who thinks that cosmetic enhancements make you better can walk right out the door and play Call of Duty. If you don't have skins, you're poor, a hacker, or a smurf. If you have skins, you're a 12-year-old lucky bastard who made €500 from 3 cases and is bragging about it like a total tool. If you have a knife, you're the king of the dust heap. To acquire skins, there are two options again: 1. Buy the few pixels for unbelievable amounts on the market. 2. Buy keys, FOR €2.30 OR MORE, and open cases where in 80% of cases a return of -98% is guaranteed. 3. Use your parents' credit card – they'll be thrilled. Conclusion: Anyone who plays this game just to have fun can't go wrong here. But anyone who also plays to win competitively should find a full lobby of friends before starting the game. If you can't stand it and want to play at a higher level, sign up for ESEA or FaceIt. A good alternative to avoid the hackers (WARNING! Pros play there too, who can actually... yeah, really play...) Always remember: CS:GO is like roulette, fun until it gets Russian.

translation_en: I thought for a long time about whether or not to recommend this game. In the end, I decided on the latter. Why? I'll explain below. I've owned the game for close to 3 years, and I've seen and experienced a lot regarding how the developers fix certain bugs, or how they somehow manage to turn good things into bad ones. I've noticed that the more I play, the more cheaters and sus individuals I run into during matches. The hitbox is straight-up bad, unreal. I can barely damage a guy from close to half a meter away while aiming right at his head and carefully watching the trajectory of my shots, only for him to simply drop me to the floor in a single shot with the weakest weapon. The same goes for several other weapons, like sniper rifles (e.g., AWP, etc.). You don't even aim at the head (you aim at the leg instead) and it gives you a headshot, or vice versa, you aim for the head and it either misses or barely does any damage. A lot of people say this is the server's "wildcard," it either registers or it doesn't. Please...!! If I'm aiming somewhere, I expect the bullet to be within the crosshair with a high probability of hitting, not see the shot I fired hitting a wall thirty meters away! I guess that's the bare minimum you'd expect. And then we've arrived at the very interesting recoil mechanics. Let's take assault rifles as an example (e.g., AK-47, M4A1 and company), where if you shoot at a wall standing in one place, you can verify the weapon's recoil, and consequently see what kind of pattern they form, or rather, in what direction the bullet impacts can be seen. Well now, to actually shoot well and accurately, during sustained fire you have to pull your cursor/crosshair down, which just crosses over into the realm of the ridiculous. You practically have to pull the crosshair down so much that you're aiming at the floor just to land any decent hit on the enemy. This is just sheer nonsense! The other major problem is the community. You should definitely not play alone, because it might increase your risk of a nervous breakdown! Why am I writing this? In most matches, be it even the most basic casual match, tons of players do nothing but microspam—meaning they spout bullshit into their mics at an ear-piercingly high frequency—yes, I'm talking about teenagers, most of whom haven't even hit puberty yet. On top of all that with the utmost arrogance, combined with insults that if our parents had ever heard us use, we'd have gotten such a slap to the back of the head our snot would've gone into orbit. Approaching 26 years old, and having experienced other things in life, I simply have zero patience left to listen to this and argue with these little c*nts. But the older ones aren't any better either. The late teens don't possess much mature thinking either. Is anyone surprised after this that even a patient person can be pushed over the edge??? I don't think so... Another annoying type of microspam is when some bottom-of-the-barrel "unce-unce" music is blasting out of an already shitty mic that crackles and pops and ruins your ears. On top of that, you have to mute these guys one by one just so you have to suffer through it while playing. Another highlight is the stupidity and toxic behavior of the community found on the forums. Either someone is trying to scam (trying to steal someone's account access, or steal weapon skins collected in CS:GO from their inventory), or they're crying about why they got a VAC ban. Naturally, this is spiced up with enough whining and broken English that a few comments later they end up admitting themselves that they weren't playing fair. This usually makes me want to laugh and cry at the same time. As a result, a few months ago the developers added a mode called Overwatch to the game, which serves to give us a 10-minute footage of someone suspected of cheating, and after the video ends we can decide their fate—what cheat they used, or if they were actually playing well and clean. This is partly good, partly not. I won't go into details, everyone can decide for themselves whether it's necessary or not. But it's just appalling, and shows the standard of the game and the players alike, how many cheaters you run into during your gameplay experience. I think this game is the cesspool of multiplayer. And then I'd touch on MM, or otherwise known as the competitive system. Here, the server divides players into 5v5 teams to fight each other so you can eventually rank up. Well, this has been completely fucked up too, thanks to everything listed above. That's also why I wrote 1-2 paragraphs ago that it's worth playing with at least 2 friends, because in many cases it assigns teammates to you who are simply retarded. The kind of guy who starts shouting and acting like an asshole after losing two or three rounds, abandons the match, and thus your chances of winning are gone and besides that, the game becomes totally unenjoyable. Everyone is pissed off and just rushing things. Not to mention that there's a high chance the team against you has a cheater or a smurf (people whose 2nd account this is, visibly with low hours, or who bought the game again out of fear of getting a VAC ban on their main profile or losing their high rank). But in quite a few cases, it's "not just" 1, but multiple people using some cheating software that the VAC system doesn't detect, so even if you report the person, there's no guarantee they'll get the punishment they deserve... And these things I've written down are just the tip of the iceberg. I genuinely suggest playing MM with at least 2 people, but if you can scrape together a full 5-stack, you better play like that, that way the fun factor of the game actually stays intact! But so I'm not being so stone-hearted—though realist would probably suit me better in this regard—I'll briefly talk about the positive side of the game too. As I mentioned before, it's really only worth playing with friends or people you trust and know can play fair. There are many game modes besides casual and MM that are genuinely fun and guarantee a simple recharge. My favorite is zombie escape, although even here the community's careless and abandoning-your-team mentality rears its head. The game is properly optimized, it runs great even on a simpler, older PC. The graphics, light and shadow effects are handled really well. There's light reflection on tiles and floors. Dust kicking up, etc., can be found in it. There are in-game item drops, where if you sell some of them you make some pocket money that you can even redeem during a sale for a completely new game (if you have enough of course). However, this is also its downside, because many people think that if you don't have at least a 20 EUR skin, you're a nobody; it serves as a sort of in-game dick-measuring contest. Not to mention the scammers who target naive players, robbing them of their high-value skins which they'll never see again. On the other hand, anyone who isn't careful will sooner or later spend their last penny thanks to the constant case opening. It's like a virtual casino, spiced up with a bit of Russian roulette (and a whole lot of *suka blyat*). This game might be very popular, but I'm certain that it's not good. I regret all the time I've poured into it, but most of my acquaintances only play this, they don't really know anything else. :( Thanks for reading! If you disagree with anything, I await your counter-arguments! Have a nice day!

translation_en: Have you ever wanted to get into a verbal fistfight with total strangers? Have you ever wanted to know how many 12-year-olds have hooked up with your mum? Welcome to CS:GO! Here you'll learn Russian within a few weeks and master the top 100 insults in any language. After just a few games, you'll know more Russian insults than in your native tongue. Anyone who thinks they'll get anywhere using English in this game is dead wrong. Conflicts are resolved through team kills, and if that's not enough, a "Nazi, blyat" gets thrown in for good measure. If you fall behind in the first quarter of matchmaking, the first teammate already abandons the game. Okay, jokes aside. With almost 1000 hours of playtime, I've seen a lot in this game and have some experience of how a standard matchmaking game goes down. Teams: Once even the last funny creature hits "Accept" at the very last second, the teams are picked. They usually look like this: 1. You 2. Russian 1 3. Russian 2 4. Russian 3 5. Russian kid As soon as one of them says "Cy*a" in voice chat – if that even gets used – you already know, "another fu*king russian in our team..." Since this is a team-based game, the Eastern Europeans naturally realize that English is a absolute no-go. So you might as well disable voice chat right away. With a bit of luck, you'll actually get a competent player on your team once in a while, but otherwise it's: keep your dictionary ready. Gameplay: Since the game is so realistic (I'm deployed in Afghanistan myself and die to a decoy grenade, easy!), the gameplay naturally has to be structured accordingly. While the RPG isn't available as a weapon, every other weapon does that job with flying colors. When you stand behind your enemy, empty your whole magazine because not a single shot hit, and then move a millimeter, they greet you with a 180° MLG spin-bot flick executed right in mid-air. What happens? You get your face bashed in so hard that you just chill in the corner, and your keyboard, mouse, headset, or even your monitor might end up broken. Then there's the AWP. If you know how to use it, it's the deadliest weapon you can hold. But hardly anyone can actually use it, and yet everybody buys it anyway. Why? Just to lose it again because not a single shot hit. Rank system: Anyone who thinks that the ranking system means you only play against equals is, again, dead wrong. Because for many weeks after a CS:GO sale, the place is crawling with hackers, and don't even get me started on smurfs. Then there's Prime Matchmaking, a pointless button that fulfills its function about as well... Skins: Skins are the key to success. Anyone who thinks that cosmetics make you play better can walk right out the door and play Call of Duty. If you don't have skins, you're poor, a hacker, or a smurf. translation_en: What do we have here? Obviously, CS is CS. I remember starting to play 1.6 in basement computer clubs back when I didn't even have a PC at home. Nostalgia and all that. It was insanely interesting. A lot of water has gone under the bridge since then, of course, and the gaming industry has taken a huge leap forward. 1.6 is morally outdated. Only old-schoolers who don't recognize other games in principle or stubborn freaks play it. It's 2016 after all, not 2005-2008. Then came CS:Source, or just CSS. Pretty decent actually, like a breath of fresh air after 1.6, but still somehow not quite right and missing something. And then CS:GO came out, instantly gaining massive popularity among players thanks to Valve's support, as they pushed this game really hard. And what do we have now? A pretty good game, well-made, lots of maps, a decent engine, almost no bugs, etc. Valve is constantly trying to improve something. They change gun sounds or mess with other minor stuff. So logically, the game doesn't need anything, everything is smooth and good. You'd think everything is just ideal, a solid 10/10 right? Well, fuck no! Now for the main problem of CS:GO. Why? Because the whole issue is the fucking community and a million cheaters. Seriously. 10 cheaters out of 10. JUST FUCKING everywhere. Name me another game where there are so many fucking cheaters? You won't, because it's just the end of the line. Cheaters in low ranks, all sorts of 10-13 year old noobs with cheats in gold novas, cheaters in high ranks, LEMs, Supremes, Globals. Cheaters in the pro scene. Cheaters even in casual public servers. Cheaters just everywhere. The whole issue is a normal anti-cheat. Why don't we see it? Because for Valve, cheaters are a huge percentage of their income. Ask why? I'll answer. Take your average piece of shit with cheats. The scumbag bought the game, paid Gabe, bought a key, paid Gabe, bought a knife, gave a % to Gabe, got a VAC. Bought an account, paid Gabe for a copy of the game, bought skins again - paid, raised his Steam level - bought cards and paid. And so on in a loop. Naturally, we will never see a normal anti-cheat, while at the same time the cheats themselves have become much more advanced and more accessible. Now downloading a legit-looking cheat or buying one is as easy as pie, there are tons of varieties, etc. For example, back in CS 1.6, there was one type of aimbot, the crosshair would just jump half the screen and even a kid with Down syndrome could see it. And what about now? Now these are cheats where you can configure literally anything. The spread, where the bullet will hit, what kind of spread this or that weapon will have, how wallhack will work, all sorts of radar hacks, etc. A BUNCH of stuff, seriously. Even now, for example, for someone like me with 12 years of gaming experience, it's sometimes very hard to distinguish skill from cheats. I have to watch a demo and review every moment 2-3 times. And what will it be like in 2 years, for example? The cheat industry will grow exponentially, and Overwatch will only catch the most blatant retards. And on the pro scene, cheats will be even more widespread. Because it's way easier to dome people left and right with cheats than to learn how to aim yourself. And there have already been plenty of examples in the esports scene. And lots of VAC scandals with pro players. The situation will only get worse in the future. Conclusion: Until there is a total fight against cheaters—not just a normal VAC, but making it so a cheater can't just buy another account, like banning by hard drive serial number, or something else—the game won't improve. Right now, it's just "treading water." They tweak sounds, add some skins, slightly change a few maps, etc. Nothing global. At this stage, playing MM will only cause disgust. Seriously, normal people play it either out of desperation, or those who don't give a fuck who they play with. Who don't give a shit if some little school kid with software is going to ram your whole team's asses over and over again, or if a cheater on your team does the exact same thing to the opponents. Bottom line: The game itself is 9/10, provided cheaters are minimized. At this stage, 5/10. Don't play with cheats. Don't ruin the game for yourself and everyone else. Don't make the community even worse than it already is... Thanks. UPD 24.11.16 Situation update: Shitty sounds were added, nobody asked for graffiti, and that's it. BRAVO! Great job. GJ. UPD 08.08.17 A year has passed. Yeah, it was harsh, BUT. What actually changed? F-O-C-K-I-N-G N-O-T-H-I-N-G. There aren't fewer cheaters. If anything, there are fewer bans, judging by the stats from vac-ban.com.... so VAC works even worse. They added a dull operation, finished the missions in a day. Now you have to grind 3 game modes 10 times over just for crates and a medal.

translation_en: I finally decided to post a review on CS:GO, after a few years spent collecting virtual dust in my Steam library. [b]CS:GO, what is it?[/b] First of all, you should know that CS:GO is a first-person shooter, based almost exclusively on multiplayer, with a competitive aspect (no story, campaign, or anything like that). Next, seasoned FPS players, be aware that here you can only aim down sights (zoom) with sniper rifles, so you have to be precise, shoot "from the hip" and have actual skill. It's not really like CoD or a lot of other generic FPS games. You could say that CS is extremely played and popular: its low price attracts a good number of players. [b]CS:GO, the premise[/b] Win! By eliminating players from the opposing team (Counter-Terrorists vs. Terrorists). Among several game modes like competitive (the dominant aspect of the game), team deathmatch, casual, arms race (not sure that means much to you, but ain't nobody got ti... time to explain). To play properly, you have to understand the weapons, how they work, recoil... tons of YouTube tutorials are at your disposal. Players are ranked by playing competitive matches (5 vs. 5 with a bomb/defusal scenario). I'll add that teamwork is very important in this game, vital to succeed. [b]CS:GO, slot machine?[/b] There's a whole economy revolving around SKINS (weapon appearances), which sell like hotcakes, from 3 cents to several hundred euros! To get good ones: - buy keys and cases (€2-3) to win a random skin... - buy the skin you want on the community market at full price. They also make you pay for music and other USELESS things. Anyway, you should know that spending money in CS:GO is purely cosmetic and won't affect gameplay in any way. I advise against getting into it at the risk of wanting more and wasting your money just to show off in front of mostly idiotic people you'll never see again. In short, Valve is getting rich off the backs of poor, innocent, and oblivious pre-pubescent teenagers. [b]CS:GO, community?[/b] 500 thousand players constantly online. That's huge, right? But the CS:GO community is one of the most criticized, why? It's crammed with squeakers, players who hurl insults for no reason, 7-year-old kids doing their first beatbox, or preteens constantly shouting "bruh" or "noob". Not to mention the Russians, and even though you shouldn't generalize, a good number of them insult people and have a pathetic attitude. Okay, maybe I'm exaggerating, we don't only have that... A quick note, players often vote to play the same maps (shoutout Dust II) so there's little variety (even if a recent update limits this problem). The miracle technique? Bring your own reliable friends to have fun, hassle-free games. [b]+BONUS:[/b] CS:GO + Workshop -> BOOM, lots of extra community-created maps to practice handling certain weapons, admire, play hide & seek maps—an interesting aspect. Plus, players submit skins on the Workshop that sometimes get included in the game if they get enough upvotes. [b]Conclusion:[/b] Good with a team, or when you stumble upon a good match, can be rage-inducing, addictive. That's CS:GO. [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bo5ZVe1LHxU].[/url] Edit: I gave up on CS; probably too many "cancers" and ultimately no real point. You end up playing it without knowing why, out of a-ddic-tion. Having a competitive rank encourages you to come back and play over and over to get better, it wastes your time. If you want strategy games, there are better ones, if you're looking for an FPS, same thing. [b]Pessimistic conclusion:[/b] In the end, ideal for brainless gamers or those who have time to waste. That is not the case for me.

translation_en: CS GO, a love-hate story where with every chapter you get more and more involved, a game that first started as a mod and today is one of the most played shooters out there. Counter-Strike Global Offensive was released in mid-2012 and to this day it still gets various updates, from small bug fixes to new operations, which include weapon skins, new maps, missions with a unique story, and a campaign medal. The game might seem repetitive, with that same old cliché story of CTs versus TRs, and honestly it is, but what makes it repetitive and at the same time lovely is the fact that it delivers an enjoyable gameplay experience, with a huge balance among the weapons that forces players to rely solely on their own skill and experience to win each round. Despite looking simple, the game brings attractive graphics, though not for the most demanding audience, and it also features a competitive rank and tier system. For me, it's one of the best online FPSs out there today, and it will provide hours and hours of gameplay. As for the game's community being toxic, I don't think that's a CS GO problem; most online games have those kinds of people, and I don't think that's a flaw or an excuse to call it "trash." Valve does what it can, but there are always people who will break the rules. And speaking of smurfs, I have a 2nd account myself, I don't think it's a problem, not for me anyway. Despite looking simple, the game brings attractive graphics, though not for the most demanding audience, and it also features a competitive rank and tier system where, once you hit level 40, you can trade it for a service medal for that respective year. It's easily one of the best online FPSs out there today and will give you hours and hours of gameplay.

translation_en: "Although this is a game, it is not something to be played with." —Akihiko Kayaba, Creator of "SAO Sword Art Online" CSGO, the dream of mice worldwide. CSGO, the most popular FPS in the world. A toxic game. Don't compare any of Tencent's FPS games to CSGO, because CSGO completely fucking bodies them. After all, it's the goddamn founding father of FPS, or rather, Tencent's games don't even fucking deserve to stand next to CS. As the little brother of the CS series, CSGO's performance still leaves us amazed to this day. Four years have passed, and instead of fading, CS's international popularity is continuously rising. The only thing that can rival its fame is *Dota 2*, and in 2016, CSGO finally started getting popular in China too. Tyloo's activity gave us a glimpse of hope for Chinese CSGO. When they beat LG, the whole country went wild, and at the same time, Tyloo told the whole wide world: the legendary Chinese dragon is starting to awaken. (Tip) None of CSGO's skins have stat boosts, meaning new players and pros use the exact same guns. Totally fair. What... you read this far and still haven't hit "Add to Cart"? Well... considering CSGO was once as cheap as 24 bucks, it's normal not to buy it. But during the last sale, the Counter-Strike Complete bundle was priced even lower than CSGO at just 22 RMB, so what you choose to buy is up to you. Main Review: First, my rating: 9.5/10. The only reason it's not a full 10 is because VAC still isn't perfect and can't completely stop cheaters. However, once you reach 100 competitive wins in CSGO, it unlocks "Overwatch" (porn inspection lmao) where you get to judge whether someone is a "Hacker". This is probably Valve's fix to make up for VAC's shortcomings. For Beginners: 0. The strongest boss in the whole game: The Chicken. 1. Click "Play" in the top left corner of the game, select Weapon Course (the tutorial), and start getting a basic understanding of the game. 2. After finishing 1, you can go to the Steam Workshop and find: - `crashz' Crosshair Generator v2` (most subscribed #1) to tweak your favorite crosshair (just shoot the crosshair with a gun). - `Aim Botz` (most subscribed #2) aim training map, figure out how to use it yourself. - `Dust 2 - Smoke Practice` (most subscribed #7) smoke throwing map for Dust II (because there's a 99% chance you'll queue into Dust II, which is why the game is also called CS Dust II, bracket laugh, since Dust II is the fairest map anyway). 3. (Optional) ① Open game settings - Game Settings, turn on [Enable Developer Console (~)], then press "~" to bring up the console. ② Type `net_graph 1` (1 can be changed to 2 or 3) in the little console box. This is the command to show CSGO network stats. Important commands explained below: - FPS: Frames Per Second, basically how smooth the game looks. - Ping: The time it takes from sending a data packet to the server until receiving the reply. Basically lag, or your network status. - Loss: Packet loss rate. In-game, it means what percentage of data packets sent to you by the server were lost. Could be a transmission channel issue, but more likely a receiver-side issue. Basically how much of your data isn't reaching the server in real-time. Having this usually means your home internet sucks. - Chock (Choke): Choked packets, meaning outbound data packets weren't sent out in time. Network issue. (Simply put, having loss and choke is bad, it ruins the gaming experience.) Competitive Matchmaking (Requires Rank: Private Rank 3) How to get weapon skins: 1. Random drops upon leveling up. 2. Guaranteed drops from opening cases (wear unknown). Skin wear order (from best to worst, though some guns don't follow this exact order): Factory New > Minimal Wear > Field-Tested > Well-Worn > Battle-Scarred Weapon types: - Normal: Exactly what it sounds like. - StatTrak™: Commonly known as StatTrak guns, comes with a built-in kill counter (red text). - Souvenir: Dropped during tournaments in free-to-open souvenir packages, special yellowish color. translation_en: This is a review, but also a status update, and a farewell. 1011 hours. If it were you, what would you use it for? There are millions of possibilities, yet I chose CS:GO. I used to be immersed in the passion, fun, and thrill that competitive play brought me. From Silver all the way through casual lobbies to Double AK, dropping ranks after the rank shift, and grinding back up to AK. I used to spend time practicing and researching, watching demos, practicing aim, learning grenade lineups. It all feels like it was just yesterday, flashing back one by one. I remember my first 1v5. 400 hours, Dust 2. Every detail, every spot where I got a kill, I still remember clearly. My hands wouldn't stop shaking after the ace. Matched with another 1v5 in the same clutch situation, but we lost that one because there was no defuse kit. After that, I played countless clutches and pulled off countless comebacks, but I don't remember any of them. At 800 hours, I got my dearest big kitty cat. Big kitty said to me, "You could do so many things with 800 hours! You're just wasting time!" That was the second semester of my sophomore year. Later, I thought about it over and over, and finally uninstalled Steam. But after Kitty went abroad, lonely me went right back to playing until now. It wasn't just CS:GO during that time; whenever I saw a game I liked, I'd buy it, and many of I bought and never played, but Steam and CS:GO had already blended into my life. Some say games are spiritual opium; some say games are the ninth art. In my view, a game is a feast that never ends. At first, I was intoxicated, obsessed, unable to pull myself away from the colorful delicacies; then came confusion, hesitation, and self-blame for wasting time like that; and finally, numbness, treating this banquet as a lifestyle and state of being. There is a quote that I have kept firmly in my mind ever since I first heard it, and I'll share it here with those of you who can see this review: *For what it's worth, it's never too late, or in my case, too early, to be whoever you want to be. There's no time limit, stop whenever you want. You can change or stay the same. There's no rules to this thing. We can make the best or the worst of it. I hope you make the best of it. I hope you see things that startle you. I hope you feel things you never felt before. I hope you meet people with a different point of view. I hope you live a life you're proud of. If you find that you are not, I hope you have the strength to start all over again.* For me, I think it's time to experience a different lifestyle, to meet another group of people, to seek out once again the things that leave me in awe. I originally thought I would write a lot, but words stop at the heart, leaving nothing to say. 2016-4-22 2:10 AM ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Lately, I missed Vitaliy, so I came to check if his bot was renewed, only to find he's gone—probably VAC banned. Wolf's M4 and AK are still as crisp as ever. ROCK's M249 still headshots me from long distance in mid. Steel still occasionally catches me from behind while I'm not wearing headphones... And that guy whose name I can never remember, who forces a shotgun every single round no matter if it's round 2 or round 16... They are still accompanying me just like before. When I play like an idiot and die, they don't give me shit. When I 1v5, they don't hop on WoW and type "Jesus Christ". When I drop them guns, they still acting all too proud to pick them up, every round throwing me the gun they picked up even when they're on eco. Yet sometimes when I turn on my mic to rage buy to vent or type out that they're a bunch of morons, they don't make a peep. Everything is just like the first time I met them three Christmases ago. The only thing that has changed is me in front of the screen. About that quote, today I ran into a totally different situation, with a completely different outcome. Took a cab to go take my IELTS speaking test. The taxi driver really wanted to chat with me, even though I wanted to quietly listen to some listening practice to calm my jittery heart (I only found out this morning that my speaking test was today; I thought the whole damn time it was the same day as the written test). But thinking that usually no one talks to me anyway, I went ahead and chatted with him. The driver was a middle-aged man around 40, talking to me about going abroad and about himself. He mentioned that when he was young, he was sent abroad on assignments to quite a few countries. Though none of them were developed nations, he still went to a lot of places and experienced some different local customs and cultures. But later he got divorced, and has a son in middle school who sounds like he's doing fine with his studies. When talking about going abroad, he said that back when the kid was little, his ex-girlfriend wanted to take the kid abroad, but his family didn't agree (I wouldn't have agreed either—wait, I don't even have a girlfriend). He sounds pretty regretful about that decision back then. Later on, he told me that last year his old man fell ill, and he immediately asked for leave to take care of his dad at the hospital, but he worried about people at work playing dirty behind his back if he took too much time off. Anyway, that period was rough. Later his dad passed away, his mindset completely changed, and he stopped going on business trips. Now he drives a cab, but only drives 4 or 4.5 hours a day and leases the car out the rest of the time. After getting out and saying goodbye, I couldn't shake the feeling for a long time. He reminded me of a lot of things, including myself. I figure when he was young he definitely saw things most people never see in a lifetime; he also met all kinds of people from all over the place, different industries, different ages, even different nationalities. I figure when he was young he must have had his glory days, going to sleep at night with a smile on his face. He's also spent different kinds of nights with quite a few women—though he never told me about that, I mean, would your ex-girlfriend help raise your kid? (Sorry guys, forgot you don't have girlfriends). He has been living out my life motto, yet now on his face, apart from the marks left by his wild and unbridled youth, there's mostly just the vicissitudes of time. This is not what I want. Maybe there are some things you can only do when you're young, but what's the point? In the end, it's just talking points, leaving behind nothing but memories and sorrow. Finally, I'll let you guys know, that quote is from a movie called *The Curious Case of Benjamin Button*. There's another line in it that goes like this: *You can be mad like a mad dog at the way things went. You can swear and curse the fates. But when it comes to the end, you have to let it go.* 2016/5/5 0:05

translation_en: He's Global Elite in CS:GO. Impeccable skills, insane game sense. P90? One-taps people with 553s from across the map; AK47? Running headshots on everyone; AWP? No one survives once they're in his scope; Negev? Ever heard of a 1v5 clutch to hold the site? Deagle? Uses only the Deagle all game, gets MVP every round, and wins 16:0. Countless people have fallen to his gun, countless people used to call him a Hacker, but he knew it was his own true skill. Because other than himself, nobody knew how he practiced his aim for hours on end, nobody knew how he played against N bots all by himself just to train his game sense. Going from a negative K/D ratio to over 3, even close to 4—only he knew the blood, sweat, and tears that went into it. He had a hundred-game win streak in competitive mode. Yet he couldn't get lost in games forever. Pushed by his parents, he finally found a girlfriend. At the same time, he also found a job. Every day, coming home only in the evening and feeling burnt out from work, he stopped playing competitive mode altogether. His match history also froze at that 100-game win streak. Every day when he got home, he would only play CS:GO for an hour—only by playing with his "battle buddies" could he cast away the day's worries and misery. His girlfriend never understood why he locked himself in his room every night, laughing and chatting away. Since their place had two computers, one for each of them, she had no clue what he was actually up to. Normally he wasn't that nice to her, mostly because he wasn't much of a talker, and she wasn't a talker either. But the silent care he showed when she was sick, and having her heavy clothes and umbrella ready when the weather turned cold, made her very happy. Just like that, a few months passed. Until one day, she learned that because of work, he had to do a month of straight overtime, couldn't come home at noon, and wouldn't get back until midnight every day. She specifically took a month off to take care of him. After all, her salary wasn't that high, and she genuinely felt bad for him. She brought him lunch every day, and at night she wouldn't start cooking until 11:40, taking care of him until bedtime. But she was always curious about the laughter coming from his room every night; she wanted to know why. Finally, one afternoon, she turned on his computer and found only one game sitting on his desktop—CS:GO. Driven by curiosity, she opened the game... A month later, he booted up CS:GO for the first time in forever, only to notice something was off—his rank had dropped from Global Elite to Silver I. He checked his match stats and saw that his most recent games were all losses. His K/D ratio had also plummeted from 3.8 to 1.2. He knew his account was only used by him, so all of this could only have been done by her, cooking away in the kitchen. "Did you do this?" He pointed at the Silver I icon on the computer screen. She looked a bit nervous, twisting the hem of her shirt with both hands: "Y-yeah... I did it..." "Why'd you mess with my computer?" From his tone, she seemed to catch a hint of seriousness and anger—he was always exceptionally gentle with her. "Because... because I wanted to understand you... I wanted to make you happy too... I didn't want you to only be happy when you're with those friends of yours." By the end, her voice was so quiet she could barely hear it herself. "Ah!" She was startled by a sudden move—he had her pinned against the wall (*kabe-don'd*), his left index finger lifting her chin: "So you've met all of them, huh? Chatted with them?" "Mm... mm..." She looked a bit flustered. "How many competitive matches have you lost?" "About 100 games..." She lowered her head as low as it could go, feeling the stinging pain of a slap across her face coming in the next second. "Did you get flamed to shit?" She was a college graduate, of course she understood words like "noob," "f*ck you," and "f*cking noob" coming out of foreigners' mouths, let alone local insults. She wasn't one to back down; she wanted to fight back and prove she could play, but frustratingly, she'd die without even seeing the enemies. Every time she lost, she would secretly cry for a bit to vent the emotions bottled up inside. Thinking of this, she nodded. "Wanna play and prove to them you can do it?" "Yeah!" Against all odds, she yelled it out super loud. "Alright then, I'll teach you." Just like that, he started training her in CS:GO, coaching her aim, helping her learn the maps, teaching her everything he possibly could. Meanwhile, their relationship grew better and better. He changed his ID to NoobTeam No1. She took the ID NoobTeam No2. Every time, he would only use 50% of his actual skill, letting her be the main character. Finally, she successfully ranked up to Double AK. Until one day, she asked him: "Where'd you get this knife? It looks so dope!" "Oh, this? I unboxed it!" "How do you open them?" "Remember the cases you drop at the end of matches? You just buy keys and open them. Like this. But it's all RNG, though." "Oh! Is that how it is? I've got over a hundred cases here, let's open all of 'em!" Just like that, the two of them opened cases and blew their entire life savings. "Welcome to Counter-Strike: Global Dereanking - Case Opening Edition!" Rumor has it, that's what the two of them told the bank teller when they withdrew their very last deposit.

translation_en: Well, I was actually pretty torn before writing this review. After all, other people have already written the good reviews, and I don't really have anything to add. So, I'll just talk about my journey from first playing this game to becoming a pro. I can't remember when I bought this game, nor do I remember how pathetic I was during my first game or my first hour. It feels like I once quit the game because I couldn't stand those weird bullet trajectories and sliding mechanics, and I even wanted to refund it at one point. But I hung in there. Looking at those pros with dozens or even thousands of hours under their belt, I felt somewhat inspired. For the first few hours, I was just playing against bots—basically running around the whole map following computer teammates and getting assists. Someone might ask why I didn't play against real players, and the answer is that I used to have multiplayer anxiety. You'd probably find an answer like that even more confusing, right? But that was the problem I faced back then: just the thought of getting into gunfights with real opponents made my hand holding the mouse tremble and my whole body go cold. Maybe I wasn't cut out for this game or for playing against other people at all—hell, even when playing League of Legends, I was an eternal bot-match king who played 1,400 bot games! However, as I grew and matured, I felt myself gradually drawn in by the charm of this game. After watching a bunch of shooting videos on Bilibili, I solidified my belief in picking the game back up. Entering the game once again, hearing that familiar symphony on the main menu, I was quite moved. Still, I more or less carried some lingering trauma regarding player matches, so I chose to keep playing against bots—Easy, Normal, Hard, Expert: From having zero accuracy in close-range gunfights, to getting a decent feel for long-range tapping; From blindly mimicking snap-shots, to a one-shot-kill knife-switch flick shot. Gradually, my skills reached mastery, and before I knew it, my playtime exceeded forty hours. I fucking played over forty hours against bots! Still, occasionally posting screenshots of my scoreboards where I utterly crushed Expert bots was pretty damn satisfying. Until I clicked random matchmaking and joined a casual match. I seemed not to be so afraid of player matches anymore. But sometimes my hands would still shake blindly: in one match, I was the last one left on the team, and as I walked around a corner a big guy suddenly appeared right in front of me. Panic struck my heart, my mouse violently whipped my view up to the upper-right, and predictably, I got one-tapped. A foreigner on my team even typed a message expressing shock: "Horrible?" Yet I didn't give up there. Instead, I immersed myself even more in casual communities to hone my skills. I believe that one day I'll be like the pro gods—calm under pressure, capable of utterly ruining the enemy team from all three lanes. 120 hours have passed just like that, and today I can be considered an expert. In this brief time, my skills have skyrocketed and improved shockingly: From always getting sold out by teammates whenever I saw an enemy, which taught me the art of being a coward; From watching teammates who couldn't suppress their urge to flank the enemy rear, which taught me the ways of base-infiltrating; Which spots are easier to sneak up on people from, how to pull off surprise attacks, and which camping spots are easy to defend—I know them inside out. To the point where I'm so ratty and scheming now! Hear footsteps? No fear, hide, switch to the taser. Hear reloading? No rush, hide, wait for the opportunity to flank. Hear the defusal sound? Throw a flashbang, but don't rush in—play mind games. And to the point where I'm so proficient and badass now! Dual pistols blazing, recoil-controlled headshots, consciously and viciously aiming straight for the enemy's head! Auto-shotgun in their face, hide in the smoke, wait to distinguish sights and sounds, then ruthlessly strip away multiple lives! SMG and Desert Eagle, roaming all three lanes, occasionally stealing a kill, following teammates to rush and secure bomb sites! Got a double kill in a knife round, three players remaining, plant the bomb, one-versus-two. Occasionally getting a triple kill, using a pump-action, auto-shotgun, or the M249. Lucky enough to get a quad kill, rifle and pistol firing without hesitation, killing anyone in sight. ... Well, having said all that, the above can be considered my growth experience and personal insights. I'm dedicating this to commemorate my passing youth (jk), and leaving it here for my future self. I also hope those who read this won't laugh at me.

translation_en: The game has gone through various changes since late 2012 when I started playing it (although half of my hours are from watching Overwatch, watching demos, watching tournaments, trading and leaving the game open without playing) and I admit it's one of the best competitive shooters out there, but I must say that I still don't recommend this game for several reasons: -Back in its beginnings in 2012, this game showed potential to be a worthy successor to 1.6, but nowadays it has become an easy money-making machine where more importance is given to skins than to the game itself. -Prioritizing the skin market over the actual game and constantly trying to monetize everything, pins, gloves, graffiti, character skins, patches and any sh#t they can come up with (something that in previous Counters was completely free), with a virtual knife ending up costing triple a real-life one, and extremely rare items like sapphires, rubies, emeralds, black pearls or souvenir AWP Dragon Lores selling for thousands of euros for some pixels we see on a screen. -Very deficient anti-cheat system. In all the years I've been playing it, to this day I still run into hackers with wallhacks, spinbots, aimbots, triggerbots, aim assist, etc., which leaves a lot to be desired considering that having been on the market since 2012, it still has security flaws that completely ruin the gaming experience. -Almost total waste of the workshop, where thousands of very well-crafted maps and skins with many hours of work behind them are left sitting there, only for the paid cases that drop in the game to mostly feature—almost always—horrible, low-effort designs. The same goes for maps; they add absolute trash while there are hundreds of brilliantly made ones that never get featured... I encourage you to take a look at the workshop and judge for yourselves. -Very shameful performance and optimization. After so many years on the market, I find myself more and more limited in playing it due to massive fps drops. Instead of improving its performance, it keeps getting worse, and we are still waiting for them to officially announce if the Source 2 engine will arrive and solve these performance issues, rather than this sh#tly patched engine from over 15 years ago with constant, brutal fps drops. -Bugs everywhere. Every time they release an update, they fix 1 bug and a bunch of new ones pop up. -Going from a paid game to free-to-play, they've managed to completely f#ck it up by filling it with sons of b#tches with multi-accounts to use hacks and completely ruin the game. -Competitive mode plagued by hackers, and on top of that, add tons of smurf accounts created when the game went free-to-play, which somewhat ruins the gaming experience since you're playing against accounts with levels way below their actual ranks and against hackers who don't have a f#cking clue how to play and go flying across the maps, which is also quite annoying. -I also want to point out the great servers implemented in this game, and with all the money this game generates we're still stuck with sh#tty servers, pathetic tickrates, bullet registration issues, and where in competitive matches you're always matched against people with lower ping—what kind of fairness is there in a match like that? When are you planning to upgrade the servers to 128-tick and stop with the cases and bullshit? Like I said, pathetic. My conclusion to all this is that you've turned a high-quality shooter into a simple money-making tool, plagued by bugs, terrible optimization, cheaters, and bad servers. Graphics: 7 Sound: 8 Gameplay: 8 Playtime: unlimited ____________ Score: 8 / 10

My cute little noob friend, are you dragging the team down? 3. Stopping rushes at the start of the round is the eternal meta; make good use of your nades. 4. Learn to look at the radar. 5. Fastest T run out of B-Tunnels is 11s. My dear, do you know how to fight for B-Tunnels control now? 7. Fastest CT push to short / cat corner is 10s (without teammate boost). Fastest T run to the short corner is also 10s (going through dark / lower tunnels), running onto platform takes 12s. Fastest T running from B2 to B1 is 10s. My dear, do you know how to fight for close short control now? ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Original review below: Faster pace than CS 1.6, spray control is harder, but regardless of graphics, textures, or physics engine, it's one of the best competitive FPS games out there right now. Game balance is beyond doubt, and most importantly, CS:GO has way more tactical depth than your average FPS. It's a game where you actually need to use your brain. Update: A friend asked if bunny hopping can be used to save time. Very interesting question; I thought the same thing when I first got into KZ, but applying it in actual matches doesn't yield ideal results. In theory, if you hit your bhops and get good speed, it should save a tiny bit of time, though I haven't tested exactly how much. I've never seen anyone heavily abuse bunny hopping just to save time in matches—maybe I'm just ignorant. However, I don't recommend doing it, for these reasons: 1. Risk vs. reward doesn't add up. If you hit it, you might be slightly faster, but whether you'll beat your opponent to position is questionable. If you mess up and stutter-step, the lag penalty will definitely outweigh any time you saved, making the loss greater than the gain. 2. During the fast opening movement of a round, you aren't just blindly running forward; you also have to throw utility, turn away from flashes, etc. Sure, technically you can seamlessly chain forward and backward bhops while turning away from flashes, but the difficulty is too high, and it's hard to control nade force and throwing trajectories. 3. Generally speaking, your mouse sensitivity for KZ is higher than for competitive matches. They have different goals: KZ wants speed, competitive play wants steady aim. Swapping back and forth hurts your muscle memory. So the best approach is to communicate strats with your teammates during freeze time, plan your routes, and the second the round starts, pull out your knife and speed run (in 1.6 you could pull off certain movements to run a tiny bit faster than just holding W; not sure if that's still a thing in CS:GO).

translation_en: Dazhu has been playing CS for fourteen years. He met Cuihua when he was playing CS 1.6. That was also ten years ago. Cuihua was the exact match of his dream girl, with braided pigtails reaching down to her waist. Dazhu would often have a lit cigarette dangling from his mouth, stealing glances at Cuihua. Being the only female playing CS in the shady internet café, Cuihua naturally had pro players swarming around her, and Dogdan, the king of quick-scoping, was universally acknowledged as the number one in the café. Dogdan would often bring Cuihua along to play against other people in the café, which naturally included Dazhu. And Dazhu was more than happy to suck up to Cuihua, jumping around repeatedly and trying his best to stick his head out into Cuihua's flowing line of fire. Naturally, Dazhu's K/D ratio was rock-bottom year-round, and his signature super-jump getting farmed for bullets was mocked by the little kids in the shady internet café. Yet Dazhu wasn't sad; seeing the smile on Cuihua's face when she headshot him made him feel it was all worth it. One day, Dazhu had just sneaked out of the shady internet café. Seeming in a good mood, he wasn't in a hurry to go home. He squatted down against a corner of the wall, casually picked up a cigarette butt and put it in his mouth, reminiscing about Cuihua killing him over and over again, and also about the sneers and jeers from the punk kids watching around them. He chuckled, took a deep drag of the cigarette butt, stubbed the filter out on the ground, and patted his pants as he got up to go home. Just then, he saw Cuihua and Dogdan coming out of the internet café, holding hands quite intimately. Dazhu's eyes bloodshot slightly, his brain stopped functioning, and he tiptoed after Dogdan and Cuihua. Not long after they walked away from the internet café, Cuihua linked her arm through Dogdan's. Dazhu felt the blood rush to his head, but he didn't blow up. He thought he might have misunderstood Cuihua, so he took no action. Shortly after, Dogdan and Cuihua turned into a place called "Happy Village Hotel". Dazhu breathed a sigh of relief. So they were just going to watch TV. Time flies, five years passed. One day, while Dazhu was showing off his movement, a little kid behind him asked why he was still playing CS? The graphics and textures of CS were completely crushed by CF. Dazhu felt his sense of superiority had been battered beyond recognition, but switching to play CF just because of that was way too trashy. He considered if there were any other reasons to transition into a great CF pro, and later found out, there were none. He still curled up in the corner playing his CS, transitioning from internet café matches to platform matchmaking. He played his rank, higher and higher, higher and higher. He even spotted Dogdan's ID in there: 丿Quick-Scope丶Tyrant. Figures it's Dogdan, Dazhu thought. Another two years passed, and Dazhu had climbed to a ridiculously high rank on the platform. Cheaters or no cheaters, his movement ensured he never took more than 2 bullets in a single round. Many people still sticking with CS had vaguely heard of this king of movement who could stroll in and out freely amidst a hail of bullets. Dazhu was getting ready to pull an all-nighter again that day. At 3 AM, Dogdan suddenly walked into the internet café, and he brought along a woman dressed up like a demolition turkey. The smokey eye makeup and explosive pink hair made Dazhu a bit nauseous, but he knew this was the most popular style in the village. Dogdan scanned the place, naturally spotting Dazhu in the corner. He walked over happily and said to him, "Why are you still playing CS? Come on, go chase some chicks with your bro!" Dazhu took a look at the turkey beside him and naturally got a bit scared. "You go have fun, Brother Dogdan, I'll play a couple rounds of CS." Dogdan spat on the ground and sneered, "What a loser." Then he went to the counter to load five bucks on a PC, and sat down right next to Dazhu. Dazhu felt a bit awkward and wanted to make conversation, "Brother Dogdan, you're coming online so late?" "Done working, came out for a walk to stretch and take a break," Dogdan said impatiently. The turkey chick behind him had a cigarette dangling from her mouth with a nonchalant look. "Play a couple?" "Alright." Dazhu invited Dogdan, and the two of them opened a lobby on the platform to party up. Two rounds later, Dazhu was consistently in first place, while Dogdan was dead last the whole time. Dogdan slammed his keyboard with a bang, "What a piece of sh*t game!" and left in a huff with the turkey chick in tow, without even logging his PC out. Dazhu logged off his PC and spent a buck and a half to buy a bottle of mineral water. "My life is truly f*cking great," Dazhu thought to himself. A week later, the CS platform did a questionnaire survey. Dazhu filled in his information, hoping to win something. Things gradually turned out for the better; he won a Valve mega bundle and could finally play the official game. Dazhu saw that the latest CS in there was CS:GO, and felt he could finally rival those CF little kids on graphics. The next day, based on the info he provided, a manager from the platform contacted him. He asked Dazhu if he wanted to play professionally, and Dazhu said, yes. Dazhu indeed wanted to, he kept thinking about making money because deep down in his heart lay something he could call a dream. Over the course of a few years, Dazhu had played many tournaments. He was also turning 25, and his reflexes and aim could no longer keep up with the youngsters. Today was his last match, and also his first time playing abroad. He felt this world tournament was no different from playing in the shady internet café back in the day; he just wanted to take this massive prize money and do that one thing he had always wanted to do. Getting on stage, he rubbed his hands together, as if he saw Cuihua sitting across from him back at the shady internet café. He took a deep breath, looked up and saw the $1M banner for the championship team. It seemed he found a faith in his heart, a resolution. From the start of the match to the end, there didn't seem to be any suspense, at least that's what Dazhu thought. Coming all the way through the quarterfinals, playing against Russians or red-heads made no difference. His exquisite positioning and movement made up for his reflexes and aim. He stopped thinking about all that. He got the prize money and told the manager, I'm retiring. Today, Dazhu clutched the cash from the tournament in his arms. He had made up his mind, the thing he always wanted to do, the thing he had worked half his life for. He bought keys, opened cases, and then blew all the prize money.

translation_en: After playing for 300 hours and looking back at this version of Counter-Strike, I think it's a great version. What's that saying again? Growing fond of something over time? I used to complain about the accuracy in Global Offensive. Coming from 1.6 and Source, I was used to being able to run and gun right dead-center of the screen, so even if you were dodging bullets with some epileptic, invincible ninja footwork, you could still drop the sniper across the bridge. Now, you just have to rely on luck. I really couldn't understand that mechanic back then, but once you actually fire a single shot with any weapon, you realize how unscientific the old games were—because even while walking, you're just thanking God you didn't shoot your own big toe. As the versions evolved, I watched weapons get buffed and nerfed. Every single update brought a bunch of sighs and groans, and they got ruthlessly swept away by the river of time, leaving behind only your memories. Oh, that's your youth right there. It's like you still remember the morning you first saw Counter-Strike, how you were blown away by this brilliant game and resolved in your heart to only ever love CS for the rest of your life; countless days and nights of hard practice, 1vN clutches, and the whole LAN cafe going nuts. But now, you don't see CS in LAN cafes anymore, just like WoW back in the day. These vanished things fiercely mark those good old times that are never coming back. I genuinely remembered running into the sunset that year—because I was at the internet cafe playing CS and forgot to go home for dinner... As for Global Offensive, like its predecessors, it's very hardware-friendly while delivering solid graphics. We can tell some little shit, "Yeah, this is your shooter grandpa's new grandson, pretty right?" As for cases and skins, as a fake military nerd whose gun knowledge came from playing original CS, I like the original dark, matte weapons. Those battle-scared wear and tear marks are badges of honor. Of course, when I run into a group of enemies, I'm shooting the guy with the skin first. —————————— I'd rather use stock guns for the rest of my life and play Surf than ever open a case. Fucking delicious.

translation_en: [h1]Preface - A dream round[/h1] Dust 2. The score is 8:0 for the others... those damn T's. The "eco round" and the subsequent "full equip" round both did nothing twice already. It's like a curse. Out of desperation, four guys buy HE grenades and go "Long". Actually, all of them were supposed to buy an HE, but there's always one troll. Three grenades fly into the "Long Doors"... One guy is once again too stupid to throw and his lands in "Pit". Four Terrorists die from the grenades. The team cheers. This is the turning point, and with 16:11 the Counter-Terrorists win the game that seemed already lost. These are the moments that make Counter-Strike so remarkable - so unique. A review for Counter-Strike: Global Offensive? That's nonsense. With an average of half a million players a day, the success story of Counter-Strike 1.6 and Source, and a permanent spot in the Steam Top 5 since its release in 2012, there's hardly anyone left who doesn't know this game. So this is meant more as a tribute to Counter-Strike than a review. [h1]What does Counter-Strike demand from us?[/h1] All of you who actually haven't played Counter-Strike online to this day, be warned. Counter-Strike sucks the time right out of you, and because of the specific nature of the core "Competitive" mode, you can't just stop playing when something else - namely real life - "interrupts". If you abandon a competitive match (60 - 90 minutes), you get a cooldown and can't join competitive matches for a certain period. These cooldowns keep getting longer, so you hardly ever find anyone who willingly abandons a game. So you sit in front of your PC and game... no matter what happens... no matter who wants something from you... whether the phone rings... the mailman rings... all of that fades into the background. Without much thought, I can remember at least three major arguments with my girlfriend where this was the exact issue. This... concept of competitive matches she somehow never seemed to fully understand.^^ So besides time, Counter-Strike wants something else entirely from you... and that's your money. Just like Team Fortress, for example, Counter-Strike doesn't skimp on pretty and sometimes super rare "skins" that you can use to trick out your weapons. While these have zero gameplay impact, it's just a nice change of pace after 500 or 1000 hours of playtime to finally look at a different M4, see a different knife animation, or let a "StatTrak" weapon count your kills. With individual skin prices ranging from 0.03 to 300.00 Euros, this collecting can add up and get out of hand really fast. Knives, for instance, are rarely found under 50.00 Euros (which is four times the price of the game!!!). Even so - at a guess - every fourth or fifth active player has one of these skins. To illustrate this, here is my very personal balance sheet: Hours played: 2100 Price of the game: 14.00 Euros Money spent on skins and operations: 300.00 Euros [i](I estimated the last number using the Steam market overview. I'm well aware that I can sell a skin again. The only things factored in here are the actual market transaction fees, meaning the money I actually "lost" directly to Valve.)[/i] For anyone now throwing their hands up in horror and asking how anyone could spend so much on a game, here's a pretty interesting calculation: Let's start with another game, namely Call of Duty: Black Ops II. On my friends list (750 people, a mixed bunch, mostly German), there's hardly anyone who has spent more than 10 hours on this game. Hours played: 10 Price of the game: 60.00 Euros [b]60 Euros : 10 hours = 6 Euros / hour[/b] So for every single hour of fun here, you paid 6 Euros! Now, one could rightly argue that Counter-Strike is also a very time-intensive game that you play much longer than a Call of Duty, of which a new one comes out every year. Okay... let's take Skyrim and, as the average playtime, the values from my friends list again: Hours played: 200 Price of the game (Legendary Edition): 60.00 Euros [i](Yeah, I know. It's cheaper now, but many even paid a lot more when they bought Skyrim and the DLCs separately.)[/i] [b]60 Euros : 200 hours = 0.3 Euros / hour[/b] In Skyrim, you pay 30 cents for an hour of fun. Sounds better already. Now let's calculate again using my Counter-Strike numbers from above: [b]14 Euros + 300 Euros : 2100 hours = 0.15 Euros / hour[/b] So as much as that might have looked at first glance... at the end of the day, Counter-Strike is a real bargain - even if you indulge in weapon skins. Of course, anyone who doesn't fall for the skins essentially plays for free (14 Euros : 2100 hours = 0.01 Euros / hour^^). And an average playtime of 1000 hours is totally normal. You regularly find values of over 3000 hours among other players, or even multiple accounts where just the "smurf" has 500 hours. So this calculation actually holds up ;-) [h1]What does Counter-Strike give us in return?[/h1] Counter-Strike is simply a fantastic game. The evolution you go through as a player: from bot slayer to "unranked" competitive beginner, the "spray 'n' pray" Silver ranks, all the way to your first proper team play in the Gold ranks. Starting around MGE/DMG, you either have to play very well or play well together to keep having success. A "P90 run" or distraction maneuvers with "decoys" rarely get you to your goal anymore. Plus, players from all conceivable countries (yeah... except the ones from Russia -.-) suddenly learn the English "map callouts", meaning the individual positions on the map, so they can tell their teammates where an enemy is... or was. Finally, there are the "nades". On many maps, it makes sense to smoke off the camping CTs while the T's rush the bomb spot (if that's too many CS terms, send me a PM. Maybe I'll write a translation^^). On Mirage, you'll frequently see Terrorists sitting in front of all kinds of walls, aiming at their feet or some roof beams, and on command throwing a massive amount of smokes onto the A-spot, while one guy holds "Action / T-Ramp" and prays that there's no rush while his teammates are literally staring holes in the sky. Counter-Strike is, as this language shows, a world entirely of its own, but one that knows how to thrill. [h1]Afterword - Farewell[/h1] For me, these were truly entertaining and emotional 2100 hours, where shouts of joy and moments when I wanted to hurl my keyboard out the window alternated, sometimes by the minute. Unfortunately, I didn't reach the final rank of "Global Elite", but I really think you can be satisfied with "Legendary Eagle Master" too. And so, after 3 1/2 years, I've decided it's time for other games (no: not Fallout 4^^) and clicked "Delete Local Content...". Of course, I'm going to miss Counter-Strike and the fun hours with you in this game, but there are just sooo many other games in the library that want to be played, and then the Steam Winter Sale is coming up soon too, and and and... and at the latest with Counter-Strike V.R., I'll be back in action ;-)
