translation_en: Now, I consider CS one of the best games I've ever played, certainly the best FPS. But... I can't recommend it. For one single reason: the community, which I think is easily the worst here on Steam. It doesn't matter how good you are, in 50% of the cases (statistic) you'll end up in a team of Russian kids between 9 and 12 years old. Needless to say, these kids (who only Christ knows how it's possible for them to be sitting in front of a computer all day at that age, looking at their accounts they play an average of 50-60 hours every 15 days, I don't consider that normal) don't know how to speak English (and this makes any kind of tactics impossible, turning CS into a "run around and shoot" game, thus killing it and making it like a normal FPS, with worse graphics, fewer weapons, and fewer maps) they aren't capable of using the guns, which here in CS have a very different and more complicated feel compared to normal ones (basically they only spray in full auto, landing the first 3 bullets and sending the rest into orbit at the cruising altitude of a space shuttle) and last but not least, made hysterical and paranoid (I'm not kidding) by hours and hours in front of a PC, they'll call you a cheater and start insulting you, until you report them all for chat abuse, buy a shotgun in the next round, shoot them in the head and while they start screaming in squeaky little voices (all documented) you reach the fateful moment of the rage quit. Aside from killing the very nature of Counter-Strike, all these factors just piss you off and in those moments the only thing to do is turn off the computer and go read something with a cup of tea, playing nervously and rushed only decreases your chances of hitting anything that moves, and increases your sense of distress. The remaining 50% of the community is made up of 25% people with super high ranks and stratospheric levels (as well as several years of gaming behind them) who by some arcane mystery end up playing in the same matches as silvers (weird, huh?), 10% poor bastards trying to have fun, a good 10% of people who do anything else while playing (usually going afk at the start of every round) and finally... a good 5% of blatant cheaters! The worst part is that without a community like this (and with matchmaking that doesn't blatantly favor long-time players) this game could actually be fantastic: great and diversified weapons, maps designed down to the smallest detail, from spots to spawns, a shooting system that if mastered is genuinely fun and very rewarding. And it could also be more welcoming to newcomers (who otherwise just get insulted and never helped) with dedicated servers and a community of people who talk to you in-game like they would in real life, because nobody would ever talk to you the way they do from behind a keyboard, least of all a 10-year-old kid. So Valve... Improve the matchmaking, make sure super players play against people their own level, and don't come breaking our balls at lower ranks, raise awareness for quick comms (add new phrases and commands so people can communicate through those) and finally, Russian parents, will you please do something to stop your kids from ruining their lives spending 5 hours a day behind a video game? Oh, and the ones who use profile pictures of anime girls that look straight out of an hentai and try to pass them off as their girlfriends or themselves (I even saw two in the same match with the exact same pic), they just make me kind of sad...

translation_en: After sinking a hell of a lot of hours into this game, I can finally say it's clearly worth the candle. You can see a good amount of positive aspects in this game, but they also come with their fair share of negatives. In this little review, I'll mostly talk about the Competitive mode, in-game purchases, the community, ... Let's start with the positives: Game balance: It's nothing new, CS:GO is a worthy successor to its predecessors—a relatively well-balanced game, both in terms of weapons and "teams". By that I mean whether you're playing as a Terrorist or a Counter-Terrorist, the game is made in such a way that there's no disadvantage whether you're on one side or the other. The only differences will come down to the maps and your individual skill. Graphics: Even though it's not on the graphical level of what you might find in Battlefield and other Arma games, CS:GO's graphics are clean, crisp, and pleasing to the eye. The game takes very few resources to run (the graphics engine being a decade old already). In-game purchases: I consider this a plus; the purchases you can make in-game are only weapon skins, nothing that can allow you to be better than someone else or help you progress faster. This part of the game is relatively well-developed, and a good chunk of the community is into trading and buying/selling weapon skins. Clarity of the game: In CS:GO you immediately know what you need to do. The tutorial is practically non-existent, and it's by referring to the on-screen help when you start the game that you'll know what to do. In the classic mode, called Competitive, two teams, the Counter-Terrorists and the Terrorists (CT and T) face off to win the round. For the Ts, there are two ways to win the round: kill all the opponents, or plant the bomb and make it blow up. The CTs' objective is therefore either to kill all the opponents, or defuse the bomb in case it gets planted. As you will have understood, the principle of the game is simple and you will take great pleasure in learning how to play it. Personally, I only have one problem with CS:GO, and that's its community: The CS:GO community reeks of toxicity, so I strongly advise you to play with friends, that way you won't get matched with strangers who are very often toxic. CS:GO is a team game, and most of the people you'll get matched with in low-medium ELO don't know how to communicate to give you crucial info, won't be cooperative, etc., ... To conclude, I advise you to play CS:GO with friends, take the time to learn (Rome wasn't built in a day) and above all do everything to have fun, even with a tryhard mindset :) Thanks for taking the time to read all that, feel free to react in the review comments.

If you have any objections, why don't you come over here, face to face, and... hit me, you fucker~~~ The CS:GO series is the latest installment in the CS series as we know it. Its unique FPS experience has made many gamers find a new partner to kill time with, and of course I'm one of them. First of all, I want to thank Steam for this powerful logistical platform. It's what gives CSGO such an extraordinary game quality and experience. It's much luckier and more blessed than its father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—from a game mod dragged into the community, to the community launching tournaments, which eventually drove the entire competitive gaming industry. That is a truly remarkable decision. I also want to thank CS's father (the developer): when you play Dust 2, please notice the wall on A-site platform with the green graffiti; that's the autograph of the old man of CS himself. Oh right, I've written so much bullshit, and not a single sentence is actually a review of the game. Let's talk about CSGO. How should I put it, what CSGO gives people... I've dabbled in basically all mainstream FPS games, but CSGO is the one I've played the longest. The reason is very simple: CSGO is fair enough. Fairness is the soul of a competitive game; stripped of this attribute, no matter how great a game is, it cannot escape the clutches of being eliminated. So, is CSGO really worth spending our time and energy squandering on? Does it actually achieve fairness? Without Steam's logistical supplies (and VAC, OW), without timely patch updates and remedies, CSGO wouldn't have the achievements it has today. By contrast, its forefathers were much more miserable, even though they were brilliant in their time. It is precisely this attribute of fairness that gives the game itself lasting entertainment value, and its stable performance is built upon this very value: there are quite a few people like me who have been playing the CS series for at least 10 years, growing up from ignorant kids into adults, still enjoying the fair experience CS brings us. In this world, there is too much injustice and a lack of virtue; at least here, we have a spiritual sanctuary we can still call our own. Many years ago, some people said that CS is a kind of spirit, while others said CS is a kind of mental illness. Who knows? People who love to play will always love to play, and there are plenty of people who dislike it. It's very easy to refute that latter view from a gaming perspective, but do you even care to argue? Just as CSGO's performance shows, it doesn't have the graphics of BF4, the realistic feel of ARMA, or the smooth handling of COD. Most machines can run it smoothly, and its network optimization and server caching mechanism allow friends from all over the world to compete on the same stage. What more could we possibly ask for? translation_en: [b] My beginnings in Counter Strike [/b] Ever since I was little, around 5 or 6 years old, I used to play Counter Strike 1.6 on my older brother's PC against bots. My favorite map back then was Assault, because my brother only played on it and that was the only one I knew. Even though I was really bad at playing against easy bots, I loved the idea of shooting your enemies to win. I usually played as Tero and, since I was a kid, I almost always killed the hostages. Later, in 2011, I got internet, but it was via modem. I started playing zombie, then base builder, where I was even an owner. After that, I started playing classic with a good friend of mine, usually on Indungi community servers. Later I got into respawn and war3ft, but this time on the Freakz community. Back then FPS didn't matter, I didn't even know what those were, but I was pissed off that I had high ping because of shitty net. I kept going until 2013, when I quit and discovered a new game that I loved like crazy, Minecraft. [b] Brief history in Counter Strike : Global Offensive [/b] I found out about CS:GO from 1.6. translation_en: When I was a kid, the two of us would happily ditch school and go to the internet cafe to play CS, carefree, like we never had a single worry in the world. But after entering middle school, everything changed. A guy in our class would brag about his CF skills every single day, and to show off what a big shot he was, he even bought her a butcher axe, stealing her away from me. Just like that, she left for CF, leaving me all alone. After school, the gloomy sky had already started raining. Upon finding out she went to play CF, I was practically having a mental breakdown. I walked home in the rain, only to get splashed with muddy water by a bicycle. The person riding the bike was that guy. "Country bumpkin, go back to playing your dumbass CS!" he yelled, and sped off. There was neither joy nor sorrow on my face, but it hurt like hell inside. That night, I cried my eyes out the whole night. ----- Eight years later, she’s tall and attractive, but seems to have given up her studies and is playing in some CF internet cafe tournament. She lost a few games in a row, a few drops of sweat hanging on the tip of her delicate nose. Her elementary schooler teammate next to her was playing on a Private Second Class account, not even a single RMB item on him. This round was a guaranteed loss. I saw her, walked over, and sat down, chasing the kid away. But she was too focused to even notice me. Four people were already dead on the field, leaving only me, a SAS holding an AK-74. Clutch time. I peeked out, one-tapped the enemy who leaned out, and then continued spraying down the enemies coming to pinch me. After that, relying on my movement, I dodged the bullets of a Fire Qilin and headshot him dead with the 12 rounds of a Glock. I picked up the Fire Qilin and clutched the round for them. She took off her headphones, looked at me with eyes full of surprise, and asked, "Where the hell have you been all these years? You got so good, I've been waiting for you in CF this whole time." I looked at her, expressionless, and said: "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS: GO) expands upon the team-based action gameplay that it pioneered when the franchise launched 12 years ago. CS: GO features new maps, characters, and weapons and delivers updated versions of the classic CS content (de_dust, etc.). In addition, CS: GO introduces new game modes, matchmaking, leaderboards, and more. 'Counter-Strike took the gaming industry by surprise when the unassuming mod became the most played online PC action game in the world almost immediately after its release in August 1999,' said Doug Lombardi at Valve. 'For the past 12 years, it has been one of the most-played games in the world, headlining competitive gaming tournaments and selling over 25 million units worldwide across the franchise. CS: GO promises to expand on CS' award-winning gameplay and deliver it to gamers on the PC as well as the next gen consoles and the Mac.'" Tears streamed down her face, and she came with me to CS:GO. Then she opened cases and blew all her life savings.

translation_en: Counter-Strike Global Offensive is an extremely popular game on Steam (it has a console version too, but yeah...) developed by the almighty Valve and released in 2012. Any self-respecting gamer has already played or at least heard of Counter-Strike (CS for close friends), a game that started as a Half-Life mod in 1999 and ended up becoming more famous than the original game itself, as well as being responsible for the popularization of LAN houses around the world, creating an absurd legion of fans who locked themselves in front of the PC and spent hours playing with friends. This brings us to Global Offensive, a game that has everything from the classic and a little more. CS GO is a heavily played game on Steam, has a very affordable price (currently 24.99 Reais), making it easy for everyone to play. The game is extremely fun either alone or with friends, featuring the following game modes: Deathmatch, Arms Race, Demolition, Casual, and Competitive. It's very easy to find matches in any of them, usually taking only a few seconds. CS GO's graphics, at least personally speaking, are quite pretty and please me a lot. The game isn't that heavy and doesn't require a NASA PC, even to play with everything maxed out. The game's bots are as stupid as ever, it's very easy to see them standing still, trying to walk into a wall, shooting like there's no tomorrow, or getting stuck somewhere, but even so they are much "smarter" than the bots from previous versions. There are things that are quite disappointing about the game; personally speaking, what bothers me the most is the Brazilian community that keeps ruining the game. The amount of toxic, ill-mannered people who do nothing but bitch and whine about everything is a pain in the ass! The easiest thing to do is start an argument with some asshole during a match, the amount of retards playing is no joke, there's always someone to ruin your gaming experience. As for cheaters, they aren't that common, at least I haven't seen many. They exist, unfortunately that's a fact, Valve tries to control it but can't always do so and that's a flaw. In the end, Counter-Strike Global Offensive is a game I highly recommend. For those who are fans of the classic, the game is a must-have, and for FPS fans, CS GO is a great bet. The game definitely has its problems, but it still remains that classic sneaky CS with friends that is always a lot of fun and makes and will make you lose hours and hours playing, swearing, smiling, and having a good time. Rating: 9.5

Since this game requires special skills that can be acquired over time, it definitely stands out from any shooter, CSGO being a strategic game. To sum it up, considering its price and the amount of fun that awaits you, I recommend buying it, and mind you, don't quit like many do at the beginning just because you get low scores, you'll see that you will manage to improve and stand out from other players very soon.

translation_en: If we're talking about FPS games on Steam, this one is without a doubt bound to be mentioned. It's a huge hit, and ever since the first game came out in 1999, its momentum hasn't stopped. This title, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO), is a somewhat old game released in 2012, but it has a massive player base and is so lively that it's no exaggeration to call it the most played FPS in the world. With that much popularity, sooner or later some people are gonna think about buying and playing it themselves. Well, actually, probably everyone thinks that. But hold on for a second. This game is a little different from your typical modern FPS. I'm writing this review so that new buyers don't end up going, "Wait, I bought it and played it, but isn't this CS:GO a bit different from that famous field game or that famous duty game?! This isn't what I expected! It feels so wrong!!" First off, one way it differs from modern typical FPS games is that some weapons cannot be aimed down sights (ADS). In this game, depending on the weapon, some you can look down the sights to shoot, and some you can't. And the vast majority of weapons that appear in CS:GO do not let you aim down sights. Matches basically play out relying on hip-firing. There are still more differences. The second difference is that weapons are on a purchase system. You might be thinking, "A purchase system? Like saving up money in-game to unlock weapons?" That way of thinking is slightly off in terms of nuance. First off, the flow of this game is that in the few seconds before a match starts, you buy your primary and secondary weapons, plus extras like consumables such as grenades. As long as you don't die, the weapons you bought can be used in the next round too, but if you die, you have to buy a new weapon all over again. But don't worry, weapon pricing is set at a pretty fair balance, so it doesn't get to the point of, "Ah, I died. Man, gotta save up money again," but rather stops at the level of, "Ah, I died. Alright, what should I use next?" Third, and this depends on the game mode, but basically once you die in this game, you cannot respawn until the next round. Even though you can't respawn, a single round is only about 2 minutes long, and matches move fast and end quickly so there isn't that much stress. Fourth, weapons are already almost entirely unlocked right from the start. It's not a system where you raise your rank and unlock weapons accordingly—almost everything is unlocked from the get-go. If you fight hard in matches and stack up money, you can rapidly use the weapons everyone else is using. Fifth, plenty of community servers and weapon skins. As for community servers, I only really know them as servers set up by users, so I can't really say much. On that topic, feel free to look it up on your own or just skip it. The main point here is skins. By the time you heard in point four that weapon unlocks are practically done from the start, some of you might have already figured it out, but I can't exactly call CS:GO's weapon variety abundant. It probably falls into the category of having quite a low number of weapon types among FPS games. However, the system that resolves this lack of variety is weapon skins. The number of skins in this game is massive, an unfathomable amount. I definitely want you to look for your favorite skins. I can say for sure there's enough volume that you can thoroughly enjoy just looking at them. Sixth, random distribution of weapon skins or weapon cases after a match ends. When a CS:GO match ends, you get a random drop of either a weapon or a weapon case. Naturally, the weapons you get here can be used in matches. Now, what is a weapon case? You could call it a bit of a lucky grab bag. Depending on the type of weapon case, you get one skinned weapon. There are various types of weapon cases, and whether you hit a good skin depends entirely on the case. And guess what, these weapon cases don't open for free. You have to buy a weapon case key for about 300 yen to open them. This system is kind of a bottleneck, isn't it... Whether you consider this 300 yen for a weapon case to be expensive or cheap probably depends on the person. It seems like ranks and stuff were added in updates later on, but I don't really know much about that. Anyway, the big differences from a typical FPS are just those six points, so if you grasp those, I don't think you'll be surprised by anything. Actually, the thing that surprises you the most isn't the system, but the bullets when you fire full-auto... But I'll dare not talk about that. I'll leave that surprise for whoever buys the game to experience themselves. Well then, have a good Counter-Strike life.

Yeah, what do I even have to say about CS? Back in the day when internet cafes just became a thing, I learned how to join LAN matches before I even knew how to type. Back then, the version most people played was 1.5, and later 1.6 somehow felt like a total revolution. Back then, I got owned so hard I learned what flick shots, jump shots, spray control, and tapping actually meant. Later on, the people who used to play CS with me all drifted apart, because we all knew we weren't that important to each other anyway. Later on, I got into Steam because a friend nagged me to play KOF with him. Later on, I got bored of KOF and bought CS:GO, didn't know anything about community servers or VPNs, and played the whole night with high ping. Later on, I met a Thai girl who would always secretly drop by my streams; she said she couldn't understand a word, but she liked listening to my voice. Later on, that girl became an influencer with tons of followers on FB, while I'm still just a nobody. Later on, I conquered every major console and my game library just kept growing, and just like before, I put CS down again. Back to the beginning, do I have anything to say about CS? translation_en: To anyone planning to buy this game who has never played CS in their life, I warn you right off the bat that this is not Call of Duty, it's a tactical game that focuses on teamwork, individual patience, and reflexes. Let's break it down. I think CS:GO is a fucking awesome game. If I compare it to 1.4 and 1.6, I'd say it's the one I like the most, having put over 1000 hours into its predecessors back when I was a kid playing in LAN centers. (A lot of people overrated the older versions of CS and I don't know why. Please don't kill me). If you've never played this game before, I recommend patience and investing a minimum of 20-30 hours to figure out whether you like it or not, because you're going to get frustrated dying every two seconds, and you'll complain about shooting some guy in the head when a gun's recoil is just the way it is. I have to point out that if you have friends—at least 4, making 5 with you—play matchmaking or competitive matches, because if you know each other you can have a blast and actually understand one another. If you play solo, you'll get matched with some foreigner or a 4-man premade, and if you suck, they'll kick you. Another thing is the community. I've run into all kinds of people: aggressive, funny, weird, or even mute—which is weird because you always need to communicate with your team. I can also tell you that you can make money in this game. Although it all sounds like a bed of roses and shit, it's not easy at all; either you've got horseshoes up your ass as a buddy of mine says, or you lose more than you invest. The method is either opening cases, or selling the weapon drops you get in the game until you have enough money to buy a key and open a case. You could drop anything from a €200 knife to a €0.02 gun. This is all based on luck. I'm keeping it all pretty brief, but my conclusion is: If you like challenges, you're competitive, and you have buddies who play it, this is your game. If you don't have at least one of those things, forget it and go play Call of Duty. I've left out a thousand things, but I repeat that this is just a brief overview of my opinion and explanation of the game, and I definitely recommend it.

translation_en: Being a big fan of the Counter-Strike franchise for quite some time now, I feel it's my duty to at least leave a review for one of the games, and little CS:GO is the lucky chosen one! If you want to learn Russian-Polish, completely forget conventional methods (like classes, books, and all that bullshit app stuff), just grab this game and it'll teach you all the insults, and words of every kind! Counter-Strike is a franchise famous for its genuinely difficult gameplay, and it's often described by fans (and I'm one of them) as the ONLY real FPS out there right now. The hardest part is sticking with it because in competitive you'll find some truly shit teammates in Silver and Nova rank, but once you hit MG1, this "shitty" community starts to thin out. The big problem with CS:GO is that, compared to the older titles, it got "mainstreamed" and consequently is full of little kids screaming "OMMMGG THAT WAS SOOO EASY!" when they win 16-14... Oh yeah... Therefore, it's totally up to you whether you buy this game or not. But think about it carefully because if you do buy it, I advise you to dive the fuck IN! Well, there you go, that actually wasn't so hard..

translation_en: Have you always had a masochistic urge to be insulted by complete strangers? Do you want to be called a 'noob' even though you're clearly better? Did you want to know how many Eastern Europeans your mom has slept with? Then CS:GO is EXACTLY the right place for you! And not only that, the gaming experience goes even further... You'll find out within your first few hours that you are actually Hitler (for that, your profile just needs to be public and your location set to Germany), and you'll also learn why the Red Army took so long to stop the numerically vastly inferior Wehrmacht (it would be funny now if it was 4:1 like in CS:GO), namely because tactical, logical, and analytical thinking are not particularly common among a large portion of Eastern European/Eurasian players. On top of that, you'll feel like a CIA agent during the Cold War tapping a telephone line. You really get to hear unfiltered what your Polish/Russian/Ukrainian/Romanian teammates are thinking—no, thinking was already explained above. A wise man from the East once told me: "CS:GO is like roulette, funny until it gets Russian." Such wise words that will make sense to every player. I don't want to bash the teammates too much, I've actually met competent ones, and very nice ones too. It generally seems that you always meet the biggest morons in this game, no matter where they're from. Germans too. So: Find yourselves friends to play with. (Premade lobbies: recommended by dentists. Because of all the bad toothpaste commercials, oh whatever...) I love this game, with almost all its facets. Whether it's eSports, surfing, I've pretty much tried it all. Valve is also very active as a developer and updates the game regularly. With lots of new skins that people are supposed to buy. Whatever. Weapons are well-balanced, and all playable in their own way, and useful for various tips and tricks, for example the Scout is accurate while jumping, the Mag-7 is too, and the AWP doesn't make a zoom sound if you don't press the zoom button but instead switch weapons. And here are the basics you should bring along: 1. Patience You weren't born a master and won't be one overnight, that takes time and practice. 2. Social skills You have to get along with your teammates, and that is CONSIDERABLY easier if you don't insult them, but treat them with respect and friendliness. 3. English skills At least the numbers, so you can call out to your teammates whether someone has high or low HP, you can find the callout locations on the internet. More isn't harmful of course, but you should at least have that much. 4. A microphone PLEASE. STOP IT. GET A MICROPHONE. I despair every single time I play a competitive match and I'm the only one talking, while the rest are typing in chat, which NOBODY has the time to read. And if possible, not too shitty of one, so your tender little voice (or courageous roaring, depending on the situation) doesn't get lost in the static hiss. Thanks. To all the people leaving a negative review: Please have the balls to say what you didn't like. And to everyone who wants to read a really good review: [url=http://steamcommunity.com/id/Sirius87/recommended/730/] Review by Sirius [/url]

translation_en: A comprehensive guide to cop-and-robber combat, the go-to textbook for basic small arms, which kept me company from elementary school all the way until college graduation. 8 years ago, an FPS browser game called "CrossFire" burst onto the scene and ruined my 300 million brothers in the blink of an eye. "Yet the funniest part is, as times change, the main user base of CrossFire is still elementary schoolers." Tips: If you're looking for something technical, like "how to improve your headshot rate" or "how to breathe and position yourself," then I advise you not to read any further: totally useless. ——————————————————————————————————————————— -Built on the Source engine, purebred. Building upon "Source," it enhances the dynamic HDR rendering effects, features an excellent physics engine, and makes textures much more detailed. -Rich map selection, reasonable design, with a decent degree of tactical viability. The stage design fits the theme of "Global Offensive" very well: sweltering Middle Eastern dust towns, Gothic-style European small towns, modern business-style office buildings... conflict is everywhere. The T and CT characters differ on every map, and the radio voice lines are primarily in English, but all feature heavy regional accents. -Before buying the game, I downloaded the standalone version of Source, messing around with bots in my spare time, and my skills improved somewhat over the years. But this didn't give me even the slightest upper hand the moment I touched CS:GO. The firearm model designs and sound effects are solidly middle-of-the-road and traceable; inheriting the fine traditions of its predecessor, I am gladdened to see that Valve still hasn't abandoned the weapon weight mechanic, which still noticeably impacts a character's mobility—a design element that many shooting games have already discarded. -Online matchmaking is a epoch-making design. Although a small minority of domestic players hold a negative attitude towards ping and server stability, the matchmaking system greatly enhances international communication, meaning domestic users' gaming scope is no longer limited to community servers and LAN/platform battles. For just $7.49, this might be the cheapest way to communicate directly with foreigners. Some phenomena are quite interesting, for instance: Indians' accents are irreversible, it feels like something splattered on a wall that you can never scrape off; Russians speak so fast you can only guess what they're saying from their tone; Koreans are mostly silent, but the moment they open their mouth you'll want to greet them with a gun butt; foreigners are flesh-and-blood with dicks, and sometimes even have more issues than domestic players, so you come to realize that while player skill might be significantly higher than bots, people with rock-bottom EQs know no national borders. [h1] Anyone who has played "The Witcher 3" is certainly familiar with Gwent, a mini-game that can be described as "overshadowing the main game." Unfortunately, there is one here too, and this mini-game is called "The next case drops a knife." [/h1] All of this probably starts when a matchmaking game settles. Back then, I was getting utterly destroyed by players of unknown nationalities, and while I was still brooding over my negative K/D ratio, I suddenly noticed an extra yellow box in my inventory. "Keys cost $2.49, not too expensive. Let's try it." "Holy shit, there are so many good guns, and they have qualities?!" "What the fuck, it gave me something worth less than $1? I don't believe it. Open another!" → "Why history always repeats itself is simply because human nature is greedy." Actually, calling this box an urn or Satan's box wouldn't be going too far. If a player who previously played some online RPGs with loot boxes and enhancement systems enters CS:GO for the first time, this thing caters extremely well to their gambler's psychology. Some make a fortune because of it, while others rage-delete the game over it. The weapons unboxed range from a fraction of a dollar to hundreds of dollars. ①When you look at their appearances you might exclaim: Valve finally stopped letting colorblind people handle weapon model development. The weapon models in this game finally don't look as lifeless as before, because from the earliest versions all the way to Source, all weapon textures were as monotonously charcoal-colored as a pile of burnt wood, and the paint kept chipping! ②Even more considerate is that some can even help you count your kills (excluding deaths and assists). ③Too bad, depending on their quality (orange, purple, blue, light blue, gray), they still suffer from varying degrees of paint chipping. It is recommended that you visit a 4S shop for maintenance after firing 5,000 rounds or about 3 months, or you can just spend money to buy a new one. → "The perfect definition of all flash, no substance." What weapon has a usage rate of less than 1% in the game? That's right, you guessed it, the knife. Aside from switching to it and pressing F to inspect (show off) for a bit, it seems to have no other use (does holding a knife make you run faster? I don't know if this setting is still kept in GO. But running around randomly with a knife when things aren't totally safe and running into a gun-wielding enemy at a corner, I guarantee your mind will be full of alpacas). Valve's art team put in some real effort this time, and the M9 Bayonet isn't hogging all the spotlight anymore. At the same time, they are encouraging more players and third-party creators to participate in weapon skin development. When you hold these legendary weapons in your hands, feel their heavy, cold texture, and examine those exquisite and gorgeous patterns, you will surely exclaim from the bottom of your heart: Hey, look at you, old buddy! Look at this, it's practically a work of art! As for their prices, to maximize the visual impact, you'd better go check the market yourself. → "I am surrounded by shills." Having played WoW for so many years, I've always been a loser: play battlegrounds and the Alliance loses, play Horde and the Horde loses. When walking away with those pathetic honor points, I used to wonder: who the hell is winning all these matches? A lot of friends in my friends list open cases, and looking at others flexing their knives and guns, then looking at the sub-$1 low-tier junk I unboxed, I truly fail to comprehend the mystery behind it. → "Absolute fairness" As a CFer who jumped into the game in 2007 and came back this June only to get scammed into matching with 9-year-olds after a month, I must say Valve is a conscientious developer that genuinely makes "skin guns" without ever upending their core nature: no matter how much money you spend, you are genuinely just buying a skin. → "On the wondrous uses of the F key" This is written purely for beginners! The F key is a pretty important button in this game, and if you want to play well, you should increase its usage frequency (Audition players have a blood feud with the space bar, but here you should treat the F key the same way). Uh, especially in clutch situations where all your teammates are dead and everyone is watching you from spectator mode. Don't forget, take two steps and press F! Why am I choosing to write this crap today? Because today is Children's Day, and channeling my inner child, I top-ended $50 to be reckless, with the result once again being joyous and celebratory. ——————————————————————————————————————————— -To those who read this review and come begging for a free copy of CS:GO (including international friends), all I want to say is you beggars, don't make things hard for a poor bastard like me! Push me too far, and since I've already opened so many damn cases, what else is there that I wouldn't dare do?! -At the same time, thanks to those friends who frequently invite me to play this game, thanks for your good intentions. Though I've consistently declined or left you on read, it's because I uninstalled this game long ago. Ten years ago I might have been a skill-based player, but later I became a capital-based player. I admit I got played by the game; if I can't unbox good stuff, why the hell should I even play?! But I'm also speechless. Originally, I was the kind of pillar of talent who, in my parents' eyes in childhood, would at worst go to Tsinghua or Peking University, and who resolved to grow up to be the country's Chairman; now I've nearly degenerated into a gambler, and I have Valve and their excellent work "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive" to thank for all of this! "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive"! "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive"! That's right, important things always need to be said three times. But in the end, I still wish you all unbox knives. *Though I don't want to stir up drama, this is indeed entirely my own damn opinion. *If you want to flame me, please buy a SPAS-12, that's my favorite.

translation_en: The layout of internet cafes in Luzhen is different from anywhere else: there's always an L-shaped counter right on the street, where prepaid gaming cards are ready to be issued at any time. School kids, as soon as school let out around noon or evening, would often spend four coppers for an hour—this was over twenty years ago, now it's gone up to ten coppers an hour—standing outside the net admin, playing a heated game of CS. If they were willing to shell out one more copper, they could buy a pack of spicy strips or a bottle of Coke as a gaming companion. If they forked over a dozen or so coppers, they could even call a e-girl companion, but most of these customers were elementary schoolers and generally not that well-off. Only those wearing school uniforms would pace into the private rooms next to the shop floor, ordering drinks and company to play at a leisurely pace. From the age of twelve, I'd been a shop assistant at the Xianheng Internet Cafe at the town entrance. The net admin said I looked too slow and might not be able to handle the high school uniform clientele, so I should just do odd jobs outside. The elementary schoolers outside, though easy enough to talk to, were full of nagging and endless nitpicking. They'd often want to see with their own eyes the gaming card being printed from the counter, check if there was actually money on it, and watch the RMB get put into the cash drawer before feeling relieved. Under such strict supervision, scamming money out of them was pretty tough. So after a few days, the net admin said I couldn't handle this either. Fortunately, the person who recommended me had a lot of clout and I couldn't be fired, so my job was changed to the mindless duty of solely sweeping the floor. From then on, I spent all day standing in the bathroom, entirely devoted to my duties. While I hadn't made any mistakes, it always felt a bit monotonous and boring. The net admin had a fierce face and the customers never had a pleasant tone, making it impossible to feel lively; only when Fu Yiji came to the shop could I get a few laughs in, which is why I still remember him to this day. Fu Yiji was the only guy who wore a school uniform while playing CS:GO outside. He was pretty tall, with a pale face and scars often wedged between his wrinkles, and he carried some cheap domestic smartphone from a few years ago. Even though he wore a school uniform, it was filthy and torn, looking like it hadn't been patched or washed in over a decade. Whenever he talked to people, it was always full of "no knife used" and other gibberish that left people half-understanding. Because his surname was Fu, others took that half-understood phrase "Superior Master Fu Yiji" from tracing practice paper and gave him the nickname "Fu Yiji." As soon as Fu Yiji arrived at the shop, all the guys drinking would look at him and laugh. Some would shout, "Fu Yiji! You've got a fresh scar on your face again!" He wouldn't answer, just saying to the counter, "Give me two hours, and a pack of spicy strips," laying out nine big coppers. They'd deliberately raise their voices and yell, "You must've opened Gaben's cases again!" Fu Yiji would open his eyes wide and say, "How can you falsely accuse an innocent person out of nowhere..." "Innocent? I saw you live-streaming the latest case openings the day before yesterday, crying like a bitch." Fu Yiji would blush deeply, the veins on his forehead bulging out, and argue, "Opening cases can't be considered unlucra... Case opening!... Can an African's business be considered unlucrative?" Followed by a stream of hard-to-understand words like "A gentleman is stubbornly unlucrative" and "knife," causing everyone to burst into loud laughter: the inside and outside of the shop were filled with a toxic atmosphere. According to what people said behind his back, Fu Yiji used to play matchmaking too, but he never made it to Silver and didn't even know how to idle; so he grew poorer and poorer, down to the point of almost begging. Fortunately, he was good at boosting, so he'd grind StatTrak skins for people in exchange for a bowl of rice. Unfortunately, he had another bad habit: he loved to drink and hated to work. After sitting around for less than a few days, he and his steam friends would completely disappear together. After doing this a few times, nobody left him with any StatTrak skins to grind. With no other choice, Fu Yiji inevitably resorted to occasionally opening cases. But his conduct at our shop was better than anyone else's—he never defaulted on his payments. Even if he occasionally didn't have cash and temporarily put it on the chalk slate, within a month he'd definitely pay it off in full and have Fu Yiji's name wiped from the slate. After eating half a pack of spicy strips, the flush on Fu Yiji's face would gradually fade back to normal, and someone would inevitably ask him again, "Fu Yiji, did you really play ranked?" Fu Yiji would look at the person asking, showing an expression of disdain to argue. They'd follow up with, "How come you couldn't even scrape together half a Silver rank?" Fu Yiji would immediately look dejected and uneasy, a layer of gray casting over his face, mumbling some words. This time it was all about lag and getting screwed over, completely incomprehensible stuff. At this moment, everyone would burst into laughter again: the inside and outside of the shop were filled with a toxic atmosphere. At times like these, I could join in the laughter, and the net admin would never scold me. Furthermore, whenever the net admin saw Fu Yiji, he'd often ask him the same things to provoke laughter. Fu Yiji knew he couldn't chat with them, so he'd have no choice but to talk to the kids. Once, he said to me, "Have you played CS?" I nodded slightly. He said, "Played it... then let me test you. When playing Terrorist on Dust 2 mid, how do you smoke it off?" I thought to myself, a beggar like him is even qualified to test me? So I turned my head away and ignored him. Fu Yiji waited for a long time and said earnestly, "Don't know how to smoke it off? ...I'll teach you, remember! You gotta remember these smokes. In the future when you become a net admin, you'll need to use them to flex." I thought to myself that I was still a long way from the net admin's rank, and our net admin never even played CS:GO; amused and impatient, I lazily replied, "Who needs you to teach me, don't you just throw a smoke from CT spawn?" Fu Yiji showed an extremely pleased expression, tapping the counter with his long fingernails on two fingers, nodding and saying, "Right, right! ...There are four ways to smoke it, do you know?" I grew even more impatient, pouting and walking away. Fu Yiji had just opened matchmaking, wanting to smoke off mid, but seeing my complete lack of enthusiasm, he let out another sigh, showing an expression of extreme regret. A few times, the neighborhood kids heard the laughter and came over to watch the fun, surrounding Fu Yiji. He'd feed them one kill each. Once the kids finished getting themselves killed, they still wouldn't disperse, their eyes glued to the screen. Fu Yiji would panic, spread his fingers to cover the keyboard, hunch over, and say, "I'm kicked, I've already been kicked." He'd straighten up, take another look at the screen, shake his head, and mutter, "Kicked out, kicked out! Why the hell kick me? WTF." Then this group of kids would disperse amidst laughter. Fu Yiji made people so cheerful, but without him, people just went on living their lives anyway. One day, probably two or three days before the Mid-Autumn Festival, the net admin was slowly closing out the accounts, took down the chalk slate, and suddenly said, "Fu Yiji hasn't been here in a long time. He still owes nineteen coppers!" Only then did I realize that he really hadn't been around for a long time. Someone eating a tea egg said, "How could he come? ...He got sodomized." The net admin said, "Oh!" "He was still opening cases as usual. This time he lost his mind and actually opened 100 cases. Can you just go opening newly released cases like that?" "What happened after?" "What happened? First he wrote a suicide note, then he chopped off his hands, chopped away for most of the night, and then got sodomized." "And then?" "And then he got sodomized." "What happened after he got sodomized?" "What happened? ...Who knows? Maybe he went to go work as a male hooker." The net admin didn't ask anymore and slowly went back to calculating his accounts. After the Mid-Autumn Festival, the autumn wind grew colder day by day, looking like early winter was approaching; leaning against the heater all day, I even had to put on a cotton-padded jacket. One late afternoon without a single customer, I was sitting there with my eyes closed. Suddenly I heard a voice: "Open for an hour." Though extremely quiet, this voice was very familiar. Looking over, there was absolutely nobody there. I stood up and looked outside, and there was Fu Yiji, sitting by the threshold under the counter. His face was black and thin, completely unrecognizable; wearing a tattered lined jacket, sitting cross-legged with a straw cushion underneath tied to his shoulders with grass rope. Seeing me, he said again, "Open for an hour." The net admin poked his head out too, saying, "Is that Fu Yiji? You still owe nineteen coppers!" Fu Yiji raised his head despondently and replied, "This... I'll pay it back next time. This time it's cash, and I need a good PC." The net admin smiled at him just like usual and said, "Fu Yiji, you opened cases again!" But this time he didn't argue much, simply saying, "Don't make fun of me!" "Make fun of you? If you hadn't opened them, how'd you end up chopping your hands off?" Fu Yiji muttered softly, "+1 to library, +1, +1..." His expression looked a lot like he was begging the net admin not to bring it up anymore. By this time a few people had gathered, and both the net admin and I laughed. I activated the card, brought it out, and placed it on the threshold. He fished four big coppers out of his tattered pocket and put them in my hand. I saw his hands were covered in mud—turns out he had walked here using those very hands. Before long, he started a match, and amidst the banter and laughter of the others, he sat down and slowly walked away using those hands. From then on, I didn't see Fu Yiji for a long time. By the end of the year, the net admin took down the chalk slate and said, "Fu Yiji still owes nineteen coppers!" By the Dragon Boat Festival the following year, he said again, "Fu Yiji still owes nineteen coppers!" By the Mid-Autumn Festival, however, he didn't mention it, and by the end of that year, he wasn't seen at all. To this day, I still haven't seen him—presumably Fu Yiji has indeed quit the game for good. Written in the winter of 1918.

translation_en: A very strange game. Instead of a foreword: a young guy, 17 years old, gaming experience of only about 5 years, and even then, only familiar with the basic online shooters like "Battlefield" and "Call of Duty", never played past CS games, and this one was gifted to me, I’d hardly ever have decided to buy it myself. And that's a pity. Let's move on to the game itself. In my opinion, this game is one of the few that during matches truly requires maximum concentration, decent erudition, a "well-hung tongue", competent tactics, the ability to think outside the box and make lightning-fast decisions. And all this for shouting matches in chat. Yes, yes, unlike the other games I mentioned, where the element of interaction between players is reduced to "beep-beep, get in, I'll drop you off at the point and f*ck you with a defibrillator to get points" ("Battlefield") and "uhhhhh, well.... let me drop a radar on the ground" ("Call of Duty"), CS is much better in this regard: after all, the game is considered a more or less team-based shooter. That's where the catch lies. Apparently, only a chosen few know about its team-based nature. That is exactly why you will have to sort things out in the game chat so much. Moreover, I'm not even talking about casual mode, where you have no hope of anything good anyway, but specifically about competitive mode. Casual mode is a mode where everyone just runs around, flexing their karambits and Asiimovs, challenging you to "one-on-one, knives or pistols," trying to become your stepdad, blasting music in voice chat or straight up holding the mic to the TV, telling you about their hard and sweaty lives, or just hurling ethnic slurs. Naturally, [strike]no one gives a f*ck[/strike] nobody cares about teamwork there, they only think about their "frag" count. In other words, standard, thoughtless fodder. It's a whole different story in competitive mode. Playing with friends here is an absolute pleasure, this is when the full charm of the game is revealed: you plot tactics, cover each other, play stealthy, everyone knows their place, their abilities, the sniper will never be left without an AWP, a "rush B" will never get screwed over by a ridiculous smoke, the "bomb carrier" will never run to A when B has already been cleared. And after the game... oooohhh that feeling... so much shit, so much shit is poured on you, the happy winners, by the opponents during those brief seconds after the match when everyone is in a single voice chat, so much debris of exploded assholes flying at you from the monitors... It feels like you could reach out and catch them, catch these almost material echoes of someone else's overflowing hatred. However, all of this looks completely different if you play with random players. Even if by some incredible chance you happen to get an ADEQUATE team (I’m not even hoping for a good one, let it at least be adequate), then in the very next game you are in for a moral shock. I advise playing in absolute silence in this situation for two reasons. 1. By entering into a dialogue with them, you automatically drop to their level, and with the pressure drop that occurs from a sudden immersion into this sea abyss, you risk dying. 2. According to statistics, in 73% of cases one of your four allies is a Pole. If you utter even a single word, he will recognize you, smell the Russian spirit, and shower you with "kurwas", "vodkas", and "Putins", despite your stellar play, "carrying" the team, and EVEN having a CD Projekt RED avatar like mine. Nevertheless, although I advise keeping silent, that's not entirely right, because if you manage to show what you're worth in the first rounds, then as the alpha of the pack you can further lead the team and TRY to give them instructions, in English of course, since we respect other nations, and of course, if a leader hasn't already emerged before you, because "Too many leaders spoil the bomb site." I say TRY because if there actually is a Pole with you, you won't be able to command, and in general, there are people out there who can't even be called human, and they still won't listen to basic things and always run around like "lone wolves" trying to pad their "frag" count. And of course, I couldn't ignore the feature that "haters" love the most: cases and skins. Yes, CS has cases, weapon skins, exclusive music, and weapon stickers for real money. But no one forces you to buy them, they give no gameplay advantages, and even, despite rumors, they do not increase your manhood (though who the hell knows). Having at least the rudiments of willpower in your soft little skull, you will be able to control yourself and not buy virtual guns for thousands of rubles. RECOMMENDED.

translation_en: Playing the Counter-Strike series for the first time? Decided to start with CS:GO? Here is an encyclopedia of certain terms you will be hearing in the game in the future. Pub, public server - A place where a noob with a five-thousand-ruble skin is respected, unlike pro players with stock weapons. MM (Matchmaking) - A place where you will sweat your balls off trying your absolute hardest until round twenty. After that, the game switches to a "fuck this shit" playstyle. Poles - Famous inhabitants of MM, creatures who are dissatisfied with ABSOLUTELY everything you do. Literally anything. Even if you clutch a 1v5 with just one pistol on 1 HP. The main rule: not a single word in Russian. Russians - Famous inhabitants of MM and public servers who clog up the chat with swearing. If you suddenly need info from your random Russian teammate, you'll hear something like "He ran past somewhere over there," "Looks like he was around there," and "I think right here." After doing a 180-degree turn and checking those angles, the enemy turns out to be behind you. Cases - Gabe's loot boxes. You shove 120 rubles ($1.5) into them and pull out literally pennies in return. Skins - Weapon paint jobs that determine a player's skill. Awap, A-V-P, AVP - If you think the best way to learn is in actual combat, throw that thought out of your head and never run with this sniper rifle, which, judging by your movement while scoped, weighs about 50 kilos if not more. M4 - Counter-Terrorist weapon that Terrorists always prefer to pick up as a trophy. AK - Terrorist weapon that Counter-Terrorists always prefer to pick up as a trophy. General impressions of the game / Comparison with previous versions: Like about 60-70% of the Counter-Strike community, I've been playing since 1.6. How is GO different? - The shooting is more random than in 1.6. You'll think there's a magnet hanging in the sky of every map that attracts bullets. Actually, it's not like that. I checked. Weird, right? - Grenade physics. Even though real grenades weigh about half a kilo, here they bounce off surfaces like shit hitting a public restroom tile. Be careful with the alternative throw button when using grenades. - Physics in general. If you suddenly see a terrorist's corpse twist after death as if they don't have a spine at all — don't be surprised. The modified engine lets you capture the best breakdance moments from dead bodies. Don't believe me? Check the GO community screenshots. - Graphics. If you think your girlfriend asks too much of you (if you even have one, and you know what a female human is), you're wrong. This game will devour all of your RAM and give you a pathetic 100 FPS if you have less than two gigs of RAM. A slideshow during gunfights is guaranteed. - Weapons. There are new ones. There's a lot to say about them. Buy it and see for yourself. After writing this totally useless review that maybe two or three people will look at max, I want to wrap it up with a general conclusion. The game is really good. Once you get the hang of it after about 100 hours, you'll figure out what makes it tick. But unfortunately, the game is merciless to beginners. If you really don't want to get matched with players who think your pistol barrel is edible and try to bite it when you're executing a rush together, you have to train your reaction time, aim, grenade setups, and overall tactics. And remember — never lose heart. This game will eat away at your nerves, just like it did mine. The main thing is not to give up. Someday you'll become just like the pros. Patience is key.

In a competitive match you'll depend only on your skill and your teammates'. -> It's Counter Strike!! In this installment, the developers planned to gather the best of Counter-Strike 1.6 & the best of Counter-Strike: Source to unite these two types of Counter players; That is, to bring together the 1.6 players with the Source ones and in my opinion they've achieved it, I see many 1.6 players who are very good and have been playing CS:GO for a long time and the same with the Source players. Bad Points. -> The VAC is trash. VAC (Valve Anticheat) is Valve's anti-cheat system and with all due respect, IT'S TRASH! In many high-rank competitive matches you'll run into players with hacks, and the worst part is that VAC takes 1 MONTH to figure out if they have hacks, that's why they created Overwatch which consists of us working for Valve as their slaves to see if people have hacks because they know their anti-cheat system is useless. -> The community is infested. Many times you'll run into annoying people (Russians, Brazilians, squeakers, people who treat you like trash for being a "Noob", etc.) -> Smurfs and Hackers. I've decided to add this con because recently (1 or 2 months ago) I've had the curiosity to check the profiles of people who get a ridiculous amount of kills in the match, and funnily enough those people don't have more than 40 hours played, they don't have other games, their steam level is 0 or 1 at most, or they even have their profile set to private, so no matter how good you are, if you go up against a smurf or a hacker, you're screwed. Well, having given my most important points about CS:GO I have finished my review. See you soon & GG.

translation_en: Back then I was a Call of Duty fan like many others, but then my eyes laid upon the irresistible offer of a discounted Counter-Strike on Steam. Ok, straight to the point: For beginners and Call of Duty fans, the game takes a VEEERY long time to get used to, since you can only hip-fire with almost all weapons and they also recoil like crazy, which will especially scare off the CoD people. (Which is actually a good thing, CoD is trash... at least compared to CS) Also, your teammates and opponents are mostly FUCKING brutal hardcore gamers who give you a headshot with a Deagle EVERY damn time... EVERY TIME. Anyway, moving on :D If you are neither put off by the gunplay nor by the other players, all you need is practice. And quite a lot of it. You have to find the weapon you're immediately good with, then improve your aim with it, and try to play with foresight, and above all improve your reflexes, just so you don't completely shit the bed. Quick tip: Don't just play some mainstream weapons just because you keep getting killed by them, you can do just as well with another weapon.. so leave the AK in the closet for now (Heh, Kollegah reference :D ) Up to this point, this all sounds like a very critical list, but it isn't. CS:GO is just an insanely fast, demanding, but also genuinely learnable first-person shooter (I'm deliberately avoiding the word "tactical shooter", because that's not the right term, at least in my opinion), which is actually completely based on skill, and not on OP weapons like in certain other shooters *COUGH*. You actually still need proper aim here :D With my 93 hours of playtime at this point, I'm still far away from being "good", but I'm very confident and just have fun with this game every single day anew. The so-called weapon skins are just a visual upgrade for weapons and can either be unboxed from weapon cases (Current price for a key: €2.29, skin value is COMPLETELY random), dropped randomly (for free) or bought on the market for the specified price. Just a quick summary again: - Skill-based - Fast - Demanding - Sometimes brutal teammates/opponents - Really hard for beginners and CoD gamers at first - Learnable - Keys for skins very expensive - Wonderful insult trainer in all world languages (Fun fact :D ) In my opinion, the best first-person shooter I know of (besides Quake 3 Arena) that I have played / seen so far. Definite buy recommendation.

translation_en: Best way to learn Russian. 10/10 More seriously, very good base game, completely ruined by its community. I spent over a thousand hours on CS 1.6, so needless to say I had a rude awakening with CS:GO. On the very first installment, the vibe was good, people helped each other out, hackers got banned quickly. On CS:GO, 80% of the community consists of: - smurfs who come back in full force every time there's a sale (may you die a slow and painful disease, guys) and who completely ruin competitive, - hackers everywhere, - tryhards, raging sweatlords who will kick you and/or insult you for free just because you're still getting the hang of the game, - squeakers who will drool all over your mom if you kill them (or call you a hacker if you hit a headshot), - Russians who make zero effort to adapt and play in their own little world (when they aren't screaming "C.yka Blyat"). "u f*cking noob", "get cancer", "gtfo" or "I f*cked your mom" are the standard polite greetings down here. Forget the fantasy of a somewhat tight-knit community like the one I knew on the original game. Here, team kills are legion. The matchmaking also needs an overhaul; after several matches, I ended up playing against totally overpowered guys as well as absolute noobs who were staring at a wall or asking "How u grab weapon lol?". In short, matches are never balanced, I gave up quickly. Last point of this review, and not the least: Valve's thirst for cash, selling skins and other weapon customizations at indecent prices. Sorry, Gaben, I'm not blowing my savings account to get my M-16 in fuchsia pink. I'm not dropping 100 bucks for a neon knife when the Carrefour down the street sells the same ones for 2 euros. Microtransactions were already the cancer of TF2, they're turning into metastases on CS. What's the point of lugging around a piss-yellow AWP other than showing off that you've got dough? More profitable than hunting down the clowns who piss all over the spirit of the game... I recommend it because the base game has enormous potential and playing with mates is genuinely exhilarating, with CS:GO relying much more on teamwork than its predecessors. More realistic, the graphics are very nice and the game runs without a hitch on the toaster I use as a computer. Buy it to play with friends. And run away at all costs from competitive, and online play in general if you expect to have any fun. In ten hours of gameplay, I didn't play more than three matches without seeing hacks/smurfs/insults/kicks/bans/Russians/kevins. People will tell me "But that's normal, you haven't played enough, rank up and it'll get better." But funnily enough, the prospect of shortening my life expectancy by enduring a hundred hours of gameplay in such terrible company to FINALLY start enjoying the software doesn't really appeal to me. Give me back the spirit of CS 1.6, please. translation_en: My old man is a absolute Counter-Strike fanatic. Half the apartment is covered in his jerseys with his nickname on the back, posters, and game boxes. About once a month he buys a new mouse for around 150-200 PLN because he chucks the old one out the window in a rage when his aim "gets scuffed". In my 22 years of life I've run to MediaMarkt like 30 times already for a new MX518 or Deathadder. A week ago I just walked into the store and the kid working there immediately handed me a Logitech G4 and asked if I'm sponsoring some multi-gaming team. The other half of the apartment is clogged with gaming accessories, old mice, keyboards, gamer clothes like wristbands, and computer magazines. CD-Action, Click!, Komputer Świat, Cybermycha, Retro Gamer, etc. Every week my old man does a tour of all the local newsstands and press shops, dropping massive amounts of cash on this waste of paper. Back in the day he only played with bots and that gave him joy, he played 2 hours a day and got bored. I was stupid enough to introduce him to the internet and he started playing online multiplayer. At first he picked one FFA server where he had regular "homies", they'd always greet him when he logged on: "sup art", "hi art", "what's up art". He played there for half a year and then went to a meetup of that server's players where they were gonna play, drink, and vote for admins. He came back Sunday evening, pissed off, clothes torn, with a black eye. He got into a fight with some guy named Jaro because they didn't vote him for admin even though he'd been playing there so long, and they used the argument "you don't even know what an MX is", so he lost his shit and started throwing hands xd He came back wrecked and never went on that server again, except on some other nickname just to talk trash. Those were the CS 1.5 days so with our Neostrada connection he could change his IP at will (which I also needlessly told him about). More than once he spent whole days changing his IP, logging back onto the server, and insulting Jaro and the rest of the admins. He also made an account on a few Counter-Strike forums: Wiaderko, In Memories of CS 1.5, Proxion, etc. On all of them he slandered and insulted the administration and the head admin Jaro xd I got a huge kick out of it because as a casual player I was watching it from the sidelines, until... My old man met "Duży" (Big) on some other server, Duży was a guy my age and invited my old man to a clan. Fuck! My old man in a clan. Now he didn't spend 5 hours a day during the work week grinding CS, but 8-10. He'd come home from work, first thing he sits at the PC and grinds some FFA (warming up, that's what he called it). After 3 hours of warmup his clan crew would gather and they'd start playing scrims and matchmaking. They'd play these scrims and matches for an average of 3 hours on weekdays because most of them had to go to sleep since they had middle school or high school the next morning, but my old man didn't give a fuck about work because he had his own business, and with the ones who stayed he'd sit until 2 AM more than once, working out tactics on where to flash, where to throw a smoke, who goes where and at what second, etc. They'd spend fucking 2 weeks analyzing a single map. That's how they played de_inferno, which they called "their map" xd Never mind that after 50 hours they were just figuring out basic tactics that people on public servers already know, but they had *their* map! Regularly for the past 8 years, every month or two, my old man buggers off with his current or some other clan to meetups or LAN parties, blowing a ton of cash on gas, hotels, food, and alcohol. He has literally never won anything. Oh wait, sorry, once they won 500 PLN, after splitting it 100 per head it covered the gas. When my old man isn't eating at the computer, which mostly happens on Sundays when grandma—his mother—has dinner with us, he talks the whole damn time about Counter-Strike, tactics, his clan mates' lives... For fuck's sake. My mother and I don't know what to do anymore. At first it was cool when I was like 13, but now I'm embarrassed in front of my friends. My old man doesn't give a shit what's going on. Every weekend Saturday/Sunday he's in my room from 6:30-7:00 AM. He gets up, washes up or doesn't, makes coffee and scrambled eggs, then sits at the PC and starts blasting. Every Saturday and Sunday I'm woken up by the sounds of Kalashnikov gunfire and screams of *Go go go! Fire in the hole!* One weekend my girlfriend was sleeping over, naturally we were sleeping naked after a night full of passion. It doesn't phase the old man, he walks in at 6:40 like it's nothing, fires up the PC and starts grinding. I told my girlfriend this sort of thing happens and she wouldn't believe me. So she lay naked until 11:30 (even though she wanted to go home at 10) because she couldn't get up since my old man was sitting at the computer. Only when he had to pee and the map changed did she quickly leap out of the bed. Absolute nightmare. I won't even mention the fact that my dad talks in all internet-Counter-Strike slang, which nowadays I don't even understand. In high school, my buddies were over and we were drinking a beer, talking—my old man was sitting in my room with us playing. Then he stands up, walks over, pokes his head through the door and says: "You guys want some ice loles?" And I fucking blushed so hard, while my friends cracked up. A minute later he brought us some nut-flavored ice cream. Non-stop repeating "Look at that headshot", "What a fucking lucker", "Fuck, de_dust again." That's still not the worst. The worst is when he plays in the evenings/nights, that's when I have no right to sleep at all, just like on weekend mornings. All I hear the whole time is "Water water water! Bridge bridge! Morgue! Be be be be be! Help! I'm going house! Peek him!" etc. Yesterday's situation: 11:40 PM, I have to be up for work at 8, he's shooting with an AWP, he dies (someone knife'd him), screams his head off about what a fucking noob he is, then turns around to see my pissed-off face, hits Tab and says, "Look, I'm first." And I'm like "Fine, dad" and shove my face back into the pillow. This year for Christmas he bought himself a mouse for 500+ PLN. Some super tricked-out one with weights, one of those adjustable ones that molds to your hand. Of course he bought it around the 20th before Christmas because he couldn't wait. By Christmas Eve the mouse was already trashed because he was playing drunk around 1 AM (I had just gotten back from Midnight Mass) and I saw he was playing on one of the old ones. I asked what happened and he said that piece of shit mouse doesn't work like it's supposed to. Once he took me to his 40th birthday at a player meetup, I mean sure, cool present. Not only did I have to watch my 40+ year old dad running around shirtless with teenagers in an internet cafe pouring vodka for them, but he also made me play and then yelled at me that I'm a noob and don't get it. What a birthday. Once he shows me his stats, he must have been like 80/3, I tell him "nice, nice", then a round starts and I look—he's seeing through walls, there are lasers, his crosshair isn't even moving, basically my old man was a cheater. They uploaded him to a Counter forum's "cheater blacklist", of course he denied it, made a million multi-accounts where he trolled them and wrote that he was clean, legit, nothing to see, etc. Never mind that he was tracking people through walls and didn't even try to hide it. They banned all his Steam accounts linked to ESL and the forums. He immediately bought 10 new ones, some of which got banned too because he kept cheating. For fuck's sake. The worst thing in all of this is that my old man decided to visit the AC (anti-cheat admin) who judged him and put him on the blacklist. Turns out it was Jaro from years ago, my old man came back with a wrecked face and a torn jacket + 2 weeks later he got a court summons. The trial is in a month, and he's still trolling on the forum, writing posts as himself saying he's clean and a good player and he doesn't know what they want from him. On top of that, he's looking for a clan and writing in his application that he used to play in PGS, MYM, NiP, SK, etc. Mom left us 3 years ago, she's living a happy life with a guy she'd been having an affair with for a long time because dad was playing the game. I don't know if he's even noticed she's gone yet.

translation_en: There isn't much more to say about Counter-Strike – the world's most popular FPS, which started its career as a Half-Life mod back in 1999. Global Offensive is the 4th installment of this cult production, featuring the best graphics and plenty of new features, such as: - a ranking system similar to the one known from League of Legends (ranging from the lowest Silver I to Global Elite); - tradeable and marketable weapon skins (prices reach up to several hundred €, you can also open cases with weapons or weapon stickers); - periodic special operations (campaigns where you win weapon skins, weapon cases, or play new maps); - the ability to watch matches via the in-game spectator system (watching your friends' matches or pro-level gameplay). However, we mustn't forget that Counter-Strike is still one of the hardest FPS games available on the market. Mastering weapon recoil is a major challenge and requires a lot of practice. Learning how to properly throw grenades or grasping team tactics, which often ensure success in a match, requires no less skill. Yes, Global Offensive is a game that heavily relies on teamwork, even if the individuals don't know each other. To avoid painting too rosy a picture, CS has a few flaws. Currently, the most annoying thing is so-called smurfs, which are low-level accounts played by people of a much higher skill level. This significantly hinders ranking up and is incredibly frustrating when you lose matches to players who belong to a higher league. It's common to encounter 2 smurfs per game or across 3 matches in a row. The second problem is the servers, where the tick rate is a major issue and often dictates whether a bullet hits the enemy or not. Despite Valve making huge amounts of money, they dodge upgrading the servers by pleading a lack of cash. To sum up, if you are looking for an FPS that heavily rewards self-improvement, that will require you to learn, and will give you a lot of satisfaction when you rank up, then Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is just for you. On the other hand, the game can really piss you off, especially if you get a bunch of Russian-speaking teammates and run into smurfs on the enemy team. Personally, I recommend it.

translation_en: [Classic, Microtransactions, First-Person Shooter] I'm sure everyone has heard of the Counter-Strike franchise. This installment also adds a fair few new systems—probably the biggest update since the original 1.6!!! The game is vastly different from the CoD and BF series currently on the market; it's a small-map-based game. It uses a round-based format, and the team that gets the most points by the end of the game wins. This version adds official Valve servers, gun skins, and a microtransaction system. The Competitive mode played on official Valve servers is basically ranked mode, which matches you with players of similar skill based on your number of wins. As for gun skins and the microtransaction system, they can basically be used to make some extra Steam wallet cash. After a match ends, there's a chance to drop gun skins or cases. Gun skins, as the name implies, are used to change the look of your weapons. Recently, they also added stickers, which you can stick on your guns to make them unique. Cases need keys to be opened, and if you're lucky, you have a chance to get good-looking skins, or even sell them to other players via the Marketplace to pad your Steam wallet.
