translation_en: [h1]There is probably no one who hasn't played Counter-Strike at least once in their life. This game series is so popular that probably only the blind, deaf, and mute haven't heard of it. So let's not beat around the bush and jump straight to the analysis. Yes, this isn't the same Counter-Strike we played with friends over the LAN back at the turn of the century, but did it have to stay unchanged?[/h1] [b]GL HF[/b] For the sake of balance, a lot of our favorite guns from the first part were nerfed. The "deagle" got "uncontrollable" as a payment for its power, the silenced "m4" got its ammo reduced to just 20 rounds in exchange for low recoil, AWP's "zoom" was tweaked to make it as blurry as possible while moving, and the "USP-S" spare magazines were dropped down to two, which often forces thriftless players to scavenge the floor for anything that can shoot at the end of the round. Of course, new guns weren't left out either, including the "CZ-75" submachine gun, the insanely [strike]op[/strike] accurate "Tec-9" pistol, and the "PP-Bizon", a light submachine gun with low lethality but a huge ammo capacity. All this heavily affected the gameplay, adding a solid dose of randomness to shooting. For instance, the new ballistics make it easier to shoot on the run, and thanks to the new, more powerful pistols, forcing eco rounds has gotten quite a bit easier. Whether that's good or bad is entirely up to you. A major contribution to the good qualities of CS:GO is the new kill reward system. For example, getting a kill with a weaker weapon gives a bigger reward and vice versa (if you knife an opponent, you get $1500, which is 5 times the default reward, while a kill with the [strike]op[/strike] AWP only pays out $100, a third of the default). This feature brings a healthy dose of variety into the game and often forces gamblers to take risks and fight to the bitter end, which makes competitive matches more thrilling, tense, and spectacular. [b]To pay, or not to pay[/b] Let's talk about microtransactions. In CS:GO, this means the ability to buy unique weapon finishes and seasonal DLCs called Operations. People make money off the former, so let's talk about the latter instead. The standard contents of an operation: [olist] [*]5-7 maps (made by the community) that are available even to those who didn't buy the operation, but only for the duration of the operation (usually 5-6 months, though lately operations have been coming out more and more often... tsk tsk tsk) [*]12-18 pretty weapon finishes (made by the community) and accordingly a new case where you can get those finishes, assuming you leveled up your "Luck" skill in the "S.P.E.C.I.A.L." system on time—damn, wrong game, my apologies. [*][strike]Compendium[/strike] an animated book with your match stats and operation progress. [*]A few more nice little things, like an operation medal, a new knife model (not to be confused with a finish), and usually that's about it. There's nothing you can do with the first one except keep it as a memento of the operation, and you'll most likely never have the second one unless you're ready to drop 50 or more evergreen bucks on the Steam Market, or spend dozens of times more trying to unbox it from cases. [*]In the latest operation (Falchion), a profile level (not to be M.M. rank) and a bunch of missions were added to these "perks", completion of which grants XP for that very level. It's worth mentioning that besides the Falchion operation itself, which costs $5.99, you can buy two additional storylines (an extra two dozen missions, really) for just $2.99 each. In my opinion, the price for all these "innovations" is already overpriced, and now they're selling it in pieces, and twice as expensive too. Overkill, don't you think? [*]Finally, it's worth mentioning that these—let's be honest—not-so-original missions actually have a plot, which is pretty decent by modern FPS standards, delivered via short text blurbs before the missions. A pretty interesting move, I'd even say: "the only interesting move in this operation". [/olist] In the end, we get two overpriced DLCs a year with minimal content, most of which is made by the community rather than the developer. Not bad, Gabe, pretty damn bad... Verdict: Counter-Strike: Global Offensive definitely has flaws, yet it has way more merits. If the developers paid more attention to creating new content instead of adding new weapon finishes—which they didn't even make, by the way—the game would be times better. But until then... go buy the add-on to the add-on for just $2.99.

translation_en: [b]A bit of Counter-Strike history[/b] I started playing Counter-Strike pretty much since it came out, around '99. When I was a kid I used to play in the local LAN room in my apartment block with friends until 2005 when my parents bought me a PC. That's when I made my first Steam account (which unfortunately got stolen > kid > naive > the end). I didn't make another Steam account until I opened my first Deathrun server on Counter-Strike 1.6. I should point out that since 2008 I only played deathrun / surf / kz / bhop / hns, definitely not classic.. so my shooting accuracy wasn't that great anymore until I started playing CS:GO. [b]Since when do I play CS:GO?[/b] I've been playing CS:GO since the skill groups (ranks) came out in the winter of 2012. Until they added Operation Payback and implicitly weapon skins, I barely played at all because the game felt very poorly optimized. I started playing alongside the Indungi Administration (TucsoN / iBen), they're the ones who urged me to buy my first Operation Payback, but back then I couldn't wrap my head around the idea of putting money into a virtual game (I still don't get it to this day). I started to like the game when the second operation, Phoenix, dropped, but given that I had a pretty weak PC I only played the Nuke map and hit the "performance" of 30/40 FPS. I only played this map until I learned the callouts. The FPS in the game didn't help me much.. when I was 1vs1 with an M4A4 / AK-47 the game would stutter and I didn't have that many chances to take down the enemy, so I started playing with the P90 taking my friends' advice. I bought the second operation, "BRAVO," because you had better chances of weapon / case drops plus the perks it offered. After that, I started to like that icon you automatically get when buying an operation and I started collecting every badge / icon / operation. Why did I like the idea? Because it tracks all your matches / MVPs besides the perks offered by the operation itself, which gives you a gateway to financial growth. So that's when trading started. [b]How did I get the items?[/b] During that period I had an SA:MP server and that helped me a lot with the items part because like I told you above.. I don't agree with putting money into a virtual game, so I started getting myself some items like (AWP Boom / Glock Fade / AK-47 Fire Serpent / M4A4 Howl / AWP and M4A4 Asiimov / Karambit and Bayonet Crimson Web and many others that you can still see in the screenshots on my profile) all of it bought from the profit of the SA:MP server. [b]What did I do with them?[/b] After a long time I decided it made no sense to keep ~1500 euros in my inventory and play at 40 FPS, so I sold all my items for real money and that's how I invested in the PC and peripherals I have today > http://www.pcgarage.ro/vizualizare-wishlist/1097152/ [b]What are my intentions in this game?[/b] Generally I don't like to lose so I want to win every match. Because of this I don't play with just anyone. I will collect all the operations and try to make them GOLD (except the Payback one which I didn't get to finish due to the reasons mentioned above). I don't care about rank but I try to keep it high. I still don't consider myself a good player so I practice daily and train on FFA servers / 1vs1 arenas / and workshop aim maps. As for the items in my inventory, I keep / buy strictly only the ones I like (there's no accounting for taste). [b]What advice do I have for other people reading this review?[/b] 1. The game is enjoyable if you have a PC that runs over 100/150 FPS, otherwise there's no point in getting into the game because you'll just get pissed off, you won't know how to shoot / you'll never achieve any performance in the game. 2. Don't take the food out of your mouth, your allowance, your mom's money to buy weapons / operations etc. 3. Be very cautious if you have items because you are easy prey for "scammers". 4. The game is fun until you run into cheaters. So if you run into cheaters you'll get pissed off > the temptation to buy cheats pops up > you get a VAC BAN > you lose your Steam account and the money invested in it > you throw your computer out the window and your mom beats you too, so.. calm down for those who want to buy cheats. 5. Train on FFA (free for all) / Arena (1vs1 / aim map) servers and play a lot with bots to learn how to do SPRAY CONTROL > like pashabiceps. 6. NEVER play alone.. people will drag you down and trying to be the one who "carries" and carries everyone else is hard, my advice > make a team of 5 (+1 sub). [b]That being said, I want to thank you if you read this review and I hope it helped you! [/b] -----------------(you can leave questions or opinions via a comment on this article)---------------- Respects, Alexandru Bălan aka. Colo.

I gotta say, it feels amazing, just pure satisfaction, nothing else. It brought back that feeling from middle school of playing CS 1.6 in the school computer lab behind the teacher's back. Compared to COD 4, 6, 8, 11 and that bullshit Online, BF3 and BF4, Titanfall, CS:GO has much purer competitive gameplay. It doesn't have COD's fast-paced kills and getting killed, it doesn't have Battlefield's 64-player chaos, and it doesn't have Titanfall's explosive mechs, but every single bullet, every grenade, every piece of positioning gets your heart pounding. I want to say this is the essence of FPS competition. The problem with Battlefield is that having that many players on the screen looks great and feels like a battlefield, but on some maps like Caspian Border the match becomes a total mess, and on tight maps like Operation Locker it just turns into pure bullet dumping and firepower suppression. CS:GO perfectly overcomes these flaws, or rather, it perfectly avoids them. It's precisely this core game mechanic that strips away all the messy, flashy elements, making players focus on every little detail in the game and fully explore the fun in it. Actually, I just started playing, so what I'm saying might be a bit one-sided and arbitrary, and my FPS skill is the noobiest of noobs, with still a lot of unknown stuff waiting for me to discover. But one thing's for sure: this game, which inherits the excellent tradition of its predecessor, will definitely become an endless rave for hardcore fans, just like Dota 2. Update 24/11/2016: Now that I'm studying in the UK, matchmaking ping is smooth as silk, but what's killing me is that my rank win rate is probably close to 90%. Because I got placed in Silver, I still haven't climbed out to Gold. What happened to ranking up after winning three games in a row?

translation_en: First of all, I'd like to say that this game is pretty tricky to review because it's very iconic and has a lot of aspects where opinions are all over the place and "good" players are divided (don't pay attention to the little shits who tell you "Best FPS!!!" or "This game is so good!"). I'm going to offer a more or less complete review of the game that will speak to the most hardcore among you, to the real gamers. First, I'd like to talk about the community and cooperative aspect, which is unique in this new installment that follows the evolution of Counter-Strikes. In previous episodes, when you played CSS alone without caring about those around you and just handled weapons all by yourself, well that's over! And yeah, because now we actually discover that CS:GO leans towards a barely explored side of Counter-Strike: cooperation is essential to guarantee optimal gaming pleasure. And on that subject, I have a few important examples to flesh out: This game is not made for lone wolves, arm yourself with friends even if they aren't very good, because if you don't, the internal communication of the team you play with will be weak. Whereas if you end up with your 4 friends on your team, the game will already be that much more enjoyable yet more strategic, cooperation is the keystone of this game. As for the community aspect, frankly I'm disappointed, apart from a few good people, the community is limited to mocking bastards and toddlers with screaming and rage to spare. If you want good social relations, don't go looking in the enemy team. Next, as for the value for money, hats off, 14 Euros I find that very fair and above all it allows people strapped for cash to afford an FPS at a low cost, I'm stoked to see players from developing countries who really had to fight to get this game. (well I'm imagining weird things, I know). On the flip side, we will notice a clear increase in immature players in the community, but also a business side in the sale of weapon skins and other fancies, a knife is nice and all, but not for 150 euros... On the sound side, the soundtrack is really not bad even though it's short and the menu music gets somewhat annoying the more you open the game. They released a whole new concept, which are music kits that replace the in-game ones (even though, hey, by messing with the game files you can put your own custom ones in huehue). Graphics-wise, there's nothing to complain about, it's pretty promising. Different modes that are very good, but once you start competitive mode, especially with friends, it's pretty hard to go back to the other gamemodes, and plus there are really fun community modes too like surf, jailbreak, deathrun, and others... Overall, (lol best joke ever) the game is really enjoyable to play especially with battle buddies even if they each have their own gaming preferences. Another Valve success that draws a crowd and will remain a success following in the CS lineage. Thanks, thanks to this game, I have those little moments of fun that I've never encountered in other games.

translation_en: My personal review of Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. I've been playing CS:GO on and off since the beta. Even though it had the Counter-Strike name slapped on it, to me it was a completely new game.. It had a few similar aspects, but the color palette was different, I couldn't tell enemies apart, and at first it felt really awkward and shooting guns was hard. But after buying a PC back in August and enjoying it with a fresh mindset, there were way more players than I thought and it was actually pretty playable. Also, compared to the previous game (Source), they patched out almost all the exploits(?) and bugs I knew and made it a fair game to play. And I feel like they lowered the barrier to entry a lot. The game got a lot easier compared to its predecessor, and I got the strong feeling it was made for people trying out CS for the first time. (Though I personally find GO harder.) Also, there's this new content in Global Offensive called skins. In fact, it feels like a lot of people play this game just to get good skins. A lot of my friends trade them a lot.. Though I think the default skins are the best, but hey, it's a matter of taste. I respect that~ The Good: 1. I liked the better hit feedback compared to Source. 2. The fact that you can freely customize your viewmodel. 3. Being able to make maps and share them on the Workshop. The Bad: 1. When you queue for quick match, there are no Korean servers so your ping goes over 80. That's why I don't play it often and enjoy 5v5 matches on community servers.^^ Edit: (Community servers like WB or anyone-goes servers have had way too low skill levels for a long time now, can't stand playing on them.) 2. There seem to be quite a few cheaters when you play quick matches. 3. The lack of a microphone receiving volume slider in the sound options. (Edit: Type `voice_scale "0.5"` in the console to lower voice volume. Default: 1.0) (Edit: You can now adjust voice_scale in the sound options) Regardless of all that, I love this game. Thanks for reading my long review. Leave your thoughts. I'll come back to make edits if anything needs changing.

translation_en: Counter-Strike Global Offensive, this game is hard to review... but let's go. This game kind of depends a lot on who's playing it. I have friends who claim this game is the best CS that ever existed, others who say 1.6 / Source is better, and I have friends who keep insisting this is the best game ever made (exaggeration...), but in my opinion, this game is actually good, though it has various problems included, but let's start with the good side, right? This is the only current CS with official servers, so you don't need to spend hours and hours looking for a vanilla server with an acceptable ping, like you used to. There are a lot of Brazilian servers, so ping is finally something we don't need to worry about. It also has new game modes, 2 of which already existed in other CSs, but weren't official, made by the community instead. The game modes are: "Arms Race, Demolition and Deathmatch", and it also has an amazingly well-thought-out rank system (explained at the end of the review), you'll always get matched with people at your level, thus having to give your best to wipe out the enemy team, work as a team and all that. New guns were also added, and others removed. The removed ones are the "M3", the "MP5" and the "Scout", they were replaced by the "Nova", "MP7" and "SSG08". Other guns had changes too, but nothing major, you'll probably only notice the texture change. The other guns added were the "PP-Bizon", "Mag-7", "Sawn-Off", "CZ", "Negev", "R8 Revolver", and new grenades also came along, which are the "Decoy", "Molotov", and the "Incendiary Grenade" (you probably know what these last two are for ^^) and a "Taser" was also added, known as "Zeus", [strike] which is only available in "casual" mode [/strike] (after a recent update, it's available for competitive too), which kills with one shot but you have to be close to the enemy (a knife, but with a bit more range and lethal). These must have been the new things I liked, but let's get to what I didn't like: The community is ruining the game with stupid stuff. Join a Casual with 20 people. At least 17 will be using glitches and ignoring the objective of the game, just wanting to get kills. They're also using only OP weapons, like the P90, which over time became known as "PNojenta" [P-Disgusting], from the sheer rage it caused people here. Not to mention the snipers except for the SSG, the AWP continues to be overpower just like in the other CSs, and the auto-sniper is a living hell. So, playing a game that you'll enjoy is going to be a matter of pure luck if you want to play without glitches, play "clean". This ended up leading to another subject, which is the other thing that irritates me, the OP weapons. The community is only using them because they can only feel good about themselves if they kill someone. Therefore, my rating for the game currently is 7/10. If Valve removed some glitches, it would probably go up to 9/10, or even 10/10, who knows. But with this community playing... I guess it'll have to be 4/10. Don't judge me, I met some incredible people playing, but they were well hidden :P Extras: I'll talk a bit now about the new game modes I mentioned and the differences between "Casual" and "Competitive" mode. [b] Arms Race: [/b] This mode is one of the most fun for me. It's known in other games as "Gungame", so if you're a fan of FPSs, you probably know this mode. But for those who don't know, it's about "getting kills to get a new weapon", it's a team match, 5x5, where upon killing someone from the enemy team, you get the next weapon, until you reach the Golden Knife (weapon exclusive to this game mode), then, by getting a kill with it, you win. So, you'll have a dispute with the enemy team and your own team, so it gets really fun. [b] Demolition: [/b] Another 5x5 game mode, but here it's a bit more serious. It's very similar to the traditional mode, but here, just like in Arms Race mode, players will receive a weapon at the start and will have to get kills to earn the new weapon, however, here, you only get that new weapon in the next round. There are 20 rounds each match, the first team to win 11 rounds wins. [b] Deathmatch: [/b] This game mode is famous. Here there will be two teams with 10 players, where there will also be a dispute between the team. By getting kills, you'll earn points, and at the end of the 10-minute match, whoever has the most points wins. It's quite simple, but fun. [b] Classic: [/b] The famous classic Counter-Strike mode, whether it's planting the bomb or rescuing hostages, is for me always the most fun game mode. However, in CS:GO, Classic mode is split into 2 game modes, "Casual" and "Competitive". [b] Casual: [/b] Casual mode is a 10x10, where the game is pretty... casual (explains the name), since there are 10 players on each team, you can join and leave the game at any time and it won't make a difference to your rank (I'll explain this "rank" later), Friendly Fire is turned off (you can't deal damage to your teammates), Team Collision is turned off (you don't "bump" into your teammates, you walk "through" them) and the maximum number of rounds is 15, thus, the first team to win eight rounds wins. [b] Competitive: [/b] Here the game gets more serious. Here there are five players for each team, Friendly Fire is turned on (you can hit your teammates and even kill them), Team Collision is turned on (you can "bump" into your teammates), the maximum number of rounds is 30, thus, the team that wins 16 rounds first wins. Here, you can't just join and leave whenever you want. There's the "Match Making" system, where you'll search for a match, and the game will search for nine other players, and everyone will have to play from the start, and if you leave, you'll get a temporary ban from competitive mode. Having fewer players and more time (it can last up to 90 minutes), communication with the team will be essential, and if one person dies, the team will already have a gigantic disadvantage. The rewards for kills are twice as high and it has the rank system. [b] Rank: [/b] After winning 10 competitive matches, you'll receive your rank, which defines your "skill level", and you'll get matched with teams with the same rank as you, as I explained at the beginning of this review, so, the game won't be easy nor all that hard. That is, in Competitive mode, which is the best one, it's the serious CS. [b] Catchphrases: [/b] In life, admitting your imperfection is fundamental to achieving perfection. In Counter-Strike, it's no different. Getting good at CS isn't about fun, it's not about skill, but rather a unique and time-consuming process of learning the plays and maps. Discover your mistakes, deal with them, and if you lose, instead of blaming your team, see how you could have helped, accept that you share some of the blame, and always try to improve. [b] Good Luck, Have Fun [/b]

translation_en: Counter-Strike fans are a special breed. Many of them still argue about whether 1.5 was better than 1.6, let alone a complete remake. The last attempt to replace the morally outdated 1.6 happened back in 2004 and pretty much bombed: Counter-Strike: Source looked great and bragged about realistic physics, but esports players fiercely rejected it. They bitched that running felt off and grenades didn't fly right. Source and GO are separated by a whole eight years. Valve had plenty of time to weigh things, figure it out, and craft a proper remake where everything would be right. That's why the core concept in GO didn't budge even a millimeter: two teams of five (or more) people, terrorists and counter-terrorists. The secret to Counter-Strike's popularity is its simplicity (though there's always room to hone your skills), so it would be stupid to expect skills, leveling up, and drivable vehicles in GO. Buy your guns at the start of the round and run out to kill the enemies—it doesn't get any simpler than that! There isn't even a right-click ironsight aiming mode: we shoot on the move, old-school style. There are now four main modes—an official record for CS. The old-school pastimes of «Hold or rescue hostages» and «plant or defuse the bomb» were joined by the ex-mod GunGame, which is now called "Arms Race." The second newcomer is "Demolition." This is a two-minute blitzkrieg for two teams. One tries to blow up a key site, while the other stops them. Skirmishes take place on very small maps packed with hiding spots and camper positions. These locations are painfully similar to multiplayer maps from Modern Warfare. And the action's pacing feels like the Domination mode from Unreal Tournament. Except there's only one control point on the map—each team has to get to it first and hold it. Most of the weapons were carried over to CS intact, and some obsolete models were swapped out for something more trendy (the Steyr TMP and KM.45 are gone, the MP9 and P2000 are in). All the firearms are licensed this time around, and the Kalashnikov stopped masquerading as the vague CV-47. 27. Along with the AK from Russia, they brought in the Bizon submachine gun (PP-19). The maps got tweaked for better balance, and the guns don't seem to have any glaring imbalances—for every "terrorist" argument, the counter-terrorists have a worthy response ready. There are flaws, though: for instance, the terrorists' hold-up shotgun is way worse than the automatic MAG-7, which can reach enemies even at medium ranges. As usual, the balance is slowly being tweaked with patches. GO refused to bow to trends: there is no leveling system outside of matches, and both sides start every skirmish on equal footing. Money in CS is earned by killing enemies and through tactical maneuvers (planting the bomb or rescuing hostages). At the start of the round, you use your blood money to buy weapons, armor, and grenades. Among the latter, some hot new items make their debut: the Molotov cocktail and incendiary grenades, which make it easy to block off corridors and set careless fighters on fire. Added to those are decoy grenades that mimic weapon sounds—which can be useful in certain situations, since experienced players often rely on audio cues. On top of that, there's the Zeus x27 taser, which kills at point-blank range with a single hit. The only catch is that it's single-use. If you miss, the taser's gone for nothing, and the operator is left empty-handed. For a fraction of a second, but still... Online, that kind of delay is all an enemy needs, so the usefulness of the "Zeus" is pretty questionable for now. On the bright side, dying to it is almost more humiliating than dying to a knife. This new installment of Counter-Strike hardly breaks with tradition. But even so, "loyalty to tradition" is GO's main feature. That's both its greatest strength and its biggest flaw. Essentially, we got the exact same CS: Source with polished graphics, physics, and integration with current Steam services. Plus—updated maps and an expanded arsenal. The developers combined modern tech with nostalgia for the old-school CS, but they didn't bother inventing anything fundamentally new.

translation_en: Counter-Strike: Global Offensive takes the competitive FPS experience a step further. Just like the other games in the series, every weapon, map, and the economy system in the game are perfectly balanced. You have to think about every move you make and spray carefully, and the slightest reckless move can cause you to lose the match. Alongside the competitive mode, there are also casual fun game modes like casual, hostage, and arms race. But the competitive mode is pure madness. Following in the footsteps of the previous games in the series, Global Offensive fulfills its mission worthily. Having adopted simplicity as its mission, it has also embraced the core idea of "easy to learn, hard to master," as foreigners say. Of course, this has its pros and cons. When we evaluate it overall, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive more than fulfills its duty and frankly screams "buy me" with its $15 price tag, especially if you catch it on sale, it's just icing on the cake. If we were to give an average rating: 1- Sounds 9/10 2- Graphics 7/10 3- Animations 7/10 4- Physics engine 8/10 5- Playability 9.5/10 And overall, the game gets a 9.5 out of 10 from me.

translation_en: I decided to redo my review because I think the game I have by far the most hours in on Steam deserves a somewhat more comprehensive evaluation. Unfortunately, this comes with a language problem, and since this review will be a bit longer than all the ones I've written so far and my English isn't quite 100%, I've decided to write it in my native language and I apologize to all foreigners for this (yeah, I know they won't translate it anyway). Counter Strike: Global Offensive is, in my opinion, one of the best games on Steam in terms of price-to-replayability. You can spend hundreds of hours in it and it still won't get boring. After all, take a look at the community yourself and you'll find that the overwhelming majority of people have a lot of hours played compared to other games. If anyone is interested in the exact number, according to data from 2014, CS:GO is the ninth most played game on Steam by hours played (source: [url]http://arstechnica.com/gaming/2014/04/introducing-steam-gauge-ars-reveals-steams-most-popular-games/2/[/url]). The investment in the game also pays off quickly, depending on the playtime and the user's trading skills. As a reward for played matches, you get weapon cases that can be sold on the market and thus get some euros back into your account. New case collections are gradually released, and new items can be sold for a decent price in the first few days. On the first day, maybe even for 2-3€, which means the game can pay for itself with just one sold case. On sale, it can be bought for around 3€, which is a real steal for that price. I already touched on the topic of weapon skins here, and so before I get to the actual gameplay, I'd like to explain what it's all about. These are basically graphics on weapons that can be bought on the market, dropped after playing games, or obtained from cases that are unlocked with keys that must be bought in-game. The principle is similar to Team Fortress 2, for example. The appearance of weapons can also be customized with stickers and the like. However, it is important to emphasize that these are purely cosmetic changes, and as for the gameplay itself, they do not give players any advantages, meaning the game is definitely not pay-to-win. As for weapons, both teams have a choice of many weapons, which may differ between teams, but have similar power. The weapon arsenal is gradually expanded; since the game's release, additions include the M4A1-S with a silencer or our Czech classic, the automatic CZ75. For newbies, I will elaborate that by teams I mean terrorists and counter-terrorists. The game, like previous installments, includes two basic game modes. In the first, terrorists try to plant the bomb at designated sites and then detonate it, and counter-terrorist units try to prevent them. The second is the classic hostage rescue. This depends on the game maps, which are mostly specially created for individual modes. These game modes can be played either in Casual mode or Competitive mode. As the name suggests, competitive mode is a matchmaking mode and determines the player's rank. Rank is basically an indicator of a player's skill, and based on ranks, players are matched to servers in competitive matches. The player is therefore sure that they are playing against people who are of similar skill. For an idea, here is a link to an overview of all ranks: [url]http://cloud-4.steampowered.com/ugc/1117158766046342923/31403BEFD00407DF9D16EBDDE500EB7FE32E18B3/[/url] Competitive mode is the most played game mode, but it also has some negatives. The main one I would name is the community, which generally I cannot say much positive about compared to the communities of other games. I often encounter players who know nothing about teamwork, which is the absolute cornerstone of success in competitive mode and you can't win without it. Frequently, these are people who don't understand English, which is an important feature for playing comp. mode. Teams are often international and players communicate with each other mostly in English. Basics like telling the team where and how many enemies are located should be learned by everyone over time, because uncommunicative players are generally not very popular. Another problem is with so-called griefers, which are players who intentionally ruin the game, but fortunately there aren't that many of them. Significantly more are cheaters; they pop up in the game like mushrooms after rain, especially after sales when they can buy a new copy of the game at a favorable price after being banned on their previous account. The only defense against them is to report them, which can be done through the in-game scoreboard. Likewise, you can commend a player who willingly helped you or led the team well. Players who have many commends from the community can watch demo recordings of reported cheaters, express their opinion on whether the given player was actually cheating or not, and thus help improve the community of the game. However, if you don't feel like playing serious matches where you have to communicate, or just don't have time for a full competitive match that can drag on for up to 90 minutes, CS:GO offers many other modes. Apart from Casual, which I already mentioned and is basically the same as Competitive, only maps rotate faster and the player can leave the match at any time without a penalty, there are also Deathmatch modes where you play for points gained by getting kills. Each weapon is scored differently based on how hard it is to get a kill with, so the most points are awarded for the weakest weapons. Furthermore, there is Arms Race, where to win you need to record a kill with every weapon in the game, and Demolition, which is somewhat similar to Casual mode. I would recommend these game modes especially to beginners before they dive into competitive matches. Through the game, you can also watch pro matches, and the main advantage compared to regular streams is that you can switch to any player from both teams, eliminating the need to watch just the player who is currently being streamed. Of course, you do lose the commentary, which is usually present especially during major tournaments. By watching tournament events, you can also get expensive items that are randomly dropped to viewers. Now I am coming to the very conclusion. I definitely recommend the game. It doesn't have many negatives, except for the community—which, with a few exceptions, isn't a very bright spot of the game—and also some updates from Valve that tend to make the game worse. However, developers are willing to revert updates after community feedback, like recently after the sniper scope change, which received very negative feedback. The best game mode is, as I already mentioned, Competitive, which is an obvious choice if you have a few capable friends. So that's all, I hope you liked the review. Any feedback is welcome so I know whether to redo my other reviews into Czech and elaborate on them a bit more. See you on the battlefield.

translation_en: Counter-Strike.. a game that is a worldwide phenomenon. Practically everyone has heard of it and has played a few matches in one of its various versions. Unstoppable success yesterday, today and tomorrow.. you can bet on it. A success that expands into championships that are gaining more and more strength and showing that electronic games have a place as a sport. Such is its popularity that one of its championships was broadcast live on SporTV. For those who don't know it, a brief summary is enough: a first-person shooter game where a Counter-Terrorist (CT) team tries to inhibit the attack of the Terrorist (TR) team, whose mission is to plant a bomb or keep hostages, and the CT team must disarm the bomb or rescue hostages. Simple. But much deeper when it comes to the gameplay involved in a match. The current version, Global Offensive, released in 2012, has constant updates and, from time to time, brings a lot of new stuff for the players. It features game modes to please most players, from the most tactical ones who want a serious and competitive game, even to those who just want to shoot around and have fun, to pass the time, without much commitment: [list] [*][b]Arms Race:[/b] a very fun CT versus TR version where whoever gets the most kills the fastest wins. Starting with powerful weapons and, as you eliminate enemies, you change to a less powerful weapon until your last weapon is the Golden Knife, and if you manage to kill an enemy with it, you win the match. [*][b]Demolition:[/b] the two teams face each other with the objective of planting/disarming the bomb on a much smaller map than usual, for faster and more dynamic matches. Where, for each enemy you eliminate, you get better weapons in the next Round. [*][b]Deathmatch:[/b] CT versus TR, whoever gets the most kills the fastest, reaching the highest score by the end of the time. But there is only one winner. Great for practicing your skills with several different weapons. Since you kill and die stupidly fast. The objective is to get the highest score. [*][b]Casual:[/b] casual matches, where the two CT and TR teams face each other until there are no survivors left from a certain team, or until the bomb is defused in case the TR team planted it. Also, there are phases where the objective of the CTs is to rescue hostages from the hands of the terrorists. In this mode, players already start with kits and vests, and friendly fire is disabled. [*][b]Competitive:[/b] the same style of play as the casual match. However, friendly fire is enabled and you must buy vests and kits. They are 5 versus 5 teams, where the entire match can last more than 1h30min (the first team to score 16 matches wins), with fierce rounds that require you to be serious to participate. The matches are leveled according to your current Rank, and as you win, you end up in increasingly experienced teams. There are 18 Ranks, from Silver to Global Elite. Likewise, you can lose matches and drop in rank. Leaving an ongoing competitive match repeatedly generates punishments (being kicked or for abandoning), depending on the frequency, you can stay 30min, 2h, 24h or 7 days without being able to play competitive matches. [*][b]Custom:[/b] This type depends exclusively on custom servers made by the players themselves, where they can find a range of possibilities and very unusual maps. [/list] Whatever your playstyle, know that you will never have a match equal to the previous one. Each match is a different one that will involve tactics, skill, luck, and team cooperation. Every kind of emotion is guaranteed. There will be days when you'll be playing very well, others, when you'll always be at the bottom of the scoreboard (there's no denying that). And, when playing with random people, you'll always have a chance to end up with a nice team, but just as well, the chance to end up with horrible people.. and I don't just mean SKILL, in MANNERS too (you can imagine the kind of characters that show up, right?). Besides the so famous [i]Cheaters[/i], huh!? Unfortunately it's common to bump into players who use cheats to get ahead. It will be rare times that a [i]cheater[/i] is banned during the match. After reports, subsequent analyses will be made to assess whether the accused is one or not, and then, the [i]VAC BAN[/i] is applied. And still there will be those who you swear are cheaters, but no, they're just guys having a lucky day, or who are really skilled. We also have the Community Market to mention, which moves an absurd amount of money with the famous weapon [i]Skins[/i] that the game promotes. They are weapons that range from a few cents to even a few thousand reals. No joke. At the end of each match, depending on the server, there is a possibility of random [i]drops[/i] of cases for all players involved and even some weapon [i]skins[/i]. From these cases, by opening them with a specific key (which you have to buy), if you are very lucky, you can get a valued [i]skin[/i] to show off in your matches or sell and make a few bucks in your Steam wallet. [b]But one thing is more than certain:[/b] you are going to need a lot of patience here and there when playing this game. Even those who just log in to have fun. Everyone wants to have fun, but everyone wants to win too! This is the game that will amuse you and piss you off, satisfy and dissatisfy you, make you proud and ashamed, suffer and practice "[i]bullying[/i]", be called "[i]noob trash easy[/i]" when you lose and "[i]noob trash hacker[/i]" when you win, make friendships and enmities, take your money and give you some change (depending on luck), make you quit but you'll come back sooner or later, because very few will manage to stop playing... yeah, there's no way around it.. translation_en: If there is one thing Counter-Strike has stood out for so much and continues to be so recognized for, it's for being a 100% skill-based game. There is no room for the luck factor here and the game always offers the exact same tools to all players, so in the end, the ones who know how to play best almost always win. Forget about any modern FPS and all their innovations. Here you won't find any XP progression system to get increasingly destructive upgrades or pinpoint-accurate weapons that give you an advantage just for having played longer than someone who just started. Here, hours played translate into more "real" experience; we are better because by playing more we've learned its mechanics, how the weapons work, and the strategic spots on the map, not because a system hands us artificial advantages. In essence, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is the good old Counter-Strike 1.6, with updated graphics to adapt to what's demanded nowadays and with a few minor tweaks and changes that we'll discuss later. But at the end of the day, what we have is the exact same game as always. Valve knows very well what they're doing, and altering the original formula probably would have resulted in complaints from the fans, who despite the years still want the same old formula, which by the way, hasn't aged at all and is still in great shape. For newcomers, if you plan to step into this battlefield and you're coming from other current FPS games like Call of Duty, the best thing you can do is forget everything you've learned in them. Here you shoot from the hip and if you want to aim you can only do it with weapons that have scopes, there is no automatic health regeneration, so all the damage we take is permanent, and there are no respawns, so if we get killed we won't get back into the action until the next round. Basically, the game asks us to join either the terrorist or the counter-terrorist team. Depending on the map we're on, the terrorists will have to plant a bomb and detonate it or the counter-terrorists will have to rescue hostages. All of this within a set time limit. To win we either have to complete the objective or kill the entire enemy team. Easy, simple to understand, and with a gameplay depth that has defined an era. If we run around shooting like crazy and expecting to land a few bullets, we'll end up dead over and over again. If we want to survive we'll have to constantly keep an eye on the radar, play as a team with the rest of our teammates, know that if we hold the knife we run faster, set up ambushes to catch people by surprise, be aware that when we crouch we improve our accuracy, calculate very well when to reload, etc. In addition, each round we will earn money, whether by getting kills, winning, losing, rescuing hostages, or defusing bombs. This will be used to buy weapons and equipment in a shop (which now features a radial layout to make it easier to use with a controller) located at each team's spawn point. This adds a certain strategic value, since we'll have to decide what to spend our cash on each round. Furthermore, if we die, we lose everything we've acquired, which makes surviving each assault even more valuable and pushes us not to do crazy things and to measure our movements carefully.

translation_en: [b]A different kind of shooter.[/b] That's how you'd have to define Counter-Strike: Global Offensive in the current First Person Shooter landscape. And why is that? It's simple, CS:GO isn't just any Battlefield or Call of Duty, it's an FPS where skill and reflexes matter a whole lot more and where you'll need quite a few hours to handle yourself decently in a public match. These are some of the things that set it apart from the competition: [i]AIM[/i]: In this game there's no aim assist, you can't aim down sights (except with snipers), everything depends on your reflexes and the skill you have to hit headshots or chest shots so you don't have to fire multiple bullets to kill an enemy. [i]RECOIL[/i]: Realistic weapon recoil, you won't be able to spray a burst of, say, 6 bullets with an assault rifle because most of them won't go where you're aiming. Plus, everything matters when shooting: if you move, jump, crouch, or are on a ladder, every situation is different. If we compare recoil in CS:GO and CoD, we could say that in CoD the weapons are static and very easy to control. [i]HEALTH[/i]: This is perhaps one of the most important points; in any other FPS you get shot, you hide, and you come out unscathed. In CS:GO every mistake has a price. Health never regenerates, and that'll make you think twice before leaving cover. Those 3 aspects, which are fundamental pillars in an FPS, completely change the gameplay and make CS:GO a pretty damn good game that I would undoubtedly recommend to anyone who likes first-person shooters because, to me, it's a MUST-PLAY of the genre. 8.5/10.

translation_en: [i]Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is my absolute favorite game. In this review, I will go into detail on many points why buying this game is worth it. However, this review is aimed more at those who want to start with CS:GO and haven't played CSS or CS 1.6 before. I can't explain the differences between the parts myself or say what all has changed (except for the graphics, of course).[/i] [b][u]Introduction[/u][/b] First of all, I have to say that CS:GO is not a casual game and you therefore have to spend a few hours with the game to become a "good" player, so to speak. A small tip: if you've decided to buy the game after this review, play against bots first and get familiar with the weapon recoil, because just blindly holding down the trigger at a target won't lead to success... [b][u]Game Modes[/u][/b] CS:GO offers the following game modes in total: Hostage Rescue, Bomb Defusal (both in Casual and Competitive versions), Arms Race, Demolition, and Deathmatch. All modes are a lot of fun, but long-term you'll be playing Hostage Rescue and/or Bomb Defusal. In both modes, and actually in all the others too, the core is the fight between Terrorists and Counter-Terrorists, basically good versus evil. In Bomb Defusal, the terrorists have to plant a bomb at so-called "sites", and in Hostage Rescue, the CTs (Counter-Terrorists) have to rescue the hostages who are guarded by the terrorists. A classic game of cat and mouse that can hook you for hours. Simple but good is the motto here. [b][u]Teamplay[/u][/b] Unlike in other first-person shooters (at least most of them), CS doesn't depend on the individual, but on the team. Teamwork is everything! Anyone who doesn't play as a team, but explores the map on their own, won't see any success. Communication is key! That's why a headset is a must to max out the fun, but it gets especially funny when you know your mates (teammates) and can wipe out the enemy team together and take the victory. [b][u]Not for Everyone[/u][/b] As you can see, CS isn't a game for just a few hours, so the price of 15 euros is definitely worth it! You don't even need to wait for a sale at this price. Despite the high praise, you have to say that CS isn't for everyone either. You need to be very resistant to frustration, because defeats and quick deaths at the beginning are the order of the day, but you'll be all the more hyped when you see your learning curve going up, albeit very slowly, but better than nothing at all. No pain, no gain, I'd say at this point. [b][u]Conclusion[/u][/b] In my opinion, you'll have fun with this game, and with that, I wish you a lot of fun in your battles in Counter-Strike.

translation_en: Hello. In this review I'm going to highlight my own experiences that I've gathered in this game. When I got the game, downloaded and installed it, I found myself in a completely new game mode, since Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is my very first first-person shooter ever. So, started the game up and I see a pretty manageable game menu, except for 1-2 points that I, as a total beginner, had to ask about first. For example, as a beginner I didn't know right away that a Competitive match is something like a ranked game and that you can only enter your clan tag via a Steam group. However, these are such tiny points that they really aren't worth mentioning. So, with the game now open and everything adjusted to my satisfaction after some settings, my first game could actually start. So if you play a competitive game at a time of day when the servers are well populated and you don't have any special map requests, the queue time is usually less than a minute. 90% of the time, the team you get is roughly around your rank – so either unranked or pretty much in your league. Rarely, mostly in the evenings, it can also happen that you get people who are below or above your rank – simply because the right players can't be found, but somehow a game has to happen naturally. When you finally find a game, on your selected map or a random map that just happened to be found, you are in the game after a short loading time. During the loading screen you still see a tip on the left side and on the right side you find a brief overview of the map – which I think is very practical since the maps were completely foreign to me. When you click into the game, you can buy all weapons via the buy menu during the warm-up phase, which lasts about 2 minutes. The in-game money is capped at 16,000 and that's also the amount you enter the warm-up phase with so you can buy weapons. Then the game begins and because the controls are very simple and you can configure everything yourself (crosshair, keybinds, mouse sensitivity, etc.), you get the hang of the controls very quickly. The engine is also very easy to handle, so you have a totally ordinary first-person shooter from a first-person perspective – another one isn't possible either, which would probably ruin the whole game. That's about as much as I can say about the game. It's easy to understand, is a ton of fun, and handles well. What I also think is really great, besides the option for voice chat, is the ability to communicate via radio commands. That way you can let the others know what's going on even if you don't have a microphone. That's also quite easy to understand and really easy to follow thanks to the position callouts. What also turned out well since the last patch is the ability to assign yourself a unique color on the minimap – although it's not very advantageous that colors can also appear twice, so I think they could work on that a bit more. Otherwise, though, this simplifies communication, especially when there are Asian or Russian names in your team, for example, instead of the name you can just say "Green" or "Blue". So much for Competitive and "In-game". If I had to mention something else, it would immediately occur to me that, win or lose, by means of a random generator, everyone involved in the game gets a gimmick from the game in the form of skins, weapon cases, or other little things that contribute to the customization of the game. I think I've talked enough. If you have any questions, feel free to ask them. If you found this post helpful, I'd appreciate some feedback. :)

[u]PROS[/u] - Great graphics - Great gameplay - Huge player base - Great weapon balancing - In-game VoIP for better team coordination - Low price [u]CONS[/u] - Quite demanding to run on low-to-mid-range PCs - Hard to get into the game, especially if you run into experienced players - The experience on official servers isn't always positive (lag and, rarely, server crashes that can lead to a temporary ban of your game account) - Some weapon skins (e.g., equipped with StatTrak) can only be won by opening Cases with paid keys In conclusion, Counter-Strike is a great game that's well worth its modest price. More information: [url=http://blog.counter-strike.net/] Official Website [/url] [i]- Recommended for those who often play with friends -[/i]

translation_en: [b]I get asked from time to time whether people should buy "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive". I personally really like it, but it's not for everyone. Anyone who has the spare cash and just wants to try it out is strongly advised to do so. Anyone who is unsure should think about it first. That's why I'm taking a different approach in this review:[/b] [u][b]Who is CS:GO NOT for?[/b][/u] [i]1) Level-uppers and perk lovers[/i] There are no unlockable weapons, no perks, or variable weapon skills. You buy your gear together every round and can do so from the very first minute of the game. It's not for everyone, but it guarantees a very balanced skill level with a focus on your own abilities. Small downside: There are weapon skins that let you "personalise" your own weapons. You either find these randomly at the end of a game or can buy them in the community market (or trade them with other players). There are also recurring season passes, so-called "Operations". Leveling up is somewhat possible there. [i]2) Lone wolves.[/i] It's a genuinely tactical team shooter. If you want to have fun for a bit longer and more professionally, you need to be able to play in a team. That means: Help your team by calling out where you saw enemies. Your money isn't your money, it's the team's money. If you have enough cash and someone asks you if you can buy them a weapon (obviously doesn't mean a blank check for everything), then do it. Hold the position you've been entrusted with. You lose as a team and you win as a team. - Period! [i]3) People who care endlessly about their K/D.[/i] This actually ties into #2. It's a team shooter and no matter how many enemies you take down, what ultimately counts after the rounds is whether you won the most or not. Your K/D has no bearing on that (holding positions is way more important than just running around fragging). [i]4) People who only want to play a single quick round within a certain timeframe.[/i] Counter-Strike has always been defined by its round-based nature. You get money round after round and have to, for example, either plant or defuse a bomb (rescue or guard hostages, etc.) within a time limit. Not everyone likes that, but it increases the tactical quality. [i]5) Quickscopers and SMG snipers.[/i] Sure, exceptions prove the rule, but unlike in many genre competitors, you shouldn't go into close quarters with a sniper rifle or snipe around with a submachine gun here. Why? It rarely ever works out, since weapon range and recoil play a massive role. [i]6) Realism lovers.[/i] "The crosshair doesn't sway with the sniper rifle - totally unrealistic!!" Yes, that's true, and there's also no aiming down sights. But in my opinion, the point here isn't to be the most realistic shooter (especially since that's never possible anyway, and all the ones that try are still so wildly unrealistic in many places because otherwise it just wouldn't be fun to play). It's about your skill, your team, and balance. ________________ So, anyone who has read this far might just have wanted to check if they fit the bill. Anyone who hasn't been put off yet can look forward to an exciting team shooter (the way you sometimes sit in front of your PC when the bomb is planted and it's down to a 1vs1... ;)), which includes a few nice, classic game modes (Bomb-Defuse, Hostage Scenario, Arms Race [get a kill, get the next weapon], Deathmatch, Battle Royale, 2vs2, and tons of community servers with various special features) and runs on practically any PC. It doesn't come with a tacked-on, lazy single-player campaign, it's cheap, suits casual and competitive players alike, and has a huge community. [b]So it's a recommendation from me, with the caveat that not everyone will like it! :-)[/b]

translation_en: Counter-Strike never dies! Since the late 90s, this old Half-Life mod has evolved particularly well, eventually becoming one of the most played online franchises. Just like that. But awards aside, is Global Offensive the worthy successor to the series? Counter-Strike: Global Offensive While the Counter-Strike community is more than flourishing, it's also aging. It's rare for newcomers today to be more attracted to a CS 1.6 than a Battlefield 3. It must be said that those big globs of pixels meant to represent blood might shock novices. Thus, Valve is trying to relaunch this formidable machine and recreate a buzz around its series with Global Offensive, going all-in: trying to seduce console players in addition to PC gamers. If PC gamers are already widening their eyes at this "terrible blasphemy," they can rest assured, no real concessions were made and they will find their bearings very quickly. Phew, didn't even have time to plant my bomb... And since we're talking about potential novices, let's not forget to mention the basic rules of Counter-Strike just in case a few of them are reading these lines. Terrorists and Counter-Terrorists face off on a closed map according to different game modes. Unsurprisingly, we find the great classics, where you either have to save hostages or plant / defame a bomb. However, other types of matches are available to us, notably Arms Race, in which you have to kill your opponents with almost every weapon in the game, one by one. Every time you get a frag, you move straight on to the next weapon, until you get the famous golden knife. Anyone who kills with this golden blade instantly wins the match! Note that you can knock an opponent down a level by killing them with your default knife, which is always rewarding. Sure, regulars will recognize a mod that already existed in CS, but you have to admit it's pretty thrilling, especially since instant respawn and map size spice up the action. Nevertheless, we can regret the possibility for team members to camp the opponent's spawn point, because even if you have a period of invincibility at each respawn, you aren't safe from getting peppered in the back after three seconds. Arms Race matches are sometimes full of suspense. The other mode making its "appearance" is Demolition, which looks like a classic match where you can't buy anything. At the start of each round, you get a new weapon if you got a frag in the previous game, along with grenade(s) if you pulled off a multikill. But the end goal remains winning the round, either by killing the entire opposing team, or by planting / defusing a bomb. Just like Arms Race, the maps are very small and it's not uncommon for first blood to be spilled in less than ten seconds. In short, these two modes seem entirely suited to the series' usual gameplay by offering action-packed matches, which should also delight e-sports fans. Besides, there's no doubt that Valve designed the game with this in mind from the start. That doesn't mean novices have been forgotten, with the direct inclusion of playable offline matches with bots or even a Training mode that lets us use a small panel of weapons in dedicated exercises. There's even a Casual Classic mode with a few quirks like the absence of friendly fire and player collision, for example. The training mode might help newbies get the hang of the game. On the other hand, when it comes to gameplay, old-school vets will be happy to find old-school handling, which undoubtedly won't please all newcomers. No ridiculous aim assist, but rather old-school FPS sensations that are always a pleasure, with demanding recoil and a crosshair that does the absolute minimum. It probably sits somewhere between CSS and CS 1.6, and there's no denying that a certain level of skill will inevitably be required for those who want a positive K/D ratio. While this is a plus for those who have been playing the series for years, we can still question the lack of evolution we can't help but notice. Sure, you can also tell yourself "if it ain't broke, don't fix it," but sometimes it feels more like a big update than a new game. Since it's still sold for around fifteen euros, we could have expected more new features. The same goes for the weapons, among which brand new ones are rare. In fact, we mostly get recent versions of weapons that already existed, like the M4A1 turning into the M4A4. We do note the presence of a few extra submachine guns, a taser, and decoy and incendiary grenades. Unfortunately, in classic modes, everything suggests that the stars of previous installments will still make up 95% of players' choices. Too bad, as that was a flaw that needed fixing. Classic maps have however benefited from a few tweaks. Regarding console controller handling, we notice the non-negligible addition of a quick-turn button, even if the lack of nimbleness compared to the keyboard/mouse combo is felt. Demolition mode maps are very small. Whatever happens, there's no doubt that the future of this Global Offensive looks bright, especially since modders will be able to have a field day on PC. From what we've seen on console, the servers seem stable and lag didn't seem frequent to us, even if complaints on the forums are worth noting. However, even if fans show up and it will undoubtedly still be played in a few years, the series' stagnation over more than ten years is unfortunate for a title sold for around fifteen euros. The question we can ask ourselves is this: would Global Offensive have had the same success if it wasn't a Counter-Strike? Not sure... SCORES Graphics 13/20 We suspected it, this isn't where Counter-Strike: Global Offensive intended to bare its teeth. The upside is that it will run on old PCs without stressing the components. On the other hand, some animations look straight out of hell. Console versions are probably a tiny bit worse, but broadly speaking, it's the same deal. Gameplay 16/20 Pure Counter-Strike, no doubt about it. The proposed game modes take full advantage of the snappy gameplay and you're right in the thick of an old-school FPS. That said, we don't really see any elements that would encourage CS 1.6 or even CSS players to leave their domain for Global Offensive. Lifespan 18/20 An already present community, modes with very different concepts, gameplay leaning towards competition, Global Offensive will still be around for several years, there's no doubt about that. Soundtrack 12/20 Efforts clearly weren't put into the soundscape during the design of Global Offensive, and it shows. A few new voices and jingles here and there but nothing mind-blowing. Let's just say you shouldn't play Battlefield 3 right before, that's all. - Overall Score 15/20

[/h1] [code] Valve is like a Norse god who fucked up big time and delighted bored mortals with his gifts, but over time transformed from a giver and muse into some kind of tempting tyrant, attracting the newly arrived generation exclusively with gambling and empty promises. And I'm only talking about the persona of the developer, the hearth keeper, the judge of a tight-knit community, and all that kind of stuff. If you've played competitive games from this studio hard, you understand me perfectly. [/code] It was an unexpected encounter, but I no longer plan to log into Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, so with this review I am putting a definitive end to our relationship. The game attracted me for a long time with item collecting, and later turned into something resembling a job altogether, but when each of your skins exceeds a hundred thousand rubles in price and there's nowhere higher to go, your eyes are suddenly opened to how pathetic the whole situation is. The game stopped bringing any pleasure, and every subsequent login is exclusively tied to being a slave to your own habits. Closing the personal stories, let's move on to the game itself. Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a first-person competitive shooter that offers players a pretty large selection of diverse matches. And there really is a lot to play here, because under the hood of the shooter fit a battle royale, two-player duels, classic team deathmatches with bomb defusal and hostage rescue, a bunch of mini-games each of which pulls off being a self-sufficient game, and if even that's not enough, you can find third-party entertainment on custom servers, drowning in a countless variety of modifications and sheer madness. Surfing, hide and seek, obstacle courses, boss fights, what isn't there, folks, people have long known how to entertain themselves. If we look at the classic game modes, Global Offensive almost completely copies its predecessors, offering players a familiar selection of maps, a rich arsenal of firearms which, by the way, has once again split into two factions, allowing you to buy a certain rifle only for the chosen side, which leads to a constant search for looted weapons after a battle. In other words, comrades, if you've played Counter-Strike even once, you'll figure out the local skirmishes right away. The new weapons, grenades, and economy might surprise a beginner, but you get used to it quickly. [h1] Run, you poor bastards! [/h1] As for the cons, everything is clear here without me. The game was switched to a free-to-play model, thereby giving a chance to dishonest crooks who use all sorts of programs. There really are a lot of cheaters in the game, and besides them, there are classic morons who intentionally ruin the game for their own team. And this happens so often that it has already become a sort of norm for the competitive part of the game. By the way, folks, since we brought up the competitive mode with personal rank leveling, it's worth mentioning the whole horde of boosters who drop down to lower ranks just to smash less nimble players. All of this is deeply off-putting, drives you up the wall, and ultimately breeds a disgust for the game. [list] [*] A black hole for your time and life. [*] A casino for the gullible, a springboard for the enterprising. [*] The game is free now. [/list] Counter-Strike: Global Offensive can't be called a forgotten project. The game is constantly updated, new maps are added, old ones are modernized, they experiment with modes and pamper players with events that are fully capable of padding the pockets of diligent fighters. And while conditional Team Fortress 2 has been lying in a corner and mournfully dying off for the past few years, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is only just beginning its journey. Why beat around the bush, right? I don't regret the time spent, because I cashed out a truly insane amount of money from the game. At this point in time, the game has stopped bringing pleasure, so think hard before logging in, friends, do you really need it? Even if you've played a thousand hours, or maybe even more, just think about the alternatives. How many wonderful games, books, and movies you can soak in instead of another match with irritating personalities. translation_en: How to describe Counter-Strike 2? - It took everything CS:GO had and improved every single aspect. Now smokes aren't just "a static barrier," they're volumetric, so you can shoot through them and see small holes to peek through, and throwing an HE grenade clears it for 1 second (just enough to get a kill). - The Subtick system is way better than the old 64-tick; shots actually register a lot more than before and give you that satisfying feeling when hits land. - The new world ranking system is phenomenal! If you have a really good team, you can really stand out in the scene because of your rank, and I'll tell you more: lots of new pro players are going to get signed because of this leaderboard. - Aside from that, there's the new per-map skill group system, meaning that to be Global Elite you really gotta grind and dedicate yourself to every single map, instead of just being a Global on Mirage alone. - The anti-cheat system has also been improved. Now if someone is cheating, the match is automatically cancelled, and if one of your teammates gets banned for cheating while you're in the same lobby, you end up losing rank, making matches much fairer. - The graphics are way better than before, and everything we complained was missing or needed changing in CS:GO has been improved and fixed in this game. This is a game for life, whether you want to play casually with your friends or compete to make it big.

translation_en: [b]tl; dr:[/b] It's simply the best competitive shooter out there. [*] Unlike other titles with yearly releases that divide the community, CS:GO has weekly updates that keep the game fresh. You can be confident investing in a game that will have support for years and years. [*] The community actively participates by creating maps or weapon skins. Not only that, the best work is included in season passes and creators are rewarded from their sales. [*] Competitive matchmaking that tests you against people of your own skill level. [*] Mod support. [*] CS:GO has one of the best spectator modes I've ever used. Whether you're watching highlights of your past matches, your friends' matches, or live professional players' matches. [*] The new casual game modes are perfect for people who haven't had experience with Counter-Strike before and might feel intimidated in competitive mode. [*] It truly is a competitive game: There are no killstreaks, unlockable weapons (skins are purely cosmetic), nor perks... The team with the most skill and better strategies wins. Valve has made sure since the beta to balance all the weapons in the game as much as possible.

translation_en: Counter-Strike: Global Offensive brings back the old-school gameplay of its predecessors. When it comes to gameplay, not much has changed since the original Counter-Strike; anyone familiar with those other titles definitely won't have any trouble with CS:GO. The game keeps that traditional team combat dynamic going, with Counter-Terrorists on one side and Terrorists on the other. Among the game modes, "Classic Competitive" stands out, where two 5-player teams battle it out following competitive rules in a thirty-round match. Without a doubt, it's the most strategic mode in the game and the one that demands the most teamwork. The cool thing about this mode is that the developers made it more enjoyable, from how matches are set up (using lobbies where you can form your team with friends before joining a match) to the ranking system (a sort of performance rating aimed at keeping the game mode more balanced). A downside, especially in Classic Competitive, is the existence of a lot of cheating players, the famous "cheaters." However, it might sound like a cliché, but crime doesn't pay because justice is slow but sure. Generally, these cheaters don't last long in the game; while the anti-cheat system isn't always effective, they end up getting banned within a few days. Plus, there's the Overwatch system, which relies on experienced players in this mode to review reports of suspected cheaters in matches, contributing to a better, cheater-free game. All in all, the game is excellent and totally worth buying.
